papers.title: Cautious Conflict-Free Inverse Gradient Methods
papers.abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) are indispensable tools for modeling complex phenomena in physics and engineering. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful alternative to traditional numerical solvers by directly incorporating physical constraints into neural network loss functions. Despite their advantages, PINN training requires multi-objective optimization, which often leads to significant gradient conflicts among boundary, initial, and residual loss terms. The Conflict-Free Inverse Gradient (ConFIG) method addresses these conflicts; however, integrating ConFIG with adaptive optimizers such as Adam introduces a critical vulnerability: the conflict-free direction generated by ConFIG is further processed by the optimizer, and the resulting weight update may no longer be conflict-free with respect to the task gradients. To address this issue, Cautious ConFIG is proposed as a concise three-line extension to the ConFIG algorithm that empirically restores the conflict-freeness guarantee prior to the weight update. The method is evaluated on three PINN benchmarks: the 1D Viscous Burgers' equation, the 1D Nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation, and the 2D Kovasznay flow. Experimental results demonstrate consistent performance improvements over the standard ConFIG baseline. Additionally, the stabilizing effect of cautious masking and its reaction to conflict severity, task number, and optimizer lag are investigated using a simple toy system.

papers.intro:
Partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely applied in physics Sommerfeld (1949), chemistry Jamwal et al. (2025), engineering Ames (1965), and finance Duffy (2013) to model complex phenomena that evolve over space and time. These equations implicitly define a function of several variables, and solving a PDE with given initial and boundary conditions involves determining this function. Traditionally, PDEs and their initial boundary value (IBV) problems are solved using numerical methods that discretize the domain into a finite set of subregions. The solution function is then represented as a set of values corresponding to these subregions. For example, the PDE can be reformulated as a time-stepping rule by approximating partial derivatives with finite differences. Discretization may introduce artifacts, particularly for complex geometries, and the number of subregions can increase exponentially with the number of dimensions, a phenomenon known as the curse of dimensionality Bellman (2015). Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) Raissi et al. (2019) have gained significant attention in recent years by directly parameterizing the solution function with a neural network. This approach mitigates discretization errors and alleviates the curse of dimensionality. As a mesh-free method, it is well-suited for complex geometries. Furthermore, formulating IBV problems as neural network training enables the utilization of recent advances in deep learning architectures and optimization techniques. However, PINNs also present limitations, as deep learning methods are less well-understood regarding error analysis and generalization compared to classical numerical approaches. While numerical methods reliably yield solutions when conditions such as the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy criterion Courant et al. (1952) are satisfied, training a neural network in a high-dimensional loss landscape can be unpredictable. One notable challenge in PINN training is gradient interference. Each IBV condition is formulated as a separate loss function, and the resulting gradients can interact adversely, severely hindering convergence. The ConFIG method Liu et al. (2025) was developed to address the gradient interference problem by computing an update direction that is conflict-free with respect to all task gradients. However, the ConFIG direction typically serves as an input to another optimizer, such as Adam Kingma and Ba (2014), and the resulting update direction may not remain conflict-free with respect to the task gradients. Consequently, the conflict-freeness property is often lost before the weight update is applied. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce Cautious ConFIG, a simple three-line extension compatible with any ConFIG-optimizer combination. It incurs negligible computational overhead, is easily parallelizable on the GPU, and effectively restores ConFIG’s mathematical properties. • We evaluate Cautious ConFIG on three challenging PINN benchmarks: the 1D viscous Burgers equation, the 1D nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and the 2D Kovasznay flow, observing substantial performance improvements over the baseline (19% to 28% relative improvement). • We analyze the effectiveness of Cautious ConFIG by monitoring key metrics during PINN training and present a computational model demonstrating that Cautious ConFIG produces update directions that align more closely with task gradients under conditions of severe conflict, numerous tasks, and significant optimizer lag.

papers.title: A Benchmark for Controllable Speaking-Style Captioning in Audio-Language Models
papers.abstract: Speaking-style captioning (SSC) aims to generate natural language descriptions of how speech is delivered, capturing paralinguistic attributes such as vocal timbre, prosody, and expressivity. Many downstream applications, including conversational AI agents, controllable speech generation, and large-scale audio annotation, require dimension-specific style captions that describe targeted aspects of speech (e.g., speaker traits, emotion, or delivery style), rather than a single undifferentiated description. However, existing work lacks a unified formulation for controllable speaking-style captioning. We address this gap by formulating SSC as an instruction-following audio-language task, where explicit instructions specify the speaking-style dimensions to be described. We introduce StyleInstructCaps, the first standardized benchmark for controllable speaking-style captioning in audio-language models. StyleInstructCaps provides a dataset and evaluation framework that measures metadata groundedness, hallucination, instruction-following ability, generalization to unseen instructions and audio datasets, and speaker-style consistency. Across nine state-of-the-art audio-language models, we find that strong instruction-following ability does not necessarily imply grounded speaking-style understanding, and that SSC-specific instruction-diverse training substantially improves groundedness, controllability, and speaker consistency.

papers.title: Graph Spectral Series and Its Signatures
papers.abstract: Bandlimitedness is a central modeling assumption in graph signal processing (GSP), but many graph signals exhibit substantial energy throughout the graph-frequency domain. We introduce a new framework for analyzing such non-bandlimited signals by treating their graph Fourier spectra as ordered sequences and representing them with path signatures. Specifically, motivated by the observation that non-bandlimited graph spectra often display rough, time-series like behavior, we introduce the notion of graph spectral series and develop a signature-based representation that captures global spectral structure without frequency truncation. We establish conditions under which the proposed representation is continuous and characterize its information-preserving properties. We further provide an asymptotic interpretation of graph spectral series for sequences of expanding graphs. Experiments on real-world trend-prediction and change-detection tasks show that signature features can improve performance over representations based directly on the original graph signals. The proposed approach provides a novel principled signature-based tool for analyzing non-bandlimited graph signals.

Many contemporary data analysis problems involve structured data, with graphs being a prominent example. Graph signal processing (GSP) provides principled methods for analyzing signals defined on graphs, including sampling, reconstruction, and filtering [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. In parallel, graph neural networks (GNNs) introduce nonlinear, trainable models specifically designed for graph-structured data and have become a central tool in modern machine learning [9, 10, 11]. Both lines of work emphasize that the topology of the underlying graph can provide essential information beyond that contained in node attributes alone [12, 13, 14, 15].

In the GSP literature, “bandlimitedness” is a commonly used notion for characterizing graph signals [1, 3, 16, 4, 17]. Intuitively, a graph signal 𝐱\mathbf{x} is bandlimited if most of its energy is concentrated in only a small number of GFT components. In many studies, these components are assumed to lie in the low-frequency range, reflecting the idea that informative graph signals tend to vary smoothly over the graph. As a result, high-frequency components, which correspond to rapid changes across neighboring nodes, are typically small or negligible.

However, in practice, the bandlimited assumption can be far from realistic. As illustrated in \creffig:wse, the frequency responses of graph signals may exhibit non-negligible energy across the entire frequency domain. In such cases, overly simplifying a signal as bandlimited can lead to misrepresentation and misinterpretation. In some scenarios, a graph signal may appear to have a single dominant leading component under a Laplacian-based GFT. They can reveal additional fine-grained and informative structures that would otherwise be obscured.

papers.title: ProMo3D: Probing Motion Cues in Frozen 3D Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D foundation models have recently reshaped multi-view reconstruction, yet dynamic 4D understanding still often relies on large-scale motion supervision or hand-crafted, architecture-specific heuristics. We ask whether frozen 3D foundation model tokens already encode motion-relevant information that can be exposed by lightweight readout functions, rather than re-learning motion-specific features with high-capacity decoders. Through probing on three representative backbones, we find that static--dynamic separation is decodable from frozen token representations. Our rank-restricted and spectral analyses on $\pi^3$X reveal that the recovered motion cues are concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this, we propose Probing-based Motion Distillation (PMD), which converts pairwise motion-state compatibility scores against a fixed anchor token into dense motion masks. Trained on only 160 YouTube-VOS videos using a single 16 GB GPU, PMD transfers zero-shot to DAVIS, SegTrackv2, and FBMS-59 without target-benchmark fine-tuning. With multi-view pretrained geometric backbones, PMD outperforms training-free heuristics and approaches substantially heavier supervised and self-supervised methods, suggesting that motion decoding from frozen 3D foundation models can be lightweight and data-efficient.

papers.title: Surface Functionalization with Lasers: from Nanostructures to Applications
papers.abstract: Pulsed laser sources stand out as remarkable and versatile tools in the growing interdisciplinary field of materials science, offering capabilities for tailoring and customizing materials to meet specific requirements. Their ability to induce different controlled material alterations allows enhancing material properties that might otherwise remain elusive. In essence, laser-induced material modifications encompass a spectrum of transformative processes, ranging from subtle topographical changes in the nano- and microscale, to intricate chemical modifications. Among the challenges to overcome are the creation of approaches that allow tuning the properties of light to optimize interactions on various types of solids, including metals, semiconductors, and dielectrics. Understanding these interactions is paramount towards efficiency increase of the processing techniques. This chapter embarks on a comprehensive exploration of the intricate dance between pulsed laser beams and their interaction with matter at the surface. The applications of laser-induced surface modifications are far-reaching and extend into widespread industrial fields. Examples of these include tribology, where the study of friction, wear, and lubrication is paramount. Besides that, the modified surfaces find applications in wetting phenomena, changing surface energy and contact angle control, enhanced welding processes, and optimizing molecular adhesion for stronger and durable interfaces. The ability to precisely engineer material surface properties through laser processing opens new frontiers in materials and surface sciences, offering innovative solutions and pushing the boundaries of what can be achieved in various industrial and technological domains.

papers.title: Optimal Riesz mean inequalities for the Coulomb Hamiltonian
papers.abstract: We are interested in whether the Riesz means of the eigenvalues of the Coulomb Hamiltonian can be bounded by the corresponding semiclassical phase space integral. In dimensions two and three we determine the optimal Riesz exponent above which this bound holds.

papers.title: Rethinking Data Imbalance in Class Incremental Surgical Instrument Segmentation
papers.abstract: In surgical instrument segmentation, the increasing variety of instruments over time poses a significant challenge for existing neural networks, as they are unable to effectively learn such incremental tasks and suffer from catastrophic forgetting. When learning new data, the model experiences a sharp performance drop on previously learned data. Although several continual learning methods have been proposed for incremental understanding tasks in surgical scenarios, the issue of data imbalance often leads to a strong bias in the segmentation head, resulting in poor performance. Data imbalance can occur in two forms: (i) class imbalance between new and old data, and (ii) class imbalance within the same time point of data. Such imbalances often cause the dominant classes to take over the training process of continual semantic segmentation (CSS). To address this issue, we propose SurgCSS, a novel plug-and-play CSS framework for surgical instrument segmentation under data imbalance. Specifically, we generate realistic surgical backgrounds through inpainting and blend instrument foregrounds with the generated backgrounds in a class-aware manner to balance the data distribution in various scenarios. We further propose the Class Desensitization Loss by employing contrastive learning to correct edge biases caused by data imbalance. Moreover, we dynamically fuse the weight parameters of the old and new models to achieve a better trade-off between the biased and unbiased model weights. To investigate the data imbalance problem in surgical scenarios, we construct a new benchmark for surgical instrument CSS by integrating datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving significant performance improvement against existing baselines.

papers.intro:
Image segmentation of surgical instruments is crucial for advancing fully autonomous robotic surgery, as it provides critical information to understand dynamic and complex surgical scenes (Chen et al., 2024; Nwoye et al., 2023; Maier-Hein et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2024b; Ranem et al., 2024). Recently, deep learning-based methods have shown promising results in solving increasingly challenging tasks (Garcia-Peraza-Herrera et al., 2021; Colleoni et al., 2022; Lou et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2021; Alabi et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2024a). However, collecting and aggregating a large-scale dataset for surgical scenarios is difficult in practice due to high storage costs, licensing, and privacy concerns, and the frequent updating of instruments (Zia et al., 2023; Razzak et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2023b; Bai et al., 2023). Most approaches suffer from catastrophic forgetting, where the performance has a significant degradation when the past data are not available. To address this challenge, Continual Learning (CL) methods aim to enable models to learn new classes or tasks by training on new data while alleviating the catastrophic forgetting problem (Chaudhry et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2024; Li and Hoiem, 2017; Douillard et al., 2020; Li et al., 2025; Ayromlou et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023c). Nevertheless, previous methods suffer significant performance degradation in robotic surgical scenarios due to biased incremental learning updates, as illustrated in Figure 1, which shows a pronounced bias in the segmentation head weights for new and old classes.

Why is continual segmentation more challenging in robotic surgical scenarios? We believe this stems from the combination of three factors: (i) the data distribution for instrument classes is highly imbalanced due to variations in surgical workflow, with different phase durations and erratic occurrences; (ii) the imbalance is exacerbated as the new class has a high probability of occurrence and is highly concentrated, whereas the old class has a low probability of occurrence and is more dispersed; and (iii) the visual similarity of instruments, with minimal differences near class boundaries, further complicates segmentation. Even worse, the unavailability of exemplar samples due to licensing and privacy constraints makes the task even more challenging. Additionally, attributes specific to surgical scenes lead to increased difficulty. Unlike the relatively stable illumination in general settings, surgical illumination is highly directional and often positioned to highlight specific areas. The anatomical complexity also leads to various illumination degradation scenes. The diversity of surgical instruments and the similar visual characteristics also introduce further complexity. Besides, in surgical scenes, camera viewpoints are often highly constrained, leading to noise and reduced image quality, which further increases the difficulty of applying segmentation models.

To address the class imbalance challenges, classical techniques have been widely explored in machine learning to mitigate imbalanced distributions. Recent studies (He et al., 2021) have analyzed the relationship between class incremental learning and class imbalanced learning, demonstrating that techniques from class imbalanced learning are similar to class incremental learning methods. (Wu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2020) have attributed the performance degradation caused by sample imbalance to biases in the final fully connected layer. These biases are mitigated by incorporating a bias correction layer trained using a balanced validation set (Wu et al., 2019) or normalizing the output weights (Zhao et al., 2020). While these methods provide some improvement, they fall short in the context of continual learning for surgical instrument segmentation, where data imbalance is further exacerbated by privacy restrictions and the inherent complexity of surgical workflows. Current continual semantic segmentation approaches still lack effective strategies to improve performance under imbalanced distribution scenarios, which are typical in surgical environments.

In medical image analysis, data scarcity is often addressed by generating synthetic data, enabling knowledge sharing without exposing patient-level information (Colleoni and Stoyanov, 2021; Colleoni et al., 2022). Similarly, continual learning utilizes generative models to replay synthesized data (Shin et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2018). However, updating generative models incrementally introduces challenges, including high resource consumption and reduced system stability. In this case, Xu (Xu et al., 2024) blended and augmented the foreground to the synthetic background to avoid generating model updates. These methods provide the flexibility to create a class-balanced dataset using any preferred instrument, while also automatically generating the instrument annotations. However, they simply crop patches without instruments from the images and use these patches to train a generative model. In this case, (i) the generated backgrounds are often distorted and may contain unforeseen artifacts and inconsistencies, (ii) the model can only learn foreground information based on segmentation annotations from such data, but due to the distorted backgrounds, it is challenging for the model to extract effective discriminative information between the foreground and the background, and (iii) this approach limits the model to generated background patches, neglecting the effective utilization of the scarce real samples available. Therefore, although this method is straightforward, there is still significant room for improvement.

papers.title: High Scores, Hidden Failures: Evaluating Codebook-Based LLM Content Analysis
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for codebook-based content analysis in computational social science, where codebooks translate theoretical concepts into labeling schemes. While prior work reports strong predictive performance, it remains unclear whether these systems produce reliable and robust text annotations. We conduct a large-scale empirical failure-mode analysis of LLM-based coding pipelines across four datasets and five models by systematically evaluating their stability, robustness, and conceptual validity under controlled perturbations, domain shifts, and optimization procedures. We uncover multiple failure modes that are largely invisible under standard metrics, showing that high aggregate scores frequently coexist with severe label-level disparities, instability across runs, domain sensitivity, and shifts in label interpretation. Importantly, these failure modes persist under widely used optimization strategies and remain largely invisible under standard metrics such as accuracy and micro-F1. Our results demonstrate that current LLM-based coding pipelines cannot be treated as stable measurement tools without targeted validation beyond aggregate performance.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate text data using natural language instructions, enabling scalable labeling for tasks such as dataset construction, qualitative coding, and content analysis (Törnberg, 2024; Abraham et al., 2025; Rytting et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2023). In computational social science (CSS), these instructions are typically formalized as codebooks, structured annotation guidelines that map theoretical concepts onto predefined labels. For example, a codebook for analysing news coverage of minimum wage policies might define labels such as Prices, Government, Welfare, and Justice to classify the different concepts through which minimum wage policies are discussed in each text. By incorporating the codebook’s labels and their definitions directly into prompts, recent studies report strong predictive performance and substantial agreement between human and LLM annotations, suggesting that LLMs could serve as scalable substitutes for human coders (Rytting et al., 2023; Ramanathan et al., 2025; Ruckdeschel, 2025; Farjam et al., 2025).

In computational social science (CSS), these instructions are typically formalized as codebooks, structured annotation guidelines that map theoretical concepts onto predefined labels. For example, a codebook for analysing news coverage of minimum wage policies might define labels such as Prices, Government, Welfare, and Justice to classify the different concepts through which minimum wage policies are discussed in each text. By incorporating the codebook’s labels and their definitions directly into prompts, recent studies report strong predictive performance and substantial agreement between human and LLM annotations, suggesting that LLMs could serve as scalable substitutes for human coders (Rytting et al., 2023; Ramanathan et al., 2025; Ruckdeschel, 2025; Farjam et al., 2025).

However, the use of LLMs for codebook-based annotation introduces two sources of potential failure. First, LLMs may fail to apply codebook instructions consistently during inference. A growing body of NLP research highlights prompt sensitivity (Shu et al., 2024; Mizrahi et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2023), where model predictions change under seemingly minor prompt variations, such as formatting choices, label ordering, or wording differences. Beyond prompt sensitivity, LLM-based coding pipelines may also exhibit broader robustness issues, including instability across repeated runs, inconsistent adherence to codebook definitions, and large disparities in performance across individual labels. Second, LLMs are increasingly used not only to apply annotation instructions but also to refine or optimize the prompts themselves. Recent approaches employ automatic prompt optimization or multi-agent prompting frameworks to iteratively modify prompts in order to improve predictive performance (Abraham et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025). While these methods can yield improvements on standard evaluation metrics, they also introduce additional risks. For instance, modifying prompts that encode coding schemes can implicitly alter label definitions, amplify disparities in label-level performance, or shift the conceptual meaning of the constructs being measured (see Section 5). These issues are consequential in content analysis, where annotations function as measurements (Krippendorff, 2018). They feed downstream statistical analyses (frequency comparisons, regressions, hypothesis testing), as well as qualitative interpretation, including conceptual and relational analysis. This requires that performance is balanced across labels for frequency-based claims to hold (Egami et al., 2023), results are comparable across runs, models, and corpora for findings to replicate, and the labels must retain the theoretical constructs the codebook was designed to measure (Halterman and Keith, 2025).

In this paper, we operationalize the risks around faithful LLM coding by defining controlled experiments and complementary metrics. Then, we empirically demonstrate that current LLM-based codebook methods systematically fail in predictable ways. We organize our study around a set of failure modes, spanning two stages of practical CSS pipelines: (1) inference failure modes, which arise when an LLM applies a fixed codebook (see Section 4), and (2) optimization-induced failure modes, which arise when an LLM is used to refine a codebook prior to inference (see Section 5). papers.title: Anisotropic magneto-elastic coupling in the quasi-2D Ising magnet Li$_2$FeSiO$_4$ and thermodynamic signature of low-energy orbital excitations
papers.abstract: The relevance of spin, lattice and orbital degrees of freedom in the quasi-2D Ising-like magnet Li$_2$FeSiO$_4$ is demonstrated by thermal expansion and specific heat measurements supported by numerical studies. By means of thermodynamic and Gr\"uneisen analysis, we separate the orbital signatures and quantify the energy gap and its pressure dependence from the experimental data as $\Delta\sim 300 - 350$ K and $\partial \ln \Delta/\partial p_{\rm c} \approx -4.6$ %/GPa). Both values excellently agree with the theoretical DFT predictions. The thermal expansion anomalies associated with the onset of long-range magnetic order imply significant magneto-elastic coupling and are used to determine the anisotropic uniaxial strain dependencies of $T_{\rm N}$. They are dominated by the in-plane (i.e., $c$ axis) response $(\partial \ln{ T_{\rm N}} )/\partial p_{\rm c} \simeq 15$ %/GPa while the (negative) $a$ axis and (positive) out-of-plane ($b$ axis) pressure dependencies are much smaller. Short-range magnetic order extends well above $T_{\rm N}$ but is not driven by the same energy scale as $T_{\rm N}$ as evidenced by the observation of non-monotonic in-plane distortion, sign-change of the Gr\"uneisen parameter, and failure of Gr\"uneisen scaling.

papers.intro:
Transition‑metal compounds display a wealth of unexpected and spectacular phenomena – including complex electronic phases and exotic quantum states – originating from their intertwined charge, spin, lattice, and orbital degrees of freedom. Although charge and spin have been initially in the research focus, it has become increasingly evident that orbital physics is equally essential for deciphering and tuning the properties of these materials. [43, 42, 22, 10, 6] In transition metal compounds, the partially filled dd orbitals are split by the local crystal field, electron correlations, or spin-orbit coupling so that their degeneracy can be fully or partly lifted and orbital degrees of freedom become a relevant local electronic property. Associated orbital ordering phenomena are strongly linked to the crystal lattice, e.g., via Jahn–Teller distortions, leading to cooperative structural changes that stabilize particular orbital configurations. [13] The orbital occupancy and arrangement also govern magnetic superexchange interactions such as Kugel-Khomskii coupling or the Goodenough–Kanamori-Anderson exchange [2, 14, 21, 29, 30] which further corroborates the orbital’s role as a key ingredient of the complex physics of emergent phenomena in transition metal compounds.

Typically, orbital excitations in transition metal materials are studied via optical methods [37, 44, 5] or resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) [32, 11, 46, 39]. Orbital degrees of freedom are also detected by thermodynamic properties, e.g., by entropy or lattice changes associated with short- or long-range orbital ordering phenomena or orbital rearrangements and redistribution. [9, 8, 27, 23, 38, 41, 3, 31, 33, 36, 20] Here, we report thermal expansion and specific heat studies on the quasi-2D Ising-like magnet Li2FeSiO4. We find significant magneto-elastic coupling and quantify the uniaxial pressure dependencies. In addition to short-range spin-ordering evidenced by anisotropic lattice changes, our data reveal entropy changes associated with numerically predicted low-lying orbital excitations in Li2FeSiO4 which are further confirmed by the temperature dependence of the Grüneisen parameter. The numerical orbital configuration is corroborated by excellent agreement of the experimental and theoretically predicted uniaxial pressure dependence of the lowest orbital energy gap. In summary, our data allow us to disentangle long- and short-range magnetic order, the lattice degrees of freedom, and the low-energy orbital excitations.

papers.title: Beyond Data Schedule: Fast LLM Pretraining on Data Mixtures by Loss-Reweighting
papers.abstract: Large language models often acquire specialized capabilities through successive pretraining stages, but these gains can come at the cost of forgetting earlier knowledge. In this work, we investigate whether such trade-offs can be improved by changing how strongly each domain contributes to learning while keeping its data exposure fixed. We find that, in controlled knowledge--mathematics experiments, loss reweighting produces a single checkpoint that surpasses the best knowledge and reasoning scores attained along either stage trajectory. This reveals an independent control that data-mixture ratios alone do not capture. Building on this finding, we propose LARE (Loss-Adaptive Reweighting under fixed Exposure), which automatically adjusts domain weights from running loss statistics. Motivated by a theoretical analysis of gradient noise, its normalized inverse-square-root rule balances relative loss scales without changing the sampled mixture or requiring additional runs to search for weights. Across knowledge, mathematics, and code, \Method{} improves all five evaluated benchmarks for a 1.5B model trained on 240B tokens, averaging +7.84 pp over a matched direct mixture, including gains of +17.06 pp on GSM8K and +9.00 pp on MATH. These findings demonstrate that adjusting domain loss scales can improve joint capabilities without additional domain exposure.

papers.title: Trajectory Matching: Discrete Flow Matching with Structured Actions
papers.abstract: The natural units of structured discrete generation are often not independent single-component edits but richer actions: attaching a fragment to a molecule, inserting a node together with an incident edge, or growing a hierarchy by adding a child. Yet most existing discrete flow matching methods (DFM) are restricted to independent component-wise edits over fixed-size states. This restriction stems from endpoint conditioning: endpoints fix the source and target during training but not the action sequence between them, making tractable conditional rates hard to define for complex actions that cannot be factorized component-wise. We propose trajectory matching, which conditions the flow on a full sequence of actions connecting the endpoints. This yields principled, simulation-free training targets for user-defined action spaces, including actions that change state size, modify multiple components, or depend on earlier actions. We prove that the resulting objective recovers the marginal flow and that trajectory matching strictly subsumes factorized DFM, while additionally capturing actions with prerequisite structure such as hierarchy growth or fragment-based molecule generation. Empirically, on tree and molecular graph generation, trajectory matching with domain-aligned actions matches or surpasses factorized DFM baselines (lifting MOSES validity from 92.8% to 99.2%) and transfers without retraining to substructure extension and linking. Trajectory matching enlarges the design space of discrete flow matching by turning the action vocabulary into a modeling choice. An interactive explanation of trajectory matching is available at https://niklaskemper.com/blog/trajectory-matching/.

papers.intro:
Many structured generation problems are most naturally expressed in terms of actions that reflect the structure of the domain rather than the structure of the representation. In molecular graph generation, for example, the natural actions are not single-component edits but operations like attaching a fragment to a partial structure or inserting an atom together with a bond. Such actions can change the size of the state, modify several components at once, and depend on one another—an atom can only be attached to atoms that have already been inserted. The value of such structured actions is well established in autoregressive models: fragment-based molecule generation (Jin et al., 2019), grammar-based code generation (Yin & Neubig, 2017), and insertion-based graph models (You et al., 2018) all exploit domain-aligned actions to achieve strong empirical performance.

However, existing discrete flow matching (DFM) (Campbell et al., 2024; Gat et al., 2024) and related non-autoregressive methods such as discrete diffusion (Austin et al., 2021) cannot easily express such actions. The reason is structural: DFM prescribes a conditional flow between sampled endpoints, and the corresponding rate must be tractable for training. To achieve this over combinatorially large state spaces, existing methods factorize the rate across components. This commits the model to fixed-size states, single-component edits, and independence between actions. Recent extensions (Havasi et al., 2025; Deutschmann et al., 2026; Lüdke et al., 2026) lift the fixed-size constraint by supporting insertions and deletions in specific domains, but they do so by mapping these operations into augmented state spaces where they again reduce to factorized single-component edits. Actions that modify multiple components or depend on one another therefore remain out of reach.

We address this gap with trajectory matching: rather than conditioning on endpoints alone, we condition on a full trajectory of actions connecting them. A trajectory specifies which actions are applied and in what order, leaving the conditional flow to determine only when each action is taken. This makes the conditional rate straightforward to define for general action spaces, including actions that change state size, modify multiple components, or depend on one another. The resulting training objective is still simulation-free and provably recovers the marginal data-generating flow. To make training efficient, we require an efficiently sampleable distribution over trajectories connecting the endpoints. We give explicit constructions for several settings, including actions with hierarchical dependencies. Our framework also recovers standard factorized DFM as the special case of independent component-wise actions with uniformly sampled orderings, placing factorized updates and actions with prerequisites within a common framework.

papers.title: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search
papers.abstract: Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs. However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD. LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation. KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.7 p.p. that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 19%. Project page and code: https://lems-svd.github.io

papers.intro:
The rapid scaling of LLMs (Yang et al., 2025; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2023) has enabled previously unattainable capabilities, but introduced substantial computational and memory requirements that limit deployment in resource-constrained environments. To address these limitations, low-rank approximation using SVD has emerged as a principled and effective compression strategy (Qinsi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025d; Wang et al., 2025c; Chekalina et al., 2025). By decomposing dense weight matrices into smaller factors, SVD substantially reduces parameter counts and computational complexity while retaining easy-to-accelerate dense tensor computations. This ensures immediate compatibility with standard inference engines, avoiding the specialized hardware or sparse kernels that are often required by semi-structured or unstructured pruning approaches. Prior work has demonstrated that SVD-based methods yield significant inference acceleration, particularly in memory-bound regimes, while achieving performance competitive with state-of-the-art pruning techniques (Qinsi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025d). They also demonstrate that low-rank approximation is orthogonal to quantization, allowing the two methods to be combined effectively for maximum efficiency.

They also demonstrate that low-rank approximation is orthogonal to quantization, allowing the two methods to be combined effectively for maximum efficiency.

However, the full potential of SVD in modern LLMs is limited by two fundamental challenges: global rank allocation and decomposition quality. The primary bottleneck is the global allocation problem, which requires determining the optimal rank for each layer under a fixed parameter budget. Existing strategies fail to solve this optimization effectively, as they rely on uncalibrated local sensitivity proxies (Azizi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b) or expensive measurements (Thoma et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2024) to determine layer importance. These methods typically neglect the non-linear error explosion inherent in deep networks (Huang et al., 2025), creating a critical misalignment between error proxy and actual degradation. Consequently, their ability to identify high-performance rank allocations remains limited. Further, high decomposition quality requires distinguishing and preserving the weight directions that are most critical for the downstream task. While Fisher-weighted SVD theoretically addresses this by aligning reconstruction error with the loss landscape (curvature), existing work (Chekalina et al., 2025) suffers from rank deficiencies under reasonable sample counts, limiting its effectiveness.

In this work, we address both challenges by introducing LEMS for global rank allocation and KFAC-SVD for robust decomposition. LEMS introduces a layer-wise error model that integrates local sensitivity, empirical calibration, and a bias correcting error propagation. By explicitly modeling layer-wise error accumulation, we can formulate the search as an ILP and solve it efficiently. KFAC-SVD mitigates the rank deficiency that limits the decomposition quality of prior Fisher-based SVD by transitioning from sequence-based to token-wise statistics for the Fisher approximation. By accumulating token-level loss curvature information, we effectively prevent rank collapse, yielding a decomposition of significantly higher fidelity. Our contributions are threefold: 1. LEMS. We propose a layer-wise error model for rank allocation in SVD that captures both local sensitivity and global error propagation modeling error propagation via a bias. To obtain global rank allocations we search the error model with an ILP formulation. 2. Robust Fisher Decomposition (KFAC-SVD). We leverage a token-wise Kronecker-factor estimation in SVD to mitigate the rank bottleneck of prior Fisher-based SVD and improve its decomposition quality. 3. Empirical Validation. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3, KFAC-SVD improves WikiText2 perplexity by an average of 19% over baselines. LEMS further drives substantial accuracy gains of 2.1-4.7 p.p. compared to the best existing rank allocation methods. Crucially, it also generalizes to activation-based SVD and scales to the 70B parameter regime, achieving a 4.0 p.p. improvement over uniform rank allocation.

papers.title: EviGround-CT: Sentence-to-Volume Grounding for Verifying LLM-Generated Chest CT Reports
papers.abstract: Chest computed tomography (CT) reports generated by large language models (LLMs) can describe positive findings that lack localized evidence in the scan. We propose EviGround-CT to verify these findings after report generation. A deterministic extractor identifies positive finding sentences, and a 3D grounding model predicts an evidence mask for each sentence. Using the full sentence retains anatomical location, laterality, and descriptive modifiers in the grounding query. We evaluate report generation on CT-RATE, and grounding and verification on a held-out 100-case ReXGroundingCT subset. Using the available annotations, sentence-grounded verification raises evidence-supported precision (ESP) from 0.263 to 0.365 across 137 extracted in-scope positives, compared with category conditioning. The corresponding unsupported positive finding rate falls from 0.737 to 0.635. The paired case-level bootstrap ESP difference is +0.102 (95% confidence interval: [0.028, 0.181]). The predicted masks associate individual report statements with spatial evidence that can be inspected alongside the CT.

papers.intro:
Full-volume chest computed tomography (CT) report generation must summarize hundreds of slices containing abnormalities that may be small, diffuse, or spatially distributed. Recent volumetric datasets and CT-oriented systems enable report generation from these scans [1, 2]. Spatial correspondence is also central to multimodal image-guided systems [3, 4, 5]. Evaluating the generated findings requires checking where their evidence lies. For a statement such as “a small pulmonary nodule is present in the right upper lobe,” the relevant evidence is a nodule in the specified lobe. Lexical similarity and finding-level agreement assess text or labels without explicitly testing this spatial correspondence. Category agreement, for example, treats mentions of a nodule in different lobes alike. Sentence-to-volume grounding includes the stated location in the evidence query.

papers.title: Investigating the trackability of landmarks in NBI and WLI
papers.abstract: Reliable visual tracking of anatomical landmarks in endoscopic video is a key prerequisite for computer-assisted interventions in laryngeal surgery. While Narrow Band Imaging (NBI) is clinically established for enhancing vascular contrast, its effect on automated tracking relative to conventional White Light Imaging (WLI) remains unexplored. We present a quantitative comparison of landmark trackability in NBI and WLI using a forward-backward error framework applied to 61 endoscopic videos from 39 patients. Two regions of interest are evaluated: the vocal folds (VF) and mucosa with a prominent vascular pattern (MPVP). We compare a classical feature-based tracker (CSRT) against learning-based point trackers (CoTracker3-Online and TrackOnR) across both modalities. NBI consistently reduced the forward-backward error in both regions, reaching statistical significance for the vocal folds, while failure rates stayed low. These findings indicate that NBI can improve tracking robustness in laryngeal endoscopy, with implications for motion analysis, navigation, and robotic assistance.

papers.intro:
Reliable markerless tracking of natural landmarks in endoscopic videos is an important prerequisite for many computer-assisted interventions and analysis tasks, including motion compensation [7] and navigation [5]. In laryngeal endoscopy, robust tracking of anatomical landmarks is particularly challenging due to frequent camera motion, tissue deformation, illumination changes, and partial occlusions. Accurate temporal tracking of structures such as the vocal folds could nonetheless support downstream applications such as automated screening workflows and robotic assistance systems.

In laryngeal endoscopy, robust tracking of anatomical landmarks is particularly challenging due to frequent camera motion, tissue deformation, illumination changes, and partial occlusions. Accurate temporal tracking of structures such as the vocal folds could nonetheless support downstream applications such as automated screening workflows and robotic assistance systems.

Besides conventional White Light Imaging (WLI), Narrow Band Imaging (NBI) is widely used in clinical practice to enhance the visualization of vascular structures and mucosal patterns. Soft tissue tracking in surgical scenes has been studied extensively for WLI [3], but the performance of modern trackers on NBI remains unexplored. From a computer vision perspective, the enhanced vascular texture in NBI could improve the temporal stability of visual features and thereby tracking robustness, while the altered image appearance and stronger local contrast may instead degrade certain methods. It thus remains unclear whether NBI generally improves trackability over WLI, and whether any benefit depends on the tracked anatomical region or the tracking algorithm.

From a computer vision perspective, the enhanced vascular texture in NBI could improve the temporal stability of visual features and thereby tracking robustness, while the altered image appearance and stronger local contrast may instead degrade certain methods. It thus remains unclear whether NBI generally improves trackability over WLI, and whether any benefit depends on the tracked anatomical region or the tracking algorithm.

In this work, we present a quantitative comparison of landmark trackability in NBI and WLI laryngeal endoscopic videos. We evaluate tracking consistency on two regions of interest (ROIs) using the forward–backward tracking error across 61 videos from 39 patients, employing two state-of-the-art point trackers and one baseline box tracker.

papers.title: MDPO: Multi-constraint Dexterous Policy Optimization with Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation requires high-dimensional control policies to accomplish complex contact-rich tasks while simultaneously satisfying multiple safety requirements, such as joint limits, unsafe finger configurations, arm collisions, and unstable object interactions. Constrained reinforcement learning (RL) provides a principled framework for incorporating these requirements into dexterous manipulation policy learning. However, existing constrained RL methods for dexterous manipulation primarily focus on cumulative cost constraints and struggle to simultaneously handle multiple heterogeneous constraints during dexterous policy learning. In this work, we propose Multi-constraint Dexterous Policy Optimization (MDPO) for safe dexterous manipulation. We first formulate dexterous manipulation as a multi-constraint policy optimization problem involving both cumulative cost constraints and state-wise cost constraints. Based on this formulation, we integrate multi-constraint projection into the dexterous manipulation policy optimization process. Specifically, we employ constraint-specific policy projections to map the intermediate policy that maximizes task performance onto the feasible regions defined by the cumulative cost constraint and the state-wise cost constraint. Extensive experiments on ReDMan, including safe joint control, finger safety, and grasping tasks, demonstrate that MDPO achieves superior constraint satisfaction while maintaining competitive task performance compared with the baselines. Our code is available at this link.

papers.intro:
Dexterous manipulation is a fundamental capability for embodied robots, enabling them to perform complex tasks that require high-dimensional coordination, precise contact control, and flexible interactions with objects [1]. Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) have demonstrated considerable potential for learning dexterous manipulation policies directly through interactions with the environment [2]. Unlike conventional model-based approaches that rely on accurate dynamics models and manually designed controllers [3], RL provides a data-driven paradigm that optimizes manipulation strategies directly from environmental feedback [4]. This characteristic makes RL particularly attractive for high-dimensional dexterous manipulation tasks involving complex contact dynamics and nonlinear interactions. However, applying RL to real-world dexterous manipulation remains challenging due to the presence of multiple physical cost constraints. For example, excessive joint motions and repeated unsafe interactions should remain within tolerable limits throughout the manipulation process, whereas critical unsafe states, such as severe violations of joint limits or hazardous finger and arm configurations, should be strictly avoided [5]. Therefore, simultaneously considering dexterous manipulation performance, cumulative safety constraints, and state-wise safety constraints is crucial for achieving reliable dexterous manipulation.

Although constrained RL has improved the safety of dexterous manipulation policies [5], existing methods mainly focus on a single cumulative cost constraint and rarely consider the simultaneous regulation of cumulative and state-wise safety requirements [7]. Conventional penalty or Lagrangian approaches handle constraints by introducing manually designed or adaptively learned coefficients [8, 9]. However, extending such methods to heterogeneous constraints requires multiple penalty factors, increasing optimization difficulty and potentially leading to unstable or overly conservative policy updates. Projection-based methods provide an alternative by mapping updated policies back into feasible constraint regions [10, 11, 12], but are still primarily developed for the single constraint settings. Moreover, cumulative and state-wise constraints exhibit different temporal characteristics and may interact during dexterous manipulation: improving task performance by relaxing cumulative safety can increase instantaneous safety risks. Therefore, an effective multi-constraint RL algorithm is needed to jointly regulate long-term cumulative risks and state-wise safety violations while preserving manipulation performance.

papers.title: Security evaluation of 6G-oriented and O-RAN networks through targeted attacks
papers.abstract: The sixth generation (6G) of networks is supported by increased bandwidth, automation through the use of O-RAN technologies. Simultaneously though autonomous operation leads to an extensive threat surface and sophisticated attacks. Understanding the attack impact, the Tactics, Techniques and Procedures that are used by attackers is extremely challenging, but however is crucial for developing defense and mitigation strategies against them. This paper evaluates a targeted attack chain against a virtualized, 6G-oriented O-RAN testbed in which the F1 midhaul interface is accessible to an attacker and transport-layer protection is not enabled. The attack disrupts the legitimate O-DU association, introduces a rogue O-DU using observed configuration parameters, and intercepts user-plane traffic. The attack was evaluated in a fully virtualized testbed based on Open5GS, the srsRAN Project, FlexRIC, and an Electric Vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure based on OCPP 1.6.

The evolution towards 6G networks is expected to rely heavily on openness, virtualization, automation, and intelligence at the edge. Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architectures are central to this transition, since they decompose traditional base-station functionality into interoperable components such as the O-CU, O-DU, and O-RU, while exposing standardized interfaces for control, monitoring, and optimization. These properties enable flexible deployment models, lower vendor dependency, and support for emerging vertical applications, including industrial IoT, and EV charging infrastructures.

Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architectures are central to this transition, since they decompose traditional base-station functionality into interoperable components such as the O-CU, O-DU, and O-RU, while exposing standardized interfaces for control, monitoring, and optimization. These properties enable flexible deployment models, lower vendor dependency, and support for emerging vertical applications, including industrial IoT, and EV charging infrastructures.

However, the same openness and disaggregation that make O-RAN attractive also expand the network attack surface. Interfaces that were previously hidden inside proprietary equipment are now transported over IP-based midhaul and fronthaul networks, often across virtualized or software-defined environments. If these interfaces are insufficiently protected, adversaries with access to the transport network may be able to observe signaling traffic, extract configuration parameters, disrupt legitimate associations, or impersonate trusted RAN components. This risk becomes particularly important in private 5G and 6G-oriented deployments, where operators may prioritize low latency, reduced computational overhead, or simplified configuration over strict security enforcement.

papers.title: C-DFF: Concept-Level Diagnostics for Mechanism Parity in Simulation-Based Validation of Autonomous Driving Perception
papers.abstract: Simulation is widely used in autonomous-driving validation, but matching task outputs between real and synthetic images does not guarantee that a system relies on the same visual evidence. This creates a validation gap for transfer, especially in safety-critical perception functions. We present Concept-Decisive Feature Fidelity (C-DFF), a concept-level mechanism-parity diagnostic for paired real-synthetic evaluation. Starting from decisive evidence extracted from a frozen system-under-test (SUT), C-DFF projects that evidence into a shared semantic concept space using off-the-shelf segmentation and compares real and synthetic concept-importance vectors. The result is not only a scalar mechanism-parity score, but also a concept-shift diagnostic that identifies which scene concepts become more or less decisive in simulation. We evaluate C-DFF on KITTI $\leftrightarrow$ Virtual KITTI 2 with 2126 matched pairs across three frozen SUTs (steering regression, YOLOP drivable-area, YOLOP lane-line). Across these tasks, C-DFF is SUT-discriminative and yields interpretable concept-level summaries that support validation triage and simulator debugging. When reported alongside task-specific output-value context metrics, C-DFF shows that output agreement does not by itself establish mechanism parity. These results position C-DFF as a practical semantic diagnostic layer for validation and verification workflows in simulation-based AV testing.

papers.intro:
Simulation is now a core component of autonomous-driving development and safety evaluation because it enables scalable testing across scenarios that are rare, risky, or expensive to reproduce on-road [1, 2, 25]. However, simulation-based validation still faces a key question: when a real scene and its synthetic counterpart produce similar model outputs, did the system rely on the same evidence to make that decision? This question matters because output agreement alone can hide “right output for the wrong reason” behavior. A perception or driving model may preserve the final prediction while shifting its reliance toward spurious or non-transferable cues, which weakens the validity of simulation-based conclusions [5, 6]. For validation and verification workflows, practitioners therefore need metrics that test not only output similarity, but also mechanism parity. Prior work introduced Decisive Feature Fidelity (DFF) as a way to compare decisive evidence maps extracted from a frozen system-under-test (SUT) [4]. DFF captures mechanism-level differences that output metrics can miss, but raw decisive-map differences are still difficult to translate into engineering action. A heatmap mismatch indicates that the mechanism changed, but it does not directly reveal which semantic parts of the scene became more or less decisive. This paper addresses that interpretability and actionability gap. We introduce Concept-Decisive Feature Fidelity (C-DFF), a concept-level mechanism-parity diagnostic for paired real–synthetic evaluation. C-DFF combines decisive evidence extraction on a frozen SUT with off-the-shelf semantic segmentation to project decisive evidence into a shared concept vocabulary (e.g., road, sidewalk, building, sky). The output is a scalar mechanism-parity score together with concept-shift summaries that are directly usable for simulator, renderer, and synthetic-data debugging. We evaluate C-DFF on KITTI ↔\leftrightarrow Virtual KITTI 2 using 21262126 matched real–synthetic pairs and three frozen SUTs (steering regression, YOLOP drivable-area, YOLOP lane-line). Across these tasks, C-DFF is SUT-discriminative. Reported alongside task-specific output-value context metrics, it shows that output agreement does not by itself establish mechanism parity and therefore captures a different aspect of real–synthetic transfer. The concept-level diagnostics further identify which scene concepts are responsible for the mismatch, which makes the metric operational for simulation-based validation and verification.

papers.title: TrackTok: Object-Centric Video Tokenization with Semantically Persistent Tokens
papers.abstract: We introduce TrackTok, an efficient video tokenization framework that produces object-centric tokens, i.e., tokens that consistently encode the same semantic objects across time, even as it moves, deforms, or undergoes partial occlusion. Conventional patch-based or existing holistic tokenizers produce token identities often tied to fixed image locations. In contrast, our approach learns temporally persistent object-centric representations that bind visual features across frames into stable semantic units. This enables substantially more compact, continuous latent video representations, reducing the number of tokens required for downstream generative modeling with state-of-the-art flow models, while preserving the semantic structure needed for high-quality synthesis. Our tokenizer offers a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. TrackTok achieves comparable class-conditional generative FVD on UCF-101 dataset at 8 times fewer latent tokens and better latency, and outperforms existing 1D tokenization baselines on frame prediction task on Kinetics-600 across low token budgets. These results suggest that object-aligned and temporally persistent tokenization is a promising direction for scalable video generation, where reducing latent token counts is critical for efficient modeling. Our code for this work is available at https://github.com/phamleyennhi/tracktok.

papers.intro:
Autoencoding videos into compressed latent spaces is an active research area with large impact on efficient video streaming and generative modeling Xing et al. (2024); Yin et al. (2025); HaCohen et al. (2026). An optimal autoencoder should encode videos into a representation that is (1) highly compressive and (2) allows for high-quality video generation in latent space, i.e., being easy to process by current-gen, large-scale generative models, such as video diffusion models Blattmann et al. (2023); Yang et al. (2025); Wan et al. (2025) or autoregressive transformers Hong et al. (2023); Yu et al. (2023); Wang et al. (2024b). We refer to compression as the number of latent tokens a video is encoded into, as it is the quantity that primarily governs the cost of the downstream generative model: attention in diffusion transformers over continuous latents scales in the token count, while for autoregressive transformers over discrete latents the token count directly equals the number of network function evaluations (NFEs). A promising recent direction are tokenizers that map videos into unstructured sets of tokens, which are not aligned with the spatiotemporal grid of input video tokens Wang et al. (2025); Tan et al. (2025). In this paper, we present TrackTok, a novel tokenizer of this category that represents videos as semantic, object-centric tokens, achieving a state-of-the-art trade-off in compression vs. generation quality (c.f. Fig. 1 left).

papers.title: RoboLongR: Causally Consistent Rewards Teach Robots to Progressively Master Long-Horizon Manipulation
papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires actions whose validity depends on earlier interactions, yet visual progress can conceal missing task prerequisites. We propose RoboLongR, an offline-to-online framework that learns history-dependent rewards to guide policy adaptation to new tasks. Its central objective is causal consistency: aligning rewarded progress with prerequisites supported by execution history. Stage-shuffle supervision encourages execution-order sensitivity, recurrent memory preserves evidence of earlier interactions, and two-round training refines trajectory segments using predicted progress. The resulting rewards guide stage-conditioned policy refinement from behavior cloning to online reinforcement learning. Sparse terminal feedback connects policy experience to reward learning by triggering correction for repeated high-scoring failures. Pretrained on demonstrations from 88 RLBench tasks and Open-X data, RoboLongR achieves 31.8% average success on 18 long-horizon tasks excluded from reward pretraining, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.2 percentage points. Across four real-robot tasks, it achieves 57.5% success, a 32.5-percentage-point improvement over the comparison method. Reward-level controls probe sensitivity to synthetic order perturbations, while ablations examine the contributions of individual components to policy improvement.

papers.title: New developments in the geometry and topology of 3D head-direction coding
papers.abstract: The head-direction (HD) system is a neuronal compass that represents head orientation in 3D. Its encoding of 3D head orientation can be decomposed into a multiplexed representation of 2D head tilt relative to gravity and 1D head orientation in the horizontal plane (azimuth). Defining azimuth during 3D motion is not trivial, and recent studies have indicated that the HD system implements a so-called dual-axis/tilted-azimuth (DA/TA) rule, a representation that is well supported experimentally but remains mathematically and mechanistically difficult to interpret. Here, I introduce a new formulation of DA/TA based directly on the elements of a rotation matrix describing 3D head orientation. In this formulation, TA is represented by a 2D vector, whose direction encode TA and whose norm depends on tilt, consistent with a tilt-dependent gain of HD tuning reported by experimental studies. I provide a geometrical interpretation of this formulation and use it to characterize the topology of the resulting representation. More generally, I introduce a framework in which head orientation is represented by a rotation matrix and neuronal responses arise from linear combinations of its elements followed by nonlinear transformations. Within this framework, the linear stage specifies which aspects of 3D orientation are encoded, and therefore allow relating neuronal representation to linear algebra concepts. Classical HD tuning, gravity tuning, and DA/TA can all be described within this common framework. Together, these results provide a new mathematical, geometrical, and topological perspective on 3D HD coding.

papers.title: HNSecW: A Logarithmic-Time MPC Protocol for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.abstract: As a core component of modern RAG systems, approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search has been extensively studied for decades. In practice, deploying ANN often requires symmetric privacy, where the querier's query and the database owner's data must remain hidden from each other, necessitating a secure multi-party computation (MPC) solution. So far, most MPC-based ANN protocols follow a cluster-based approach: they evaluate distances for the query over a large candidate set and rely on heavyweight primitives such as distributed ORAM to hide access patterns. As a result, each search typically requires $O(\sqrt{N})$ time. We propose HNSecW, a novel MPC protocol for ANN search that achieves the $O(\log N)$ search time for the first time. We first study the single-query setting. Starting from HNSW, the state-of-the-art ANN algorithm, we redesign its control flow and data structures to achieve fully data-independent execution. To further achieve logarithmic search time, we employ offline reshuffling and partial database duplication. Furthermore, we extend our protocol to support multiple sequential queries by introducing a "double visited" caching structure that eliminates redundant cross-query memory accesses, thereby avoiding per-query online shuffling. In addition, we develop a batch-query protocol that exploits higher parallelism to reduce both round complexity and the circuit's critical path. Our experiments show that HNSecW preserves the high accuracy of plaintext HNSW ($\geq 90\%$ recall) and delivers over a $20\times$ efficiency improvement over prior work on million-scale datasets.

During the collaboration, disclosing the query may reveal the institute’s research details; disclosing the hospital’s database and patient data would violate regulations such as HIPAA.

A naive approach to achieving symmetric privacy is to introduce a trusted third party, such as a cloud provider: both the database owner and the querier submit their plaintext vector database and queries to the third party, which then performs the ANN search and returns only the results to the querier. However, delegating all sensitive information in plaintext to a single, fully trusted entity may violate privacy regulations like GDPR and introduce severe risks of data breaches or misuse.

This motivates people to seek cryptographic solutions that can remove the need for trusted third parties. One natural solution is to implement ANN search in the secure multi-party computation (MPC) model (Yao, 1986). In these solutions, the database owner and the querier secret-share the vector database and queries across multiple servers. The servers then jointly execute the ANN search protocol on these shares. The security of MPC ensures that no single server can reconstruct any input. Several recent efforts pursue this direction. However, most existing solutions either relax privacy guarantees by assuming a public database (Zhou et al., 2025), or incur high computational overhead (Chen et al., 2020; Li et al., 2025). Specifically, the two closest MPC solutions to our setting (Chen et al., 2020; Li et al., 2025) rely on cluster-based ANN pipelines: the database of size NN is partitioned into clusters, and the protocol identifies and searches the clusters most relevant to a query. Their efficiency depends heavily on the number of clusters, which is typically set to N\sqrt{N} to balance cluster selection and in-cluster search costs. As a result, their search time becomes O⁡(N)O(\sqrt{N}) for each query. This quickly becomes impractical at modern database scales, because under MPC, each additional vector access incurs heavy communication, particularly for high-dimensional vectors. papers.title: Conviction Without Evidence: Verdict Stability Is Independent of Visual Grounding in Medical Vision--Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision--language models applied to medical question answering can reach correct diagnoses without using the diagnostic image, inferring instead from the clinical vignette. We ask whether this is visible in how \emph{firmly} a model holds its answer: does a model defend a diagnosis derived from a blank placeholder as tenaciously as one derived from a real medical image? Crossing an image-substitution protocol with two levels of adversarial pressure on 60 Italian State Examination items, we find no evidence that ungrounded verdicts are more fragile. In a paired item-level analysis, fabricated consensus (L4) overturns 94.4\% of verdicts with the real image and 98.1\% without ($\Delta = +0.037$; one-sided 95\% upper bound $+0.105$); contentless doubt (L1) overturns 62.5\% and 51.8\% ($\Delta = -0.107$, 95\% CI $[-0.209, -0.001]$), the point estimate running opposite to the direction a grounding detector requires. The two levels nonetheless produce opposite \emph{dynamics}: under L4 the model flips once, always to the exact option argued for (110/110 first-turn flips), and then freezes, averaging 1.9 verdict changes over ten turns; under L1 it never settles, averaging 7.4 changes. Instability under contentless doubt tracks intrinsic item ambiguity rather than evidence availability, and so does not serve as a grounding signal. Flips are almost entirely corrupting (99/100 across both levels). The model is not unaware of the missing evidence---it flags the blank image at baseline on 35 of 60 items and abstains on 4--6---yet those abstentions do not survive contact with pressure. None of the epistemic signals a user could plausibly consult distinguishes a grounded diagnosis from a confabulated one.

papers.intro:
Epistemic failure in deployed systems is often not a failure to compute an answer but a failure to represent the limits of one’s own knowledge (Hüllermeier and Waegeman, 2021). A medical vision–language model that reaches a correct diagnosis without consulting the diagnostic image has not made an error by the usual metric, yet it has produced a verdict whose evidentiary basis is entirely different from what its presentation implies. Prior work established that this occurs frequently, and that models fabricate supporting visual observations for images they cannot see (Felizzi et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023).

papers.title: CVM-Store: A Secure Storage System for Confidential Virtual Machines
papers.abstract:
Stateful cloud workloads require high-performance persistent storage when running on untrusted cloud infrastructure. Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs) promise to protect these workloads through hardware-enforced memory encryption and isolation without requiring application changes. However, they protect only data in use; persistent storage lies outside the CVM trust boundary, exposing all stateful data to the cloud provider.
  Extending the trust boundary to persistent storage presents inherent challenges. High-bandwidth workloads require near-raw NVMe throughput, yet the default kernel CVM I/O stacks are inadequate, and userspace I/O libraries are not designed with CVM use cases in mind. Access patterns and storage semantics vary between workloads, necessitating access-pattern-aware security abstractions rather than uniform block-level encryption. In order to mitigate against rollback, freshness is needed, but CVMs lack hardware primitives for this purpose, requiring alternative solutions.
  We present CVM-Store, a storage system that co-designs a high-throughput userspace I/O engine with CIF (confidentiality, integrity, freshness) data protection. The key insight is that neither authenticated encryption nor I/O is a bottleneck by itself, but their naive combination is. CVM-Store exploits this by interleaving them, eliminating redundant copies and OS/hypervisor mediation. CIF guarantees are provided as composable primitives that adapt protection to workload access patterns, from which we derive three concrete authenticated abstractions: a KVS, a log, and a filesystem. An asynchronous trusted counter service provides freshness guarantees with epoch-based batching, which enables rollback protection without dedicated hardware support. CVM-Store delivers full CIF guarantees within $\approx$1% (write) and 1-19% (read) of raw NVMe bandwidth for large objects.

A broad range of sensitive workloads are increasingly deployed in public clouds and require performant persistent storage. These include container runtimes that provision large, immutable image layers and datasets [61, 127, 29], checkpointing and audit-logging services [70, 11], and HPC, AI training and inference pipelines [115, 73, 84, 126], spanning sensitive domains such as healthcare record management and financial transaction processing. In all cases, the cloud provider controls the entire workload lifecycle and may try to undermine the security guarantees such workloads depend on [80, 64].

CVMs protect entire VMs with hardware-enforced memory encryption and isolation, enabling unmodified applications to run securely on untrusted infrastructure. Major cloud providers [43, 71, 47] have deployed CVMs, offered by various vendors (e.g., AMD SEV-SNP [7], Intel TDX [50], Arm CCA [12]), at scale, making them the de facto foundation for running security-sensitive workloads.

However, CVMs protect only data in use, leaving persistent storage outside their trust boundary. NVMe devices, storage controllers, and the I/O stack remain under full control of the untrusted cloud provider. Thus, a malicious operator can read, corrupt, or replay persistent data, exposing every workload that requires storage outside CVM memory and relies on local storage such as NVMe SSDs. Importantly, fully closing this threat requires not only cryptographic protection of stored data, but also a mechanism to bind that data to a verified, trusted identity. Therefore, designing such secure storage systems for CVMs is necessary but non-trivial.

Simply layering existing confidential-storage techniques [59, 72] onto the CVM I/O path compounds the problem: CVMs encrypt their guest memory by default, preventing devices from performing direct memory access (DMA) to it. All I/O must instead pass through bounce buffers [93], unencrypted shared memory regions where data is copied to and copied back, along with multiple context switches, further degrading I/O performance compared to conventional VMs [59, 83]. This mismatch between a fast I/O path built for trusted devices and the CVMs’ untrusted-device reality makes securing CVM storage fundamentally challenging (§​ III).

papers.title: RefinedGAW: A Refined German Academic Web Dataset
papers.abstract: The largest open German text datasets are built from broad web crawls, which provide scale but limited coverage of specific domains. We introduce RefinedGAW, a processed and annotated resource derived from 26 semi-annual crawls of the German Academic Web, totaling 122 million documents and 314 billion tokens, with full crawl and capture history of every text. Documents labeled as academic research account for 84% of German RefinedGAW tokens across HTML and PDF. At 87.6 billion tokens, this exceeds the 64.9 billion tokens in the German subsets of FineWeb2 and FinePDFs, despite their almost five-times-larger combined size. RefinedGAW also contains substantial amounts of educational, math-heavy, and expert-oriented content with minimal commercial bias. Across HTML and PDF, 88% of German RefinedGAW documents have no near-duplicate candidate match in the three evaluated reference datasets, supporting complementary coverage. We release a queryable metadata index for fine-grained data selection and a rehydration tool for retrieving and processing source documents.

papers.intro:
Large language models have increased demand for text datasets at substantial scale. The largest open text datasets are derived from broad web crawls, such as Common Crawl (Common Crawl Foundation, 2026). Focused crawls can complement these resources by covering specific domains more exhaustively, surfacing specialized material.

The German Academic Web11 1 https://german-academic-web.de/ (GAW) archive is a domain-specific crawling effort containing semi-annual snapshots of the public web presence of German academic institutions from 2012 onwards (Paris and Jäschke, 2020), starting from around 150 seed domains. A potentially high concentration of scientific and educational text, which improves language-model performance on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks (Penedo et al., 2024a), makes academic websites a promising domain. However, raw web archive captures require substantial processing before they can support downstream research and model development. Resources such as C4, mC4, RefinedWeb, MADLAD-400, FineWeb, and HPLT illustrate the extensive processing and documentation needed to turn web captures into usable text datasets (Raffel et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2021; Penedo et al., 2023; Kudugunta et al., 2023; Penedo et al., 2024a; Oepen et al., 2026).
