With RefinedGAW22 2 Available at https://hf.co/datasets/ellamind/RefinedGAW., we introduce a processed and richly annotated resource derived from the GAW. In two separate pipelines we extract text from HTML pages and PDFs, deduplicate identical text across crawls while retaining all occurrences and source versions, add rich document-level annotations with propella (Idahl et al., 2026), and package a dataset of 122 million unique documents totaling 314 billion tokens. We further characterize RefinedGAW in language, source, and content composition, and compare its German subset to large German reference datasets. Automatic document-level annotations indicate a high concentration and substantial volume of academic research content in RefinedGAW’s German subset (Figure 1(a)). Our broader characterization also identifies substantial educational, math-heavy, and expert-oriented material, while marketing-heavy content is rare (Figure 1(b)). Across HTML and PDF, 88% of German RefinedGAW documents have no near-duplicate candidate match in the three evaluated reference datasets, supporting complementary coverage. We publicly release a queryable metadata index including document-level annotations and source provenance, together with software for retrieving and processing source documents. The annotations enable fine-grained corpus analysis and subset selection, the retained URLs, crawl occurrences, capture times, and source versions enable longitudinal study of institutional web content.

papers.title: Constructions of Secure Convertible Codes
papers.abstract: Secure convertible codes, introduced by Zhang and Rashmi, achieve secrecy capacity under a passive eavesdropper model in which an eavesdropper is allowed to access any $\ell$ symbols from the initial and final codewords. In this paper, we construct two families of access-optimal secure convertible codes. The first family of codes based on Maximum Rank Distance (MRD) codes is constructed for all parameters in the merge and split regimes and requires a large field size. The second family of codes, constructed using Generalized Reed-Solomon codes, uses smaller fields but is applicable only for certain parameters in the merge and split regimes.

papers.title: Compositional Approximately Bisimilar Abstractions of Stochastic Interconnected Systems
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of constructing (alternating) bisimilar symbolic models for discrete-time, stochastic, interconnected systems. By leveraging a refined over-approximation of the stochastic reachable sets and the q-th moment input-to-state stability (delta-ISS-Mq) property, we establish an approximate bisimulation relation between stochastic systems and their deterministic (noise-free) counterparts. This approach significantly simplifies the analysis of the approximate (alternating) bisimulation between the global interconnected stochastic system and its symbolic model. We derive formal conditions under which local bisimulation relations are preserved when composing subsystems into a global interconnected system. The engineering relevance of the proposed compositional framework is demonstrated through temperature regulation case studies involving a fixed ten-room building and a circular cascade interconnection scaled from six to fourteen rooms. The results show that, beyond a small number of subsystems, the proposed method achieves substantially faster abstraction computation times than standard monolithic approaches, with the performance gap widening as the number of interconnected subsystems grows and the monolithic approach failing to converge beyond ten rooms.

In recent years, formal synthesis methods have emerged as a rigorous paradigm for the design of stochastic control systems, attracting significant attention for their ability to automatically generate controllers that are correct-by-construction Lavaei et al. (2022). These approaches are particularly valuable for handling complex specifications, such as those expressed in linear temporal logic (LTL) or represented by automata on infinite strings Baier and Katoen (2008). Despite these advances, the automated synthesis of controllers for interconnected stochastic systems remains inherently challenging.

To address this complexity, the utilization of finite abstractions has become a standard methodology. This process involves abstracting the continuous dynamics into a finite set of states, performing analysis and synthesis on this abstract model using algorithmic techniques from the formal methods community Baier and Katoen (2008); Majumdar et al. (2024), and mapping the controller back to the concrete system with guaranteed error bounds. The existing literature encompasses various abstraction techniques for stochastic systems, including finite bisimilar abstractions for randomly switched systems Zamani et al. (2014), incrementally stable switched systems Zamani et al. (2015), and continuous control systems Zamani and Abate (2014). Alternative approaches focus on constructing infinite abstractions for jump-diffusion systems using small-gain conditions Zamani et al. (2016), utilizing stochastic reachability analysis for discrete-time hybrid systems Abate et al. (2008), or proposing symbolic models based on input set discretization Zamani et al. (2017) and omega-regular objectives Dutreix et al. (2022).

However, monolithic abstraction procedures frequently encounter the curse of dimensionality, rendering them computationally intractable for large-scale interconnected systems. To circumvent this, compositional approaches have been advocated, wherein a global abstraction is synthesized from local subsystem abstractions by exploiting the inherent modularity and interconnection topology of the underlying dynamics. This compositional paradigm imparts modularity, enabling the reconfiguration of interconnection topologies without necessitating a global re-computation, thus maintaining computational efficiency when integrating auxiliary subsystems.

Early contributions in the compositional domain predominantly addressed deterministic dynamics. Notable works include the employment of simulation functions and small-gain conditions Pola et al. (2016), partial feedback linearizability Hussien et al. (2017), joint dissipativity properties Zamani and Arcak (2017), and alternating simulation functions Swikir and Zamani (2019). Furthermore, Saoud et al. (2021b) introduced a generalized framework based on “approximate composition” that obviates the need for standard small-gain conditions. More recently, compositional methodologies have been extended to the stochastic domain. Studies such as Awan and Zamani (2023); Lavaei et al. (2020a) leverage small-gain theorems and stochastic simulation functions, while others address finite Markov decision processes for switched systems Lavaei et al. (2020b) or employ dissipativity-type properties Lavaei and Zamani (2022).

Crucially, however, these existing stochastic frameworks typically establish an approximate (alternating) simulation relation. The primary impetus for this research lies in the derivation of approximate (alternating) bisimulation relations for the class of discrete-time stochastic interconnected systems. Existing compositional frameworks predominantly rely on simulation relations, which characterize a unidirectional behavioral inclusion essentially establishing that the abstract model over-approximates the reachable sets of the concrete dynamics. While such inclusion suffices for safety verification, it inherently introduces conservatism in control synthesis; specifically, the inability to synthesize a controller in the abstract domain does not strictly preclude its existence in the concrete system. In contrast, the proposed (alternating) bisimulation relation enforces a bidirectional behavioral equivalence between the stochastic interconnected system and its deterministic abstraction. This stronger relational property is significant because, within the general theory of (alternating) bisimulation for symbolic control Tabuada (2009), such bidirectional equivalence enables a control policy synthesized over the finite abstraction to be refined to the concrete stochastic domain with quantifiable error bounds, and underlies decidability results for the existence of valid control policies with respect to a broad class of specifications. In this paper, we rather focus on establishing this bisimulation relation compositionally for stochastic interconnected systems. We demonstrate the practical use of the constructed relation through a safety-controller case study (Section 5).

papers.title: Calibration requirements for Epoch of Reionization 21-cm signal observations - V. Bias and variance in the cylindrical power spectrum from uGMRT Band 3 observations of the ELAIS-N1 field
papers.abstract: Detection of the redshifted 21-cm signal from neutral hydrogen requires precise control of systematic effects arising from instrumental calibration. In this work, we investigate the impact of both time- and frequency-dependent residual gain and bandpass errors on the estimation of the multifrequency angular power spectrum (MAPS) using radio interferometric observations. We discuss our previously developed analytical framework for estimating bias and excess variance in 21-cm signal MAPS in the presence of these residual errors and apply it to uGMRT Band-3 observations. The statistical properties of the residual gains are derived from the data themselves, including their temporal and spectral correlations. We introduce a robust technique for additionally flagging poor-quality data. Our results show that the excess variance induced by residual gain and bandpass errors dominates over the bias across the range of angular multipoles considered. The amplitude of this variance is comparable to the expected power spectrum upper limit at redshift $z \sim 2.2$, indicating that residual calibration errors can significantly affect the detectability of the 21-cm signal. We further transform the estimated MAPS into ($k_{\perp}, k_{ll}$) space and find the expected foreground wedge structure. Importantly, we observe a significant power leakage into the nominal EoR window, which we attribute to residual calibration systematics. This highlights that even after standard foreground mitigation, time- and frequency-correlated gain errors can introduce mode-mixing and contaminate the EoR window. Our results emphasise the necessity of improved calibration accuracy and robust characterisation of residual gain statistics for current and upcoming interferometric experiments such as the uGMRT and SKA, to enable reliable detection of the cosmological 21-cm signal.

papers.intro:
The redshifted 21-cm signal from neutral hydrogen (Hi ) is the ideal probe to study large-scale structure of the early universe and its evolution over cosmic time [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. As the 21-cm signal is weak, directly imaging it at high redshift is difficult. Alternatively, we use the method of intensity mapping, a statistical measurement tool that estimates the two-point correlation function or the angular power spectrum [6, 7] to extract information about the underlying large-scale distribution of Hi [8, 9, 10, 11]. We can directly measure the visibility function of the sky brightness distribution with radio interferometers, and by correlating visibilities corresponding to nearby baselines and frequencies, we can estimate the multifrequency angular power spectrum of the redshifted 21-cm signal [12, 13, 14, 15].

We can directly measure the visibility function of the sky brightness distribution with radio interferometers, and by correlating visibilities corresponding to nearby baselines and frequencies, we can estimate the multifrequency angular power spectrum of the redshifted 21-cm signal [12, 13, 14, 15].

In the same frequency band as that of the redshifted 21-cm signal, there is radio emission from a variety of other astrophysical sources in our Galaxy and external galaxies, including compact extragalactic point sources, diffuse Galactic synchrotron emission, and free-free emission. These emissions are collectively called foregrounds and are typically several orders of magnitude stronger than the expected 21-cm signal, making its detection challenging (16, 17, 18, 10, 19, 20, 21, 22, e.g.). Several foreground mitigation techniques have been proposed in the literature to overcome this challenge. One commonly used approach is the foreground subtraction, where an accurate foreground model is subtracted from the observed visibilities or the reconstructed images, and the 21-cm power spectrum is then estimated from residual data [23, 24, 25]. Another promising approach is the foreground avoidance technique (26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34). Here the cylindrically averaged power spectrum P⁡(k⟂,k∥)P(k_{\perp},k_{\parallel}) is estimated, where the contribution from the foreground remains confined to a wedge-shaped region in the (k⟂,k∥)(k_{\perp},k_{\parallel}) plane known as the “foreground wedge”. The Hi power spectrum is then estimated from the rest of the region of the (k⟂,k∥)(k_{\perp},k_{\parallel}) plane (referred to as the “EoR window”). In addition to these, further foreground suppression techniques have been developed to improve the robustness of the measurements (35, 36, 37, 38, 39).

papers.title: The Language of Deformation: Semantic Failure Analysis as a Prerequisite for Dexterous Manipulation of Deformable Objects
papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation of rigid objects has reached a level of maturity where grasp stability, control, and planning strategies are successfully applied in industry and logistics. In contrast, manipulating deformable objects (cables, plastic pieces, cloth) remains far more challenging, as rigid-object methods do not account for their additional complexity. This paper identifies semantic failure analysis as a key step toward mature deformable-object manipulation and supports this claim with proof-of-concept experiments. Unlike rigid-object manipulation, where goals are well-defined in terms of criteria such as force balance and slippage, deformable-object manipulation involves a broader variety of failure modes arising from differences in materials, geometry, and behaviour. Typical failures include buckling, plastic deformation, pressure variations, and tearing. These diverse and often hard-to-detect events require distinct corrective strategies, making semantic failure analysis necessary. We define its key components and challenges and present experimental results supporting its potential as a research direction.

papers.intro:
A driver would not react to a brake failure in the same way as to a skid on ice. The difference lies in the semantic understanding of each event: brake failure (a sinking pedal) demands pumping the brakes, while traction loss (locked wheels) requires the opposite action of easing off them. The same principle applies to deformable-object manipulation, where failure modes differ widely in their characteristics and behaviour, each requiring a different — and sometimes non-intuitive — response.

The difference lies in the semantic understanding of each event: brake failure (a sinking pedal) demands pumping the brakes, while traction loss (locked wheels) requires the opposite action of easing off them. The same principle applies to deformable-object manipulation, where failure modes differ widely in their characteristics and behaviour, each requiring a different — and sometimes non-intuitive — response.

For example, the corrective action needed to maintain a grasp on an object undergoing plastic compression differs sharply from that required when an object is about to buckle. In the first case, maintaining a tight grasp is essential, since even a slight reduction in compression may cause the permanently deformed object to slip. In the buckling case, however, the system should reduce compressive forces to prevent a sudden snap that releases the accumulated elastic energy. A capable manipulator must therefore distinguish these failure modes and respond accordingly.

papers.title: Regularization and Full Support for the CBO Equation with Measure Initial Data
papers.abstract: We prove global well-posedness and regularization for the isotropic consensus-based optimization equation with initial probability measures of finite fourth moment. Under suitable weight decay assumptions, after any nonconstant consensus motion, both the density and the consensus trajectory become smooth, and all spatial Sobolev norms are locally bounded in time. The proof uses a Fourier commutator estimate, localization and iteration, followed by a nonlinear time bootstrap. Counterexamples show that smoothing can fail at a stationary consensus point. For non-Dirac initial data, we also prove positivity away from the consensus point and full support at every positive time in all dimensions.

papers.title: Rigid Particle-Induced Anomalous Softening in Elastomer Composites
papers.abstract: Particle-filled soft composites generally stiffen as particle loading increases, imposing a trade-off between functionality and compliance. Here, we show that this trade-off can be overcome by designing particles to actively direct gelation rather than act as passive fillers. In a sol-rich elastomer matrix, sol-phase kinetics redirect network formation towards particle-mediated assembly, yielding anomalous softening despite increasing particle content. This response is governed by topological reconfiguration of the load-bearing network during gelation rather than by filler loading alone. A structure-based model captures the composition-dependent onset of this behaviour, and the same response is reproduced across distinct particle systems. The resulting materials combine functionality with softness, energy dissipation, and recoverability under large deformation. These findings establish topology-guided gelation as a general strategy for engineering compliant functional composites for soft robotic actuation, conformal interfaces, and other systems that require both deformability and embedded material functionality.

papers.title: INVAR-Agri: Detecting Discrepancies in Multilingual Operator Manuals of Agricultural Implements with a Fine-Tuned LLM
papers.abstract: Operator manuals of agricultural implements are delivered in many languages, and the standards require that competent persons review every translation, which makes this review the bottleneck. This paper presents a proof of concept that compares two training workflows on the same LLM, EuroLLM-1.7B-Instruct, trained on operator manuals of one manufacturer. In approach A, a back-translator translates each language version back into English, and an English reader compares it with the English version. In approach B, a checker reads the English version and the translation together, where the checker reports differences. The test sets contain errors planted in numbers, units, opposite words, obligations, negations, and conditions in 24 languages, and they include unmodified text and meaning-preserving edits for alerts and false alarms. The trained back-translator concealed many planted errors, most of all weakened obligations, while translation-quality scores rose. In contrast, the separately trained checker detected most planted errors, although it was weak for units and for number changes unlike those in training. A check by the author confirmed the concealment. In addition, a simple rule check caught the number and unit changes, but it alerted on harmless rewrites. A check of alerts on real Finnish translations showed that most alerts were false, caused by language-specific wording, so the precision on real text remains a limitation. Within this setting, a trained checker might support, not replace, the review by competent persons, and firmer conclusions need more data.

papers.intro:
A manufacturer of agricultural implements produces an operator manual for every machine type, which is delivered in the languages of the markets where the machine is sold. In the corpus of this study, each operator manual exists in 16 to 26 languages. The operator manual provides instructions for coupling, adjustment, field operation, transport on public roads, and maintenance. Safety-relevant content sits in small details, for example, tightening torques, speed limits, obligations such as “must”, prohibitions such as “do not”, and conditions such as “when the engine is running”. One wrong number, unit, or word in a translation means the operator in that country receives a different instruction than the English version gives. Such a different instruction creates a risk of injury or machine damage. Every language version of an operator manual carries the same responsibility as the English version. In an earlier study, locally run LLMs answered operator questions from six language versions of one operator manual, where the answers on the non-English versions were less accurate than on the English version [1]. It concluded that native-language manuals are preferable to relying on the translation abilities of the LLM for safety-critical use.

Machine translation and large language models (LLM) can translate a complete operator manual into many languages within hours at low cost. However, the check of each translation still needs a reviewer who reads that language and understands the machine. For example, an operator manual in 20 languages may require 20 reviewers, with one reviewer per language. The manufacturer rarely has such reviewers for every language and often relies on the translation provider. Consequently, checking, and not translating, is the bottleneck of multilingual operator manuals. The practical aim is that a technical expert reads English and checks all language versions with the support of an LLM, which is a proposed application that this paper does not test. However, this paper tests a precondition of such support, namely whether automatic checks keep visible or detect discrepancies in translated instructions.

In this paper, there are two ways to let one technical expert who reads English check every language version of an operator manual. Our approach A uses back-translation, where an LLM translates each language version back into English and the expert compares the back-translation with the English version. Users of machine translation, such as physicians, already rely on back-translation [2]. However, a back-translation can repair an error on its way back, so that the error disappears [3]. In contrast, approach B uses direct checking, where an LLM reads the English version and the translation together and reports what differs. The same idea underlies quality estimation and the detection of critical errors in machine translation [4, 5]. Both approaches depend on an LLM, which can be trained on the manufacturer’s own operator manuals. This paper investigates how training each workflow changes whether planted discrepancies stay visible in approach A or are detected in approach B, how often each workflow alerts on unmodified text and on meaning-preserving edits, and how detection transfers to text not copied from training manuals and to changes unlike those in training.

papers.title: Indication of Electron Antineutrinos from the Diffuse Supernova Neutrino Background
papers.abstract:
We report an indication of $ ar{
u}_e$ from the diffuse supernova neutrino background (DSNB) based on a spectral fit analysis of a 5003.0-day dataset in Super-Kamiokande. Key improvements over previous searches include enhanced rejection of atmospheric $
u$ backgrounds, updated evaluations of systematic uncertainties, and a refined spectral fitting method. Using a representative DSNB model, the best-fit flux was determined to be $3.6^{+1.6}_{-1.5}~\mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ for $E_
u>13.3$~MeV, corresponding to a $2.6\sigma$ tension with a null hypothesis ($99.5\%$ C.L., one-sided). Similar significances were obtained with signal models of varying spectral shapes.

papers.title: Theoretical description of high-harmonic spectroscopy for uniaxial nematic and isotropic liquid crystals
papers.abstract: Enabled by their controllable optical anisotropy, liquid crystals form a cornerstone of linear optical and display technologies. Bringing the versatile platform into the nonlinear regime, we explore its nonlinear optical anisotropy by high-order harmonic generation spectroscopy. Through a comprehensive study targeting gas, liquid, nematic, and crystalline phases, we present a semi-empirical tight-binding approach that provides insight into the intermolecular character of ultrafast light-driven electron dynamics across soft-matter mesophases. We demonstrate how intermolecular electron hybridization enables spectroscopic access to structural properties, such as the nematic director and order parameter. Outlining such foundational mechanisms opens avenues towards nonlinear liquid crystal devices and ultrafast soft-matter spectroscopies.

papers.intro:
Liquid crystals (LCs) are soft-matter systems that combine fluidity with a degree of molecular order, bridging the gap between liquids and solids. In most of the cases, they consist of uniaxial rod- or disk-like molecules that can translate, tumble, or rotate while attaining certain degrees of macroscopic structural order and yielding specific crystalline features such as optical birefringence or other electrical, magnetic, and optical anisotropic properties [1]. They exist in various thermodynamic mesophases with different structural orders, many of which consist of partially aligned molecules along a common axis called the director, such as what governs the nematic phase. Some are further arranged into layers to form e.g. the smectic phase, achieving even higher degrees of combined positional and orientational order. Crucially, thermotropic LCs exhibit controllable structural order, as their macroscopic structural mesophase can be tuned by temperature [1]. Further, for partially ordered phases such as the nematic phase, the microscopic molecular structure, i.e. the orientation of the molecular director, can be controlled by electric fields. Their tunable structural and optical properties have been employed with decades of expertise in linear optics applications such as the multibillion-dollar display technology industry [2]. Advancing the LC technologies from the linear towards the nonlinear optical regime gives prospects for exploiting controllable material structure to open a playground for rich light-driven electron dynamics to achieve innovative controllable nonlinear optical devices.

Across such systems, the microscopic generation mechanism is often described in terms of a three-step model, consisting of ionization/excitation, propagation, and recollision/recombination, in which electrons can acquire energy from a strong driving field to emit a nonlinear higher harmonic response [22, 23, 24, 25].

Most recently, the HHG process in liquid systems has gained increased interest due to the observation of a relatively constant maximal cut-off energy in the spectral response across different wavelengths, intensities, and compounds. A striking contrast to the well-established quadratic and linear electric field strength scaling of, respectively, gas and solid state targets [26, 9, 20, 27, 28]. A microscopic interpretation was proposed, and corroborated by experiments, considering a collection of single molecular emitters, from which the most energetic electron trajectories could be attenuated due to scattering off neighboring molecules [28].

When advancing to the more complex systems of liquid solutions, interpretations based on single-molecular emitters again showed success, as some solutions are well described as a simple sum of the solute and solvents harmonic yields [29]. For solutions with characteristic localized solvation shells, a strong suppression of specific harmonics was interpreted as a sign of electron scattering off molecules in the solvation shell. In contrast, a pronounced second spectral plateau was also observed and interpreted as arising from electrons that recombine at neighboring molecules [30]. Such interpretation requires the electronic states in question, the highest-occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO), to be delocalized across full solvation shells, reminiscent of the delocalized Bloch state interpretation of condensed matter systems. Intermolecular interactions thereby attain a contradictory role, both attributed to suppressing harmonic generation through scattering and dephasing, and also offering additional channels for electron recombination. To elucidate the fundamental role of intermolecular interactions, LCs provide an ideal platform, due to the unique possibility to shape and control the microscopic structural properties on demand. Furthermore, the anisotropic optical properties of LCs hold great potential to provide additional spectroscopic information about the fundamental microscopic electron processes at hand. Optical anisotropy has, for instance, historically enabled tomographic imaging of molecular orbitals [31, 32], tracking attosecond nuclear motion [33] and resolving ultrafast electronic charge migration [34] in optically aligned gaseous targets. Additionally, for solids, optical anisotropies have been utilized to probe crystal structure symmetries [9, 35], unravel anisotropic couplings and curvatures of the energy band structure [36, 37] and distinguish between underlying driven-electron or exciton mechanisms [38]. LCs represent a natural extension of this paradigm, offering a highly tunable anisotropic environment where nonlinear optical processes can be tailored through macroscopic order.

papers.title: Connectivity rewiring and filament formation by active region emergence observed with Solar Orbiter
papers.abstract: Using an 11-day dataset from Solar Orbiter, combining EUV imaging, H$\alpha$ observations, vector magnetograms and nonlinear force-free field extrapolations, we track the evolution from the emergence of a new active region to the reconfiguration of coronal connectivity. We find that the restructuring proceeds through a sequence of localized reconnection events that propagate along the filament channel, producing successive brightenings and bidirectional flows. This process leads to the gradual erosion of the original filament and the simultaneous formation of a new, highly sheared filament connecting the two regions. Magnetic modeling reveals a transition from a sheared arcade supporting the initial filament to a twisted flux rope underlying the newly formed structure. Our results demonstrate that flux emergence can reorganize filament channels through a spatially and temporally ordered sequence of reconnection events, rather than a single impulsive episode. This sequential reconnection front provides a natural mechanism for filament formation in evolving active regions and highlights the importance of continuously changing magnetic connectivity in the corona.

papers.intro:
Solar active regions (ARs) are the visible manifestations of magnetic flux emerging from the solar interior into the photosphere and above, where it concentrates into bipolar magnetic patches that can evolve into pores and sunspots and, ultimately, mature AR magnetic systems (Parker, 1955; Fan, 2021). The emergence process is not merely a surface phenomenon: as flux accumulates and reorganizes, the coupled photosphere–chromosphere–corona system develops increasingly structured magnetic connectivity that shapes the coronal structures (loops, arcades, fan systems) and governs how and where energy can be stored (Cheung and Isobe, 2014; Toriumi and Wang, 2019). Because the most damaging space-weather drivers originate in magnetically complex regions, understanding how flux emergence builds active regions, particularly in their earliest, most rapidly evolving phases, is a central problem in contemporary solar physics.

Because the most damaging space-weather drivers originate in magnetically complex regions, understanding how flux emergence builds active regions, particularly in their earliest, most rapidly evolving phases, is a central problem in contemporary solar physics.

In the photosphere, the earliest emergence often appears as small, opposite-polarity concentrations that grow and separate while horizontal field becomes prominent between them, consistent with an emerging Ω\Omega-loop geometry that arises as rising flux interacts with convection (Fan, 2001; Archontis et al., 2004). Chromospheric and transition-region signatures frequently accompany these photospheric changes. For example, arch filament systems are widely regarded as atmospheric tracers of emerging flux (Bruzek, 1967; Bruzek, 1969), and recent high-resolution/high-cadence observations have shown that small-scale brightenings within such systems can be associated with reconnection-related dynamics and may reflect the interaction of newly emerging flux with preexisting field structures (Tiwari et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2024). These early interactions are important because they can precondition the developing region by creating shear, mixed polarities, and stressed connectivity that later support energetic activity.

A mature active region can host a coronal magnetic field that departs substantially from its potential configuration, storing significant amounts of free magnetic energy in electric currents (Priest and Forbes, 2002). Solar eruptions are widely understood to be powered by this stored energy, which is gradually built up through the combined action of flux emergence and photospheric motions that stress the coronal field (Forbes, 2000; Sun et al., 2012; Green et al., 2018). In particular, flux emergence plays a central role in transporting magnetic flux, helicity, and free energy from the convection zone into the corona, where these quantities accumulate and contribute to the formation of strongly non-potential magnetic configurations, especially along polarity inversion lines (PILs) (Fang et al., 2012; Georgoulis et al., 2012; Kontogiannis et al., 2025). Numerical simulations further show that the Lorentz force associated with emerging flux naturally drives shear and rotational flows, injecting Poynting flux into the corona and promoting the formation of sheared arcades and, in some cases, flux-rope-like structures through reconnection and flux cancellation (Moore et al., 2001; Aulanier et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2026).

Beyond the buildup of non-potentiality, the interaction between emerging flux and the preexisting coronal field critically determines the subsequent evolution of the system (Török et al., 2024). Depending on the magnetic configuration and the efficiency of reconnection with the overlying field, emerging regions may either remain confined or develop into eruptive systems (Török and Kliem, 2005; McKevitt et al., 2026). Observations and simulations indicate that flux emergence can destabilize preexisting coronal structures, including filaments and their overlying arcades, through magnetic interaction with the ambient field, often triggering eruptions (Feynman and Martin, 1995; Wang and Sheeley, 1999; Chen and Shibata, 2000; Li et al., 2023). At the same time, flux emergence can also stabilize coronal structures by enhancing the confining magnetic tension or reducing the upward net force (Chen and Shibata, 2000; Zhou et al., 2025). In this framework, flux emergence is not only a driver of energy buildup, but also a key agent of large-scale magnetic restructuring, capable of modifying coronal connectivity over extended regions.

In particular, how reconnection driven by flux emergence propagates through preexisting magnetic systems, and how this process contributes to the formation, transformation, or disappearance of filament channels, is still not fully understood. Addressing these questions requires observations that can simultaneously capture long-term evolution, multilayer coupling, and the spatial progression of coronal restructuring.

The Solar Orbiter (Müller et al., 2020) mission provides a unique opportunity to meet these requirements. It includes a dedicated observing plan (SOOP; Zouganelis et al. 2020), the Active Region Long-Term Evolution SOOP (R_SMALL_MRES_MCAD_AR-Long-Term), designed to monitor solar active regions continuously over extended periods. This SOOP coordinates multiple remote-sensing instruments to obtain multiwavelength observations from the photosphere to the corona. papers.title: Estimating Treatment Effects in Complex Disease Dynamics: Immortal Time, Varying Hazards, and Multiple Time Scales
papers.abstract: In observational survival studies, delayed treatment initiation can induce immortal time bias in effect estimation when treatment groups are defined by future uptake. Despite originating from distinct predictive or causal inference paradigms, time-dependent approaches (e.g. the time-dependent Cox model, landmark supermodel, multi-state model, and g-formula) are often treated as interchangeable in applied research when addressing immortal time bias. These models effectively reclassify person-time according to time-varying exposure, yet the interpretation of their target estimands depends on assumptions about the underlying disease process and clinically relevant time scales. We study effect estimation for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation under baseline intention-to-transplant strategies in acute myeloid leukemia (i.e. transplantation is planned for a prespecified time, subject to the patient's eligibility), within a multi-state framework allowing time-inhomogeneous Markov, semi-Markov, and state arrival extended semi-Markov dynamics. Using target trial emulation, we benchmark, on the probability scale, estimates derived from Cox-type time-dependent models and the g-formula against the corresponding theoretical values implied by the stochastic data-generating process. Decomposing the partial likelihood score, we show that single-time-scale models can be systematically biased when death intensities from different originating states are not proportional on a common time scale, as can occur when the clock is reset after intermediate events. We quantify these findings in a phase III simulation study and illustrate their implications in an application to data from three acute myeloid leukemia trials.

papers.intro:
In many clinical settings, the treatment of interest following an initial therapy can be started only after a delay and only in patients who remain eligible until then, so that its receipt depends on the evolving patient history. This raises the question of how to quantify its population-level effect, relative to alternative treatments, in patients who are, once eligible, scheduled to receive it after a prespecified waiting time. A typical example is allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), which, where indicated, is given as consolidation after remission induction and can no longer be performed as planned if the patient becomes ineligible due to disease progression or dies beforehand (Döhner et al., 2022). Defining treatment groups by eventual receipt of allo-HSCT therefore introduces immortal time bias. For decision making at the time of eligibility (i.e. at baseline), the relevant contrast is instead between strategies decided at that point, such as allo-HSCT planned for a prespecified time, irrespective of eventual receipt, versus chemotherapy only, in terms of the risk of the outcome within a given time horizon. The aim of this work is to examine whether, and under which assumptions about the disease process, commonly used approaches to immortal time bias (i.e. the time-dependent Cox model, landmark supermodel, multi-state model, and g-formula) recover such contrasts on the probability scale when the process involves intermediate events and multiple clinically relevant time scales. Before formalizing this question and addressing it by simulation and an application to AML trial data, we review the issues that motivate it: immortal time bias and its usual remedies, assumptions about the disease process and its time scales implicit in these remedies, and the causal interpretation of hazard ratios in this setting.

In survival analysis, treatment effects are typically evaluated by contrasting intensity (hazard) functions between groups receiving different treatments, defined to start from a clinically relevant time origin (e.g. disease diagnosis or treatment allocation). With a parametric or semi-parametric hazard model, the effects are often summarized by a hazard ratio comparing the groups’ instantaneous event rates throughout, under a proportional hazards assumption. In randomized controlled trials, any delays in the initiation of treatment after allocation are accommodated under the intention-to-treat principle, which aligns with the treatment policy strategy in the estimand framework (Kahan et al., 2024), and randomization ensures baseline exchangeability between groups. However, in non-randomized studies, systematic differences in the timing of treatment initiation between groups due to reasons such as delayed donor availability or varying durations of preparative therapy can introduce immortal time bias (Suissa, 2008; Lévesque et al., 2010). The term ‘immortal time’ refers to the period between the time origin and the initiation of the intended treatment, during which patients who eventually receive that treatment must, by design, remain event-free and may be offered the same standard of care as those in the control group. Therefore, this pre-treatment event-free period is a structural guarantee induced by defining treatment groups based on future initiation, rather than a protective effect of the treatment itself.

Immortal time bias has often been framed as a misclassification of person-time between exposure groups, which may reflect, at least in part, that ‘immortal time’ is rhetorically striking and can inadvertently encourage a simplified interpretation as merely a classification problem. Under this view, converging evidence from systematic reviews of published literature, simulation studies, and mathematical derivations suggests that such misclassification systematically distorts estimates towards showing a beneficial effect when immortal time is incorrectly assigned to the treated group, often by a standard time-fixed Cox model with a baseline (ever/never) treatment indicator (van Walraven et al., 2004; Austin et al., 2006; Beyersmann et al., 2008). This concept motivates the widespread use of Cox-type time-dependent (CTD) models, including the extended time-dependent Cox model and the landmark supermodel, among other related formulations, to reclassify person-time according to actual exposure status (Mantel and Byar, 1974; Anderson et al., 1983; van Houwelingen and Putter, 2011; Gleiss et al., 2018; de Wreede et al., 2022). However, in applications of CTD models, assumptions about the hazards and the stochastic process that governs the evolving disease history and upon which the estimand targeted by these models depends are rarely made explicit.

Under this view, converging evidence from systematic reviews of published literature, simulation studies, and mathematical derivations suggests that such misclassification systematically distorts estimates towards showing a beneficial effect when immortal time is incorrectly assigned to the treated group, often by a standard time-fixed Cox model with a baseline (ever/never) treatment indicator (van Walraven et al., 2004; Austin et al., 2006; Beyersmann et al., 2008). This concept motivates the widespread use of Cox-type time-dependent (CTD) models, including the extended time-dependent Cox model and the landmark supermodel, among other related formulations, to reclassify person-time according to actual exposure status (Mantel and Byar, 1974; Anderson et al., 1983; van Houwelingen and Putter, 2011; Gleiss et al., 2018; de Wreede et al., 2022). However, in applications of CTD models, assumptions about the hazards and the stochastic process that governs the evolving disease history and upon which the estimand targeted by these models depends are rarely made explicit.

From a process perspective, CTD methods are built on an instantaneous event rate defined relative to the current risk set and conditioned on the information available just before a given time point. The modeling step is then to separate the baseline component from a multiplicative covariate component, often within a single time scale (i.e. the event process is treated as a single transition from the chosen origin to the outcome of interest), typically allowing the baseline hazard to change freely over time. Assuming the hazard at a given time not to depend on earlier history in any further way beyond what is captured by the covariate history yields a Markov-like description of the event process, conditional on the observed history (i.e. the process is memoryless given the observed history). The process need not be time-homogeneous; indeed, time-inhomogeneity is clinically more plausible, as risks typically change over the course of the disease, reflecting the evolving clinical trajectory towards the absorbing state, which depends on the starting distribution of the process and on changes induced by intermediate events (Aalen and Gjessing, 2001).

papers.title: Nuclear recoil effects with a realistic nuclear charge form factor
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel two-parameter Gamma model of the nuclear charge distribution as an alternative to the widely used Fermi distribution. The model yields simple analytical formulas for all moments of the charge distribution and closed-form expressions for the electrostatic potential and momentum-space form factor, the latter satisfying the correct analyticity requirements for a physical charged particle. We apply the model to calculate the nuclear recoil correction to the Lamb shift in electronic and muonic atoms and analyze its nuclear-model dependence. We find that the nuclear-size recoil corrections to energy levels of heavy muonic atoms are strongly sensitive to higher moments of the nuclear charge distribution, highlighting the importance of realistic nuclear modeling. To facilitate further calculations, we also provide the Fortran code RECFNS, designed for computing the nuclear recoil correction within the QED framework. The present work establishes a basis for future extensions to higher orders in the electron-to-nucleus mass ratio, hyperfine splitting, and radiative corrections.

Atomic energy levels are affected by the finite charge distribution of the nucleus. In the approximation of an infinitely heavy nucleus, the finite nuclear size (fns) effect can be readily taken into account by using the appropriately modified Coulomb potential in the Dirac equation. The fns energy shifts are approximately proportional to the mean-square charge radius of the nucleus, rC2r_{C}^{2}, which provides the basis for determining nuclear charge radii from atomic spectroscopy, in particular from muonic atoms [1].

The theoretical treatment of fns effects becomes much more complicated for nuclei of finite mass. In the relativistic theory, the dependence of atomic energy levels on the nuclear mass is highly nontrivial. The well-known reduced mass can be meaningfully introduced only in the nonrelativistic limit, i.e., for the Schrödinger equation. The use of the reduced mass in the Dirac equation – even though it sometimes appears in the literature [2, 3, 4, 5] – is inconsistent with relativistic theory. In fact, a proper treatment of nuclear recoil effects requires a systematic QED treatment.

papers.title: Accelerating high-fidelity gyrokinetic fusion simulations with iGENE
papers.abstract: We present the latest version of iGENE, a differentiable implementation of the local (flux-tube) gyrokinetic code GENE, now fully rewritten in JAX. iGENE features a multispecies, collisional, fully electromagnetic nonlinear gyrokinetic model while preserving end-to-end differentiability. The code is verified against GENE for linear ITG, TEM and KBM physics and for nonlinear turbulent fluxes with adiabatic and kinetic electrons. Forward-mode derivatives of the linear growth rate agree with finite differences for all five parameters tested, resolving the 30--50\% discrepancy in $\hat{s}$ and $\epsilon$ reported for the earlier TensorFlow version. All collectives are native JAX operations, and the code strong-scales from 2 to 32 H100 GPUs with 86\% parallel efficiency. We then assess three routes to a shorter time to solution. Custom CUDA FFT kernels operating in bfloat16 are up to $3.97\times$ faster than fp32 cuFFT on the transforms, and on a single H100 iGENE is $2.63\times$ faster per time step than single-precision GENE. Multi-rate sub-cycling of the parallel dynamics yields a further $1.89\times$ speedup with kinetic electrons. Finally, a Hermite-Laguerre velocity-space representation is implemented, offering tunable fidelity.

Fusion energy is one of the most formidable scientific and engineering challenges, among others because of the complex, nonlinear, multi-scale, multi-physics phenomena that determine the behavior of a confined plasma. Simulation tools remain critical for fusion research and for probing physics that experiments cannot currently access. Specific numerical methods have been and are continuously developed to produce more and better data. An obvious question is thus how to accelerate such simulations, often requiring extreme computational effort, while maintaining the necessary degree of fidelity for the downstream tasks.

This work reports our efforts to accelerate high fidelity local gyrokinetic simulations, which are the workhorse for characterizing turbulent transport in magnetically confined plasmas. Following the proof of principle discussed in [1], we have further developed the iGENE code, adding all the missing physics elements that were originally not available in the TensorFlow implementation and are necessary for a high fidelity description of a fusion plasma. The code now implements a fully electromagnetic collisional model, is interfaced to most common tokamak and stellarator equilibrium solvers and has been verified against the Fortran version of GENE [2]. The code has been fully rewritten in JAX [3], keeping end-to-end automatic differentiability as a crucial property. It can therefore be used in optimization workflows as well as AI/ML pipelines.

We have verified the code results and measured its parallel performance, which has improved from the TensorFlow port. The iGENE algorithm, a faithful translation of the GENE one, is already extremely optimized on massively parallel architectures, but it remains computationally expensive. We have therefore explored different paths to reduce the time to solution. In particular, modifications to the time stepping scheme enabling sub-cycling of the parallel dynamics, the usage of mixed precision arithmetic and a spectral description of velocity space. The latter is a new feature added to iGENE motivated by the success of similar representations including e.g. the GX code [4] or GENE-X [5]. It is targeted specifically to a multi fidelity approach to turbulence, where the number of moments can be selected to reduce the cost of a run. Furthermore, thanks to the use of agentic AI, the code has been strongly optimized for GPU usage by writing custom FFT kernels that outperform vendor library, an effort that was made easier by adopting JAX. Thanks to these efforts iGENE is now faster than the original GENE code, by 2.63×2.63\times per time step on a single H100 for the kinetic-electron case of Sec. 5.2 when compared with GENE in single precision, although certain optimization strategies could be backported to Fortran and equivalently applied there.

papers.title: Explosive instability, quiet plasma: phase-space cascades, coherent vortices, and transport suppression in a dipole pair plasma
papers.abstract: Turbulence in a magnetised dipole pair plasma can transfer electrostatic energy into coherent flows while carrying entropy to small scales. This occurs via a dual cascade in a four-dimensional phase space, whereby advection by the fluctuating electric field nonlinearly phase-mixes the transit-averaged particle motion. Below a critical pressure gradient, zonal bands suppress the kinetic mode, leaving a transport floor. When the fluid mode is unstable, an explosive burst collapses into a zonal condensate on which two vortices "breathe" by reversible energy exchange, without causing net transport.

papers.title: Recently launched AGN-driven outflow in a lensed quiescent galaxy at Cosmic Noon
papers.abstract: We analyze JWST/NIRSpec IFU spectroscopy of MRG-M0150, a gravitationally lensed, massive quiescent galaxy at $z=2.6$ from the INQUEST-JWST survey. Thanks to the combination of lensing magnification with JWST's angular resolution, we are able to build spatially resolved maps of the ionized gas spatial distribution, kinematics, and ionization properties in this system. We detect ionized gas emission throughout the galaxy: the lack of residual star formation inferred from line-ratio diagnostic diagrams, together with the decoupling between the gas and stellar kinematics, suggest that the ionized gas is in a wind. We use the 3D gas kinematics modeling code \texttt{MOKA3D} to constrain the geometry and physical properties of the ionized gas wind. We find that the observations are consistent with a biconical wind driven by the low-luminosity AGN at the center of the galaxy, which is detected in X-rays. The wind reaches high velocities of $1000-1400$ km/s, implying that part of the gas may escape the halo. The ionized gas mass outflow rate, $(0.6 \pm 0.2)$~${\rm M}_{\odot}$~yr${}^{-1}$, is modest but exceeds the upper limit on the residual star formation rate, and it is likely that the wind is multiphase and carries more mass. We show that typical unresolved observations would not detect the wind, suggesting that the incidence of such outflows may be higher than previously recognized. Simple geometric arguments show that the observed outflow must have been launched $\approx 0.45$~Myr ago from the time of observation. This evidence suggests that low-level AGN activity is an important mechanism for maintaining quiescence in massive galaxies at cosmic noon, potentially over cosmological timescales.

papers.intro:
The physical processes responsible for the quenching of star-formation in massive galaxies remain one of the key open problems in galaxy formation and evolution. Numerous mechanisms have been proposed to explain the quenching of massive galaxies, including active galactic nuclei (AGN), stellar feedback, and virial shock heating (see Whitaker and Bezanson, 2026, for a recent review), but no single mechanism seems to be universally applicable. Semi-analytical models and cosmological hydrodynamical simulations typically invoke AGN feedback as a mechanism capable of quenching massive galaxies. Feedback from the AGN can drive galaxy-scale outflows in multiple gas phases, quenching the galaxy both by expelling gas from the system and by heating the circumgalactic medium, thereby preventing the cooling and accretion of gas that could otherwise fuel subsequent star formation (Di Matteo et al., 2005; Hopkins et al., 2006; Bower et al., 2006; Somerville et al., 2008; Davé et al., 2019, e.g.). However, direct observational evidence linking AGN feedback to the quenching of star formation remains elusive. At cosmic noon (z∼2−3z\sim 2-3), a significant fraction of massive galaxies stopped forming new stars (Muzzin et al., 2013; Straatman et al., 2014; Tomczak et al., 2014; Weaver et al., 2023, e.g.). Observing recently quenched systems at this epoch is crucial for investigating the main mechanisms responsible for quenching star formation in the most massive galaxies.

Galaxy-scale gas outflows have been extensively studied at z∼1−3z\sim 1-3 through large galaxy surveys. It has been found that outflows are ubiquitous in massive star-forming galaxies at cosmic noon (Steidel et al., 2010; Weiner et al., 2009; Förster Schreiber et al., 2019) and in those hosting the most luminous AGN (Cano-Díaz et al., 2012; Cresci et al., 2015a; Kakkad et al., 2016; Davies et al., 2020b), where they are expected to be powerful enough to be able to suppress star formation. However, the study of gas outflows and nuclear activity in the first quiescent galaxies at high redshift is challenging from the ground, relying either on deep exposures of individual galaxies (Kriek et al., 2024; Belli et al., 2017, e.g.) or stacked spectra (Belli et al., 2019, e.g.).

Early JWST spectra of individual galaxies have revealed the presence of AGN activity in these systems (Carnall et al., 2023b; Belli et al., 2024; D’Eugenio et al., 2024; Wu, 2025) and subsequent studies with larger samples have confirmed a high AGN incidence in massive quiescent galaxies at z>2z>2 (Bugiani et al., 2025; Skarbinski et al., 2026). These AGN, for the most part, have been classified as low-luminosity AGN (LL-AGN), based on their faint inferred bolometric luminosities and the lack of more overt tracers of powerful AGN activity such as X-rays detection or IR excess (Almaini et al., 2025; Hewitt et al., 2026).

Early JWST spectra of individual galaxies have revealed the presence of AGN activity in these systems (Carnall et al., 2023b; Belli et al., 2024; D’Eugenio et al., 2024; Wu, 2025) and subsequent studies with larger samples have confirmed a high AGN incidence in massive quiescent galaxies at z>2z>2 (Bugiani et al., 2025; Skarbinski et al., 2026). These AGN, for the most part, have been classified as low-luminosity AGN (LL-AGN), based on their faint inferred bolometric luminosities and the lack of more overt tracers of powerful AGN activity such as X-rays detection or IR excess (Almaini et al., 2025; Hewitt et al., 2026).

At the same time, JWST observations have revealed a widespread presence of gas outflows in massive quiescent galaxies at high redshift, detected both in the neutral and ionized phases (Davies et al., 2024; Taylor et al., 2026; Valentino et al., 2025; Sapori et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). These outflows can be remarkably powerful, often carrying large amounts of cold gas. In particular, observations of neutral-phase outflows in z>2z>2 galaxies through the Na D absorption line have shown that powerful winds are prevalent among massive galaxies at cosmic noon and may represent the dominant pathway for quenching at this epoch (Davies et al., 2024; Sapori et al., 2026). In some systems, the inferred neutral-phase mass outflow rates exceed the current star-formation rates by more than an order of magnitude, suggesting that efficient removal of cold gas may contribute directly to the rapid quenching observed in these galaxies (Belli et al., 2024; D’Eugenio et al., 2024).

However, the origin of these galactic winds and their connection to star-formation quenching remain unclear, as the low-level AGN activity observed in many massive systems struggles to explain the high energy and momentum rates characterizing the observed outflows. While some studies attribute the origin of the observed winds to ongoing LL-AGN activity (Belli et al., 2024; Wu, 2025; Bugiani et al., 2025, e.g.), others interpret them as relics of past starburst episodes or previous periods of more powerful black hole activity, with the central AGN having since faded into a low-accretion state (Valentino et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Taylor et al., 2026). Distinguishing between these scenarios is therefore crucial for establishing whether the outflows observed in massive quiescent galaxies represent ongoing AGN feedback or the remnants of the events that originally quenched the galaxy.

With only a few exceptions (Gangula et al., 2026; D’Eugenio et al., 2024), most studies rely on spatially unresolved data and therefore are not able to directly constrain the geometry, kinematics, and timescales of the outflows. While the ionized phase may represent a small contribution to the total outflowing mass, as observed in high-zz quiescent galaxies (Belli et al., 2024) and predicted by simulations of galactic winds (Kim et al., 2020), it is the best suited to measuring these properties. Ionized gas can be detected directly in emission without requiring a bright background continuum. Its emission traces the full spatial extent of the wind, and, provided that it can be spatially resolved, yields detailed information about the kinematics and 3D structure of the outflow. This can reduce some of the uncertainties associated with assumptions about the geometry and kinematics when deriving mass outflow rates and energetics. Moreover, reconstructing the extent, geometry, and velocity of the winds provides a way to constrain their characteristic timescales, which can be used to distinguish between winds powered by ongoing AGN activity and fossil outflows launched by a past quasar or starburst event. Resolved observations of the ionized phase can therefore offer a unique view on the connection between AGN activity, galactic outflows, and the maintenance of quiescence in massive galaxies at high redshift.

papers.title: The origin and distribution of diffuse HI in the close interacting MHONGOOSE galaxy systems
papers.abstract: We present the deepest HI observations of the two systems with Dproj < 100 kpc, and $\Delta$ vsys < 200 km/s in the MHONGOOSE survey. The MeerKAT observations have a 3$\sigma$ NHI = 10$^{17.9}$ cm$^{-2}$ over 16 km/s at 4 kpc scales. The new data detect HI in seven galaxies -- the interacting NGC 3511/3513 pair, and an interacting triplet (NGC 4781, NGC 4790 and UGCA 308) along with two new (2MASX J1255 and MKT 25413) dwarf satellites. Six galaxies lie on the star-forming main sequence, and their HI gas fractions are typical for such systems. In contrast, MKT 25413 has a log(MHI/Msun) = 5.7, which is the lowest MHI detected of a galaxy that is not a Milky Way satellite. This low surface brightness dwarf galaxy shows an anomalously low star formation and HI fraction for its stellar mass. We find ubiquitous low column density HI surrounding the galaxies, which is likely a consequence of mild tidal interactions from fly-bys in the past few hundred megayears. We derive the stellar and H$\alpha$ kinematics from VLT/MUSE observations and the H2 kinematics from ALMA observations. The kinematics of the stellar and multiphase interstellar medium of the interacting galaxies display ordered rotation, and the atomic-to-molecular gas ratios are indistinguishable from star-forming field galaxies. The stellar morphology of all the interacting galaxies (except the low-mass dwarf UGCA 308) does not show major disruptions, and there is no stellar component associated with the HI tails, bridges or clouds in the intra-group mediums, down to $\mu_{g}$ = 29 mag arcsec$^{-2}$. We surmise that the mild environmental interactions in the close systems are able to pull the diffuse HI out of the disk and redistribute it. The gas is not in equilibrium, although it remains bound and is in the process of falling back onto the disk.

papers.intro:
The availability of a gas reservoir underpins the evolution of galaxies. When there is a sufficient gas supply, under the right conditions the gas can cool and further collapse to form stars (Kennicutt et al., 1994; Kennicutt, 1998; Schinnerer and Leroy, 2024, e.g). If the gas reservoir has been removed or the available gas is unable to cool, star-formation (SF) ceases, and the galaxy will be quenched (e.g. see Cortese et al., 2021, and references within). By using more sensitive observations and refined simulations, we are forming a detailed picture of the baryon cycle that traces the gas and SF processes in and around galaxies.

If the gas reservoir has been removed or the available gas is unable to cool, star-formation (SF) ceases, and the galaxy will be quenched (e.g. see Cortese et al., 2021, and references within). By using more sensitive observations and refined simulations, we are forming a detailed picture of the baryon cycle that traces the gas and SF processes in and around galaxies.

There has been extensive observational and theoretical work showing that gas from the interstellar medium (ISM) can be heated or ejected via different internal processes. For example, stellar winds, radiation or supernova explosions can prevent cooling (Hopkins et al., 2012; Strickland et al., 2000; Chevance et al., 2022, e.g.). This feedback is most efficient in galaxies lower than log(M⋆M_{\mathrm{\star}}/M⊙\rm{M_{\odot}}) = 10, whereas galaxies above this mass are more likely to have active galactic nuclei (AGN) inject energy into the ISM that heat the surrounding gas and create outflows (Croton et al., 2006; Fabian, 2012; Pillepich et al., 2018, e.g.). Another pathway to remove the gas reservoir of a galaxy is through external interactions directly related to the galactic ecosystem. Gas stripping efficiency correlates with the galaxy environment (i.e. with the galaxy number density), and ram pressure appears to be the dominant and most efficient method to strip the ISM in dense galaxy cluster environments (Chung et al., 2007; Jaffé et al., 2018; Rohr et al., 2023; Edler et al., 2025, e.g.). The influence of tidal fields as galaxies orbit each other in close proximity has shown to profoundly disturb and sometimes strip the ISM in a wide range of environments (de Blok et al., 2018; Kleiner et al., 2021; Serra et al., 2023; Rhee et al., 2026, e.g.). Tidal fields can strip the stars and ISM in galaxy pairs, low density groups and clusters, and is thought to be the main quenching mechanism in galaxy groups due to their cooler intra-group medium (IGM), lower orbital velocities and therefore long-lasting encounters (Wu et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023, e.g.). As tidal fields operate over a broad range of strengths, there are many factors that determine if the stellar component is affected, and whether the ISM is disturbed or completely stripped. The situation is even less clear for galaxy pairs. In some pairs, tidal torques funnel the gas inward and boost central star formation (Barnes and Hernquist, 1996; Mihos and Hernquist, 1996), resulting in enhanced atomic and molecular gas fractions (Violino et al., 2018; Ellison et al., 2018, e.g.), consistent with tidal tails channelling diffuse gas that condenses out of the surrounding hot halo (Wang et al., 2023, e.g.). Other studies report on atomic gas stripping and star-formation suppression in pairs (Yu et al., 2022, e.g.), and both enhancement and suppression are seen even within the same interacting samples depending on pair separation (Šiljeg et al., 2025, e.g.). Galaxy pairs show larger scatter in gas content than isolated galaxies at fixed stellar mass, with comparable median values (Bok et al., 2020, e.g.), indicating that whether a given pair is gas-rich and star-forming or gas-poor and quenched likely depends on factors such as separation, mass ratio, and orbital stage.

In the low-zz Universe, the dominant component of the multiphase ISM is neutral atomic hydrogen (H i), which has historically been shown to be one of the best observational tracers for ISM perturbations and stripping. As the interaction strength determines whether the gas reservoir is removed from the galaxy, resolved observations of H i have provided many insights into the quenching stage of interacting galaxies (Koribalski and Dickey, 2004; Boselli and Gavazzi, 2006; de Blok et al., 2018; Pearson et al., 2018; Luber et al., 2022, e.g.). In the past two decades, a number of H i interferometric surveys were completed to observe the ISM and extended gaseous disk of nearby star-forming galaxies. Two important examples are; The H i Nearby Galaxy Survey (Walter et al., 2008, THINGS;) with the Very Large Array (VLA) and Hydrogen Accretion in LOcal GAlaxieS (Heald et al., 2011, HALOGAS;) with the Westerbork Synthesis Radio Telescope (WSRT). The 3σ\sigma H i column density (NHIN_{\mathrm{HI}}) – normalised to a velocity width of 16 km s-1– of THINGS is sensitive down to NHIN_{\mathrm{HI}} = 1019.5 cm-2 at a spatial resolution of a few hundred pc, which focused mainly on the kinematics and star-forming process of the dense H i in the disk (de Blok et al., 2008; Leroy et al., 2008; Bigiel et al., 2010, e.g). HALOGAS on the other hand is sensitive down to NHIN_{\mathrm{HI}} = 1019 cm-2) over the same velocity width, at a spatial resolution of approximately one kiloparsec, and was able to detect and quantify the behaviour of extra-planar H i in nearby gas-rich, star-forming galaxies (de Blok et al., 2014; Vargas et al., 2017; Marasco et al., 2019, e.g.). While these surveys were able to measure the H i properties of galaxies in a column density regime approximately two orders of magnitude lower than where star formation occurs, they were limited to the higher density H i that only moderate-to-strong interactions are able to disrupt. Tidal interactions in groups that strip H i above NHIN_{\mathrm{HI}} ∼\sim 1019 cm-2 are typically strong enough to produce massive (e.g. log(MHIM_{\mathrm{HI}}/M⊙\rm{M_{\odot}}) >> 8.5) H i tails, and disturb the stellar component (Koribalski and Manthey, 2005; Serra et al., 2013; Saponara et al., 2018, e.g.).

papers.title: Theoretical Pulsation Properties of RR Lyrae and Type II Cepheids in the JWST and Roman photometric systems
papers.abstract: RR Lyrae (RRL) stars and Type II Cepheids (T2Cs) are key standard candles and tracers of old stellar populations. The deep, wide-field capabilities of facilities such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will significantly expand their utility as a Population II alternative to Classical Cepheids for distance scale calibrations. We present theoretical pulsation properties-including light-curve morphologies, amplitudes, and multi-filter relations for RRLs (Z = 0.0001 - 0.02, M = 0.51 - 0.80, Msun) and T2Cs (Z = 0.0001 - 0.01, M = 0.495 - 0.65, Msun) to enable detailed studies of Galactic and extragalactic populations. Using alreday available non-linear convective pulsation models, we converted their predicted bolometric light curves across various chemical compositions and evolutionary stages into the JWST and Roman photometric systems. From these, we derived multi-filter Period-Amplitude and Color-Color diagrams, alongside Period-Luminosity and Period-Wesenheit relations with explicit metallicity terms. RRL relations display a significantly stronger zero-point metallicity dependence than those of T2Cs, despite sharing similar slopes. Consequently, T2Cs offer a distance scale indicator that is remarkably robust against metallicity uncertainties. As a preliminary test, we applied our metal-dependent Period-Wesenheit relations to a subset of JWST-observed RRLs in the WLM galaxy, deriving a distance modulus of mu_0 = 24.85 +/- 0.03 mag (assuming the literature average metallicity). The derived distance to WLM is consistent with most literature values, though slightly shorter than determinations based on Classical Cepheids and the Tip of the Red Giant Branch. These theoretical relations pave the way for future high-precision distance determinations and asteroseismic diagnostics with JWST and Roman.

papers.intro:
RR Lyrae (RRL) stars and Type II Cepheids (T2Cs) are well known standard candles and tracers of the formation and evolution of old stellar populations. In the case of RRL, their use as distance indicators has traditionally relied upon the well-established luminosity–metallicity relation (see, e.g., Caputo et al. 2000; Di Criscienzo et al. 2004; Marconi et al. 2018; Muraveva et al. 2018, and references therein) and a period–luminosity (PL) relation in the near-infrared (NIR) filters (Longmore et al. 1986; Bono et al. 2001; Bono et al. 2003; Catelan et al. 2004; Dall’Ora et al. 2006; Coppola et al. 2011; Navarrete et al. 2015; Marconi et al. 2015; Muraveva et al. 2015; Marconi et al. 2022, see, e.g.,). Moreover, accurate two-filter and three-filter Period-Wesenheit (PW) relations can be derived for these pulsators (Marconi et al. 2015, see, e.g.,). While the physical basis for these relations is robust, the precise values of coefficients and the role of metallicity in the NIR PL and PW remain a subject of active debate (Bono et al. 2003; Borissova et al. 2009; Marconi et al. 2015; Muraveva et al. 2018; Marconi et al. 2022; Bhardwaj et al. 2023; Zgirski et al. 2023; Prudil et al. 2024, see, e.g.,).

However, recent high-precision calibrations (Bhardwaj et al. 2023, see, e.g.,) quite closely align with theoretical predictions for the metallicity term coefficient both in PL and PW relations of RRL.

T2Cs are significantly more luminous than RRL, typically by more than 0.2 dex, making them powerful distance indicators across diverse stellar environments. They have been identified in the Galactic Bulge (Matsunaga et al. 2013; Bhardwaj et al. 2017; Braga et al. 2019, e.g.,), in Galactic Globular Clusters (Matsunaga et al. 2006; Ngeow et al. 2022, GGCs,), in the Galactic Halo (Wielgórski et al. 2022; Ripepi et al. 2023) and in the Magellanic Clouds (Soszyński et al. 2018; Sicignano et al. 2024, e.g.,). Classified by their pulsation periods, T2Cs are traditionally divided into three sub-groups: BL Herculis stars (P<4P<4 days), W Virginis stars (4<P<204<P<20 days), and RV Tauri stars (P>20P>20 days). While foundational stellar evolution models for T2Cs were established by Gingold (1976, 1985), more recent investigations have focused primarily on the pulsation properties of the BL Herculis subclass (Di Criscienzo et al. 2007; Bono et al. 2020; Das et al. 2021; Das et al. 2025, e.g.,). In Marconi et al. (2025), we expanded upon this theoretical landscape by computing the oscillation properties of post-Zero-Age Horizontal Branch (ZAHB) stars directly along their evolutionary tracks. On this basis, we presented—for the first time—a detailed pulsation analysis across three distinct metallicity values, bridging the gap between evolutionary theory and observed pulsation properties. The next era of time-domain astronomy is defined by a shift toward high-cadence, deep-sky infrared and optical mapping. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time (Ivezić et al. 2019, LSST,) is expected to revolutionize our census of variable stars by providing a 10-year "movie" of the southern sky. Complementing this is the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (Akeson et al. 2019, Roman,), whose Wide Field Instrument will provide Hubble-like resolution over a field of view 100 times larger, focusing on the Galactic Bulge and high-latitude fields. Together with the JWST, these missions will extend our reach to variable stars in distant, obscured environments that were previously inaccessible, allowing us to use them as precision distance markers across the Local Universe.

papers.title: Multiphase Gas Structure in JWST Little Red Dots
papers.abstract: JWST has uncovered a population of compact high-redshift galaxies, 'little red dots' (LRDs), exhibiting broad Balmer emission lines that often show narrow absorption features and strong Balmer breaks - spectral signatures attributed to dense gas surrounding rapidly growing black holes, but whose small-scale structure remains unknown. A striking feature of LRD spectra is that the H$\beta$ absorption is systematically deeper than H$\alpha$, yet in any homogeneous gas this ordering is physically impossible. Here we model the H$\alpha$ and H$\beta$ line profiles using radiative transfer simulations for 11 LRDs with JWST sensitive high resolution spectroscopy, and independently constrain the $n=2$ hydrogen column density, $N_{\rm HI,\mathit{n}=2}$, from the Balmer-break continuum. We find that the $N_{\rm HI,\mathit{n}=2}$ from H$\alpha$ in a homogeneous medium cannot reproduce the observed H$\beta$ absorption in several objects, and that this $N_{\rm HI,\mathit{n}=2}$ typically falls two orders of magnitude below the lower bound set by the Balmer break. Both tensions are simultaneously resolved by a multiphase medium of dense clumps within diffuse hot ionized gas. This multiphase gas structure is a necessary ingredient for any viable LRD model, regardless of the nature of the central engine.

papers.title: Radio view of the Peanut cluster: merger-induced stripping and a radio halo shortly after pericentric passage
papers.abstract: The Peanut galaxy cluster (SRGe CL0238.3+2005) offers a rare opportunity to investigate thermal and nonthermal processes only $\sim0.1$\,Gyr after pericentric passage. We present a multi-frequency radio study of this system at $z=0.42$ using new MeerKAT and uGMRT observations, complemented by Chandra and MUSTANG-2 data. We identify two morphologically and spectrally distinct radio components: a double-lobed source in the northern subcluster and extended diffuse emission across the cluster center. The double-lobed source has a strongly curved, ultra-steep spectrum and is offset by $\sim22$\,kpc from the nearest brightest cluster galaxy. Its spectral curvature and positional offset are consistent with remnant AGN plasma that may have been displaced during the merger or reshaped by a shock. The diffuse emission extends over $\sim1$~Mpc and is classified as an ultra-steep spectrum ($\alpha=-1.77\pm0.11$ between 400\,MHz and 1.28\,GHz) radio halo. Its volume-averaged radio emissivity, $(1.1\pm0.1)\times10^{-41}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-3}$ Hz$^{-1}$ at 1.4\,GHz, is an order of magnitude higher than the characteristic value for other halos. The radial profile of the halo is well described by a single exponential fit and its radio emission correlates tightly with the X-ray, with a best-fit slope of $1.11\pm0.05$. Chandra and MUSTANG-2 observations reveal candidate surface brightness discontinuities, with the most prominent inner feature coinciding with a region of flatter spectral index, potentially tracing localized particle (re)-acceleration. The coexistence of an extended ultra-steep spectrum radio halo, high radio emissivity, remnant AGN plasma, and candidate X-ray/SZ discontinuities makes the Peanut cluster an important test case for understanding the evolution of diffuse radio emission and its connection to the dynamical state of the intracluster medium in early-stage mergers.
