papers.intro:
Galaxy clusters grow through hierarchical accretion and mergers, which are among the most energetic events in the Universe. These mergers profoundly affect the intracluster medium (ICM), driving shocks, turbulence, and large scale gas motions, ultimately accelerating relativistic particles. Systems observed shortly after pericentric passage are rare because this phase is short-lived. The Peanut cluster (SRGe CL0238.3+2005) was recently identified in the all-sky survey conducted with the extended ROentgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array (eROSITA) aboard the Spectrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) observatory (Sunyaev et al., 2021; Predehl et al., 2021; Burenin et al., 2022; Lyskova et al., 2025). Located at z=0.42z=0.42, the cluster has a mass of M500≃1015​M⊙M_{500}\simeq 10^{15}\,M_{\odot} and an ICM temperature of k​T≃10kT\simeq 10 keV. Multi-wavelength observations indicate that the system is undergoing a major merger, approximately 0.10.1 Gyr after pericentric passage (Lyskova et al., 2025; Zaznobin et al., 2026). Such massive systems at this redshift are rare and only a few dozen galaxy clusters with M500>1015​M⊙M_{500}>10^{15}\,M_{\odot} are expected to be found across the whole sky (Tinker et al., 2008; Mortonson et al., 2011; Harrison and Hotchkiss, 2013).

The Chandra 40-ks X-ray image of the Peanut cluster reveals two bright X-ray clumps to the north and south, separated by a pronounced surface brightness depression (Lyskova et al., 2025). Comparison with optical observations shows that the X-ray bright gas component is offset from the subcluster galaxies, reminiscent of the Bullet cluster merger (Markevitch et al., 2004; Clowe et al., 2006; Paraficz et al., 2016, see, e.g.,). In contrast to the Bullet cluster, however, the Peanut cluster appears to involve two “bullets” in an almost head-on collision. Lyskova et al. (2025) reported that the cluster experienced an almost head-on merger only ≲0.1​Gyr\lesssim 0.1\,{\rm Gyr} ago, i.e., it is observed in a particularly energetic phase of the merger (just after the pericenter passage of the two merging sub-halos).

Diffuse radio emission associated with galaxy clusters, known as radio halos and radio relics, provides a direct probe of the nonthermal processes in the ICM (Markevitch and Vikhlinin, 2007; van Weeren et al., 2019; Adam et al., 2025). These sources and fossil plasma from active galactic nuclei (AGN) (Mandal et al., 2020; Brienza et al., 2022; Botteon et al., 2026a; Rajpurohit et al., 2024, e.g., ) trace the distribution of relativistic particles and magnetic fields, (re)-accelerated by processes like shocks and turbulence. The Peanut cluster offers a rare opportunity to investigate diffuse radio emission in a massive cluster merger shortly after pericentric passage. However, despite its unusual dynamical state, the system remains poorly studied at radio wavelengths. Survey observations, including the Rapid Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) Continuum Survey (McConnell et al., 2020, RACS;) and the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT) Sky Survey (Intema et al., 2017, TGSS;) presented by Lyskova et al. (2025) revealed extended steep spectrum radio emission, potentially indicative of aged radio plasma. However, the sensitivity and angular resolution were insufficient to establish the nature of radio emission or to investigate its spectral properties in detail.

papers.title: An Intermediate Mass Stripped Star in a 4.2-hour Orbit around a Compact Object
papers.abstract: From their discovery as radio pulsars to landmark multi-messenger observations of their mergers, double neutron stars have transformed our understanding of the extreme Universe and the formation of heavy elements (Drout et al. 2017; Abbott et al. 2017). Yet, uncertainties in their formation result in predicted merger rates spanning orders of magnitude (Tauris et al. 2017; Mandel & Broekgaarden 2022). The most critical stage occurs when a star is stripped of its hydrogen-rich envelope, causing the binary orbit to shrink drastically. Despite its fundamental role, the resulting tight binaries comprising a stripped star and neutron star have remained elusive. Here we report a $\sim$$3.4\,M_{\odot}$ stripped star (Ludwig et al. 2026; Drout et al. 2023; G\"otberg et al. 2023) orbiting an unseen companion every 4.2 hours. Our orbital and spectroscopic analysis excludes a normal star, which would not fit within the orbit, as well as a second stripped star which would have been detectable in our spectra. Adding constraints from high cadence photometry gives a 99.4% probability that the companion is too massive to be a white dwarf, making a neutron star the most likely companion. We model the system's future and predict that the stripped star will transfer mass again before exploding as a hydrogen-free supernova, leaving a bound pair of neutron stars that will merge after 220 Myr. This system reveals a previously unconstrained phase of binary evolution, uncovering a new class of systems that probes the uncertain physics of massive stars, linking to observable gravitational-wave sources.

papers.title: Role of site-specific coordination for the structural and electronic properties of a Co-HATCN network on silver
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional metal-organic porous networks (2DMOPNs) on metal surfaces provide a versatile platform for exploring emergent electronic and magnetic phenomena in designed surface nanostructures. While the porous architecture is governed by coordination between molecular building blocks and metal centers, most 2DMOPNs utilize only one type of coordination site, leaving the impact of multiple coordination sites largely unexplored. We address this question by investigating the structural formation of a Co-coordinated 2DMOPN on Ag(111) with the linker molecule hexaazatriphenylene-hexacarbonitrile (HATCN), which has two chemically distinct nitrogen coordination sites at the peripheral nitrile groups and pyrazine-type core nitrogen atoms. Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) reveals the transformation from a simple honeycomb HATCN structure to a Co-coordinated porous network with three structurally and electronically inequivalent molecules in a 6:3:1 ratio. The existence of two distinct coordination sites leads to selective Co coordination geometries for all three molecules, accompanied by site-specific charge transfer from Co into the former lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO), as revealed by momentum-resolved photoemission and density functional theory. Our results demonstrate that site-selective Co coordination not only controls the overall architecture of the porous network structure but also strongly influences the local electronic properties through site-specific metal-molecule interaction, providing a route to tailor the site-specific electronic structure of 2DMOPNs at the molecular level.

papers.intro:
Two-dimensional metal–organic porous networks (2DMOPNs) on noble metal surfaces have emerged as a highly flexible platform for engineering the electronic properties of surfaces on the nanoscale [4, 5, 36]. The key control parameter is the long-range ordered porous architecture. This architecture determines the periodic surface potential landscape and thus governs the strength of quantum confinement of the two-dimensional electron gas of Shockley surface states and image potential states within the nanopores, as well as the coupling between neighboring pores [23, 36, 38, 26]. For instance, the band dispersion of the quantum-confined surface states depends on the pore size [20, 35], the barrier width between adjacent pores [37], and the geometry and symmetry of the scattering potential landscape [19, 36]. These structural parameters can even be tuned by external stimuli such as temperature [27]. Understanding the relationship between the structural motif and intralayer interactions within 2DMOPN structures is therefore crucial for achieving active control of the interfacial electron structure.

The key control parameter is the long-range ordered porous architecture. This architecture determines the periodic surface potential landscape and thus governs the strength of quantum confinement of the two-dimensional electron gas of Shockley surface states and image potential states within the nanopores, as well as the coupling between neighboring pores [23, 36, 38, 26]. For instance, the band dispersion of the quantum-confined surface states depends on the pore size [20, 35], the barrier width between adjacent pores [37], and the geometry and symmetry of the scattering potential landscape [19, 36]. These structural parameters can even be tuned by external stimuli such as temperature [27]. Understanding the relationship between the structural motif and intralayer interactions within 2DMOPN structures is therefore crucial for achieving active control of the interfacial electron structure.

The most descriptive intralayer interaction for the overall network structure is the metal–ligand coordination, i.e., the interaction between the reactive molecular site and the linker atoms. These interactions are highly selective and directional, with interaction energies that can exceed those of mere van der Waals or hydrogen bonds [5]. As a result, metal–ligand coordination dominates the relative arrangement between the metallic linker atoms and the molecular building blocks, thus determining the overall periodicity and symmetry of the network structure. In addition, metal–ligand bonding substantially modifies the electronic structure of the organic building blocks. For strong electron acceptors, metal coordination induces a charge transfer into the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) of the ligand, whose magnitude depends on the type of metal center and its coordination number [14]. In extended 2D metal–organic networks, the hybridization between metal 3d states and ligand π\pi orbitals even leads to the formation of hybrid dispersive bands [3, 29, 6], and the charge transfer from the metal center to the ligands also alters the scattering potential of the metal centers for surface electrons [20]. So far, however, the coordination in most 2DMOPNs is mediated by only one type of coordination site of the organic ligand, for instance by carboxylate [41, 15], pyridyl [45, 42, 38], or carbonitrile groups [40, 20, 1]. In these systems, structural complexity arises mainly from a variation of the coordination number of the metal centers, as observed for the coexistence of three- and fourfold Co–carbonitrile nodes [28] or for even more complex arrangements including quasicrystalline tilings [13, 44]. In addition, chemically distinct coordination sites have so far been exploited for the selective binding of different metal species, for instance Gd atoms at the peripheral nitrile groups and Co atoms in the macrocycle of a porphyrin derivative [43]. However, the competition among coordination sites of the same ligand for the same metal center, and its impact on the structural properties of the network, have remained largely unexplored.

Therefore, we investigate the structure formation of a cobalt-coordinated HATCN (hexaazatriphenylene-hexacarbonitrile) porous network structure on Ag(111). HATCN is a planar, highly symmetric π\pi-conjugated molecule and a strong electron acceptor on noble metal surfaces [8, 9]. On Ag(111), its adsorption is accompanied by a charge transfer from the substrate into the LUMO [32], which amounts to approximately one electron per molecule and lifts the twofold degeneracy of the gas-phase LUMO [10]. Most importantly for our study, HATCN has two chemically distinct types of nitrogen atoms for metal coordination: six peripheral nitrile groups, which constitute the prototypical coordination motif of carbonitrile-based networks [40, 28] and six pyrazine-type nitrogen atoms of the hexaazatriphenylene core, which coordinate Cu atoms in Cu–HAT frameworks on coinage metal surfaces [25]. HATCN therefore represents an ideal model system to explore how the competition between two coordination sites governs the structure formation and the electronic properties of a metal–organic network.

papers.title: An extended red wing of the 5797 {\AA} diffuse interstellar band in the Red Rectangle nebula
papers.abstract: Diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) are interstellar molecular absorption features that are ubiquitous in the interstellar medium (ISM). So far, there was only one known sight line where DIBs show an extend tail towards the red (ETR), namely Herschel 36. Such sight lines are essential to illuminate the DIB problem, namely the identification of their carriers, because they show more DIB variation than standard ISM sight lines. To report a new detection of the 5797 {\AA} DIB in the Red Rectangle nebula with an ETR, which adds a new observational constraint for the DIB carrier. We analysed archival GIRAFFE/FLAMES integral field spectroscopy to extract all spectral features between 5776 and 5810 {\AA} at different spatial positions. We used time series spectra to identify stellar and circumstellar features, and data from different instruments to exclude instrumental effects. We report the firm detection of the 5797 {\AA} DIB that is localised in the Red Rectangle nebula, or in the ISM in the sight line towards it. Curiously, while the 5797 {\AA} DIB shows an ETR in the Red Rectangle, the 5780 {\AA} DIB does not. Further, we report an exceptionally high equivalent ratio of EW(5797)/EW(5780) = 1.79 higher than any other literature value.

papers.intro:
The diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) continue to be a mystery in astrochemistry since being discovered more than a century ago (Heger, 1922). They are ubiquitous in the Milky Way (Zasowski et al., 2015) and even in other galaxies (Heckman and Lehnert, 2000; Ehrenfreund et al., 2002; Cordiner et al., 2008). Besides the cationic fullerene C+60{}_{60}^{+} (Campbell et al., 2015; Spieler et al., 2017), no other DIB carrier is identified at this point. A lot of progress was made, but the DIB carriers remain elusive. Profile variation in DIBs is generally very subtle in sight lines through the diffuse ISM. The only sight line with large profile variation is towards Herschel 36, the O-star illuminating the Hourglass region of the Lagoon Nebula (Dahlstrom et al., 2013). Several strong DIBs show an extended tail towards the red (ETR), which was interpreted as rotational contours of highly excited carriers. Anomalous sight lines like Herschel 36 are essential to solving the DIB puzzle, as they show extreme DIB profile variations.

In this Letter, we present a second sight line where at least one DIB has an ETR: the Red Rectangle nebula (RR). The RR is a unique object for studying the formation and evolution of circumstellar and interstellar molecules in a broad wavelength range. At its centre is the binary star system HD 44179 consisting of a post-asymptotic giant branch (post-AGB) star that is losing mass and a solar-type main sequence companion (Witt et al., 2009). The resulting accretion disc around the secondary star ejects a bipolar mass outflow of dust and molecules, and is the source of ionising photons. The binary system cannot be seen directly, but is obscured by a circumbinary dusty disk, where the dust scatters the optical star light, so the spectrum of HD 44179 is still observable (Thomas et al., 2013). The disk is extending outward more than 10 arcseconds and can be approximated by a spherical structure, only punctured by the ouflow (Men’shchikov et al., 2002). The outflow is a bright source of aromatic infrared bands (AIBs), and exhibits class B profiles in the centre (Peeters et al., 2002), which is typical for circumstellar environments. But it completely transforms to class A at larger separations (Ebenbichler et al., 2026), which is typical for the ISM. In the optical, the outflow shows strong extended red emission (ERE), a very broad emission feature, giving the nebula its red colour (Schmidt et al., 1980). Additionally, there are narrow emission features superimposed on the ERE, called the red rectangle bands (RRBs). Their peak wavelengths are very close to the wavelengths of some DIBs, leading to the assumption that they could be caused by DIB carriers in emission (Scarrott et al., 1992; Sarre et al., 1995). However, the absence of most DIBs in the central source HD 44179 (Hobbs et al., 2004) casts doubt on this hypothesis. Here, we report the detection of a 5797 Å DIB with an ETR in the spectrum of HD 44179, which significantly enforces the idea of common DIB and RRB carriers and is only the second source of a DIB showing an ETR.

papers.title: A theoretically exact filtered back-propagationformula for single-time wave inversion
papers.abstract: We consider single-time wave inversion, that is, recovering the initial pressure $f$ from the wave field $\mathcal{W}_T f = u(\cdot,T)$ at a single time $T$, where $u$ solves the wave equation with sound speed $c$ and initial data $(f,0)$. In two dimensions this is the main reconstruction step of full-field photoacoustic projection imaging, where each camera image is a two-dimensional wave field at a single time instant. An efficient direct method is back-propagation by the Fourier multiplier $2\cos(cT|\xi|)$. It yields exact inversion in odd dimensions but not in two. We give its error in closed form, with bounds, and derive an exact explicit filtered back-propagation $f = 2\mathcal{W}_T \mathcal{M}_K \mathcal{W}_T f$ in analogy to filtered backprojection for the Radon transform.
papers.intro:
In camera-based full-field photoacoustic tomography (PAT), an optical phase-contrast system and a camera record projections of the 3D acoustic pressure field at a single time TT after the laser pulse [1], instead of time-resolved signals on a detection surface as in standard PAT [2]. Because the X-ray projection commutes with the Laplacian, every camera image is itself a two-dimensional wave field whose initial value is the linear projection of the initial pressure [1]. Reconstruction thus splits into a 2D single-time wave inversion per projection, followed by a Radon inversion across projections. This is how camera-based PAT is processed in practice [3, 4]. It is modular and fast: every camera image is processed independently at the cost of a few FFTs. It also lets incomplete images be completed in 2D first before the final image formation step. Note that the reduction to 2D uses a constant speed of sound; for variable sound speed, full 3D methods are a natural alternative [5, 6].

papers.title: Uncertainty Evaluation to Support Safety of the Intended Functionality Analysis for Determining the Applicability of Performance Targets Across Triggering Conditions in ML-Based LiDAR Object Detection
papers.abstract: For safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF) analysis according to ISO 21448, a machine learning object detector for light detection and ranging (LiDAR) point clouds can meet a performance target, a limit on the mean per-frame share of wrong detections among accepted detections, by rejecting detections above an uncertainty threshold. A threshold selected on data of one condition carries a statistical guarantee only for data distributed like its selection data, whereas SOTIF analysis covers every triggering condition. This paper presents an uncertainty evaluation in which the threshold is transferred into a triggering condition, a test decides at a stated error probability whether the target is applicable there, not applicable or not determined, and a lower bound counts the independent units an applicable outcome requires. For PointPillars ensembles on KITTI and nuScenes, counted in recorded sequences, as the dependence between frames requires, neither dataset held enough independent units for any target limit, and no transfer had a not applicable outcome. Counted in frames, the same data gave not applicable outcomes at limits fixed in advance after transfers into far distance, into rain and between two separately trained detectors, thresholds that met the target limit after a transfer rejected most correct detections, and in rain the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve did not decrease. A performance target met under one condition therefore counts as evidence under a triggering condition only after a test there, reported with its share of accepted correct detections and its number of independent recorded sequences.

papers.intro:
An automated vehicle perceives its surroundings with object detectors, among them detectors for point clouds from light detection and ranging (LiDAR) sensors. A detector based on machine learning (ML) outputs a three-dimensional box, called a detection, for each object that it recognises in a frame, one point cloud of the sensor. The motion planner, which plans the path and speed of the vehicle, acts on these detections. This paper considers detections of cars, the object class with the most annotations in the KITTI and nuScenes datasets used here [1, 2]. A detection is wrong if it does not match a car marked by the annotators of the dataset (an annotated car), for example because no object lies in its box or because the box misses the position or size of the car. A wrong detection can make the vehicle brake or steer for an object that does not exist, or misjudge the position of one that does.

A wrong detection can make the vehicle brake or steer for an object that does not exist, or misjudge the position of one that does.

ISO 21448, the standard on the safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF), requires that the residual risk of a driving function meets acceptance criteria at vehicle level [3]. Performance targets for system elements, for example a limit on how often a sensor reports an object that does not exist, can be derived from these criteria. A detector can meet such a target by rejecting uncertain detections. In this paper, the detector is an ensemble of separately trained networks, called members, and two indicators compute the uncertainty of a detection from the outputs of the members. The spatial indicator usu_{\mathrm{s}} grows as the members disagree more on the position and size of the box, and the existence indicator ueu_{\mathrm{e}} grows as their confidence that an object is present falls. A detection whose indicator value exceeds the uncertainty threshold τ\tau is rejected and does not reach the motion planner. The other detections are accepted. The performance target of this paper bounds the false acceptance proportion (FAP), the share of wrong detections among the accepted detections of a frame averaged over frames, by a limit α\alpha. A lower threshold rejects more wrong detections but also more correct ones, and every rejected correct detection is a car that the motion planner does not receive.

The guarantee therefore holds only for data distributed like the data on which the threshold was selected [5, 6], with their mix of distances, weather and locations.

ISO 21448 describes a triggering condition (TC) as a specific condition of a scenario that initiates a system reaction contributing to a hazardous behaviour, and it requires the response of the system to TCs to be evaluated. Its example of a statistical argument (Clause C.6.3.2) assumes one environment and does not state what holds in another. ISO/PAS 8800 considers the case in which the safety requirements of an artificial intelligence system are fulfilled only for a limited part of the input space. It requires that such a case is identified and reported to the development of the encompassing system [7]. A SOTIF analysis therefore has to establish under which conditions a performance target is met. Whether a threshold selected under one condition meets the target under another has to be tested.

The conference paper extended here [8] reported the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUROC). AUROC measures how well an indicator separates correct from wrong detections (0.5 is chance level, 1 is perfect separation), not whether a threshold meets a limit. It is therefore not known whether AUROC shows a change of condition under which the threshold no longer meets the limit.

Recorded data can show that a limit is met only if they hold enough independent units (frames or recorded sequences). Frames of one recorded sequence, a continuous recording such as a nuScenes scene or a KITTI drive, are not independent of each other. The number of independent frames or recorded sequences needed to show that a limit is met sets the minimum amount of data to record per condition.

In the uncertainty evaluation of this paper, a statistical test, the applicability test, decides whether a performance target met under one condition is also met under another condition. A threshold is transferred when it is selected on recorded data of one condition, the condition of selection, and used unchanged on recorded data of another, the condition of use. For example, a threshold selected on the detections at near distance is transferred when it is used unchanged on the detections at far distance. At a stated error probability, the performance target is applicable in the condition of use if the data show that the FAP with the transferred threshold does not exceed the limit there, and not applicable if they show that it exceeds the limit. The applicability is not determined if the data show neither. The test examines whether the target is met under the condition of use, not whether it is required there. This paper takes the target as required under every condition of the operational design domain (ODD). Figure 1 shows, for two transfers, one recorded frame in which the transferred threshold accepts a wrong detection that the threshold selected in the condition of use rejects. Both frames were chosen to show this case. In the KITTI frame, an unannotated object under the box of the wrong detection cannot be excluded.

papers.title: On the symmetric Morrey problem in three dimensions
papers.abstract: We study the relations between seven generalized notions of convexity for continuous integrands in the space of symmetric $3\times 3$ matrices. Here, symmetric quasiconvexity is defined through symmetrized gradients, and symmetric rank-one convexity through symmetrized rank-one lines. We construct a symmetric quasiconvex integrand that is not polyconvex at symmetric matrices, and an integrand that is both symmetric rank-one convex and Hessian quasiconvex but not symmetric quasiconvex. We also establish a transfer principle that converts smooth rank-one convex functions that lack Hessian quasiconvexity into symmetric rank-one convex integrands while preserving this lack of of Hessian quasiconvexity. Applying this scheme to already existing counterexamples yields the existence of symmetric rank-one convex integrands that are not Hessian quasiconvex. Together with known examples, these results determine all pairwise implications among the seven notions considered here.

papers.title: On the power of adaption and randomization 2: Non-symmetric convex sets
papers.abstract: Let $S:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator between real Banach spaces, and let $F\subset X$ be nonempty, bounded and convex. We prove $$a_{2n-1}(S,F)\le 27n\min \{ e^{\rm ran}_n (S,F), e^{\rm ada}_n (S,F)\}.$$ Here $a_k$ is the minimal worst-case error of continuous affine algorithms of rank at most $k$, and $e_n^{\rm ran}$ and $e_n^{\rm ada}$ are the minimal errors of adaptive randomized and deterministic algorithms using at most $n$ continuous linear measurements. This shows that the gain of adaption and randomization, and even nonlinearity, is limited by a factor $27n$ for approximation in convex sets. We discuss the optimality of the result by examples.

papers.title: The closed convex hull of all associative copulas is a Z-set in the family of all bivariate Schur concave copulas, and related results
papers.abstract: Very recently, Problem 2.5 stated by Mesiar and Sarkoci in \cite{MeSa} and originally formulated by Durante was answered in the negative by \v{S}eliga \cite{Sel}. The author showed that the closed convex hull of all bivariate associative copulas is a proper subset of the family of all Schur concave copulas, and even computed the exact uniform distance of his counterexamples to the closed convex hull (so that the Hausdorff distance between the two families is at least $\frac32-\sqrt{2}$). Using the fact that every bivariate associative copula can be represented as a (finite or countably infinite) ordinal sum of Archimedean copulas and the minimum copula $M$, and working with the Markov kernels of Archimedean copulas, we first give an alternative, simple proof of the strict inclusion. We do so by showing that convex combinations of associative copulas can assign only very little mass to \new{staircase-shaped unions of small squares covering} certain line segments parallel to the main diagonal, a result we later extend to so-called chains and staircases. Building on the first observation, we then go one step further and show that, from a topological perspective, the closed convex hull of all associative copulas is a very small subset of the Schur concave family, namely a so-called $Z$-set, and that the family of associative copulas is, in turn, a $Z$-set in its closed convex hull.

papers.intro:
It is well-known and straightforward to verify that the widely used family 𝒞a​r\mathcal{C}^{ar} of bivariate Archimedean copulas is not closed with respect to the uniform metric d∞d_{\infty} and that its closure is the family 𝒞a​s​s​o​c\mathcal{C}^{assoc} of associative copulas (see [11]). In accordance with 𝒞a​r\mathcal{C}^{ar}, the family 𝒞a​s​s​o​c\mathcal{C}^{assoc} is easily shown not to be convex. Moreover, according to [2, 12], every associative copula admits a (finite or countably infinite) ordinal sum representation with Archimedean copulas and the minimum copula MM serving as building blocks. Since each associative copula CC is obviously symmetric and easily verified to be Schur concave (see [1, 5]) and since the family 𝒞s​c\mathcal{C}^{sc} of all Schur concave copulas is closed and convex it may seem natural to conjecture that the closed convex hull of 𝒞a​s​s​o​c\mathcal{C}^{assoc} is 𝒞s​c\mathcal{C}^{sc}, i.e., that convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)=𝒞sc\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc})=\mathcal{C}^{sc} holds. This very question was formulated as Problem 2.5 in [14] and goes back to Fabrizio Durante. Problem 2.5 has recently been answered in the negative by Šeliga [17], who constructed a one-parameter family of Schur concave shuffles of MM outside convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}) and determined their distance to convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}). He also proved that every extreme point of convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}) is associative and reformulated the second part of Problem 2.6 in [14] as the question whether the extreme points of convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}) are exactly the associative copulas which are extreme points of the full family of copulas 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The objective of this note is twofold. Firstly, we give an independent proof of the fact that convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}) is a proper subset of 𝒞s​c\mathcal{C}^{sc}, based on a different mechanism: elements of convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}) assign very little mass to staircase-shaped unions of small squares covering line segments parallel to the main diagonal, whereas Schur concave copulas may assign these sets much more mass. Since the resulting counterexamples are not extreme points of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the extremality argument used in [17] does not apply to them. Secondly, and this is our main contribution, we show that convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}) is a so-called ZZ-set in 𝒞s​c\mathcal{C}^{sc} and that 𝒞a​s​s​o​c\mathcal{C}^{assoc} is, in turn, a ZZ-set in convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}), i.e., topologically speaking convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}) is negligible in 𝒞s​c\mathcal{C}^{sc} and 𝒞a​s​s​o​c\mathcal{C}^{assoc} is negligible in convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}). The rest of this note is organized as follows: Section 2 gathers some background on the involved families of copulas and on Markov kernels, which serve as key tool. Section 3 then studies one concrete example of a Schur concave copula which is not an element of convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}), and, working with tools from infinite-dimensional topology then uses this example in order to show that convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}) is topologically negligible in 𝒞s​c\mathcal{C}^{sc}. Section 4 generalizes the underlying mass bound to arbitrary staircases, shows that the elements of convh¯⁡(𝒞assoc)\cconvh(\mathcal{C}^{assoc}) do not charge chains off the main diagonal and compares this approach with the one in [17], showing in particular that these necessary conditions are not sufficient. Section 5 contains further topological results, and Section 6 concludes the paper.

papers.title: Approximating the Euclidean Ball by Polytopes: Surprising Rates in High Dimensions
papers.abstract: We determine the sharp dimensional dependence of the asymptotic approximation error for the Euclidean unit ball $B_2^d\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ by polytopes with a prescribed number of vertices in the relative symmetric difference metric. Specifically, we prove that $$\lim_{N\to\infty}N^{2/(d-1)}\inf_{P\in P_d(N)}\frac{\operatorname{vol}_d(P\triangle B_2^d)}{\operatorname{vol}_d(B_2^d)}=\Theta(d^{-1/2}),$$ where $P_d(N)$ consists of polytopes with at most $N$ vertices and no containment restriction. Equivalently, the classical Laguerre-Delone triangulation numbers satisfy $\operatorname{ldel}_{d-1}=\Theta(d^{-1/2})$. This improves the lower bound $\Omega(d^{-1})$ of B\"or\"oczky (2000) and the upper bound $O(1)$ of Ludwig, Sch\"utt and Werner (2006). In contrast, the corresponding asymptotic coefficient for approximation with a prescribed number of facets has order one, as shown by Kur (2020). We also establish non-asymptotic bounds showing that, for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, the ball admits an $\varepsilon$-approximation with at most $\exp(C(\varepsilon)\sqrt d)$ vertices, whereas approximating the hypercube to the same accuracy requires at least $\exp(c(\varepsilon)d)$ vertices. Consequently, the ball does not maximize the optimal relative approximation error among convex bodies, even up to an absolute multiplicative constant at the same vertex budget. Thus Macbeath's theorem (1951) on the extremality of the ball for inscribed approximation does not extend to polytopes in arbitrary position.

papers.title: Attack logics, not outputs: Concept-based Property Attacks for Shortcut Elimination in Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (NNs) for computer vision are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, such that minuscule malicious changes to inputs may induce unintuitive outputs. One key approach to verify and mitigate such robustness issues is to falsify expected output behavior, which enables local robustness guarantees and adversarial training. Due to the black-box nature of NNs, current attacks only falsify a class of the final output, such as flipping from $\text{\texttt{stop_sign}}$ to $\neg \text{\texttt{stop_sign}}$. In this work we argue that robustness analysis should focus more generally on logical inconsistencies in concept-level reasoning rather than solely on output misclassification. We formalize this perspective through concept-based properties, i.e., constraints over human-interpretable concepts such as $\text{\texttt{red}} \land \text{\texttt{octogonal}} \implies \text{\texttt{stop_sign}}$ and study the falsification of such properties as a principled form of adversarial attack. Furthermore, an implementation of concept-based properties on already trained NNs is proposed using techniques from concept-based explainable artificial intelligence (C-XAI). For that we formally prove that attacks on concept-based properties are expected to have a reduced search space compared to simple class falsification, whilst arguably be more aligned with intuitive robustness targets. The practical effectiveness of our approach for logically informed adversarial training is shown in an empirical study across multiple models and datasets, including both vision and a security-relevant code processing task. Our results demonstrate that concept-level falsification generalizes classical adversarial attacks: Retraining on our novel attacks maintains robustness gains as compared to classical adversarial retraining whilst better eliminating semantic biases.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Monocular Depth Estimation for Visual Perception in Lower-Limb Prostheses
papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation has advanced rapidly with the development of foundation models that demonstrate strong zero-shot generalisation across diverse visual domains. However, the applicability of these models to visual perception for lower-limb prosthetics remains largely unexplored. Reliable depth perception is particularly important for prosthesis users, who often experience significant challenges when navigating stairs, uneven terrain, and other complex environments. To address this gap, we introduce the Lower-Limb Prosthesis (LP) dataset, a benchmark designed to evaluate depth perception from an emulated knee-level prosthetic viewpoint. Using this dataset, we evaluate four state-of-the-art monocular depth estimation foundation models. Our results provide the first systematic benchmark of monocular depth estimation performance from a prosthetic viewpoint, while highlighting both the challenges and the potential of deploying foundation models in prosthetic perception systems. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Ishivijay/lp_dataset.

papers.intro:
Visual perception is fundamental to autonomous navigation and environmental understanding. In the context of medical prosthetics, the ability to accurately perceive and interpret the surrounding environment is critical for safe and effective device operation. However, current lower-limb prostheses lack robust perceptual capabilities, leaving users at significantly increased risk of falls, particularly when navigating stairs, uneven terrain, and cluttered environments [1]. Integrating reliable depth perception into prosthetic systems could enable real-time hazard detection, adaptive gait planning, and enhanced environmental awareness. By improving the ability to navigate complex environments safely, such capabilities could reduce fall risk, enhance mobility, and increase user confidence in daily activities.

By improving the ability to navigate complex environments safely, such capabilities could reduce fall risk, enhance mobility, and increase user confidence in daily activities.

Computer vision approaches are increasingly being integrated into lower-limb wearable robotics to provide active environmental awareness. In lower-limb prosthetics, vision-in-the-loop control using gaze-tracking cues can be used to identify user intention and anticipate terrain transitions, providing volitional control of active knee-ankle prostheses [2]. Visual-inertial odometry can be combined with 3D terrain reconstruction to classify locomotion [3]. Similarly, depth-aware pose estimation has also been integrated into lower-limb exoskeleton systems to enable real-time gait analysis and prevent asymmetric locomotion and falls [4], as well as to facilitate gesture-driven control interfaces leveraging monocular depth features [5]. While these approaches demonstrate the value of vision, they generally rely on task-specific training, custom multicamera setups, or cooperative rehabilitation environments.

While prior datasets have captured egocentric or wearable camera images of locomotion environments, they focus mainly on RGB-based scene classification or activity recognition and do not provide paired ground-truth depth annotations. Existing depth estimation benchmarks, on the other hand, target indoor scenes NYUv2 [11], ScanNet [12], or autonomous driving KITTI [13], none of which reflect the specific viewing angle, motion patterns, and close-range stair navigation experienced by a prosthesis user. To our knowledge, no existing dataset provides paired RGB-depth data recorded from a lower-limb-mounted camera during locomotion, capturing the perspective of a lower-limb prosthesis.

The dataset covers a variety of scene elements, including staircases, corridors, landings, and doorways, all captured from an emulated knee-level prosthetic viewpoint during locomotion.

papers.title: Compression of Vision Foundation Models for Retinal OCT via Growing-Neural-Gas Codebooks and Graph-Guided Masked Image Modeling
papers.abstract: Vision foundation models for retinal imaging are large and computationally demanding, limiting point-of-care deployment. We ask how much of such a model's downstream utility survives compression into a smaller network. We propose a topology-aware discretization framework that distills a continuous foundation model into a discrete codebook, then uses it as the reconstruction target for masked image modeling (MIM). It combines gradient-free codebook learning via Growing Neural Gas, which yields an adjacency graph over the codes, with a graph-distance soft cross-entropy loss that replaces one-hot MIM targets with topologically graded supervision. With student pretraining on 383 public Duke iAMD optical coherence tomography (OCT) volumes, the pipeline distills an 86M-parameter teacher into a 22M-parameter student with at least 3.6x fewer FLOPs. The student performs close to, and in some settings above, its teacher across three classification and two segmentation benchmarks, with the magnitude and direction of the difference depending on the teacher, task, metric, and student capacity. On the external OLIVES benchmark, it surpasses its MIRAGE teacher on every metric (98.06% vs. 95.22% balanced accuracy). It works with two Vision Transformer (ViT-Base) teachers, retinal (MIRAGE) and natural-image (DINOv3); with the out-of-domain teacher, the student outperforms it on retinal-layer segmentation, indicating that the added value of retina-specific pretraining is task-dependent: largest for segmentation, while a general-domain teacher is competitive for classification. These results yield compact retinal models potentially suitable for deployment, transferring across OCT datasets, devices, and clinical tasks, including three datasets not used in the student's pretraining.

papers.intro:
Retinal diseases including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic macular edema (DME), and choroidal neovascularization (CNV) impose a major and growing clinical burden worldwide, driven by population aging and the diabetes epidemic, and represent leading causes of vision impairment and blindness (Wong et al., 2014). Optical coherence tomography (OCT) has become the indispensable workhorse imaging modality for screening, diagnosis, and longitudinal monitoring of these conditions, delivering high-resolution, non-invasive cross-sectional visualization of retinal microstructure that directly informs anti-VEGF treatment decisions and disease activity assessment (Flaxel et al., 2020). Deep learning has become integral to automated OCT interpretation, yet conventional supervised approaches remain constrained by the scarcity of large, expert-annotated retinal datasets, motivating a shift toward self-supervised pretraining that learns directly from unlabeled scans (Morano et al., 2025). Within this paradigm, Vision Transformer-based foundation models—including the general-domain DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) and retina-specific models such as RETFound (Zhou et al., 2023), VisionFM (Qiu et al., 2024), EyeCLIP (Shi et al., 2025), and MIRAGE (Morano et al., 2025)—have demonstrated that large-scale self-supervised pretraining yields transferable representations that consistently outperform models trained from scratch or pretrained on ImageNet across diagnostic and prognostic retinal tasks. A single such backbone can deliver strong performance across both classification and segmentation of OCT images, making vision foundation models an increasingly attractive basis for retinal image analysis.

Despite this promise, the foundation models driving these gains are typically large, GPU-intensive architectures, and their substantial computational and infrastructure requirements remain a major obstacle to real-time deployment on portable devices or in resource-constrained clinical settings (Jin et al., 2026; Chia et al., 2024). Compounding this barrier, building a foundation model with broad generalizability typically demands pretraining on large, heterogeneous datasets pooled across institutions and imaging devices, a scale of data acquisition and curation that is logistically and financially prohibitive for most individual research groups or clinical centers (Chia et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2026). A natural avenue to sidestep the data constraint is masked image modeling (MIM), a self-supervised paradigm that eliminates the need for labeled data and, in principle, allows pretraining on more modest unlabeled datasets. Pixel-level MIM approaches reconstruct raw image patches from masked inputs, an objective that is easy to optimize but biases the encoder toward low-level texture statistics rather than high-level semantic features (He et al., 2022). Lifting the reconstruction target to the semantic level — by predicting discrete visual tokens produced by a vector-quantized tokenizer rather than raw pixels — was proposed as a remedy (Bao et al., 2022; Ramesh et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2023); yet standard vector quantization imposes no relational structure among learned tokens, and the one-hot MIM target treats every incorrect code as equally wrong. Crucially, both MIM generations were developed for large, GPU-intensive encoders, and neither was designed to transfer the semantic knowledge embedded in those models into a lightweight backbone suitable for point-of-care inference. Distillation into compact Vision Transformers has been studied on natural images, for example by DeiT, which transfers a teacher’s class predictions through a dedicated distillation token during supervised ImageNet training (Touvron et al., 2021), and by TinyMIM, which transfers token relations from larger MIM-pretrained ViTs to smaller ones on ImageNet (Ren et al., 2023). Both were developed on large natural-image corpora with labels or continuous targets; they do not consider distillation from a foundation model through graph-structured discrete targets on a small, unlabeled in-domain medical cohort.

papers.title: Dynamics of two-dimensional Bose gases in the focusing case
papers.abstract: We prove the propagation of Bose--Einstein condensation and a norm approximation for the dynamics of a Bose gas with localized initial data in two dimensions with singular interactions that may have a small attractive part. We allow the scaling of the interaction to be any polynomial scaling $N^\beta$ for $0<\beta<\infty$ and even exponential scaling $e^{N^\kappa}$ for $0<\kappa<1/4$. Our approach covers external potentials that are time-dependent, at most quadratic, and bounded below, including the situation without an external potential.

papers.title: Grounding on Request: Learning Modality Control in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: When an image and its caption disagree, can a user reliably control which one a vision-language model (VLM) follows? Accuracy alone cannot answer this question, since a model might give the correct answer from parametric knowledge without following the requested evidence. We therefore evaluate modality grounding control through conflict-preserving counterfactual interventions. Specifically, Flip measures whether an initially correct answer follows an edit to the requested modality, while Stay measures whether it remains stable when the competing modality is edited. To learn this control, we build on neologism learning by introducing new words for visual and textual grounding, training only their embeddings while keeping the pretrained model fixed. We also introduce Counterfactual Twin-Margin (CTM) supervision, which uses paired interventions to teach how answer probabilities should change when the requested evidence changes. Across three VLMs on three existing benchmarks and our multi-attribute Ground-CF benchmark, we find that learned modality words improve control over natural-language instructions. Surprisingly, a single learned embedding per modality provides strong lightweight visual control and shows little average degradation on held-out values. LoRA remains strongest overall, although its visual advantage narrows under held-out evaluation. Moreover, counterfactual supervision improves control in several settings where standard supervision is weaker. Finally, we test our method on real-world news video and find that visual control improves when the relevant evidence is made easier to access. Overall, our results show that reliable modality control requires testing not only whether an answer is correct, but whether it continues to follow edits to the modality of choice.

Vision-language models increasingly receive several modalities at the same time, including images, videos, and accompanying text (Bordes et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2026; Sanders et al., 2024; Sanders et al., 2023). Often these sources agree, but what should happen when these modalities do not? In settings with cross-modal conflict Zhang et al. (2025); Zhu et al. In practice, however, VLMs can exhibit modality dominance, favoring one modality (often text) even when explicitly asked to use another (Ghatkesar et al., 2025; Hua et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2025). Previous work has therefore focused largely on either strengthening visual grounding or reducing the influence of dominant textual information (Ghatkesar et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2025). Rather than pushing the model permanently toward one modality, we seek to understand how we can allow the user to choose either modality on demand.

papers.title: Style over Substance? Linguistic Bias in LLM-based Peer Review Copy title
papers.abstract: The number of paper submissions to major AI conferences has increased dramatically in recent years, substantially increasing the peer-review workload of researchers. At the same time, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support peer review, both by individual reviewers and by conference organizations. While LLM capabilities have improved considerably, their evaluations may be influenced by linguistic characteristics that are unrelated to scientific content. In this work, we introduce a controlled experimental framework for studying such effects by systematically perturbing the linguistic style of research papers. Specifically, we rewrite papers to exhibit (i) linguistic features associated with native or non-native English writing, and (ii) high- or low-confidence linguistic features. To construct these interventions, we derive fine-grained rewriting instructions grounded in the linguistic literature and apply them using LLMs. Crucially, our interventions are designed to preserve the underlying scientific content. We then evaluate the resulting papers using different LLM reviewers. Our experiments expose a critical vulnerability in LLM-based peer review: reviewers systematically reward confident rhetoric independent of scientific content, raising serious concerns about the robustness of their assessments.

papers.intro:
The peer-review process is an integral part of scientific publishing, but also requires substantial time and effort from researchers. This challenge has become increasingly pronounced with the growing number of submissions to major AI conferences. In parallel, recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have opened up new opportunities to automate or support parts of the reviewing process (Jin et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025; Dycke and Gurevych, 2026). Individual reviewers use LLMs to assist with the review process, while LLMs are also increasingly seen as systematic tools for generating or supporting peer review (Demetrio et al., 2025; Baumann et al., 2026).

This challenge has become increasingly pronounced with the growing number of submissions to major AI conferences. In parallel, recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have opened up new opportunities to automate or support parts of the reviewing process (Jin et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025; Dycke and Gurevych, 2026). Individual reviewers use LLMs to assist with the review process, while LLMs are also increasingly seen as systematic tools for generating or supporting peer review (Demetrio et al., 2025; Baumann et al., 2026).

However, the use of LLMs for peer review also introduces new risks. LLM judgments can be influenced by properties that are unrelated to the actual quality of the evaluated content. Prior work on LLM-as-a-judge has, for example, demonstrated biases related to the position of an answer or preferences towards outputs of the same LLM family (Liu et al., 2024; Wataoka et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025). Similar concerns have been identified specifically for LLM-based peer review as well. LLM reviewers can be susceptible to adversarial modifications of papers (Lin et al., 2025), fail to reliably identify faulty scientific reasoning (Dycke and Gurevych, 2026), and exhibit biases based on author-related information such as affiliation, seniority, or publication history (Vasu et al., 2026). Moreover, recent results suggest that even paraphrasing or stylistic properties of a paper can substantially affect LLM-generated review scores (Kaneko, 2026; Kousha and Thelwall, 2026; Baumann et al., 2026). These findings raise the central question of our paper: ”How do we systematically measure whether LLM reviewers judge the research quality, rather than the linguistic style with which the research content is presented?”

Researchers have different linguistic backgrounds, and previous work has already found evidence that language proficiency and writing style can influence human peer review (Politzer-Ahles et al., 2020; Saposnik et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2006; Sayegh et al., 2024). Motivated by these human studies, we focus on two complementary dimensions that together signal epistemic authority: (i) the language proficiency reflected in the writing, and (ii) the confidence with which the research is presented. Language proficiency can signal author credibility (Lev-Ari and Keysar, 2010), while confident linguistic framing can influence the perceived scientific credibility (Teigen, 2023). Both dimensions are well characterized in the linguistic literature (Hinkel, 2002; Hyland, 1996), and should not substantially affect the assessment of the underlying research quality.

To this end, we integrate an automated annotation procedure for identifying positive and negative aspects in reviews (Lu et al., 2025).

We therefore propose a controlled framework for perturbing a research paper along a specific linguistic dimension, while preserving its underlying research content. Specifically, we rewrite papers to exhibit (i) linguistic characteristics associated with native or non-native English writing, and (ii) high-confidence- or low-confidence linguistic characteristics. Our experiments reveal that the two linguistic dimensions affect LLM reviewers differently. Across models, expressed confidence has a strong and consistent effect on evaluation even though the underlying scientific content remains unchanged. In contrast, differences between native- and non-native associated writing are substantially smaller and more model-dependent. More importantly, our controlled rewriting framework provides a practical way to stress-test LLM reviewers by varying specific linguistic cues and measuring when these changes alter review outcomes. papers.title: A Robust, Explainable, and Efficient Deep Metric for Speech and General Audio Quality
papers.abstract: We present a robust Speech and Audio Quality Metric (SAQM) that merges features of traditional quality metrics with a CNN trained on a large amount of data using contrastive learning methods. To overcome the problem of limited amounts of human-labeled training data, we propose two pretraining strategies relying on pseudo-labels. One uses an established objective metric PEAQ-2f (based on ITU-R BS.1387) as surrogate loss, the other is based on contrasting a wide range of coding modes by a rule-of-thumb ordering based on expected perceived quality. As a key novelty, our approach lets us generate saliency maps by propagating gradients to identify which feature has the greatest impact on the final metric outcome and enables our system to provide insights regarding the type and extent of distortions present in the tested audio signal. The resulting (SAQM) operates at low computational complexity, performs comparably to (SOTA) metrics on speech while still performing well on general audio content.

In this work, we present the design of a robust SAQM (SAQM) for monitoring perceived quality of coded audio content with explainable model predictions. State-of-the-art systems can be distinguished into first, established methods that built upon hand-crafted, intricate rule-based features that are perceptually motivated [5, 20] and second, systems that build upon DNN like audio foundation models [32, 33, 9]. Systems falling into the first category exhibit strong correlation to subjective ratings for specific degradations caused by processes such as perceptual coding, speech enhancement or blind-source separation [5, 20, 1]. However, these traditional models often show low performance and struggle with reliability when evaluating modern or complex impairments, including additive noise, reverberation, or bandwidth-extended (BWE) speech and music [34, 12, 2].

papers.title: Concurrent Task Orchestration: Hierarchical Trusted Collaborator Group Formation for Constrained Resource Allocation
papers.abstract: Effective collaboration among resource-constrained mobile intelligent machines, such as Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), is essential for the completion of complex tasks. However, concurrent task demands, limited distributed resources, and dynamic collaborator availabilities make it challenging to satisfy task-specific completion goals in diverse collaborative systems. To address these challenges simultaneously, we propose a new framework of trusted collaborator group formation and the supporting resource allocation strategy for concurrent task orchestration. Specifically, a collaborative task is decomposed into subtasks subject to dynamic resource availability and inter-subtask dependencies. A task utility model is developed for collaborator group evaluation support subtask allocation according to task completion goals and unified value-risk analysis. Based on this model, concurrent task orchestration is formulated as a long-term utility maximization problem under $\alpha$-fairness. To solve the problem efficiently, we develop a hierarchical matching strategy that first clusters tasks and collaborators into coarse-grained sets and subsequently performs fine-grained collaborator group formation and task allocation within matched sets. Task-specific trust is predicted through spatial-temporal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and embedded into a fairness-aware Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework to continuously update the matching policies. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed strategy improves concurrent task completion performance by 22% over representative baselines under resource constraints.
papers.intro:
Empowered by the rapid convergence of inherent communication and computing technologies, future wireless networks will support a plethora of applications, including smart manufacturing and intelligent transportation systems, which involve increasingly complex collaborative tasks such as multi-robot assembly or vehicle platoon control [1]. Amidst the expeditious technological evolution, limited resources available at each device and growing heterogeneity among tasks necessitate intelligent and reliable collaboration among connected machines for effective task completion [2]. For instance, a group of connected intelligent machines (e.g., Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs)) with computing resources and communication capabilities, could be selected to handle tasks delegated from other resource-constrained intelligent machines (e.g., Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs)) [3]. However, selecting suitable collaborator groups is difficult due to intricate requirements for capability and reliability.

Given the heterogeneity and complexity of future collaborative systems, achieving efficient concurrent task orchestration through effective collaboration among intelligent machines under stringent resource constraints can be extremely challenging. This challenge primarily stems from the trade-off between meeting diverse requirements of concurrent tasks, possibility of involving different groups of collaborators for one same task, and drastically increased complexity to optimize overall system efficiency under fairness considerations.

This challenge primarily stems from the trade-off between meeting diverse requirements of concurrent tasks, possibility of involving different groups of collaborators for one same task, and drastically increased complexity to optimize overall system efficiency under fairness considerations.

From the perspective of an individual task execution, both the task decomposition into subtasks and the selection of a group of collaborators jointly entail task completion value and risks. On the one hand, task completion value is fulfilled through meeting diverse task completion goals such as latency and energy consumption requirements [4], thus imposing intricate criteria on how tasks are decomposed and collaborator groups are selected. Proper task decomposition supports fine-grained collaboration and aligns subtask-level completion goals with available resources. However, when task completion goals are ambiguously defined and trade-offs between competing goals are improperly balanced, the effectiveness of best-effort strategies such as Quality-of-Service (QoS)-based task offloading is significantly reduced [5]. Moreover, attacks launched by malicious machines, such as illegitimate collaborators [6] or eavesdroppers [7], further degrade task completion value. On the other hand, dynamic task requirements and varying collaborator conditions introduce significant uncertainty for collaborator group formation and task allocation, thus increasing risks for task completion [8]. While some existing approaches such as heuristic-based task offloading select suitable collaborator groups, they often rely on static and complete system information [9, 10], making them ineffective in highly dynamic scenarios.

On the other hand, dynamic task requirements and varying collaborator conditions introduce significant uncertainty for collaborator group formation and task allocation, thus increasing risks for task completion [8]. While some existing approaches such as heuristic-based task offloading select suitable collaborator groups, they often rely on static and complete system information [9, 10], making them ineffective in highly dynamic scenarios.

From the perspective of system orchestration, sharing limited resources of all collaborators among concurrent tasks remains a major challenge in guaranteeing the task completion value and tolerable risks for each task. Specifically, diverse task requirements induce increased dynamics in resource requirements, thereby intensifying uncertain contention among concurrent tasks for limited resources. This uncertainty in resource contention is eventually translated into unpredictable task completion outcomes and value. Thus, effective orchestration of concurrent tasks is needed to allocate limited resources across all completing tasks, aiming to maximize the collective task completion value and minimize associated risks simultaneously. Existing strategies typically formulate concurrent task orchestration as an optimization problem aiming to maximize the cumulative utilities of all concurrent tasks [11]. However, such objectives may lead to disproportionate outcomes, where some tasks could dominate allocated resources while others are persistently underserved. While short-term fairness is often unattainable under resource constraints, enforcing long-term fairness, i.e., fair task allocation over time, is essential to prevent persistent resource monopolization.

Task-specific trust serves as a goal-achieving mechanism to direct the selection of reliable collaborators aligned with diverse completion goals of tasks [12]. We extend this concept from a single collaborator evaluation to a group evaluation, ensuring collective capability and reliability of collaborator groups in meeting the global requirements of tasks. Machine Learning (ML) supports adaptive collaborator group selection in dynamic environments by learning complex relationships between task requirements and collaborator conditions [13]. Among ML algorithms, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) particularly supports sequential decision-making under complexity and dynamics, making it well-suited for optimizing long-term outcomes [14, 15]. Thus, the integration of task-specific trust and DRL facilitates the automatic formation and matching of reliable collaborator groups aligned with evolving task goals. However, while DRL performs well under fully observable environments, partial observability of system states complicates such integration. Moreover, DRL typically maximizes long-term rewards, i.e., the cumulative utilities of all tasks [16], without considering long-term fairness, leading to imbalanced resource allocation among tasks. In addition, DRL model training in large-scale systems often becomes time-consuming and suffers from slow convergence [17, 3].

papers.title: Spectral localizer for unbounded topological Hamiltonians
papers.abstract: In a series of joint papers with Loring, it was shown how index parings of $K$-theory classes with Fredholm modules can be computed as the half-signature of a suitably constructed finite-dimensional matrix, called the spectral localizer. After offering a novel perspective on earlier results, it is shown how the framework can be extended to unbounded gapped Hamiltonians given as second-order linear differential operators (in particular, matrix-valued Schr\"odinger and regularized Dirac operators). Important insights are the coercive phase space localization and discretizations by means of wavelets.

papers.title: Online Discrepancy of Sparse Random Vectors over Long Horizons
papers.abstract:
We study online vector balancing for independent sparse random vectors: each arrival is supported on a uniformly random set of $s$ of the $n$ coordinates, with nonzero entries equal to one (binary model) or independent random signs (signed model), and an online algorithm must sign each vector upon arrival. The prefix discrepancy is the largest $\ell_\infty$-norm of the signed sums up to the horizon $T$, the terminal discrepancy that of the sum at time $T$. For binary inputs with $2\le s\le n/2$ and $T=\Theta(n)$, Altschuler and Tikhomirov showed that both are of order $\sqrt{s}+\log\log n$; they asked how the prefix discrepancy depends on the horizon and whether a matching terminal bound holds at every prescribed time.
  Over long horizons, the two differ. For every fixed $s\ge2$ and $c>0$, every online algorithm, even a randomized one that knows the horizon, incurs with high probability prefix discrepancy $\Omega(\log\log n+(\log T/\log n)^{\alpha_s})$ for $n\le T\le e^{cn}$, where $\alpha_s=(2^{s-1}-1)/(2^s-1)$. For $s=2$, quadratic Greedy matches this bound; for fixed $s\ge3$, we give an online algorithm with prefix discrepancy $O(\log\log n+(\log T/\log n)^{1/2})$. In contrast, a deterministic algorithm that knows neither the horizon nor the failure probability keeps the terminal discrepancy $O_k(\sqrt{s}+\log\log n)$ at each prescribed time, with failure probability $n^{-k}$ for every fixed $k$, for $2\le s\le n/2$ (binary model) and $2\le s\le n$ (signed model); for $s=2$, quadratic Greedy itself does so. This answers their terminal question, and the same order is optimal for prefixes at all polynomial horizons $T\ge n$.
  The lower bound uses a finite safety game realized within the input law; the upper bounds use moments of elementary symmetric polynomials and, at terminal times, a $\cosh$ potential or a translated gauge with a Foster inequality at every state.

papers.title: Revisiting entropy and entropy-related magnitudes of a symbolic sequence and their estimation
papers.abstract: This article revisits entropy and related magnitudes (entropy density, effective measure complexity, and informational distance) for the analysis of sequential data. We present their mathematical foundations within information theory and ergodic theory, establishing connections between probabilistic Shannon entropy and algorithmic Kolmogorov complexity. A central result, Zivs theorem, demonstrates the asymptotic equivalence between the normalised number of distinct words and entropy density, providing the theoretical basis for estimation via Lempel-Ziv factorisation. We examine the convergence properties of these magnitudes and introduce estimation procedures for finite sequences, including a method for the effective measure complexity and the transfer entropy rate. An open-source software library implementing parallel algorithms for efficient Lempel-Ziv factorisation is presented. The practical utility of the framework is illustrated through three case studies: functional brain connectivity analysis from fMRI data, characterisation of spatiotemporal dynamics in coupled nonlinear oscillators, and electrocardiogram-based classification of atrial fibrillation, demonstrating how entropic measures capture meaningful structural and dynamical properties across diverse domains.

papers.intro:
Data from complex dynamical systems often appear as one or a few time series, from which the system’s dynamics must be extracted [1]. In data analysis, the usual aims are to assess regularity versus randomness, to identify patterns, to discover governing laws, or to predict future system behaviour [2]. One useful approach is to treat the dynamical system as an information source and apply information-theoretic tools alongside statistical descriptions [3]. In general, a single or just a few data sets are insufficient to fully understand the underlying dynamical system that drives the information source, yet these are often the only available data. In such cases, assuming ergodicity becomes necessary to extract the relevant information from the data [4].

In general, a single or just a few data sets are insufficient to fully understand the underlying dynamical system that drives the information source, yet these are often the only available data. In such cases, assuming ergodicity becomes necessary to extract the relevant information from the data [4].

For most systems, a fundamental quest is to find the relation between randomness and pattern in the system signal [5]. Randomness can be considered noise or, in a more useful perspective, the intrinsic uncertainty of the system, while a pattern is related to the deterministic laws that govern the system’s behaviour. It has been argued that for a complex dynamical system, the behaviour lies between complete predictability and total randomness [5]. Entropy density captures the irreducible unpredictability in a signal. Entropy density, also known as Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy, entropy rate, among other names, has been defined in several fields, including information theory, ergodic theory, and dynamical systems [3, 6]. A lesser-used measure of complexity is the effective measure of complexity, introduced by Grassberger [4], which aims to capture a system’s intrinsic memory and, in time-series analysis, its reliance on the past to define its future. Both magnitudes can be theoretically justified by Kolmogorov’s algorithmic complexity, which laid a solid foundation for the analysis of data beyond the ensemble-statistical point of view [7]. Kolmogorov’s theory of complexity builds on the existence of a universal computational machine, as demonstrated by Turing, and on the computational theory of recurrent functions [8]. From Kolmogorov theory, several concepts emerge that are closely related to entropy density and effective measure complexity; significantly, it also allows us to define the informational distance as a measure of the distance between two data sets [9].

papers.title: Distributed Predictive Flocking for a Swarm of Miniature Vibration-Driven Robots in a Confined Arena
papers.abstract: Coordinating many miniature robots in a confined arena, with no leader, central planner, or global map, is a core challenge for swarm robotics. As the swarm grows denser, collision avoidance becomes the limiting factor, and the number of safely coexisting robots depends on the formulation of the inter-robot safety constraint. We present a distributed predictive flocking controller in which each robot solves its own nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) problem, optimizing swarm cohesion and alignment costs, inter-robot and obstacle safety, and a task objective, while exchanging only predicted trajectories with local neighbors. Within this generalized controller architecture, solved in real time, we compare six barrier and control-barrier-function (CBF) safety formulations on a digital twin of an open-source vibration-driven bristlebot in a $0.64\,\mathrm{m^2}$ arena. A look-ahead discrete-time CBF performs best overall, with the fewest collisions and the widest inter-robot margins across nearly every swarm size tested. We deploy it on phototaxis, phototactic orbiting, and cohesion without a stimulus tasks, using swarm sizes starting from ten robots and up to the geometric packing limit. The swarm holds well: collisions stay low in small swarms, rising steeply as the packing limit approaches, while coordination and cohesion degrade gently rather than collapsing. The swarm is found not to trade safety for order, keeping both across the confined arena, with local alignment high at every swarm size.

papers.intro:
Autonomous multi-robot systems are a promising approach for tasks in cluttered, inaccessible, or hazardous spaces, from confined-structure inspection to search in collapsed buildings and medical micro-robotics [1]. In these settings, many miniature robots must coordinate in proximity within a tight, bounded arena. As in natural swarms, such as flocking of starlings, schooling of fish, the crowded colonies of ants and honey bees, and even the collective migration of cells, robust group behavior emerges from purely local interactions among simple agents [2, 3, 4], with no central control [1]. Miniaturization, however, tightly bounds onboard compute, memory, and power [5], demanding control that is theoretically principled yet computationally light. Moreover, when the arena is fixed, a growing number of robots increases the density of the swarm and hinders smooth motion. When it is also cluttered with obstacles, coordination is even harder. In this scenario, collision avoidance becomes the central challenge.

Miniaturization, however, tightly bounds onboard compute, memory, and power [5], demanding control that is theoretically principled yet computationally light. Moreover, when the arena is fixed, a growing number of robots increases the density of the swarm and hinders smooth motion. When it is also cluttered with obstacles, coordination is even harder. In this scenario, collision avoidance becomes the central challenge.

The standard way to coordinate such a swarm from purely local interactions is Reynolds’ boid model [6, 7], which reduces collective motion to three local rules (cohesion, alignment, and separation) that produce coherent group motion without global information [8]. Early control laws formalized these as artificial potential fields over a communication graph [9, 10], and reactive velocity-matching rules scale to tens of drones [11]. Such reactive methods, however, offer no predictive horizon, no formal safety guarantee under nonlinear dynamics, and no systematic handling of kinodynamic limits. These shortcomings are especially severe in confined, high-density settings, where many underactuated robots have little room to recover from unsafe motions.

Model predictive control (MPC) [12] addresses these limitations. For the nonlinear dynamics of mobile robots, this takes the form of nonlinear MPC (NMPC). It solves a finite-horizon optimal control problem (OCP) online, which provides closed-loop feedback, constraint satisfaction, and explicit multi-objective trade-offs. Distributed MPC (DMPC) extends this to a swarm by splitting the global problem into per-agent OCPs coupled through shared constraints [13, 14, 15, 16]. Solvers such as the Sequential Quadratic Programming real-time iteration (SQP-RTI) [17] solve each per-agent OCP in real time. Similarly, optimization-based swarm planners achieve strong real-world navigation [18, 19, 20, 21]. These methods are mainly developed for point-to-point navigation [14, 22], with collision avoidance typically encoded as geometric constraints such as separating hyperplanes or safe corridors.

The closest works embed Reynolds behaviors in NMPC. They have been demonstrated on up to 16 quadrotors [23, 24], leader-follower teams [25, 26, 27], and fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) [28]. Most share one regime. They assume sparse flight in large 3D airspace, with the swarm migrating toward a shared goal. Even when several obstacles are present, they remain sparse relative to the available space, keeping the environment effectively low-density. Few address the opposite regime that we target, where many underactuated robots coordinate at high density in a fixed, confined, and cluttered arena under a task objective such as following a light gradient. Here, the inter-robot safety formulation, not free-space planning, governs how many robots can coexist. Each of these works, however, fixes a single safety formulation in advance, usually a distance constraint or a penalty. It remains open which formulation fits the most robots into a fixed arena with minimal collisions.

The closest works embed Reynolds behaviors in NMPC. They have been demonstrated on up to 16 quadrotors [23, 24], leader-follower teams [25, 26, 27], and fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) [28]. Most share one regime. They assume sparse flight in large 3D airspace, with the swarm migrating toward a shared goal. Even when several obstacles are present, they remain sparse relative to the available space, keeping the environment effectively low-density. Few address the opposite regime that we target, where many underactuated robots coordinate at high density in a fixed, confined, and cluttered arena under a task objective such as following a light gradient.
