Each of these works, however, fixes a single safety formulation in advance, usually a distance constraint or a penalty. It remains open which formulation fits the most robots into a fixed arena with minimal collisions.

Safety formulations differ in how collision avoidance is encoded as a constraint in the OCP. Such a constraint is classically formulated using a barrier function h⁡(x)h(x) whose safe set 𝒮={x∣h⁡(x)≥0}\mathcal{S}=\{x\mid h(x)\geq 0\} is kept forward invariant to certify safety [29], typically imposed as a hard [30] or soft [31] distance constraint. A Control Barrier Function (CBF) [29] relaxes this strict boundary condition by allowing h⁡(x)h(x) to decrease at a rate bounded by a class-𝒦\mathcal{K} function, and its discrete-time form (Dt-CBF) [32] imposes this at each MPC stage. Zeng et al. [33] enforces it as a hard constraint, which is often infeasible. Feasibility is restored by softening the decay with slack variables [34, 35, 36], adding terminal barrier terms [37, 38], or anchoring a soft CBF with one hard step [39]. Beyond feasibility, when the constraint has relative degree greater than one, as for a distance constraint under unicycle dynamics, a higher-order CBF (HOCBF) [40, 41] chains the barrier conditions. Lu et al. [39] compare a distance-constraint MPC, a hard discrete-time CBF, a slacked CBF, and their combination on a common footing, but for a single robot. In the multi-robot setting, safety is enforced by reactive schemes [42, 43], by post-hoc CBF-QP (quadratic program) filters [44], or by a CBF inside a decentralized MPC with neighbors as predicted trajectories [45, 46, 47, 48]. A formulation’s collision performance, however, likely changes with the swarm density. A comparison across densities is required to find the best one.

papers.title: Multiscale MIGHT: Modeling Local and Systemic Particle Transport in the Cardiovascular System
papers.abstract: Analytical models of signaling molecule (SM) transport in the cardiovascular system (CVS) force a choice between whole-body scope and vessel-level resolution: Pharmacokinetic models for systemic transport lump each organ and lack small-scale structure, whereas synthetic molecular communication (MC) channel models resolve branched vessel networks (VNs) only for a single pass or capture recirculation only in topologically simple loops, and only partially include SM degradation. To close this gap, we propose Multiscale MIGHT, an extension of the Mixture of Inverse Gaussians for Hemodynamic Transport (MIGHT) model that jointly captures branched topologies, closed-loop circulation, organ clearance, and chemical degradation of SMs. First, we connect the ends of a branched VN to form a closed loop with local and global SM degradation, model the closed-loop channel impulse response for arbitrary transmitter (Tx) and receiver (Rx) positions as a Laplace-domain feedback system, and approximate it in closed form by an inverse Gaussian mixture over multi-pass trajectories. The model is validated against finite-element simulations in COMSOL. Second, we set up a whole-body model, where an exemplary local VN, resolved at vessel-level detail, is embedded into the remaining systemic circulation, represented by lumped organ blocks. We simulate whole-body SM transport for various Tx sites and SM species. Our results show that, at an Rx in a local VN, only the initial pass produces a distinct peak in the SM concentration, significantly shaped by the local vasculature in case of small Tx-Rx distances; subsequent passes arrive strongly dispersed and are shaped almost entirely by organ clearance and chemical degradation rather than by the local VN topology.

papers.intro:
The CVS distributes oxygen, nutrients, hormones, other endogenous SM, and administered drugs throughout the body and is thus the primary domain for diagnostic and therapeutic in-body MC applications. Designing such applications requires analytical models of SM transport in the CVS. However, to date, no such model jointly captures the three properties that arguably shape this transport most strongly: (P1) Branched topology: The CVS is a complex VN with many parallel paths, so SM reach an observation site along paths with widely differing travel times [1]. (P2) Closed loop: SM recirculate, possibly along different paths in successive circulations [1]. (P3) Degradation: SM are cleared locally by organs, e.g., liver and kidneys [2], and degraded globally, e.g., by enzymatic cleavage.

papers.title: Multimodal Concert Video Editing: System Design and Exploratory Evaluation
papers.abstract: Editing multi-camera concerts requires coordinated decisions about musical relevance, visual quality and cut timing. We present a modular framework that combines instrument activity from multitrack audio, visible instruments and image sharpness with beat-based timing and probabilistic camera selection. An interpretable scoring model links these components to the choice of views over complete shot intervals. Component tests and an exploratory expert study on a four-camera concert yield mixed assessments across the editing variants. The findings motivate extending local audiovisual relevance with contextual and sequence-level criteria. The architecture provides a basis for testing these extensions and studying how component behaviour affects the quality of complete edits.

papers.intro:
Multi-camera concert editing requires deciding when to cut and which view to show. Editors coordinate musical activity, image quality, framing and the progression of a sequence. A clear view of an active instrument can be useful, but so can a reaction or an interaction elsewhere in the ensemble. Automating this workflow therefore requires more than ranking isolated images.

Automatic camera management has been studied in lecture environments [9], concert mashups [15] and social-camera footage [1]. Concert-directing systems combine auditory and visual instrument information [17]; learned approaches address next-view selection and cut prediction [8, 6]. Temporal and candidate-view context are also modelled in multi-camera editing [12, 2], while theatre systems combine camera selection and shot-size control [16].

Named audio stems provide instrument activity and roles; visual detections describe instrument visibility, and image-gradient statistics characterise sharpness. An explicit utility combines these signals, aggregates them over a prospective shot interval and controls a probabilistic camera selector. Beat and tempo estimates determine candidate cut boundaries independently of view selection.

papers.title: Affine-invariant Cubic Newton with Weak Learners
papers.abstract: Modern gradient boosting algorithms are based on Newton's method, which excels empirically but lacks global convergence guarantees. While recent work on Gradient-Regularized Newton (GRN) boosting achieved a global $\mathcal{O}(1/\gamma^{12}k^2)$ rate, its analysis was not able to exploit the natural Hessian geometry and suffers from a heavy $\gamma^{12}$ dependence on a worst-case `weak gradient edge' $\gamma$. In this paper, we tackle these theoretical drawbacks by generalizing the Affine-Invariant Cubic Newton (AICN) scheme to convex optimization with weak learners. Our analysis is based on average cosine values $\overline{\Theta}_k$ along the optimization path and directional improvements $\delta_k$ in the Hessian-induced norm. We show that the weak-AICN update reduces to a damped weak-Newton step with an explicit stepsize determined by $\delta_k$. Under semi-strong self-concordance, we establish a global $\mathcal{O}(1/\overline{\Theta}_k^4 k^2)$ rate, significantly improving upon the weak-GRN bound. We further prove a local linear rate, global linear convergence for Hessian-dominated losses, cosine angle lower bounds, and present weak-AdaAICN, which adaptively tunes the cubic regularization. Finally, we demonstrate the broader applicability of this framework beyond gradient boosting by showing that Newton coordinate descent emerges naturally as a special case of optimization with weak learners.

papers.intro:
Modern gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT) libraries such as XGBoost [6], LightGBM [19], and CatBoost [35] use Newton’s method to fit leaf weights. However, theoretical understanding of Newton boosting [12, 37, 33, 42] has remained limited in comparison to first-order gradient boosting [24, 12, 4, 14, 38, 11, 7, 21, 22]. This stems from the fact that Newton’s method does not have global convergence guarantees, and can diverge when initialized far from the optimum, even for smooth, strictly convex losses [23, 17]. Recently [42] proved the first global O⁡(1/k2)O(1/k^{2}) rate for Newton boosting by extending the Gradient-Regularized Newton (GRN) [25, 9] scheme to weak learners. They did this via the Restricted Newton Descent framework [42], which poses boosting as a special case of Hilbert space convex optimization with iterates restricted to a scalable set of weak learners.

While the weak-GRN scheme successfully globalizes Newton boosting, its convergence analysis was not able to take advantage of the natural Hessian geometry of the problem. The weak-GRN bounds rely on standard Lipschitz continuity of the Hessian, and the proofs are fundamentally based on bounding the growth of Euclidean gradient norms [42]. Because of this geometric mismatch, the analysis does not depend on any prior established definition of weak learner edge or cosine angle [14, 37, 21]. Instead, [42] introduced the “weak gradient edge” γ\gamma, which measures the similarity between the exact gradient and the implied weak gradient in the Euclidean norm. This results in a severe 𝒪⁡(1/γ12​k2)\mathcal{O}(1/\gamma^{12}k^{2}) dependence in the convergence rate, rendering the bound highly pessimistic since γ\gamma can often be very small when using intentionally weak learners.

papers.title: Do Words Matter? What Text Contributes to Few and Full-Shot Vision-Language Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Vision-language anomaly detectors describe normal and abnormal appearance with text, and their gains are commonly credited to the semantic content of these descriptions. This attribution is plausible in the zero-shot setting, but few- and full-shot detectors interpose a trained visual adapter, and in that setting it has not been isolated. Changing a description changes both its meaning and its geometry, so accuracy comparisons cannot separate the two. We ask what a fixed pair of text embeddings, or anchors, contributes to such a detector: semantic content, effective scale, or joint anchor geometry. For a single anchor pair, the answer is effective scale alone. The score reads the anchors only through their difference, and a trained adapter can rotate to follow any replacement direction, leaving that direction, and with it the linguistic content, unidentifiable. We prove that replacement anchors with the same difference-vector length permit exactly the same probability maps and attainable losses. Across seven medical datasets, three vision backbones, both supervision regimes, and three adapter families, scale-matched random and orthogonal anchors track correct prompts; breaking the scale match opens a gap that restoring it closes without text. The same pattern holds in MVFA and when MadCLIP's learned prompts are replaced by a text-free learned scale. When one adapter serves many categories, the answer expands to their joint arrangement. Rotating all category axes together changes nothing, as predicted. For the tested CLIP prompts, these axes are nearly collinear, and meaning-free rotations that spread them apart improve performance on both industrial benchmarks. Even under frozen zero-shot transfer, a random anchor frame transfers as well as the prompt frame: coordinate consistency, not meaning. What these detectors read from their prompts is scale and arrangement, not semantic content.

papers.intro:
Anomaly detection asks a model to identify appearances it has rarely or never seen. Because anomalies are rare, visually diverse, and seldom labeled, the field has largely trained detectors on normal data alone, scoring a test image by how far it departs from the resulting model of normality (Roth et al., 2022; Deng & Li, 2022; Gudovskiy et al., 2022; Salehi et al., 2021); supervising anomalies directly only shifts the scarcity, since labeled anomalous examples are rarer still (Ding et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023). Such detectors carry no explicit representation of what constitutes abnormality, and must define it negatively, as departure from a reference distribution that has to be estimated exhaustively from images. The cost is a per-category fit: every new object or organ needs its own corpus of normal data, and accuracy degrades when only a handful of examples are available (Huang et al., 2022). The field typically attributes these gains to semantic factors, including anomaly semantics, language-compatible features, or vision–language alignment (Li et al., 2024; Zuo et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Shiri et al., 2025). In a training-free detector, the anchors directly define the scoring rule: no learned visual map can compensate when their coordinates change. papers.title: Scalar-Longitudinal Modes of Extended Electrodynamics in Perfectly Conducting Cavities and Trapped Modes of Divergence Cleaning
papers.abstract: In extended electrodynamics, the Lorenz condition is not imposed and $C=\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A}+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\partial\Phi/\partial t$ is a dynamical field, which adds a scalar-longitudinal (SL) family to the TE, TM and TEM modes of a cavity. With $C=0$ on the wall of a closed perfectly conducting cavity, the classical resonances remain unchanged, while the SL modes are the Dirichlet eigenmodes of the volume, with $\mathbf{B}=0$ and an electric field along $\nabla C$. In uniform cavities they share the frequencies of the TM modes that vary along the axis, and for a connected wall the fundamental remains classical. Matching at a conductor described by its constitutive laws gives $\partial C/\partial n=0$ instead and couples the scalar-bearing modes to the Maxwell field. The results belong to the $C=0$ problem, the condition that separates the sectors and the one divergence cleaning imposes. The rectangular, circular cylinder and coaxial cavities provide benchmarks, together with the damping time that gives the slowest scalar mode its fastest decay.

papers.intro:
In a perfectly conducting cavity of uniform cross-section, the classical source-free field is a superposition of transverse-electric (TE), transverse-magnetic (TM) and, on multiply connected cross-sections, transverse-electromagnetic (TEM) standing modes [1, 2, 3]. Extended electrodynamics adds a scalar-longitudinal (SL) sector by retaining the scalar that the Lorenz gauge sets to zero and allowing it to evolve as a dynamical field [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. The companion paper, Ref. [10], derives the extended system and solves it for a closed waveguide with a specified scalar wall condition. The formulation, its energy law and the wall condition at a physical conductor are those of Minotti and Modanese [9, 11]. There, the SL modes share the TM cutoffs. The present paper carries that analysis into closed cavities, treating resonances for general shapes and giving explicit solutions for uniform cavities by adding conducting end walls to the guides. Derivations that carry over unchanged are cited from the companion paper.

papers.title: Deep Scientific Reasoning under Physical Constraints: Structure-Aware Spectrum Prediction
papers.abstract: Structured scientific spectra encode rich physical information while obeying hard constraints, such as conservation laws and characteristic spectral geometry. Accurate prediction of these spectra is central to materials discovery, yet existing methods often treat them as unconstrained sequences and therefore fail to enforce the underlying physical structure. Taking electronic density of states (eDOS) as the prototypical example, we introduce DeepSciReasoner, a general paradigm for predicting scientific spectra under physical constraints. The framework combines structure-aware spectrum decoding with constraint-preserving physical reasoning, allowing predictions to capture rich spectral structure while respecting the underlying physics. We evaluate DeepSciReasoner on eDOS, phonon density of states (phDOS), X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), and Raman spectra, where it substantially improves prediction accuracy while maintaining physical consistency. These results establish DeepSciReasoner as a reusable blueprint for structured scientific spectrum prediction under hard physical constraints.

These spectra encode rich mechanistic information while obeying hard physical constraints. These constraints include conservation laws (e.g., mass/charge/state counts) and spectral geometry (e.g., sharp discontinuities at band edges and peaks) that are essential for correct downstream observables.

Machine learning has made rapid progress on crystal property prediction for scalar targets (Xie & Grossman, 2018; Schütt et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019). Predicting physical spectra is more challenging because the output is a high-dimensional sequence over a spectral axis (energy, wavenumber, or frequency) whose validity depends on physical constraints and spectral geometry. Beyond basic nonnegativity, physically meaningful predictions must preserve the total spectral mass (the integral over the spectral axis) and accurately capture where spectral mass lies, including sharp band edges, prominent peaks, and sparse vibrational lines. Taking eDOS as the prototypical example, total-state conservation, band-edge sharpness, and the placement of Van Hove singularities (Van Hove, 1953) all need to be respected for the prediction to be physically faithful; analogous geometric and conservation considerations recur in phDOS, XANES, and Raman.

For example, there are three key limitations in previous eDOS prediction methods. First, they predict the band gap and spectrum separately and reconcile them post hoc, which misaligns band edges near the Fermi level and introduces spurious in-gap density. Third, the total eDOS is theoretically a sum of atom-projected DOS (pDOS) (Mulliken, 1955); however, prior models collapse a crystal into a single global embedding, reducing interpretability and ignoring atom-projected contribution. papers.title: Benchmarks Are Surprisingly Compaction-Friendly
papers.abstract: Long horizon agentic tasks are now pushing LLM agents past their context window. To continue the task, the agent scaffold has to free up the context window, a process known as context compaction. Compaction is generally lossy by design: agents can silently lose task constraints, instructions, or their reasoning behind earlier decisions. Although compaction is a standard component of coding agent scaffolds, it has not been studied systematically with frontier models on realistic, long horizon agentic tasks. Previous work evaluate smaller open weight models on toy or synthetic trajectories. We fix the agent scaffold (OpenCode), implement five compaction strategies inside it, and evaluate three frontier models on three long horizon benchmarks (PaperBench, ProgramBench, PostTrainBench). For the two 1M context models, the compaction threshold does not measurably affect the task performance, whereas GPT-5.3-Codex, the model with the smallest context window, performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench and, less clearly, on PostTrainBench. No compaction method outperforms default self-summarization, and methods that discard more content cost some models up to 20 points while leaving other models the same. Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build. We argue that current benchmarks are compaction-friendly: i.e., the objective is fixed and the agent's progress stays on disk, so most of what compaction discards can be recovered, except constraints that don't exist anywhere else.

papers.intro:
LLM agents can now run for multiple hours on a single task autonomously. For example, a single run of PostTrainBench (Rank et al., 2026) or ProgramBench (Yang et al., 2026) produces on average several hundreds of thousands of tokens, more than many LLMs’ context windows. Widely used agent scaffolds like Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenHands, and OpenCode mostly handle this with some form of summarization: when the context is near the limit, the scaffold asks a model to summarize the work so far, discards the current context, and continues from the summary (Cassano and Rush, 2026; Anthropic, 2026a; Smith, 2025; OpenCode contributors, 2026). This process is called context compaction.

Widely used agent scaffolds like Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenHands, and OpenCode mostly handle this with some form of summarization: when the context is near the limit, the scaffold asks a model to summarize the work so far, discards the current context, and continues from the summary (Cassano and Rush, 2026; Anthropic, 2026a; Smith, 2025; OpenCode contributors, 2026). This process is called context compaction.

Most compaction methods are lossy by design. If the summary removes something, the agent can then lose task constraints, certain instructions, or the chain of thought behind previous decisions. This raises two questions: can the agent still solve the task, and does it still respect the rules it was given? Previous works have shown that constraints specified by the user often do not survive compaction (Wang et al., 2026). Other work compares compaction with other context management methods on downstream accuracy, but on long context question answering or web search, where the long input is given upfront (Zhang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025). However, none of these studies measure the downstream effect of compaction on realistic long horizon agentic tasks with frontier models, where the context is generated by the agent itself.

papers.title: RoboWorM: Evaluating Movement Realism, Consistency and Acceleration Affects in Embodied Video World Models
papers.abstract: Video world models (VWMs) are rapidly emerging as scalable neural simulators for robotic manipulation. However, most benchmarks only evaluate them as open-world video generators, using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that lack strict 3D spatial and kinematic reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboWorM, a comprehensive, deployment-aware benchmark that leverages known hardware priors such as robot kinematic trees and fixed camera configurations, to systematically examine structural and spatiotemporal fidelity. RoboWorM curates 1,605 episodes across single-arm, bimanual, and humanoid morphologies, spanning both Markovian and long-horizon non-Markovian tasks under single- and multi-view setups. To explicitly measure physical consistency, we propose two deterministic, VLM-free metrics: KIVA for intra-view kinematic stability, and RIGIS for multi-view geometric consistency. By exploiting intrinsic robotic invariants, KIVA improves hallucination detection alignment with human annotations by 25.8% relative to the strongest frontier VLMs, while RIGIS achieves a 130% higher Spearman correlation with human preferences. Furthermore, since real-world deployment requires low inference latency, we utilize RoboWorM to conduct the first large-scale audit of the quality-efficiency trade-off. Evaluating 9 state-of-the-art acceleration techniques across 3 leading world models (over 29,000 generated rollouts), we demonstrate how these acceleration methods can retain superficial visual quality while silently compromising deployment-critical physical constraints. Using our metrics, we achieve 2.3$\times$ maximum inference speed-up with minimal quality loss.

papers.intro:
Video world models (VWMs) have recently emerged as scalable neural simulators for robotic manipulation, mitigating physical data scarcity by generating synthetic trajectories, ranking policies, and enabling model-based planning (Jang et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026). However, the prevailing evaluation paradigms treat these models merely as open-world video generators. General-purpose benchmarks evaluate perceptual quality and text alignment (Liu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026a), while recent robotics-aligned benchmarks rely heavily on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to score task plausibility (Jiang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c; Yang et al., 2026b; Nguyen et al., 2026d). While valuable for assessing high-level semantic alignment, VLM evaluators suffer from optimism bias, struggle with strict 3D geometric reasoning, and evaluate physical AI in a vacuum. A generated robot video is not just a moving picture; it represents a physical system in motion. In reality, a robot’s mechanical arms cannot arbitrarily change length, its gripper cannot float disconnected in mid-air, and multiple cameras viewing the same workspace must capture the exact same 3D layout.

To bridge this gap, we propose shifting physical evaluation toward a complementary deployment-aware setting. In real applications, practitioners generating synthetic data already possess explicit prior knowledge of their setup, e.g., the robot’s specific kinematic structure, task instructions, and fixed camera configurations. While evaluating world models as generic video generators is useful for open-world assessment, it leaves these critical structural priors unused. By actively leveraging these priors, we can construct deterministic, physics-grounded measurements that better align with the requirements of real-world robotics. Further, deployment introduces another critical constraint: inference efficiency. The high generation latency of world models poses a severe throughput bottleneck, motivating acceleration techniques like caching, sparse attention, and token pruning (Lyu et al., 2025; Bu et al., 2026; Xi et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026d; Li et al., 2026b; Nawaz et al., 2026). Since acceleration compresses structural representations, it preserves superficial perceptual appearance while silently violating strict kinematic constraints. Evaluating this quality-efficiency trade-off is thus an essential, yet largely unexplored, dimension of practical robotic deployment.

First, we audit intra-view physical hallucinations through KIVA, which maps robot joint actions to keypoints to evaluate kinematic violations and physical plausibility. Since hallucinated videos yield out-of-distribution visual tokens, these estimates violate kinematic invariants, explicitly exposing the errors. Second, we verify cross-view consistency through RIGIS, a Robotic Inter-view Geometry & Intrinsic-Extrinsic Stability framework, which ensures that synchronized views form a unified 3D scene with temporally stable camera extrinsics and intrinsics. Armed with these deterministic metrics, we utilize RoboWorM to conduct a comprehensive audit of the quality-efficiency trade-off in robotic video generation. A Diverse Benchmark for Robot World Models: We curate a rigorous evaluation suite of 1,605 episodes encompassing three major robot morphologies (single-arm, bimanual, humanoid). The benchmark spans both short Markovian interactions and long-horizon, non-Markovian tasks involving multiple subgoals and up to four synchronized camera views. 2. papers.title: Rigid Band Shift in Electron-Doped Kagome Metal
papers.abstract: We study the effects of Sn-site doping on the electronic structure of nonmagnetic kagome metal YV$_6$Sn$_{6-x}$Sb$_x$ by infrared spectroscopy and density-functional theory. The results for samples with $x$ = 0 and 1.4 demonstrate that partial substitution of Sn by Sb acts as a rigid shift of the Fermi level while leaving the band dispersion largely intact. Our findings establish Sn-site substitution in YV$_6$Sn$_6$ as a route to systematically investigate band-filling-dependent electronic properties of nonmagnetic kagome metals.

papers.intro:
Kagome metals are layered materials in which itinerant 3dd electrons occupying the metallic kagome lattice give rise to a characteristic electronic structure featuring flat bands, Van Hove singularities, and linearly dispersing bands, which can drive a variety of electronic orders [1, 2]. The physical properties of these systems are highly sensitive to the band filling, which, together with electronic correlations and electron-phonon coupling, shapes their rich phase diagrams. The emerging phases include exotic magnetic orders, charge- and spin-density waves, unconventional superconductivity, and nematicity [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8].

R​M6​X6RM_{6}X_{6} (in short ’166’) kagome metals, with RR = rare-earth element, MM = Mn, Fe, V, Cr, Co, or Nb, and XX = Sn or Ge, provide a versatile platform for studying kagome physics, offering a broader chemical space than the widely studied AAV3Sb5 family [9]. These compounds exhibit a variety of electronic and magnetic phenomena, including helical magnetic orders [10, 11] and charge-density-wave (CDW) order in ScV6Sn6 [12] and LuNb6Sn6 [9]. Their electronic structure features characteristic signatures of the kagome lattice, including Dirac-like crossings and multiple Van Hove singularities in close proximity to the Fermi level [13, 14, 15]. The broad chemical flexibility of the 166 family therefore provides an attractive setting for exploring how changes in band filling influence the electronic properties of kagome systems.

The CDW states observed in ScV6Sn6 and LuNb6Sn6 have transition temperatures comparable to those of the AAV3Sb5 compounds. In contrast to AAV3Sb5, however, these CDW states are associated with structural modifications involving predominantly out-of-plane displacements of the Sn atoms, while the kagome network and the V/Nb-derived electronic states remain largely unaffected [12, 16, 17, 18, 19]. Competing ordering vectors have been linked to the softening of flat phonon modes and the resulting structural instability [20, 16, 17, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25]. This structural instability has been attributed to the size of the ion occupying the RR site [26]. In ScV6Sn6, the CDW can be suppressed by as little as 5% substitution of Sc by Y or Lu and is generally absent in 166 compounds with sufficiently large RR-site ions.

Here, we investigate the possibility of tuning the Fermi level in nonmagnetic YV6Sn6 [27, 28] by replacing Sn. We perform Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy and density-functional theory calculations and find that Sb substitution modifies the low-energy electrodynamic response while leaving the underlying band dispersion largely intact. The observed evolution can be understood in terms of a rigid shift of the Fermi level relative to the band structure. Our findings demonstrate that substitution on the pp-block site provides a route to tuning the Fermi level in nonmagnetic 166 kagome metals, enabling to study how band filling influences their electronic properties in systems where the RR-site-size-driven structural instability is suppressed.

papers.title: Gaussian Episodic Memory for Long-Term Spatiotemporal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Real-world environments undergo continual semi-static changes, requiring a memory representation that captures both the spatial and temporal evolution of a scene. Existing spatio-temporal memories for robots typically rely either on structured representations, which are limited to the entities and attributes captured during construction, or on image-based memories, which are constrained to previously observed viewpoints. We introduce GEMS, a framework that combines a persistent spatio-temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) map with an agentic reasoning pipeline. The 3DGS map is reconstructed once and subsequently updated only in regions where the scene changes, storing only these modifications while preserving visual detail across time. The agentic pipeline leverages this map to render novel views on demand, iteratively accumulating evidence to answer spatio-temporal questions and ground objects from natural-language queries. To advance future research, we introduce GEMS-Bench, a spatiotemporal question-answering benchmark focused on semi-static environments. It comprises 3 real-world and 12 synthetic environments, spanning 473 question-answer pairs. We evaluate GEMS on novel-view synthesis quality across scene updates, 3D object grounding, spatiotemporal question answering, and storage efficiency. GEMS outperforms recent baselines in 3D object grounding and spatiotemporal question answering, while achieving rendering quality on par with dedicated scene-update methods. Code and data: https://abwerby.github.io/GEMS/

papers.intro:
Robots operating for long periods in human-centered environments must model not only the geometry and semantics of their surroundings but also how those surroundings evolve over time. Real-world environments, such as homes and offices, experience frequent semi-static changes in which objects are moved, furniture is rearranged, and equipment may appear, disappear, or change state. Modeling these changes and building episodic memory that captures when and where they occurred enables robots to reason about the environment’s history and answer spatial, semantic, and temporal questions, such as where an object was previously located, when a change occurred, or how the current state of a scene differs from an earlier one.

Real-world environments, such as homes and offices, experience frequent semi-static changes in which objects are moved, furniture is rearranged, and equipment may appear, disappear, or change state. Modeling these changes and building episodic memory that captures when and where they occurred enables robots to reason about the environment’s history and answer spatial, semantic, and temporal questions, such as where an object was previously located, when a change occurred, or how the current state of a scene differs from an earlier one.

3D scene graphs (3DSGs) [1, 2, 3] have emerged as compact, structured representations that organize spatial-semantic concepts. However, typical 3DSGs represent a single snapshot of the environment. More recent 3DSG approaches incorporate temporal information into scene representations to model semi-static changes [4, 5, 6, 7]. However, they either preserve only object-level states and textual descriptions, precommitting to objects segmented at construction time, or preserve observations only from fixed viewpoints, limiting access to the underlying visual evidence. Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [8] has emerged as a high-fidelity representation that preserves fine-grained visual details, supports novel-view synthesis, and enables localized updates [9, 10], making it well suited for long-term embodied reasoning. Existing 3DGS-based mapping and reasoning methods, however, either address static scenes [11, 12] or maintain only the latest scene state [13].

3D scene graphs (3DSGs) [1, 2, 3] have emerged as compact, structured representations that organize spatial-semantic concepts. However, typical 3DSGs represent a single snapshot of the environment. More recent 3DSG approaches incorporate temporal information into scene representations to model semi-static changes [4, 5, 6, 7]. However, they either preserve only object-level states and textual descriptions, precommitting to objects segmented at construction time, or preserve observations only from fixed viewpoints, limiting access to the underlying visual evidence. Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [8] has emerged as a high-fidelity representation that preserves fine-grained visual details, supports novel-view synthesis, and enables localized updates [9, 10], making it well suited for long-term embodied reasoning. To this end, we present GEMS, a persistent spatiotemporal episodic memory based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), coupled with an agentic reasoning pipeline. GEMS construct an initial 3DGS map, then detect changes from observations collected during each subsequent scene revisit and locally update the Gaussian primitives in affected regions. Unchanged Gaussians are shared across temporal states, while additions, removals, and modifications are stored as temporal deltas. As a result, storage grows with environmental changes rather than the number of revisits. Given a query, the agentic pipeline can select informative viewpoints for reconstructed regions rather than being restricted to a fixed set of viewpoints. The 3DGS-based memory enables the agent to render the map from a consistent virtual camera pose across different timesteps. This controlled alignment supports cross-temporal visual comparison and reasoning about object motion and state changes. Moreover, photorealistic novel-view rendering enables the agent to perform on-demand segmentation of target objects from informative, query-dependent viewpoints.

papers.title: First-order magnetostructural transition in Ni-Mn-Sn powder - A matter of particle and grain size
papers.abstract: In Ni-Mn-based Heusler alloys, the magnetocaloric effect originates from a first-order magnetostructural transition (FOMST). However, the influence of particle and grain size on thermal hysteresis, transition width, and nucleation and growth mechanism remains poorly understood, as mechanical grinding can introduce residual stresses and processing-induced defects. In this study, we examined the size dependence of the FOMST in gas-atomized Ni-Mn-Sn powder by combining microstructural characterization with temperature-dependent XRD, magnetometry, calorimetry and single-particle measurements, enabling decoupling of size dependence from processing-related influences. We observed a pronounced size dependence of the transition ranges (Ms-Mf) and (Af-As), which decrease with decreasing particle size and approach zero for single-crystalline particles below ~20-30 micrometer. The thermal hysteresis decreases with increasing particle size, reaching a lower limit of 17 K for large polycrystalline particles above 100 micrometer. EBSD reveals a nearly constant grain size, implying a transition from polycrystalline to single-crystalline particles as particle size decreases. In polycrystalline particles, multiple grains transform gradually over an extended temperature interval because grain boundaries act as barriers to the progression of transformation. In contrast, single-grain particles lack preferred nucleation sites, resulting in larger hysteresis, while the absence of barriers to transformation propagation causes the entire particle to transform in a narrow range. These results demonstrate that the size dependence of the FOMST is governed by the interplay between particle size, grain boundaries, and the free particle surface.

papers.intro: The past decade has seen record-high global mean temperatures, with 2024 being the warmest year on record [34]. Continued global warming is expected to increase the demand for cooling over the coming decades. Currently used conventional cooling devices rely on the vapor-compression technique, which is more than a hundred years old, and require the use of environmentally harmful refrigerants. A significant increase in cooling efficiency and the elimination of harmful refrigerants demand the search for alternative cooling technologies. Solid-state caloric cooling, utilizing caloric effects, is seen as a promising alternative for the vapor-compression technique [22, 8, 12, 7, 11, 30, 9]. Magnetocaloric cooling uses magnetic solid-state material as refrigerant and operates entirely without refrigerant gases, which makes it a potentially more environmentally friendly and energy-efficient cooling alternative [13]. Ni-Mn-X (X= In, Sn, Sb, Ti) Heusler alloys are considered as potential caloric refrigerants, as the alloys show an inverse magnetocaloric effect (MCE) and a conventional elastocaloric effect (ECE) making these materials suitable for magnetocaloric, elastocaloric or multicaloric cooling [15, 27, 18, 10, 35, 2]. The caloric effects arise from the first-order magnetostructural transition (FOMST), involving a martensitic transformation that is driven by a nucleation and growth mechanism [15, 18]. The nucleation and growth mechanism and the related FOMST properties, thermal hysteresis Δ​Th​y​s​t\Delta T_{hyst} and transition widths (Ms−Mf)(M_{s}-M_{f}) and (Af−As)(A_{f}-A_{s}), depend on a variety of intrinsic and extrinsic properties [11, 30]. Chemical composition [38], transition temperature TtT_{t} [1] and microstructural aspects like homogeneity [37], grain size [25], secondary phases [26, 32] and texture [25] have a significant impact on the FOMST properties and the related MCE in Ni-Mn-based Heusler alloys. In view of the fact that the active magnetocaloric material is typically incorporated into the refrigeration device in packed powder beds, parallel plate arrays or microchannel geometries with sizes below 500 µm [46], it is necessary to establish a better understanding of how decreasing the characteristic length scales in terms of sample dimension or particle size impacts the nucleation and growth process of the martensitic transformation. The possibility to process spherical powders by gas-atomization for additive manufacturing techniques like laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) or direct energy deposition (DED) [31, 36] opened up a new possibility to study the size dependence of the FOMST, and tailor the FOMST properties by selecting a specific particle size. Early studies of size effects on the martensitic transformation in shape memory alloys focused on non-magnetic Cu-based microwires, considering both stress-induced and temperature-induced transformations. Reported effects include changes in transformation temperatures, transformation stresses, hysteresis, and stored elastic energy [5, 41, 42, 40]. Chen et al. observed larger hysteresis and greater energy dissipation in thinner wires, which they attributed to enhanced internal frictional work arising from stronger surface pinning of the phase boundary at higher surface-to-volume ratios [5]. Shifts in transformation temperatures and stresses, in contrast, were attributed to the relief of elastic transformation stresses at free surfaces [5, 41]. Wire diameter has also been reported to affect transformation morphology. Ueland et al. observed a transition from multi-domain to single-domain transformation behavior with decreasing wire diameter. In thinner wires, transformation proceeded through the nucleation and subsequent growth of a single martensite plate, whereas thicker wires exhibited continued nucleation and growth of additional plates [42]. Studies regarding the size dependence of the martensitic transformation in Ni-Mn-based Heusler alloys were conducted on thin films [48], milled particles [9, 4, 14] and gas-atomized powders [49, 16]. For Ni-Mn-Sn thin films, Zhang et al. found that Δ​Th​y​s​t\Delta T_{hyst} of the films does not depend on the grain size, but increases with decreasing film thickness according to a power law model [48]. In another study on gas-atomized Ni-Co-Mn-Sn single particles (38 µm to 9 µm), Zhang et al. confirm the trend of an increasing Δ​Th​y​s​t\Delta T_{hyst} with decreasing particle size [49], which is also found by Lago el al. in gas-atomized Ni-Co-Mn-In single particles (42 µm to 8 µm) [16]. In each case, the authors attribute this to greater energy dissipation through enhanced frictional work in smaller particles and a limitation of nucleation due to a reduced probability of finding potent defects acting as nucleation sites [49, 16]. Additionally, different types of transformation characteristics are revealed in these particles, ranging from continuous transformations with broader transition temperature ranges (>>15 K) to abrupt transformations with narrow ranges (<<1 K). In addition to the studies on atomized spherical powder, several studies on milled Ni-Mn-based Heusler alloy particles have been reported, although grinding and milling can introduce plastic deformation and lattice defects, such as dislocations, and generate internal stresses and associated lattice strains in these alloys [9, 4, 14, 20, 19, 29, 43, 39]. For irregular large particles, Gottschall et al. describe a significant broadening of Δ​Th​y​s​t\Delta T_{hyst} and (Ms−Mf)(M_{s}-M_{f}) and (Af−As)(A_{f}-A_{s}) with decreasing particle size (250 µm to 100 µm) [9]. Cavazzini et al. demonstrate a size dependence of the martensitic transformation in hand-ground and annealed Ni-Mn-In-Co particles (250 µm to 66 µm) [4]. Specifically, Δ​Th​y​s​t\Delta T_{hyst} is significantly broadened as a result of a broadening of (Ms−Mf)(M_{s}-M_{f}) towards lower temperatures, whereas MsM_{s} and (Af−As)(A_{f}-A_{s}) are not affected by particle size. In addition, an increased amount of retained austenite in smaller particles below MfM_{f} is confirmed by magnetometry and XRD, which the authors attribute to larger residual stress in smaller particles, as a direct result of the powder-synthesis process. As the particle size decreases, these residual stresses increasingly suppress the martensitic transformation and thus lead to a broadening of the hysteresis. In another recent study, Khanna et al. also describe a correlation between particle size and degree of deformation in milled Ni-Mn-In-Co particles, which leads to a broadening of the FOMST [14]. Besides lattice defects like dislocations and internal stress and strain, the defects introduced by mechanical processing can also include antiphase boundaries associated with dislocations. In ball-milled Ni-Mn-Ga, the dissociation of full dislocations into partial dislocations and their subsequent motion have been proposed to produce antiphase boundaries or reduce atomic order, depending on the displacement vector [39]. Such defects can affect magnetic properties even without detectable atomic disordering. In mechanically treated Ni-Mn-Sn, a reduction in saturation magnetization was attributed to antiferromagnetic coupling between Mn-atoms across dislocation-associated antiphase boundaries [43]. Under sufficiently severe milling conditions, atomic disordering can additionally contribute to the suppression of the martensitic transformation [39, 4]. Substantial lattice distortions can arise even during hand grinding. For example, a microstrain of up to 0.93 % has been reported in hand-ground Ni-Mn-Sn particles [20]. The extent of these processing-induced changes depend on the milling conditions [4]. These findings illustrate the difficulty of disentangling particle size effects from the effects of lattice defects, internal stresses and strains, and particle morphology. To disentangle the influence of particle size from effects related to powder morphology and processing-induced defects, such as dislocations, associated antiphase boundaries or atomic disorder [39, 4, 20, 43], we used gas-atomized Ni-Mn-Sn powder in this study. Owing to its spherical morphology and preparation without mechanical grinding or milling, this material system provides a suitable model to systematically investigate the size dependence of the FOMST while avoiding the additional defects and internal stresses introduced by these processing steps. Despite previous studies, it remains unclear how particle size and the associated grain structure influence the FOMST, particularly with respect to thermal hysteresis, transition widths, and the underlying nucleation and growth mechanisms. Zhang et al. [49] investigated individual Ni-Co-Mn-Sn particles, including larger polycrystalline particles, but their statistical analysis of transformation behaviour focused only on particles classified as single crystals, with diameters of approximately 9–38 µm. The present study examines individual particles over a wider diameter range of 13–127 µm, including both single-crystalline and polycrystalline particles. We relate their transformation behaviour to particle microstructure and direct in-situ observations of the martensite nucleation and growth. In this context, we hypothesize that the observed size dependence of the FOMST is closely linked to the microstructure and presence of grain boundaries within a particle, which is expected to affect the nucleation and growth behavior of the martensitic transformation. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a systematic study of gas-atomized Ni-Mn-Sn powders. The FOMST is characterized by a combination of structural (XRD), microstructural (SEM, EBSD), calorimetric (DSC), and magnetic measurements, including both powder-based and single-particle analyses. Within this framework, we identified a correlation between particle size and crystallinity, providing the basis for a detailed investigation of size-dependent transformation behavior for Δ​Th​y​s​t\Delta T_{hyst} and (Ms−Mf)(M_{s}-M_{f}) and (Af−As)(A_{f}-A_{s}).

papers.title: Joint End-to-End Training of Weighted BP Decoder Ensembles
papers.abstract: Ensemble decoding improves decoding reliability by combining component decoders with complementary failure events. Existing approaches typically obtain this diversity from code-specific structure, such as code automorphisms, multiple parity-check representations, or targeted modifications of the message-passing graph. In this work, we instead learn the diversity of an ensemble of weighted belief propagation decoders by jointly optimizing trainable Tanner-graph edge weights. A central design question is how the training objective should distribute gradient among the ensemble members to promote complementary decoding behavior. To this end, we compare four ensemble objectives under direct gradient-based optimization and identify best-member training as the most effective approach. For a (64,32) progressive edge-growth (PEG) low-density parity-check (LDPC) code, the resulting ensemble outperforms the considered trained and untrained belief-propagation-based ensemble baselines. With 10 members, it provides a gain of approximately 0.66 dB over a single belief propagation decoder at a target frame error rate (FER) of $10^{-4}$. Similar behavior is observed for a (128,64) CCSDS LDPC code, indicating that the learned complementarity is not specific to PEG. Although the ensemble performance improves substantially, all trained members show a higher standalone FER. The gain therefore results from learned specialization and complementary failure events rather than uniformly improved component decoders.

Ensemble decoding improves the FER-performance of short block codes by exploiting diversity among several constituent decoders and selecting the most likely candidate from their combined output list [1]. Conventional approaches create such diversity structurally, e.g., through multiple parity-check representations [2], code automorphisms [3], or decoder-side modifications of the message-passing process [4]. In contrast, learned message-passing decoders, like WBP (WBP), improve an individual iterative decoder by optimizing trainable parameters of the decoding algorithm [5, 6].

In [8], a decoder is trained on words that remain uncorrected by a preceding learned decoder. Both approaches therefore promote specialization through prescribed or sequentially defined training subsets.

This distinguishes ensemble training from single-decoder training: improving every member on average typically does not lead to the best improvement of the ensemble, because the final decision benefits from members that correct different frames. Conversely, assigning every frame equally to every member encourages similar decoding behavior.

papers.title: Relative delooping levels on intervals of torsion classes
papers.abstract: Let $U$ be a support $\tau$-tilting module over a finite-dimensional algebra $A$, and let $\mathcal{V}\subseteq\operatorname{Fac}U$ be any torsion class. The exact heart $\mathcal{H}=\operatorname{Fac}U\cap\mathcal{V}^{\perp}$ has an Ext-progenerator $P$. We prove that $\operatorname{Hom}_A(P,-)$ realizes $\mathcal{H}$ as a submodule-closed exact subcategory of $\operatorname{mod}B$, where $B=\text{End}_A(P)$, and preserves minimal syzygies. The global relative $k$-delooping levels are independent of $k\geq1$. Writing $g=\operatorname{glo}\text{-}\operatorname{dell}\mathcal{H}$, we obtain the sharp comparison $g\leq\operatorname{glo}\text{-}\operatorname{dell}B\leq g+1$ and $\operatorname{findim}B^{\mathrm{op}}\leq g+1$. Thus the two global levels are finite simultaneously. For wide hearts the relative levels equal their classical counterparts. We also characterize syzygy finiteness of $B$ by a finite relative syzygy stratum and obtain explicit bounds for both finitistic dimensions. If the heart is Frobenius, it is exactly the category of finitely generated Gorenstein-projective $B$-modules under this realization, and both self-injective dimensions of $B$ are at most one. We also give examples to show the main results.

Let AA be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field 𝕜\Bbbk. The finitistic dimension conjecture asks whether the projective dimensions of the finitely generated modules of finite projective dimension have a common finite bound. Gélinas [11] introduced the delooping level and proved findim⁡Aop≤dell⁡A\findim A^{\mathrm{op}}\leq\dell A, where dell⁡A\dell A is computed on simple right AA-modules. This relates finitistic dimension to the occurrence of modules as stable direct summands of higher syzygies. Kershaw and Rickard [15] showed that the delooping level can be infinite. Guo and Igusa [13] introduced the derived delooping level, while Barrios, Lanzilotta and Mata [4] studied global delooping levels and their relation to other homological dimensions. Further developments concern left–right symmetry [12] and derived equivalences: Chen [6] showed that finiteness of the ordinary delooping level is not preserved by derived equivalences, whereas Wei, Wu and Cao [17] study comparisons for derived delooping with a shift in the delooping degree.

papers.title: Rigorous Lower Bounds for Atomic and Ionic Ground-State Energies
papers.abstract: We establish a new iterative method for computing rigorous lower bounds for the ground-state energies of all atoms and ions. The accuracy of the resulting bounds depends on two ingredients: the quality of the initial energy estimate and the quality of the used upper bound for the maximum number of bound electrons, $N_c(Z)$, as a function of the nuclear charge $Z>0$. In particular, this new method allows us to establish the explicit lower bound $E(N,Z) \geq -0.8710\,N^{1/3}Z^2$ for the ground-state energy $E(N,Z)$ of the atom/ion with $N \in \mathbb{N}$ electrons and nuclear charge $Z \in (0,N]$, thereby considerably improving the best known constant $A=(3/2)^{1/3} \approx 1.1447$ in the estimate $E(N,Z) \geq -A\,N^{1/3}Z^2$ for $0 < Z \leq N$ and coming much closer to the best possible constant given by the Thomas-Fermi asymptotics $\lim_{N \to \infty} |E(N,N)|N^{-7/3}= -E_{\text{TF}}(1)\approx 0.7687$ derived in Adv. Math., 23(1) by Lieb and Simon. To demonstrate the potential and the limits of our method, we also compute explicit lower bounds for the ground-state energies $E(N,N)$ of all atoms with $2 \leq N \leq 86$ and we compare them with the bounds obtained in J. Chem. Phys., 62(8) by Hertel, Lieb, Thirring and the bounds obtained by Seco in his dissertation. Finally, we also provide a uniqueness result for the expectation values of the kinetic, potential and interaction energies on the ground-state space.

papers.intro:
Since the early days of quantum mechanics, considerable effort has been devoted to determining the ground-state energies of atoms and molecules as accurately as possible, both experimentally and theoretically. High numerical accuracy is particularly important when differences of several energy levels are considered, as for example is the case of chemical reactions and radiative processes. Furthermore, lower bounds for atomic and molecular ground-state energies play a fundamental role in the study of the stability of matter, since their asymptotic behavior as the number of electrons N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} tends to infinity determines whether matter is stable or not Lieb and Seiringer (2010). Deriving an upper bound for a given atomic or molecular ground-state energy is relatively straightforward. Indeed, by the variational principle (cf. Eq. (3) below), it suffices to compute the expectation value of the corresponding Hamiltonian with respect to an arbitrary trial state ψ\psi belonging to its domain. However, one can only expect that the resulting upper bound is close to the (typically unknown) exact value of the ground-state energy if ψ\psi provides a sufficiently good approximation of the true ground state. Over the years, a large toolbox of methods has been developed in quantum chemistry for constructing such approximate ground states. A prominent example is the self-consistent field (SCF) method based on the Hartree-Fock-Roothaan equations. Its accuracy can be further improved by employing Post-Hartree-Fock methods, which also account for electron correlation. For details concerning the SCF method and related approaches, we refer to standard textbooks on quantum chemistry (see, e.g., Lewars (2024)). The primary objective of this work is the derivation of lower bounds for atomic and ionic ground-state energies. From a mathematical perspective, this is a considerably more challenging problem, and correspondingly much less rigorous results are available. For small atoms and ions, highly accurate lower bounds have been obtained using, for example, the Bazley-Fox method Bazley (1960), the Temple inequality and related methods Alexander and Coldwell (2002); King (1995); Stevenson and Crawford (1938), as well as subsequent refinements of these approaches Ireland et al. (2022); Marmorino et al. (2012). For larger systems, however, these methods become increasingly inefficient due to the growing dimensionality of the problem and the associated computational costs. In this regime, the approaches developed in Hertel et al. (1975) and Seco (1989) yield stronger lower bounds, although these bounds still differ from the expected ground-state energies (e.g. upper bounds obtained from extensive numerical computations) by several percent. Moreover, both approaches rely on substantial numerical computations at intermediate stages, making it difficult to derive explicit bounds in terms of the electron number N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}. At the current state of research, the absence of sufficiently strong lower bounds for atomic and ionic ground-state energies seems to be one of the main obstacles to resolving several prominent open problems in mathematical physics, including the monotonicity of the ionization energies Simon (1984) and the derivation of the van der Waals law without additional assumptions Anapolitanos (2016); Anapolitanos and Sigal (2013).

papers.title: Adaptive Control for General Nonlinear Stochastic Systems
papers.abstract: This paper extends the least-squares and certainty-equivalence minimum-variance framework of classical linear self-tuning regulators to a broad class of nonlinearly parameterized systems with compact parameter spaces, including commonly used deep neural network models. First, historical nonlinear least-squares fitting guarantees are converted into online one-step prediction bounds under a general modulus of continuity, with explicit regret rates under parameter Lipschitz continuity and finite-moment noise. Second, approximate NLS estimation combined with certainty-equivalence control achieves closed-loop stability and asymptotically optimal tracking under mild conditions without requiring excitation or parameter identifiability. Explicit closed-loop regret and tracking error rates are established in the parameter-Lipschitz case, and closed-loop examples show that the regret rates cannot, in general, be improved for this regulator. Finally, robustness to small unmodeled dynamics is established by showing that closed-loop stability is preserved and the tracking error bounds comprise a vanishing term and a residual term determined by the model discrepancy.

papers.intro:
Modern applications in embodied robotics, intelligent manufacturing, and energy systems increasingly combine feedback control with dynamical models that are estimated from data and may be highly nonlinear [1]. Accurate models may be difficult to obtain before operation, while measured input–output data can be used to update the model and improve control performance during operation. The self-tuning regulator (STR) provides a direct way to incorporate this information into feedback: estimate the model from past observations and compute the next control input using the current estimate. Its classical realization combines least-squares (LS) estimation with certainty-equivalence (CE) control [2, 3]. Extending this approach to nonlinear model classes would provide a theoretical basis for adaptive regulation using general nonlinear models estimated from data.

The self-tuning regulator (STR) provides a direct way to incorporate this information into feedback: estimate the model from past observations and compute the next control input using the current estimate. Its classical realization combines least-squares (LS) estimation with certainty-equivalence (CE) control [2, 3]. Extending this approach to nonlinear model classes would provide a theoretical basis for adaptive regulation using general nonlinear models estimated from data.

The central difficulty is the interaction between open-loop prediction and closed-loop feedback control. The estimated model determines the control input, which in turn affects the subsequent system trajectory and the observations available for estimation. The predictor must therefore remain accurate along the trajectory generated by the adaptive regulator. For nonlinear parameterizations, a small fitting error over past observations alone does not ensure a small one-step prediction error, and feedback may amplify prediction errors before sufficient information has been obtained. Stability and tracking analysis must therefore account for prediction errors before boundedness of the closed-loop signals has been established.

This paper studies general nonlinearly parameterized stochastic systems with finite output and input memory, where the unknown parameter belongs to a known compact set. At each time, the estimator approximately minimizes the cumulative squared output residuals, and the control input is determined according to the CE principle. The objective is to establish closed-loop stability and asymptotically optimal tracking for this nonlinear STR. To this end, a one-step prediction analysis is developed from the historical least-squares comparison, allowing the regressors to be unbounded, dependent, and nonstationary.

For linear stochastic systems, the stability and optimality of the Åström–Wittenmark self-tuning regulator and an extended least-squares adaptive tracker were established in [4]. A unified treatment of stability, optimality, consistency, and logarithmic convergence rates for LS-based regulators was subsequently developed in [5]. These classical works provide a methodological foundation for the present study through their analysis of the interaction between prediction errors and closed-loop signal growth.

However, extensions to nonlinear systems are subject to fundamental limitations that apply to any causal controller. A critical growth phenomenon for scalar-parameter nonlinear stochastic systems was identified in [6], while limitations arising from uncertainty growth and parameter dimension were established in [7, 8]. For nonlinear parameterizations, feedback capability was related to parameter sensitivity and model structure in [9]. These results motivate the search for conditions under which nonlinear adaptive regulation can be achieved.

Early work on nonlinear adaptive prediction in [10] studied nonlinear autoregressive and control models with unknown parameters in a compact set and established an asymptotically exact logarithmic law for cumulative nonlinear least squares (NLS) one-step prediction errors under smoothness, identification, and a positive-definite limiting information condition. Subsequently, [11] used NLS to achieve simultaneous identification and stabilization for scalar-parameter systems. In the analysis of control regret, [12] related prediction regret to control regret for linearly parameterized systems under suitable incremental stability conditions. More recently, [13] established asymptotically optimal output regulation with stable, nonlinearly parameterized exosystems and derived NLS identification rates, while [14] obtained polylogarithmic expected regret across episodes for nonlinearly parameterized systems under a uniformly bounded dynamics map, an identifying initial policy, and excitation of the optimal policy. Recent recursive approaches include a nonlinear WLS-type estimator and adaptive feedback under quantitative monotonicity and Lipschitz conditions [15], and a modified stochastic-gradient predictor with prediction and CE control rates under a weak-convexity condition on the prediction loss [16]. The present work establishes stability and tracking properties of an adaptive regulator that combines approximate cumulative NLS estimation with CE control for general nonlinearly parameterized systems. The analysis requires neither excitation nor parameter convergence and does not impose additional model structure conditions such as uniformly bounded dynamics, identifying information conditions, or monotonicity or convexity assumptions used in the respective studies above.

From a statistical learning perspective, [17] obtained rate-optimal non-asymptotic bounds for the quadratic prediction error method under dependence and identifiability conditions. Their performance criterion evaluates the final model estimate on an independent copy of the regressor trajectory. The criterion considered here is the cumulative one-step prediction error along the actual system trajectory, with the model estimate updated at each time. Under heavy-tailed errors, [18, 19] characterized how noise moments, function-class complexity, and local envelopes govern least-squares rates. Those results concern statistical prediction risk based on independent sample pairs. The present analysis allows predictable regressors generated from past observations, as occurs under feedback control.

papers.title: mdRNAcat: A Molecular Dynamics RNA Catalog of REST2 Conformational Ensembles
papers.abstract: Learning molecular models of RNA requires simulation data that capture conformational variability and provide consistent physical training signals. Here, we introduce mdRNAcat, a curated dataset of all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of 48 RNA systems selected to promote sequence diversity. Each system is simulated using replica-exchange with solute scaling (REST2), with 32 Hamiltonian states and production lengths of 200-300 ns per state. The dataset provides atomic coordinates, instantaneous forces, and forces reevaluated under the unscaled reference Hamiltonian, together with structural annotations and replica-exchange metadata. Coordinates and forces are available at 1 ps intervals for the reference state and 100 ps intervals across all states in a standardized HDF5 format. We characterize conformational sampling, exchange behavior, base pairing, and sugar-pucker distributions to document the properties of the simulated ensembles. mdRNAcat provides a reusable resource for developing and evaluating data-driven RNA models, including coarse-grained force fields.

papers.intro:
At the sub-cellular scale, life is an intricate choreography of biomolecules in motion, whose understanding requires to know both their structure and dynamics. Despite major advances in experimental techniques, many important biomolecules remain structurally unresolved, with their conformational dynamics, at best, partially characterized. In principle, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide atomistic access to such dynamics, but the relevant time scales are often out of reach due to prohibitive computational expenses (Hollingsworth and Dror (2018)). Recently, machine learning methods have made substantial progress in structure prediction, such as Alphafold 3 (Abramson et al. (2024)) but also for learning molecular interactions and dynamics (Kovács et al. (2025)). However, much of this progress and the underlying training data have centered on proteins rather than RNA. This is in part due to differences in available data. Machine learning methods rely on available data to achieve the aforementioned results. For proteins, large collections of experimentally determined structures (Berman et al. (2000)), MD data sets, such as mdCATH and ATLAS (Mirarchi et al. (2024); Vander Meersche et al. (2024)), and data sets of quantum-mechanical properties (Levine et al. (2025); Eastman et al. (2024)) are available. In contrast, RNA lacks a comparably large and systematically generated MD resource. While curated RNA structure collections and nucleic-acid simulation repositories exist Upadhyay et al. (2025); Hospital et al. (2016), they do not provide the combination of scale, homogeneous protocols, large-scale conformational sampling, and consistently available force information targeted by mdRNAcat. To our knowledge, no existing RNA MD dataset combines these properties. This gap is particularly relevant given the growing interest in data-driven RNA modeling Upadhyay et al. (2026) and the need for large, consistent training datasets for coarse-grained machine-learned force fields Li and Chen (2026).

papers.title: The metastability phenomen for a radiative gas model
papers.abstract: We study the time-asymptotic behaviour of solutions to a singular perturbation of the inviscid Burgers problem describing sound propagation in a radiating gas. This radiating gas model exhibits the interesting phenomenon known as metastability that has been first identified for the viscous Burgers equation. Precisely, on an initial time span, that scales linearly in the inverse of the perturbation parameter, we can quantify the L1-distance of the solution to the so-called sharp N-wave solution of the inviscid Burgers problem and to a diffusive N-wave. On a second long-time stage that scales exponentially in the inverse of the perturbation parameter, the solutions still remain close to a diffusive N-wave before finally collapsing into diffusion waves. Besides our analysis of the radiating gas model, we also provide an alternative description of metastability in the viscous Burgers model which, unlike other studies, relies on L1-estimates and does not require the passage to similarity variables.

papers.title: Model-Aware Generation of Safety-Critical Scenes for Robust End-to-End Driving via Distilled Planner Surrogates
papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models perform well on standard benchmarks but collide frequently in safety-critical scenarios. We present a failure-mode analysis on NeuroNCAP which shows that 95.9% of DiffusionDrive's collisions are planning failures despite reliable detection, pinpointing the bottleneck in planning rather than perception. We attribute this to a fundamental data imbalance, as safety-critical interactions are rare in real driving logs, so planners are hardly ever trained on them. We close this gap with a novel model-aware framework that generates safety-critical training scenes against a specific planner. Each planner is attacked at the bird's-eye-view (BEV) level through a differentiable surrogate distilled from its own planning head. This keeps the expensive video renderer out of the attack loop. We extract 50 scenes per planner, each pairing an attack with a safe escape trajectory that serves as the fine-tuning label. A fully automated quality-diversity search generates both the attacks and the escapes, so that their variety is not specified by hand. Only these scenes are rendered to fine-tune the planner, which reduces the computational cost significantly. Fine-tuning on these scenes roughly halves the closed-loop collision rate of two planners on NeuroNCAP (SparseDrive 28.0% to 12.2%, DiffusionDrive 37.5% to 19.2%) while largely preserving normal driving. A cross-planner transfer experiment shows that the gain comes from targeting the specific planner. Each planner improves most on the scenes generated against itself, and DiffusionDrive fine-tuned on SparseDrive's scenes retains only 6.7 of its 18.3-point collision-rate reduction.

papers.intro:
End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has shown strong performance on standard benchmarks, yet the models are limited by the data they are trained on. Real-world driving datasets are heavily skewed toward normal, uneventful driving, with safety-critical interactions accounting for less than 0.03% of real-world driving time [1]. Such situations are inherently rare in naturalistic driving and cannot be deliberately staged at scale for safety, cost, and legal reasons. As soon as these models encounter scenarios outside their training distribution, performance degrades sharply. On Challenger, which generates physically plausible videos for adversarial scenarios such as cut-ins, sudden lane changes, and blind-spot intrusions, the collision rate of state-of-the-art E2E models increases by up to 26×\times compared to standard nuScenes evaluation [2]. While Challenger stress-tests models through video-based adversarial replay, NeuroNCAP evaluates in closed-loop, where the ego executes its own plan and failures hidden in open loop appear, on harder scenarios including oncoming vehicles, stationary vehicles, and side collisions [3]. There SparseDrive results in a collision rate of 28.0% and DiffusionDrive in 37.5%.

Since collecting safety-critical driving data at scale remains impractical, several directions have been explored to synthetically close this gap. Video generation models such as MagicDriveV2 [4] can synthesize photorealistic multi-view driving videos. Methods that do generate training data for the planner either derive it from validation failures without closed-loop evaluation [7] or simulate hundreds of thousands of scenes reconstructed from logged drives [8]. In both cases the scenarios come from existing data rather than being designed as interactions. Adversarial scenario generation designs such interactions deliberately, but either at the state level without photorealistic rendering [9, 10, 11] or, as in Challenger [2], against the logged ego trajectory rather than against a planner. No existing method generates photorealistic adversarial scenes optimized against a specific vision-based planner.

Targeting this weakness with generated scenes requires the gradient of a collision objective with respect to the adversary’s behavior. For a vision-based planner, whose input is rendered video, this gradient would have to pass through the video renderer, which is computationally infeasible. We therefore attack a surrogate instead. We distill the target planner π\pi into a differentiable surrogate planner π^\hat{\pi}, which consists of the planner’s own planning head, copied and frozen, behind a small trained adapter that takes ground-truth bird’s-eye-view (BEV) state instead of images. The failure analysis justifies this construction, since perception is reliable. Gradients through π^\hat{\pi} are cheap and point at the planner’s specific failure modes rather than at a generic driving prior. Every generated scene is therefore optimized against the planner to be fine-tuned.

papers.title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
papers.abstract: Software engineering agents resend their entire trajectory to an LLM at every turn, motivating online trajectory reduction. Prior work shows that randomly deleting 75% of tokens in old turns may preserve agent effectiveness, but it remains unclear why, how agents compensate for missing content, and whether it actually reduces costs. This paper presents an empirical study of 42 trajectory-reduction configurations, focusing on effectiveness, agent behavior, and cost. We systematically explore deleting content from old turns by varying the scope, granularity, amount, and timing of deletion across 9,400 runs with two state-of-the-art agents on SWE-bench Verified. We find deleting large amounts of trajectory content (e.g., up to 100% of reasoning text) can preserve overall effectiveness. Importantly, such deletion must be applied with a delay, as immediate deletion tends to significantly degrade effectiveness. Agents often compensate for deleted content by re-fetching it, increasing both the number of turns taken and the input/output tokens. Whether trajectory reduction reduces costs depends on the pricing model: Under a flat pricing model, estimated costs fall in 26 of 42 evaluations. Surprisingly, under a caching-aware pricing model, zero evaluations yield lower costs, since reducing the trajectory breaks the cached prefix billed at a lower rate. Our findings have three implications: First, token counts alone are misleading; trajectory reduction techniques must consider overall costs under a realistic pricing model. Second, analyzing trajectories is crucial to understand agent behavior, as end-to-end effectiveness hides differences such as excessive re-fetching. Finally, these results highlight the need for future work on memory management to reduce costs without sacrificing effectiveness.

papers.title: Context-Aware Generation and Modulation of Expressive Motion Behavior using Multimodal Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Expressive robot motion positively impacts human-robot interaction by improving user engagement, likability, or task performance. We present a novel approach to automatically generate and modulate complex, expressive full-body gesture sequences from a multimodal (text, audio, video) context description. Based on a unified mathematical implementation of the Principles of Animation using Dynamic Movement Primitives, we use multimodal foundation models to generate such sequences along with parametric motion variations that are highly context-aware. This method extends the state of the art in terms of flexibility and generality by being interpretable, composable, and working across different robot morphologies. Moreover, we integrate the system into a continuous control framework and leverage knowledge distillation to learn a much smaller model, significantly improving token efficiency and system latency. Results from a user study with a human-like platform indicate that participants judged our system's motions to be better aligned with the interaction context than motions produced under a non-modulated or API-level condition. We also demonstrate how the system generates expressive motion for robots with different kinematics, showcasing its versatility. Paper webpage: https://gen-mod-expressive-motion-behavior.github.io/.
