papers.intro:
Non-verbal communication via gaze, gestures, or facial expressions is a crucial component of socially intelligent behavior for humans and robots. Robot-performed gestures are often seen as a defining property of social robots (De Wit et al., 2023), and by using their physical embodiment and presence, they are perceived more positively and persuasive than, for example, interactive virtual agents (Li, 2015). Therefore, the design and use of expressive robotic body motion are critical for achieving natural and effective communication with socially interactive robots. Key questions include how movements are shaped, selected, and timed, the extent of their expression, and their integration with speech, context, and the course of interaction. This paper tackles several of the above questions, namely how body motion can be represented to facilitate learning, execution, and modulation – i.e., context-sensitive variations of the same motion –, and how basic gestures can be automatically selected, timed, and varied such that interlocutors perceive the robot’s behavior as aligned with the interaction context.

This paper tackles several of the above questions, namely how body motion can be represented to facilitate learning, execution, and modulation – i.e., context-sensitive variations of the same motion –, and how basic gestures can be automatically selected, timed, and varied such that interlocutors perceive the robot’s behavior as aligned with the interaction context.

The variety of expressive human body motion appears to be open-ended. One way to tackle this complexity practically is categorizing gestures into communicative functions such as deictic, iconic, or symbolic, and reusing standardized sets of pre-recorded gestures (Tan et al., 2021). By providing a small set of exemplars for each function, a robot can cover many real-world situations without the need to generate joint-level trajectories on the fly. We build on such motion datasets and adopt recent work (Hielscher et al., 2025) that employs Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) to represent, modulate, and compose basic gestures into expressive body language. Originally developed for motor skill learning from imitation or demonstration, e.g., for robot manipulation, DMPs offer properties highly relevant for this task. As shown in (Hielscher et al., 2025), they provide a unified implementation of the Principles of Animation and enable modulation of key principles through a low-dimensional, interpretable parameter set. This allows animators – and large language models – to stylize full-body motion along the well-established dimensions of the Principles of Animation across different kinematic configurations. They are also online adaptive in the sense that gestures are parametrized by a static or dynamic goal in space towards which gestures are executed.

papers.title: Lanthanide Crystal Field Theory in the J-Mixing Regime: $f^n$ Configurations
papers.abstract: The low-energy sector of the lanthanide $f^n$ shell is to first approximation governed by the interplay of three interactions: Coulomb repulsion, spin-same-orbit coupling and the ligand crystal field potential. To rationalize the energy landscape in different chemical environments, it is desirable to extract the phenomenological crystal field parameters from experimental data; however, in practice, high-dimensional fitting procedures complicate their routine determination. Here, we present a computational extraction procedure based on real tensorial sets and the $U(7)$ canonical chain that, unlike existing operator equivalent methods, takes all $J$ multiplets of the lowest-energy $LS$ term into account, ensuring meaningful results even in the presence of considerable $J$-mixing. Two series of lanthanide compounds, [Ln(III)(C$_8$H$_8$)$_2$]$^-$} and doped Ln(III):Y$_2$O$_3$} (Ln $\in$ {Ce, Pr, Nd, Sm, Eu}) serve as examples for high- ($D_{8h}$) and low-symmetry ($C_2$) scenarios. Consequences for the generalisation toward actinides are briefly discussed.

papers.title: The dominance of feedback mechanisms for perception in the central visual field: the flip tilt illusion by backward masking and the Feedforward-Feedback-Verify-reWeight algorithm
papers.abstract: The flip tilt illusion is the misperception of the orientation of the alignment between a pair of dots by 90 degrees. It occurs when the dot-pair contains one black dot and one white dot, is typically visible only in the peripheral visual field. It is predicted by the central-peripheral dichotomy (CPD) theory. Along the visual pathway from retina to downstream stages, our brain admits only a tiny fraction of visual input information for recognition due to a processing bottleneck that starts from the output of the primary visual cortex (V1) along the visual pathway. Accordingly, perception downstream from V1 relies on impoverished information, selected largely by gaze shifts to center the selected content at fovea and additionally by the capacity of the bottleneck even in the central visual field, likely making perceptual hypotheses about the visual scene ambiguous or illusory. To overcome, downstream areas send feedback to upstream areas such as V1 to query for additional information, thereby re-assessing the weights of the initial hypotheses. This perceptual algorithm is termed Feedforward-Feedback-Verify-reWeight (FFVW). To save resources, the feedback query is limited largely to the central visual field. The peripheral visual field is thus vulnerable to perceptual ambiguities and illusions. The CPD theory further predicts that impairing the feedback renders the flip tilt illusion visible in the central visual field. This paper reports a confirmation of the prediction. The feedback is disrupted by masking the visual inputs after a short viewing duration t. Furthermore, the FFVW algorithm is studied by a computational model of the perceptual data as a function of t. It reveals that the initial feedforward sweep of visual information explains the flip tilt illusion for t shorter than 20 ms, whereas the feedback mechanism dominates perception for longer t.

Figure 1 demonstrates the flip tilt illusion (Zhaoping, 2020), using homo- and hetero-pairs of dots tilted parallel or orthogonal to the tangent of the rings. Ring A contains 100% homo-pairs tilted tangential to the ring. Ring D is like ring A, except all dot pairs a hetero-pairs. In noise, ring A is highly conspicuous, but ring D is hard to spot. Wherever one directs the gaze on each image, most segments of the ring is in the peripheral visual field. The flip tilt illusion, normally only visible in the peripheral visual field, makes one perceive a hetero-pair of dots as if it is tilted orthogonal to the actual tilt of the dot pair. This illusion makes the dot pairs in ring D appear orthogonal to the tangent of the ring, making ring D inconspicuous in noise. In the recent decades, converging evidence is supporting the V1 Saliency Hypothesis (V1SH) (Li, 1999; Li, 2002) which proposed that the primary visual cortex (V1) supports looking by constructing a saliency map from external inputs to guide gaze exogenously to the salient locations (reviewed in (Zhaoping, 2014; Zhaoping, 2026b)). Although other brain areas such as the frontal eye field (FEF) and the parietal cortex also control attention and gaze shifts through endogenous and goal-dependent factors (Buschman and Miller, 2007; Bisley and Goldberg, 2010; Zhou and Desimone, 2011), V1’s critical role in looking motivated the idea that the bottleneck starts at V1’s output to downstream visual areas along the visual pathway, see Figure 2A. Indeed, by V2, the first cortical area downstream from V1 along the visual pathway, information about the eye of origin of visual inputs is largely lost, since V1 is the only cortical area with a substantial percentage of neurons that are monocular to encode eye of origin, which is not discriminable by human observers. Indeed, a V2 binocular neuron preferring a particular orientation can pool inputs from V1 monocular neurons preferring the same orientation but a diversity of preferences for eye of origin. Future investigations should ascertain how much and what other information are starting to be lost from the output of V1.

papers.title: Do vision models know that three is three?
papers.abstract: Do vision models encode the transition $2{\to}3$ the same way whether it appears in handwritten digits or in hand gestures, and do they "understand" that clean${\to}$dirty is the same transformation regardless of whether it is applied to a kitchen or a carpet? The linear representation hypothesis (LRH) answers this for language models: concept changes correspond to directions in (language) embedding space. In vision, the same concept can manifest in visually unrelated "regimes" that rarely co-occur: images of digits and hands do not share much in common in pixel space. To understand whether vision models still encode the underlying abstract concepts, we study 46 vision encoders across architectures, training objectives, and scales, on 10 concept families including numerosity, age, object identity, and MIT-States attributes. Within each regime, we find statistically significant concept directions near-universally across our tested models. However, two distinct regimes do not always share the same concept direction. Several models learn multiple linear structures for the same concept transition, split across regimes. We call this phenomenon "fragmented linearity": strong local linearity coexisting with near-absent global linearity. Fragmentation is, however, not fixed: models with stronger local linearity progressively escape it (local-global linearity correlated with $\tau \in [0.38, 0.89]$ across all concepts), and where global linearity does emerge, concept directions can transfer as linear probes across regimes.

The linear representation hypothesis (LRH) [1, 2] claims that the embedding spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain linear directions corresponding to high-level concept changes, enabling interpretability and algebraic interventions in representation space. Yet as vision encoders increasingly serve as the perceptual backbone of multimodal systems [3, 4], understanding whether the same linear structure holds in vision is essential to completing the picture.

Yet as vision encoders increasingly serve as the perceptual backbone of multimodal systems [3, 4], understanding whether the same linear structure holds in vision is essential to completing the picture.

Vision is fundamentally different from language in that the same concept often manifests in visually drastically different ways. For instance, the concept of “3” can be represented using handwritten digits [5], the number of objects in an image [6] or hand gestures [7]. While these different groups (regimes) of images do not share much in common in pixel space, a human would understand that the same underlying concept is being manipulated; do vision embedding spaces encode the same abstractions? A linear representation in embedding space would hint that they do.

Linear structure (linearity) in the embedding space is indeed often an assumption (implicit or otherwise) in prior works that attempt to interpret vision embeddings [8, 9, 10]. Prior work has also studied linearity of vision embeddings after projection onto a tangent space [11], with respect to ordinal attributes [12], and its emergence as a consequence of data diversity [13]. While these findings hint toward the presence of linear structure in vision embeddings, a more rigorous study exploring whether it survives across drastically unrelated visual regimes remains missing.

papers.title: Aligning Large Language Models with Human Feedback: Mathematical Foundations and Algorithm Design
papers.abstract: This article provides an introduction to the mathematical foundations and algorithmic frameworks used to align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human intentions, preferences, and values. We discuss standard alignment techniques, such as fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF), and direct preference optimization (DPO). We also explore the theoretical underpinnings of learning from human preferences, drawing connections to inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and discrete choice models. We present state-of-the-art algorithms in a tutorial style, discuss their advantages and limitations, and offer insights into practical implementation. Our exposition is intended to serve as a comprehensive resource for researchers and practitioners, providing both a foundational understanding of alignment methodologies and a framework for developing more robust and scalable alignment techniques.

Background. As large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm, it is clear that generative AI systems will soon become ubiquitous in our lives. LLMs have been applied beyond chatbots and personal assistants to tackle complex challenges, including video gaming [8] and autonomous control [7]. After the successful introduction and demonstrated efficacy of alignment training in LLMs [5, 38], the concept of alignment has been playing an increasingly important role in the design and training of AI systems. Loosely speaking, alignment refers to the performance guarantee that the AI system will generate outcomes that are intended or preferred by the human user without undesirable side effects or behaviors such as deception or manipulation.

More technically, the LLM alignment problem involves fine-tuning or adjusting a base model that was originally trained on extensive, diverse datasets. While such a base model is trained to learn core behaviors and general knowledge, it often falls short when applied to specific tasks or to meeting the nuanced preferences of a human user. To better align the model, additional feedback is gathered from human experts who evaluate and/or rank the model’s performance within a specific task context. As demonstrated in [38, 19], reinforcement learning (RL) holds significant promise for LLM alignment by leveraging additional feedback to enhance their performance. This feedback embodies expert judgments regarding both the accuracy of the model’s responses and any particular preferences they may have. The goal is to refine the model to better meet these specific requirements, ultimately enhancing its task relevance and user satisfaction. Generally, it is observed that after the alignment process, LLMs can follow human instructions well, and can avoid providing toxic and non-preferable responses. Despite extensive study of the alignment problem in recent literature, this research area remains young, and it is still evolving rapidly with many unresolved theoretical challenges. A primary contribution of this article is to introduce the signal processing community to the fundamentals of alignment, highlight state-of-the-art algorithms and approaches, and clarify the intersection

between alignment methodologies and various techniques relevant to signal processing (SP). We believe that our article will foster interdisciplinary contributions and expand the role of SP in LLM alignment research. By understanding the alignment problem, SP researchers can leverage their expertise in mathematical modeling, noise handling, inverse problem-solving, and optimization to address a number of key challenges. For instance, similar to reconstructing signals from observed data in SP, many alignment approaches involve solving inverse problems, such as learning the human preference models from the data. Therefore, we expect that introducing the alignment to SP professionals can foster innovation in AI safety, inspire novel techniques, and accelerate the development of robust, generalizable alignment frameworks that can be applied across diverse applications.

papers.title: Detection and Validation of Hidden Subgroup Disparities in Clinical AI
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) models used in clinical workflows often perform systematically differently across patient groups, raising concerns about equity and patient safety. Traditional subgroup analyses can expose such disparities only when rich metadata (e.g., patient demographics) is available and captures the sources of performance variation, conditions rarely met in practice. Algorithmic subgroup discovery methods offer a solution by identifying coherent groups from learned feature representations, but because true underlying stratifications are unknown, these methods are hard to evaluate. As a result, subgroup discovery has not been systematically applied or assessed for performance monitoring. Our main objective is to evaluate algorithmic subgroup discovery for performance monitoring, assessing the discovered subgroups' performance gaps and semantic coherence. Investigating cardiomegaly classification in a dataset of 223,228 chest X-rays, we showed that the discovered subgroups exhibited larger performance gaps (accuracies of 0.61-0.90) than traditional metadata-based analysis (0.80-0.94) and were frequently interpretable using patient, acquisition, and model metadata. As a proof of concept, we also showed that annotations from learned subgroups can be used to mitigate the biases they expose. We conclude that subgroup discovery is a practical and effective tool to enhance the performance validation and monitoring of ML systems in healthcare.

In the US, for example, the FDA had approved 1,247 AI-assisted medical devices by May 2025, with 523 of these approvals occurring within the last 24 months [30]. This growth reflects the vast potential of AI for patient care. However, research shows that even the most capable AI models can reinforce societal biases and fail unpredictably in clinical settings [33]. Consequently, regulatory agencies worldwide are tightening policies governing the development and deployment of medical AI to enhance its fairness and robustness.

A critical concern is that ML models may perform systematically differently across patient subgroups [27, 6, 14, 20]. This has hampered past attempts at safely deploying medical AI, particularly in underserved populations [27, 6]. Model performance can depend on many factors [10], including patient attributes (e.g., sex, age, ethnicity) and image characteristics (e.g., image quality, artifacts, device manufacturer). Chest X-rays model’s performances, for example, were shown to depend on biological sex [15, 31], support devices such as tracheotomy tubes and chest drains [13, 21], artifacts (e.g., laterality markers, highlight arrows) [8], and projection views [8] (anterior-posterior (AP) and posterior-anterior (PA)). Not understanding when and why an ML model systematically fails poses an avoidable danger to patients and delays the development of more robust models. Furthermore, systematic hidden model failures may violate regulators’ demands for safety and effectiveness for all intended use populations of a medical device.

These challenges are central to ensuring the safe and equitable application of AI in healthcare. Recent guidelines for trustworthy medical AI development, reporting, and deployment increasingly stress the importance of detailed subgroup analyses (e.g., TRIPOD+AI [7]) and systematic bias assessments (e.g., FUTURE-AI [16], PROBAST+AI [17]). In response, current frameworks call on AI developers and dataset curators to explicitly identify and annotate potential sources of bias throughout the model development pipeline. Together with clinical metadata, such as patient attributes and data-specific characteristics, the annotation can then be used to define patient subgroups to assess group fairness and evaluate model robustness. In general, the richer the available annotations, the more precisely relevant subgroups can be defined, increasing the chance of uncovering meaningful performance gaps.

However, acquiring such rich metadata is inherently challenging: dataset collection is both time- and personnel-intensive, and privacy concerns can limit the scope of metadata collection. In practice, this can lead to severe reporting gaps, as exposed by a recent scoping review of FDA-approved medical AI devices [18]. According to their analysis, less than 4% of approved devices provide information on race or ethnicity, less than 1% report on socioeconomic factors, and less than 19% report on age subgroups [18].

Even under ideal conditions, where multiple metadata attributes are available for a large, heterogeneous population, metadata may only partially align with the major hidden factors of variation that affect ML model performance. As a result, traditional metadata-defined subgroups may fail to reveal relevant performance gaps. Metadata annotations often reflect concepts that are meaningful for human interpretation and categorization, yet may be irrelevant to how machine learning models stratify data to make predictions. For example, stratifying a chest X-ray dataset by patient sex may be of limited value for auditing performance, since observed differences are often driven by correlated factors such as the presence of support devices (e.g., tubes and lines) rather than sex itself [31, 21]. In contrast, stratifying by projection (AP vs PA) is crucial. Standard radiology interpretation emphasizes that the PA view is preferred for assessing cardiomegaly because the AP view magnifies the cardiac silhouette [23]. Accordingly, deep learning models perform better on PA studies than on AP studies for cardiomegaly-related labels (see Table 2). Unrecognized subsets of data are referred to as hidden stratifications. As we will demonstrate in this study, even in one of the most comprehensively annotated large-scale datasets available, CheXpertPlus [5], which contains over 80 annotated factors including patient socio-demographics, comorbidities, and image characteristics for more than 200,000 samples, hidden stratifications remain prevalent. While manual inspection of model errors can sometimes reveal these issues, it is generally infeasible at scale and particularly challenging in medical imaging, where relevant differences across samples are often subtle.

Algorithmic subgroup discovery [9, 28] appears as a potential solution for this problem, as it can learn data stratifications that are relevant to a specific ML prediction model and dataset. The subgroup divisions are found by training unsupervised clustering methods (e.g., mixture models, k-means) on learned feature representations of the data. Aside from the predictions from the investigated model, subgroup discovery methods also leverage complementary knowledge from models trained with different objectives (e.g., multi-modal, generative) or with more data. These models have been used so far only on toy datasets with predefined biases for easier evaluation. We believe they might also be useful for performance evaluation and model surveillance, but they have yet to be proven effective in real-world medical contexts. The main challenge of using subgroup discovery techniques is how to validate the discovered subgroups, as hidden stratifications by definition lack ground-truth labels for evaluation.

papers.title: Magnetoelastic avalanches in magnetar crusts with plastic islands
papers.abstract: High-energy outbursts from magnetars may be associated with crustal failures or quakes. The magnetoelastic modes of the star can be excited to large amplitudes in such a framework, providing a natural explanation for the quasi-periodic oscillations observed in the X-ray tails of some events. However, previous calculations of torsional modes have been carried out assuming an intact crust without accounting for the failure itself. We develop a code in this paper that solves the axial sector of the linearised Einstein-Maxwell-Euler equations in a cavity that hosts inelastic regions or 'plastic islands'. As crustal elements are displaced, shear stresses are tracked as a function of time to allow cells to dynamically switch from elastic to inelastic states. The presence of islands in the crust promotes phase mixing and, when reflected waves mix constructively, large sections fail collectively ('avalanche') if the initial kick is strong enough. Transient spectral features are observed as a result of the progressive loss of elastic support, which may explain the temperamental nature of the oscillations observed following giant flares and magnetar storms.

papers.intro:
Magnetars are observationally classified by their propensity for bursting and flaring in the X- and gamma-ray bands. The giant flares unleashed from these sources constitute the brightest events ever observed in the local universe in terms of peak luminosity (Mazets et al., 1979; Palmer et al., 2005). Theoretical efforts to model the trigger of flares, including their rarity, rise times, and durations have led to significant shifts in our collective understanding of neutron-star phenomena (see Sotani, 2024, for a review). Given that quantum-electrodynamic, chromodynamic, and general-relativistic (GR) effects all interact non-trivially in magnetar environments (Suvorov and Pons, 2025; Wadiasingh et al., 2026, e.g.,), it is worth trying to understand how observed characteristics translate into a theoretical picture and vice versa.

A noteworthy feature associated with high-energy outbursts are quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs). Data from Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) for the August 1998 giant flare from SGR 1900+14, for instance, reveal a rich forest of spectral peaks throughout the decaying, pulsed tail spanning hundreds of seconds (Strohmayer and Watts, 2005). One interpretation of QPOs is that the quasinormal modes of the star were excited and subsequently imprinted on the signal (Strohmayer and Watts, 2006, e.g.,). By matching observed frequencies to the perturbed spectra of model stars one can, in principle, approach the inverse problem of constraining nuclear and magnetic substructure (Sotani et al., 2008; Gabler et al., 2018). As an example, Colaiuda and Kokkotas (2011) found that, for a 1.4​M⊙1.4M_{\odot} star with a field strength of ≈4×1015\approx 4\times 10^{15} G, the 28, 53 and 84 Hz QPOs observed from SGR 1900+14 could be identified as discrete Alfvén modes for some equations of state (EOS) or global modes in a star of the same mass but different EOS. Aside from this ambiguity, many subtle aspects complicate the identification problem; superfluidity (Gabler et al., 2012; Gabler et al., 2013) plus crust-core (van Hoven and Levin, 2011; Keer and Jones, 2015), crust-magnetosphere (Burnaz et al., 2025), and non-axisymmetric (Passamonti and Lander, 2013) couplings all shape the spectrum and excitation amplitudes.

Mechanical stresses build up over time in a magnetar crust through the combined actions of Hall drift and Ohmic dissipation (Pons and Viganò, 2019), which strain the lattice and inject twist into the magnetosphere (Beloborodov, 2009). In this respect, the two main models put forward to explain outbursts are either that (i) the magnetosphere becomes overtwisted and a reconnection is triggered, or (ii) those same mechanical stresses overwhelm the ionic lattice and instigate crustal failure (see Kaspi and Beloborodov, 2017, for a review). Although the sub-ms rise times of giant flares hint towards a magnetospheric origin (Lyutikov, 2015), the quake picture finds some favour in that modes are naturally excited to large amplitudes. Long-term magnetothermal evolutions allowing for quakes also reproduce observed outburst rates rather well (Pons and Perna, 2011; Perna and Pons, 2011).

However, previous quake-centered models for QPOs do not account for the fact that the crust must fail in the first place to excite the modes. In this paper, we explore how crustal failure itself affects the development of magnetoelastic modes, purportedly tied to QPOs, by tracking stresses in a time-domain simulation that can dynamically switch a cell from an elastic to an inelastic state. Generally speaking, the loss of elastic support in overstressed zones tends to decrease the frequency of torsional modes in a state-dependent manner that adjusts with the failure geometry. Moreover, if the crust is already in a volatile, prestressed state when some section fails, the torrent of magnetoelastic waves that are launched will induce further stresses at mode crests as they propagate, potentially driving an avalanche (Li et al., 2016). The formalism developed here has the added benefit that the choice of initial data can be tied directly to the initial quake geometry and is thus (arguably) less ad hoc.

We describe, and present the first results of, a new code that evolves the linearised conservation equations in an elastic crust with a prespecified failure geometry (‘plastic island’). Stresses are tracked during the evolution and, if further cells exceed a nominal von Mises threshold, have their elastic traction removed before the simulation resumes. We observe both prompt avalanching and beat-frequency phenomena such that, as more cells fail over time, the character of magnetoelastic modes drifts in time with energy cascading to smaller scales as fragmentary patterns emerge due to mode mixing (Heyvaerts and Priest, 1983; Gabler et al., 2012, see, e.g.,). Although linear, a time-domain solution to the mode problem with a dynamical elastic response adds a step of realism towards the characterisation of QPO phenomena.

Indeed, a key feature of the QPOs that has thus-far resisted adequate description is mode transience: dynamic spectra show oscillations apparently being excited and then decaying and/or re-emerging at later times with different frequencies, amplitudes, and longevities (Huppenkothen et al., 2014c; Pumpe et al., 2018). For instance, we show in Figure 1 the spectrum determined by Miller et al. (2019) following the December 2004 giant flare from SGR 1806–20. By eye one can see a feature around ∼25\sim 25 Hz that seems to become excited and then fade away, only to sporadically reemerge with a slightly different frequency and amplitude. Whether it is the ‘same mode’ is unclear; nevertheless, transient features may hint towards nonlinear phenomena such as mode-mode seeding (Sotani et al., 2024; Pnigouras and Lander, 2025), damping due to various couplings (Gabler et al., 2016), or – as we investigate here – dynamical mode mixing promoted by the progressive loss of elasticity (Kojima, 2024; Caplan and Bransgrove, 2026; Caplan et al., 2026, see also).

papers.title: ePNGCAT: the first eROSITA all-sky data release
papers.abstract: The eROSITA telescope array aboard the joint German--Russian Spektrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) mission delivered the deepest soft all-sky X-ray survey to date, scanning the entire sky more than four times between December 2019 and February 2022. The potential of the survey remains, however, hampered by the fact that only data for the half of the sky owned by the German consortium have been released publicly, whereas the other half remains accessible only to the Russian consortium, effectively making eROSITA a "half-sky" survey for most applications. The only publicly accessible all-sky "data product" as of 2026 is a single press-release image published in June 2020 jointly by both consortia to celebrate the completion of the first all-sky survey (eRASS1). Here I present the first all-sky eROSITA catalogue based on this image, containing around 63 thousand sources with an estimated completeness of about 50% above $3\times10^{-13}$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ in the 0.2-2.3 keV band and a positional accuracy of $\sim$1 arcmin, validated against the full eRASS1 catalogue for half the sky and against several external catalogues. The catalogue is thus comparable with 2RXS, the deepest truly all-sky survey generally available, and gives a first glimpse of the eastern Galactic hemisphere with eROSITA. In this hemisphere, about 11000 detected sources have no counterpart in ROSAT or other public X-ray catalogues and are expected to be genuine new X-ray sources. Besides the catalogue, I release calibrated HEALPix maps to facilitate studies of large-scale extended emission, such as the eROSITA bubbles, or of Galactic absorption that require full sky coverage (https://zenodo.org/records/23640281), as well as the complete analysis pipeline to make the results fully reproducible (https://github.com/doroshv/eropngcat).
papers.intro:
The joint German–Russian Spektrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) mission, carrying the eROSITA X-ray telescope array, was launched on 13 July 2019 (Sunyaev et al., 2021; Predehl et al., 2021) with the primary goal of conducting the first all-sky X-ray survey since ROSAT with major improvements in sensitivity, spatial resolution, and energy coverage. According to the collaboration agreement, data rights were split between the national scientific consortia, each getting half of the sky in Galactic coordinates separated by the meridian passing through the Galactic centre: the Russian consortium exploits half of the sky mostly observable from the Northern hemisphere (eastern), and the German consortium the other half. The survey can now be considered complete, and the German consortium (eROSITA_DE) has already released most of the data for general access in two data releases. The first included source catalogues, photon lists and source products for the first half-sky survey eRASS1 (Merloni et al., 2024), and the second includes data for the first three surveys (eRASS:3) and contains only source catalogues (Ramos-Ceja et al., 2026).

papers.title: Torque lags from magnetic unlocking in neutron stars and gravitational-wave smearing
papers.abstract: In canonical twisted-torus models of hydromagnetic equilibrium in neutron stars, the toroidal field is confined to regions where the poloidal field lines are closed. As spindown torques applied at the stellar surface need not be communicated efficiently to such magnetically-unlocked regions, toroidal zones or magnetic voids may rotate faster than the electromagnetically braked part of the star. Continuous gravitational radiation from the associated non-corotating quadrupole may therefore be emitted at higher frequencies than poloidal ones to a degree that depends on the diffusive microphysics controlling angular momentum transport. Dissipative processes can suppress long-lived lags, and we estimate the relevant timescales and their sensitivity to microphysics. Nevertheless, we show that a quadrupole component whose pattern speed differs from the observed spin is shifted, or smeared, over a finite frequency band. Single-template or narrowband upper limits therefore constrain only the quadrupole contribution lying inside the searched frequency window, not necessarily the full frequency-integrated quadrupole. Using simple models, we quantify this spectral redistribution over finite observation windows and discuss its implications for continuous-wave searches.

papers.intro:
Multimessenger data from the landmark gravitational-wave (GW) event GW170817 have proven invaluable in constraining both micro- (Ripley and others, 2023; Suvorov et al., 2024) and macrophysical (Bauswein and others, 2017; Abbott and others, 2018) elements of neutron star interiors. Another type of signal that is hoped to be observed soon involves continuous GW emission (Jaranowski et al., 1998; Abbott and others, 2008; Wette, 2023), as it holds promise for additional information that is inaccessible electromagnetically. For instance, hydromagnetic deformations produce a mass-quadrupole moment that varies in time as the star spins, leading to persistent radiation that encodes the magnetic geometry (Chandrasekhar and Fermi, 1953; Frieben and Rezzolla, 2012; Lasky and Melatos, 2013). With the exception of precession (Jones and Andersson, 2002; Gao and others, 2020; Suvorov and Kokkotas, 2021, e.g.,), estimates for continuous strains from magnetic deformations have thus far been explored in the context of rigid rotation: if the whole body spins at a linear frequency of νR\nu_{\rm R}, the dominant spectral feature resides at 2​νR2\nu_{\rm R}, which simplifies the analysis significantly.

Within minutes after birth, a solid crust forms and then grows as crystallisation proceeds through the outer layers as the neutron star cools. The magnetic field anchored there induces a torque which acts at the surface, leading to gradual spindown. However, causality demands that there is a delay, related to the propagation speed of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) modes or otherwise, before the core can respond (Easson, 1979). The theory behind torque lags has been studied extensively (Link and Epstein, 1991; Melatos, 2012) and has important implications for GW emission: if some regions of the star rotate differentially then the overall spectrum may not consist of a single peak but rather could be smeared.

Both analytic (Glampedakis and Lasky, 2015) and numerical (Anzuini and Melatos, 2020) investigations indicate that the magnetic field plays a crucial rôle in relieving torque lags. This is because the field is frozen into the fluid due to the conductivity of neutron-star matter (Baym et al., 1969), so that angular momentum is transported on the (fast) Alfvén timescale. On the other hand, the prevailing ‘twisted torus’ equilibrium model for the interior consists of a threading poloidal field with a stabilising toroidal field that is confined within the neutral curves (Braithwaite and Nordlund, 2006). Meissner expulsions in superconducting regions could also lead to disconnected, and possibly quite complicated magnetic topologies (Lander, 2024; Das et al., 2025; Das et al., 2026; Sedrakian and Rau, 2026).

In single-template searches, where phase-locking between electromagnetic and GW signals is assumed, any smearing will be missed and thus ‘toroidal quadrupoles’ could escape detection. In narrowband searches, by contrast, a typical mismatch of order δ=Δ​ν/νR∼10−3\delta=\Delta\nu/\nu_{\rm R}\sim 10^{-3} is permitted to account for possible mismatches between the electromagnetic and GW-emitting components (Aasi and others, 2015; Abbott and others, 2017; Abbott and others, 2019; Abbott and others, 2022a). Searches around harmonics of the spin frequency have also been carried out for known pulsars (Abbott and others, 2022b). These are related in spirit, although do not by themselves cover the quadrupole-weighted frequency distributions considered here. While a mismatch of order 10−310^{-3} may be sufficient for neutron stars within the band of ground-based interferometers if the poloidal field is sufficiently weak (Melatos, 2012), the key argument here is that signals associated with magnetic deformations should be spread over a range of frequencies rather than simply concentrated at ones that are electromagnetically out-of-phase.

papers.title: Bach-flat metrics and global regularity of conformal structures
papers.abstract: We study global regularity properties of conformal structures on compact manifolds with applications to conformally invariant variational problems. We find sharp conditions ensuring that a manifold equipped with a Riemannian metric of Sobolev class is conformally diffeomorphic to a smooth one. In particular, we prove that $W^{2,q}$ Bach-flat four-manifolds with $q > 2$ are smooth up to conformal diffeomorphisms. We also solve the Yamabe problem for $W^{2,q}$ metrics with $q > 2$ on three-manifolds under a mild conformal condition.

papers.title: Explicit Coleman integration over finite extensions of $\mathbb{Q}_p$
papers.abstract: Coleman integration is an important computational ingredient of the Chabauty--Coleman method and its extensions. We extend the Balakrishnan--Tuitman algorithm to general smooth projective curves with good reduction over arbitrary finite extensions of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, allowing both ramification and nontrivial residue degree. Given a suitable plane model and integral bases, we provide explicit precision bounds and an accompanying Magma implementation. As an application, a single-prime computation at $p=19$ over the unramified quadratic extension $\mathbb{Q}_{19^2}/\mathbb{Q}_{19}$ recovers all $35$ affine sporadic quadratic divisors on $X(s3,ns5)$ over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt5)$. Completeness is proved in an appendix using symmetric Chabauty and a Mordell--Weil sieve.

papers.title: The design and flight of the Payload for Ultrahigh Energy Observations (PUEO)
papers.abstract: Sources of cosmic rays at ultrahigh energies (UHE, $\gtrsim$ 1 EeV) are anticipated to give rise to neutrinos at similar energies by production via propagation interactions either within the source region or on cosmological scales. Measurements of the neutrino flux, flavor, and energy provide significant insight into those underlying processes governing UHE cosmic ray acceleration and propagation. Detecting neutrinos at these energies requires immense detector volumes due to their low predicted flux. We present the balloon-borne mission PUEO (Payload for Ultrahigh Energy Observations) which is an antenna array designed to detect the Askaryan emission from UHE neutrino interactions in the Antarctic ice. This paper reports on the design considerations and implementations for constructing PUEO, from the design parameters to the as-built validations.

papers.intro:
The Payload for Ultrahigh Energy Observations (PUEO) is a NASA Astrophysics Pioneers long-duration balloon mission designed to study ultrahigh-energy (UHE) particles (≳\gtrsim 1 EeV), UHE neutrinos in particular, from astrophysical and cosmogenic sources [1]. PUEO completed its 23-day flight over the Antarctic continent in the 2025–2026 austral summer aboard a 34.4334.43-Heavy MCF (million cubic feet) high-altitude balloon. After briefly summarizing the case for radio searches for UHE neutrinos, this paper is organized as follows. The description of event backgrounds and neutrino signals is discussed in section 2. The science instrument and gondola design including antenna validation and description of subsystems is presented in section 3. Section 4 presents the telemetry pathways and section 5 describes the preflight validation tests, followed by the calibration systems for in-flight performance validation in section 6. Finally, section 7 presents the flight path and a first look at the quality of the flight data.

UHE neutrinos serve as a unique probe of the highest energy phenomena in the Universe. As messengers, cosmic rays are susceptible to deflection in magnetic fields and to interactions with matter and radiation in the interstellar medium [2, 3]. Gamma rays are not susceptible to magnetic deflection, but at TeV energies and above, their horizon is limited by their ≲\lesssim Mpc attenuation lengths due to interactions with extragalactic background light and the cosmic microwave background [4]. It is expected that UHE neutrinos travel unimpeded by these effects and are capable of pointing back to their sources throughout the Universe. Instead, the difficulty in their use as messengers lies in their predicted extremely low flux at ultrahigh energies, and their very low interaction cross section in a detector target, compared to hadrons or photons. This necessitates the use of large detector volumes on the order of hundreds of cubic kilometers water equivalent to achieve measurements of the UHE neutrino flux on reasonable timescales.

IceCube has measured the neutrino spectrum up to PeV energies, but, due to the constraints of optical detection, its sensitivity is limited in the EeV energy range [5, 6]. This range includes the expected energies of cosmogenic neutrinos – neutrinos produced via interactions between UHE cosmic rays (UHECRs) and the cosmic microwave background [7, 8, 9]. The flux of astrophysical neutrinos, those produced directly from sources, is predicted to extend to these energies as well [10].

Optical neutrino detector experiments, such as IceCube and KM3Net, detect the Cherenkov light emitted by the particle showers resulting from neutrino interactions in their instrumented media. Rather than optical observations, PUEO detects the radio emission from these particle showers, which generated by the Askaryan effect [11]: neutrino interactions in the ice produce relativistic particle cascades that develop a negative charge excess, resulting in coherent broadband radio signatures emitted at and near the Cherenkov angle. The Askaryan effect has been observed in accelerator experiments using various forms of natural media, including ice, as the propagation medium [12, 13, 14].

Unlike optical light, radio waves at frequencies below ∼1.2\sim 1.2 GHz have kilometer-scale attenuation lengths in suitably cold polar ice [15], and this enables significantly larger detector volumes. Radio monitoring for Askaryan emission has been used in-ice by the RICE [16], ARA [17], ARIANNA [18], and RNO-G [19] projects. Monitoring the Antarctic ice sheet for these radio signatures has also been achieved from a long-duration balloon platform by four flights of the ANITA project [20].

Balloon-borne radio detectors trade limited flight times for the ability to observe large instantaneous volumes, 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) million km3, of ice from above. This large instantaneous volume necessitates low triggering thresholds, as signals can originate far from the instrument. PUEO and its predecessor ANITA were able to observe such large volumes by using large cylindrically-arranged broadband horn antennas, pointed in a manner that their fields-of-regard covered nearly the entire ice sheet below the payload from a suborbital vantage. The antennas had significant overlap in their views with many of their neighbors, which enabled interferometric imaging and geolocation of any impulse observed, to accuracies of fractions of a degree, far better than the 40∘ diameter beams of the individual antennas.

papers.title: Ethics by Configuration: AI Ethics Principles in Coding Agent Instructions
papers.abstract: As AI coding agents become integral to software development, projects increasingly utilise configuration files, such as context files and skills, to govern agent behaviour. While AI ethics principles are widely used in research and policy, little is known about whether and how they are reflected when developers configure coding agents. We studied ethics principles in 40,079 configuration files across 8,893 GitHub repositories. Using a validated large language model (LLM) classification, we measured the prevalence of ethics-related statements, and qualitatively analysed 702 stratified samples across 679 files to uncover the ethical considerations reflected in these files and the parties they concern. Ethics-related statements appeared in 39.4% of files and 61.5% of repositories; concentrated on accountability, transparency, privacy protection, and reliability; and occurred more often in task-specific files such as skills than in project-wide context files. Our qualitative analysis identified 30 categories of ethical considerations, which take the form of concrete rules for the agent. Accountability appeared mainly as requirements for human approval, transparency as explain and honestly report the agent's work, and fairness as accessibility and localisation. These considerations reveal a difference in focus. Whereas public ethics frameworks aim to protect society and end users, configuration files mainly concern developers, maintainers, and community members in the development workflow. Ethics-related content appeared mainly in prose-based files, and whether agents follow these instructions remains untested. We discuss the implications for practitioners, researchers, and policymakers.

papers.intro:
With the rise of AI coding agents, developers increasingly use them across software development activities, including requirements analysis, code writing, test generation, and documentation maintenance [35, 33], with autonomy ranging from close human supervision to independent operation [15]. Their outputs, from intermediate responses to final deliverables, can impact stakeholders across the software development life cycle (SDLC). For example, hallucinated or overly long responses can frustrate the developer working with the agent [38], while end users may benefit from added accessibility features [41]. Meanwhile, agent configuration files, such as AGENTS.md [8] and skills [20], provide additional context and guidance for the agent to achieve specific tasks. Against the backdrop of Agentic AI governance, ethics, and risk management – to “effectively deploy and de-risk the powerful capabilities of the technology” [24] – it is increasingly important to understand how ethical considerations are reflected in these configurations, which guide agent behaviour in software development.

Against the backdrop of Agentic AI governance, ethics, and risk management – to “effectively deploy and de-risk the powerful capabilities of the technology” [24] – it is increasingly important to understand how ethical considerations are reflected in these configurations, which guide agent behaviour in software development.

AI ethics principles, such as fairness and transparency, are widely discussed in research and policy [32]. For example, Australia’s AI Ethics Principles [2] and the EU’s Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI [14] set out principles AI systems should follow throughout their lifecycle. However, putting them into practice remains difficult. From a humanistic or philosophical perspective, “principles might be too vague, unenforceable, or downright clash with each other” [48] (citing [9]), and some frameworks are hard to enforce [26]. From an implementation perspective, Pant et al. [43] surveyed 100 AI practitioners and found that, while most were familiar with AI ethics, they faced general, technology-related, and human-related challenges in applying these principles. Gao et al. [22] analysed open-source AI model documentation and found ethical considerations mostly written as problem statements and use-case restrictions. These studies examine ethics through what practitioners report or document for human readers. With AI coding agents, however, developers can write ethical expectations into configuration files as instructions for agents to follow. Treude et al. [48] described these files as a developer-authored governance layer turning abstract ethics principles into natural-language directives. Inspecting 25 repositories, they found early examples of guidance on fairness, accessibility, sustainability, and tone. Yet, beyond this small sample, it remains unknown how common such guidance is, which principles it reflects, and in what form.

[17] to 40,079 configuration files from 8,893 open-source repositories across eight configuration mechanisms, such as context files, skills, and hooks. We use Australia’s AI Ethics Principles [2] to define the scope of ethics we considered. We classified each file with two open-source large language models (LLMs) and verified the classification against human annotations, checking both whether a file is ethics-related and whether its assigned principles are correct. We then drew 702 samples across 679 files for the eight principles and analysed them qualitatively, identifying 30 categories of ethical considerations reflected and the parties these considerations explicitly mention.

We use Australia’s AI Ethics Principles [2] to define the scope of ethics we considered. We classified each file with two open-source large language models (LLMs) and verified the classification against human annotations, checking both whether a file is ethics-related and whether its assigned principles are correct. Using this verified classification, we measured how prevalent ethics-related statements are and which principles they concern, and how repositories cover principles across their configuration files. We then drew 702 samples across 679 files for the eight principles and analysed them qualitatively, identifying 30 categories of ethical considerations reflected and the parties these considerations explicitly mention.

Our results show that ethics-related statements are common in agent configuration files, appearing in 39.4% of files and 61.5% of repositories, and concentrate on accountability, transparency and explainability, privacy protection and security, and reliability and safety. These statements appear more often in task-specific files, such as skills, commands, and subagents, than in project-wide context files. However, these statements have a narrower focus than the principles, concentrating on developers rather than on end users and society at large. In configuration files, the statements mostly concern the people closest to the agent: the developers working with it, project maintainers, and community members. Users of the resulting software are addressed less often, and society and the environment rarely. Transparency shows this focus clearly. Although explanations could be directed at the people who use the resulting software, almost all transparency excerpts concern reporting to developers and maintainers. We finally discuss the implications of these findings. Practitioners could complement approval with review and use hooks and permission settings to enforce specific constraints on agent actions. Researchers could build benchmarks that test whether ethical instructions change agent behaviour, and policymakers could provide guidance on how each principle applies when configuring an agent.

papers.title: Why Emission Spectral Profile of Diverse Fluoro-phores Look Alike with Thick Polymer Overlayers?
papers.abstract: Fluorescence from fluorophore-polymer overlayers reflects an interplay between molecular photo-physics and thickness dependent optical propagation. Combining spectrally resolved single mole-cule measurements, transition dipole moment orientation analysis and ensemble fluorescence, we show that structurally and photophysically distinct fluorophores can exhibit similar red shifted emission profiles under thick polymer overlayers even without additional reflecting surface. This similarity indicates a common optical transfer function imposed by the overlayer rather than a pure-ly fluorophore specific molecular response. Although local molecular interactions, excited state dy-namics and vibronic coupling govern intrinsic emission, the overlayer modifies detected spectra through refractive index contrast, dielectric boundary reflections, cavity effects and collection ge-ometry. Vibronic energy spacing distributions remain largely preserved as thickness changes, whereas spectral positions and relative intensities vary systematically. Thus, polymer thickness pri-marily reshapes detected spectrum through optical propagation and outcoupling while retaining vi-brational modes. Time dependent density functional theory identifies candidate Franck-Condon and Herzberg-Teller active dye modes contributing to spectral fluctuations and dipole reorientation.

papers.title: What Will Replace Pull Requests? Rethinking Software Collaboration for AI Agents
papers.abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) coding agents has put pull requests under pressure: agents open millions of pull requests per month, while some open-source projects have begun to restrict or disable external contributions. We investigate which alternatives to pull requests practitioners are proposing or adopting and what these changes mean for empirical software engineering research. We reviewed 50 gray-literature documents from 31 organizations or individuals published between October 2025 and October 2026, coding the problems each named, the mechanisms it proposed or adopted, which of five roles of pull requests (integration, review, rationale, accountability, and external contribution) each mechanism takes over, and the evidence offered. Most responses retained pull requests in some form, whether by adding tooling, attaching a new artifact, or restricting access, and restriction was the response most often reported as adopted. Several proposed alternatives moved review and rationale into agent conversations and session records, but only Zed reported using a replacement in practice. Only two documents outlined a replacement for external contribution, and neither reported adoption. Pull requests are changing in ways that pull-request datasets will not capture: reviews conducted in agent conversations leave no pull-request comments, and projects that disable pull requests disappear from samples of newly opened ones. We outline a research agenda on the effectiveness of the emerging alternatives, their consequences for open-source participation, and the adaptation of empirical methods.

papers.title: How Do Coding-Agent Harnesses Self-Evolve? An Empirical Study of Retrospective Adaptation
papers.abstract: Coding agents can adapt their harnesses, the software, configuration, and instructions used to run them, based on experience from earlier tasks, but whether these adaptations improve their behavior on later tasks remains unclear. We study \retro, a skill that asks an agent to review a completed session and propose harness changes, and ask what changes it proposes and whether implemented changes reduce repeated work on later tasks. We ran Claude Code on 30 SWE-bench Verified issues, qualitatively coded the 125 proposals from \retro, implemented 24, and evaluated 12 harness changes on later issues from the same repositories in fresh sessions with and without each change. Most proposals referred to an event in the session, but 18 of 43 lint-related proposals recommended a practice regardless of what had happened. Among the seven evaluations in which sessions without the change encountered the targeted problem, two changes eliminated the targeted action, one reduced its occurrence, four showed no reduction, and some changes added work on unrelated issues. Harness self-evolution requires more than generating and implementing changes: it needs ways to establish whether a change helps on later tasks and to revise or remove changes that do not.

papers.intro:
Coding agents such as Claude Code run inside a harness: the software, configuration, and instructions used to run the agent, including context files such as CLAUDE.md that the agent reads at the start of each session. A session that identifies how to run a repository’s tests or which tests already fail can retain this information in the harness for later sessions on the same repository. Retaining changes from completed sessions for use on later tasks, without retraining the model, is harness self-evolution [1]. Whether a retained change helps is a separate question: a change can describe one task rather than the repository, can stay outside a later session’s context, or can be read without changing what the agent does.

The /retro skill is one mechanism for producing such changes. It instructs a coding agent to conduct a retrospective: a review of a completed session that generates numbered proposals for harness changes requiring human approval [2]. In our study, Claude Code completed the task sessions, generated the retrospectives, and implemented approved proposals. Two large language models (LLMs) coded the proposals, and we selected which proposals to implement, chose the later issues, and labeled the outcomes, so the process we study is self-evolution with human selection and evaluation rather than an autonomous loop. We ask two research questions. RQ1: What harness changes does /retro propose, and to what extent are they based on events in the session? RQ2: Under what conditions do implemented adaptations prevent targeted actions on later issues from the same repository?

An implemented harness change is an adaptation. For each adaptation, we operationalize repeated work as a later session performing a specific action that the adaptation was intended to prevent, such as running tests with pytest when it is not installed, or rerunning tests on unmodified code to check whether an unrelated failure was already present. This is a behavioral measure, not a judgment that the action was unnecessary or that preventing it improved the task outcome. We transferred individual adaptations, each proposed after one session, to other issues in the same repository. By recording whether later sessions encountered the targeted problem, consulted the adaptation, and repeated the targeted action, we examine when a retained adaptation changes what the agent does.

papers.title: Toward Evidence-Based Agentic Software Engineering
papers.abstract: Task success rates and execution costs of agentic coding tools depend on both model and harness. The harness manages context, provides tools, and runs the agent loop. In empirical software engineering (SE) studies, comparisons that change model and harness together cannot isolate their effects. We qualitatively annotated 325 experiments reported in 146 peer-reviewed full papers published between 2025 and 2026. We examined the reported configurations and whether comparisons isolated harness effects, including harness configuration and version, model, tasks, and user interaction. The exact version of every harness used was reported for only 15 experiments. For five, the paper reported when the experiments were run, and for 31, authors shared execution traces for every session. Of the 226 experiments comparing harnesses, 35 never varied the harness in isolation. Based on this analysis, we derive requirements for a reference harness that the SE community can use for experiments. We call on the community to report all degrees of freedom of experiments with agentic coding tools and on SE venues to pilot dedicated tracks or special issues around a specified reference harness release. In these tracks, papers would hold the harness version fixed and vary features through separately versioned extensions to isolate feature effects and test their interactions.

papers.intro:
Task success rates and execution costs of agentic coding tools depend on both model and harness. An empirical software engineering (SE) study can attribute an outcome difference to the model or to the harness only if it identifies which model and which harness ran. The harness manages context, offers tools, enforces permissions, and runs the agent loop, in which a model chooses an action and receives its result. The inner harness comprises the code, including the built-in system prompt and tool schemas, while the outer harness is the configuration that users add, such as context files, settings, and hooks [1]. Model and harness interact as well. Zhang et al. ran three models on three harnesses and found that changing the harness reversed the ranking of two models in six of nine comparisons [2]. Kapoor et al. found that Claude models scored highest with one harness and OpenAI models with another [3].

papers.title: A Sharp Distributional Lower Bound for Planar Discrepancy
papers.abstract: We prove that the unnormalized discrepancy function of every $n$-point set in the unit square has absolute value at least $c\sqrt{1+\log n}$ on a set of measure at least $\eta$, with absolute constants $c,\eta>0$. Consequently, its $L_p$-quasinorm is bounded below by $c\,\eta^{1/p} \sqrt{1+\log n}$ for every $p>0$.

papers.title: A Borsuk-Ulam theorem for adaptive continuous measurements
papers.abstract: We prove a Borsuk-Ulam theorem for adaptive measurements: if $2^n\le m$, then any $n$ adaptively chosen continuous functionals take identical values at two antipodal points of any sphere in $\mathbb{R}^m$. Consequently, at least $\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil$ adaptive continuous measurements are needed to learn the vectors of a ball in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with an error smaller than its radius, which matches the recently obtained upper bound up to one measurement. The bound extends to Bernstein widths in Banach spaces. The main idea of the proof was found by Claude Fable 5, an AI model developed by Anthropic, and we document the development in a last section.

papers.title: Control of the Electronic and Atomic Structure of the Altermagnetic {\alpha}-MnTe Surface via Substrate-Induced Surfactants
papers.abstract: Altermagnets are a novel class of materials with unique momentum dependent spin-polarization of the electronic band structure, which opens up new avenues for spintronic devices. Altermagnetic {\alpha}-MnTe is particularly interesting for such applications due to its giant spin splitting and the persistence of altermagnetic order up to room temperature. Growth of thin films is, however, challenging and governed by interactions with the substrate. As a result, the surface of {\alpha}-MnTe thin films exhibits very different atomic structures in dependence of the substrate material. Whereas on SrF2(111) an atomically clean, perfectly (2x2) reconstructed surface forms, on InP(111)A the MnTe surface is always InTe terminated due to super-segregation of In from the substrate to the surface. Most strikingly, the InTe surfactant layer displays a quasi-periodic dislocation network to accommodate the InTe/MnTe lattice mismatch. This leads to the emergence of distinct surface states in dependence of surface termination that strongly affect the electronic band structure at the surface as shown by angle resolved photoemission and tunneling spectroscopy. Thus, control and characterization of the atomic structure of the surface is fundamentally important for understanding the properties of altermagnets and provides room for engineering and tailoring of spin-polarized states in actual devices.

The recent discovery of altermagnetism as a distinct new magnetic phase by Šmejkal et al. [33] has triggered tremendous theoretical and experimental efforts to explore its physical manifestations and to identify promising material candidates. The concept is based on symmetry considerations well established in topology and superconductivity, and applies them to unconventional forms of magnetism that combine a unique spin-polarized band structure with zero net magnetization. Consequently, altermagnets open up promising routes for power efficient electrical control of spin currents in spintronic devices via charge-to-spin conversion, anomalous Hall effect, and giant magnetoresistance [34, 35].

Finally, while this study focuses on MnTe on InP and SrF2\mathrm{SrF}_{2}, we emphasize that similar effects are expected for films grown on other substrates such as GaAs or van der Waals bonded V-VI chalcogenide buffer layers, offering a new paradigm for engineering altermagnetic heterostructures.

papers.title: Contributions of massive stars and classical novae to Galactic 26Al
papers.abstract: The radioactive isotope 26Al is believed to be mainly produced by massive stars and ejected into the interstellar medium through their winds and supernovae. Due to its lifetime of 1.04 Myr, it traces recent nucleosynthesis and star formation. 60Fe is a similarly long-lived (lifetime 3.8 Myr) isotope, and only originating in ccSNe. Stellar evolution models in combination with Galactic Chemical Evolution (GCE) models tend to over-predict the 60Fe/26Al ratio. Population synthesis models that attempt to explain both, the 26Al mass in the Galaxy and its spatial distribution, only match the observational constraints with an enhanced star formation rate (SFR) of >5 Msun/yr. Classical novae may contribute to the 26Al production, potentially lowering the SFR inferred from massive stars and alleviating tension in the 60Fe/26Al ratio. However, previous studies suggest their contribution is negligible or < 10%. In this work we aim to determine the mass distribution of 26Al as a function of Galactocentric radius and estimate the contribution of (very) massive stars and classical novae to the 1.8 MeV signal. We are using 20 yr of INTEGRAL/SPI observations of the gamma-ray line at 1.8 MeV to test different assumptions on the radial structure of 26Al and compare the resulting mass distribution to different GCE models. For our baseline analysis, all tested source models prefer substantial nova contributions, with best-fit fractions of 77-84%. This alleviates tension in the 60Fe/26Al ratio and lowers the SFR from 26Al measurements accordingly to 1-2 Msun/yr. While it is difficult to gauge both contributions directly, next generation MeV telescopes can potentially identify individual massive stars, such as Gamma-2-Velorum.

The radioactive isotope 
ucAl26 is characterized by its 1.8091.809 MeV γ\gamma-ray line. Due to its intermediate lifetime of τ=1.04	au=1.04 Myr, it is considered to be an excellent tracer of the ongoing nucleosynthesis in our Galaxy (Diehl et al., 2006). It is long-lived enough to be ejected from stars into the interstellar medium (ISM), either during the wind phase or through core-collapse supernovae (ccSNe), before decaying. Compared to the timescale of Galactic evolution, the lifetime is still small, so that we only observe recently produced 
ucAl26. The most recent 1.8 MeV all-sky map from measurements with INTEGRAL/SPI (Winkler et al., 2003; Vedrenne et al., 2003), Fig. 1 (Bouchet et al., 2015), shows extended emission along the Galactic plane, supporting the consensus idea that the isotope originates in regions of massive-star groups, based on the clumpy morphology that is coincident with nearby OB associations (Knödlseder, 1999).

papers.title: Virtual defect mediated quantum melting in supersolids
papers.abstract: The current understanding of supersolid melting is largely based on mean-field theories predicting that such transitions arise from a structural energy minimization mechanism. Here, we show that soft-core quasi-one-dimensional supersolids stabilized by a shallow external lattice can instead melt at zero temperature into a superfluid phase with quasi-long-range positional order through the proliferation of virtual soliton--antisoliton pairs, leading to a Kosterlitz--Thouless transition. We derive the corresponding Renormalization Group equations from first principles and use them to determine the critical properties of the system. Remarkably, the proliferation of topological defects near criticality strongly renormalizes both the density modulation and the superfluidity behavior. The transition described is intrinsically a beyond mean-field effect, since the external lattice produces only a smooth crossover between weakly and strongly modulated states at the mean-field level.

papers.title: From Data Footprints to Researcher Fingerprints: Temporal Ego-centric Research Group Detection in Scientific Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Understanding who researchers collaborate with, when and how their research groups form, and how these evolve over time is a foundational prerequisite for constructing multidimensional, evidence-based researcher fingerprints -- a requirement that has become increasingly urgent in the context of ongoing reforms in research evaluation advocated by initiatives such as DORA, the Leiden Manifesto, and CoARA. In this paper, we propose an egocentric approach for fine-grained research group detection, operating at the scale of individual researchers' ego networks, as extracted from Scientific Knowledge Graphs (SKGs), and requiring the ego node to be present in all identified research groups -- a constraint that is not merely technical but reflects a commitment to researcher-centred analysis. Our approach builds on the Leiden algorithm as its computational core and is grounded in SKGs, which provide the heterogeneous, open scholarly metadata necessary to trace collaboration patterns at scale in a reproducible and transparent manner. We evaluate the proposed method through a user evaluation involving 10 researchers with diverse backgrounds and career stages, demonstrating its ability to surface meaningful and interpretable collaboration structures. The research groups identified constitute the structural scaffold upon which richer characterisations of scholarly identity -- including roles, seniority, contribution types, and publication patterns -- can be built in subsequent work, contributing to the broader goal of fairer and more transparent research assessment.

papers.title: Task Relevance-Driven Prompt Expansion for Federated Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Federated continual learning (FCL) has attracted considerable interest by enabling local clients to continually acquire knowledge from new tasks. However, most FCL methods assume that the global server has prior knowledge of the arrival times and number of categories for new tasks, which is unrealistic in the real world. Furthermore, they neglect the importance of positive inter-task semantic relationships when learning new tasks and are significantly affected by irrelevant relationships from old tasks, thereby exacerbating catastrophic forgetting. To resolve the above challenges, we develop a novel Task Relevance-driven Prompt Expansion (TRPE) model. Specifically, to eliminate the reliance on prior knowledge of new tasks, we propose an out-of-distribution detector to identify the arrival of new tasks within local clients, along with a radius-adaptive DBSCAN to infer the quantity of categories in new tasks on the proxy server. Moreover, to explore positive inter-task relationships, we calculate the affinity between the original gradient for learning new task and its gradient orthogonal to the feature space of old tasks to evaluate semantic relevance between old and new tasks from a global perspective. Then, we use this global task relevance to determine the key-prompt pair for new tasks and identify highly related old tasks. After concatenating their prompts for training, we can leverage such positive inter-task relations to improve the continual learning of newly arriving tasks. To balance the learning of new tasks and the forgetting of old ones, a soft orthogonality constraint is applied to the local key and prompt gradients. Experiments spanning diverse datasets and backbones confirm the efficacy of our TRPE model.

papers.intro:
Federated learning (FL) [60, 73, 23, 25] is a widely adopted collaborative training paradigm that enables multiple distributed local clients to develop a global model while protecting the privacy of their local data [55, 75]. Unlike traditional approaches that require centralizing data, FL allows each client to train the model locally on their own data and communicate only the necessary model updates with a global server [58, 23, 25]. In recent decades, federated learning has achieved significant success in addressing growing concerns over data privacy and security [6, 38, 25], making it particularly valuable in information-sensitive applications such as finance [32], healthcare [9], and mobile technology [31]. While successful, most FL approaches [58, 6] aim to learn a single task with a fixed dataset on local clients. They struggle to continually learn a sequence of new tasks over time and may experience catastrophic forgetting [44, 74] of old tasks when local clients do not have memory to store all training samples from previous tasks. To tackle this limitation, recent studies have focused on federated continual learning (FCL) [13, 69, 10]. As presented in Fig. 1, FCL allows local clients to learn new tasks consecutively while retaining knowledge from previous tasks, facilitating applications in areas such as healthcare and smart cities.

They struggle to continually learn a sequence of new tasks over time and may experience catastrophic forgetting [44, 74] of old tasks when local clients do not have memory to store all training samples from previous tasks. To tackle this limitation, recent studies have focused on federated continual learning (FCL) [13, 69, 10]. As presented in Fig. 1, FCL allows local clients to learn new tasks consecutively while retaining knowledge from previous tasks, facilitating applications in areas such as healthcare and smart cities.

Generally, mainstream studies on FCL [37, 12, 34, 17] can be broadly classified into two categories: rehearsal-based and rehearsal-free methods. The former allocates a fixed rehearsal buffer to retain some samples from old tasks [13, 10], which can help mitigate catastrophic forgetting by retraining the global model using the training data from both old and new tasks. Unfortunately, this exemplar buffer may raise privacy concerns in many applications [54], further limiting its practical adoption. To address this issue, rehearsal-free FCL approaches apply a regularization term to the global model to preserve the semantic information of old tasks [34, 69] or utilize generative models to replay the training data of old tasks [28, 2]. Nevertheless, they require transmitting the entire model to learn new tasks continuously, resulting in high communication overhead. In light of this, some rehearsal-free FCL methods [41, 37] incorporate prompt learning [65, 62] with FL to enhance communication efficiency. They inject task-specific prompts into a pretrained vision transformer (ViT) [14], achieving state-of-the-art performance in tackling catastrophic forgetting and thereby driving recent advancements in FCL [17].

However, the aforementioned FCL methods [13, 69, 34, 10, 28] unreasonably assume that the global server knows both the arrival times and the total class number of new tasks in advance. This assumption violates privacy protection requirement of FCL [54]. Once this prior knowledge is unavailable, they cannot continue to learn new tasks. Moreover, existing FCL methods [29, 54, 17] overlook the importance of inherent semantic relationships between new and old tasks in addressing forgetting of previous tasks while facilitating the learning of newly arriving tasks. They cannot determine which types of inter-task relationships are effective for facilitating the learning of new tasks from a global perspective, and the improper use of irrelevant semantic relations may exacerbate catastrophic forgetting. To better comprehend these challenges, we introduce an intuitive example in this paper. The structural information of the bus learned from old tasks can provide positive guidance for learning the truck in new tasks, and their shared characteristics help mitigate forgetting related to the bus. Some irrelevant relations, such as correlations in modalities and appearances between the bus and truck, may hinder the learning of new tasks. To explore positive semantic relations between the bus and truck, the global server is assumed to know in advance when local clients receive novel tasks, which is not realistic in the real world.

papers.title: Lax Pair for the Kirchhoff-Pohozaev equation
papers.abstract: We prove that the Kirchhoff-Pohozaev equation on any compact connected Riemannian manifold without boundary admits a Lax pair $(L,B)$, where $L$ is a self-adjoint finite-rank perturbation of the Laplace-Beltrami operator and $B$ is a skew-adjoint operator of finite rank, both depending analytically on the phase space variables. We study the spectrum of $L$ using the perturbative determinant which is known to determine its spectrum and to admit a product representation similar to that of the generating function in KdV. We use this to show that the dynamics of the integrals of motion constructed in \cite{BoitiManfrin2026,BHMP,campos} admits a Lax pair formulation with the same operator $L$ and to get a new proof of the involutivity of these integrals.
