papers.title: SoFTg: A hybrid segmentation framework for solar granulation revealing turbulent convection statistics at DKIST scales
papers.abstract: In this work, we present Solar Feature Tracking: granules (SoFTg), a new hybrid algorithm within the SoFT library designed for the segmentation and tracking of solar granulation. By combining a heuristic approach based on a custom adaptive-thresholding technique with the speed and robustness of deep-learning methods, SoFTg provides a fast, reliable and user-friendly solution for granule segmentation, followed by the standard SoFT approach for tracking. We present a comprehensive evaluation of the algorithm's performance using multiple metrics and analyse the different stages of the processing pipeline. The method is tested on three datasets acquired with the Visible Broadband Imager operating in the red continuum at the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope in Maui, Hawaii. We present distributions of both the lifetime and equivalent diameter of the thousands of granules tracked, providing, for the first time, statistically robust evidence of turbulent convection at the spatial scales now accessible through the high-resolution imaging capabilities of DKIST.

papers.title: Multiplex relational event models of self-reported and perceived gossip
papers.abstract:
Gossiping is a complex social phenomenon that unfolds through multiple types of relations. Among other things, individuals may initiate gossiping about others as a result of believing themselves to be the target of gossip. These two processes, i.e., gossiping and gossip perception, form a dynamic multiplex network, where self-reported and perceived gossip ties coexist and can influence each other over time. We develop a multiplex relational event model to study the joint evolution of these two processes.
  The proposed model includes endogeneous covariates that capture the influence of events occurring within one layer, as well as events occurring on the other layer, on the rate of self-reported and perceived gossiping. We analyze survey data collected annually from 44 secondary schools in Hungary. We show how a multiplex relational event model, including linear, smooth and random effects, is able to describe the social mechanisms operating within and between self-reported and perceived gossiping and to capture how these two layers influence each other over time.
papers.intro:
Gossiping consists of interactions among individuals who exchange information and opinions about others. Such interactions can be of a positive nature, and result in the strengthening of social bonds, but also of a negative nature, such as when they contribute to bullying (Espelage et al., 2007; Kisfalusi, 2018). The general aim of this paper is to describe the underlying dynamics of gossiping. To this end, different dimensions of gossiping are important. Individual gossiping about another person may be affected, among other things, by the gossiper perceiving that gossiping is directed towards them by that person. This means that the two processes are interdependent, with perceived gossiping influencing subsequent gossiping behaviour, and vice versa. In order to account for these different processes, and have a more complete characterization of the gossiping dynamics, this paper considers a multiplex representation of gossiping, where different types of gossiping can influence each other over time.

Several approaches have been developed for modelling multiplex networks, both in the case of static and dynamic networks (Wang, 2013; Chen, 2021; Snijders et al., 2013). These approaches are primarily formulated in terms of network ties or network states, rather than time-ordered relational events. The latter is instead the case of gossiping, where events happen instantaneously in continuous time. Motivated by this, Poda et al. (2026) develop a relational event model of self-reported gossiping. However, they do not account for the effect of perceived gossiping, or, in general, of other types of gossiping that may effect self-reporting gossiping. Hong and Niezink (2026), on the other hand, study specifically the dependence between self-reported and perceived gossiping. However, the multiplex p2p_{2} model that they develop is only suitable for static gossiping data, while information on time ordering plays a key role in understanding the dynamics of gossiping. Moreover, their analysis focuses primarily on whether individuals accurately perceive gossiping directed towards them, rather than on the role of perceived gossiping in influencing future gossiping behaviour and vice versa.

To address these limitations, in this paper, we propose a multiplex Relational Event Model (REM). This is an extension of standard REMs for jointly modelling time-ordered events across multiple relational layers. In the specific case of gossiping, this model allows to account for self-reported and perceived gossiping as two interdependent relational event processes, allowing past interactions in one layer to affect subsequent interactions in the other. We illustrate the proposed framework with an empirical application to longitudinal school survey data collected annually from a number of secondary school classes in Hungary (Vörös et al., 2025). Two questions in the survey specifically focus on self-reported and perceived gossiping, allowing us to study their interconnected dynamics.

We define endogenous covariates that explicitly account for the multiplex nature of the relations. In this way, the model accounts for dependences both within each event type and between different event types. We then develop statistical inference for multiplex REMs on rather generic relational data structures. In particular, we start from the availability of complete relational event data and then move to the case of aggregated counts across time intervals. Finally, we also consider the case of right-censored interval-time data. This is particularly relevant for the empirical illustration, where for each layer we only know whether at least one gossiping event of that type occurred during the time period covered by each survey. In all these cases, we show how efficient generalized additive models can be used to fit multiplex REMs. A combination of linear, smooth and random effects can therefore be included to capture the complexity of the underlying process and quantify the effects of important drivers.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 motivates the methodological development using the school survey data from Vörös et al. (2025). We then introduce the multiplex REM in section 3, including the definition of endogenous covariates across the different multiplex layers. Section 4 presents inferential approaches for complete, aggregated and censored relational event data. Section 5 evaluates the proposed method through simulation studies, showing the advantages of a multiplex formulation of the problem compared to using standard REMs on each separate layer with no cross-layer dependences. Finally, section 6 goes back to the motivating example and studies the dynamics of perceived and self-reported gossiping via a suitably defined multiplex REM, with complex within-layer and between-layer linear and smooth effects.

papers.title: Morse index characterization of the Veronese projective plane
papers.abstract: Following Simons' seminal work in 1968, every closed, connected, embedded minimal surface in the four-sphere that is not totally geodesic has Morse index at least five. In this paper, we prove that equality holds if and only if the surface is congruent to the Veronese projective plane. Relying on recent advances by Bernstein and Ketover, this characterization settles Kusner's 1996 conjecture on the minimizers of the Willmore functional in dimension four for surfaces whose normal bundle has nonzero Euler number. This is always the case, in particular, for embeddings of nonorientable surfaces whose orientation double cover has even genus.

papers.intro:
Minimal surfaces are critical points of the area functional, and their Morse index is the maximal dimension of a space of smooth normal variations on which the second variation is negative definite. The index thus quantifies instability. It also connects variational existence theorems to geometric classification: an upper bound on the index of a surface produced by a variational construction can become a rigidity statement when the surfaces of low index are understood.

papers.title: A Congestion-Aware RDMA Front-End for LST Advanced Camera Readout
papers.abstract: The Advanced Camera (AdvCam) upgrade of the Large-Sized Telescopes (LSTs) calls for a fully digital readout in which each front-end board streams data to the event-building servers over commercial 10 Gb/s Ethernet, using an FPGA implementation of Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) over Converged Ethernet v2 (RoCEv2). In a previous work, a customized RoCEv2 core integrated with the SLAC SURF UDP/MAC stack was shown to sustain near-line-rate data transfers from a Xilinx KCU105 to a server equipped with a Mellanox ConnectX-5 NIC. However, the AdvCam topology is an incast funnel: many 10 GbE links converge onto a single uplink, and bare Priority Flow Control (PFC) congestion management protocol is known to be unfair and to suffer from head-of-line blocking. This work extends the previous design with the Data Center Quantized Congestion Notification (DCQCN) algorithm. A protocol-level ns-3 simulation is used to validate the DCQCN dynamics and to explore the parameter space; an FPGA rate-limiter integrated into the SURF MAC reacts to incoming Congestion Notification Packets (CNPs) according to the DCQCN state machine; a cocotb testbench with an emulated Python switch verifies the firmware end-to-end against a Soft-RoCE receiver; and a three-sender incast hardware test on a DCQCN-enabled commercial switch reproduces the canonical fair-share, reactive-redistribution, and saw-tooth behaviour expected from a commercial RDMA NIC. The internal rate-limiter register is shown to track the measured RoCEv2 throughput cycle by cycle.

papers.intro:
The Large-Sized Telescopes (LSTs) are designed to capture the lowest-energy gamma rays observed by ground-based imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescope arrays. Their Advanced Camera (AdvCam) upgrade [1], based on Silicon Photo Multipliers (SiPMs), is expected to increase the number of channels by a factor of four (to about 8000 pixels per camera) and to raise the data throughput by roughly an order of magnitude relative to the legacy PhotoMultiplier Tube (PMT) design [2]. To cope with this throughput while keeping the on-detector electronics affordable and serviceable, the AdvCam readout adopts a fully digital architecture in which the front-end board itself performs digitization, local triggering, packetization, and direct RDMA WRITE transfer to the event-building servers over a commercial Ethernet fabric, with no intermediate custom backend layer.

RDMA assumes a lossless fabric: a single dropped packet triggers a Go-Back-N retransmission [4] that collapses throughput. It is now the standard congestion-control algorithm in commercial RDMA deployments and is supported, with varying levels of compliance, by all major vendors of RDMA-capable NICs.

papers.title: Critical velocity and dissipation mechanism in finite superfluid $^4$He nanodroplets
papers.abstract: A hallmark of superfluidity is the frictionless motion of an object below the Landau critical velocity; Whether this concept applies to nanoscale droplets remains unclear. Using time-dependent density functional theory, we investigate the motion of a sodium atom on the surface and inside a superfluid helium nanodroplet. For surface motion, we identify a critical velocity above which energy dissipation through ripplon excitation and the formation of surface-bound quantized vortices leads to rapid deceleration. Inside the droplet, the atom is slowed down to a steady-state velocity that depends on the initial speed, contrasting experiments reporting a critical velocity for dopants ejected from droplets [Phys. Rev. Lett. 111, 153002 (2013)]. Remarkably, the velocity of the ejected atom is nearly independent of its initial velocity. We demonstrate that this behavior results from the bursting of the bubble surrounding the atom at the droplet surface, challenging the previous experimental interpretation.

papers.title: Learning Structured Sparsity for Large Models: Bridging Model Compressibility and Efficient Inference
papers.abstract: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

papers.intro:
Scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020) motivate larger models for improved quality, while their memory and computational demands increase reliance on cloud infrastructure with high-end accelerators. However, network connectivity can be unstable in underwater and rescue operations (Stojanovic & Preisig, 2009; Deng et al., 2013; Gunn & Anderson, 2015). Safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving require on-device decisions to avoid cloud communication delays (Liu et al., 2019; Kuutti et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2025; Bodmer et al., 2026), while privacy requirements can prevent sensitive data from being uploaded (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016; Shi et al., 2016). These constraints require large-model inference to move from the cloud to resource-constrained edge devices. Fitting large models within limited memory and achieving low inference latency with the available computational resources are the two critical challenges of this transition. The latency requirement is particularly important in feedback control, where inference latency adds to loop delay and excessive delays can degrade closed-loop performance or destabilize the system, compromising safety (Shin & Cui, 1995; Findeisen & Allgöwer, 2004; Ma et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2023; Nan et al., 2026).

Varying memory budgets across edge devices call for elastic compression of a single trained checkpoint to multiple model sizes. SALAAD (Ma et al., 2026a) enables such elastic compression by learning sparse-and-low-rank (SLR) representations for each linear projection11 1 Here, linear projection refers to a learned linear map in the attention (query/key/value/output) or multi-layer perceptron (MLP; up/gate/down) modules. Embeddings and the language model head are excluded unless noted. during pretraining. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into lower inference latency. Unstructured SLR saves static memory but incurs higher inference latency (see Appendix A.1). We identify the overhead from irregular memory access in unstructured sparse operations as a critical barrier to deploying large models on edge devices. We therefore induce structured sparsity during pretraining, allowing the SLR components to adapt jointly to the structural constraints.

papers.title: Phronix: The Capability-Centric Learning Paradigm for Agents
papers.abstract: Scientific computing increasingly relies on large language model-based agents for performance engineering tasks such as instrumentation, analysis, and workflow porting. However, agent effectiveness depends heavily on the surrounding harness, which typically relies on manually written skills and curated memory. This limits autonomous learning, forcing agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions rather than retain and reuse knowledge from prior executions. We introduce Phronix, a capability-centric learning paradigm that enables agentic harnesses to acquire, validate, and refine reusable capabilities from their own executions. Phronix operates through a predictor-validator-corrector loop: MCP tools and associated skills propose solutions, tool executions validate them, and observed outcomes refine the stored capabilities. It distills every observed interaction into a capability store and researches a failing task rather than abandoning it. First, such learned capabilities solve a recurring task on the first attempt in 93-95% of cases across every model, significantly reducing solution non-determinism and improving reliability. Second, Phronix turns an agent's own execution into 7.6-30.8 durable capabilities per task without user instruction, and creation falls below two once the needed capability exists. Third, warm-start runs consume only 0.38-0.40 million tokens per task, which is three to four times less than a single baseline attempt, while a cold-start costs no more than the baseline. On the 1000 Genome Pegasus workflow, instrumenting a production application for I/O performance analysis, Phronix passes all 11 correctness checks against six for the baseline harness, and also lifts the task solving rates of two cheaper models from 29% and 27% of SWE-bench tasks solved to 91% and 87%, respectively, matching the performance of the most expensive evaluated model.

papers.intro:
Scientific computing has begun to delegate its routine engineering to LLM (LLM) agents, which auto-tune HPC code on production supercomputers [13], diagnose parallel I/O performance [11], and work on the repositories and pipelines behind published results [10, 5]. The work delegated there is repetitive rather than novel, such as instrumenting an application, characterizing where a run spends its time, and repeating that for the next application, input scale, and system. An agent, however, is more than a model which operates withing a harness [34], where the LLM proposes each step and observes its result [35], tools exposed through interfaces such as the MCP (MCP) [29, 3] let it touch the world, skills accumulate how a class of task is done [33, 1], memory carries what earlier sessions learned past the context window [24], and the harness orchestrates them into the loop the agent runs. An agent that is good at such a task once should be good at it every time, and it is the harness, not the model, that determines whether it is, because the harness governs how much human steering a task requires and how many tokens and retries it consumes. Improving agent effectiveness is consequently as much a harness problem as it is a model problem.

Traditionally, LLM were accessed through web chat interfaces such as Open WebUI [20], ChatGPT [21], and Claude [2], which wrap a model in a conversation backed by a fixed set of tools [19, 29, 27]. As these interfaces matured, developers built more complex and capable command-line harnesses such as Codex [22] and OpenCode [23], which let users plug in different skills and agents for each task. State-of-the-art harnesses such as Claude Code [1] and Stakpak [31] add memory that persists across sessions, together with rulebooks that curate the standard operating procedure for a class of task. Along this timeline, each harness has become more adaptable than the last, and that adaptation is increasingly carried by skills and memory rather than by the interface itself [33, 30, 25, 24]. All of them are driven primarily by human, who writes the skill or rulebook that a complex task needs before it is assigned.

As these interfaces matured, developers built more complex and capable command-line harnesses such as Codex [22] and OpenCode [23], which let users plug in different skills and agents for each task. State-of-the-art harnesses such as Claude Code [1] and Stakpak [31] add memory that persists across sessions, together with rulebooks that curate the standard operating procedure for a class of task. Along this timeline, each harness has become more adaptable than the last, and that adaptation is increasingly carried by skills and memory rather than by the interface itself [33, 30, 25, 24]. All of them are driven primarily by human, who writes the skill or rulebook that a complex task needs before it is assigned.

Despite support for skills and persistent memory, existing harnesses often rely on users to decide what knowledge to retain and reuse, limiting their ability to learn autonomously from completed tasks. For an agent to learn from its own work instead, the harness must overcome three challenges that each keep the user in the learning loop. First, solution non-determinism prevents an agent from reproducing a solution it has already found, because the skills and models of the harness keep changing how they solve the same problem, so a task solved once may be solved differently or not at all when it recurs. Second, manual tracking requires users to identify and preserve useful information from agent executions, so the experience a task produced is lost before it can be reused. Third, manual learning leaves the conversion of that experience into reusable knowledge to a user who must ask for a skill by name, so an agent that repeats a task never becomes better at it. These challenges are particularly significant in scientific computing, where the same instrumentation, performance analysis, and workflow porting recur across applications and systems. Addressing them requires a learning paradigm in which agents organically build, correct, and learn capabilities without waiting for a user to do so on their behalf.

For an agent to learn from its own work instead, the harness must overcome three challenges that each keep the user in the learning loop. First, solution non-determinism prevents an agent from reproducing a solution it has already found, because the skills and models of the harness keep changing how they solve the same problem, so a task solved once may be solved differently or not at all when it recurs. Second, manual tracking requires users to identify and preserve useful information from agent executions, so the experience a task produced is lost before it can be reused. Third, manual learning leaves the conversion of that experience into reusable knowledge to a user who must ask for a skill by name, so an agent that repeats a task never becomes better at it. These challenges are particularly significant in scientific computing, where the same instrumentation, performance analysis, and workflow porting recur across applications and systems. Addressing them requires a learning paradigm in which agents organically build, correct, and learn capabilities without waiting for a user to do so on their behalf.

We present Phronix, a learning paradigm that makes building capabilities the first-class citizen of the harness and runs every one of them as a predictor–validator–corrector loop, where a capability generates an artifact, tool-based validation deterministically rules on its correctness, and the findings of that ruling correct the capability for future use rather than working around it. papers.title: Agentic Hazard Mapper: Emulating Expert Map-Making with AI Agents for Risk Communication
papers.abstract: Hazard maps are essential tools for public risk communication, preparedness, and evacuation planning, yet effective cartographic design is not always ensured due to limited access to cartographic expertise across local governments and communities. We present Agentic Hazard Mapper, a multi-agent system that automates hazard-map production by emulating professional cartographic workflows and iterative design trade-offs while adapting design decisions to different data, locations, and hazard contexts. We conducted a formative study with map experts to inform the system design, followed by a user study and interviews with map experts and hazard practitioners. The generated maps improved participants' spatial understanding and evacuation-planning performance, reduced perceived workload and task completion time, and were generally preferred over corresponding municipal maps. We further discuss human oversight, adaptation across users and communication contexts, and opportunities to extend agentic support across broader stages of hazard-map production and risk communication.

papers.title: A Composite Rest-Frame UV Spectrum of Galaxies at $5.7 < z < 6.9$: Ionization, Outflows, and Implications for Intergalactic Metal Enrichment
papers.abstract: We present a stacked JWST/NIRSpec spectrum of 104 galaxies at $\lambda_{\rm rest}=1200\unicode{x2013}2000\;\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$ to study nebular emission and absorption from the interstellar medium (ISM) and stellar winds. The sample is drawn from known [O III] emitters with mean redshift $z=6.50$, absolute UV magnitude $M_\mathrm{UV}=-20.7$, and stellar mass $M_{\star}=10^{8.93}\;\mathrm{M_\odot}$. The stacked continuum closely resembles lower-redshift Lyman Break Galaxy composites, with a few notable differences. Ly$\;\alpha$ has comparable strength and is redshifted relative to the [O III] systemic frame, consistent with production in gaseous outflows. High-ionization emission lines including O III], C III], and He II are slightly stronger than in lower-redshift stacks but exhibit narrow widths, disfavoring ionization from a broad-line AGN. Emission-line ratios slightly favor ionization by a hard stellar continuum, though a contribution from a narrow-line nuclear source cannot be strictly excluded. Numerous strong absorption lines at both high and low ionization are blueshifted by $\sim200\;\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, again indicating outflows driven by stellar winds or entrained metal-enriched ISM. A simple model suggests that at $z\sim6.5$ most star-forming galaxies are too young for winds at these velocities to propagate beyond $\sim3\unicode{x2013}9$ proper kpc, implying that the observed [O III] emitter population alone cannot explain the frequency of heavy-element absorbers seen in quasar spectra. In this picture, early enrichment of the intergalactic medium likely arises from undetected low-mass galaxies ($M_\star\sim10^5\unicode{x2013}10^6\;\mathrm{M_\odot}$) clustered around the more massive systems detected in JWST/NIRCam WFSS surveys.

papers.title: Informative inference on the average treatment effect with instrumental variables
papers.abstract: Policy decisions often depend on whether the average treatment effect (ATE) exceeds a specific cutoff. In instrumental variable (IV) settings, point identification of the ATE requires strong assumptions that are often difficult to justify. Therefore, many researchers shift their attention to identification of the local (L) ATE or target bounds of the ATE. Both strategies have well-known drawbacks: the substantive relevance of the LATE is frequently questioned, and the bounds are often too wide to be informative. We propose a simple sensitivity analysis that allows researchers to maintain focus on the ATE, and then discuss its connection to related bounding procedures. Based on these results, researchers can decide, in a principled manner, whether the sign of the ATE is inferable under assumptions they deem credible. The proposed strategies are easy to apply, and we illustrate their value with two real-data examples. The R package ivate implements our procedures.

In instrumental variable (IV) settings, point identification of the average treatment effect (ATE) requires strong assumptions that are often difficult to justify in practice. Many researchers therefore shift their attention to an alternative estimand: the local average treatment effect (LATE), also known as the complier average causal effect (CACE) (Angrist et al., 1996). The practical relevance of the LATE has been widely questioned (Deaton, 2010; Heckman and Urzúa, 2010; Manski, 2020; Swanson and Hernán, 2018). Indeed, when the ATE is of primary interest, a point-identified LATE gives only a partial answer to the substantive research question.

Indeed, when the ATE is of primary interest, a point-identified LATE gives only a partial answer to the substantive research question.

To maintain focus on the ATE under the same or weaker assumptions, partial identification approaches that target bounds on the ATE have been proposed; see Swanson et al. (2018) for an overview in the binary setting. While partial identification methods have received substantial attention in the methodological literature, applications remain rare: a recent survey found that in a sample of more than 300 IV studies published in leading journals across epidemiology, medicine, political science, and economics, none applied partial identification methods (Locher et al., 2025). One potential reason is that without additional assumptions, the resulting bounds represent extreme scenarios, thus are typically wide, and hence often fail to resolve the research question.

papers.title: The Emergence and Sparsification of a Syntactic Circuit
papers.abstract: To understand the emergence of grammatical behavior in language models, we track circuits for subject-verb number agreement in pythia-1b and ten seeds of pythia-410m across training. We find that subject-verb agreement is learned early, and is initially handled by a diffuse collection of neurons. However, after agreement behavior has stabilized, the mechanisms responsible for it continue to reorganize. The attention heads which mediate agreement often shift during training: in the case of pythia-1b, behavior is controlled by two heads early in training but by a third (different) head later. Furthermore, the circuit shrinks over training, with pythia-1b's final circuit being strikingly sparse. We take these results to be informative about how linguistic knowledge emerges and is represented in a language model.

papers.intro:
Our goal is to tell the story, in as much detail as possible, of how subject–verb number agreement emerges across training in language models (LMs). Number agreement has long served as a probe for syntactic competence in language models (Linzen et al., 2016; Gulordava et al., 2018; Marvin and Linzen, 2018; Futrell et al., 2019; Mueller et al., 2020; Warstadt et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2021). It has also been used to probe how these models encode grammatical information internally (Finlayson et al., 2021; Lasri et al., 2022; Arora et al., 2024). Notably, this task’s historical interest results from its symbolic specification, which, despite being simple, resists classic statistical methods.11 1 E.g., it requires tracking structural information — grammatical subjecthood — over potentially unbounded distances, and can thus not be solved by simple Markov models. A minimal circuit for handling it has to (1) recognize and store the grammatical number of the subject, (2) transport this information to the prediction position, and (3) license the corresponding output form.

In this work, we first (Experiment 1) trace the emergence of such a circuit over the course of language model training, studying ten seeds of pythia-410m and one seed of pythia-1b. We find that agreement is learned quickly and is initially controlled by a diffuse circuit. Over the course of training, however, we find that while the model’s performance remains mostly unchanged, the underlying circuit gradually evolves: it both sparsifies (concentrating in a smaller set of neurons) and is rerouted within the model (being implemented by different attention heads). By the end of training, a surprisingly sparse circuit captures most of the agreement signal in pythia-1b (Figure 1).

papers.title: Tight Learned Event-Inertial Odometry (TLEIO): a Transformer-Based Architecture for End-to-End Motion from Event Streams
papers.abstract: Event cameras provide microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range, and sparse asynchronous measurements, making them compelling for odometry under fast motion and challenging illumination. Yet, accurate event-based state estimation remains difficult: existing systems often use events as a complement to frames or rely on feature tracking, correspondence search, and optimization-heavy backends, limiting the efficiency promised by event sensing. We introduce Tight Learned Event-Inertial Odometry (TLEIO), a compact filter-based pipeline that learns short-window relative motion directly from voxelized event streams and tightly fuses the resulting constraints with IMU propagation. Its learned front-end, EventsFormer, predicts local displacements and per-axis uncertainty from event voxels in a single forward pass, while a stochastic-cloning EKF fuses these overlapping predictions with IMU propagation, producing metric trajectories without explicit feature tracks and pose optimization at inference time. The network is trained directly from pose displacements, without requiring event-flow labels. We evaluate TLEIO on the TartanAir/TartanEvent benchmark and on real DAVIS240c sequences. On TartanAir, TLEIO reduces average ATE from 2.26 m to 1.10 m over the IMU-only TLIO baseline, while achieving up to 48.9% lower runtime than optimization-based event odometry methods.
papers.intro:
Visual Odometry (VO) is an essential component in AR/VR and robotics applications, but standard frame-based pipelines remain limited by conventional cameras. Motion blur, low-light scenes, and high dynamic range can degrade feature tracking and dense alignment, even when the downstream estimator is strong. Event cameras address these limitations at the sensor level by asynchronously reporting brightness changes with microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range, and low power consumption. These properties make them well suited to fast motion and challenging illumination, but their sparse and irregular output makes odometry from events fundamentally different from frame-based VO [1].

papers.title: Component Pooling Trained Across Orientations for Few-Shot Remote Sensing Scene Classification
papers.abstract: Few-shot remote sensing scene classification (FSRSSC) aims to recognize novel scene categories from only a few labeled images. Most FSRSSC methods summarize the feature map of an image by global average pooling, which treats the few objects that define an aerial scene and the large background around them alike, and they rarely consider that aerial images have no canonical orientation. To address these issues, we propose RoCoP, a parameter-free component pooling network trained across orientations. RoCoP consists of a feature extractor, a non-negative decomposition module (NDM) and a component scoring module (CSM). NDM factorizes the local descriptors of each image into a few additive components with a deterministic initialization and a single multiplicative update, so that the positions of one object are grouped together. CSM weights each component by its activation magnitude and converts the weights into a soft mask for pooling. Because both modules are invariant to permutations of feature positions, the only rotation-sensitive part of the pipeline is the backbone, which we train to classify randomly rotated views of every image. Experiments on NWPU-RESISC45, AID and UC Merced show that component pooling and rotated-view training are complementary: together they improve a strong transfer-learning baseline by about 2.5 points in 5-way 1-shot accuracy on NWPU-RESISC45 and AID, without adding parameters at inference. Under an identical protocol, RoCoP outperforms re-implemented metric-based and task-adaptive methods, and NDM and CSM also improve existing methods when plugged into them. We further identify the regime in which the method does not apply, namely very small base sets.
papers.intro:
Remote sensing scene classification assigns a semantic label, such as airport, farmland or residential area, to an aerial or satellite image, and supports land-use mapping, urban planning and environmental monitoring [1, 2]. Deep convolutional networks have made this task largely solved when thousands of labeled images per class are available [4, 1]. Labeling remote sensing images, however, requires expert knowledge, and new categories appear as applications change. Few-shot remote sensing scene classification (FSRSSC) therefore asks a model trained on a set of base classes to recognize novel classes from one or five labeled images per class [5, 23, 24].

Existing few-shot methods follow three main paradigms. Optimization-based meta-learning learns an initialization that adapts quickly to a new task [6]. Metric-based methods learn an embedding in which a query is classified by its distance to the labeled support samples [7, 8, 9]. Transfer-learning methods train an embedding on all base classes and fit a simple classifier on the support set of each task, and they have proved to be strong baselines [10, 11, 12]. In remote sensing, these ideas have been extended with attention [23, 33], prototype calibration [24, 31, 36], kernel and subspace metrics [25, 34], contrastive and self-supervised learning [26, 27, 29, 41], relation modeling [35, 28], multi-scale feature fusion [43, 44], and, more recently, vision–language and pretrained models [46, 45].

Two properties of aerial scenes are, however, rarely addressed together. First, the evidence for a scene class is usually carried by a few ground objects, such as the runways of an airport or the courts of a sports field, while bare land, vegetation or water fills most of the image. Most FSRSSC pipelines nevertheless summarize the feature map by global average pooling (GAP), which weights object and background positions equally. Methods that keep local descriptors [15, 16, 17, 39, 40] or weight them with attention [33, 38] judge each position independently or learn attention parameters on the base classes, so the positions of one object may receive inconsistent weights on novel classes. Second, aerial images are taken from above and have no canonical orientation. Rotation is usually handled by data augmentation or by self-supervised rotation prediction [63, 29], independently of how the features are pooled.

In this paper, we propose RoCoP, which pools features over components rather than positions and trains the backbone across orientations. A non-negative decomposition module (NDM) groups positions whose channel responses are alike into a few additive components by non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) [53], and a component scoring module (CSM) weights each component as a unit, so that all positions of one object share one weight. Neither module has learnable parameters. We show that both modules are invariant to permutations of feature positions, so the only rotation-sensitive part of the pipeline is the backbone; RoCoP therefore trains the backbone to classify randomly rotated views of every image, instead of adding constraints to the pooling. Our experiments show that component pooling alone brings a modest gain, that the gain becomes much larger when the backbone is trained with rotated views, and that two natural extensions, an explicit mask-consistency loss and a task-level calibration of the component scores, do not help.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows. (1) We propose a parameter-free component pooling for FSRSSC, composed of NDM and CSM. A deterministic NNDSVD initialization and a single multiplicative update make the decomposition reproducible for every image, cheap and differentiable, so it can be trained end to end while inference remains inductive. (2) We show that component pooling and rotated-view training are complementary. The analysis is supported by paired comparisons on identical test episodes and by the stability of the pooling masks under rotation, and it shows that the plain rotated-view objective is preferable to explicit consistency constraints. (3) We conduct extensive experiments on three benchmarks, including same-protocol re-implementations of representative methods, plug-in studies, and analyses of the classifier, the calibration and the number of components. RoCoP outperforms the re-implemented methods, improves other methods as a plug-in module, and its limitation on very small base sets is identified.

papers.title: Scalable Unrolled Chains for MRI Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Unrolled variational networks achieve state-of-the-art performance for accelerated MRI reconstruction, but standard end-to-end training becomes prohibitively memory intensive as the number and width of cascades increase. We propose a memory-efficient training framework that updates a randomly sampled cascade while retaining supervision from the final reconstruction loss. The error signal is propagated from the end of the chain to the sampled cascade using an activation-light backward pass that avoids storing full chain activations, thereby decoupling training memory from chain length. A time-conditioned network shared across cascades further keeps the parameter count independent of chain length. The backward pass is approximate only through frozen normalization statistics, and a trained exact gradient control shows the approximation leaves reconstruction quality unchanged. The framework remains trainable at chain lengths and cascade widths where standard end-to-end backpropagation exhausts GPU memory. On fastMRI single-coil knee and multi-coil brain reconstruction, our method consistently outperforms other local training approaches. On high-SNR knee slices, our method surpasses E2E-VarNet at $8\times$ and matches it at $4\times$, while on the complete brain validation set it surpasses E2E-VarNet at $8\times$ and achieves comparable performance at $4\times$, with fewer parameters, lower peak memory, and faster per-iteration training. Code is available at https://github.com/emehillaj/scalable-unrolled-mri.

papers.intro:
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) provides excellent soft tissue contrast without ionizing radiation, but its sequential acquisition leads to long scan times and sensitivity to motion. Accelerated MRI addresses this by undersampling k-space and using reconstruction algorithms to recover diagnostically reliable images from incomplete measurements. Supervised deep learning, particularly unrolled variational networks [7, 20], has substantially improved reconstruction quality by repeatedly applying learned refinement and data consistency in a sequence of cascades. These cascades can be interpreted as successive iterations of a discretized MR reconstruction algorithm [7]. Unrolled networks’ capacity can be increased through wider refinement networks or longer chains, with the latter resembling multi-step generative inference procedures such as diffusion models [8]. However, end-to-end training stores activations from every cascade, making peak memory scale with both network width and chain depth. Consequently, scaling either dimension quickly becomes impractical under realistic GPU memory budgets.

Existing approaches trade activation memory for additional computation, architectural constraints, or approximate gradients. Checkpointing recomputes discarded activations [5], while reversible, in-place, and computational imaging methods recover them through reversible architectures, locally reconstructible layers, or model-specific inverse operations [6, 2, 10]. Other approaches compress activations or modify error propagation or supervision, including activation compression [4], synthetic gradients [9], local objectives [1], and surrogate or sparsified backpropagation [3, 21, 13]. These approaches add computation, impose architecture-specific constraints, or approximate the gradient, while decoupled local supervision methods instead modify the training objective by supervising intermediate layers.

Intermediate reconstruction states in unrolled MRI provide natural points for decoupling training across cascades. Existing approaches decouple learning at these intermediate cascade outputs by defining targets or reconstruction states along a prescribed sequence. GLEAM directly supervises intermediate cascade outputs against the fully sampled reference [14], while k-space cold diffusion progressively modifies the supervising sampling mask from undersampled to fully sampled, and FLAT interpolates between undersampled and fully sampled states to reconstruct intermediate targets [18, 16]. These approaches avoid or modify full chain backpropagation, but their intermediate targets or prescribed sequences may not align with optimizing the final reconstruction and may therefore constrain the solutions learned by the complete chain.

We propose an efficient sampled training framework for a shared, cascade-conditioned unrolled network that derives its training signal directly from the final reconstruction loss rather than from intermediate objectives. Unlike synthetic gradients, local learning, and trajectory supervision, our framework retains the final loss signal while computing parameter gradients for only one sampled cascade at each iteration. The full chain is evaluated forward, with the cascades preceding the sampled one forming a forward only prefix and the remaining cascades forming a frozen suffix. The suffix propagates the final loss error signal back to the sampled cascade using an activation-light backward pass, where only the sampled cascade performs a standard parameter backward pass. Thus, the method combines cascade sampling with memory-efficient propagation of the final loss signal through the suffix.

Unlike checkpointing and activation reconstruction, our framework neither recomputes discarded activations nor requires invertible architectures. Instead, we construct a lightweight backward pass that requires little or no activation storage in the suffix. For linear layers, the input gradient can be computed directly from the layer weights without storing activations, while for LeakyReLU, a one-bit sign mask is sufficient to recover the exact input gradient. The only approximation arises at normalization layers, where we hold the forward statistics fixed to linearize the backward map. Sec. 3.1 shows that the resulting error signal closely matches exact suffix backpropagation and leads to indistinguishable training behavior.

papers.title: Price's law for scalar waves on 1+4 dimensional subextremal Myers-Perry spacetimes
papers.abstract:
We consider Myers--Perry spacetimes $(M,g_{\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathfrak{m}})$ in $1+4$ dimensions with two spin parameters $(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})\in\mathbb{R}^2$, which are a direct generalization of the well known Kerr spacetime in $1+3$ dimensions. We prove that the Hamiltonian flow associated to $g_{\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathfrak{m}}^{-1}$ is normally hyperbolically trapped for the full subextremal range \[
  (|\mathbf{a}|+|\mathbf{b}|)^2<2\mathfrak{m}. \] As an application, we prove a Price law with explicit leading order terms for solutions $\phi(t,x)$ of the scalar wave equation \[
  \Box_{g_{\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathfrak{m}}}\phi=0 \] under the assumption of real mode stability. Our precise asymptotics imply that $\phi(t,x)=ct^{-3}+\mathcal{O}(t^{-4+})$, where $c\in\mathbb{C}$ is an explicitly computable constant.

papers.title: DRILS: Dependency-based Requirement Change Impact Analysis Using LLMs
papers.abstract: Change is inevitable in software systems, where requirements must continuously adapt to evolving stakeholder needs, regulations, and project scopes. Managing such changes is a fundamental software engineering challenge, as manually identifying the impact of a change request, given high requirements volume, Natural Language (NL) complexity, and intricate interdependencies, is error-prone and time-consuming. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising solutions for requirements change impact analysis (CIA), yet their effectiveness when enhanced with advanced techniques remains underexplored. We present DRILS, an LLM-based agentic framework for requirements Change Impact Analysis, employing a multi-agent architecture to generate candidate impact sets, with an LLM-as-a-judge promoting diversity during selection. DRILS features two key components: RE-RAG, a carefully engineered RAG technique providing focused domain context, and a requirement dependency graph (RDG) as an additional knowledge source. Evaluation across three manually curated datasets demonstrates superior performance over state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average recall of 87.1%, precision of 76.3%, and F1 score of 81% at a lower cost. Precision gains are particularly significant, 41.1%, 83.4%, and 149.8% over the closest baseline per dataset, as higher precision directly reduces false positives and manual validation effort. We also contribute three annotated CIA datasets to support future research.

papers.intro:
Requirements form the foundation of system development and maintenance (Sommerville and Ransom, 2005). They specify what a system should do, the constraints under which it should operate, and the properties it is expected to satisfy. These descriptive documents are most commonly formalized as Requirements Specifications, which establish a shared understanding of the system among all stakeholders involved (Zowghi and Coulin, 2005). Requirements are particularly important because they provide the basis for system design, verification, and validation. Therefore, maintaining accurate and consistent requirements documentation is essential throughout the system lifecycle (Pohl, 1994).

They specify what a system should do, the constraints under which it should operate, and the properties it is expected to satisfy. These descriptive documents are most commonly formalized as Requirements Specifications, which establish a shared understanding of the system among all stakeholders involved (Zowghi and Coulin, 2005). Requirements are particularly important because they provide the basis for system design, verification, and validation. Therefore, maintaining accurate and consistent requirements documentation is essential throughout the system lifecycle (Pohl, 1994).

Among the most inevitable realities of any system’s lifecycle is change. No system, regardless of how thoroughly it is specified or carefully it is designed, remains static throughout its operational life. Change is driven by different reasons such as evolving regulations, shifting stakeholder needs, discovered system defects, environmental adjustments, technological advancements, or the natural growth of the domain the system serves (Nuseibeh and Easterbrook, 2000). Such changes extend to the requirements specifications themselves, requiring engineers to revisit, revise, and realign the documentation to accurately reflect the system’s new state. Since requirements are interdependent, a change to one requirement can affect other requirements that depend on it (Regnell et al., 2008). Maintaining consistency between the evolving system and its requirements documentation demands careful analysis of which requirements are affected and how changes may propagate through their dependencies. Failure to keep requirements documentation synchronized with actual system changes risks introducing ambiguity, inconsistency, and a growing disconnect between what the system is documented to do and what it actually does. This process is formally known as inter-requirement Change Impact Analysis (CIA), a core practice within the Requirements Engineering (RE) domain (Pohl, 2016).

Performing CIA throughout a system’s lifecycle is inherently challenging, particularly in large-scale systems where requirements documentation is extensive. This challenge is particularly pronounced for safety-critical systems due to their additional certification constraints. Under such conditions, the process becomes increasingly time- and resource-intensive, and the likelihood of overlooking affected requirements or misassessing a change’s scope also increases.

This challenge is particularly pronounced for safety-critical systems due to their additional certification constraints. Under such conditions, the process becomes increasingly time- and resource-intensive, and the likelihood of overlooking affected requirements or misassessing a change’s scope also increases.

To address these challenges, researchers have proposed various techniques to automate the CIA task. Dependency-based approaches rely on dependencies between requirements or other system artifacts to identify impacted requirements and propagate change impact (Nonsiri et al., 2013; Aryani et al., 2009; Kchaou et al., 2017; Alkaf et al., 2019; Nejati et al., 2016; Göknil et al., 2008; Goknil et al., 2011; Goknil et al., 2014a; Rahim et al., 2026). However, structural dependencies alone are generally insufficient to capture the full semantic implications of a change request. Model-based approaches utilize formal representations of requirements and software artifacts to assess whether they are impacted (Aryani et al., 2009; Nejati et al., 2016; Kchaou et al., 2017; Alkaf et al., 2019). However, these approaches require requirements and artifacts to conform to specific modeling formalisms, which limits their applicability across different development contexts. Natural Language Processing (NLP) approaches analyze the linguistic content of requirements and other software artifacts, often leveraging semantic similarity to assess change impact (Arora et al., 2015a; Arora et al., 2015b). However, they often rely on shallow linguistic features that fail to capture deeper semantic relationships, and some of them still require substantial human involvement, limiting scalability and automation. Furthermore, across these three categories, many existing approaches primarily focus on propagating change impact across requirements and other software artifacts rather than directly identifying impacted requirements in response to a specific change request.

With the recent advent of Large Language Models (LLMs), researchers have explored their application to various software engineering activities. LLMs are advanced language models trained on large-scale textual data and capable of understanding and generating human-like text. Their natural language processing capabilities, combined with their ability to be fine-tuned for specialized tasks, make them relevant solutions for requirements engineering activities (Naveed et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024). However, the application of LLMs to requirements CIA remains underexplored. Only a few approaches have been proposed to address this task (Etezadi et al., 2025; Rusdianto et al., 2024), leveraging prompt engineering and basic RAG techniques. To the best of our knowledge, no existing work has combined the analytical capabilities of LLMs with the structured representation provided by requirements dependency graphs while also leveraging the technical knowledge embedded in the requirements specification for change impact analysis.

papers.title: Recovering fractal boundary dimensions from Robin eigenvalues
papers.abstract: We study Robin problems in which a small local boundary coefficient competes with the increasing surface measure of a finite-depth fractal approximation. For a fixed smooth domain, layer potentials give Green function and eigenpair expansions; contour residues and a finite-rank reduction yield a quantitative spectral-gap-dependent eigenvalue remainder. For varying Lipschitz domains, a uniform Poincar\'e inequality and a trace estimate with respect to normalized surface measure give a uniform ground-state expansion and a rank-one resolvent singularity as the total Robin boundary mass tends to zero. Under the boundary-resolution hypothesis and the condition on the approximation scales, ground-state measurements with known Robin coefficients recover the lower and upper Minkowski dimensions for sequences with bounded total Robin boundary mass. We describe Neumann, generalized Robin, and Dirichlet-type operator limits under the corresponding compact Mosco convergence hypotheses. Koch snowflake computations illustrate the reconstruction formulas, and an exact finite-stage area correction improves the adjacent-stage dimension estimator.

papers.title: Nodeless d-wave pairing in monolayer FeSe revealed by intra-unit-cell Josephson interferometry
papers.abstract: The Josephson effect provides a direct phase-sensitive probe of superconducting order and has played a central role in identifying unconventional pairing symmetries1-6. Conventional Josephson interferometry, however, extracts phase information through engineered junction geometries and crystallographic orientations, rather than by resolving the internal phase structure of the pair state within a single unit cell. Here, we use a superconducting Nb tip to realize atomic-scale Josephson interferometry in monolayer FeSe/SrTiO3. Despite a fully gapped quasiparticle spectrum, the local Josephson response exhibits a striking intra-unit-cell pattern, with maxima centred on Fe-Fe bonds and robust nodal lines along the Fe-Se directions. We show that these nodal lines arise from destructive interference between Josephson tunnelling amplitudes associated with opposite-sign pairing components. Microscopic calculations reproduce the observed spatial pattern and identify it as a fingerprint of nodeless d-wave pairing. Our results establish intra-unit-cell Josephson interferometry as a local phase-sensitive probe of pairing symmetry in unconventional superconductors.

papers.title: End-to-End Neural Modeling of EM Response and Design Performance for Free-Form RFIC Passives
papers.abstract: Passive matching networks are critical components in radio-frequency integrated circuits (RFICs), but their design is bottlenecked by expensive finite-difference-based electromagnetic (EM) simulation. We propose an end-to-end neural framework for free-form RFIC passives that predicts both EM response and downstream design performance under varying frequency and circuit contexts, combining a frequency-conditioned neural simulator with a circuit-conditioned neural solver. To improve design performance prediction, the simulator outputs a neural EM response consisting of both the explicit EM response and a complementary response, together with a dependence regularizer that encourages the two responses to capture orthogonal information. To evaluate the proposed framework, we construct a large-scale dataset of free-form passive layouts, synthesized from both expert-designed contours and random paths. Our 21M-parameter model achieves high accuracy across a broad frequency range, circuit contexts and passive matching settings, with $R^2>0.98$ for almost all targets, while providing orders-of-magnitude faster evaluation than traditional EM simulation. Code available at https://github.com/ETH-IDEAS/RFIC-NeuralSim.

Existing neural approaches have made progress on RFIC passive modeling, but their coverage remains limited, as summarized in Table 1. First, many prior methods operate on templated or otherwise restricted passive layouts, which simplifies modeling but significantly narrows the design space. Second, most prior work focuses on EM response prediction without modeling downstream design performance. This is a serious but overlooked limitation because small EM-response errors can cause large design-performance degradations when passed to a ground-truth solver, as shown in Figure 1. Third, prior methods often omit explicit auxiliary circuit conditioning, operate on narrow or sparse frequency regimes, or require retraining when the frequency grid changes. These gaps leave open the central problem we study here: end-to-end neural modeling of free-form passive matching networks, from layout to both EM response and design performance, under varying circuit and frequency settings.

papers.title: Reliability Assessment of FRP-RC Columns Using AK-MCS with a Piecewise Two-Branch Approach
papers.abstract: Slender concrete columns reinforced with fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) bars fail at medium to high axial load levels either by concrete crushing or by loss of stability, while the tensile strains in the reinforcement remain far below the rupture strain. Each non-linear finite element (FE) analysis yields only the capacity of the governing failure mode, and the governing mode changes over a broad zone in which both capacities are nearly equal. Both characteristics conflict with active-learning Kriging-assisted Monte Carlo simulation (AK-MCS), which assumes a single, smooth limit-state function. This paper proposes a piecewise, two-branch AK-MCS framework in which each failure mode is represented by its own Kriging model, trained only on the FE analyses in which that mode governs, and the governing prediction is the minimum of both. Safeguards against data starvation keep rarely governing branches usable. After convergence, additional FE analyses are placed based on a leave-one-out calibration check and on the width of the confidence interval on the reliability index. A design-point search on the surrogate and importance sampling at the design points provide the reliability index even where direct Monte Carlo simulation finds no failure. For an FRP-reinforced concrete column example with mixed failure, 79% and 62% of the training points lie near the mode boundary. The reliability index from the design-point search agrees with the Monte Carlo estimate to within 0.05, and an FE analysis at the design point confirms the surrogate to within 0.6%.

papers.title: Post-Progression Treatment Regimes and the Limits of Cross-Trial Survival Transport
papers.abstract: Models transporting overall survival (OS) effects across clinical trials fail when they ignore the "post-progression treatment regime"---the subsequent therapy rates across biomarker strata and randomized arms. Because this trial-level regime is systematically omitted from published reports, standard correction families are structurally inadequate: crossover adjustments target an unrealistic counterfactual with zero subsequent therapy, erasing critical environmental differences; population adjustments (including MAIC, STC, AIPW, and density ratios) match baseline individual covariates, leaving trial-level regimes mismatched. We show that these correction approaches carry near-identical bias, proving the failure is informational rather than methodological. Simulations demonstrate that ignoring the target setting's landscape can leave the directional sign of the transported effect completely undetermined, even when mechanisms are fully known. Conversely, providing the target regime to a regime-aware estimator successfully recovers the true treatment effect. Code is available at https://github.com/felizzi/post-progression-transport-WMHS-NeurIPS-2026.
papers.intro:
Cross-trial transport underlies indirect treatment comparison, network meta-analysis, and synthetic control arms (Signorovitch et al., 2010; Phillippo et al., 2018), and is increasingly performed with learned representations of patients or trials (Johansson et al., 2016; Shalit et al., 2017). A patient world model that generates OS conditional on PFS is, in effect, an estimator of this transport, fitted to published trial reports. We ask what such a model can learn from that evidence base, and identify a specific and consequential gap.

A randomised trial identifies a treatment effect in the population it enrolled. Transport asks for the effect in a different target population—another trial’s population, a reimbursement jurisdiction, or a real-world cohort—usually with individual data from the source trial and only summary data from the target. Standard methods assume that, conditional on a set of baseline effect modifiers, the treatment effect is the same in source and target; differences in the distribution of those modifiers are then removed by reweighting or regression (Colnet et al., 2024). The assumption fails whenever something that modifies the effect differs between source and target but is not a baseline covariate.

OS is the sum of PFS and post-progression survival (PPS). Subsequent therapy is given after progression, so it can change PPS but not PFS. If the probability of receiving it differs by arm, by biomarker stratum, or between trials, OS effects differ even when the drug and the biology are identical. The probability is set by the treatment landscape a trial runs in, not by any patient characteristic, so methods that adjust for patient characteristics cannot account for it.

Consider a trial in which the progression-free survival hazard ratio is essentially identical in a biomarker-positive subgroup and its complement, yet the overall survival hazard ratios diverge sharply—a pronounced OS benefit in the biomarker-negative stratum and none in the biomarker-positive—while the marginal rate of subsequent therapy is balanced across arms. The natural reading is that the biomarker modifies the drug’s effect on survival. Our results show that this reading is not licensed by the data. Because PFS precedes subsequent therapy it is invariant to the post-progression regime, whereas OS is not (Figure 1); and a regime that is balanced in the marginal—the quantity a standard switching assessment inspects—can be sharply arm-differential within strata in offsetting directions (regime S2, Section 3). Holding drug and biology fixed and changing only the regime, the biomarker-positive OS hazard ratio in our simulation moves from 0.9730.973 to 1.2351.235 to 1.5181.518 while the PFS hazard ratio does not move (Table 2): the regime alone can produce a stratum-wise divergence of exactly this kind. A careful analyst would not stop at the marginal check but would examine the four arm ×\times biomarker cells. That is the right analysis, and it fails only because published reports do not contain the subsequent-therapy rate in each of the four cells: they give at most a rate by arm. With the four cell rates the regime’s contribution would be visible at once; without them, a stratum-specific divergence in OS hazard ratios cannot be attributed to biology rather than to the within-stratum, by-arm subsequent-therapy pattern. This paper makes that non-identification precise.

The quantity transport requires is the treatment effect in the target population under the target’s own post-progression treatment regime. We define a regime as the table q​[m]​[t]q[m][t] giving the probability that a patient in biomarker stratum mm and randomised arm tt receives subsequent targeted therapy after progression. Regimes differ across trials for reasons unrelated to the drug under study: approval timelines, reimbursement, geography, and biomarker-based eligibility for later agents. The gap is not hypothetical. A cross-sectional review of 275 published oncology trials and 77 registration trials leading to FDA approval found post-progression treatment assessable in only 36%36\% and 48%48\% of them, and, where assessable, judged it below the standard of care in 55%55\% and 76%76\% (Olivier et al., 2023). The regime is thus often unreported, and often different from the setting into which results are transported.

papers.title: Active Flux and Polygons: why a stabilisation and how to implement boundary conditions
papers.abstract: In a recent paper, the authors developed an Active Flux-type algorithm for polygonal meshes (see \cite{BP_Pampa_VEM}). The main difference between Active Flux methods on polygonal meshes and those on Cartesian or simplex meshes is that the basis functions are not explicitly known. These functions describe the solution using point-value approximations on the polygon boundaries and the average value within the polygons. In \cite{BP_Pampa_VEM}, it was shown that directly transposing the algorithm from simplexes to polygons leads to a mild instability, and a remedy was proposed without a rigorous explanation. In the present paper, we clarify this issue and demonstrate that the solution presented in \cite{BP_Pampa_VEM} is indeed correct. Furthermore, another challenge-the implementation of boundary conditions-was previously solved heuristically. Building on \cite{pampa_dg}, we show how to properly implement these boundary conditions. Finally, the method is illustrated through several examples with hybrid meshes.

papers.intro:
We developed in [8] a scheme for polygonal meshes that follows the Active Flux methodology [16, 17, 19, 18, 13, 20, 23, 14, 2, 1]. In each polygon, the solution is described by its average value and its point values on the boundary. The vertices of the polygons are included among these interpolation points, while the others correspond to Gauss–Lobatto points on each face. Compared to [3, 7], which were developed for triangles, and even compared to schemes designed purely for Cartesian meshes (such as [9, 10, 15, 20, 23, 14]), this scheme requires a rather unconventional filtering term. The reason is as follows: unlike standard elements such as simplexes, there is no reference polygon. Consequently, the user must either explicitly define (and store) the basis functions needed to evaluate the functional approximation for each element, or adopt an alternative approach. In [8], we utilize the Virtual Element Method (VEM) framework (see [12] for a review and Section 2 for a brief summary). This VEM space is constructed such that the set of polynomials of degree kk (here k=2k=2) is a subspace; that is, the VEM space V⁡(K)V(K) contains ℙk\mathbb{P}_{k}. This implies that we forgot explicit knowledge of the basis functions, knowing simply that they exist. Instead, we compute the L2L^{2} projection of any function from the VEM space onto polynomials of degree kk, which is sufficient for approximation purposes. In the scheme of [8], we need to compute the gradient of the solution—specifically, the gradient of its projection onto ℙk\mathbb{P}_{k}. In doing so, information is lost because ℙk\mathbb{P}_{k} is a proper subspace of the VEM space. This issue does not arise in [3] or in other Active Flux-type methods. Therefore, a filtering term is required to damp out the unresolved modes without compromising accuracy. In [8], a heuristic solution was found based on pragmatic analysis, though it lacked clear theoretical justification.

papers.title: Singular set estimates in quasilinear Alt-Caffarelli problems
papers.abstract: For a nonnegative, uniformly convex function $\Phi$, we study nonnegative minimizers of the quasilinear Alt-Caffarelli energy $\int_{\Omega}\Phi(\nabla u)+\chi_{\{u>0\}}$. Under mild regularity assumptions on $\Phi$, we show that the codimension of the singular set of the free boundary is at least $2+\eta$ for a positive $\eta$. With a singular minimizer in three dimensions in a forthcoming work, this result is sharp as long as integer dimensions are considered. Our proof method is flexible, and we use it to also prove a similar result for minimizers of the $p$-Laplacian counterpart of the Alt-Caffarelli energy.

papers.title: Domain-Adapted Latent Diffusion Models for CT-to-PET Image Translation
papers.abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) provides important metabolic information for tumor detection and staging but remains significantly less accessible than Computed Tomography (CT) due to its high cost, infrastructure requirements, and reliance on injected radioactive tracers. CT-to-PET image translation using generative models aims to address this disparity, yet state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods are limited by the scarcity of paired training data. To overcome this, we propose a domain-adapted latent diffusion framework that transfers natural-image priors using a relatively small dataset of 21,930 paired CT/PET slices, incorporating a signed power transform to resolve extreme intensity sparsity in PET data. Compared to CPDM, a state-ofthe-art baseline for CT-to-PET image translation, our approach yields superior performance in pixel-wise reconstruction and localized tumor fidelity, demonstrating effective transfer of natural-image priors to the medical domain. We further provide a systematic analysis of evaluation metric reliability for sparse PET data, showing that standard full-image metrics can be misleading indicators of translated image quality, and propose background-filtered and mask-restricted metrics as more clinically meaningful alternatives.

papers.intro:
Positron Emission Tomography (PET) and Computed Tomography (CT) are complementary medical imaging modalities that capture anatomical and metabolic information, e.g., for tumor detection, staging, and treatment monitoring. Specifically, CT scans provide high-resolution anatomical information through X-ray attenuation, while PET scans reveal metabolic activity via radiotracer distribution, typically 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG). Used together, they offer a more complete diagnostic picture than either modality alone. However, PET scanners require costly infrastructure and radiotracer production facilities, making PET imaging less accessible than CT, particularly in low-resource healthcare settings.

In particular, latent diffusion models (LDMs) [16] offer a compelling option due to the learned latent space that they operate in, which allows generation of high-resolution images at lower computational cost. [14] recently introduced the CT-to-PET Diffusion Model (CPDM), a conditional diffusion model based on a Brownian Bridge process that defines a stochastic bridge between CT and PET latents rather than corrupting toward pure Gaussian noise, and additionally incorporates domain knowledge through attention and attenuation map modules. Notably, the authors report that LDM priors were inferior to CPDM in their experiments [14]—a finding we revisit in this work.

papers.title: Transient Supercriticality in Hawkes Processes: Detection, Identifiability, and Apparent Criticality
papers.abstract: Self-exciting (Hawkes) models of epidemics, earthquakes, financial markets, and social cascades are usually calibrated with a branching ratio $n$ below one. This is a condition for stationarity, not for existence: a process with $n>1$ grows exponentially but remains finite on any finite horizon. Imposing stationarity is also misleading, because transient supercritical episodes then masquerade as near-criticality. Reconstructing the latent genealogy of events, we show that a single finite record can reveal an excursion into the regime $n(t)>1$, and back, and date its onset and end. Detectability is governed by the excess $n-1$ times the square root of the number of exposed parents. Even when the memory time of the triggering is unknown, the data determine the growth rate of activity during the episode nearly as precisely as when it is known, and hence whether $n$ crossed unity, whereas the value of $n$ requires independent knowledge of the memory time. Letting the data choose between endogenous amplification and external forcing prevents confusing the two. In the 2015 Korean MERS outbreak, our reconstruction shows that transmission by hospital cohorts had collapsed by 28 May, before the incidence peak and two weeks before the instantaneous reproduction number fell below one; in real time, it establishes the collapse a few days earlier than this standard indicator. Our framework separates stationarity, non-explosion, and transient supercritical amplification, and provides a practical route for detecting short-lived endogenous instabilities in self-exciting systems.

papers.intro:
Many self-exciting systems appear to pass through transient phases in which each event triggers, on average, more than one further event, before the amplification subsides. Every epidemic wave begins with a reproduction number above one and ends when interventions, behavioral change, or the depletion of susceptibles bring it below one [1, 2, 3]. In seismicity, spatially resolved inversions of the epidemic-type aftershock sequence (ETAS) model for California return branching ratios nn up to about 1.21.2 in several regions, values that can only be temporary [4], although finite catalogues, missing events, and truncation also bias such estimates [5]. In financial markets, Hawkes calibrations of high-frequency activity find an endogeneity that has risen over the years towards the critical value n=1n=1 [6] or lies close to it [7, 8]. On social media, a fraction of retweet cascades are estimated to be supercritical during their first minutes to hours [9], and bursts of collective attention display the signatures of endogenous, near-critical cascades [10, 11]. In the brain, epileptic seizures share the statistics of earthquakes and have been described as departures from the near-critical dynamics of normal activity [12, 13]. More generally, transient phases of supercritical amplification are a natural mechanism for the outsized events called dragon-kings [14, 15].

We argue that this is not only unnecessary on a finite horizon, as recalled below, but also misleading. A stationary fit to a record that contains a transient supercritical episode returns a branching ratio just below unity: for an episode with n=1.35n=1.35 lasting eight memory times within a subcritical regime with n=0.65n=0.65, the median estimate is 0.960.96, against a time average of 0.790.79, and criticality cannot be rejected in 86%86\% of the catalogues (Sec. IV.2). A system that alternates between subcritical and supercritical phases is thus diagnosed as stationary and near-critical. This provides an alternative explanation for the branching ratios close to unity reported in many systems, and for the claims of criticality built on them [7, 16], in the spirit of the sweeping of an instability as an alternative to self-organized criticality [17], and complementary to the apparent criticality produced by an unmodelled nonstationary background [18, 19, 20]. Allowing the data to test for transient supercriticality, rather than excluding it a priori, may therefore change conclusions drawn from stationary calibrations.
