The branching ratio is the central control parameter of a linear Hawkes process: in the cluster representation, it is the expected number of direct offspring generated by one event [21, 22]. The familiar condition n<1n<1 guarantees a stationary cluster process with finite mean intensity. It is therefore built into a large fraction of statistical theory and applied calibration, either explicitly as a parameter constraint or implicitly through a locally stationary approximation [23, 24, 25]. It is also built into the way nn is commonly measured. In a stationary process the mean intensity is Λ=μ/(1−n)\Lambda=\mu/(1-n), so that the fraction of immigrants is μ/Λ=1−n\mu/\Lambda=1-n and the fraction of triggered events is exactly nn. The branching ratio is therefore often estimated and interpreted as the fraction of endogenous events, n=1−μ/Λn=1-\mu/\Lambda, for instance as a measure of the endogeneity, or reflexivity, of financial markets [6], or as the fraction of events attributed to triggering by stochastic declustering [26]. Such an estimate is bounded by unity by construction, since a fraction cannot exceed one. The identification of the two quantities, however, holds only in the stationary regime. In a finite window that contains an interval with n⁡(t)>1n(t)>1, the fraction of triggered events remains below one while the mean number of offspring per parent exceeds one: in the catalogues of Sec. IV.2 with an episode n+=1.35n_{+}=1.35, triggered events make up a median 92%92\% of all events, a value that would be read as a near-critical branching ratio. As a result, a mathematical condition for stationarity has become an inferential prior, enforced either by a parameter constraint or by the very definition of the estimated quantity: the model is prevented from asking whether the data contain a finite interval with n⁡(t)>1n(t)>1. We instead estimate nn as the mean number of offspring per exposed parent, a quantity that is not bounded by unity.

The restriction of stationarity is stronger than finite-time well-posedness requires. In point-process terminology, “explosion” means the accumulation of infinitely many events before a finite time. For a standard linear Hawkes process with a regular exponential kernel and finite mean fertility, n>1n>1 destroys stationarity but does not by itself imply finite-time explosion; instead, the mean activity grows asymptotically at a positive Malthusian rate. Nonstationary and time-varying Hawkes processes have been studied theoretically and statistically [27, 28], although their inference is generally developed under stability or local-stationarity assumptions, while supercritical Hawkes dynamics has also become an explicit object of mathematical analysis [29]. In the ETAS context, Helmstetter and Sornette showed that a finite branching ratio n>1n>1 produces an exponentially accelerating seismicity rate at sufficiently long times [30]. An even more singular regime arises when event fertilities are power-law distributed with tail index below unity, so that the mean fertility and formally the branching ratio, diverges. Sornette and Helmstetter showed that the resulting anomalous branching dynamics can generate genuine stochastic finite-time singularities of the activity rate [31]. These results show that the conventional boundary n=1n=1 separates stationary from supercritical branching dynamics, rather than admissible from inadmissible finite-time realizations. This motivates the inference problem considered here: to determine from a single finite realization whether the process enters a transient regime with n⁡(t)>1n(t)>1, and to estimate its onset, duration, and amplitude while discriminating endogenous amplification from exogenous forcing.

papers.title: General Relativity for Mathematicians - Part I
papers.abstract: These notes cover the first part of a course of the same title taught by Filippo Fila-Robattino and Manuel Tecchiolli at the University of Zurich in the Winter Semester of 2025. Topics include variational principles in classical mechanics, special relativity, smooth manifolds and tensor calculus, connections and curvature, geodesic motion, and the derivation of Einstein's equations from the Einstein-Hilbert action. The treatment is aimed at a mathematical audience, combining physical motivation with precise definitions, detailed proofs, and explicit calculations.

papers.title: Can Open Be Too Open? On the Security and Trustworthiness of Fully Transparent LLMs
papers.abstract: There are different levels of transparency for LLMs: open weights, open data, and/or open pipeline. Recently, more interest has emerged in fully transparent LLMs, i.e., LLMs with fully open weights, data, and training pipeline. Drawing analogies to other fields such as software security, it is often believed that increasing transparency inherently increases the security and trustworthiness of the LLM. However, we argue that such claims need to be critically re-evaluated in the context of LLMs. In this paper, we analyze the impact of transparency on LLM security and trustworthiness by reviewing the relevant literature. Our core findings are that, due to the limited reproducibility of LLM pipelines, in practice, users cannot verify the correspondence between open weights and the associated open data and pipeline. Thus, in order to trust a model, users still need to trust that developers acted honestly, reducing the benefits over models that provide less "transparency". Moreover, we find that even when LLMs are fully transparent and trusted, this openness can favor adversaries. Open weights in particular, but also open data and pipelines, can increase the success rate of attacks. Although the same mechanisms can be used to improve the model and protect it against attacks, the current lack of robust lightweight mechanisms to patch LLM vulnerabilities limits the benefits of openness at this time. We note that our analysis is based on current LLM capabilities and analysis tools, and that future developments may require a re-evaluation of these points.
papers.intro:
In the current LLM landscape, there are different levels of model transparency (also called openness). Models can be made available with their weights (open-weight models), their data (open-data models), and/or their training pipeline (open-pipeline models). A model could have any combination of open/closed weights, open/closed data, and open/closed pipeline. However, most commonly used models are either fully closed, meaning that they are only accessible over an API and nothing is published (e.g., OpenAI GPT-5, Anthropic Claude Opus, Google Gemini 3), only open-weight (e.g., Meta Llama 4, Alibaba Qwen 3, Mistral Large 3), or fully open, meaning open weights, open data, and open pipeline (e.g., Ai2 OLMo, EleutherAI Pythia, Apertus 1.5, Lucie-7B). It must be noted that even for fully transparent LLMs, opaque components may have been used. For example, open data means that all data used for training is published; however, parts of the data are often generated by an LLM that may not be fully transparent, which is an opaque component. Increased transparency is often seen as improving security and trustworthiness [69, 188, 118, 92, 112], similarly to how open-source software is often seen as providing better security guarantees and higher trustworthiness than closed-source software (i.e., the “Many-Eyes Principle” that states that given enough independent reviewers all bugs are shallow [130]).

It must be noted that even for fully transparent LLMs, opaque components may have been used. For example, open data means that all data used for training is published; however, parts of the data are often generated by an LLM that may not be fully transparent, which is an opaque component. Increased transparency is often seen as improving security and trustworthiness [69, 188, 118, 92, 112], similarly to how open-source software is often seen as providing better security guarantees and higher trustworthiness than closed-source software (i.e., the “Many-Eyes Principle” that states that given enough independent reviewers all bugs are shallow [130]).

In this work, we argue, however, that these claims need to be evaluated carefully since the analogy between LLMs and software does not hold in the context of security and trustworthiness. Software code was designed to be read and edited by humans and can be deterministically and inexpensively compiled into a binary. In contrast, LLMs are less amenable to public scrutiny, even under full transparency, due to a combination of factors including the way in which the training data is selected, the non-determinism of training, the cost of training, and the lack of interpretability of the weights. Some may argue that transparency alone may lead to more honest development processes as even a slightly increased risk of detection could disincentivize malicious behavior. However, if unwarranted, this can also give a false sense of security, and thus, we believe it is important to identify the impact of transparency on the trust and security of LLMs.

To evaluate the security of an LLM, different adversaries must be considered: a) an inference-time adversary who attempts to use the model for malicious purposes, b) an external model poisoner who posts malicious data to frequently scraped websites or redistributes a malicious version of the model, c) a malicious insider who tries to inject weaknesses into a model by changing the training pipeline, training data, or weights, and d) a malicious model developer (i.e., the organization that develops the model) who ships or serves a different model than the one the user expects. These correspond to general classes of adversaries for software, namely a malicious user, a software supply-chain attacker, a malicious insider, and a malicious vendor. For software, open-sourcing can help against all of these adversaries; for LLMs, this is not the case.

To evaluate the security of an LLM, different adversaries must be considered: a) an inference-time adversary who attempts to use the model for malicious purposes, b) an external model poisoner who posts malicious data to frequently scraped websites or redistributes a malicious version of the model, c) a malicious insider who tries to inject weaknesses into a model by changing the training pipeline, training data, or weights, and d) a malicious model developer (i.e., the organization that develops the model) who ships or serves a different model than the one the user expects. These correspond to general classes of adversaries for software, namely a malicious user, a software supply-chain attacker, a malicious insider, and a malicious vendor. For software, open-sourcing can help against all of these adversaries; for LLMs, this is not the case.

Transparency and Trust. The discussion of trust in LLMs focuses primarily on adversary (d), i.e., whether a user can verify that the LLM they run has the advertised properties. Transparency is usually seen as a way to reduce the need for users to trust the model developer. In open-source software, the user can inspect the code and can verify that the program they are running resulted from the published code (e.g., through reproducible builds). Even more importantly, the user can verify that the implementation largely corresponds to the specification and the functionality that the software is supposed to implement. Given that there is a clear semantic link between the code and the program behavior, it is difficult for the developer to insert hidden functionality into the open-source code without eventually being detected by reviewers of the code. Thus, one can, with appropriate care (i.e., the software is indeed reviewed by many and is written and built in a way that can be understood and verified), rely on popular open-source codebases being trustworthy.

Thus, one can, with appropriate care (i.e., the software is indeed reviewed by many and is written and built in a way that can be understood and verified), rely on popular open-source codebases being trustworthy.

For LLMs, this is usually not the case, even if a developer publishes the weights, data, and training pipeline of the model. The model weights do not provide a clear semantic link to the model’s behavior, and the training data is too vast to inspect in sufficient depth, whether manually or with automated tools. A malicious developer can poison an LLM by inserting a backdoor in the data, which often requires only a few poisoned documents in the dataset, and can be hidden to make detection more difficult [28, 146, 44, 61]. This means that it would be hard for a user to identify a poisoned model even if they have access to the data and training pipeline. Furthermore, even if a malicious backdoor is found, it is hard to provably attribute it to the developer, since the data they collected could already have been poisoned by another party. Even if we assume that the user can be certain that the published training data does not contain any backdoors, they may not be able to trust the weights that they received. Current frontier training processes are non-deterministic (i.e., using the same training pipeline on the same training data twice will not result in the same weights) [131, 125, 185], making it harder for users to verify that the weights actually resulted from applying the published training pipeline on the published data. Furthermore, even if training were deterministic, there are very few entities that could retrain a model to verify its correctness given the high effort required for training and the difficulty of replicating exact training hardware and entire training pipelines. Thus, unlike for open-source software, the user of a transparent LLM still needs to trust the developer to a significant degree. An overview of these differences is shown in Table I.

papers.title: OrthoRF: Exploring Orthogonality in Object-Centric Representations
papers.abstract: Neural synchrony is hypothesized to help the brain organize visual scenes into structured multi-object representations. In machine learning, synchrony-based models analogously learn object-centric representations by storing binding in the phase of complex-valued features. Rotating Features (RF) instantiate this idea with vector-valued activations, encoding object presence in magnitudes and affiliation in orientations. We propose Orthogonal Rotating Features (OrthoRF), which enforces orthogonality in RF's orientation space via an inner-product loss and architectural modifications. This yields sharper phase alignment and more reliable grouping. In evaluations of unsupervised object discovery, including settings with overlapping objects, noise, and out-of-distribution tests, OrthoRF matches or outperforms current models while producing more interpretable representations, and it eliminates the post-hoc clustering required by many synchrony-based approaches. Unlike current models, OrthoRF also recovers occluded object parts, indicating stronger grouping under occlusion. Overall, orthogonality emerges as a simple, effective inductive bias for synchrony-based object-centric learning.

papers.intro:
Decomposing scenes into constituent parts is a long-standing strategy in computer vision. Classical approaches factorized images into surfaces and objects with properties like reflectance, albedo, and geometry (Coakley, 2003). Deep learning has renewed this effort by learning structured representations (Zhang et al., 2013; Dittadi, 2023). In practice, this is often operationalized as Object-Centric Learning (OCL) (Greff et al., 2020), where models discover modular, compositional object representations that support generalization and relational reasoning on many downstream visual tasks (Ding et al., 2021; Bapst et al., 2019; Mandikal and Grauman, 2021).

Deep learning has renewed this effort by learning structured representations (Zhang et al., 2013; Dittadi, 2023). In practice, this is often operationalized as Object-Centric Learning (OCL) (Greff et al., 2020), where models discover modular, compositional object representations that support generalization and relational reasoning on many downstream visual tasks (Ding et al., 2021; Bapst et al., 2019; Mandikal and Grauman, 2021).

At its core, much like human perception (Spelke, 1990), OCL addresses the binding problem (Roskies, 1999): flexibly integrating features (such as color, shape, texture) into a unified perception. This view aligns with cognitive and neuroscientific accounts that posit neural synchrony (Singer, 2007) as a key mechanism, whereby temporally synchronized oscillations bind distributed information into coherent objects (see Fig 1).

This view aligns with cognitive and neuroscientific accounts that posit neural synchrony (Singer, 2007) as a key mechanism, whereby temporally synchronized oscillations bind distributed information into coherent objects (see Fig 1).

A dominant OCL design to binding uses a collection of discrete latent vectors, named ”slots“ (Locatello et al., 2020), each dedicated to the features of a single object. As slot-based methods evolve, radically new ideas are emerging in OCL, some of which are inspired by synchrony (Mozer et al., 1991; Reichert and Serre, 2013). In this less-explored paradigm, binding is expressed via the relative phases of complex-valued neural activations, with phase-space distances serving as an implicit relational metric between object instances. Recently, synchrony-based models (Löwe et al., 2022; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2024; Miyato et al., 2024) have achieved unsupervised object discovery on synthetic and more naturalistic scenes, surpassing prior supervised approaches (Mozer et al., 1991).

Current state-of-the-art synchrony-based models, such as Complex-valued Autoencoders (CAE) (Löwe et al., 2022), use real-valued weights to process complex-valued activations, by sharing weights across the real and imaginary parts. In these models, magnitudes encode feature presence, whereas phases encode object affiliation. During training, they leverage the natural constructive/destructive interference through the addition of complex activations in every layer, promoting phase alignment for features of the same object and phase separation for different objects. A related work, named Rotating Features (RF) (Löwe et al., 2024a), replaces complex-valued with vector-valued (i.e., nn-dimensional) activations that rotate on a hypersphere, extending representational capacity beyond 2D complex planes. To (de)synchronize phases for object representation, these models use an additional inductive bias via a gating mechanism (Reichert and Serre, 2013) that strengthens interactions among similarly oriented features and weakens those among dissimilarly oriented ones. However, this mechanism can be hard to interpret. To improve interpretability, Löwe et al. (2024b) introduced cosine binding, a more transparent alternative that is based on cosine similarity between activations. This, however, entails substantial memory overhead, since it requires computing and storing many similarities between inputs and intermediate outputs.

Synchrony-based models have important limitations. Unlike slot-based methods, which yield discrete, object-aligned slots (one slot ≈\approx one object), state-of-the-art synchrony-based models (Löwe et al., 2022; Löwe et al., 2024a; Stanić et al., 2023; Miyato et al., 2024; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2024) produce distributed representations. While this can be more flexible, it makes the output hard to use without extra machinery. In practice, they require post-hoc clustering in phase space to recover objects, grouping features by phase. This distributed coding also degrades performance in overlap regions: features from occluding objects become uncertain and drift farther from cluster centers (Löwe et al., 2024a), complicating object assignment. As a result, evaluations of these models often exclude overlapping regions, potentially underrepresenting the regimes where robust binding is most needed.

In this paper, we advance synchrony-based models, specifically the RF autoencoder (Löwe et al., 2024a), by improving both interpretability and representational capacity. Motivated by evidence that orthogonality enhances efficiency and encourages disentanglement (Ranasinghe et al., 2021), we propose Orthogonal Rotating Features (OrthoRF), an RF extension that enforces orthogonal object encoding in the phase space. Our approach has two components: (i) a softmax-based competitive binding that drives nn-dimensional activations to specialize on distinct input components (objects), and (ii) an inner-product-based orthogonality loss that enforces a 90∘90^{\circ} separation between object representations in phase space. Together, these yield sharper phase alignment and more reliable grouping: features of the same object concentrate along a single vector dimension, producing one-hot–like object encodings. These results underscore orthogonality as a simple yet powerful inductive bias for synchrony-based object-centric learning.

papers.title: Who Pays for Thinking? Billing Hidden Reasoning Tokens in Model Cloud Contracts
papers.abstract: In token-priced language model services, users can see the prompts they submit and the answers they receive, but may also pay for internal reasoning and candidate answers that are not shown in the final response. This paper develops a three-party service model to study how charging for this intermediate computation shapes providers' decisions and social welfare. Users purchase answers from a model firm that pays an execution cloud, with either supplier controlling the computation budget. The model separates user billing from upstream payments and identifies when metered pricing encourages excessive generation, when fixed service prices restrict valuable computation, and how responsibility for execution costs changes these choices. A LiveCodeBench study measures answer quality, latency, token use, and resource consumption across five model deployments, with numerical billing comparisons for the three covered by archived tariffs. At equal average charges on the reference workload, the calibrated comparisons show that billing structure changes both service participation and the computation budgets suppliers select. For accepted services with different budgets, the measured outcomes define the user-value thresholds at which their welfare ranking reverses. Metered pricing yields higher welfare when the additional inference it induces creates net social value, whereas fixed service pricing is preferable when the costs of that computation outweigh its benefits.

papers.intro:
Artificial intelligence (AI) applications built on large language models (LLMs), including chatbots and coding assistants, have become an important part of the Web. Similarweb estimates that generative AI platforms received an average of 9.5 billion Web visits per month between June 2025 and May 2026 (Similarweb, 2026). Token-priced AI services can charge for internal reasoning and for candidates that an application generates but does not deliver to its end user (Google, 2026a; Google, 2026b). How does charging for this unseen generation shape providers’ computation choices, and when does the additional computation create enough value for users to justify its cost?

In cloud-hosted services, users pay a model firm that purchases computation from a cloud provider. Existing studies analyze incentives to expand inference, price menus for users with different valuations, and manipulation of reported token counts (Artola Velasco et al., 2026a; Bergemann et al., 2026; Artola Velasco et al., 2026b). These studies focus on the user–provider transaction, leaving the model–cloud allocation of incentives largely implicit. A larger bill can reward the model firm while additional execution costs fall on the cloud, making both the payment between them and control over generation relevant to service provision.

This paper compares metered billing for intermediate generation with fixed service pricing at equal average charges on the reference workload. A three-party model separates this retail choice from the payment to the execution cloud and the right to choose the attempt budget. Payments for compute time, fixed capacity fees, and revenue sharing give the suppliers different returns to another candidate. The analysis determines which services satisfy participation and selects the controller’s most profitable budget, retaining ties and exit. It identifies when metered pricing supports more computation and when that computation improves welfare. Pooling, which submits multiple tasks in one generation call, enters through two channels. A lower cost increment can change the cloud’s preferred budget, and lower cost levels can make a previously rejected budget tradable. Either response can lower welfare even when each fixed service becomes cheaper.

papers.title: Transverse detuned loading for modulation bandwidth enhancement in VCSELs
papers.abstract: Directly modulated vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers (VCSELs) are central to short-reach optical interconnects, where modulation bandwidth and power efficiency are critical factors for increasing data transfer capacity. Conventional oxide VCSELs still require power-hungry signal processing to achieve high-speed data transmission above 100 Gb/s. Here we report an experimental implementation of detuned loading in a VCSEL to enhance the modulation bandwidth. The detuned loading is achieved by carrier-induced index variations that reshape an engineered transverse mode so its overlap with spatially selective optical losses decreases with increased carrier density. This produces a negative differential loss reminiscent of that in detuned-loaded DBR lasers lasing on the long-wavelength reflectivity flank. The resulting 850 nm single-mode VCSEL exhibits an enhanced carrier-photon relaxation frequency of 44 GHz, yielding a 3dB electrical modulation bandwidth exceeding 50 GHz. The enhancement persists from 25 {\deg}C to 75 {\deg}C showing the robustness of the mechanism introduced. The same device supports 106.25 Gb/s NRZ transmission without digital signal processing, transmitter pre-emphasis or receiver equalization. These results establish transverse detuned loading as a robust alternative approach for extending the modulation bandwidth of vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers.

papers.title: Post-DART impact ejecta re-accumulation on Dimorphos and implications for Hera gravity measurements
papers.abstract:
Context. The DART impact might have substantially modified the surface and near-surface structure of Dimorphos, affecting the morphology and gravity field that is to be measured by ESA's Hera mission.
  Aims. We investigate the post-impact redistribution of ejecta and its dependence on the assumed internal structure of Dimorphos.
  Methods. We performed high-resolution SPH simulations of the DART impact into two low-cohesion rubble-pile models, with and without a large central boulder. We followed the processes of ejecta re-accumulation and gravity evolution for six hours.
  Results. The impact ejects about 13% of Dimorphos's mass, most of which is re-accreted, producing near-global resurfacing. The ejecta blanket exceeds 8 m around the impact depression but is only a few tens of centimetres thick near the antipode, with similar large-scale deposition in both interior models. Local gravity changes reach about 10% of the pre-impact value. The central boulder affects the surface gravity only within the impact depression, where the removal of overlying material enhances its gravitational contribution.
  Conclusions. Hera will observe a surface and gravity field substantially modified by DART, which must be considered when interpreting measurements in terms of the internal structure of Dimorphos.

papers.intro:
On 26 September 2022, NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft impacted Dimorphos, the secondary of the Didymos binary asteroid system, and successfully altered its orbit around Didymos (Daly et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2023; Chabot et al., 2024). The impact produced an amount of ejecta, which was observed by ground- and space-based telescopes (Li et al., 2023) and by the LICIACube (Dotto et al., 2024). The measured momentum transfer and morphology of the evolving ejecta suggest that Dimorphos is a low-cohesion rubble-pile asteroid (Raducan et al., 2024a). However, different interior structures can produce outcomes that are consistent with existing observations. These differences might be reflected in the distribution of re-accumulated ejecta and the post-impact gravity field, providing diagnostics of the surface and internal properties of Dimorphos.

ESA’s Hera mission (Michel et al., 2022) will arrive at the Didymos system in late 2026 to complete the DART experiment. Hera will determine the shape, mass, composition, and dynamical properties of the binary, while the Juventas CubeSat will probe Dimorphos with the JuRa low-frequency radar and measure the local gravity vector with the GRASS gravimeter after landing (Michel et al., 2022). Together with hyperspectral observations from HyperScout-H (Popescu et al., 2025; Prodan et al., 2026), these measurements will constrain the surface, near-surface, and interior properties of Dimorphos.

papers.title: The counts of parity-odd vs even late-growing permutations in the group $\mathbb{S}_{2p-1}$ differ by $(-1)^p$
papers.abstract: A permutation $\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_n$ of objects $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ is called \emph{late-growing} if its partial sums never exceed the respective partial sums of the `average' permutation (with the arithmetic mean $n^{-1}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^n i = (n+1)/2$ of $1,\ldots,n$ on average at each entry $\sigma(i)$): $\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma(i) \leqslant k\cdot (n+1)/2$ for all positive $k\leqslant n$. We prove that for $n=2p-1$ odd, the set $\Phi_p\subseteq \mathbb{S}_{2p-1}$ of late-growing permutations is partitioned into parity-even vs odd elements, $\Phi_p = \Phi_p^{+} \sqcup \Phi_p^{-}$, in an almost symmetric way: $| \Phi_p^{+} | - | \Phi_p^{-} | = (-1)^{p+1}$. The proof is constructive: by viewing the permutations $\sigma\in\Phi_p$ as constrained walks on the integral lattice $\mathbb{Z}$, we describe two filters that pair all but one element in $\Phi_p^{+}$ versus $\Phi_p^{-}$; the remaining walk $\sigma^*$ with monotonically growing step amplitudes determines the dominant parity subset.

papers.title: The generic structure of the singular set in the Stefan problem
papers.abstract: We show that, in every space dimension $n\ge2$, the singular set $\Sigma$ of a generic (in the Baire-category sense) solution of the Stefan problem is countably parabolically $(n-2)$-rectifiable. In particular, $\dim_{\mathrm{par}}(\Sigma)\le n-2$. This is achieved by proving the following sharp result: in every space dimension, points of the maximal stratum of a generic solution are discrete in space-time.

The Stefan problem [Ste90] is one of the most classical free boundary problems and it aims to describe the evolution of free interfaces such as ice melting into water. papers.title: Hidden Singularity and Fractal Dimensions for Extended Harper Operators
papers.abstract: We prove that, for every irrational frequency, the spectra of the extended Harper family throughout the zero-measure regime have finite $1/2$-dimensional Hausdorff measure and lower box dimension at most $1/2$. Both numbers improve to $1/3$ on the isotropic critical boundary. The proof is based on a family of unitary transformations, that specializes to the chiral transform of [BJK] for the case of the critical almost Mathieu. This family allows to make every operator in this regime spectrally equivalent to a singular Jacobi operator. Using these singular representatives, we apply the method of [BJK] to construct covers by $O(q_n)$ intervals of total length $O(q_n^{-1})$, improving to $O(q_n^{-2})$ on the isotropic boundary, where $q_n$ is the denominator of a canonical approximant to $\alpha$. The covers give upper box bounds and, with packing estimates, examples where the box-counting dimension fails to exist.

papers.title: Nonabelian Higgs fields from minimal submanifolds
papers.abstract: We construct $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ Yang-Mills-Higgs fields on a broad class of noncompact Riemannian manifolds, concentrating in the large-mass limit along prescribed nondegenerate minimal submanifolds of codimension three. The solutions have uniformly bounded rescaled energy. On closed manifolds with $b_1(M)=0$, adding a suitably scaled Higgs potential gives an analogous concentration result. Our construction completes one direction of the correspondence proposed by Parise, Pigati and Stern, realising prescribed minimal submanifolds of codimension three as concentration sets of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ Yang--Mills--Higgs fields.

papers.intro:
The emergence of minimal hypersurfaces from nonlinear elliptic equations has been a central theme in geometric analysis since the 1970s. The work of Modica and Mortola [20] revealed how hypersurface area arises as the limit of diffuse phase-transition energies. This insight initiated a programme that has since established a rich correspondence between minimal hypersurfaces and the transition layers of solutions to the Allen–Cahn equation [17, 16, 15, 8, 7].

papers.title: Differentiable Contact Dynamics for Legged Locomotion: Policy Learning and Contact-Implicit Trajectory Optimization
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a smooth analytic gradient for frictional contact and applies it to policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization for legged locomotion. The exact contact sensitivity is available in closed form but describes changes within the current contact mode, providing no first-order information toward neighboring contact modes. The proposed gradient replaces this sensitivity only in the backward pass, leaving the hard-contact forward solve unchanged and the realized rollout feasible. A central-path relaxation of the de Saxc\'e-corrected second-order-cone complementarity problem for Coulomb friction smooths the conditions defining the separating, clamping, and sliding modes. The relaxed sensitivity is evaluated at a point on the central path obtained by a Newton iteration initialized from the hard-contact solution. The sensitivity remains continuous through contact-mode transitions and converges to the exact sensitivity as the relaxation vanishes. Using 100,000 samples and less than 2 min of training on a desktop PC, policy learning with the proposed gradient produces a policy that transfers to hardware without fine-tuning. On hardware, the robot under a trotting policy withstands pushes and traverses debris and slippery ground. In trajectory optimization, the proposed gradient reaches contact-rich solutions missed by exact and Signorini-relaxed gradients. Project page: https://diffcontact.github.io

papers.intro:
The first-order gradient through contact in a differentiable physics simulator provides a common computational primitive for two classes of methods in contact-rich robot control. The first is policy learning, in which model-free reinforcement learning is widely used and policy-gradient estimates are computed from rollouts across thousands of parallel environments [1, 2, 3]. First-order policy learning [4, 5] preserves the same objective but replaces the score-function (REINFORCE) estimate [6, 7] with a typically lower-variance first-order estimate [8]. This estimate can be obtained by differentiating through the simulator, with comparable policies learned from fewer samples [9]. The second is trajectory optimization. Contact-implicit trajectory optimization (CITO) methods determine when and where contacts are made and broken without a prescribed contact-mode sequence [10, 11, 12]. Shooting-based DDP/iLQR methods [13, 14] use the same transition Jacobians as the policy-learning estimator and have been applied online in receding-horizon control for contact-rich locomotion [15].

This estimate can be obtained by differentiating through the simulator, with comparable policies learned from fewer samples [9]. The second is trajectory optimization. Contact-implicit trajectory optimization (CITO) methods determine when and where contacts are made and broken without a prescribed contact-mode sequence [10, 11, 12]. Shooting-based DDP/iLQR methods [13, 14] use the same transition Jacobians as the policy-learning estimator and have been applied online in receding-horizon control for contact-rich locomotion [15].

For legged robots, both tools are limited by the contact sensitivity provided by differentiable simulation. A simulator may be differentiable without providing a useful first-order direction toward a neighboring contact mode [16, 17]. The exact contact sensitivity is available in closed form [18, 19], but it is evaluated with the active set, or contact-mode assignment, held fixed and therefore describes only the response within the current mode. A clamped contact is linearized as remaining clamped, providing no first-order information toward liftoff or slip, and the sensitivity changes discontinuously when the active set changes. In contact-implicit optimization, this mode-restricted sensitivity keeps the local search near the contact sequence of the nominal trajectory [15, 18, 20]. In first-order policy learning, the same Jacobians enter backpropagation through time (BPTT), where they can produce fragile or ineffective optimization in contact-rich systems [16, 17, 21, 22].

Prior work addresses contact sensitivity in policy learning and CITO in different ways. In policy learning, methods shorten the differentiation horizon [9, 22], use a reduced-order model for the backward pass [23], or smooth contact in the forward rollout [24]. Shorter horizons can help with long-horizon gradient instability, but do not change the contact sensitivity within each window. In CITO, transcription methods optimize contact impulses alongside the trajectory [11, 12, 25], whereas shooting methods rely on transition Jacobians from the contact dynamics [13, 14, 15]. Other approaches smooth the forward contact model [26, 20], differentiate relaxed contact solutions [27, 28], or estimate gradients across perturbed solves [29, 30]. For shooting-based CITO with a hard-contact forward solve, however, the exact contact sensitivity remains tied to the current contact mode and offers limited first-order guidance toward a different mode [18]. Relaxing only the Signorini condition during differentiation [15] partly addresses this limitation by providing directions for contact make/break transitions, but leaves sliding and normal–tangential coupling unaddressed.

We therefore propose a contact sensitivity obtained by relaxing the full frictional contact condition only in the backward pass, providing search directions toward neighboring contact modes while retaining the hard-contact forward solve. The de Saxcé correction expresses frictional contact as a single second-order-cone complementarity condition [31, 32]. Relaxing this condition along a central path [33] couples normal and tangential contact sensitivities across separation, clamping, and sliding. These coupled sensitivities are available in every contact mode, allowing the optimizer to change modes through gradient-based updates. We further investigate their role in guiding transitions to sliding, where a normal-only relaxation lacks the required tangential information.

papers.title: Heavy Heisenberg Algebras, Zero Modes and Modularity
papers.abstract: It is known due to a result of Miyamoto that zero mode correlators of weight $1$ vectors of vertex operator algebras are quasi-modular forms, and that their generating series are Jacobi forms. In this article we generalize this to higher weight vectors. We consider weight 2 vectors that generate what we call heavy Heisenberg algebras. We prove that their zero mode correlators are a specific type of quasi-modular forms. As a consequence, they too can be summed up into a generating series with Jacobi-like modular transformation properties. As an application of our results, we sketch an argument that gives the asymptotic behavior of the dimensions of states of our VOAs.

papers.title: Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design
papers.abstract: De novo protein design campaigns remain bottlenecked by the inference compute time required to generate and rank candidates, limiting wider functional exploration. Here, we introduce and evaluate an epitope excision approach that truncates targets to local interface windows to accelerate both backbone diffusion and structure prediction. Across 15 targets and 3,666 designs, excised windows closely reproduced full-target binding interfaces (median C\alpha RMSD of 0.37 \AA) and made it practical to design binders against the 719-residue extracellular domain of fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) by cutting RFdiffusion and AlphaFold3 GPU time by ~ 88% in one of the epitopes. Pairing this workflow with an agentic optimization loop allowed the system to autonomously identify catalytic-site targeting strategies. Under a fixed compute budget, a human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflow raised the computational hit rate from 5.06% to 9.33% while further cutting GPU hours by ~ 42%. We also found that omitting target multiple sequence alignments during refolding roughly substantially increased the apparent yield. Wet-lab validation with yeast display identified nanomolar binders from the generated designs with the HITL and the fully autonomous agent (human-out-of-the-loop, HOOTL) arms recovering more enriched designs than the PI-alone baseline. Together, target excision and agent-guided search offer a practical way to scale de novo binder design to large, therapeutically relevant proteins.
papers.intro:
Structure-based de novo binder design routinely generates thousands of candidate backbones and sequences per target, combining backbone generators such as RFdiffusion [1] with sequence design tools like ProteinMPNN [2] in end-to-end pipelines such as BindCraft [3]. Because only a small fraction of generated candidates actually bind in vitro, campaigns depend on an in silico filtering step in which each candidate is refolded with its target (for example with AlphaFold3 [4], building on AlphaFold2 [5]) and ranked by an interface-confidence metric. One such metric, ipSAE [6], is derived from AlphaFold predicted aligned error and has been shown to outperform earlier scores including pDockQ [7] and pDockQ2 [8]. How well this computational screen separates true binders from non-binders has been shown to correlate with the hit rate of downstream wet-lab testing.

The refolding step is also the primary compute bottleneck. AlphaFold3 has been demonstrated to be a reliable refolding method, and its runtime is governed by discrete token buckets, with complex lengths rounded up to the next multiple of 256 tokens. Many biologically important targets, including cell-surface receptors, multi-domain ectodomains, viral glycoproteins, and enzymes are much larger than the designed binder and the local patch it contacts. Consequently, most of the tokens processed during refolding belong to target regions far from the binding site. For a 719-residue enzyme ectodomain of a disease target, fibroblast activation protein α\alpha (FAP), repeated full-structure diffusion and full-complex refolding is prohibitively slow, even though the targetable epitope is a relatively small rim around the catalytic opening [9].

To get around the compute bottleneck, previous studies have targeted structurally independent folding units. However, many drug targets containing functional pockets are not confined to a single, small domain. Recent work has demonstrated that the global fold of a target may not be strictly necessary for generative design, as discontinuous structural fragments can successfully guide backbone generation [10]. However, target truncation requires rigorously auditing of its downstream consequences for larger wet-lab campaigns. It remains unknown how aggressive cropping impacts the precise interface geometry and the ranking signal required to separate true binders from non-binders during in silico triage. Furthermore, discontinuous 3D patches do not map cleanly to the discrete token-bucket economics of modern predictive triages like AlphaFold3, nor do they readily support the multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) often required for reliable refolding. This asymmetry motivates epitope excision: cropping the target down to the residues immediately surrounding the designed interface (the contact shell plus a tunable surrounding halo) and folding this local pocket in place of the intact protein. For excision to be useful in practice, it must preserve the local geometry of the designed interface, maintain the relative ranking of true binders against non-binders, and cross a token-bucket boundary to deliver actual wall-clock speedups. Instead of treating aggressive cropping as a free speedup, the first half of this study tests all three requirements systematically across a 15-target benchmark.

Beyond reducing fold times, excision turns otherwise intractable targets into manageable sub-problems. Running a productive campaign still requires iterative choices about where to target, how much of the surrounding structure to retain, and how to allocate compute across candidate backbones and sequences. Large language model (LLM) agents are well suited to this type of iterative, data-driven optimization. Equipped with external tools, state memory, and quantitative feedback, modern LLMs can plan multi-step workflows, launch jobs, inspect intermediate results, and adjust their search policy from round to round, closely mirroring how a researcher runs a design campaign. Similar multi-agent frameworks built on Gemini, such as Google’s AI co-scientist, have recently been used to generate, critique, and refine experimentally validated biomedical hypotheses [11]. De novo binder design provides a clean testbed for evaluating how much autonomy to give such an agent, because campaign performance can be measured directly as the computational hit rate under a fixed structural threshold and a fixed GPU budget.

The two parts of the study address complementary questions: the 15-target benchmark defines the physical and statistical operating limits of epitope excision, and the FAP campaign tests how best to direct that pipeline in practice. We find that the human–agent hybrid produces the most high-confidence designs per GPU-hour. Along the way, we also observe that omitting target multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) substantially shifts AF3 interface-confidence scores on several targets, indicating that single-sequence refolding can be an effective option depending on alignment depth. Finally, we test these computational predictions experimentally through yeast display and identify nanomolar binders from the generated designs.

papers.title: MOSHO: A Native Discrete Shark-Inspired Metaheuristic for Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search
papers.abstract: Hardware-aware neural architecture search (NAS) requires jointly optimizing predictive accuracy and device-specific latency over discrete search spaces. While multi-objective swarm optimizers show promise, continuous formulations such as the Multi-Objective White Shark Optimizer (MOWSO) can suffer from quantization noise when rounded to integer-encoded architecture vectors. To address this limitation, we propose MOSHO (Multi-Objective Shark Hunting Optimization), a native discrete metaheuristic that replaces continuous motion equations with discrete architecture-editing operators. MOSHO integrates adaptive operator scheduling, energy-regulated restarts, and deferred crowding-distance truncation to enhance exploration and search efficiency. On the merged NAS-Bench-201/HW-NAS-Bench benchmark across 18 contexts, MOSHO achieves a median normalized hypervolume of 0.9987 and IGD+ of 0.0064, yielding Pareto fronts competitive with NSGA-II while reducing search runtime by 96.4% (0.64 s vs. 17.72 s). These results demonstrate that tailored discrete search mechanisms can enable swarm optimizers to achieve high-quality multi-objective solution quality with substantially lower search cost in hardware-aware NAS.

papers.intro:
Deep learning has become a fundamental approach for image classification and visual recognition, with Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) achieving strong performance across a wide range of applications (Elsken et al., 2019). The performance of a CNN depends not only on its learned parameters but also on architectural choices, including operation types, kernel sizes, channel widths, activation functions, and connectivity patterns. Manually designing these configurations is challenging because the number of possible combinations grows rapidly with the number of architectural decisions. Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO) addresses this challenge by automatically searching for effective training and model hyperparameters, typically while keeping the network architecture fixed. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) extends this optimization paradigm by treating the architecture itself as a search variable (Elsken et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2021). NAS therefore searches an architecture space 𝒳\mathcal{X} for configurations offering desirable predictive performance. Early NAS approaches based on reinforcement learning and evolutionary algorithms demonstrated the potential of automated architecture design but often required substantial computational resources (Zoph and Le, 2017; Real et al., 2019). Subsequent weight-sharing approaches and tabular NAS benchmarks have made architecture search more practical and reproducible (Liu et al., 2019; Dong and Yang, 2020).

papers.title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use exhibit inconsistent behavior across independent runs from identical states, calling different tools, producing contradictory outputs, or pursuing divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), an unsupervised trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces the variation in task progress from 132% to 91% on tau2-bench and from 90% to 44% on toolsandbox, while improving performance across benchmarks and model scales. Training with RSD as an additional reward signal matches supervised fine-tuning performance with substantially lower variance, without requiring ground-truth labels.

papers.intro:
With recent advances, Large language models (LLMs) agents can execute complex workflows and multi-step tasks via tool calling functions (Yao et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). These agentic systems are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that interact with users and tools over multiple turns. For long-horizon tasks such as code generation agents (Shinn et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024), as well as agents built for critical applications such as healthcare systems (Tu et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2024), both correctness and reliability are important but manifest in different ways. In long- horizon tasks, like code generation, small errors in the beginning can accumulate over time, leading to compounding errors that deviate significantly from the expected solution trajectory. In critical applications such as healthcare systems, reliability is further challenged by the need for consistent agent behavior in repeated executions. However, in reality, we observe that given the same task to solve, the agent may still yield different decision paths across executions, such as calling entirely different tools, provide contradictory information to users, or follow divergent strategies that lead to different outcomes.

While LLM decoding strategies such as setting the temperature to zero, or using greedy decoding reduce stochasticity at the token level, they do not necessarily ensure consistency at the agent-level. For a multi-step or multi-turn LLM agent, the behavior is determined by sequences of decisions conditioned on evolving trajectories, where small differences in the trajectories due to stochastic tool output responses or environmental feedback can lead to divergent agent trajectories even under deterministic decoding strategies. Additionally, even when the underlying LLM is the same, the decoding strategy is deterministic, and the agent interaction history is fixed, there are additional sources of non-determinism such as floating-point precision and hardware-level variability which can lead to inconsistent agent behavior.

Existing evaluation metrics (Chang et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024) focus primarily on reporting task correctness using full or partial task completion metrics, often do not capture consistency in the agent performance. The p​a​s​spass^kk metric (Yao et al., 2024; Barres et al., 2025), which measures the chance that all kk i.i.d. task trials are successful, is the closest existing metric to capturing agent consistency, but it remains binary and is used for reporting rather than enforcing consistency in the agent behavior. Notably, agent consistency is independent of correctness, as agents may exhibit stable behavior patterns that are either consistently successful or consistently failing across executions.

papers.title: DTCA: Denoising Token Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning in Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, enabling bidirectional context modeling and parallel token refinement. Recent studies have applied reinforcement learning (RL) to DLMs and improved their reasoning performance. However, the iterative denoising process makes credit assignment more challenging, as final outcome rewards provide limited information about how different tokens contribute to the final output. In this paper, we propose Denoising Token Credit Assignment (DTCA), a framework for token-level credit assignment in reinforcement learning for diffusion language models. DTCA estimates token contributions by measuring the improvement in prediction confidence of remaining masked positions after token commitment and groups these signals according to part-of-speech (POS) categories. These contribution weights are used to select informative denoising timesteps and assign token-level learning signals during RL training. DTCA further calibrates these learning signals according to token-level entropy changes induced by policy updates. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct show that DTCA consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance across different generation budgets, with gains of up to 9.0 points on MATH500 and 5.3 points on GSM8K over the base model.

papers.title: A Truthful-in-Expectation 2-Approximation for Pair-Specific Cascade Auctions in AI-Generated Content
papers.abstract:
Generative AI interfaces can insert sponsored content at multiple points in an answer, where click-through rates (CTRs) depend on the advertiser-position pair. Under the cascade model, users read ads sequentially and stop after their first click, so both ad assignment and display order affect welfare. For arbitrary pair-specific CTRs, Balseiro et al. (WWW 2026) gave a $4/(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation whose monotonicity has not been established, and a monotone $O(\log m)$-approximation for $m$ candidate positions. Earlier truthful constant-factor mechanisms require factorized CTR models and do not apply. Whether monotonicity is compatible with a constant-factor approximation in this general setting was left open by that work.
  We give a polynomial-time mechanism for arbitrary pair-specific CTRs and any limit on displayed ads that is truthful and individually rational in expectation and achieves a 2-approximation to optimal cascade welfare. Our mechanism selects an advertiser-position matching and a designated last ad, then randomly thins earlier ads so that each selected ad's expected cascade CTR is the same fraction of its standalone CTR. This yields an exact closed-form expression for expected welfare, which we maximize over a bid-independent lottery range using linear programming. Exact optimization ensures monotonicity, while a random-prefix decomposition proves the factor-two guarantee, which is tight for this range. We also show that exactly optimizing the previous welfare surrogate can violate monotonicity, and evaluate welfare and running time on synthetic instances.

In such content, the click-through rate (CTR) of an ad may depend on both the advertiser and the position where the ad appears. Balseiro et al. Advertisers therefore compete both for positions and for the user’s attention as the user reads.

papers.title: Calibration of robust covariance estimation under heavy tails
papers.abstract: The Minimum Covariance Determinant (MCD) estimator is one of the most widely used high-breakdown estimators of multivariate location and scatter. Its practical success relies on suitable corrections, which remove the asymptotic and small-sample biases introduced by trimming. While explicit consistency factors are available under the multivariate normal distribution and, more recently, under multivariate Student-t models, these corrections only address the asymptotic behavior of the estimator. In the Gaussian case, it is known showed that the MCD also exhibits a non-negligible finite-sample bias, particularly for small sample sizes and relatively large dimensions. Such bias propagates to robust Mahalanobis distances and may affect subsequent procedures, including multivariate outlier detection and robust inference. This paper investigates the finite-sample behavior of the MCD estimator and of the related robust distances under multivariate Student-t distributions, a potentially relevant scenario in many application fields. Extensive Monte Carlo experiments are carried out over a broad range of sample sizes, dimensions, trimming levels and degrees of freedom. Based on these experiments, empirical correction factors are obtained and approximated by smooth functions, providing a computationally efficient calibration suitable for practical implementations to heavy-tailed data. The proposed corrections are developed both for the scatter bias and the robust distance quantiles, thus leading to improved approximations for robust inference.

papers.title: Patch-Derived or Register Tokens? Comparing Variable-Length Image Tokenizers
papers.abstract: Image tokenizers convert pixels into compact latent sequences for efficient generative modeling. Most approaches arrange latents on a downsampled two-dimensional grid, tying sequence length to image resolution. We compare two variable-length strategies: computationally efficient patch-derived tokens, which inherit explicit spatial organization, and more demanding register tokens, which have no predefined spatial layout. Our reconstruction results reveal that patch-derived tokens perform substantially better under extreme compression, whereas register tokens achieve slightly better reconstruction quality at intermediate budgets. At high token budgets, both approaches achieve similar reconstruction quality. For downstream generative tasks, register tokens outperform patch-derived tokens. Adding representation alignment with external pretrained visual encoders substantially improves the generative performance of patch-derived tokens, allowing them to match or outperform register tokens depending on the token budget. We further find that both approaches learn spatially localized representations. Patch-derived tokens largely retain their explicitly imposed spatial organization, while register tokens develop an implicit two-dimensional spatial structure despite having no predefined layout. Representation alignment reduces this spatial organizational constraint, enabling individual tokens to exert a stronger non-local influence.

Image tokenization plays a crucial role in reducing the computational costs of subsequent generative models [22, 3, 20]. An image tokenizer [16] encodes an image into a compact latent token representation. Most tokenizers preserve the spatial structure of the image by arranging the tokens on a downsampled grid, with each token corresponding to a fixed image region [6, 14]. Consequently, the number of tokens grows with the image resolution, resulting in prohibitively long sequences in the case of high-resolution image generation, video generation, and world modeling.

Consequently, the number of tokens grows with the image resolution, resulting in prohibitively long sequences in the case of high-resolution image generation, video generation, and world modeling.

Recent work such as TiTok [30] has challenged these grid-structured latent representations by encoding images into sequences whose length is not determined by the number of input patches. This decoupling enables substantially shorter representations while maintaining high reconstruction fidelity and supporting competitive generative modeling. A common approach introduces KK learned tokens, also called register tokens, concatenates them with the PP image-patch embeddings, and jointly processes the resulting P+KP+K tokens in the encoder. The updated KK register tokens are retained as the image representation and passed to the decoder, while the patch tokens are discarded. Although effective, this design increases the model’s sequence length from PP to P+KP+K, adding computational overhead.

A commonly used approach is nested dropout [19], in which the latent sequence is randomly truncated during training. The decoder must therefore reconstruct images from sequences of varying lengths, allowing the tokenizer to support multiple representation sizes at inference time.

These differences make it difficult to determine which observed effects can be attributed specifically to the bottleneck design. We address this gap by isolating the bottleneck design and systematically evaluating its effects on reconstruction quality, generation quality, computational cost, and the spatial organization of the resulting representations. papers.title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains
papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown impressive capabilities in high-level reasoning and task planning for robots. However, specialized domains remain a challenge for VLMs' image interpretation and grounding abilities. We introduce TrySee, a modular closed-loop robot task planning pipeline integrating general-purpose VLM reasoning with domain-specific perception and established robotics components. The system consists of an inherently reactive cyclic planning pipeline, augmented with domain-specific modular vision preprocessing, to provide online grounding. Finally, a dynamic preprocessing selection mechanism contributes to the scalability of the pipeline. The system requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations and adapts through replaceable perception modules and motion planning. The approach is evaluated on planning tasks across 5 widely different domains, including a real-world robot disassembly task. The field tests in a brownfield environment demonstrate the approach's practicality in integrating VLM planning into specialized robotic systems with limited domain-specific training data.

A fundamental requirement for VLMs to generate effective robot task plans is the ability to ground their language understanding in the robot’s perception and action capabilities. In other words, the objects and features comprising the robot’s environment must be linked to the semantics used in the given task, and these, in turn, must be linked to the concrete movements and poses necessary to interact with them. General-purpose VLMs often fail at the first step for recondite objects, and their image-level outputs alone do not provide sufficiently reliable geometric targets for robot execution. papers.title: Learning Nonlinear Waveform Fusion Across Scales for Integrated Sensing and Communication
papers.abstract: Fixed source superposition and frequency partitioning constrain how communication content interacts with a probing reference in integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). We learn nonlinear waveform fusion across scales for image transmission and localization of multiple targets in range and angle. Reception uses the information available at each end. Adaptive temporal feature weighting and spectral updates combine image features and a deterministic linearly frequency-modulated reference in a shared complex state, generating a waveform with fixed total energy over the array frame. At the user equipment (UE), the reference and channel state information condition a neural demixer for image reconstruction. At the base station, the realized transmit pulse defines a coherent dictionary for sequential localization with learned local correction, physical refinement, and residual updates. We compare the proposed waveforms with superposition in the time domain and learned spectral linear fusion on 512 independent test images, using a shared fixed UE receiver and a baseline sensing receiver using coherent peak search. Averaged across eleven task weights, the proposed waveforms reduce normalized localization error by 29.0\% and 27.0\%, respectively, while increasing mean peak signal-to-noise ratio by 1.40 and 0.82~dB. With the proposed waveforms fixed, learned local correction reduces mean normalized localization error by 12.2\% relative to the same sequential receiver without learned correction.

Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) uses a shared radio platform for information delivery and environmental sensing [1, 2]. A shared waveform must deliver recoverable information to a communication terminal and illuminate targets for parameter estimation [3, 4]. For image transmission and target localization, we optimize the shared waveform directly in terms of image reconstruction error and errors in range and angle.

Designs centered on communication reuse the structure of communication signals for sensing. Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) supports radar processing through known symbols and subcarriers [5]; adaptive designs adjust their allocation to communication and sensing requirements [6]. Designs centered on sensing instead embed information into signals designed for radar. Sidelobe control and waveform diversity preserve selected probing properties while carrying data [7], and chirp modulation provides another mechanism for embedding information [8]. Tunable filter design controls sidelobe levels, range sidelobe modulation, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) loss for waveforms integrating radar and communication [9]. In these approaches, prescribed signal structures guide information embedding and radar processing.

Multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) radar and MIMO communication designs serving multiple users optimize transmission and beamforming for both functions [10, 11]. Criteria based on beampatterns and estimation bounds connect sensing quality to communication constraints [12, 13]. Analyses of the Cramér–Rao bound (CRB) and communication rate characterize the attainable tradeoffs for specified Gaussian and MIMO models [14, 15], while symbol-level precoding also uses instantaneous data symbols in waveform design [16]. These formulations provide flexible waveform parameterizations, but their objectives at the signal level need not coincide with reconstruction and localization error.

papers.title: A Universal Constitutive Relation for Static Droplet Retention
papers.abstract: Under applied forcing, static droplet retention is accompanied by contact angle asymmetry, with unequal apparent contact angles on opposite sides. Yet, the relation between the asymmetry and forcing lacks a common constitutive basis. Here, we show that the asymmetry emerges from minimizing the forcing-dependent free energy. The response of the asymmetry to forcing defines a susceptibility whose zero-forcing value yields a universal constitutive relation between the asymmetry and forcing. The constitutive relation is quantitatively validated across liquids, volumes, and forcing levels.

A basic manifestation of such retention under forcing is static contact angle asymmetry, in which a stationary droplet exhibits different apparent contact angles on its fore and aft sides [9, 16]. Droplet retention on solid substrates is widespread in nature, as seen in raindrops clinging to leaves and windows, and is important in technologies including coating [8], printing [7], and liquid manipulation [6]. A basic manifestation of such retention under forcing is static contact angle asymmetry, in which a stationary droplet exhibits different apparent contact angles on its fore and aft sides [9, 16]. How this asymmetry relates to the applied forcing is therefore central to understanding droplet retention.

For decades, the forcing–asymmetry relation has been formulated from different physical viewpoints. Three representative formulations are summarized as follows: (i) The Kawasaki–Furmidge model [12, 10] starts from the capillary traction acting along the contact line; integrating its component along the forcing direction yields a force proportional to contact angle asymmetry, with the contact line geometry entering through a empirical factor. (ii)The McHale model [14, 15] recasts droplet retention as an Amontons-like friction law, in which the normal load is replaced by a capillary normal force. The applied forcing is then related to this load through an effective friction coefficient determined by contact angle asymmetry. (iii) The Tadmor model [20, 19] attributes the forcing–asymmetry coupling to interfacial deformation induced by the uncompensated normal component of surface tension. The strength of this coupling is governed by an interfacial modulus. Despite these distinct formulations, whether the forcing–asymmetry relation admits a common constitutive basis remains unresolved.

In this Letter, we resolve this long-standing ambiguity by demonstrating that the forcing–asymmetry relation emerges as a macroscopic equilibrium response governed by the free energy landscape. We incorporate the pressure field generated by the applied forcing consistently into both the interfacial and bulk contributions to the droplet free energy. Minimization over the resulting free energy landscape selects the equilibrium state, from which both apparent contact angles and their asymmetry follow. As the forcing varies, these selected states trace a branch, with the local variation of the asymmetry quantified by a susceptibility. Near the unforced state, we obtain a constitutive relation linking the forcing to the contact angle asymmetry, with the zero-forcing susceptibility as the response coefficient.

papers.title: SEDATE: Do Large Language Models Share an Aggression Circuit Across Languages?
papers.abstract: As the applications of AI continue to expand across various multimodal and multilingual domains, ensuring safe and responsible deployment of these systems has become an important concern. A wide-range of interventions have been proposed to make AI responses safer and more reliable. They often incur substantial computational or annotation costs, or cannot be extended to multilingual settings. In this work, we propose Selective Detection And Targeted Editing (SEDATE), a training-free approach based on detect-edit-verify strategy. SEDATE first detects the responsible neurons, edits them as and when necessary and finally verifies the model responses; all without any additional model training. We evaluate SEDATE across 7 languages and 4 model families. We further evaluate its effectiveness across 4 out-of-distribution languages and 4 additional datasets. We show that SEDATE achieves substantially superior safety scores across all languages and models over the best-performing baseline while retaining the general capabilities and incurring negligible overhead. Our results are robust, with the trends remaining similar for out-of-distribution languages and datasets.

Research Question Does aggressive generation rely on different neurons in different languages, or is there a shared set of neurons that consistently responds to aggressive content across languages?

Answering this question is important for both interpretability and safety control. If aggressive behaviour is partly supported by a language-invariant set of neurons, these neurons can provide a common mechanistic target for controlling harmful generation across languages Kojima et al. (2024). In contrast, if aggression-related neurons are largely language-specific, multilingual safety interventions may need to be designed separately for every language Zhang et al. (2026).

To investigate this question, we identify feed-forward network neurons that activate selectively for aggressive rather than non-aggressive content. For each language, we compute AAPE (aggression activation probability entropy) Tang et al. (2024), which measures how strongly a neuron prefers aggressive over benign text. Neurons with low entropy and higher activation probability on aggressive content are selected as aggression-sensitive neurons. We then measure the agreement between language-specific neuron sets using CLAO (cross-lingual aggression overlap) and define their intersection as a cross-lingual core set. This core contains neurons that are consistently associated with aggressive content across all evaluated languages Xu et al. (2025).

Identifying these neurons alone, however, is not sufficient for reliable behavioural control. A straightforward approach would be to mask them throughout the entire generation process. Such static masking is overly restrictive because it modifies the model even when it is producing harmless content and may reduce fluency, relevance, or general utility. Moreover, suppressing an undesirable activation does not indicate what the model should generate instead.

We therefore propose SeDATE, a training-free inference-time framework based on a detect-edit-verify strategy. At every decoding step, SeDATE monitors an aggression signal computed from the activation of the identified neurons. When the signal remains below a threshold calibrated on benign validation data, the model proceeds without modification. When the signal exceeds the threshold, SeDATE applies two complementary interventions: it softly suppresses the aggression-sensitive neurons and redirects the residual stream toward a representation derived from non-aggressive text. The suppression weakens the aggressive activation, while the redirection guides the model toward a safer continuation. If the signal remains elevated for several consecutive steps, generation is terminated and replaced with a fixed refusal response. Unlike static neuron masking, SeDATE intervenes only when the model’s internal trajectory indicates a potential shift toward aggressive generation. Unlike conventional activation steering, it combines sparse neuron-level suppression with residual-stream redirection. Most importantly, the same cross-lingual neuron set serves two connected roles: it acts as an internal indicator of aggressive generation and as the target of the corrective intervention.

papers.title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback
papers.abstract: Can AI agents autonomously train useful language models and improve them using feedback from users? We introduce RSI Arena, a two-stage study of autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement. Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base. During a six-day first stage, each agent has 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU cluster, independently selecting data, implementing training procedures, and choosing checkpoints. We evaluate their models on 20 benchmarks and through blind human evaluations. All ten agents produce working assistants, with the strongest model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closing a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks. Its human-preference rating is also close to NVIDIA Instruct after statistical adjustment for answer length and formatting. In Stage 2, each agent receives the comparison records and votes involving its Stage 1 model and is given three additional days for further training. Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference across the two evaluation rounds, we observe an improvement from Stage 1 to Stage 2 in the style-adjusted relative rating of eight of the ten models. We show that benchmark gains were modest, with no clear link to preference gains, while some agents encouraged longer responses and one model showed increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT. RSI Arena provides an auditable setting for studying how human feedback can guide autonomous model development. It takes a step toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what improvement means for the AI systems they use.

Recursive self-improvement is a long-term vision in which AI systems develop more capable successors that can, in turn, advance further AI development (Good, 1966; Schmidhuber, 2007). If successful, this process could accelerate AI progress beyond the pace of human research alone. Leading AI developers are actively pursuing this vision: OpenAI aims for an automated AI researcher by 2028 (Bellan, 2025), and Anthropic reports that its models already lead about a quarter of its AI research and development (Favaro and Wright, 2026). A practical step toward this vision is to establish whether AI agents can develop models end to end under realistic resource constraints and evaluation requirements.
