Compared with optimizing for a single benchmark, post-training a language model for real-world use poses a broader challenge: turning a pretrained model into an assistant that people find useful. Starting from a base model, a team selects data, writes or adapts training code, runs supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization, and evaluates the results (Ouyang et al., 2022; Lambert et al., 2024). This process requires substantial GPU resources and repeated cycles of training and evaluation, and success cannot be captured by a single metric. Because these models are built to serve people, the ultimate test is whether users prefer them. Benchmarks assess specific capabilities through fixed response formats; to capture user preferences more directly, we also ask people to compare the models in a blind Human Arena modeled on Chatbot Arena (Chiang et al., 2024).

RSI Arena delegates this entire process to AI agents. No human selects the training data or writes the training code; people only evaluate the resulting models. The arena consists of two stages that mirror how models are developed in practice (Figure 1). Stage 1 captures pre-release post-training. Ten frontier models, acting as autonomous research agents, each post-trained the same base model for six days with the same budget on a shared cluster. The agents chose their own data, training code, and internal evaluations, while we livestreamed their work. We then evaluated the ten final models on 20 benchmarks and in a blind human evaluation, where participants compared pairs of model responses side by side at COLM 2026 and online. Stage 2 captures post-release improvement, when developers use user ratings and preferences to train the next version. Each agent received the arena battles involving its own model and had three additional days to improve it. This stage tests another part of the self-improvement loop: whether agents can use feedback from their models’ users to drive further improvement.

This report covers both stages. Our main findings from Stage 1 are as follows: 1. Every agent produced a working assistant, and with style control people rate the best one level with NVIDIA Instruct. The best agent model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closed a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 benchmarks. Without style control, people rated NVIDIA Instruct highest (1,182, against 1,161); with answer length and formatting controlled, the two are level at 1,095 and 1,094. 2. The agents used similar recipes. All fine-tuned on public instruction data, and six then ran preference optimization. Six trained LoRA adapters and four trained all weights. Memory errors, storage quotas, job limits and queues took much of their time. 3. Budget use did not predict results. Gemini 3.8 Flash stopped after 12 hours and 19 GPU-hours. People rated its model above the models of Muse Spark 1.3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which used about 1,000 GPU-hours each. 4. Benchmarks and people agreed only in part. Benchmark progress and human ratings correlate at ρ=0.73\rho=0.73. LLM-judged chat benchmarks track people best, WildBench at ρ=0.95\rho=0.95, and competition mathematics does not. The longer answer won 72% of decisive votes. The model with the best AIME 2026 score placed eighth of ten in human evaluation. 5. Safety was not part of the task, and some models regressed. Eight of the ten agents narrowed their model’s style-controlled gap to NVIDIA Instruct; across all ten, the median gain was 28 points. The model trained by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash gained most, from −207 to −35 points, as its median answer grew from 61 to 508 tokens. 2. NVIDIA Instruct is still first without style control. With style control, the two are level (1,061 and 1,054). 3. The agents left much of their budget unused. They used 2,880 of their 5,051 GPU-hours and $541 of their $1,500 of API credit; Gemini 3.8 Flash used 10 GPU-hours. 4. Benchmarks changed little. papers.title: GeoPrompt: Geometry-Conditioned Prompt Learning for Underwater Open-Vocabulary Instance Segmentation
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary instance segmentation (OVIS) provides a promising solution for marine perception by recognizing and segmenting categories beyond predefined label spaces. Existing OVIS methods usually rely on vision-language alignment, where visual region features are matched with textual category embeddings to recognize both seen and unseen classes. However, this alignment assumption becomes fragile in underwater environments. Color attenuation, scattering, turbidity, and low contrast distort visual appearance, causing region features to deviate from their corresponding semantic concepts. As a result, the similarity between degraded visual features and textual classifiers becomes unreliable, which particularly weakens the recognition of unseen underwater categories that cannot be corrected by category-specific supervision. To address these issues, we propose GeoPrompt, a geometry-conditioned prompt learning framework for underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation. Our key insight is that geometric structure is more stable than visual appearance in degraded underwater scenes. Specifically, GeoPrompt introduces a geometry-guided visual adaptation module (GVAM) to extract depth-derived structural priors and inject them into multi-scale visual features. It further develops a geometry-conditioned prompt learning (GCPL) that generates geometry-aware textual classifiers from structural representations. These geometry-aware classifiers are integrated with fixed and image-conditioned textual classifiers to improve open-vocabulary semantic alignment. Experiments on the MARIS-OpenIS benchmark show that GeoPrompt achieves state-of-the-art performance and brings consistent improvements on underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation.

Open-vocabulary instance segmentation (OVIS) aims to segment object instances from both seen and unseen categories by aligning visual region representations with textual category embeddings (Radford et al. 2021; Li et al. 2022; Ding et al. 2022; Liang et al. 2023; Xu et al. 2023a; Xu et al. 2023b; Qin et al. 2023; Yu et al. 2023). Benefiting from vision-language models, OVIS reduces the dependence on closed-set category annotations and provides a promising paradigm for marine perception, where underwater environments contain diverse, fine-grained, and long-tail object categories. This ability is especially important for underwater scene understanding, since many marine objects are difficult to predefine and annotate in practical applications (Li et al. 2026).

Geometry provides a natural complementary cue to alleviate this problem. Prior RGB-D, monocular depth estimation, and depth-aware segmentation studies have shown that geometric information can complement RGB appearance by providing object boundaries, spatial layout, and shape cues for dense prediction tasks (Hazirbas et al. 2017; Park et al. 2017; Jiang et al. 2018; Chen et al. 2020; Ranftl et al. 2021; Yang et al. 2024a; Yang et al. 2024b). Importantly, our method does not require ground-truth depth annotations or explicit depth supervision. Instead of treating monocular depth as a target prediction, we exploit depth-derived features to provide geometry-aware cues that are complementary to degraded RGB appearance. papers.title: Singular Limits of Frame Bundles of Noncollapsing Positively Curved Manifolds
papers.abstract: For each dimension $n\ge 2$, we construct noncollapsing sequences of metrics on $S^n$ with a uniform positive lower bound on sectional curvature whose oriented orthonormal frame bundles, equipped with the canonically induced connection metrics, converge to nonmanifold metric spaces homeomorphic to $\Sigma(S^{n-1}\times\SO(n))$. In even dimensions, real projective quotients give connected full frame bundles with the same limits, disproving the manifold conclusion in Yamaguchi's frame bundle conjecture. In odd dimensions, each component of the full projective frame bundle, with its intrinsic metric, converges to the quotient of the spherical limit by a free involution. The singularities are detected by local homology, and we obtain quantitative equivariant Gromov--Hausdorff estimates. We also compare the frame bundle limits with the intrinsic completions of their regular limiting frame metrics, and present and discuss alternatives to Yamaguchi's original conjecture.

papers.title: Optimal $K_t$-free list colorings and the Pollyanna property of graphs with no triangular wheel
papers.abstract: A wheel consists of an induced cycle of length at least four and a vertex with at least three neighbors on the cycle. Let $\cal T$ be the class of graphs with no wheel containing a triangle. We prove that, for every $G\in\cal T$ and every integer $t\ge3$, the $K_t$-free chromatic and choice numbers both equal $\lceil{\omega(G)/(t-1)}\rceil$. We further prove that $\cal T$ is $k$-strongly linear-Pollyanna for every integer $k\ge2$, and hence is linear-Pollyanna. In particular, the class of wheel-free graphs is Pollyanna, answering Problem 10.2 of Chudnovsky, Cook, Davies and Oum.

papers.title: Combinatorial decompositions of strict partitions and multi-sum Rogers-Ramanujan type identities
papers.abstract: While multi-sum Rogers-Ramanujan type identities have been extensively investigated through Bailey pairs, the constant term method, complex contour integration, and related techniques, many still lack an intrinsic combinatorial understanding. In this paper, we establish combinatorial interpretations for several families of triple-sum identities via structural decompositions of strict partitions. For one of these families, we extend the underlying combinatorial framework to obtain a general $(m+1)$-fold multi-sum identity. Leveraging these partition-theoretic interpretations, we construct explicit bijective proofs for all the corresponding identities. As an application, this constructive approach naturally yields some parameterized generalizations.

Rogers-Ramanujan type identities are sum-to-product identities expressing a qq-hypergeometric series, often in the form of a multisum, as an infinite product (or a linear combination of infinite products). The prototypical examples are the celebrated Rogers-Ramanujan identities: (1.1) ∑n≥0qn2(q,q)n=1(q,q4,q5)∞,∑n≥0qn2+n(q,q)n=1(q2,q3,q5)∞.\displaystyle\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{q^{n^{2}}}{(q;q)_{n}}=\frac{1}{(q,q^{4};q^{5})_{\infty}},\quad\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{q^{n^{2}+n}}{(q;q)_{n}}=\frac{1}{(q^{2},q^{3};q^{5})_{\infty}}. The identities in (1.1) were first discovered and proved by Rogers [21], subsequently rediscovered by Ramanujan [19, 20], and independently established by Schur [22]. Rogers-Ramanujan type identities play a fundamental role across combinatorics, number theory, the representation theory of affine Lie algebras, and solvable lattice models in statistical mechanics; for a comprehensive exposition, see Sills’ monograph [23]. A monumental collection of such identities was systematically developed through the Bailey machinery by Slater [24].

Analytically, a central problem connecting Rogers-Ramanujan type series with the theory of modular forms is the systematic classification of modular qq-hypergeometric series. This investigation is intimately tied to the study of Nahm sums and their deep interplay with conformal field theory, the Bloch group, and the dilogarithm function [18, 30]. However, this analytic perspective requires careful demarcation: Nahm’s original conjecture is known to fail in general, as explicit counterexamples were constructed by Vlasenko and Zwegers [25]. Consequently, multivariable parameterized series cannot simply be presumed to yield modular forms without dedicated analysis. The objective of the present paper is combinatorial: we seek to explain how specific multisums arise from partition structures and to construct explicit bijective proofs for their product sides.

papers.title: Boundedness and continuity of phase-corrected gradients on Sobolev spaces
papers.abstract:
For a function $\psi: \mathbb{R}^d ightarrow \mathbb{C}$, we define the phase-corrected gradient $
abla_{\!\circ} \psi = |\psi|^{-1} \overline{\psi}\,
abla\psi$ and study the regularity of the map $\psi \mapsto 
abla_{\!\circ} \psi$ on Sobolev spaces. Since $\mathrm{Re}[
abla_{\!\circ} \psi] = 
abla |\psi|$, the phase-corrected gradient fits naturally into the framework of nonlinear composition operators. Its imaginary part $\Lambda = \mathrm{Im}[
abla_{\!\circ} \psi]$, on the other hand, plays a key role in quantum hydrodynamic models. We prove that $\psi \mapsto 
abla_{\!\circ} \psi$ is bounded and continuous from $W^{s,2}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ to $W^{s-1,2}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for $1 \leq s <  rac32$, and we show that the threshold $s =  rac32$ is sharp. In particular, this answers an open question concerning the continuity of the map $\psi \mapsto |\psi|$ on Sobolev spaces. We also show that our results remain valid for functions that do not necessarily decay at infinity, a relevant setting in the context of Ginzburg--Landau theory. Finally, we extend our analysis to more general phase-corrected gradients of the form $f(|\psi|^{-1} \psi) 
abla \psi$, where $f: \mathbb{S}^1 ightarrow \mathbb{C}$ is Lipschitz, and discuss implications for certain parabolic PDEs.

papers.title: Hierarchical Skill Evolution for Coding Agent
papers.abstract: Skills provide agents with reusable experience to guide future decisions without modifying the underlying model. However, coding trajectories are often entangled with task- and repository-specific contexts, making it challenging to distill procedural skills that generalize across diverse coding environments. To address this challenge, we present Hierarchical Skill Evolution (HSE), which progressively distills procedural knowledge from coding trajectories through hierarchical evidence aggregation. HSE first extracts task-level evidence from individual trajectories, then aggregates recurring evidence within the same repository to form repository-specific skill candidates, and finally consolidates consistent patterns across repositories into transferable skills across repositories. The evolution is driven by an external writer-evaluator loop that generates and assesses skills while keeping the underlying coding model frozen. The loop externally updates the writer and evaluator policies to improve subsequent skill generation and assessment. This hierarchy progressively filters task-specific details while preserving procedures that generalize across diverse coding environments. Successful trajectories yield reusable guidance for future tasks, while failed trajectories reveal recurring failure modes that guide avoidance and recovery. We evaluate HSE on SWE-bench Verified and DeepSWE, using GLM-5.2 across Pi and Claude Code harnesses and GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 with Pi. Across both benchmarks, 10 skills evolved solely from SWE-Gym improve coding performance across all evaluated settings, demonstrating transfer across benchmarks, coding models, and agent harnesses. We further evolve the skill library from target-benchmark trajectories without verifier feedback, relying solely on the learned evaluator for candidate assessment and achieving additional gains through benchmark-tailored skills.

papers.intro:
Skills allow coding agents to reuse experience from previous tasks without modifying the underlying model (Wang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2026b). This is particularly attractive for repository-level coding, where every attempt produces a rich trajectory of searches, code inspection, edits, tests, and recovery actions (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). Reusing these trajectories could prevent an agent from repeatedly rediscovering the same repair strategies. A trajectory, however, is not yet a reusable skill. It is entangled with a particular issue, repository structure, file paths, and patch, whereas a useful skill should guide future decisions without assuming that these task-specific details transfer.

Existing forms of agent experience expose both sides of this problem. Raw trajectory retrieval preserves concrete evidence but can encourage agents to copy solutions that are specific to a previous task or repository (Chen et al., 2025). SWESkillsBench provides broadly applicable domain knowledge, but this guidance may not tell an agent how to localize a particular bug, constrain a patch, validate the affected behavior, or recover after an incorrect edit (Han et al., 2026). Methods that synthesize or optimize skills from trajectories demonstrate that experience can be converted into reusable instructions (Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2026b; Ni et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a; Agrawal et al., 2026), but a central challenge remains: at what level should evidence be aggregated so that task-specific details are removed without also discarding the procedure that made the experience useful?

An external writer–evaluator loop jointly evolves the skill library and the policies governing skill generation and assessment (Shinn et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2026b; Pryzant et al., 2023; Agrawal et al., 2026), while the coding model remains frozen and receives only the evolved skills.

papers.title: Degree-list Kempe equivalence for 3-connected graphs
papers.abstract: In a proper coloring, a Kempe change interchanges two colors on a connected component of the subgraph they induce. For a fixed list assignment $L$, a Kempe change is $L$-valid if it transforms an $L$-coloring into another $L$-coloring. We prove that if $G$ is a $3$-connected graph other than a complete graph or the triangular prism, and $L$ is a list assignment with $|L(v)|\ge d_G(v)$ for every vertex $v$, then $G$ has a proper $L$-coloring and any two such colorings can be transformed into one another by a finite sequence of $L$-valid Kempe changes. This proves a conjecture of Chakraborty, Feghali and Mahmoud.

papers.title: pbhalo: computing primordial black hole and minihalo populations from a single primordial perturbation spectrum
papers.abstract: An enhancement of the primordial curvature power spectrum on small scales can give rise to two populations of compact objects: primordial black holes (PBHs), which form during radiation domination, and dark matter minihalos, including ultracompact minihalos (UCMHs), which form from the same modes during matter domination. We present pbhalo, an open-source Python package that computes the PBH mass function, the halo mass function and the UCMH abundance from a single spectrum in a given cosmology and applies observational constraints on the PBH abundance and on the spectrum jointly. The package components are validated against colossus (a code for halo mass functions and cosmological quantities), pbhstat (a code for the PBH mass function from a given spectrum) and published results; joint constraints are illustrated for lognormal peaks. The code is distributed under the MIT license.

papers.intro:
Primordial black holes, first considered by Zeldovich and Novikov [1], Hawking [2], and Carr and Hawking [3], are one of the candidates for a component of dark matter [4, 5, see the reviews]. The same primordial perturbation modes that produce PBHs can, at lower amplitude, give rise to dark matter minihalos. Moreover, PBHs themselves can act as seeds for dark matter accretion, around which dense halos form, and they can affect the distribution of dark matter in galactic halos [6, 7]. It is therefore natural to treat both populations together, starting from the same primordial spectrum. The aim of this work is a software package that computes both the PBH population and the dark matter minihalo population from a single spectrum in a given cosmology.

Treating the two branches together is more than a matter of convenience. First, the amplitudes at which the PBH and UCMH constraints operate differ by four to five orders of magnitude, so the question of which of them sets the allowed region for a given spectral feature cannot be answered without computing both quantities for the same spectrum. Second, both branches are sensitive to the same modelling choices (the smoothing window, the transfer function and the normalisation of the growth factor), and in separate calculations these choices easily become inconsistent. papers.title: $El\ Ascua$: An ultra-luminous, radio-loud, Compton-thick AGN at $z\sim 3.8$ hiding in plain sight revealed by MINERVA multi-band MIRI observations
papers.abstract: Heavily dust-obscured active galactic nuclei (AGN) are crucial for understanding supermassive black hole growth. Using multi-band MIRI photometry from the MINERVA survey, we report the discovery in the UDS field of an extremely mid-infrared bright Compton-thick AGN (CT AGN) at $z \sim 3.8$, \textit{el Ascua} (the Ember). The AGN and/or its host galaxy is detected at 870\,$\mu$m with ALMA and at 1.4\,GHz with the VLA. With UV-to-radio spectral energy distribution modeling, we estimate that the dusty host galaxy has a stellar mass of $\log\left( M_\star / M_\odot \right)=10.82 \pm 0.57$ and a star formation rate of ${\rm{SFR}} =157 \pm 8 \,M_\odot\,{\rm yr^{-1}}$, and we confirm the presence of a powerful dusty AGN with an intrinsic accretion luminosity of $\log\left( L_{\rm{acc}} /{\rm erg\,s^{-1}} \right)=47.12 \pm 0.58$. CT obscuration is revealed by comparing the upper limit on the X-ray luminosity over $2-10 \,{\rm{keV}}$ with the $6 \,{\rm\mu{m}}$ mid-IR AGN luminosity. We additionally find evidence for a radio excess by comparing its total IR-to-radio ratio to those of typical star-forming galaxies and radio-quiet AGN, implying that \textit{el Ascua} could be a rare radio-loud CT AGN. With an extremely high ratio between black hole accretion rate and SFR, the AGN is likely nearing the peak of a deeply obscured phase of black hole growth before AGN feedback blows away the obscuring material. Our work demonstrates the power of MIRI to reveal heavily obscured AGN missing from our supermassive black hole census.

papers.intro:
Most active galactic nuclei (AGN) are obscured by interstellar gas and dust [52, e.g.,], and at z>0z>0 these obscured AGN are the dominant mode for the growth of supermassive black holes [110, 18, SMBHs; e.g.,]. In particular, Compton-thick AGN (CT AGN), with gas column densities of NH≳1.5×1024​cm−2N_{H}\gtrsim 1.5\times 10^{24}\,\rm cm^{-2} attenuating soft X-ray emission (i.e., of energy <10​keV<10\;\rm keV) from hot coronal gas near the accretion disk, are required to match the cosmic X-ray background [41, 36, e.g.,]. CT AGN make up a significant fraction of AGN at z=0z=0, though the exact number is uncertain with estimates ranging from ∼20%\sim 20\% to ∼50%\sim 50\% of AGN [19, 16, 69, 4]. In the local universe, CT AGN can be found in the heavily buried nuclei of luminous and ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs/ULIRGs), with ∼20−40%\sim 20-40\% of nearby ULIRGs hosting CT AGN [81, 13, 108, 37, 55, e.g.,]. At z≳1z\gtrsim 1, CT AGN account for anywhere from ∼33%\sim 33\% to >50%>50\% of AGN [12, 16, 17, 30, 69, 66, 22, e.g.,], meaning that a similar or even higher fraction of AGN are CT in the distant universe compared to z=0z=0 [100]. CT AGN consequently reflect a key evolutionary phase in SMBH growth, and studying their accretion properties, interstellar environments, and host galaxies is critical for comprehensive models of black hole growth, obscuration, fueling, and feedback.

In the local universe, CT AGN can be found in the heavily buried nuclei of luminous and ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs/ULIRGs), with ∼20−40%\sim 20-40\% of nearby ULIRGs hosting CT AGN [81, 13, 108, 37, 55, e.g.,]. At z≳1z\gtrsim 1, CT AGN account for anywhere from ∼33%\sim 33\% to >50%>50\% of AGN [12, 16, 17, 30, 69, 66, 22, e.g.,], meaning that a similar or even higher fraction of AGN are CT in the distant universe compared to z=0z=0 [100]. CT AGN consequently reflect a key evolutionary phase in SMBH growth, and studying their accretion properties, interstellar environments, and host galaxies is critical for comprehensive models of black hole growth, obscuration, fueling, and feedback.

CT AGN are notoriously difficult to identify and confirm beyond the local universe, as the observed X-ray luminosity at <10​keV<10\;\rm keV is tens or hundreds of times fainter than the intrinsic, unabsorbed value [26]. Furthermore, X-ray surveys are not sufficiently deep at harder rest-frame X-ray energies of >10​keV>10\;\rm keV where the obscuring material is more optically thin [41]. As a result, a significant number of distant CT AGN are missed by both soft and hard X-ray surveys.

Infrared (IR) observations are therefore crucial for identifying and characterizing CT AGN [76, 89], especially at z>0z>0 where X-ray constraints are normally unavailable [42, 106]. In lieu of X-ray detections, studies of CT AGN have often paired the weak or non-detected X-ray flux with spectral features in the rest-frame mid-IR (MIR) at 3−30​μ​m3-30\,\mu{\rm m} [28, 3, 39, 40, 44, 42, 68, 75, 47, e.g,], where the MIR flux density from an AGN originates from a warm dusty torus enveloping the SMBH and the accretion disk [52, 76, e.g.,]. The MIR features often associated with AGN include the continuum from the warm dusty torus which brightens towards redder MIR wavelengths, forbidden emission lines from ions requiring high ionization potential, and broad absorption features at 9.7​μ​m9.7\,\mu{\rm m} and 18​μ​m18\,\mu{\rm m} from silicate dust grains in the foreground of the warm dust continuum [89]. Spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling has allowed for disentangling the AGN warm dust from polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons [83, 60, 61, PAHs;]. PAHs trace star formation and the interstellar medium, and they exhibit unique spectral features in the mid-IR, whereas the warm dusty torus of an AGN shows a strong, red, power-law continuum which can outshine the PAHs. The shape of the mid-IR SED therefore is sensitive to the relative contributions of PAHs and dusty torus emission. However, at z≳1z\gtrsim 1 studies with Spitzer and Herschel are generally limited to the brightest obscured AGN [65, 3, 12, 46, 22, e.g.,], rendering larger statistical samples of distant obscured AGN difficult to compile.

The first several years of JWST results, especially with the Mid-IR Instrument (MIRI), have dramatically changed the broader landscape of obscured AGN science. The large increase in sensitivity that MIRI provides is pushing population studies of dusty galaxies and AGN to cosmic noon (z∼2z\sim 2) and beyond [62, 2, 10, e.g.,]. With up to eight broadband filters spanning 5−25​μ​m5-25\,\rm\mu m, the photometric sampling of the SED allows for more robust decomposition of AGN and PAH emission [110, 75, 18], giving stronger constraints on AGN activity across the whole luminosity function. Lyu et al. [75] demonstrate these improvements for CT AGN as part of a broader overview of the power MIRI provides for finding more complete obscured AGN samples. Even without MIRI, Maiolino et al. [78] measure AGN bolometric luminosities from JWST near-IR spectra and combine with X-ray brightness to find heavily obscured AGN at z>4z>4, where MIRI no longer probes the rest-frame mid-IR. Between JWST’s IR capabilities and archival X-ray data, we can now reliably find CT AGN beyond the local universe without relying on rare X-ray detections.

papers.title: Faint Companions to Hot Stars. Spectroscopic Detection Sensitivity and Implications for Survey Design
papers.abstract: Searches for black holes in binaries must distinguish dark companions from faint luminous stars. This is challenging for hot stars, whose spectra contain few broad lines. We develop a Fourier-domain method that converts isolated, broadened lines into calibrated constraints on faint companions. Doppler shifts are encoded in the Fourier phase, while the line profile defines a smooth amplitude envelope. A faint secondary introduces an oscillatory perturbation to the log-amplitude. Expanding to first order in the secondary-to-primary line-depth ratio, $\alpha$, yields a nearly linear model for a likelihood-ratio test against the single-star model. The method applies to single or multiple epochs without full spectral disentangling. At small velocity separation $v$, the companion signal becomes degenerate with the primary line profile, and the fractional uncertainty from the log-amplitude scales as $\Delta\alpha/\alpha \propto v^{-4}$. If the primary velocity is known, the Fourier phase provides a more favorable detection channel whose sensitivity scales as $v^{-1}$. We demonstrate the method on archival FEROS spectra of CPD$-41^\circ$7742, detecting the known secondary in He I 6678 Angstrom and obtaining a stringent non-detection in He II 5411 Angstrom, where its contribution is expected to be negligible. The framework yields detection efficiencies as functions of line-depth ratio, velocity separation, noise, and instrumental setup. These can be combined across lines, epochs, and targets to construct selection functions for spectroscopic black-hole searches, including those enabled by SDSS-V and Gaia.

More broadly, detached post-interaction binaries encode which systems survive these evolutionary phases and constrain natal kicks, fallback retention, and envelope ejection (Fryer et al., 2012; Giacobbo & Mapelli, 2018; Willcox et al., 2025, see, for example,). Large, homogeneous surveys now make it possible to study these populations at scale.

Large, homogeneous surveys now make it possible to study these populations at scale.

Among massive stars, the fraction of systems with black-hole companions is expected to be of order a few percent (Langer et al., 2020). The identification of these systems, however, is intrinsically challenging. Less massive luminous companions can reproduce similar dynamical signatures while contributing only weakly to the observed spectrum (Shenar et al., 2020; Bodensteiner et al., 2020, e.g.,). Distinguishing these luminous companions from black holes therefore requires either detecting their spectral contribution or establishing that such a contribution would have been detectable.

Early-type spectra contain few diagnostic lines, which are often broadened by rapid rotation, with projected rotational velocities of ∼100{\sim}100 km​s−1\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} or more. In this regime, spectroscopic techniques lose sensitivity and blends become difficult to interpret (Bodensteiner et al., 2020; Müller-Horn et al., 2026; Rowan et al., 2026). The inferred properties of the luminous star may also be biased, leading to incorrect conclusions about the nature of the companion (El-Badry & Quataert, 2021, e.g.,); a well-known example is LB-1, where an apparent companion signature was later traced to the broad line profile of the primary (Liu et al., 2019; Abdul-Masih et al., 2020).

Several established methods address related aspects of this problem. Two-dimensional cross-correlation techniques, such as TODCOR, search for binary signatures using two templates simultaneously (Zucker & Mazeh, 1994), while spectral disentangling and secondary-template reconstruction methods recover component spectra from multi-epoch data (González & Levato, 2006; González et al., 2024; Seeburger et al., 2024, e.g.,). More recently, data-driven spectral models and deep-learning approaches have been used to identify faint companions in large spectroscopic data sets (Ness et al., 2015; Angelo et al., 2026; Binnenfeld et al., 2025). Beyond detection, these techniques can place upper limits on the luminosity of an unseen companion, which has been central to the identification and validation of quiescent black-hole companions to massive stars (Shenar et al., 2022; Mahy et al., 2022; Bodensteiner et al., 2022).

Rotational broadening, line depth, and velocity separation all affect the ability to identify, or exclude, a secondary contribution to the observed light. More generally, analysis techniques can lose sensitivity in ways that are difficult to quantify a priori. In searches for rare non-luminous companions, this limitation translates into characterization ambiguity, which can sometimes be resolved with complementary observations (Rowan et al., 2025; Rowan et al., 2026, e.g.,). In large surveys, the same limitation becomes a selection-function problem (Rix et al., 2021; Essick & Farah, 2026). In both cases, a non-detection of secondary light is informative only if the detection efficiency can be quantified with sufficient fidelity.

Population studies and individual-system characterization therefore require practical ways to determine which companions would have been detected, and with what efficiency. Massive-star spectra offer a useful simplification. When the relevant information is carried by isolated, broadened lines, the detailed stellar spectrum can often be replaced by a low-dimensional approximation. This makes it possible to build search schemes with minimal assumptions about the underlying spectrum and to quantify the sensitivity of a given survey.

To address this need, we develop a Fourier-domain detection framework for isolated, broadened spectral lines. Fourier analysis of stellar spectra has a long history (e.g., Gray, 1973; Smith & Gray, 1976; Smith, 1976; Gray, 1992, and references therein). Here, we use it to quantify when a faint secondary produces a detectable distortion of the primary line profile. We derive analytic detection limits in the unresolved regime and demonstrate the approach on archival spectra of CPD−-41∘ 7742. The resulting line-by-line limits provide the local detection efficiencies needed to interpret non-detections and identify luminous impostors in spectroscopic searches for black holes.

papers.title: End-to-end prostate lesion segmentation and detection from undersampled diffusion-weighted MRI
papers.abstract:
Automated prostate lesion detection from diffusion-weighted MR imaging (DWI) conventionally relies on reconstructed images and does not fully use all acquisition information. We present an end-to-end network that uses complex multicoil DWI data and coil sensitivity information for prostate lesion segmentation.
  We included 269 fastMRI prostate examinations with additional voxel-level lesion annotations. Of these, 64 examinations contained PIRADS 4 or 5 lesions. The proposed network, VarNet-Seg, consists of a k-space variational network (VarNet) with six variational cascades and an image-space 3D segmentation U-Net. Comparator models used the same segmentation architecture with fully coil-combined images (CC-Seg), fixed root-sum-of-squares reconstruction (RSS-Seg), or fixed SENSE reconstruction (SENSE-Seg). We performed ablations with end-to-end training and data consistency (DC) enabled or disabled. We evaluated lesion segmentation using Dice and patient-level detection using AUROC in five-fold cross-validation with full sampling, simulated undersampling, added noise, or both.
  VarNet-Seg achieved the highest Dice at every undersampling level. At eight-fold acceleration, Dice was 0.22 for VarNet-Seg, 0.14 for SENSE-Seg and 0.16 for VarNet-Seg (no DC). The paired difference from SENSE-Seg was 0.08 (95% CI, 0.04-0.11). With full sampling, VarNet-Seg and RSS-Seg performed similarly (0.40 vs 0.39). Patient-level AUROC decreased from 0.75 with full sampling to 0.63 at eight-fold acceleration; corresponding RSS-Seg AUROCs were 0.76 and 0.64.
  The proposed multicoil network improved prostate lesion segmentation under simulated undersampling compared to conventional models. Matched ablations supported contributions from both end-to-end training and data consistency. Prospective evaluation is needed to establish whether this approach can be used clinically in accelerated prostate DWI.

Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men, and its increasing global burden places growing demands on diagnostic services James et al. (2024). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has become central to diagnosis and biopsy planning by identifying suspicious lesions and guiding targeted tissue sampling Kasivisvanathan et al. (2018); Turkbey et al. (2019). However, long examination times and limited scanner capacity constrain access to prostate MRI Ng et al. (2025). Shorter protocols would allow more patients to be examined with existing capacity, provided that they preserve the information needed to detect and localize lesions. For automated lesion assessment, we address the separation of reconstruction and segmentation by training both stages jointly to preserve lesion information under reduced sampling and added noise.

papers.title: Identification of rippling interface between laser-ablated plasma and ambient uniform plasma at rest
papers.abstract: We present laboratory experiments on the early stage of the formation process of quasi-perpendicular supercritical magnetized collisionless shocks using laser-produced plasmas in an ambient uniform nitrogen (N) gas with 1~Torr under the external magnetic field with controlled polarity. An expanding aluminum (Al) piston plasma arising from laser irradiation interacts with a magnetized ambient N plasma, producing a bright, asymmetric self-emission whose global morphology reverses with the magnetic-field polarity. Two-dimensional ideal-magnetohydrodynamics simulations reproduce the main features of the observed structures and indicate that the ripple formation is unlikely to be driven by the Kelvin--Helmholtz instability, but is instead associated with vortex formation at the rounded leading edge of the piston plasma. We show that the bright, rippling emission delineates the Al-N interface, whose intrinsic width is consistent with an electron kinetic scale, and that its upstream side is predominantly composed of N plasma. This identification allows the formation of a supercritical collisionless shock in the magnetized N plasma to be discussed with minimal Al contamination.

papers.intro:
Collisionless shocks are ubiquitous in astrophysical objects such as supernova remnants, as well as in solar-terrestrial and laboratory plasmas [1, 2]. The kinetic energy of the incoming plasma is dissipated into various components such as high-temperature ions and electrons, magnetic turbulence, and nonthermal particles [3]. In particular, supercritical magnetized collisionless shocks are of great interest in connection with astrophysical shocks associated with particle acceleration. The detailed mechanisms around magnetized collisionless shocks are still not well understood despite state-of-the-art observations [4, 5, 6, 7, 8], particle-in-cell (PIC) [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17] and hybrid [18, 19, 20, 21] simulations. Experiments using high-power lasers provide another approach to studying collisionless shocks because they can combine controlled plasma conditions with spatially and temporally resolved diagnostics. Meanwhile, for unmagnetized upstream plasmas, laser experiments have demonstrated collisionless-shock formation and electron acceleration [22]. Motivated by these experimental advances, recent PIC simulations and theoretical studies have advanced our understanding of electron heating and energy partition between electrons and ions in unmagnetized or weakly magnetized collisionless shocks and counterstreaming plasmas [23, 24, 25]. In magnetized upstream plasmas as well, comparably well-characterized shock experiments are therefore needed to clarify how collisionless shocks form and mediate the dissipation of the incoming flow energy.

In quasi-perpendicular supercritical magnetized collisionless shocks, where the external upstream magnetic field is nearly perpendicular to the shock normal, it is well known that incoming ions are reflected by the shock potential [26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32]. Experimental verification of the presence of such reflected ions would therefore provide strong evidence for the formation of supercritical magnetized collisionless shocks. A number of high-power laser experiments have reported the generation of supercritical magnetized collisionless shocks [33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39], and some of them claimed observations of reflected ions. However, whether these observations truly capture ions reflected by the shock potential requires careful examination. One of the main reasons is that, in usual experimental setups, the upstream magnetized plasma is spatially non-uniform, making it difficult to experimentally characterize the properties of the unshocked upstream plasma with sufficient accuracy. In particular, during the early stage of shock formation, the interface between the ambient magnetized plasma and the laser-ablated piston plasma is often not yet fully separated from the forming shock within the magnetized plasma. Under such circumstances, it becomes challenging to distinguish whether the observed reflected ions originate from reflection at the shock potential in the shock transition layer or from reflection at the interface itself. In the companion paper [40], we discuss reflected ions in a foot-like region and the associated ion temperature anisotropy in a forming shock. For such an interpretation, however, it is first essential to determine where the interface between the piston and ambient plasmas is located relative to the forming shock structure.

In several previous high-power-laser experiments on quasi-perpendicular supercritical magnetized collisionless-shock formation, pronounced density structures associated with the piston–ambient interaction, shock precursors, and shock formation were observed [33, 34, 35, 38, 37]. Such density structures provide important information on the shock-formation process. However, when the upstream magnetized plasma is spatially non-uniform, an observed density variation cannot always be uniquely attributed to reflected ions or to the shock front, because it may also contain contributions from pre-existing upstream non-uniformity and from the piston–ambient interaction [38, 37]. This ambiguity is particularly important during the formation stage of supercritical magnetized collisionless shocks, when a density jump is expected at the shock front and the density can become particularly large in the overshoot region within the shock transition layer. At the same time, similarly pronounced density variations may also occur at the electron-scale interface between the two plasmas when the densities of the two interacting plasmas differ substantially. Recent experiments have therefore emphasized the importance of separating the shock structure from the driving piston and of following the temporal development of the shock [38, 39]. Therefore, before discussing reflected-ion signatures in the shock transition layer, the electron-scale interface between the piston and ambient plasmas should first be identified independently.

In this paper, we extend our previous experiments on quasi-perpendicular supercritical magnetized collisionless shocks [41, 42]. In those experiments, the ambient-gas pressure was higher than in the present study, specifically by a factor of five, and the resulting brighter self-emission from the ambient plasma made the interface region difficult to identify clearly. By reducing the ambient-gas pressure, the outer bright front can be identified much more clearly. A characteristic feature of our experimental system is the almost spatially uniform mass density of the ambient magnetized plasma, which results in an approximately uniform Alfvén velocity in the region of interest. This well-controlled upstream condition allows us to identify the interface between the piston plasma and the ambient magnetized plasma unambiguously. This feature represents a clear advantage of our experimental system, especially when compared with earlier experiments in which spatial non-uniformity of the upstream plasma complicated the interpretation of the shock-formation process.

papers.title: Experimental Evidence for Reflected Ions and Ion Temperature Anisotropy in a Forming Supercritical Magnetized Collisionless Shock
papers.abstract: Supercritical magnetized collisionless shocks require ion reflection for dissipation, yet its role during formation remains unclear. Using high-power lasers, self-emission imaging, and collective Thomson scattering, we investigate a forming quasi-perpendicular shock. An upstream emission tail is consistent with a foot-like structure, while ion heating and temperature anisotropy extend upstream of a ramp-like region. These observations provide evidence of reflected-ion-related heating during early shock formation, although the incident and reflected ion populations are not separately resolved. Future measurements of ion distributions and plasma waves could clarify how this heating mediates shock dissipation and particle energization.

papers.title: EP241021a as An Off-nuclear Month-duration Transient in a Dwarf Starburst Galaxy
papers.abstract: EP241021a is a peculiar fast X-ray transient exhibiting a long X-ray plateau and an optical rebrightening, both challenging the traditional jet afterglow model. Whether its nature is a stellar explosion or a tidal disruption event (TDE) remains debated. Here we present late-time HST/WFC3 and Gemini-N/GMOS observations of its host galaxy at $z=0.748$. After $\sim300$ days post-trigger, the transient emission had faded below detection, revealing a dwarf disk galaxy with an effective radius $R_e=1.7$ kpc, a stellar mass $M_\star\sim3\times10^8M_\odot$, and a high star formation rate of $\sim5\ M_\odot\ {\rm yr}^{-1}$. Combined with previous very long baseline interferometry measurements, the transient can be located in the galactic disk with a projected physical offset of $0.95\pm0.13$ kpc from the galaxy center. Host-subtracted optical light curves show that the rebrightening ceased at $\sim47$ days, followed by a sudden drop with a power-law index steeper than $-3.3$, coincident with a similar drop in the X-ray light curve. This synchronous drop in both bands is consistent with jet shut-off, and the required month-long jet activity suggests a persistently accreting compact object fed by a TDE. Among the TDE scenarios, the off-nuclear location and the starburst host galaxy slightly favor the post-supernova micro-TDE scenario in a binary system, in which a natal kick drives the newborn compact object into a tidal disruption of its companion. Nevertheless, an off-nuclear intermediate-mass black hole TDE or a stellar-mass black hole TDE induced by dynamical scattering in a dense stellar cluster cannot yet be excluded.

papers.intro:
Fast X-ray Transients (FXTs) are a class of extragalactic astrophysical phenomena characterized by intense, brief bursts of soft X-ray emission, with durations ranging from tens to thousands of seconds and peak isotropic luminosities spanning a broad range from 104210^{42} to 105010^{50} erg s-1 [19, 44, 23, 18, 3, 52, 1, 29, 38, 37]. Unlike traditional Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs), most FXTs are not detected in the gamma-ray band, constituting a subclass of “gamma-ray dark” transients [57].

Fast X-ray Transients (FXTs) are a class of extragalactic astrophysical phenomena characterized by intense, brief bursts of soft X-ray emission, with durations ranging from tens to thousands of seconds and peak isotropic luminosities spanning a broad range from 104210^{42} to 105010^{50} erg s-1 [19, 44, 23, 18, 3, 52, 1, 29, 38, 37]. Unlike traditional Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs), most FXTs are not detected in the gamma-ray band, constituting a subclass of “gamma-ray dark” transients [57].

Although dozens of FXTs have been identified, their physical origins remain unclear and several competing theoretical models have been proposed. First, the high-redshift GRB model argues that cosmological redshift shifts the peak energy of GRB spectra into the soft X-ray band, causing them to appear as gamma-ray-dark FXTs [19]. Second, the massive star collapse model suggests that FXTs can originate from the shock breakout of core-collapse supernovae [44, 1]. Third, the compact object merger model proposes that mergers of binary neutron stars form millisecond magnetars, which trigger FXTs when they spin down [52, 29]. Fourth, the tidal disruption event (TDE) model posits that the tidal disruption of a white dwarf star by an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) triggers super-Eddington accretion, which in turn drives a relativistic jet and produces an X-ray flare [23, 35].

The Einstein Probe (EP; Yuan et al. 54) has greatly expanded the multi-wavelength observational sample of FXTs. EP has revealed several landmark events, such as EP240315a, EP240414a, and EP250108a [31, 45, 41]. Furthermore, EP has discovered a new class of FXTs characterized by X-ray plateaus lasting several days or longer. The first such case is EP240408a, which exhibits a plateau lasting about 4 days in its X-ray light curve, followed by a sudden drop to undetectable levels [56, 33]. However, follow-up observations in optical, near-infrared, and radio bands did not detect any counterparts to EP240408a, making its nature largely unknown.

EP241021a at z=0.748z=0.748 is a unique case with an even longer X-ray plateau and rich multi-wavelength emission, enabling a detailed study of its complex evolution [43, 9, 17, 53, 39]. It was triggered by EP/WXT on October 21, 2024, producing an X-ray flare lasting approximately 100 s with a peak luminosity of ∼1048\sim 10^{48} erg s-1, but no gamma-ray counterpart was detected by monitors such as Fermi-GBM and Konus-Wind. The high-energy spectral energy distribution suggests a peak energy Ep≲100E_{p}\lesssim 100 keV and an isotropic-equivalent energy Eiso≲2×1051E_{\rm iso}\lesssim 2\times 10^{51} erg. Subsequent follow-up observations extending to beyond 100 days have revealed a series of anomalous features. The X-ray emission lasts for more than one month (one of the longest FXT afterglows), and exhibits a complex evolution with an initial decay, a plateau, a rebrightening, and a late-time steep decline. The optical light curve shows multiple rebrightening episodes, peaking at an absolute magnitude of Mr≈−22M_{r}\approx-22 mag, and exhibiting persistently red colors (r−J≈0.8r-J\approx 0.8). The radio emission exhibits rapid spectral evolution and a double-peaked spectral structure at ∼70\sim 70 days, suggesting the presence of multiple emission components. Photometry and spectroscopy of the host galaxy reveal a low-mass, young galaxy with a high star formation rate. These observational facts pose serious challenges to any single-component models, and several independent works have proposed different explanations, including multiple jet ejections [43], a refreshed shock [9], an off-axis structured jet with a two-layer cocoon [17], a magnetar-powered thermal ejecta [51], and a forward shock plus supernova model [39]. Therefore, EP241021a has become a key testbed for understanding the diversity and the unified physical mechanisms of FXTs.

papers.title: ODIN: Comparison of Source Extractor and Tractor Source Detection for Lyman Alpha Emitting Galaxy Selection at z=3.1
papers.abstract: Lyman Alpha Emitting galaxies (LAEs) are young, actively star-forming galaxies identified by their strong Lyman-alpha emission at a rest-frame wavelength of 121.6 nm, making them valuable tracers of galaxy evolution and the large-scale structure of the Universe. The One-hundred-deg^2 DECam Imaging in narrow-bands (ODIN) survey collects LAE samples during Cosmic Noon. Because LAE selection is based on photometric measurements derived from source-detection algorithms, the choice of detection method can directly affect the resulting LAE samples. We therefore compare two prominent source detection methods, Source Extractor (SE) and Tractor (Tr), to determine which is better suited for LAE selection in ODIN. We investigate differences between SE and Tr in the ODIN-COSMOS field, focusing on the z=3.1 LAE sample. We find that a significant fraction of Tr LAEs have low continuum flux measurements, increasing the inferred narrow-band excess and resulting in an LAE sample nearly twice as large as SE. However, LAEs detected by Tr but not SE exhibit equivalent width estimates indicative of potential contamination. We introduce an additional LAE selection criterion based on the expected Lyman-break behavior of LAEs at z~3 to reduce low-redshift contamination without requiring a significant detection of the break itself. Our results demonstrate that differences in source detection can significantly affect narrow-band LAE selection and motivate the use of SE photometry for ODIN LAE catalogs.

papers.intro:
Lyman Alpha Emitting Galaxies (LAEs) are star-forming galaxies as seen by their strong emission of Lyα\alpha at a rest-frame wavelength of 121.6 nm [28]. Studies show that LAEs tend to be young and compact with low line-of-sight dust content [9, 13, 31], allowing Lyα\alpha photons to escape with less absorption and scattering before being observed. Therefore, LAEs can be efficiently identified and used to study the large-scale structure of the Universe and galaxy evolution over time [9, 15].

The Tractor (Tr) is another prominent source detection method used in large multi-band imaging surveys [19]. Released in 2016, Tr has gained wide-spread attention for its ability to handle complex large-area datasets and is now a core tool in surveys like the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Legacy Survey [6]. Tr measures photometry by forward modeling based on the local point spread function (PSF) for each source in an image. Model parameters are optimized to best match the image data, and forced photometry is applied to the other bands using positions and shapes derived from the detection image. This results in a catalog that contains PSF-aware flux measurements, as well as source positions, shapes, and associated uncertainties.

With DECam, ODIN collects LAE samples at redshifts of 2.4, 3.1, and 4.5 using custom narrow-band filters that correspond to each redshift [7, see]. This range allows ODIN to look into the evolution of galaxies during what is known to be the peak epoch of star formation in the Universe, Cosmic Noon. papers.title: How Quickly Did the Giants Form? Constraining the Formation Timescales of Massive Quiescent Galaxies at Cosmic Noon Using Chemical Evolution Modelling
papers.abstract: Massive quiescent galaxies (MQGs; $M_\star \sim 10^{11} \, \mathrm{M_\odot}$) at cosmic noon ($z \sim 2$) host $\alpha$-enhanced stellar populations ($\mathrm{[Mg/Fe]} \sim 0.4 - 0.5$) at near-solar [Fe/H], implying rapid formation histories that spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting alone constrains poorly. To determine the physical conditions and formation timescales that generate these abundances, we employ a one-zone chemical evolution model with nucleosynthetic yields calibrated against resolved stars in the Sculptor dwarf spheroidal. Comparing our model to a compilation of observed abundances, we find MQGs are consistent with rapid formation timescales of $\Delta t_\mathrm{SF} \sim 0.1 - 0.4 \, \mathrm{Gyr}$. The progenitors must sustain high star-formation efficiencies (approximately the molecular gas depletion time; $\tau_\star \sim 0.05 \, \mathrm{Gyr}$) and retain most of their metal-enriched ejecta ($\eta \sim 0$), consistent with high-redshift dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs). However, our model favours moderately active progenitors with typical star-formation rates (SFRs) of $200-400 \, \mathrm{M_\odot \, yr^{-1}}$, matching recently identified `NIRCam-dark' galaxies more closely than the broader DSFG population. Sustained starbursts ($\mathrm{SFR} \gtrsim 1000 \, \mathrm{M_\odot \, yr}^{-1}$) are disfavoured, since they would form most stellar mass before significant SN Ia enrichment and underproduce the observed [Fe/H]. The same framework also reproduces the central abundances of local early-type galaxies over longer timescales ($\Delta t_\mathrm{SF} \sim 0.6 - 1 \, \mathrm{Gyr}$). Chemical abundances can therefore provide powerful constraints on the formation histories of MQGs, and incorporating them into SED-fitting routines will ensure inferred histories remain consistent with the observed chemistry.

Of the abundance ratios accessible in integrated-light spectroscopy, [α\alpha/Fe]11 1 α\alpha-elements: e.g. O, Mg, Si, Ca, Ti. is the most informative tracer of how rapidly a stellar population formed. α\alpha-elements are produced almost exclusively by core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) on timescales of 1−10​Myr1-10\,\mathrm{Myr}, while Fe production is dominated by Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia), which contribute on delayed timescales of 0.1−1.0​Gyr0.1-1.0\,\mathrm{Gyr} (Matteucci and Greggio, 1986). As a result, stellar populations whose star formation completed before significant SN Ia enrichment could preserve enhanced [α\alpha/Fe], while more extended formation histories drive [α\alpha/Fe] toward solar values (Tinsley, 1979, e.g.). [α\alpha/Fe] hence acts as a chronometer of star formation duration, complementing [Fe/H] as a tracer of total enrichment (metallicity).

Massive quiescent galaxies (MQGs) observed near cosmic noon (z≳2z\gtrsim 2) are a powerful target for this chemical analysis. Having ceased significant star formation, their stellar populations are largely undisturbed by ongoing enrichment leaving a clean record of the conditions under which they formed. Observed close to their quenching epoch, they are also caught before significant ex-situ accretion expected from dry-minor merging events (Naab et al., 2009, e.g.), isolating the in-situ stellar population assembled during the galaxy’s formation. MQGs also dominate the high-mass end of the galaxy population, where the physical processes that regulate growth through the gas supply – feedback, accretion and quenching – operate most strongly and where current galaxy formation models remain most uncertain (Naab and Ostriker, 2017). Understanding how MQGs formed the bulk of their stellar mass is therefore central to a broader picture of how the most massive structures in the Universe came to be.

Most of what is known about the chemistry of massive galaxies has been established not from MQGs directly, but from their assumed descendants in the local universe, early-type galaxies (van Dokkum et al., 2010; Patel et al., 2013, ETGs;), whose proximity allows the spectroscopic detail needed to derive stellar abundances. Archaeological studies find the properties of their stellar populations correlate strongly with the stellar mass (M⋆M_{\star}) and velocity dispersion (σ\sigma), where the most massive, highest-σ\sigma galaxies host old stellar populations with systematically high metallicities and enhanced α\alpha-element abundances (Thomas et al., 2005; Graves et al., 2009a; Graves et al., 2009b; Smith et al., 2009; Conroy et al., 2014; Greene et al., 2019, typically [α\alpha/Fe] ∼\sim 0.2;). Even low-mass ETGs at z∼0z\sim 0 show super-solar [Mg/Fe], with the enhancement growing systematically with velocity dispersion (Conroy et al., 2014). Three explanations were originally proposed by Faber et al. (1992) and Worthey et al. (1992): (i) variation in the timescales over which star formation proceeded, (ii) a non-universal initial mass function (IMF), and (iii) differential entrainment or loss of Mg and Fe in winds. However, the latter explanation is disfavoured due to the absence of plausible physical mechanisms for ejecting certain species (Matteucci, 1994). Instead, variations in SF timescales are the favoured interpretation of [Mg/Fe] variations in both galactic and extragalactic archaeology (Matteucci, 1994; Thomas et al., 1999; Thomas et al., 2005; de La Rosa et al., 2011, e.g.); though, variation of the IMF in early-type galaxies remains a subject of ongoing debate (see Bastian et al., 2010; Smith, 2020, for a review).

Extending these abundance measurements to the quiescent population at z≳2z\gtrsim 2, close to when they actually formed and quenched, has only recently become feasible with near-infrared spectroscopy from instruments such as JWST/NIRSpec and Keck/MOSFIRE. Instead, observations of z∼2z\sim 2 MQGs reveal more extreme α\alpha-enhancement, with [Mg/Fe] often reaching 0.4−0.5​dex0.4-0.5\,\mathrm{dex} (Kriek et al., 2016; Jafariyazani et al., 2020; Beverage et al., 2024; Carnall et al., 2024; Beverage et al., 2025; Jafariyazani et al., 2025; McConachie et al., 2026) compared to the typical ∼0.2​dex\sim 0.2\,\mathrm{dex} found in local ETGs. It remains an open question, however, whether this offset in abundances reflects the typical formation history of all local ETG progenitors, or only of an early, rapidly-forming subset that we preferentially observe at z≳2z\gtrsim 2.

papers.title: NOEMA Observations of the Center of M33: A Parsec-scale Molecular Filament and an Ordered Gas-Star-Formation Sequence
papers.abstract: We present NOEMA CO(1-0) observations of the inner $\sim$500 pc of M33 at a resolution of $0.91''\times0.37''$ ($3.7\times1.5$ pc), resolving the compact molecular gas structures and revealing their relation to recent massive star formation. The most prominent structure is a southeastern molecular filament (SE filament) that extends 76 pc along its principal axis, is 23 pc wide, and contains three CO-bright knots. Across eight independent transverse cuts, the adjacent H$\alpha$ ridge is displaced preferentially to one side of the principal CO ridge by a median $10.0^{+0.9}_{-1.4}$ pc. Young OB candidates are more closely associated with H$\alpha$ than with compact CO. The filament shows little velocity change along its length but a resolved gradient across its minor axis. Its elongated morphology, transverse kinematics, and ordered CO-H$\alpha$ distribution are consistent with locally asymmetric molecular-gas compression and subsequent massive star formation. Across the wider field, 23 well-measured compact clumps have a median radius of 2.67 pc and a median velocity dispersion of 2.15 km s$^{-1}$. Their linewidth and apparent virial-parameter distributions show no clear difference between the SE filament and the rest of the field. Although the local spiral potential and pattern speed remain unconstrained, the observations provide a resolved view of a compression-compatible molecular-to-ionized-gas sequence in the center of M33.

papers.intro:
Molecular clouds provide the immediate material for star formation, a key process that shapes galaxies and regulates their evolution through subsequent stellar feedback. Their evolution is governed by self-gravity, pressure, turbulence, and magnetic fields [42, 10] and is modulated by galactic environment and large-scale dynamics [58, 37, 29]. Molecular-cloud structure can therefore reveal how galactic-scale gas flows affect the conditions for star formation on parsec and subparsec scales. A substantial fraction of molecular gas is organized into filaments, and star-forming clumps and cores are often concentrated along these structures. Giant molecular filaments (GMFs), with lengths of tens to hundreds of parsecs and masses of 10410^{4}–105​M⊙10^{5}~M_{\odot}, may therefore preserve information about both molecular-cloud assembly and the onset of clustered star formation [52, 67, 73]. How such long, coherent molecular structures form within galactic disks remains uncertain.

Giant molecular filaments (GMFs), with lengths of tens to hundreds of parsecs and masses of 10410^{4}–105​M⊙10^{5}~M_{\odot}, may therefore preserve information about both molecular-cloud assembly and the onset of clustered star formation [52, 67, 73]. How such long, coherent molecular structures form within galactic disks remains uncertain.

On galactic scales, elongated molecular structures may be assembled by compression associated with spiral structure. In the classical quasi-stationary density-wave picture, a long-lived spiral pattern rotates with a nearly fixed pattern speed while gas flows through the spiral potential and is compressed in a shock [36, 53]. Molecular gas should then accumulate near the compressed ridge, with massive star formation appearing downstream after a delay. Dynamic spiral models instead describe arms as transient, recurrent structures that approximately co-rotate with the disk. Gas can converge toward such an arm from both sides, so a persistent one-directional molecular-gas-to-star-formation sequence is not generally expected [17, 5]. Recent arm–interarm comparisons suggest a complementary “gatherer” picture, in which spiral arms concentrate molecular gas and star-forming regions without necessarily altering cloud lifetimes or strongly enhancing star-formation efficiency [62, 54]. The relative distributions of molecular gas and recent star formation provide an observational constraint on these flow geometries. Ordered CO–Hα\alpha offsets have been reported across the arms of the grand-design galaxy M51 and in other nearby spiral galaxies [20, 38], consistent in some cases with gas compression followed by massive star formation. Such offsets are not detected uniformly across spiral galaxies or even along individual spiral arms. Their appearance depends on the coherence of the arm, the tracers, spatial resolution, and the gas motion relative to the spiral pattern. More generally, CO-bright, overlapping CO–Hα\alpha, and Hα\alpha-bright regions statistically represent different stages of molecular-cloud evolution, whose durations depend on the local galactic environment [49]. A local offset is therefore most physically informative when it maintains a consistent direction along an extended structure and is considered together with the gas morphology, kinematics, and galactic environment.

M33 therefore provides a useful laboratory for testing whether such an ordered sequence can arise without a prominent grand-design spiral pattern. It is the nearest actively star-forming late-type spiral galaxy outside the Milky Way: at a distance of approximately 840 kpc, 1​″1\arcsec corresponds to about 4 pc [22]. Its moderate inclination of 55∘55^{\circ} also provides a comparatively unobscured external view at physical scales comparable to those accessible in Galactic studies [32]. M33 has a flocculent spiral morphology, and simulations show that gravitational instabilities, gas physics, and stellar feedback can reproduce much of its structure without a long-lived global density wave [16]. Parsec-scale observations of M33 therefore allow us to examine whether locally ordered molecular gas and recent star formation can arise within its dynamically evolving disk.

The central region of M33 also provides an environment distinct from both its outer disk and the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of the Milky Way. The Milky Way CMZ contains warm, turbulent, high-pressure molecular gas with velocity dispersions substantially above those of disk clouds [44, 31]. M33, in contrast, is a low-mass, bulgeless galaxy with no detected supermassive black hole [23]. Its parsec-scale molecular structures therefore offer a way to examine gas dynamics close to a galactic center without the deep nuclear potential of the Milky Way CMZ.

The central region of M33 also provides an environment distinct from both its outer disk and the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of the Milky Way. The Milky Way CMZ contains warm, turbulent, high-pressure molecular gas with velocity dispersions substantially above those of disk clouds [44, 31]. M33, in contrast, is a low-mass, bulgeless galaxy with no detected supermassive black hole [23]. Its parsec-scale molecular structures therefore offer a way to examine gas dynamics close to a galactic center without the deep nuclear potential of the Milky Way CMZ.

Previous CO observations have established the molecular-gas distribution and cloud population of M33 over a wide range of scales. The BIMA CO(1–0) survey showed that GMCs are closely associated with Hi filaments and Hii regions [21]. Nobeyama and combined Nobeyama–BIMA–FCRAO observations mapped the CO(1–0) distribution and its radial variations [55, 66, 48]. The IRAM 30 m CO(2–1) survey examined the association between GMCs and young stellar populations [18, 12, 9], while the ACA+IRAM survey cataloged 848 molecular clouds at approximately 30 pc resolution [45, 33]. These studies found that more massive and more gravitationally bound clouds are preferentially associated with active high-mass star formation, and interpreted systematic changes in cloud properties with Hii-region association as an evolutionary sequence. Collectively, these surveys characterize GMC-scale populations but do not resolve their parsec-scale internal structure.

papers.title: How Numerical Errors Scale with Hardware
papers.abstract: In this short technical note, we outline how to bound numerical errors with respect to computational resources. We consider algorithms with known complexity estimates that can be executed in parallel and combine these estimates with parallelization laws. We suppose that the proposed approach generalizes beyond the presented examples and argue that it provides a straightforward and fair framework for comparing algorithms, hardware systems, and software implementations. This is achieved by imposing identical resource or energy budgets on each configuration, and comparing the resulting numerical error evaluations.
papers.intro:
Energy consumption and the availability of hardware resources are among the main limiting factors in achieving better computational results. This is particularly true for highly parallel applications, where large computing systems work toward a common goal, such as estimating quantities of interest for highly uncertain processes, simulating fluid flow in three spatial dimensions, or training a large language model.

To describe the performance of algorithms on parallel hardware, Amdahl’s law [1] characterizes the maximum speedup achievable for a fixed-size problem when only a portion of the computation can be parallelized. Gustafson’s law [2] revisits this analysis by assuming that the problem size scales with the number of processing units, deriving a corresponding scaled speedup relative to serial execution.

For many numerical algorithms in scientific computing and machine learning, however, the problem size is related nonlinearly to the numerical error one seeks to minimize. Neural scaling laws [3], for example, investigate how the number of model parameters and the amount of training data influence the training loss. When the amount of training data and the number of model parameters are scaled in tandem with a compute-optimal strategy, the training loss can be expressed directly as a function of the total training compute [4].

The here outlined proposition summarizes and generalizes observations made in [5, 6, 7].

papers.title: Computing Data-Aware Diagonal Frame Decompositions
papers.abstract: We present a method for computing a specific type of matrix decomposition that combines a structured framework with data-driven adaptation. This framework allows for an efficient and stable representation of signals or images using frames by identifying sets of vectors that naturally capture the essential features of the given data. The resulting decomposition enables the development of regularization techniques that enhance the quality of reconstruction by preserving important signal characteristics while suppressing noise. We develop an optimization-based algorithm to compute the decomposition and establish convergence properties of the resulting iterates. Numerical experiments on synthetic data and tomographic image reconstruction illustrate the behavior of the proposed method and its performance compared to conventional spectral regularization methods.

The motivation for this problem comes from the use of frame decompositions for the representation and inversion of linear operators in Hilbert spaces. This diagonalized structure allows the evaluation and inversion of the operator to be analysed and implemented in terms of frame operators and scalar multiplication. The sparsity property incorporates prior information about the underlying signal class and can help stabilize the representation. Such decompositions have been used, for example, in the regularization of inverse problems [22, 21, 20, 27, 26, 9].

However, the singular vectors generally do not provide sparse representations for a given signal class. They are determined solely by the matrix 𝐀{\mathbf{A}} and therefore cannot be adapted to different signal distributions. In contrast, tight frames provide stable and redundant representations that are well suited for sparse signal representations. Moreover, their dual frames are particularly easy to compute, since the canonical dual of a tight frame differs only by a multiplicative constant. The diagonal matrix 𝐃{\mathbf{D}} plays a role analogous to the singular values and is therefore often referred to as the matrix of quasi-singular values. It represents the scaling action of the operator in the corresponding frame coordinates. Replacing orthonormal bases by tight frames therefore provides greater flexibility in the construction of such decompositions, allowing additional properties to be imposed. In particular, our sparsity condition introduces a data-dependent criterion: rather than constructing a decomposition solely from the algebraic properties of 𝐀{\mathbf{A}}, we seek a frame 𝐔\mathbf{U} whose coefficients provide sparse representations given the data 𝐗\mathbf{X}. This is motivated by the observation that suitable representations can capture the structure of signals and images more efficiently and incorporate prior information that is relevant for inverse problems [35, 12]. We note in passing that the diagonal matrix decomposition problems has applications far beyond imaging. In fact, frames are widely used for this purpose in applied mathematics, computer science, and engineering, with applications including sampling theory [23], data quantization [5, 6], image processing [10, 29], and coding theory [40].

papers.title: Finite-temperature ab-initio-Informed Nuclear Equation-of-State Tables (FINEST): Nuclear matter uncertainties in core-collapse supernovae
papers.abstract: We construct new finite-temperature, composition-dependent equation of state (EOS) tables for astrophysical simulations by implementing a recently developed energy-density functional. The functional is constrained by ab initio nuclear matter calculations and neutron-star observations. A distinguishing feature of this functional is a non-monotonic density dependence of the nucleon effective mass, with an increase beyond saturation density. Using these EOS tables, we investigate the impact of current uncertainties in nuclear matter properties on core-collapse supernova (CCSN) evolution with spherically symmetric simulations employing an effective treatment of convective mixing. The magnitude of the EOS effects depends on the progenitor compactness. Within current constraints, variations in incompressibility, symmetry energy, and high-density pressure produce only modest differences during the early post-bounce evolution. In contrast, the effective mass dependence has a much stronger influence on proto-neutron star contraction and the explosion dynamics in a stellar model with high core compactness. Its non-monotonic density dependence leads to a qualitatively different contraction history and can alter the explosion outcome compared to mean-field effective-mass behaviors. Therefore, among the nuclear matter properties considered, the density dependence of the nucleon effective masses has by far the largest impact on CCSN dynamics. This highlights the importance of realistic effective-mass parameterizations in nuclear EOSs used in astrophysical simulations.

papers.intro:
Astrophysical simulations require a description of the composition and properties of matter under a wide range of conditions. Simulations of core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) or neutron star mergers (NSMs) that involve neutron stars especially face this challenge. The equation of state (EOS) for the hot and dense nuclear matter in newly born or colliding neutron stars is not yet fully understood. Beyond the uncertainties of the EOS in neutron stars, the challenge of an EOS for astrophysical applications is to describe matter consistently over a wide range of mass density ρ\rho, temperature TT, and electron (or proton) fraction YeY_{e}: ​104 g cm−3≲ρ≲​1015 g cm−3${10}^{4}\text{\,}\mathrm{g}\text{\,}{\mathrm{cm}}^{-3}$\lesssim\rho\lesssim${10}^{15}\text{\,}\mathrm{g}\text{\,}{\mathrm{cm}}^{-3}$, 0.1 MeV≲T≲100 MeV$0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{MeV}$\lesssim T\lesssim$100\text{\,}\mathrm{MeV}$, 0.01≲Ye≲0.60.01\lesssim Y_{e}\lesssim 0.6. This extensive range of conditions includes matter in very different phases, from uniform nuclear matter through so-called pasta phases to the formation of nuclei. The EOSs that are commonly used in CCSN and NSM simulations are based on phenomenological models, e.g., employing Skyrme energy-density functionals (EDFs) [56, 93] or relativistic mean-field descriptions [95, 94, 45, 98]. However, many of the EOSs that are typically employed in astrophysical simulations are not consistent with new constraints from observations and/or from ab initio nuclear matter calculations.

There have been many advances in nuclear matter calculations based on chiral effective field theory (EFT) interactions (see, e.g., 44, 102, 61, 30, 18, 51, 104, 7, 31), from nuclear experiments (see, e.g., 108, 66, 47, 57, 97, 54), as well as observations of heavy-mass neutron stars [26, 8, 25, 36]. In addition, neutron star radius constraints from LIGO/Virgo through gravitational-wave measurements of tidal deformabilities [1, 2, 3] and from NICER using pulse-profile modeling [83, 69, 84, 70, 19, 89, 27, 107, 68] have resulted in new EOS constraints (see, e.g., 88, 52, 75, 96, 64, 67).

In addition, neutron star radius constraints from LIGO/Virgo through gravitational-wave measurements of tidal deformabilities [1, 2, 3] and from NICER using pulse-profile modeling [83, 69, 84, 70, 19, 89, 27, 107, 68] have resulted in new EOS constraints (see, e.g., 88, 52, 75, 96, 64, 67).

In this work, we use the EOS framework developed by [48], which takes into account state-of-the-art constraints from theoretical calculations at low and higher densities, as well as observational constraints from heavy pulsar mass measurements, LIGO/Virgo, and NICER. It also includes ab initio results for the density dependence of the nucleon effective masses from Carbone and Schwenk [17]. We have incorporated these novel parameterizations of the energy density and nucleon effective mass into an updated version of the SRO code [93, 90], called FINEST (Finite-temperature ab-initio-Informed Nuclear Equation-of-State Tables). We provide an extensive set of new EOS tables to the astrophysics community, systematically varying nuclear matter properties within their constraints.

These EOS tables are equally applicable in CCSN simulations, NSM simulations, or other astrophysical applications involving neutron stars. In this work, we focus on the impact on CCSNe and propagate the nuclear matter uncertainties to the explosion.
