There has been a long history of studies exploring the impact of the EOS on CCSN dynamics and observables (see, e.g., 16, 99, 62, 76, 45, 24, 101, 82, 74, 40, 14, 87). These studies demonstrated the importance of the EOS in several aspects of CCSN simulations: The central density and electron fraction at core bounce, the rate and energy at which neutrinos are radiated, and how much energy they feed to the shock. Consequently, also partly the success of explosions, the ejecta mass and composition, and explosive nucleosynthesis yields are affected by the EOS. These studies generally show a trend that simulations with a softer EOS (where the pressure increases less with density) are more prone to yield explosions (see, e.g., 50, 24). Typically, rather different EOS schemes that are popular in the CCSN community have been compared and this is still a common approach (see, e.g., 24, 101, 14). Recently, there have been new approaches of systematically varying nuclear matter properties within one theoretical framework. This allows to understand and constrain the isolated effects of a single nuclear property. [110] and [92] performed this systematic variation using Skyrme EDFs and showed that the parameter with the largest impact on the first second of the explosion, given present uncertainties, are the nucleon effective masses, which govern thermal effects. In relativistic mean-field EOS models, the nucleon effective mass also has a similar impact on CCSN simulations as shown recently [100]. The importance of thermal effects in CCSN dynamics had already been recognized from comparisons of finite-temperature EOS models, where differences in the thermal behavior of the EOS were found to affect proto-neutron star (PNS) contraction, neutrino emission, and shock evolution (see, e.g., 99, 45). papers.title: Beyond Post-Hoc Rewards: Privileged Reasoning Exploration for Multimodal Embeddings
papers.abstract: Advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have driven substantial progress in multimodal embeddings. Recent methods exploit generative capabilities by augmenting embedded inputs with self-generated reasoning to produce more informative embeddings. However, conventional retrieval supervision for training embedding models specifies pairwise relevance relations without explicitly guiding the reasoning used for input augmentation. Such reasoning is neither directly observed nor uniquely determined by the input, allowing multiple plausible traces to introduce semantic cues of varying retrieval utility. Existing approaches largely optimize reasoning conditioned on the input alone, limiting the exploration of retrieval-relevant traces. We introduce PILOT, a framework that models reasoning as a latent variable and instantiates its prior and posterior distributions as distinct reasoning modes of a shared MLLM. The prior conditions only on the input, whereas the posterior uses additional training-time relational evidence to guide reasoning exploration. To translate the posterior's broader exploration into inference-time improvements, we derive an importance-weighted variational objective and instantiate it as a prior-posterior co-evolution framework that improves both modes under a shared inference-compatible reward while selectively transferring posterior trajectories to the prior according to their utility and prior reachability. On the 78-task MMEB-V2 benchmark, PILOT outperforms the primary baseline across all 12 task groups at both 2B and 7B parameters, improving overall scores by 3.2 and 3.3 points, respectively, with the largest gains in visual-document retrieval (+6.1 and +6.4 points). Our results show that relational supervision is most valuable not as a post-hoc reward but as a signal for shaping how reasoning is explored in training reasoning-enhanced embedding models.

papers.intro:
Multimodal embeddings map heterogeneous inputs such as text, images, and videos into a shared dense representation space, supporting applications from cross-modal retrieval to clustering and recommendation (Zhai et al., 2022; Frome et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2022). Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) (Singh et al., 2025; Comanici et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025) have shifted the field beyond the dual-encoder vision–language models (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021) toward instruction-aware universal multimodal embeddings (UME) models, which follow nuanced instructions across tasks such as visual question answering and video moment retrieval (Meng et al., 2026), and generalize better in zero-shot settings (Jiang et al., 2025; Meng et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2025; Lan et al., 2025). Yet most UME models still use the MLLM purely as an encoder, leaving its generative reasoning capacity untapped.

Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning improves MLLMs performance across diverse multimodal tasks by enabling a deeper understanding of complex inputs (Zhang et al., 2024b). Several works extend this idea to UME by augmenting each query or candidate with a self-generated reasoning trace and encoding the input together with its trace into a single embedding (Cui et al., 2026; Lan et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026a). Despite their effectiveness, existing approaches face a fundamental mismatch between reasoning generation and retrieval supervision. During training, queries are paired with relevant candidates with other candidates serving as negatives. These positive–negative relations identify relevant matches but leave the reasoning needed to distinguish them unspecified. Consequently, multiple reasoning traces may be relevant to the same input yet differ substantially in their ability to distinguish positive candidates from negative ones. Existing methods sample reasoning from the individual inputs alone, with relational supervision applied only through post-hoc rewards. This creates a fundamental exploration bottleneck. Without access to relational evidence, the model is unlikely to discover the discriminative reasoning needed to distinguish relevant candidates from distractors, and post-hoc rewards can only reinforce already sampled sub-optimal trajectories.

We address this bottleneck with PILOT (Privileged-Information-guided Latent Reasoning Optimization and Transfer), a framework that models reasoning traces as latent variables. This formulation naturally distinguishes an inference-time prior conditioned only on the target input from a training-time privileged posterior that additionally uses relational evidence to infer retrieval-relevant reasoning. We instantiate both distributions as distinct reasoning modes of a single MLLM. Explicitly identifying the positive and negative counterparts allows the model to explain a given relevance relation without first determining which counterpart better matches the target. To encourage more fine-grained, discriminative reasoning, we construct a blind contrastive posterior that observes the target alongside a randomly ordered positive–negative pair with relevance labels withheld. The model must compare both candidates against the target and predict which is positive, encouraging it to identify subtle semantic distinctions that determine relevance. Using mode-specific prompt templates, a stronger annotation MLLM synthesizes reasoning traces for both distributions. Posterior traces are retained only when the annotator correctly identifies the positive counterpart. The prior traces and verified posterior traces jointly initialize the two modes in the shared embedding MLLM through supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

papers.title: Quasiparticle Interactions in the $S = 1/2$ Heisenberg Antiferromagnetic Chain CuPzN
papers.abstract: We investigate spinon--spinon interactions in the quasi-one-dimensional $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet Cu(C$_4$H$_4$N$_2$)(NO$_3$)$_2$ (CuPzN) using inelastic neutron scattering. At zero field, the spectrum exhibits the canonical multi-spinon continuum of the Heisenberg chain. With increasing field we demonstrate the appearance of an energy gap $2\Delta$ towards momentum $q\rightarrow 0$ between the uniform magnetization precession mode and the shifted spinon continuum. $2\Delta$ is a direct measure of spinon backscattering interactions. Comparison with numerical matrix-product-state calculations and a recent analytical theory shows excellent agreement. By examining the integrable spin-1/2 chain, we provide an example of how quasiparticle interactions can be quantified experimentally in isotropic quantum spin systems.

papers.title: S2SND-v2: Unified Online and Offline Speaker Diarization with Speaker-Adapted w2v-BERT 2.0
papers.abstract: This paper presents S2SND-v2, a unified online and offline speaker diarization framework built on S2SND that improves acoustic feature extraction and the use of the resulting representations. For acoustic feature extraction, we introduce a speaker-adapted w2v-BERT 2.0 front end and compare full and pruned construction routes. To better use these features, overlap-aware activity-query masking improves speaker embedding extraction under overlap, while late-speaker training aligns unknown-speaker training with online inference conditions. Combining these improvements, the pruned system achieves competitive average diarization error rates of 14.52% online and 12.03% offline across eight test sets.
papers.intro:
Speaker diarization determines who spoke when in a recording and is a core component of meeting transcription. Early diarization systems mainly relied on cascaded pipelines comprising speech activity detection, segmentation, speaker embedding extraction, and clustering. More recently, end-to-end neural diarization models have directly predicted frame-level speaker activities, while hybrid methods have combined local neural predictions with embedding-based clustering for long-form recordings [12, 15, 17]. Sequence-to-sequence prediction has also been introduced for target-speaker voice activity detection [7]. For online diarization, additional mechanisms such as speaker-tracing buffers and global/local attractors have been introduced to maintain consistent speaker identities across successive chunks [25, 16]. Although these advances have substantially improved diarization, many existing methods are still designed primarily for either offline or online use. A unified framework that supports both modes is therefore attractive in practice.

Sequence-to-sequence prediction has also been introduced for target-speaker voice activity detection [7]. For online diarization, additional mechanisms such as speaker-tracing buffers and global/local attractors have been introduced to maintain consistent speaker identities across successive chunks [25, 16]. Although these advances have substantially improved diarization, many existing methods are still designed primarily for either offline or online use. A unified framework that supports both modes is therefore attractive in practice.

A recent development in this direction is sequence-to-sequence neural diarization (S2SND), which couples a detection decoder and a representation decoder within a single framework for online and offline inference [6]. In S2SND, speaker embeddings serve as queries for activity prediction, while activity queries guide speaker embedding extraction, allowing activity estimation and speaker representation learning to reinforce each other. Embeddings accumulated during the online pass are then reused for later blocks and for offline re-decoding. However, its overall performance still depends on two factors: the quality of the acoustic representations provided to the back end, and how effectively the back end extracts and uses speaker information under realistic online conditions.

One direction for further improving S2SND is to strengthen the acoustic representations provided by its front end. The original S2SND uses a ResNet front end, whereas self-supervised learning (SSL) has recently provided stronger and more transferable speech representations for speech and speaker tasks [4]. This trend has also reached diarization, where SSL encoders such as WavLM have been adopted in hybrid and neural systems [10, 19], and recent work has further adapted and compressed SSL encoders for speaker segmentation and verification [1, 13, 14, 18]. In particular, Li et al. combine w2v-BERT 2.0 with layer adapters, multi-scale feature aggregation, low-rank adaptation (LoRA), and distillation-guided structured pruning, achieving strong speaker verification performance with both full and pruned models [18]. These results motivate revisiting the front end of S2SND with a stronger speaker-adapted SSL model that preserves frame-level temporal resolution for diarization.

Although S2SND uses non-overlapping speech duration to select and weight accepted embeddings, the activity queries used by its representation decoder can still contain overlapping frames [6]. Such overlap-contaminated queries may degrade target-speaker embedding extraction. In addition, the random speaker masking strategy used for unknown-speaker training does not reflect how unknown speakers are often encountered in online inference. In sliding-window processing, a new speaker is more likely to first become active in the latter part of the current input block, creating a mismatch between random masking during training and late-speaker conditions at test time. Together, these issues motivate improving S2SND through not only stronger acoustic representations but also cleaner embedding extraction and better-aligned unknown-speaker training.

papers.title: SN Ares: A Strongly Lensed Type IIb Supernova at $\mathbf{z=1.276}$ with a Predicted 70-Year Time Delay
papers.abstract: We present the discovery of supernova (SN) Ares, a strongly lensed supernova at $z_{\rm spec}=1.276\pm0.002$ in a massive, triply imaged host galaxy behind the MACS J0308.9+2645 galaxy cluster. JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy spanning the rest-frame optical to NIR of Ares reveals helium features at $5876\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$, $7065\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$, and $10830\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$, as well as H$\alpha$ and Pa$\beta$. A comparison to local core-collapse SN spectra and light curves leads to a classification of SN Ares as a Type IIb supernova, the highest-redshift member of its class spectroscopically identified. A comparison to local SN IIb light curves provides a phase estimate for the spectrum of $34_{-9}^{+10}$ rest-frame days post-radioactive peak, providing a unique view into a high-redshift stripped-envelope supernova in its late-photospheric evolution. A lens model of the cluster constructed using recent JWST data indicates that SN Ares is the first image to arrive and will reappear in two future images near the center of the cluster plane in $\gtrsim 70$ years, with predicted magnifications of $\sim5\times$ and $\sim1.5\times$. Planned JWST/NIRSpec Multi-Object Spectroscopy of the cluster will allow for more detailed modeling of the lensed system for tighter constraints on the time delay and magnifications, as well as a template spectrum at the location of SN Ares.

papers.intro:
The phenomenon of strong gravitational lensing occurs when a massive foreground object, such as a galaxy or galaxy cluster, distorts the light from a background source. This results in multiple magnified images appearing at different times (for reviews on galaxy- and cluster-scale strong lensing, see Shajib et al. 97 and Natarajan et al. 75). The offset in arrival time between images can be anywhere from hours to decades depending on the mass of the foreground lens and the geometry of the system, with cluster-scale lenses typically producing longer time delays [77]. The absolute and relative size of these delays is related to the physical scale of the Universe through the geometric configuration of the lens and background source [62].

Due to the direct relationship between these delays and geometric distance, a measurement of the offset in image arrival times leads to constraints on cosmological parameters such as the local expansion rate of the Universe, H0H_{0}[89]. The use of these delays for cosmological measurements is known as “time-delay cosmography” [89, 107, 108] and has found great success with galaxy-scale lensed quasar systems [113, 104, 105, 106]. Recently, strongly lensed supernovae (SNe) have emerged as incredible tools for time-delay cosmography as well. So far, four measurements of H0H_{0} have been made with strongly lensed SNe (Refsdal, H0pe, Encore, and 2025wny), finding H0H_{0} values that span the current cosmological tension, from 65​kms−1​Mpc−165\,\rm{kms^{-1}Mpc^{-1}} to 76​kms−1​Mpc−176\,\rm{kms^{-1}Mpc^{-1}} [56, 46, 82, 85, 101, 12, 52, 73, 95]. The advantages of lensed SN systems in particular are clear: the lensed SNe have predictable light curves with distinct features (such as a radioactive peak) that simplify time-delay measurements; they require short observing campaigns of weeks to months; they are resistant to the effects of chromatic microlensing [40, 86, 49], and they fade on timescales which allow for template observations after the SN has faded [27]. Regardless of whether the source is a lensed SN or quasar, cluster-scale systems possess an advantage over galaxy-scale systems in that they include multiple background sources across redshifts, which helps alleviate the mass sheet degeneracy uncertainty at the price of a more complex model [14]. Conversely, clusters are not dynamically relaxed systems. As such, traditional dynamical methods cannot be used to help constrain the multi-peaked mass model and reduce mass-sheet degeneracy. Furthermore, cluster environments and line of sight objects which contribute to the lensing potential are likely to be complex, requiring a dedicated analysis. Finally, for simply-parametrized models, residual errors in predicting image positions are of order tenths of arcseconds [12], indicating that structures with Einstein radii smaller than this are not fully accounted for. In order to better understand their relative strengths and weaknesses, it is crucial to continue building samples of strongly lensed SNe at both the galaxy and cluster scales.

Apart from their usefulness for cosmology, strongly lensed SNe also allow for unprecedented studies of high-redshift SN physics. Such studies elucidate the evolution in SN and SN progenitor properties, as well as inform us on how chemical enrichment has occurred over cosmic time. Without the magnification afforded by lensing, however, it would be impossible to detect (much less comprehensively analyze) certain classes of SNe out to high redshifts. For example, SN Refsdal (a 1987A-like core-collapse SN at z=1.49z=1.49), would have had a peak magnitude mV>27m_{V}>27 mag and would have been undetectable by HST without its μ=15\mu=15 magnification [55]. Furthermore, it would have been impossible for HST to have obtained a spectrum that could even classify this event at all. Similarly, the recently discovered Type II SN Eos at z=5.13z=5.13, would have been completely undetectable without the ∼30\sim 30x boost (∼4\sim 4 magnitudes) in brightness afforded by lensing [2, 24, 5]. Not only did lensing allow for its discovery, a remarkably high signal-to-noise spectrum obtained with JWST/NIRSpec allowed for a direct measurement of the Fe II 5018 Å absorption component, directly confirming the expectation based on its host galaxy that it was formed in a low-metallicity environment. Another recent strongly lensed SN at z≈2z\approx 2, 2025wny, a member of an intrinsically bright sub-class known as superluminous SNe [38], was also magnified by μ≳20\mu\gtrsim 20, allowing for high signal-to-noise spectroscopy from multiple ground based observatories in addition to space-based resources [53, 44, 61]. Although this SN is intrinsically bright (MUV≲−21M_{\rm UV}\lesssim-21 mag), the massive boost by lensing allows for a much more detailed study than would be possible otherwise. These recent discoveries show how strongly lensed SNe can be simultaneously valuable for precision time-delay cosmography as well as studies of high-redshift SN physics, greatly extending the parameter space in terms of SN type and brightness for which we can make spectroscopic observations. Although we can expect many more spectroscopically confirmed SNe in the field with Roman, studies such as these that probe fundamental spectroscopic properties at high redshifts will only remain possible with JWST observations of lensed SNe.

Here, we present the discovery and JWST + HST follow-up of SN Ares, a strongly lensed, core-collapse SN at z=1.276z=1.276. In Section II, we present the spectrophotometric dataset of SN Ares. The lens model analysis of MACS J0308.9+2645 and the resulting ∼70\sim 70-year reapperances of SN Ares is discussed in Section III. In Section IV, we show the JWST/NIRSpec FS observation of SN Ares and the resulting classification as an SN IIb. We combine this classification with our photometric dataset to form our best estimate for the phase of the SN in Section V. papers.title: Developers as Managers of AI Agents: A Workplace Shadowing Study
papers.abstract:
As AI coding agents become more autonomous, developers increasingly direct, coordinate, and check their work. Yet little is known about these practices in everyday professional development. We shadowed 11 professional developers across approximately 15 hours of work, coded their activities and task transitions, analyzed 255 submitted prompts, and conducted 4.6 hours of follow-up interviews.
  Developers spent an average of 33.4% of observed time formulating prompts or checking AI responses, with task-switching rates ranging from 0 to 101.6 switches per hour. Beyond producing artifacts, prompts supported understanding, requirements clarification, agent configuration, and coordination. We identified three recurring patterns: \textit{Supervisor}, involving direct artifact inspection; \textit{Delegator}, involving dialogue-based coordination and delegated implementation and checking; and \textit{Learner}, involving agents primarily to build understanding. Developers sought technical information from agents and organizational context, authority, and alignment from colleagues. Our findings suggest future studies of how developers manage attention across concurrent agent tasks and tools that support verification, coordination, and learning.

papers.intro:
Software engineering practice is being rapidly transformed by advances in large language models (LLMs). AI-enabled development tools have progressed from code completion (Ziegler et al., 2022; Barke et al., 2023) to conversational coding assistants (Lehtinen et al., 2024; Nam et al., 2024) and, more recently, coding agents capable of carrying out development tasks with increasing autonomy (Chou et al., 2026; Roychoudhury et al., 2026). As developers delegate more work to these agents, their activities extend beyond writing code to directing agents, coordinating concurrent work, and deciding how to check generated outputs. Yet these activities occur within the broader demands of professional software development, where developers must also manage ongoing tasks, information needs, tools, and collaboration. Understanding how coding agents fit into this everyday work remains an open question.

AI-enabled development tools have progressed from code completion (Ziegler et al., 2022; Barke et al., 2023) to conversational coding assistants (Lehtinen et al., 2024; Nam et al., 2024) and, more recently, coding agents capable of carrying out development tasks with increasing autonomy (Chou et al., 2026; Roychoudhury et al., 2026). As developers delegate more work to these agents, their activities extend beyond writing code to directing agents, coordinating concurrent work, and deciding how to check generated outputs. Yet these activities occur within the broader demands of professional software development, where developers must also manage ongoing tasks, information needs, tools, and collaboration. Understanding how coding agents fit into this everyday work remains an open question.

Prior research has examined AI-assisted development through repository analyses (He et al., 2026; Murphy-Hill et al., 2026), surveys (Liang et al., 2024), observations of live-streamed programming (Chou et al., 2026), and controlled experiments (Becker et al., 2025). These studies showed a substantial code outputs from developers with AI agents (He et al., 2026), and higher perceived productivity and reduced workload (Brandebusemeyer et al., 2026). However, researchers have also reported substantial time spent waiting for generated outputs (Chou et al., 2026), less code quality (He et al., 2026), effort required to assess their correctness (Gordon et al., 2023), and, in some cases, longer task-completion times (Becker et al., 2025) and review time (Cihan et al., 2025). However, these perspectives provide a limited account of how professional developers incorporate coding agents into their everyday work. Repository-level outcomes do not reveal the activities through which developers direct and check agents, while controlled tasks and publicly streamed sessions capture different conditions from workplace development (Chou et al., 2026; Alaboudi and LaToza, 2019). Professional software development already requires developers to divide their attention across multiple tasks, artifacts, and collaborators (Mark et al., 2005; Mark, 2023; Abad et al., 2018), while continually seeking answers to questions around artifacts, such as code and program behaviors (Ko et al., 2007; Sillito et al., 2008; de Souza and Redmiles, 2011). Developers must also coordinate dependencies and maintain awareness of other people and ongoing work (Begel et al., 2009; de Souza and Redmiles, 2011), sometimes across globe and teams (Al-Ani et al., 2013; Cataldo et al., 2008).

Coding agents add another source and recipient of information in this environment. Developers may now wait for agents while advancing other tasks, return later to inspect their progress or outputs, provide additional context, or seek information needed to decide what should happen next. To address this gap, we conducted a mixed-methods observational field study of 11 professional developers working with AI coding agents on their own development tasks in workplace settings during approximately 90-minute sessions. We manually coded observable activities and task transitions, then linked prompts to preceding activities and subsequent checks. papers.title: Entity Matching using Decision Models
papers.abstract: Entity matching is the task of deciding whether two records describe the same real-world entity. Current entity matching methods rely on pre-trained language models (PLMs) which require task specific fine-tuning or generative large language models (LLMs) which do not require task-specific fine-tuning but are slow and expensive at matching large record sets. Decision models are a new class of LLM-based models that return a probability for each predefined answer option rather than generate text. This paper investigates decision models as an alternative to generative LLMs and fine-tuned PLMs for entity matching. We evaluate six decision models in a zero-shot setting across eight benchmarks and compare their performance with that of the generative LLM GPT-6 Luna and the PLM-based matcher Ditto. Our experiments show that, without task-specific training data, the four strongest decision models achieve mean F1 scores close to that of GPT-6 Luna, with the best model slightly surpassing it. This model also outperforms Ditto on six of the eight benchmarks. All decision models are faster than GPT-6 Luna, and most are less expensive. For three of the four strongest decision models, the predicted match probabilities are well calibrated without requiring any task-specific recalibration. A model cascade that routes the least confident record pairs to an ensemble of generative LLMs improves the mean F1 scores of the four strongest decision models by 1.9-4.0 percentage points. Using the best decision model and its best-performing prompt for each benchmark, the cascade surpasses the highest published F1 scores from literature on four of the eight benchmarks.

papers.intro:
Entity matching (9, 2) is the task of discovering records in different data sources that describe the same real-world entity. It is a central step of data integration, for example, when offers from different shops are matched for price comparison or bibliographic records from different databases are combined. Since 2020, state-of-the-art matchers have fine-tuned pre-trained language models (PLMs) on labeled record pairs (4, 21, 29, 30, 42). These matchers need thousands of labeled training pairs and generalize poorly to entities that do not appear in the training data (32). Generative large language models (LLMs) address both shortcomings. With few or no task-specific training examples, the best LLMs perform comparably to fine-tuned PLMs (27, 31, 33). Our earlier study (33) finds that generative LLMs are more robust to unseen entities. Applying a generative LLM is also more costly and time-consuming per record pair than using a fine-tuned PLM (47, 38). This paper evaluates decision models, a new class of LLM-based models, as an alternative to generative LLMs and fine-tuned PLMs for entity matching in terms of F1, calibration, cost, and throughput.

Decision models (40) receive an input together with questions whose answer options are fixed in the request, and they return a probability for each answer option instead of generated text. TypeSafe introduced this interface with its model Jev in September 2026. Within weeks, Cloudflare, Perplexity, and an independent developer released decision models with open weights, and OpenAI launched a Decisions API (Section 2.2). Despite the name, decision models are unrelated to the decision rules (13) and Bayesian decision models (43) of probabilistic record linkage, which decide from the comparison of two records whether they match. They are also unrelated to Decision Transformers (5), which model sequential decisions in reinforcement learning.

TypeSafe introduced this interface with its model Jev in September 2026. Within weeks, Cloudflare, Perplexity, and an independent developer released decision models with open weights, and OpenAI launched a Decisions API (Section 2.2). Despite the name, decision models are unrelated to the decision rules (13) and Bayesian decision models (43) of probabilistic record linkage, which decide from the comparison of two records whether they match. They are also unrelated to Decision Transformers (5), which model sequential decisions in reinforcement learning.

For entity matching, the input is a record pair, and a yes/no question asks whether the two records describe the same real-world entity or not (Figure 1). Like a fine-tuned PLM matcher, a decision model then returns a match probability, but it requires no task-specific training. Compared with generative LLMs, decision models have three potential advantages. First, they return the match probability directly, whereas a generative LLM returns text, so that its confidence must be stated in the text or estimated from token probabilities or repeated samples (41). Second, the developers of five of the six decision models that we evaluate calibrate their probabilities during or after training. A calibrated match probability states how likely a pair is to match, which helps to choose a threshold that trades precision for recall and to defer uncertain pairs to manual review or to a stronger model. Third, decision models return no text and are billed for input tokens only, which can lower latency and, depending on the price of the endpoint, cost. Early reports mostly concern Jev (Section 9). They do not establish how decision models compare with generative LLMs and fine-tuned PLMs in F1, cost, and latency on entity matching benchmarks, nor how well their probabilities are calibrated for this task.

The models are TypeSafe’s Jev 1.13, Cloudflare’s Clef and Clef-flash, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna through its Decisions API, Perplexity Decider v1.2 (PPLX v1.2), and Kev. The models are TypeSafe’s Jev 1.13, Cloudflare’s Clef and Clef-flash, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna through its Decisions API, Perplexity Decider v1.2 (PPLX v1.2), and Kev. papers.title: CARES: Coverage-Aware Replay Exemplar Selection for Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Replay-based Continual Learning mitigates catastrophic forgetting by keeping a buffer of past samples, making buffer composition critical under a fixed memory budget. Recent coreset-based replay methods improve buffer quality using model-derived gradients, losses, or auxiliary optimization, but incur substantial computational overhead as memory is repeatedly updated. We propose CARES, a continual model-optimization-free approach for buffer construction that instead exploits the geometry of a frozen pretrained feature space using class-aware, density-weighted coverage. We evaluate CARES across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy streams under online class- and task-incremental settings. On Tiny-ImageNet, CARES is 2.3 to 8.8 times faster than existing coreset-based selectors. Although CARES achieves this speedup using no training signal from the continual learner, it ranks among the state of the art across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy streams under online class- and task-incremental settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 7.58 percentage points under class imbalance while also attaining higher average accuracy on Tiny-ImageNet. Code will be released upon publication

papers.intro:
Continual learning (CL) studies how a model can acquire knowledge while being trained on a sequence of tasks without losing performance on previously learned tasks. This setting reflects realistic learning scenarios, where data does not arrive all at once but instead appears as a stream over time (Wang et al., 2024). However, deep neural networks trained under this constraint suffer from catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen, 1989; Robins, 1995), in which updates on newer tasks overwrite representations useful for older ones. This problem is particularly challenging in class-incremental learning, where the model must distinguish among all classes observed so far without receiving the task identity at inference time.

Methods for mitigating catastrophic forgetting are commonly grouped into regularization-, architecture-, and rehearsal-based approaches. Regularization methods constrain model updates to preserve previously acquired knowledge (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Aljundi et al., 2018; Chaudhry et al., 2018; Ritter et al., 2018; Serra et al., 2018). Architecture-based approaches modify the network architecture through expansion or parameter isolation (Rusu et al., 2022; Schwarz et al., 2018; Mallya and Lazebnik, 2018; Xu and Zhu, 2018; Yoon et al., 2020; Hung et al., 2019; Sokar et al., 2021). Finally, replay-based methods maintain a buffer of samples from past tasks, which are replayed during training to address forgetting (Chaudhry et al., 2019a; Chaudhry et al., 2019b; Buzzega et al., 2020; Aljundi et al., 2019b; Aljundi et al., 2019a; Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2022).

Under a fixed memory budget, the effectiveness of rehearsal depends not only on the number of samples stored but also on which samples are retained in the buffer (Rebuffi et al., 2017; Yoon et al., 2022; Aljundi et al., 2019b). Methods such as experience replay (Chaudhry et al., 2019b) provide inexpensive buffer updates but do not select samples that accurately represent the previously seen data. Consequently, recent work has formulated buffer construction in rehearsal as a coreset selection problem (Yoon et al., 2022; Tiwari et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2023).

In a continual learning stream, buffer updates happen repeatedly and must keep pace with incoming data; selection is not a one-time cost, but one incurred at every task boundary or even every incoming batch (Wang et al., 2024). Gradient- and loss-based criteria (Aljundi et al., 2019b; Aljundi et al., 2019a; Tiwari et al., 2022; Yoon et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2023) produce effective buffers, particularly under extreme memory limits, but they rely on additional computationally heavy optimization steps. Because this cost recurs at every update rather than once, it accumulates over the lifetime of the stream and can become a substantial fraction of total training time. This computational burden creates a practical tension: the very methods designed to make rehearsal more sample-efficient often introduce overhead that undermines the efficiency gains they seek to provide, particularly when buffer updates must keep pace with a continuous data stream (Tiwari et al., 2022; Aljundi et al., 2019a).

These limitations raise a more fundamental question: must a continually updated model also provide the signal that determines what it should remember? We investigate a complementary hypothesis: a replay buffer can instead be constructed by preserving the representative structure of the observed data in a stable feature space. Features from a frozen encoder provide a continual model-independent representation space in which examples can be compared throughout the stream. Within this space, geometric coverage encourages the buffer to represent distinct regions of the data distribution. However, pure coverage may overemphasize isolated candidates, whereas prioritizing only dense regions risks selecting redundant examples from dominant modes. Density-aware coverage provides a natural compromise between these two objectives.

SubZeroCore (Moser et al., 2025) addresses this coverage-density tension in static coreset selection through a density-aware coverage objective. We build on this rather than classical geometric selectors such as herding (Welling, 2009; Rebuffi et al., 2017), or k-Center Greedy (Sener and Savarese, 2018), which primarily emphasize representativeness or coverage (Moser et al., 2026), because SubZeroCore incorporates density without requiring model-derived training signals. This makes it well suited to the repeated memory updates of online continual learning. However, it assumes simultaneous access to a fixed candidate pool, whereas continual learning requires a bounded buffer that must be updated as new task data arrives and the distribution of available candidates may become strongly imbalanced across classes. Directly applying a global geometric selector can therefore allocate disproportionate memory to classes with more candidates.

To address these challenges, we propose CARES, a continual model-optimization-free approach to replay-buffer construction for online continual learning. At each memory-update step, CARES combines the existing replay memory with a staging pool of newly observed examples and embeds the resulting candidate set using a frozen pretrained encoder. It then allocates the fixed replay budget across observed classes and applies density-aware coverage independently within each class before reconstructing the memory. papers.title: Do Language Models Understand Igbo Culture? Beyond Multiple Choice
papers.abstract: The value of language models for any community depends on whether a model actually understands the culture of the people it intends to serve. We use the Igbo language as a case study. Existing benchmarks test translated Western ideas, lacking depth. To address this, we introduce CAB-Igbo, a benchmark developed from indigenous cultural sources and verified by native speakers across six domains. We evaluated diverse models under varying conditions, incorporating regional personas. Performance was assessed using multiple-choice accuracy and human evaluations across Epistemic Fidelity, Representational Richness, Linguistic Quality, and Pragmatic Proficiency. Results reveal a stark dissociation between language fluency and cultural knowledge. Through statistical testing, we show that for most models, the severe lack of Epistemic Fidelity and Representational Richness is already present in English and does not significantly worsen when switching to Igbo. Instead, native language prompting mainly degrades Linguistic Quality and Pragmatic Proficiency. Gemini 2.0 Flash is the only model whose cultural knowledge scores improve under Igbo prompting. We find that current models struggle to demonstrate the knowledge needed for true alignment with Igbo, and multiple-choice formats allow pattern-matching to appear as understanding. Furthermore, automated judges agree with humans on linguistic quality but fail on epistemic fidelity. Ultimately, cultural evaluation must be built from community knowledge, establishing human evaluation as the gold standard to prevent misrepresenting low-resource communities globally.

papers.intro:
Language goes beyond vocabulary; it functions as the historical archive of a people’s shared experiences. As a community navigates similar circumstances generation after generation, a distinct culture evolves, holding the community’s ethical, moral, and aesthetic standards. When a society is culturally healthy, there is a natural seamless alignment uniting the words people speak, the symbols they write, and the reality of their daily interactions. But what happens when this harmony is disrupted? Historically, this fracture began within the colonial education system, which separated the language of conceptual learning from the language of everyday life. Today, we face a new frontier of this same alienation: the Large Language Model.

Language models are increasingly deployed globally to preserve heritage and process information (Zhao and Wang, 2025), yet they are overwhelmingly trained on English and other high-resource languages (Resnik, 2025). We are told that these frontier models are "multilingual," that they can speak to us in our local languages. But linguistic fluency must not be confused with cultural fidelity. As an act of resistance against this modern alienation, this research investigates whether Large Language Models genuinely grasp the depths of African cultures, centering on the Igbo language and its people. Spoken by roughly 30 million individuals in Southern Nigeria, Igbo carries a profound cultural heritage anchored in vibrant oral traditions and complex kinship networks. When an artificial intelligence processes fluent Igbo but maps it onto Western norms or pan-African stereotypes, it performs significant representational harm. It preserves surface meaning but strips away the deep cultural ontology embedded in the expression.

papers.title: Pulsed Laser Deposition of Ferroelectric SrTiO3 Shells Enables Polarization-Controlled Charge Separation in TiO2 Photoanode
papers.abstract: Ferroelectric polarization offers a powerful route to govern the interfacial charge separation in photoelectrodes; however, chemically converted ferroelectric shells lack sub-nanometer thickness control, coherent strain retention, and chemically clean interfaces. Here, we use pulsed laser deposition to fabricate stoichiometric SrTiO3 shells on hydrothermally grown TiO2 nanorod arrays, achieving atomically defined core-shell architectures while preserving the one-dimensional transport geometry. The photocurrent density followed a volcano-shaped dependence on shell thickness and reached 1.9 mA cm-2 at 1.23 V versus RHE under AM 1.5G illumination for the optimized 15-mins sample, exceeding the established hydrothermal benchmark. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed a tetragonally distorted, oxygen-stoichiometric shell, identifying coherent interfacial strain rather than defect dipoles as the origin of the ferroelectric order. Kelvin probe force microscopy directly imaged a polarization-induced built-in electric field whose magnitude scaled with charge-transfer efficiency and photocurrent density. Together, these complementary structural, chemical, electrostatic, and device-level measurements established a quantitative strain-polarization-built-in field-charge separation relationship. This work transforms ferroelectric photoanode engineering from empirical optimization into an atomically controllable and predictive materials strategy for high-efficiency solar water-splitting devices. This approach is readily extendable to visible-light absorbers and complex ferroelectric heterostructures.

papers.title: Chirpons: elementary local phase oscillations associated with complex zeros
papers.abstract: For a complex wave, the local phase variation provides the instantaneous frequency in time, the local wavenumber in space, and the local momentum in quantum mechanics. Here we study this quantity from the complex-zero structure of the analytic continuation of the wave. A single nonreal zero produces a localized Lorentzian phase variation on the real axis, whose position, width, sign, amplitude, and integrated phase are fixed by the zero itself. We call this elementary zero-associated oscillation a chirpon. The representation is exact for finite products and finite Fourier sums, and extends to entire and band-limited functions through canonical factorization. We illustrate the construction with superoscillatory sequences and discrete Fourier sums, showing how local anomalous oscillations can be reconstructed from periodic families of complex zeros. We further show how linear systems transform chirpons through the displacement of their associated complex zeros, and illustrate this dynamics for quadratic dispersive propagation and a resonant harmonic oscillator. This establishes a direct relation between local phase structure and the amplitude and phase response of the transfer function, suggesting a zero-based form of spectroscopy in which system parameters can be inferred from the motion, width, and orientation of chirpons. More broadly, the chirpon description provides a unified framework for instantaneous frequency, local wavenumber, superoscillation, backflow, and other local phase phenomena, while offering a new route for probing linear systems through the dynamics of their complex zeros.

In the local-phase picture this reversal is associated with a local phase gradient opposite to the globally allowed momentum direction. Closely related reverse-flow phenomena also occur in optical fields [16, 17, 15].

After analytic continuation of the observation variable, an individual nonreal zero produces a pole in the logarithmic derivative of the field and, consequently, a localized variation of the phase along the real axis. We identify this elementary zero-associated contribution as a chirpon. Depending on the physical variable under consideration, the same mathematical structure represents a contribution to the instantaneous frequency in time, to the local wavevector in space, or, after multiplication by ℏ\hbar, to the quantum local momentum. This viewpoint provides a common language for these apparently different local oscillatory phenomena while keeping their physical interpretations distinct.

papers.title: A Rowhammer attack on Fil-C's software capabilities
papers.abstract: Rowhammer is a hardware vulnerability in dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) in which repeated accesses to one or more aggressor rows can induce bit-flips in nearby victim rows. This phenomenon violates a core assumption of conventional programming language semantics: that reading from or writing to one memory location does not modify others. Despite the security importance of this phenomenon, there is no widely established formal framework connecting Rowhammer faults with program behaviour. This makes it difficult to reason rigorously about the efficacy of proposed Rowhammer defences and the program-level guarantees they provide. To address this gap, we present a probabilistic small-step operational semantics for an idealised imperative language subject to Rowhammer-style faults. The semantics is high-level in that it abstracts from DRAM internals and semiconductor physics. A general probabilistic fault model parameterises the semantics, representing Rowhammer-style faults by assigning probabilities to bit-flips during read or write operations within a specified victim region. The resulting distributions are propagated through programs using the standard monadic structure of probabilistic computation. As a case study, we formalise physical separation, a well-known defence that places program variables sufficiently far apart in physical memory that an access to one variable cannot disturb another. We prove a distribution-independent semantic collapse theorem: for every finite execution, including prefixes of terminating and non-terminating executions, the protected projection of the probabilistic Rowhammer semantics is the Dirac distribution of the corresponding Rowhammer-free execution. Furthermore, we develop an observation-parametric account of secure information flow.

papers.intro:
Memory-safety violations in C/C++ remain the dominant root cause of critical security vulnerabilities: Because rewriting the vast deployed base of C/C++ software is impractical, a major line of defence therefore retrofits spatial and temporal memory-safety protections onto existing code. These approaches include compiler instrumentation as in SoftBound/CETS [1] and AddressSanitizer [2], hardware-assisted capabilities as in CHERI [3], and memory tagging as in Arm Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) [4]. Fil-C [5] is a recent and unusually complete point in this space: it instruments every pointer operation at compile time and enforces complete spatial and temporal bounds checking at runtime through software capabilities, with high C/C++ compatibility to build large real-world programs unmodified. A tacit assumption underlies such systems: that the hardware faithfully preserves the metadata on which every check depends.

A tacit assumption underlies such systems: that the hardware faithfully preserves the metadata on which every check depends.

The Rowhammer vulnerability [6, 7] invalidates exactly this assumption for commodity DRAM. By repeatedly activating adjacent memory rows, an attacker induces controlled bit flips in victim rows without ever directly accessing them. Rowhammer has corrupted OS page tables [8], cryptographic keys [9], deduplication and allocator state of co-located VMs [9, 10], and JavaScript sandboxes [11, 12]. Rowhammer reads secrets it never touches [13] and survives across DRAM generations and defences [14, 15, 16, 17]. Yet compiler-managed bounds metadata, the very state on which software-defined memory safety rests, has, to our knowledge, received no systematic analysis as a Rowhammer target. This paper fills that gap with an explicitly conditional thesis: Wherever Rowhammer can land a usable bit flip in a suitable part of the stored metadata associated with a pointer, Fil-C cannot hold its spatial-safety promise for that pointer. We are not proposing a new way to hammer DRAM. We show what an existing, widely demonstrated hardware fault means for a software defence that relies on the aforementioned tacit assumption. We exploit a design choice in Fil-C 0.679: part of each heap pointer’s capability is stored as a 16-byte header inline in ordinary DRAM immediately before the object pointed to, with no mechanism to protect capabilities from corruption. Note that Rowhammer attack techniques do not let an attacker pick an arbitrary bit and force that cell to flip. They identify cells that are physically vulnerable to flipping, and then groom valuable victim data onto one of them [8, 9]. Most flips are unusable, ruled out by the cell’s page offset, its position within the Fil-C metadata, the flip polarity, the bit’s current value, or the requirement that the result remain a valid pointer (§VI-F). Our attack needs only one flip that survives all these filters. We show that such a flip silently defeats the Fil-C runtime with no panic, signal, or machine check to mark it.

papers.title: Rethinking Microscopy Generation: Co-Designed Diffusion for Biologically Interpretable Single-Cell Synthesis
papers.abstract: Generative models for microscopy can already produce realistic whole-image fields of view, but offer no principled way to control how each individual cell looks. We address this gap by recasting microscopy generation at the single-cell level and designing the input controls and the model's internal representation jointly, so that both are organized along the same biologically meaningful directions. On the input side, we aggregate a long list of standard cell measurements into a small set of semantic axes (size, elongation, brightness, texture, etc.) that are each named, measurable, and traversable. On the model side, we introduce BioVAE, an encoder-decoder whose latent space is explicitly aligned with the same set of measurements. A key finding is that the benefit of biologically structuring the latent emerges only when conditioning is also moved to the semantic axes, showing that the two ends must be designed jointly. Experiments on LIVECell show that semantic-axis conditioning substantially improves generative fidelity over high-dimensional conditioning, a blind study with biologists confirms the realism of generated cells, and per-axis traversals produce stable and interpretable phenotypic changes.

Microscopy images are pictures of a set of individual cells captured under a microscope, and the way each cell looks; its size, shape, brightness, and internal texture patterns, is defined as the phenotype. Phenotypic differences across cells are the basis of almost every quantitative question in cell biology, from how cells respond to a drug to how diseased cells differ from healthy ones [Schäfer et al.(2024)Schäfer, Nicke, Höfener, Lange, Merhof, Feuerhake, Schulz, Lotz, and Kiessling, Pearson et al.(2022)Pearson, Kremb, Butterfoss, Xie, Fahs, and Gunsalus]. Recent generative models can already generate realistic microscopy images [Liu et al.(2025)Liu, Jiang, Li, Yuan, Grzegorzek, Li, and Li, Lesmes-Leon et al.(2025)Lesmes-Leon, Dengel, and Ahmed, Osuna-Vargas et al.(2025)Osuna-Vargas, Wehrheim, Zinz, Rahm, Balakrishnan, Kaminer, Heilemann, and Kaschube, Eschweiler et al.(2024)Eschweiler, Yilmaz, Baumann, Laube, Roy, Jose, Brückner, and Stegmaier, Eschweiler et al.(2021)Eschweiler, Rethwisch, Jarchow, Koppers, and Stegmaier, Yu et al.(2023)Yu, Li, Lou, Liu, Wan, Chen, and Li], but they produce the entire field-of-view in one shot rather than building it cell by cell (Fig. 1 (a)). As a result, current models do not provide direct control over interpretable phenotype attributes such as cell size or brightness. While cellular phenotype is fundamentally defined at the level of individual cells, current generative models typically operate at the level of entire microscopy scenes.

papers.title: Existence and uniqueness of solutions for a random PDE-ODE model describing glioma invasion and radiotherapy
papers.abstract: We study a stochastic model for the growth and invasion of glioma cells in the anisotropic brain tissue, also incorporating effects of radiotherapeutic interventions and associated uncertainties. The PDE-ODE model couples glioma and healthy tissue dynamics in a nonlinear manner and explicitly includes treatment-related stochasticity through random depletion terms. The macroscopic system has been obtained by an upscaling procedure from a microscopic description in [1]. We prove the existence and uniqueness of local strong solutions to the corresponding stochastic system. The analysis addresses challenges arising from the nonlinear coupling, anisotropic diffusion, taxis mechanisms, and stochastic treatment effects, providing a first rigorous step toward the mathematical understanding of stochastic continuum models for glioma invasion and therapy response.

papers.title: Dream to Assist: Intent-Conditioned World Models for Shared Vehicle Control
papers.abstract: Assistive agents in shared-control settings face a dual challenge: acting proactively to align with the human's intentions while remaining legible enough for the human to comprehend and fluently respond in real time. We present Dream2Assist, a model-based reinforcement learning framework for tightly-coupled shared decision making that addresses both sides of this challenge. Our approach extends a recurrent state-space world model with intent inference, enabling an assistive policy trained via fictitious co-play to anticipate and support discrete human objectives without overriding human agency. Beyond the computational framework, we describe the full deployment pipeline needed to translate a world-model-based policy into a safe, human-centered system in a resource-efficient way. Crucially, we address the sim-to-real-human gap via policy down-selection and reward restructuring within an iterative human-machine interface design. We validate the framework through three human-subjects studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment spanning two qualitatively distinct domains: high-speed racing (N=30) and urban driving with richer intent structure (N=10). Our results demonstrate that intent conditioning yields measurable improvements in torque alignment and collision rate. We surface key design insights and practices for deploying learning-based assistive agents in safety-critical, real-time human-robot teaming.

papers.intro:
In shared control contexts where a human and AI assistant share the same embodiment, assistive agents face a fundamental challenge: to act proactively while remaining aligned with human intent, the agent must anticipate what the human is trying to accomplish before it intervenes. If it does so in ways that conflict with the human’s intentions, assistance can be perceived as interference rather than support. An effective embodied assistant needs to reason both about the task itself (e.g. the end-goal or overall performance of the team) as well as the human users’ objectives while performing the task.

This problem is even more apparent in safety-critical, real-time domains, where the human-AI team has to be aligned (Hadfield-Menell et al., 2016) and fluent (Hoffman, 2019), the AI has to be understood by the human (Sakai and Nagai, 2022), and the system must avoid risky events (Jamieson et al., 2022), performance degradation (Endsley, 2023), or loss of user confidence (Abbink et al., 2018). Meeting these requirements simultaneously demands tight integration of policy design, interface design, and human evaluation, and probing how algorithmic choices affect the human’s experience of the system as a collaborative partner.

The core idea is to extend a recurrent state-space world model (RSSM) with an intent predictor that infers the human partner’s discrete objectives from observed behavior, and to condition the assistive policy’s reward on the inferred intent. papers.title: DIGOM: Disentangled Interaction Graphs for Outcome prediction in Multimodal healthcare
papers.abstract: Multimodal healthcare data contain relational information that extends beyond individual patient observations. Effective clinical outcome prediction therefore requires not only integrating information from multiple modalities, but also modeling the relationships between them. Standard fusion approaches do not explicitly capture these interactions, while existing graph-based approaches typically model only a subset of them. We propose DIGOM (Disentangled Interaction Graphs for Outcome prediction in Multimodal healthcare), a graph-based framework that jointly models three complementary interaction types: Intra-patient cross-modal, Cross-patient same-modal, and Cross-patient cross-modal interactions. DIGOM learns a sparse multiplex graph with disentangled views, each encoding interactions between pairs of modalities across patients. Discrete adjacency matrices with patient-adaptive connectivity are sampled via a differentiable mechanism, enabling end-to-end learning and allowing the model to select informative relationships without imposing a fixed number of neighbors. A regularization objective maintains overall graph sparsity, while message passing integrates this relational context into patient representations for outcome prediction. We evaluate DIGOM on two multimodal healthcare datasets, MIMIC-IV and NIH-TB, across five clinical prediction tasks. DIGOM achieves the highest AUROC on all five tasks while using fewer connections than existing multi-interaction approaches. Ablation studies reveal that each interaction type's contribution varies across tasks, highlighting the need to adapt relational structures per task. DIGOM also demonstrates greater robustness to missing modalities, suggesting learned relationships provide complementary information when modalities are unavailable. Post-hoc analyses further reveal task- and outcome-specific connectivity patterns in the learned graphs.

papers.intro:
The growing availability of digital healthcare data creates new opportunities for artificial intelligence to improve patient care [1]. Depending on a patient’s condition and the available hospital resources, different types of information may be collected during their hospital stay, including demographic information, clinical notes, vital signs, laboratory test results, medical imaging, and genomic profiles. These sources of information, referred to as modalities, each provide a partial description of a patient’s condition, while together, they offer a more complete view of their health status [2]. This naturally reflects the way clinicians reason in practice, where they integrate complementary sources of information before making diagnostic or prognostic decisions. Consequently, multimodal learning has become an active area of research in medical artificial intelligence, frequently demonstrating improved predictive performance compared with unimodal approaches across a wide range of clinical applications [3, 4].

Despite this promise, effectively integrating multimodal healthcare data remains a major challenge. Standard multimodal fusion approaches are typically classified into three categories: early fusion, which concatenates modalities before learning; joint fusion, which combines latent representations learned from each modality; and late fusion, which aggregates predictions generated independently by each modality [5]. Although effective in many settings, these approaches ultimately aggregate modality-specific information into a single representation or prediction without modeling relationships between individual observations across modalities. Consequently, they may fail to capture how observations from different modalities complement or reinforce each other, limiting their ability to leverage fine-grained relationships in multimodal healthcare data.

Consequently, they may fail to capture how observations from different modalities complement or reinforce each other, limiting their ability to leverage fine-grained relationships in multimodal healthcare data.

However, medical decision-making rarely consists of simply aggregating independent observations. Instead, clinicians interpret each finding in relation to other clinical findings, as the significance of one observation often depends on the context provided by others [6]. For example, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging become suggestive of severe pneumonia when accompanied by elevated temperature and inflammatory markers. Likewise, physicians routinely compare current patients with previously encountered similar cases. A patient presenting with a chest radiograph or laboratory profile similar to previously observed cases with poor outcomes may provide valuable prognostic information [7]. Once similar patients are identified, their remaining clinical profiles, including laboratory measurements, vital signs, procedures, and treatments, can provide additional information for understanding the current patient and anticipating their clinical course [8]. As such, beyond comparing the same modality across patients, clinicians also leverage knowledge acquired from previous cases to relate findings across modalities, anticipating which abnormalities are likely to emerge next or which interventions may become necessary. Importantly, some decisions may rely primarily on complementary findings within a patient, while others may benefit more from information provided by similar patients or from other modalities.

Graph-based methods provide a natural mechanism for modeling such relational reasoning by representing patients or their modalities as nodes and their relationships as edges, through which Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) [9] propagate information for prediction. For fusion, existing approaches generally follow one of two paradigms. The first constructs patient graphs, where different modalities belonging to the same patient are connected to capture Intra-patient cross-modal interactions [10, 11]. The second builds population graphs, connecting patient modalities according to feature similarity or shared clinical characteristics to leverage Cross-patient same-modal interactions [12, 13, 14]. Although both paradigms have demonstrated promising results, they have largely evolved independently. Patient graphs ignore potentially informative cohort-level relationships, whereas population graphs overlook the rich interactions that exist between modalities within an individual patient. Consequently, neither paradigm captures the full range of relationships described above.

More recently, [15] proposed jointly modeling the three intra-patient and cross-patient interactions defined in Figure 1, bringing graph-based fusion closer to the clinical reasoning described above and demonstrating promising results. However, although a sparsity mechanism was introduced to control the graph connectivity, the resulting graphs remain relatively dense because the method does not explicitly control the number of retained edges. Such a large number of relationships increases computational cost, limits scalability to larger cohorts [16], may promote over-smoothing [17], and reduces the interpretability of the learned graph. Furthermore, this sparsity mechanism is uniform across all patients, where a single threshold determines which relationships are retained, regardless of the nodes involved. A natural extension is to make graph connectivity patient-adaptive, because clinically less complex cases may require only a few informative relationships, whereas more complex cases may benefit from integrating evidence from a larger number of related patients.

papers.title: Hybridizable Discontinuous Galerkin methods for the Keller-Segel model
papers.abstract: We propose a hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) finite element method to approximate the solution of the time-dependent Keller-Segel model, a drift-diffusion system describing chemotactic cell movement. We develop and analyze the corresponding HDG scheme, and establish theoretical convergence results for the proposed discretization. Finally, we present numerical experiments that confirm the theoretical findings.

papers.intro:
Chemotaxis, i.e. directed cell migration in response to chemical signals coming from external sources or secreted by the organisms themselves, plays a key role in a number of biological processes, from bacterial movement, to inflammation, to cancer development, to embryology. The taxis can be either positive (attractive) or negative (repulsive) due to the presence of cells/chemicals or nutrient depletion. The dynamics of many amoeboid cells, including Physarum polycephalum, Dictyostelium discoideum or leukocytes and some eukaryotic cells, shows that chemotactic movement replaces random and undirected exploration of the environment in the presence of chemical gradients: amoeba gathering to aggregate around food sources Nakagaki et al. (2000); Willard and Devreotes (2006), bacteria alternating phases of free swimming and tumbling in order to reorientate according to nutrient or even toxic external substances Berg and Brown (1972); Khan et al. (2005). The physiological mechanism in human body’s immune response to wounds or infection is regulated by chemotaxis as well. Indeed, chemokines in the inflammatory phase are responsible for the recruitment of macrophages and the promotion of angiogenesis Mantovani et al. (2003); Ridiandries et al. (2018). In the brain, chemotaxis plays a fundamental role in the neural migration for cortical development Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman (1996). The process of demyelination is regulated by chemotaxis, see Khonsari and Calvez (2007) and references therein. Regarding cancer, one of the most interesting examples of chemotaxis involves immune cells that, besides other functions crucial for the organism’s defense, have the role of detecting cancer cells and fighting them Roussos et al. (2011). The immunosurveillance in cancer inflammation involves complex relationships between cells and chemotactic factors secreted in the tumor microenvironment, as well as the interactions among cells, see Bretti et al. (2021) and references therein.

The present paper focuses on the classical Keller–Segel (KS) model Keller and Segel (1970), proposed in 1970 and still considered as a fundamental model, thanks to its basic formulation of biological processes. In spite of this apparent simplicity, such a model is able to replicate key behavior of chemosensitive populations, such as directed movement of individuals and pattern formation. The evolution of the density of individuals is described by a parabolic equation, and the concentration of chemoattractant is generally given by an elliptic/parabolic equation. Since in this model the organisms secrete chemical substances and move towards areas of higher chemical concentration, this leads to high aggregation of individuals, expressed mathematically as a blow up of their density. The high nonlinearity due to the chemotactic term makes the KS system largely intractable by analytical methods. Moreover, the model may develop two kinds of solutions: unbounded in finite time (blow up) or bounded with peaks in small areas of the domain Sleeman et al. (2005). Many analytical studies on blow-up in KS equations are described in Dejak et al. (2014) and references therein. Here, the behavior of solutions of the KS model is studied and analyzed in the bounded regime since the biological application we have in mind has a slightly different formulation where blow-up does not occur, see Braun et al. (2021). Numerical tests in the blow-up regime are also provided in order to show the capability of the method to handle such a challenging case.

The present paper focuses on the classical Keller–Segel (KS) model Keller and Segel (1970), proposed in 1970 and still considered as a fundamental model, thanks to its basic formulation of biological processes. In spite of this apparent simplicity, such a model is able to replicate key behavior of chemosensitive populations, such as directed movement of individuals and pattern formation. The evolution of the density of individuals is described by a parabolic equation, and the concentration of chemoattractant is generally given by an elliptic/parabolic equation. Since in this model the organisms secrete chemical substances and move towards areas of higher chemical concentration, this leads to high aggregation of individuals, expressed mathematically as a blow up of their density. The high nonlinearity due to the chemotactic term makes the KS system largely intractable by analytical methods. Moreover, the model may develop two kinds of solutions: unbounded in finite time (blow up) or bounded with peaks in small areas of the domain Sleeman et al. (2005). Many analytical studies on blow-up in KS equations are described in Dejak et al. (2014) and references therein. Here, the behavior of solutions of the KS model is studied and analyzed in the bounded regime since the biological application we have in mind has a slightly different formulation where blow-up does not occur, see Braun et al. (2021). Numerical tests in the blow-up regime are also provided in order to show the capability of the method to handle such a challenging case.

The KS model is hard to solve numerically due to the singular structure of solutions and to high sensitivity to changes in model parameters or in the step sizes of the numerical scheme. For the reasons described above, it is fundamental to have efficient numerical methods at our disposal, able to produce a realistic approximation of the observed phenomenon in order to describe correctly the evolution of concentration profiles. In particular, a numerical scheme for KS needs to reproduce all the relevant physical features, like the nonnegativity of the discrete approximation of the solution as well as the conservation of total mass in time in the case of no-flux boundary conditions. Moreover, since the density may grow fast in very small regions as a result of directed movement, the numerical approximation must reproduce this behavior and avoid non-physical oscillations and numerical instabilities.

papers.title: kstress: a LAMMPS package for calculating the 2D wavevector-dependent stress tensor and its anisotropy in amorphous solids
papers.abstract: The stress tensor resolved in wavevector $\qvec$ and time $t$, $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\qvec,t)$, gives access to the elastic moduli of amorphous solids as a function of the probed length scale, and to the long-range stress correlations that distinguish an amorphous solid from a liquid. Its evaluation requires the contribution of every interacting pair and therefore an interface to the force loop of the molecular dynamics code. In the current work, we present: i) an optimized implementation of the LAMMPS~\cite{lammps} module for calculating $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\qvec,t)$, in which trigonometric functions are calculated only for the basic wavevectors and, in addition, all the relevant wavevectors are supplied as an explicit list rather than generated as a full grid, so that only the wavevectors of interest are computed and stored, and ii) a validation protocol for the code illustrated for a two-dimensional polydisperse Lennard-Jones (2DpLJ) glass-forming liquid. Based on these technical achievements we elucidated how the affine moduli for the 2DpLJ model depend on the norm $q$ of the wavevector. In particular, we demonstrate that the longitudinal affine modulus shows a minimum near $q_\text{max}$ corresponding to the main peak of the structure factor. Our data also point to the peaks in the $q$-dependencies of vibrational frequencies well below $q_\text{max}$ for both transverse and longitudinal modes. The potential relevance of this feature to the ``boson peak'' is discussed as well.

The mechanical response of an amorphous material is inherently scale-dependent. In contrast to a crystalline solid, where elastic properties can be defined with respect to a unit cell and are therefore naturally associated with macroscopic material constants, an amorphous solid contains structural heterogeneities over a broad range of length scales. Local stresses and elastic responses fluctuate from one region to another [2, 3], and the mechanical response obtained from a measurement depends on the spatial scale over which the material is probed. A natural description of such systems is therefore provided by spatially resolved stress and strain fields and, equivalently, by their Fourier components at finite wavevector 𝐪\mathbf{q}, and the natural starting point is the stress tensor resolved in 𝐪\mathbf{q}, σα​β(𝐪,t)=1V∫σα​β(𝐫,t)e−i𝐪⋅𝐫ddr,\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{q},t)=\frac{1}{V}\int\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{r},t)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\mathrm{d}^{d}r, (1) where VV is the volume of the system and dd is the space dimension. Real-space approaches define local elastic moduli on coarse-graining volume and study their distribution as this volume is varied [2, 4]. The result then depends on the size and shape of the volume and on how its boundary is treated. The reciprocal-space description avoids these issues: each wavevector probes a well-defined length scale 2​π/q2\pi/q and a well-defined direction, and the full information is contained in the correlations of Eq. (1) over a set of wavevectors.

At zero wavevector the connection between stress fluctuations and elasticity is classical. The shear modulus of a solid can be written as the difference between an affine contribution, evaluated on single configurations, and a fluctuation contribution given by the variance of the shear stress [5, 6, 7]. For truncated pair potentials the affine modulus must involve an impulsive correction coming from the discontinuity at the cutoff, which must be included for the decomposition to be consistent [6]. The shear relaxation modulus G⁡(t)G(t) follows from the time correlation function of the shear stress through the fluctuation-dissipation theorem [8, 9, 10]. In glass-forming systems these relations require care: the fluctuation contribution depends on the statistical ensemble and on the sampling time [7], and in a system that does not self-average the average over independent configurations is itself a fluctuating quantity [11]. General relations between stress fluctuations and viscoelasticity, valid for amorphous polymers and glass-forming systems, have recently been established [12]. The question addressed by the wavevector-resolved description is how these quantities depend on the length scale over which the deformation is imposed.

Interest in this question has grown from two directions. The first is the observation that amorphous solids and slowly relaxing liquids carry long-range stress correlations. In a liquid with a short terminal time the stress field decorrelates over a few particle diameters, whereas in a glass-forming system it is not the case: even upon coarse-graining in time the stress correlations decay as a power law ∼r−d\sim r^{-d} in dd dimensions, with an angular dependence that survives to the largest distances the system affords [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. Their signature in reciprocal space is that ⟨|σα​β​(𝐪)|2⟩\langle|\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}\rangle retains a dependence on the direction of 𝐪\mathbf{q} down to the smallest accessible wavevectors. That anisotropy is not an artefact of a particular coordinate system, nor a sign of plastic rearrangement: it is imposed by the tensorial structure of an isotropic medium, and all components of the correlation tensor follow from the longitudinal and transverse fluctuations alone [4, 19, 20]. Establishing it quantitatively, however, requires the full tensor at many wavevectors, not a single scalar.

A physical picture at the origin of these correlations is provided by Eshelby’s inclusion problem. A localised rearrangement embedded in an elastic medium produces a stress perturbation that decays as r−dr^{-d} with a quadrupolar angular dependence, and the superposition of such events underlies both the long-range stress correlations of supercooled liquids [14, 15] and the elastoplastic description of the plasticity of amorphous solids [3]. In reciprocal space the corresponding propagator depends on the direction of 𝐪\mathbf{q} but not on its modulus, which is why the direction dependence of the stress correlations persists down to the smallest wavevectors.
