In the limit of long wavelengths the transverse and longitudinal correlation functions reduce to the hydrodynamic description involving the shear and longitudinal (second) viscosities, and the departure from that limit at finite qq measures the length scale on which the continuum description breaks down [8, 22]. In supercooled liquids the viscous response becomes increasingly non-local on approaching the glass transition [25, 26]. In liquid theory, the established approach to describe these memory effects is the Zwanzig-Mori projection-operator formalism [27, 28]. This approach has recently been applied to explore spatio-temporal stress correlations in glass-forming liquids [17, 18, 29, 30, 31]. papers.title: Lunar tidal response-induced clock frequency variations on the Moon
papers.abstract: As clock performance improves, the instability and uncertainty of the clock's fractional frequency shift (FFS) become comparable to the FFS caused by the lunar tidal response (LTR), so the influence of the LTR on lunar time needs to be investigated. In this paper, we used the Keplerian expansions method to study the FFS to the level of $10^{-18}$ caused by the LTR between two clocks placed in different positions on the Moon. We consider the case of the Moon orbiting in an elliptical orbit, which is closer to the actual situation compared to the case of the Moon moving in a circular orbit. An interesting phenomenon is found that the longitude difference between two clocks can cause a change in the amplitude and phase of the FFS due to the LTR, but the latitude difference only changes the amplitude of the FFS. We further estimated the clock difference between two clocks near the Moon caused by the LTR. When one clock is on the lunar surface, and the other is on the Earth's surface, the LTR will cause a clock difference of $% -5.68\times 10^{-7}$ $\mu $s/day between the two clocks. These are significant for the construction of a lunar time and clock synchronization near the Moon.

China is also planning to land on the Moon around 2030 [4] with many exciting results of the lunar exploration project being announced one after another [5, 6, 7, 8]. As assets on the lunar surface are expected to increase significantly in the near future, precise positioning, navigation, and time synchronization of lunar surface devices will become issues of greatest interest.

As assets on the lunar surface are expected to increase significantly in the near future, precise positioning, navigation, and time synchronization of lunar surface devices will become issues of greatest interest.

Several methods for defining lunar time have been proposed [12, 11], where the proper time measured by clocks at different locations on the lunar surface is affected by both gravitational and kinematic effects [13]. These effects are essential for constructing a consistent and high-precision lunar time system.

Tidal response is a fundamental phenomenon not only in planetary systems but also in broader astrophysical contexts. For instance, LTR can be used to infer the thermal structure of the Moon’s interior [25], while tidal responses in other bodies, such as Io [26] and even black holes [27, 28], provide insights into their internal or spacetime properties. We model the LTR in an elliptical orbit using the Keplerian expansion method, providing a more realistic description than circular-orbit approximations. We incorporate the tidal response consistently into the relativistic framework of LCRS and quantify the impact of LTR on FFS and the time difference between clocks at different locations on and near the lunar surface. papers.title: Variational Structure of Energy-Balance Climate Models with Heterogeneous Insolation
papers.abstract: We analyse stationary Sellers-type energy-balance climate models with heterogeneous insolation $Q_\varepsilon = Q_*+\varepsilon Q_1$, both on the interval $(-1,1)$ with degenerate diffusion $\kappa(x)=1-x^2$ and on $\mathbb{S}^2$ with uniformly elliptic diffusion. Assuming that the homogeneous model corresponding to $\varepsilon = 0$ admits three constant equilibria $\theta_S <\theta_M < \theta_W$ satisfying suitable non-degeneracy and spectral conditions, we prove that, for sufficiently small $\vert \varepsilon \vert $, these equilibria continue to three stationary branches $ u_S^\varepsilon$, $u_M^\varepsilon$, and $u_W^\varepsilon$. The cold and warm branches, $u_S^\varepsilon$ and $u_W^\varepsilon$ respectively, are strict local minimisers of the associated energy functional, while the intermediate branch $u_M^\varepsilon$ is non-degenerate and has Morse index one. We further establish the Palais-Smale condition and obtain a mountain-pass critical point $u^\varepsilon_{MP}$ at the minimax level between the two local minima. Under an additional isolation assumption for the homogeneous problem at the minimax level, this critical point coincides with $u_M^\varepsilon$. Lastly, a Legendre-Galerkin discretisation of the one-dimensional model numerically illustrates the three stationary branches, their discrete Morse indices, and the corresponding energy landscape.

papers.title: Constrained neural softening functions for the Mullins effect in parameter-dependent materials
papers.abstract: Accurately capturing the Mullins effect across varying material compositions remains challenging, as constitutive models must unify flexible representations of stress softening with physical consistency and robust parameter calibration. In this work, we investigate parameter-dependent physics-augmented neural network constitutive models within the pseudo-elastic modeling framework, focusing on structural constraints that ensure physically admissible neural softening functions. This paper has three key contributions: (1) We formulate different neural softening functions within the pseudo-elastic framework, including a multiplicative decomposition of the softening function that enables parameter-dependent ansatz functions satisfying common mechanical constitutive conditions by construction. (2) We derive a sufficient condition for ellipticity of pseudo-elastic constitutive models, which can be enforced in the constitutive models by construction. (3) We systematically investigate how flexibility and structural constraints influence the performance of neural softening functions in terms of prediction accuracy and calibration robustness. For this, we consider multiaxial experimental data of carbon black-filled EPDM rubber synthesized with varying amounts of curatives. The findings of our work suggest that neural softening functions are a promising extension of the classical pseudo-elastic framework and, when subject to suitable constraints, can improve predictive accuracy for highly nonlinear, parameter-dependent materials.

papers.intro:
Neural constitutive models have emerged in recent years as a promising approach to representing complex material behaviors. There is broad agreement that such models should incorporate mechanical constitutive conditions to provide mechanically reasonable predictions, while exploiting the flexibility of neural networks. This is referred to as thermodynamics-based (Masi and Stefanou, 2022), mechanics-informed (As’ad and Farhat, 2023), physics-based (Aldakheel et al., 2025), physics-constrained (Kalina et al., 2023), physics-augmented (Klein et al., 2022b), or constitutive artificial (Linka et al., 2020) neural network (NN) modeling. Throughout this work, we adopt the terminology physics-augmented neural networks (PANNs). Beyond, the paradigm of combining machine learning methods with physical and mathematical knowledge is widely used in many scientific fields (Von Rueden et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2021; Karniadakis et al., 2021; Kumar and Kochmann, 2022; Kannapinn et al., 2024; Watson et al., 2025).

As in classical approaches (Truesdell and Noll, 2004; Neff et al., 2015), an important question is which constraints should be imposed on the constitutive models and how these affect the resulting model behavior. Considerable progress has been made in hyperelastic PANNs (Fuhg et al., 2024), and various approaches have been proposed for inelasticity (Rosenkranz et al., 2024; Boes et al., 2026; Friedrichs et al., 2026) and multiphysics (Klein et al., 2022b; Kalina et al., 2024; Holthusen et al., 2026). Moreover, neural constitutive models that incorporate additional parameters that represent families of material behaviors, e.g., the geometry of microstructured materials, material constituents, or manufacturing conditions, have also been established (Linka et al., 2020; Fernández et al., 2022; Abdolazizi et al., 2025; Klein et al., 2026). In the present work, we focus on pseudo-elastic constitutive modeling of the Mullins effect and investigate suitable constraints on neural softening functions.

As in classical approaches (Truesdell and Noll, 2004; Neff et al., 2015), an important question is which constraints should be imposed on the constitutive models and how these affect the resulting model behavior. Considerable progress has been made in hyperelastic PANNs (Fuhg et al., 2024), and various approaches have been proposed for inelasticity (Rosenkranz et al., 2024; Boes et al., 2026; Friedrichs et al., 2026) and multiphysics (Klein et al., 2022b; Kalina et al., 2024; Holthusen et al., 2026). Moreover, neural constitutive models that incorporate additional parameters that represent families of material behaviors, e.g., the geometry of microstructured materials, material constituents, or manufacturing conditions, have also been established (Linka et al., 2020; Fernández et al., 2022; Abdolazizi et al., 2025; Klein et al., 2026). In the present work, we focus on pseudo-elastic constitutive modeling of the Mullins effect and investigate suitable constraints on neural softening functions.

The Mullins effect describes stress softening under mechanical loading (Mullins, 1948). Thereby, softening mainly develops upon loading to previously unattained deformation levels, although additional softening may occur during subsequent loading cycles even without exceeding the previously attained maximum deformation (Plagge and Klüppel, 2017). The Mullins effect exhibits further complexities such as temperature dependence (Plagge and Klüppel, 2017), recovery over time (Liao et al., 2023), softening-induced anisotropy (Denora and Marano, 2024), and it is frequently accompanied by other inelastic phenomena such as viscoelasticity (Alkhoury et al., 2024). The Mullins effect can be observed in a variety of soft materials, including rubber-like materials (Harwood and Payne, 1966; Mullins, 1948) and soft biological tissue (Franceschini et al., 2006; Kumar and Kumar, 2025). Moreover, it is also observed across families of materials with varying compositions or manufacturing conditions (Liao et al., 2020; Plagge and Klüppel, 2017).

Moreover, it is also observed across families of materials with varying compositions or manufacturing conditions (Liao et al., 2020; Plagge and Klüppel, 2017).

Although being most pronounced during initial loading, the consideration of the Mullins effect is important for reliable constitutive model predictions. Mechanical preconditioning, i.e., trying to remove the influence of the Mullins effect before experimentally characterizing a material specimen, can significantly affect the predictive capabilities of constitutive models (Wollner and Holzapfel, 2026). Moreover, heterogeneous deformation states in engineering components can lead to spatially heterogeneous softening, even for initially homogeneous materials (Freund, 2012, Fig. 7.6).

A variety of classical constitutive models for the Mullins effect have been proposed, including both micromechanically motivated models (Plagge and Klüppel, 2017; Göktepe and Miehe, 2005) and phenomenological approaches, such as continuum damage (Simo, 1987; Miehe, 1995) or pseudo-elastic formulations (Dorfmann and Ogden, 2004; Ogden and Roxburgh, 1999), cf. (Ricker et al., 2021). Depending on the considered phenomena, these models describe isotropic softening (Ogden and Roxburgh, 1999) or anisotropic softening (Itskov et al., 2010; Diani et al., 2006), and may additionally incorporate further effects such as recovery (Wang and Chester, 2018), temperature dependence (Plagge et al., 2020), or viscoelasticity (Caro et al., 2026). (Ricker et al., 2021). Moreover, models that include parametric dependencies of the material behavior have also been introduced (Liao et al., 2020).

Neural constitutive modeling for the Mullins effect has received only limited attention. To the best of our knowledge, the first neural constitutive model for the Mullins effect was proposed by Ghaderi et al. (2020). However, the thermodynamic consistency argument employed therein, which is based on monotonicity of the NNs, is not satisfied by the employed non-monotonic sine activation functions, cf. App. B.2 and Sec. 4 therein. Neural constitutive models based on continuum damage formulations were proposed by Zlatić and Čanađija (2024) and Tac et al. (2024), where the former employ feed-forward neural networks and the latter employ neural ordinary differential equations. In both cases, the stress response is scaled by a damage function such that softening also occurs along primary loading paths. Moreover, in Ostadrahimi et al. (2026), a neural constitutive model that accounts for viscoelasticity, temperature dependency, and softening behavior is introduced, however, thermodynamic consistency is only approximately fulfilled by promoting it through the loss function. Closely related, pseudo-elastic constitutive models based on deep symbolic regression were introduced in Abdusalamov et al. (2024). Overall, neural constitutive models for the Mullins effect are still scarce, thermodynamic consistency is not always ensured by construction, and which constraints should be imposed on the neural softening or damage functions, as well as how these affect the resulting model behavior, has not yet been systematically investigated.

papers.title: Efficient SCA Algorithms for Sparse Bayesian Learning
papers.abstract: Type-II sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) for the multiple measurement vector model recovers a sparse signal power vector by minimizing the marginal negative log-likelihood via the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, referred to as M-SBL. We revisit the covariance learning (CL) problem and develop three parallel first-order algorithms within the successive convex approximation (SCA) framework. CL-SCA minimizes per-coordinate surrogates formed by partially linearizing the log-determinant term, while CL-FP uses a damped projected fixed-point iteration derived from stationarity conditions. Both methods have closed-form updates. We prove that the fixed points of both update maps are exactly the KKT points of the CL problem, that each update direction satisfies a quantitative descent inequality, that the damped iterates achieve sufficient decrease with an $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ best-iterate stationarity rate, and we derive a backtracking rule that retains this rate without step-size tuning. If damping factors are bounded away from zero, the residual vanishes along the whole sequence and every limit point is a KKT point. Local analysis motivates CL-Hyb, which combines CL-SCA and CL-FP. Experiments on device activity detection in massive random access show that CL-Hyb-bt matches the best CL solvers' accuracy at a fraction of the runtime and is over an order of magnitude faster than EM.

papers.title: HiFiPix: Bringing High-Fidelity Real-World Super-Resolution Back to Pixel Space
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based real-world image super-resolution suffers from limited reconstruction fidelity due to information loss in VAE-based latent representations. Recently, pixel-space diffusion models offer a promising high-faithfulness alternative by avoiding latent compression, but adapting them to Real-ISR remains challenging due to inherent patch boundary artifacts and degraded generative capability. To address the issues and maximize the potential of pretrained pixel-space diffusion models, we propose HiFiPix, a pixel-space Real-ISR framework capable of ultra high-fidelity reconstruction and fine-grained visual generation effects. To suppress patch boundary artifacts, we penalize unrealistic high-frequency periodic components with a Cross-Scale Wavelet Discriminator (CWSD) for image-level supervision, and Mixup Contrastive Self-Distillation (MixCSD) for intermediate representation regularization. Furthermore, we uncover a heterogeneous generation-fidelity trade-off across low-rank adapters (LoRA) and propose Selective LoRA Pruning (LoRA-SP) to adaptively prune LoRA layers, enhancing generative capability with minimal deterioration of reconstruction fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HiFiPix consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art latent space methods in terms of both restoration accuracy and perceptual quality by a large margin. Code and models will be released.

papers.intro:
Real-world image super-resolution (Real-ISR) targets the recovery of low-quality (LQ) images suffering from complex unknown degradations, with the goal of reconstructing high-quality (HQ) counterparts that exhibit both high fidelity and satisfying perceptual quality. Initially, GAN-based algorithms Wang et al. (2021); Chen et al. (2023) employ a discriminator to match the distribution of reconstructed images with that of real-scenario images. However, lacking powerful generative priors, GAN-based models exhibit limited capability for recovering fine-grained details.

Real-world image super-resolution (Real-ISR) targets the recovery of low-quality (LQ) images suffering from complex unknown degradations, with the goal of reconstructing high-quality (HQ) counterparts that exhibit both high fidelity and satisfying perceptual quality. Initially, GAN-based algorithms Wang et al. (2021); Chen et al. (2023) employ a discriminator to match the distribution of reconstructed images with that of real-scenario images. However, lacking powerful generative priors, GAN-based models exhibit limited capability for recovering fine-grained details.

Over the past few years, diffusion-based generative models Rombach et al. (2022); Labs (2025) have advanced Real-ISR by producing highly photo-realistic details. However, existing Real-ISR methods Dong et al. (2025); Fang et al. (2026) typically rely on the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) Esser et al. (2021) to compress LQ inputs into the latent space for efficient denoising. This irreversible compression discards the subtle textures from LQ inputs, often leading to structural inconsistencies, ghosting artifacts, and ultimately compromised restoration fidelity. To mitigate this issue, prior works try to improve input quality Lin et al. (2024), reduce the VAE compression ratio Yi et al. (2025), or inject LQ features into denoising networks Yang et al. (2024). However, these strategies fail to fundamentally address the information loss introduced by latent space compression, yielding reduced generative capability (e.g., blurry leaves in the top row of Fig. 1) or limited fidelity gains (e.g., distorted characters in the bottom row of Fig. 1). As a result, restoring highly faithful textures while preserving excellent visual quality still remains a significant challenge in Real-ISR.

More recently, pixel-level text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models Yu et al. (2026); Cai et al. (2026) have demonstrated effectiveness in mitigating reconstruction accuracy issues by removing the VAE component. However, roughly fine-tuning pixel-space models to Real-ISR via LoRA adapters still faces two key challenges. First, pixel-space models typically adopt patch-based tokenization, while different tokens only interact within pure MLP-based attention blocks. Unlike VAE-based ones Saharia et al. (2022); Esser et al. (2024), whose convolutional decoders naturally preserve spatial continuity, pixel-space decoding does not explicitly enforce information interaction across patch boundaries. This leads to discontinuities between patches and periodic grid artifacts, particularly in texture-rich regions. As shown in Fig. 2 (a), under the same training strategy, pixel-space models suffer from more severe periodic artifacts than latent models Esser et al. (2024); Labs (2025), degrading the structural consistency across neighboring patches. Second, as depicted in Fig. 2 (b), although removing the VAE eliminates latent compression, it discards the compact semantic representations, making high-level semantic modeling more challenging in pure pixel space. Therefore, this weakens the generative prior and biases models toward deterministic reconstruction rather than plausible detail synthesis. Consequently, models tend to overfit reasonable but over-smoothed structures, while losing their ability to generate missing high-frequency details, especially under severe degradations.

As shown in Fig. 2 (a), under the same training strategy, pixel-space models suffer from more severe periodic artifacts than latent models Esser et al. (2024); Labs (2025), degrading the structural consistency across neighboring patches. Second, as depicted in Fig. 2 (b), although removing the VAE eliminates latent compression, it discards the compact semantic representations, making high-level semantic modeling more challenging in pure pixel space. Therefore, this weakens the generative prior and biases models toward deterministic reconstruction rather than plausible detail synthesis. Consequently, models tend to overfit reasonable but over-smoothed structures, while losing their ability to generate missing high-frequency details, especially under severe degradations.

To address these challenges, we propose HiFiPix, a pixel-space framework for high-fidelity Real-ISR. We first focus on patch-boundary artifacts arising from pixel-space decoding and observe that they mainly manifest as discontinuities in high-frequency structures. This motivates us to exploit coherent high-frequency information for cross-patch continuity. Specifically, we introduce a Cross-Scale Wavelet Discriminator (CSWD) that propagates high-frequency features across scales for boundary-aware image-level supervision, and further propose a Mixup Contrastive Self-Distillation (MixCSD) that leverages an HQ-mixed branch to regularize intermediate representations at feature levels. Together, they provide complementary external and internal supervision to suppress patch-boundary artifacts. Furthermore, we address degradation of generative capability during training. We observe that LoRA updates across layers are not equally necessary: some deep layers merely echo transformations already made by shallower layers, contributing to overfitting pixel-level characteristics rather than preserving high-level semantics. We thus propose Selective LoRA Pruning (LoRA-SP), which detects and prunes such redundant layers via Centered Kernel Alignment-based representational Kornblith et al. (2019), protects fidelity-critical layers from pruning, and progressively freezes rest, thereby constraining fine-tuning capacity precisely where overfitting risks occur.

papers.title: Yang-Mills-Higgs Limits of Reflexive Higgs Sheaves
papers.abstract: For stable Higgs bundles, Hermitian-Einstein metrics can be obtained as limits of the Yang-Mills-Higgs (Y-M-H) flow. We study the algebraic structure of subsequential limits of this flow for reflexive Higgs sheaves over compact K\"ahler manifolds, without assuming stability. We prove that the limiting reflexive Higgs sheaf is isomorphic to the double dual of the graded sheaf associated with the Harder-Narasimhan-Seshadri filtration of the initial sheaf.

papers.title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
papers.abstract: A robot policy needs to understand what a task is asking for in a scene, and how to move the robot to accomplish that task. To achieve these two skills, we introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches a small off-the-shelf vision-language model to control a robot via a simple tool harness. We use a pretrained 27B parameter model to bootstrap world understanding and reasoning, followed by supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks to teach it how to move the robot. Without any real-world robot data during training, ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness and outperforming the MolmoAct2 VLA (33.3%), while running 3x faster and 17x cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. We demonstrate that ZAP also generalizes to completely new objects, goals, strategies, and language by seating a test tube in a rack (and choosing a different hole in the rack when prompted), handing a test tube between arms mid-air, drawing an X on a tic-tac-toe board, and playing chess. These goals and types of manipulation don't appear in our training data. Furthermore, ZAP also transfers to an unseen embodiment. On a single-arm Franka, ZAP reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 percentage points ahead of the leading VLA/WAM baseline.

A robot policy has to do two difficult things at once: it needs semantic reasoning to understand instructions in a potentially unfamiliar scene, and motion control to translate that understanding into precise physical actions.

We introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), which adds motion to a small pretrained vision-language model through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), entirely in simulation. We evaluate how these skills carry over to new tasks, real hardware, and a new embodiment. Existing methods tend to trade off performance in one of these areas for the others, and broadly fall into three groups (Table 1).

We start with Qwen 3.6 27B [10], which contributes world understanding and reasoning. Our contributions are as follows: • Teacher-free training of an agent policy in simulation. We teach a pretrained vision-language model to control a robot with no frontier teacher and no real robot data. The model commands end-effector poses and gripper openings through a harness that is identical in simulation and on hardware. We seed it with successful traces mined from its own rollouts, then refine it with RL using a dense reward ladder that credits partial progress (§3). • Transfer to hardware and new embodiment. The policy handles new objects and goals, follows instructions for manipulation strategies it never practiced, and applies complex reasoning to tasks such as chess and drawing (§5).

papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB: A Hybrid Vision-Language Model for Local AI
papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, a hybrid Mamba-Transformer vision-language model that optimizes speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for local agentic workloads. Derived from the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B-A12B model family, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB combines Star Elastic compression with 2-bit Quantization-Aware Distillation for memory-constrained deployment. The model is optimized for reasoning, agentic tool use, and web & terminal interactions. We also trained a LiLiCorr speculative drafter that is released alongside the model to reach our target inference speed. The resulting model achieves a higher accuracy than leading models with similar memory footprints and speed across many benchmarks for general agentic capabilities (e.g., GDPVal v2), web browsing (e.g., BrowseComp), and terminal use (e.g., Terminal-Bench 2.1), with a relatively high TPS of 84 on RTX Spark that is comparable to models with much lower active parameter counts and more than sufficient for long-horizon agentic applications.

A compelling local agent experience requires a memory-efficient language model that can run alongside other user applications, and optimizes speed and intelligence per GB of memory used.

We present Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, a hybrid mixture-of-experts vision-language model designed for reasoning, multimodal understanding, and local agentic workloads on NVIDIA RTX Spark & DGX Spark. It fits into 24GB of memory and achieves a competitive decoding speed of 84 TPS on RTX Spark, while maximizing intelligence on benchmarks relevant to local agents: general agentic capabilities, web browsing, and terminal use. This is achieved through a combination of model compression, post-training, multimodal adaptation, low-bit quantization, and speculative decoding.

We begin from a Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B A12B model checkpoint and use Star Elastic (Taghibakhshi et al., 2026) to construct a compact backbone for our deployment budget. Guided by the deployment budget plus Knowledge Distillation (KD) signals, a router selects the routed-expert count and MoE intermediate width for each MoE layer, while preserving the hybrid architecture and hidden size to retain compatibility with the parent’s vision head. KD from the parent jointly trains the router and student weights, while a budget loss guides the architecture choices. Once the router converges on a candidate architecture that meets the target budget, we continue KD at short and long contexts to recover the parent’s accuracy.

Evaluation covers text reasoning and coding as well as visual grounding, screen understanding, and browser interaction.

papers.title: Boundary Layer Criterion for the Low Mach Number and Inviscid Limits in Compressible Fluid-Rigid Body Interaction
papers.abstract: We investigate the simultaneous low Mach number and vanishing viscosity limit for a three-dimensional compressible viscous fluid interacting with a freely moving rigid body. The fluid satisfies the compressible Navier-Stokes equations and the no-slip condition on the body surface, while the body evolves according to Newton's laws driven by the fluid stresses. We establish convergence of finite-energy weak solutions to a strong solution of the corresponding incompressible Euler-rigid body system on its interval of existence. Assuming that the initial relative energy tends to zero, convergence holds under a Kato-type condition in a boundary layer whose thickness is proportional to the viscosity. This condition combines vanishing viscous dissipation with a weighted estimate on the fluid momentum relative to the rigid body motion. The proof uses the relative entropy method and a boundary layer corrector adapted to the fluid-rigid body coupling, providing a sufficient condition for convergence in relative energy as the Mach number and viscosity tend to zero simultaneously.

papers.intro:
The simultaneous low Mach number and vanishing viscosity limit connects two distinct descriptions of fluid-rigid body interaction: a rigid body immersed in a compressible viscous fluid and a rigid body moving in an incompressible inviscid fluid. In both systems, the body evolves according to Newton’s laws under the action of the fluid stresses. The fluid equations and the interface conditions, however, change in the limit. The density approaches a constant and the fluid velocity becomes divergence-free, while the viscous no-slip condition gives way to an impermeability condition that allows tangential slip along the body surface. The question is whether solutions of the compressible Navier-Stokes-rigid body system converge to those of the incompressible Euler-rigid body system as the Mach number and viscosity tend to zero.

The simultaneous low Mach number and vanishing viscosity limit connects two distinct descriptions of fluid-rigid body interaction: a rigid body immersed in a compressible viscous fluid and a rigid body moving in an incompressible inviscid fluid. In both systems, the body evolves according to Newton’s laws under the action of the fluid stresses. The fluid equations and the interface conditions, however, change in the limit. The density approaches a constant and the fluid velocity becomes divergence-free, while the viscous no-slip condition gives way to an impermeability condition that allows tangential slip along the body surface. The question is whether solutions of the compressible Navier-Stokes-rigid body system converge to those of the incompressible Euler-rigid body system as the Mach number and viscosity tend to zero.

This passage involves two singular mechanisms. The low Mach number limit introduces the incompressibility constraint and may generate rapid acoustic oscillations, whereas the vanishing viscosity limit is sensitive to boundary layers associated with the mismatch of tangential boundary conditions. For fluids in fixed domains, these mechanisms have been studied extensively [27, 28, 24, 14, 38, 23]. In the presence of a freely moving rigid body, the boundary motion is itself an unknown, coupled to the fluid through the balance of linear and angular momentum. Establishing the limit therefore requires controlling the fluid and body motions together, including the behaviour of the fluid relative to the body in a thin neighbourhood of its surface.

The motion of rigid bodies in incompressible viscous fluids has been extensively studied. Previous contributions to the existence theory of weak solutions include [4, 5, 19, 21, 35, 6, 31]. Global weak formulations accommodating possible collisions between bodies or contact with the boundary were subsequently developed in [16, 33, 3].

The motion of rigid bodies in incompressible viscous fluids has been extensively studied. Previous contributions to the existence theory of weak solutions include [4, 5, 19, 21, 35, 6, 31]. Global weak formulations accommodating possible collisions between bodies or contact with the boundary were subsequently developed in [16, 33, 3].

For compressible viscous fluids, Boulakia and Guerrero [2] established the existence and uniqueness of strong solutions in an L2L^{2}-based Sobolev framework for small initial data, as long as no collision occurs. Hieber and Murata [20] proved local well-posedness in an LpL^{p} framework using maximal regularity methods based on ℛ\mathcal{R}-boundedness. In a related stabilization problem, Roy and Takahashi [32] obtained global strong solutions for small initial data and asymptotic stabilization of a rigid ball under a feedback force acting on the body.

For weak solutions, existence under no-slip boundary conditions was established up to collision in [6], without a smallness assumption on the initial data. Feireisl [15] subsequently constructed global weak solutions in a formulation that accommodates possible collisions. Weak–strong uniqueness for the compressible fluid–rigid body system was proved by Kreml, Nečasová and Piasecki [26], using relative energy estimates and a change of variables to compare solutions on different fluid domains. Further existence results address Navier-slip boundary conditions [29] and general inflow–outflow conditions on the outer boundary [1].

The analysis of the low Mach number limit includes the foundational work of Klainerman and Majda [24]. For viscous compressible flows, Desjardins and Grenier [8] studied the limit in the whole space, while Desjardins, Grenier, Lions and Masmoudi [7] treated bounded domains with Dirichlet boundary conditions. Broader accounts of incompressible limits and the methods used to study them can be found in [18, 34, 28, 13].

Related results are available for exterior flows with prescribed body motion. Kračmar, Nečasová and Novotný [25] proved the existence of weak solutions for a compressible viscous fluid around a rotating obstacle. Eiter, Nečasová and Oschmann [9] established weak-strong uniqueness and justified the low Mach number limit for exterior flows around a body undergoing prescribed rigid motion. In the latter result, the viscosity remains positive and the limiting equations are the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations.

The simultaneous incompressible and inviscid limit has been investigated in several fluid models. Masmoudi [27] established convergence from the isentropic compressible Navier–Stokes system to the incompressible Euler equations as the Mach number and viscosity tend to zero. For heat-conducting fluids, Feireisl and Novotný [14] studied the full Navier–Stokes–Fourier system in a regime of small Mach number and large Reynolds and Péclet numbers, identifying the Euler–Boussinesq system as the limit. Inviscid incompressible limits on expanding domains were considered by Feireisl, Nečasová and Sun [11].

For the vanishing viscosity limit in the presence of a fixed no-slip boundary, Kato [23] identified the decisive role of dissipation near the boundary. Assuming convergence of the initial data and the existence of a smooth incompressible Euler solution, convergence in the energy norm is equivalent to the vanishing of viscous dissipation in a boundary layer whose thickness is proportional to the viscosity. Sueur [36] extended this criterion to an incompressible fluid coupled to a freely moving rigid body, obtaining convergence of both the fluid and body velocities. For compressible fluids in a fixed bounded domain, Sueur [37] established a sufficient condition for the inviscid limit under no-slip boundary conditions, using the relative energy framework developed in [12, 10]. These results provide the boundary layer and relative energy methods on which the present analysis builds.

papers.title: Explicit strong blocking sets and minimal codes from expander graphs using a new graph parameter
papers.abstract: A strong blocking set is a set of points in a finite projective space that intersects every hyperplane of the space in a spanning set of the hyperplane. These objects have been studied both in finite geometry and coding theory due to their equivalence with minimal codes. We give an explicit construction of strong blocking sets using expander graphs that improves the explicit construction of Alon et al. (Noga Alon, Anurag Bishnoi, Shagnik Das, Alessandro Neri, Strong blocking sets and minimal codes from expander graphs. Transactions of the American Mathematical Society ) by introducing a new geometrically motivated graph parameter that is better suited for this problem. Using this approach, we improve the constant $C$ in the explicit construction of a strong blocking set of size $C (q+1) k$ in the $(k - 1)$-dimensional projective space over $\mathbb{F}_q$ for every prime power $q \geq 7$.

papers.title: Evolution of microstructure and crystallographic texture in a novel Zr-4Nb-2Al alloy during hot rotary swaging
papers.abstract: A multi-step induction-assisted hot rotary swaging route was developed for the novel dual-phase Zr-4Nb-2Al alloy to investigate the evolution of microstructure, crystallographic texture, and mechanical properties during sequential deformation. Phase-transformation temperatures determined by electrical resistivity measurements were used to select processing conditions in the single-phase $\beta$ field at 880{\deg}C and the $\alpha+\beta$ field at 780{\deg}C. Induction heating with thermographic temperature control enabled reduction of the initial 12 mm rod to 6.3 mm, corresponding to a total area reduction of 72%. Swaging in the $\beta$ field refined millimetre-sized prior-$\beta$ grains to approximately 100 $\mu$m, while subsequent cooling produced a fine lamellar $\alpha+\beta$ microstructure. Further deformation in the $\alpha+\beta$ field disrupted the lamellar structure, promoted globularisation and recrystallisation of the $\alpha$ phase, and refined the $\beta$ phase. The microstructural evolution was accompanied by a pronounced $\langle 11\bar{2}0\rangle_{\alpha}\parallel\mathrm{SD}$ fibre texture in the $\alpha$ phase, whereas the $\beta$ phase exhibited predominantly $\langle 110\rangle_{\beta}\parallel\mathrm{SD}$ together with a $\langle 111\rangle_{\beta}\parallel\mathrm{SD}$ component. The phase constitution remained comparatively stable, with approximately 12-15 wt.% retained $\beta$ throughout processing. Subsequent $\alpha+\beta$ swaging decreased the compressive yield strength from 1103 to 839 MPa while increasing plastic deformability, with a maximum fracture strain of 32%. Radial hardness heterogeneity was progressively eliminated. These results demonstrate that induction-assisted rotary swaging in selected phase fields provides an effective route for tailoring microstructure, texture, and mechanical response in dual-phase zirconium alloys.

papers.title: Remarks on covariant differential calculus on the non-standard quantum Podle\'s sphere
papers.abstract: An $SU_q(2)$-covariant first-order differential calculus on the non-standard quantum Podle\'s two-sphere is constructed. The module of one-forms is explicitly given in terms of modules of sections of charge $\pm 2$ line bundles associated to the quantum Hopf fibration.

papers.title: Solving Large SDPs from Flag Algebra Problems
papers.abstract:
The flag algebra method is a general tool in extremal combinatorics, which has been useful in tackling open problems concerning graphs, hypergraphs, permutations, point sets, and other structures. The method establishes combinatorial inequalities via sums of squares, which are usually obtained by a semidefinite relaxation of the original combinatorial problem.
  A typical application of the method in graph theory starts with fixing a parameter $n$ followed by constructing a semidefinite program based on the (subgraph) structure of all $n$-vertex graphs. In the standard formulation before symmetry reductions, there is a coefficient constraint for every admissible $n$-vertex graph up to isomorphism. For 3-uniform hypergraphs, there are 2,136 of them on 6 vertices and 7,013,320 on 7 vertices. While solving the resulting program for $n=6$ is an easy task on any modern computer, the programs for $n = 7$ seems out of reach, mainly because the SDP solvers need too much RAM. Yet solving such programs for as large $n$ as possible is desirable because they typically yield better bounds for the original combinatorial problems.
  We bypass the aforementioned memory requirements by linear programming with cutting planes. Although we do not guarantee that this cutting-plane procedure reaches an optimum in finitely many iterations, in many flag algebra instances it uses much less memory and yields improved bounds for well-known hypergraph Tur\'an problems.
  We use this method to obtain numerical bounds for Tur\'an densities and codegree squared densities of several 3-uniform hypergraphs including the tetrahedron, where we obtained the upper bound 0.55753 and tetrahedron without one edge with a new upper bound 0.2865. It also allows to tackle bounds on Tur\'an densities of 7-vertex 3-graphs using flag algebras, which was not possible before.

papers.title: Shaping of invariant measures of iterated function systems
papers.abstract: We study an inverse problem for iterated function systems: given maps $w_1,\dots,w_m$ on a Polish space and a target probability measure $\nu$, choose the law $\mu$ with which the maps are sampled so that the invariant measure $\pi_\mu$ of the resulting Markov chain is as close as possible to $\nu$ in the Wasserstein-1 distance. The minimization runs over the admissible set $A$ of sampling laws for which the chain has a unique invariant measure attracting every initial law; the maps need not be contractions. On bounded state spaces, regions certified by a Doeblin or splitting condition are convex unions of relatively open faces of the simplex, and they exhaust $A$ when the state space is finite; for affine systems with nonnegative matrices $A$ is a spectral sublevel set; in general $A$ is neither open, closed, convex nor connected. Existence of an optimal law reduces to the invariant measures left behind at the missing boundary $\mathrm{cl}(A)\setminus A$: boundary points without invariant measures of finite first moment repel minimizing sequences, which yields existence for all systems of homotheties of $\mathbb R^d$, and for compact state spaces a solution exists for every target if and only if the set of reachable invariant measures is closed; a two-state example shows that existence can fail. A search over a $\delta$-net returns an $\epsilon$-optimal law over any region on which $\mu\mapsto\pi_\mu$ is Lipschitz and the chains are uniformly attracting, with explicit constants and, on an interval, an explicit sample size. Under contraction on average, $\mu\mapsto\pi_\mu$ is differentiable, its derivative is injective if and only if the push-forwards $(w_i)_\#\pi_\mu$ are linearly independent, and the objective is weakly convex, so that a projected subgradient method with inexact subgradients converges to near-stationary points.

papers.title: Optimization of the second Robin eigenvalue on a planar exterior domain under fixed area constraint
papers.abstract: We consider the Robin Laplacian on a planar exterior domain with a negative boundary parameter. For a negative boundary parameter of a sufficiently large absolute value this operator has at least two negative eigenvalues below the bottom of the essential spectrum. We prove that under a fixed area constraint and convexity assumption on the bounded complement of the exterior domain the second Robin eigenvalue is maximized by the exterior of the disk. The inequality is strict for every exterior of a non-circular domain whenever the comparison disk has a negative second eigenvalue. The proof modifies the parallel-coordinate method by allowing the angular phase of a trial function to vary with the distance from the boundary. This result resolves the first item in a 2024 conjecture by the authors under an additional convexity assumption. Relaxing the convexity and the perimeter constraint remain open problems.

papers.title: The Evolution and Current State of Swift-Heavy-Ion Track Modeling
papers.abstract: This paper briefly reviews the modeling approaches to the swift heavy ion (SHI) track formation. It presents a step-by-step derivation of the two-temperature model, highlighting its underlying assumptions and approximations. Special attention is given to identifying assumptions that fail under the typical SHI track conditions, and what methods currently exist to go beyond them. As an alternative to analytical approximations, a combined Monte Carlo- molecular dynamics model is demonstrated, outlining its basic assumptions, their justifications, and validations. Finally, the paper addresses bottlenecks of the current multiscale approach, its remaining weaknesses, and necessary further developments of the theory and models.

papers.title: Proof of the Harary--Hill conjecture: an exposition
papers.abstract: The Harary--Hill conjecture states that the crossing number of the complete graph $K_n$ is exactly $\frac{1}{4}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor \left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\right\rfloor \left\lfloor\frac{n-2}{2}\right\rfloor \left\lfloor\frac{n-3}{2}\right\rfloor$. We present a streamlined variant of the proof of this conjecture recently announced by OpenAI (2026). Although the original proof is relatively short, it is quite difficult to follow. We simplify several steps and provide a concise and accessible exposition of the proof. We also combine this new result with known reductions to determine the crossing numbers of several other graph families.

papers.title: EP251129a: A Fast X-ray Transient with Two X-Ray Plateaus and Its Off-axis Afterglow
papers.abstract: Extragalactic fast X-ray transients (EFXTs) detected by the Einstein Probe are extending the parameter space of relativistic stellar explosions toward softer and longer-lived transients. Here we report EP251129a/GRB 251129A at z=0.505, which exhibits two X-ray plateaus: an early plateau lasting $\sim 10^{4}\,\rm s$ followed by a rapid decay with spectral softening, and a second plateau extending to 60 days, placing it at the extreme long-duration end of Gamma Ray Burst (GRB) plateaus. The early optical emission evolves independently of the X-ray, indicating a different origin; whereas the unusual radio afterglow shows a rapid rise of $F_\nu\propto t^{1.9-2.5}$ and a delayed peak at $\sim36-40$ days, providing strong evidence for an off-axis geometry. We find that the early X-ray behavior resembles those of ultra-long GRBs (ULGRBs) and can be naturally explained by the internal dissipation from a newborn millisecond magnetar undergoing gravitational-wave-dominated spin-down before collapsing into a black hole. The early optical, radio and late X-ray emission are well described by an off-axis two-component jet afterglow with additional energy injection, possibly powered by fallback accretion onto black hole. EP251129a therefore connects the emerging EFXT population with ULGRB-like central-engine activity and off-axis afterglow, offering a rare opportunity to probe both the evolution of central engine and jet structure in a single event.

papers.title: Convex orders in root systems and quantum tangent spaces
papers.abstract: We classify the reduced decompositions of the longest element $w_0$ of the Weyl group of a semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ for which the corresponding Lusztig quantum root vectors span a quantum tangent space in $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$. We introduce a combinatorial condition on the convex order induced by a reduced decomposition, tangency, and prove that a reduced decomposition gives rise to a quantum tangent space if and only if it is tangent. The proof relies on a description of the coproduct of quantum root vectors in terms of the convex order, and on a projection in the right weak order attached to each positive root. Up to commutation, tangent reduced decompositions are obtained by concatenating the longest minimal coset representatives along a chain of cominuscule parabolic quotients; in particular there are none in types $E_8$, $F_4$ and $G_2$.

papers.title: Structure-preserving discretisations for the quasi-incompressible, thermal Maxwell-Stefan equations
papers.abstract: We study a thermal Maxwell-Stefan-Navier-Stokes system modelling miscible mixtures under a quasi-incompressibility constraint. The system consists of the conservation laws for mass and momentum, and the balance law for entropy, which is preferred over the balance law for energy because it facilitates the development of two structure-preserving discretisation methods. The first method applies a semi-implicit Euler scheme in time, together with suitable finite elements in space, which guarantees generation of entropy and enforces the quasi-incompressibility constraint pointwise, but numerically dissipates total energy. The second method employs a continuous Petrov-Galerkin discretisation in time, which also generates entropy and satisfies the constraint pointwise, and in addition conserves the total energy and allows high-order time approximations. The structure-preserving properties and behaviour of both numerical methods are demonstrated by a series of numerical experiments.

papers.title: ImgMT: Wikipedia-based Dataset For Evaluating Text-in-Image Translation
papers.abstract:
Text-in-image translation aims to translate all textual content embedded in an image. In Text Image Translation (TIT), the output is translated text; In-Image Machine Translation (IIMT) additionally renders the translation back into the image. We introduce ImgMT, a massively multilingual dataset and benchmark mined from localized SVG illustrations on Wikimedia Commons, focusing on diagrams, maps, and infographics. ImgMT contains 35,612 aligned image pairs grouped into 1,855 image sets, spanning 129 languages, 20+ writing systems, and 4,886 language pairs.
  We propose a multi-level evaluation protocol that measures source-side text-region detection and OCR accuracy alongside target-side translation quality. We benchmark several multimodal large language models and a dedicated TIT system in English->X and X->English settings, and find that the source language and writing system substantially affect TIT quality. Finally, we show that ImgMT is not well suited for isolating the contribution of visual information in multimodal translation.

papers.title: A framework for trackable and modular rounding error analysis
papers.abstract: Robust and meaningful rounding error analysis is becoming increasingly challenging as modern numerical computations involve a rapidly evolving variety of arithmetic formats, precisions, and computational kernels. We propose a trackable and modular framework for rounding error analysis, together with a new notation for bounding accumulated rounding errors. The analysis is trackable in the sense that the origin and propagation of individual error terms remain explicit in the final result, and modular in the sense that local error bounds can be replaced according to the arithmetic, precision, or computational kernel without repeating the structural analysis. We also introduce the notation $\gamma_n=(1-{\bm u})^{-n}-1$, which provides an alternative to the classical $\gamma_n^{\mathrm h}=n{\bm u}/(1-n{\bm u})$ notation. A key feature is that our notation does not require the restriction $n{\bm u}<1$ and conveniently handles errors arising from division. Using block LU factorization as a representative example, we show that the framework distinguishes the error sources of different algorithmic variants and permits improved kernels, such as compensated summation and accurate matrix multiplication, to be incorporated directly into the resulting error bounds.

papers.title: Formation of international environmental agreements and payoff allocation
papers.abstract: Dealing with climate change requires that all countries engage in costly efforts to reduce their emissions. Reaching this objective has so far been elusive because it is in the best interest of each country to let the others do the effort and benefit itself from a better environment. The presence of negative externalities and strategic behavior have made game theory a natural paradigm to design an international environmental agreement (IEA) that codifies what countries should do. Considering that countries are sovereign and no supranational entity can impose an agreement, a stream of literature adopted a noncooperative mode of play to the formation of an environmental coalition. On the other hand, as joint optimization of all countries' payoff leads to the best outcome, cooperative games approach has also been proposed to share the cost of climate change. Both approaches have their pros and cons.

authors.name: Agnieszka Rusinowska
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Pentagon Equation in Deformation Quantization of Character Varieties
papers.abstract: Deformation quantizations of the moduli space of framed flat bundles live naturally in the Drinfeld category. Such quantizations were constructed using the so-called quantum fusion by Li-Bland and \v{S}evera. We give a complete characterization of the dependence of this quantization on combinatorial choices, and prove that these quantizations are all isomorphic, forming vertices of an explicitly constructed complete commuting graph of algebra isomorphism. To this end, we extend the Kontsevich integral methods of Le and Murakami from even associators to all associators. Finally, we also prove that bi-invariant Haar measures provide traces on these quantizations.

papers.title: Debate, Not Voting: Agentic Arbitration over Weak Optical Chemical Structure Recognition Models
papers.abstract: Optical chemical structure recognition (OCSR) turns a picture of a molecule into a machine-readable string, and it stands between decades of printed chemistry and any computational use. On real documents individual models remain unreliable. Over a 1000-molecule sample of MolParser, three readers score $46.0\%$, $43.4\%$ and $42.4\%$ exact match, yet at least one of them is right on $60.8\%$ of molecules. That gap is an ensembling problem, but not one voting can solve, because the readers seldom agree and seldom err together. We place the readers inside a multi-agent scaffold. Four language-model agents with cheminformatics tools argue about a candidate structure, write findings to an append-only knowledge base, and are held to render-and-compare gates that admit a correction only when it is demonstrably better. The debate reaches $61.9\%$, beating the best single reader by $15.9$ points and plurality voting by $9.2$ points ($p<10^{-9}$ for both, robust to correction for all $27$ tests we report), and is indistinguishable from the any-reader-right ceiling. That aggregate hides two opposing effects. On the $661$ molecules with no stereochemistry the debate is $3.9$ points above the ceiling ($p=0.004$), constructing structures no reader proposed, while on the $339$ stereochemical ones it falls below. We then swap the arbitrating model. A stronger arbitrator adds $2.2$ points (nominal $p=0.039$; neither this nor the $+3.9$ survives Bonferroni correction over all $27$ tests, so both are suggestive), and its mechanism is visible: it opens a correction on $423$ of $1000$ molecules against $120$, and an interaction test indicates it depends less on the readers (nominal $p=0.018$, not correction-robust). We conclude that the useful unit of progress is the arbitration policy rather than the reader, and that OCSR accuracy is better read against the union oracle than against the best single model.
papers.intro:
Most of what chemistry knows is drawn, not tabulated. Patents, journal articles and internal reports depict molecules as line drawings. To use any of it computationally you first need the structure as a string, usually SMILES (Weininger, 1988), and that string has to be recovered from the pixels. The task is called optical chemical structure recognition (OCSR), and deep learning has improved it a great deal (Qian et al., 2023; Rajan et al., 2021; Morin et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026). The improvement is uneven, though. On clean synthetic depictions the current readers are strong. On the drawing styles, wildcards and stereochemical annotations of real documents they are not.

papers.title: Partial Information Decomposition When Some Sources Are Known: A Source Chain Rule and a No-Go Theorem
papers.abstract: Partial information decomposition (PID) splits the information that several sources carry about a target into atoms, distinguished by which collections of sources give access to them. We ask how such a decomposition should behave when some of the sources are already known. The access structure of the atoms suggests one answer: discard the atoms that the known sources provide and regroup the rest according to which further sources unlock them. The classical construction of conditional information suggests another: recompute the decomposition under the conditional distributions and average. We show that the two answers agree, atom by atom, exactly when redundant information obeys a source chain rule, an analogue of the chain rule of mutual information: when the same sources are added to several collections, the enlarged collections share everything the added sources provide and, beyond that, exactly what the original collections share once the added sources are known. The rule divides established measures of redundant information, so that adopting or rejecting it genuinely narrows the choice of measure. Our main result is a no-go theorem: for three or more sources, the source chain rule and local positivity, the requirement that all atoms be nonnegative, cannot hold together in any PID.

papers.title: AllBRICQS: the All-sky BRIght, Complete Quasar Survey - Quasar Selection and Final Southern $G_{\rm RP}<16$ Sample
papers.abstract: We describe the final quasar sample from the Southern part of the All-sky BRIght, Complete Quasar Survey (AllBRICQS), which aimed to discover the remaining optically bright quasars using data from Gaia and WISE. We discuss our final selection and present a further 119 quasars in the redshift range $z=[0.03;4.35]$. This brings the sample of spectroscopically confirmed quasars with $G_{\rm RP}<16$ and $z>0.1$ at Dec$<+20^{\circ}$ and Galactic latitude $|b|>10^{\circ}$ to 745 objects. The spectra from the ANU 2.3m telescope at Siding Spring Observatory cover a wavelength range from 360 to 950 nm with $R\sim3000$. For redshifts of $z>0.12$, we expect the sample to be complete at $G_{\rm RP}<16$, a regime that is usually avoided by large spectroscopic surveys due to detector saturation. We note that at least one strongly lensed quasar has escaped our selection.

authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: ComBeautify: Leveraging Code Change Summaries for Conventional Commit Generation
papers.abstract:
Modern software development relies on version control systems such as Git to track changes and facilitate collaboration. While commit messages are crucial for conveying developer intent, they do not affect program functionality; as a result, developers often lack motivation to write meaningful ones. The Conventional Commits Specification (CCS) addresses this with a structured format and guidelines that help developers express the intent of a change, improving clarity and enabling automation. Yet, developers frequently struggle to express intent while adhering to the format. In particular, they may misclassify commits due to the large number of possible categories or the lack of project-specific guidance. We introduce ComBeautify, an approach that automatically generates CCS-compliant commit messages. Our hybrid approach leverages context-preserving summarization of Git diffs with large language models (LLMs) to improve commit classification accuracy under CCS. Rather than relying on manually curated category definitions, we learn them from historical commits. We also propose a method for automatically generating the CCS description component.
  Our empirical evaluation across 13 languages, 6,500 open-source repositories, and over 20 million commits provides long-term insights into CCS adoption, revealing increasing compliance. Our evaluation on twenty popular repositories reveals the limitations of approaches guided by generic category definitions, and shows that ComBeautify, when trained on project-specific data, outperforms baselines by up to 3x. Additionally, using a dataset of 2,000 manually curated commits, we validate our summarization approach, achieving up to 95.25% accuracy and surpassing baselines. These findings emphasize the need for adaptable, context-aware AI methods for commit classification and CCS-compliant commit message generation.

papers.title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
papers.abstract: Visual search is ubiquitous in daily life, from locating keys in a messy apartment to finding a tool in a cluttered workshop or an application icon on a desktop screen. While visual attention is to a large extent driven by image content, research in psychology indicates that user cognitive states have a significant influence on attention allocation. A promising way to access information about cognitive states is via Electroencephalography (EEG) recordings. Despite this potential, previous works in computational attention modeling have largely disregarded EEG, and related studies in psychology operate with abstract, simplistic stimuli, or even artificially guided search procedures. We bridge this gap with two contributions. First, we present EEGaze 140, the largest publicly available multimodal dataset of free visual search with realistic stimuli. The dataset contains synchronized EEG and eye tracking recordings from 36 participants across 140 naturalistic scenes, covering two scenarios: searching for desktop icons and finding tools in cluttered workshop scenes. Second, we introduce EEGazeNet, the first method for human attention prediction in visual search that integrates EEG signals. Our approach consists of a EEG guided refinement stage that adapts the output of a state of the art saliency prediction method to the user current cognitive state. In comprehensive evaluations on EEGaze 140, we show that EEGazeNet consistently outperforms all baselines and ablation conditions.

papers.title: Exploring the UV Fe III Emission along the Quasar Main Sequence
papers.abstract: The diversity of Type I AGNs can be organized along the Quasar Main Sequence (MS), a powerful framework primarily driven by the accretion rate and defined in the optical plane by the FWHM of $\mathrm{H\beta}$ and the Fe II strength ($R_{\rm FeII}$). Previous studies suggested that the UV Fe III evolves along this MS. However, a systematic analysis is still missing. We aim to characterize the UV Fe III emission across the MS, assess its potential as a tracer, and investigate how its properties depend on the conditions of the emitting gas. We analyzed the UV iron emission in 69 low-$z$ $(z \lesssim 1)$ AGNs observed with the Hubble Space Telescope. We fitted the 1700-2200 Angstrom range and investigated the main correlations using principal component analysis. We complemented with $\tt{CLOUDY}$ photoionization simulations to explore the dependence of the iron emission on gas density, ionization parameter, metallicity, microturbulence, column density, and spectral energy distribution. We find a positive correlation between the strengths of the UV iron emission and the optical $\mathrm{R_{FeII}}$ parameter. With this, we define a UV MS diagram using the FWHM of $\mathrm{Al III\,\lambda1860}$ and the equivalent width of $\mathrm{Fe III}$ + $\mathrm{Fe II}$. $\tt{CLOUDY}$ simulations support this result, predicting stronger Fe III emission at high $\mathrm{R_{FeII}}$. Additionally, we found object-to-object variations in the $\mathrm{Fe III}$ multiplets. Our results indicate that UV Fe III emission and $\mathrm{Al III}\,\lambda 1860$ can serve as proxies for optical Fe II and $\mathrm{H\beta}$, extending the Quasar MS into the UV domain. The variations in the Fe III multiplets demonstrate that a single template may not represent all quasars. Thus, characterizing the Fe III emission and its dependence on physical conditions is essential for improving the modeling of UV AGN spectra.

papers.title: SPAM: Survey Overview and JWST/NIRCam Multi-Band Photometry Catalog
papers.abstract: We present the Star-formation from Photometry through the Addition of Medium-bands (SPAM) survey, a 62.9 hr JWST/NIRCam imaging program to add ten new filters, nine medium-band filters, and one broad-band filter to the CEERS legacy dataset. We describe the observation strategy, present the data, and detail the data-reduction process. We include a complete reduction of imaging in the legacy CEERS footprint, inclusive of all publicly available photometric parallel and GO observations within the legacy CEERS footprint. We present a multi-band photometric and photometric redshift catalog which includes all medium- and broad-band filters available on NIRCam. We find that adding medium bands from the SPAM and MINERVA programs improves photometric redshifts. We discuss how these data advance the SPAM survey's key science goals: better-constrained photometric redshifts, identification of high-redshift overdensity members, improved recovery of emission-line strengths, and more accurate star formation histories.

authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.title: Information-thermodynamic principles unveil the response of complex networks to perturbations
papers.abstract: Understanding how complex networks respond to perturbations is key to uncovering their functional organization. We show that, for a maximum-entropy perturbation prior, standard diffusion cannot increase response entropy, a measure of the diversity of the system's response. To overcome this limitation, we develop a density-matrix-based information thermodynamics of perturbation responses along arbitrary dynamical trajectories. We show that this framework is grounded in an information-theoretic principle of least dissipation and introduces a generalized free energy that quantifies deviations from an instantaneous diffusive reference. We then illustrate the formalism using nonlinear complex networks, revealing regimes of enhanced response diversity that cannot be captured by standard diffusive descriptions.

authors.name: Manlio De Domenico
authors.institution: Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Padova

papers.title: On the Discernibility of Topology Changes in Networked LTI Systems
papers.abstract: This article investigates the discernibility of topology changes in networked linear time-invariant systems, with particular focus on edge disconnection. We introduce a new notion of discernibility motivated by a limitation of the definition commonly adopted in the literature. In consensus networks, topology changes are inherently indiscernible for all initial conditions belonging to the synchronization subspace. To overcome this issue, we first introduce the notion of dynamical discernibility of a topology change for elementary consensus networks. This notion explicitly disregards the intrinsic indiscernibility associated with states in the consensus subspace. We characterize this property for directed communication graphs and then specialize the resulting conditions to topology changes arising from either the disconnection of an edge or a variation in its weight. We then extend the analysis to networks of homogeneous agents by introducing discernibility modulo synchronization, which factors out the unavoidable indiscernibility associated with synchronized trajectories. We derive a general characterization showing how discernibility depends jointly on the topology change and on the dynamics of the individual agents. Finally, we specialize the analysis to undirected communication graphs and show that, under mild additional assumptions, discernibility modulo synchronization is equivalent to the dynamical discernibility of the corresponding topology change. This establishes a direct connection between the two notions and extends existing results on the discernibility of topology variations in dynamical networks. The resulting characterizations are then further specialized to the case of edge disconnection.

papers.title: Does Notation Matter? MusicXML Tokenisation for Symbolic Music Generation and Understanding
papers.abstract: Symbolic music representations encode musical content at varying levels of completeness, from performance-oriented formats such as MIDI to fully notated scores such as MusicXML. Yet the impact of this representational richness on deep learning models remains poorly understood. While tokenisation has been extensively studied for MIDI, score-based formats have received considerably less attention, and MusicXML in particular remains largely unexplored despite being the de-facto standard for score interchange. In this paper, we introduce the first general-purpose tokenisation framework for MusicXML, and conduct a systematic empirical study to determine whether notational richness confers a measurable advantage for deep learning on symbolic music. We train 26 autoregressive and masked language models, comparing MusicXML tokenisation against MIDI and ABC-based representations, probing the effect of different tokenisation strategies within MusicXML, and testing whether music-grammar-aware tokenisation outperforms treating scores as plain text. We evaluate music understanding tasks using linear probing across composer classification, difficulty estimation, and accompaniment suggestion, and generative tasks using objective statistical metrics and a human pairwise preference study. Our results show that MusicXML-tokenised models outperform MIDI and text-based counterparts on understanding and generative tasks.

papers.title: Homological and homotopical epimorphisms in monoidal $\infty$-categories
papers.abstract: We compare homological and homotopical epimorphisms of associative algebras in monoidal $\infty$-categories. Assume that geometric realizations and pushouts of associative algebras exist and that tensoring preserves geometric realizations. Then every homological epimorphism is homotopical. If, in addition, the ambient category is additive and tensoring preserves finite coproducts, the converse holds. This extends the result of Chuang and Lazarev for dg-algebras. In the symmetric monoidal setting, we discuss consequences for centers and commutative refinements, as well as applications to derived analytic geometry.

papers.title: Photometric Redshift Estimation with Hybrid Quantum Neural Network
papers.abstract: A Hybrid Quantum Neural Network (HQNN) is applied to recover the photometric redshift of a galaxy dataset built using data from two astronomical surveys, the Kilo-Degree Survey (KIDS) and the VISTA Kilo-Degree Infrared Galaxy (VIKING), which provide data with coverage from the optical to the near-infrared electromagnetic spectrum. The results are then compared with those obtained by a classical neural network. We see that HQNN consistently recovers the reference photometric redshift with a high statistical fidelity. Furthermore, both the $R^2$ and the MSE found by the HQNN are consistently better than those found by the classical counterpart (albeit consistent in the error range), proving the worth of further investigating these novel technologies for this particular astrophysical application.
