papers.title: Gold nanorods targeting tumor vasculature: Monte Carlo evaluation of the radioenhancement effects
papers.abstract: Gold nanoparticles targeted to tumor vasculature can raise the dose to endothelial cells, and the enhancement depends on their position relative to the vessel wall. Despite growing interest in endothelial radiosensitization, intravascular and immediate perivascular dose enhancement has not been resolved at the level of individual endothelial cells for different nanoparticle locations. Earlier vascular dosimetry scored thin wall layers, analytic endothelial slabs, or tissue-region averages. This study quantifies the dose enhancement ratio (DER) of gold nanorods (AuNRs) in individual endothelial cells and in the perivascular region for three AuNR locations. Track-structure Monte Carlo simulations in TOPAS modeled a 10 um long, 16 um diameter microvessel segmented into six endothelial cells. AuNRs were placed homogeneously in the lumen, on the inner vessel wall (vascular-targeted), or on the outer vessel wall (extravasated) at concentrations of 5 to 50 mg Au/g water within the vessel volume under 50 and 100 kVp X-rays. All DERs were corrected for the lack of charged-particle equilibrium (CPE) inherent to microscale simulations. Inner wall-attached AuNRs produced the highest microvessel-averaged DERs, reaching approximately 3.8 at 50 mg Au/g water and approximately 1.96 at 18 mg Au/g water under 50 kVp. The DER increased linearly with AuNR concentration and was higher at 50 kVp than at 100 kVp. Including AuNRs outside the simulated segment (infinite vessel approximation) increased endothelial DERs by 5 to 10 percent. In the perivascular region, the DER was highest within the first 10 um, where outer wall-attached AuNRs gave the highest values. The results establish a physical dose enhancement basis for endothelial and perivascular cells and can guide the design of vascular-targeted radiosensitization.

papers.title: Higher-harmonic spin-wave excitation by a superconducting antenna with vortices
papers.abstract: The interaction between superconductivity and magnetism provides new routes for controlling nonlinear excitations in hybrid systems. While dc-driven Abrikosov vortices (fluxons) are known to interact with spin waves, the ability of confined, nearly harmonic vortex oscillations to generate higher-frequency spin-wave modes remains unexplored. Here, by combining time-dependent Ginzburg--Landau modeling with spectral analysis of the microwave near field, we demonstrate higher-harmonic spin-wave excitation driven by a superconducting microstrip antenna in the Shubnikov phase. Unlike conventional harmonic-generation mechanisms associated with nonlinear magnetization dynamics, the magnetic layer remains a linear receiver, whereas the superconducting antenna generates the nonlinear microwave field. We show that nearly sinusoidal vortex motion and the accompanying redistribution of superconducting screening currents produce higher harmonics that couple to spin-wave modes. This response arises from spatial-to-temporal transduction, whereby harmonic vortex motion and the associated redistribution of screening currents convert a spatially nonuniform magnetic-field profile into higher temporal harmonics. Magnetic flux quanta thus act as active nonlinear elements for frequency conversion, extending the accessible spin-wave frequency range in superconducting--magnonic hybrids.

papers.title: Graph-Convolutional Reinforcement Learning for Finite-Time Stabilization of a Chaotic Chua Circuit via Unified Flexible Terminal Sliding-Mode Control
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a graph convolutional reinforcement learning framework for the finite-time stabilization of chaotic dynamics in a physical Chua circuit. The circuit is modeled directly in terms of capacitor voltages, inductor current, and physical component parameters. This preserves the connection between the mathematical model and the underlying electrical system. A unified, flexible terminal sliding-mode controller is developed to achieve stabilization within a finite time in the presence of uncertainties in the lumped model, external disturbances, and bounded control inputs. The controller incorporates state-dependent nonlinear exponents to provide flexible convergence characteristics while avoiding singular terms near equilibrium. To minimize dependence on manual controller tuning, the admissible controller parameters are optimized using an actor-critic reinforcement learning scheme with a graph convolutional network that leverages the circuit dynamics' coupling structure. The learned parameters are constrained to the ranges required by the theoretical stability conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate the rapid suppression of chaotic oscillations and the finite-time convergence of the state and sliding variables while respecting the prescribed input-saturation limits. Compared to a reference control method, the proposed approach reduces the IAE, ISE, ITAE, and ITSE by 56.27\,\%, 56.40\,\%, 61.69\,\%, and 64.70\,\%, respectively. These results suggest that graph-based reinforcement learning can effectively tune parameters while retaining the robustness and analytical structure of the underlying sliding-mode controller.

papers.title: Singular Atiyah Configurations
papers.abstract: We construct arbitrarily large configurations of distinct points in Euclidean three-space with linearly dependent Atiyah polynomials, including planar configurations. The configurations consist of two coaxial cyclic orbits and axial points. We also obtain analogous configurations in hyperbolic three-space.

The map is required to be equivariant under the action of the symmetric group. This existence problem became known as the Berry–Robbins problem.

papers.title: Synthetic Child-Adult Interactions Are Not Developmentally Plausible
papers.abstract: Synthetic data has become a common resource for training language models, and this trend has spilled over into research on developmentally plausible language modeling. However, it remains unclear whether LM-generated child-adult interactions actually resemble natural ones. We compare the synthetic TinyDialogues dataset to natural dialogue across a broad range of linguistic measures. While synthetic data matches natural data on the lexical level, it drastically underestimates the messy, fragmented nature of spoken interaction. To mitigate this, we propose instruction-tuning with data created from real dialogues, and show in a pilot study that a small model approximates the statistical tendencies of natural data after moderate parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

papers.title: Conceptizer: Next-Token Prediction Is Not All You Need
papers.abstract: Next-token prediction (NTP) rewards only the token that occurs next, penalizing every alternative. But natural language often offers many ways to express the same meaning. We introduce Conceptizer, a training framework that extends next-token prediction with a reward for meaning. Conceptizer uses a fixed, model-agnostic vocabulary of ~9K concepts, built from contextual synonyms, as units of meaning alongside tokens as units of text. It maps each next-token distribution to a concept distribution and shares the reward for the target meaning across its possible wordings. This provides a concept-level training signal without adding model parameters. Applied to 3 model families at 1B-8B parameters, Conceptizer achieves the lowest held-out NTP perplexity at concept-target positions and assigns the highest probability to contextual synonyms, against all 3 baselines. It also improves downstream performance on knowledge and sentiment tasks while remaining comparable on commonsense. These results show that language models can be directly optimized to predict meaning, not just the next token.

papers.title: Derivative-Informed Dimension Reduction of Stochastic Differential Equations: A Path-Space Sensitivity Approach
papers.abstract: Uncertainty in the drift of a stochastic differential equation (SDE) induces uncertainty in statistical observables defined as expected functionals on path space. We propose a derivative-informed method for identifying low-dimensional structure in the drift-to-observable map, with the aim of improving the tractability of uncertainty quantification. This approach can be viewed as a generalization of the active subspace method to infinite-dimensional input spaces and to path-space observables of SDEs. Representing uncertainty in the drift by random perturbations in a Hilbert space, we construct a path-space sensitivity operator using first-order Fr\'echet derivatives of the observable with respect to the perturbation. We establish conditions under which the leading eigenfunctions of this operator correspond to directions of maximum mean squared sensitivity of the observable, thus enabling low-dimensional approximation with certified error bounds. We further introduce a martingale control variate of the Fr\'echet derivative that reduces error in sample-based estimators of the operator. Using a Galerkin scheme for numerical discretization, we show that reduced representations of the drift from the derivative-informed basis yield more accurate approximations of mean first hitting times of SDEs than the Karhunen-Lo\`eve expansion of the same truncation order.

papers.intro:
Stochastic differential equations (SDEs) are used to represent stochastic processes in a wide array of domains, including physics and biology, systems engineering, mathematical finance, sampling, and diffusion-based generative modeling. In many of these settings, the drift function of the SDE is not known a priori and must be inferred from a set of observations. Data-driven models of the drift function appear in the form of machine learning force fields for molecular dynamics [3, 24], surrogates of model discrepancy in control systems [30, 14], and neural network estimates of the score of an intractable probability distribution in diffusion-based sampling [33]. In each of these examples, models of the drift function are inferred from finite data and therefore subject to statistical error, which propagates to uncertainty in statistical properties of the modelled process.

In many of these settings, the drift function of the SDE is not known a priori and must be inferred from a set of observations. Data-driven models of the drift function appear in the form of machine learning force fields for molecular dynamics [3, 24], surrogates of model discrepancy in control systems [30, 14], and neural network estimates of the score of an intractable probability distribution in diffusion-based sampling [33]. In each of these examples, models of the drift function are inferred from finite data and therefore subject to statistical error, which propagates to uncertainty in statistical properties of the modelled process.

Both the tasks of model inference and uncertainty quantification of data-driven models of SDEs suffer from the curse of dimensionality: it is more difficult to infer an accurate model of the drift function and quantify the impact of model uncertainty when its parameters are high- or infinite-dimensional. To pose an example, in forward uncertainty quantification (UQ), one aims to characterize how uncertainty in the input drift function – represented by a probability distribution of parameters of the drift function, μ\mu – influences uncertainty in an output observable quantity FF which depends nonlinearly on the drift function. This task amounts to solving for the pushforward distribution of the observable, F♯​μF_{\sharp}\mu, which is typically not available in closed form and must be characterized by Monte Carlo simulation. Rather than incur the expense of simulating the SDE for every Monte Carlo trial, a common approach to reduce the cost of forward UQ is to learn a surrogate operator which efficiently approximates the pushforward map [35, 13]. However, such operators are increasingly challenging to learn for input parameters in high dimensions.

However, such operators are increasingly challenging to learn for input parameters in high dimensions.

Dimension reduction techniques are often employed to improve the tractability of forward UQ, sensitivity analysis, and model learning. In the literature on dimension reduction for parameters of SDEs, the drift function is generally assigned a specific functional form – for instance, reduced-rank Gaussian processes [12] or a low-rank tensor decomposition of the value function in stochastic optimal control [10, 32] – which admits reduced-dimensional representations. However, these strategies reduce dimension by committing to a specific model class, which precludes the use of preexisting or alternative functional forms such as neural networks. Moreover, since the basis constructions are agnostic to variation in observable functionals of the solution of the SDE, such as path statistics or invariant statistics, truncation of the basis expansion form of the drift may lead to a loss of accuracy in the corresponding observable.

In this paper, we propose a technique for constructing a reduced representation of the drift function in terms of a data-driven, observable-adapted basis which is suitable for forward UQ and sensitivity analysis of the observable of the SDE. Our approach corresponds to solving for the derivative-informed subspace of parameters of the drift function from the spectral decomposition of a path-space sensitivity operator, constructed from data on the first-order derivative of the observable with respect to the parameters. The derivative-informed subspace is also referred to as the active subspace in literature, which was first popularized by [7] and then generalized to vector-valued observables in [39] and to infinite-dimensional parameters and observables in [20]. In the setting where the parameter is infinite-dimensional – the drift function itself is the parameter – the subspace approximation of the drift is a truncated expansion on a complete basis of a chosen function space. A key feature of derivative-informed subspaces is that under appropriate conditions, one can leverage a subspace Poincaré inequality to derive an upper bound to error in the subspace approximation of the observable.

A key feature of derivative-informed subspaces is that under appropriate conditions, one can leverage a subspace Poincaré inequality to derive an upper bound to error in the subspace approximation of the observable.

We focus the presentation of our method on its application to path-space observables of SDEs. These are quantities expressed as expectations with respect to the law of the SDE, which is a probability measure on the space of continuous paths. This type of observable appears in many forms, such as committor functions or mean first transition times which relate to reaction rates in molecular dynamics [17, 41, 9] and the cost functional in stochastic optimal control [11, 18, 26]. Our method is similar to Koopman operator approaches to dimension reduction in that both seek representations of the SDE coefficients that are adapted to a chosen class of observables. The Koopman operator characterizes the evolution of observables dependent on the process at deterministic times, such as one-point statistics or two-point correlation functions [40], and can be represented with reduced-dimensional Galerkin or extended dynamic mode decomposition approximations which preserve the selected fixed-time statistics [38, 15, 16, 29]. In contrast, the path-space observables considered here are defined expectations over path measures, where the length of paths, determined by the stopping time, is a random variable. In general, such quantities cannot be expressed as the action of a fixed-time Koopman operator on a state-space observable. Derivative-informed subspaces are a more general approach to dimension reduction in the sense that they can tailor the reduced subspace of drift functions to not only one-point or two-point statistics, but also path-dependent statistics defined by non-deterministic stopping times.

papers.title: Delayed maximum energy solar energetic particle events: Statistical analysis from Solar Orbiter
papers.abstract: Investigations of solar energetic particles (SEPs) have long utilized the dispersive nature of onset times, as in, the earlier arrival of higher-energy particles compared to lower-energy particles, to infer information such as the path length to the acceleration site at the time of initial particle release. However, recent observations by Solar Orbiter and Parker Solar Probe have begun to characterize SEP events with an apparent delay in arrival times of the higher energy portion of the particle distribution, above a critical energy separating the delayed particles from that of the typical velocity dispersion signature at lower energies. Features of these delayed maximum energy (DME) SEP events, sometimes referred to as "inverse velocity dispersion" events, could provide new insight into the impacts of magnetic connectivity to locations along an expanding coronal mass ejection-driven (CME-driven) shock wave, variations of acceleration along the shock surface, and transport effects in the inner heliosphere. This study focuses on the occurrence rate and characteristics of DME events observed by Solar Orbiter relative to their footpoint locations with respect to the initial flare site. These DME events show a bias in occurrence rate towards events when the observer's footpoints were westward of the associated flare location. Additionally, estimated locations at which the highest-energy particles of DME events are released into the flux tube suggest continued release of increasingly higher-energy particles from the CME-driven shock into the connected flux tube well into the inner heliosphere. This indicates that DME events could be attributed to inner heliospheric effects and are not actually coronal in origin. This finding is consistent with previous observations and interpretations of SEP events connected westward of the associated flare.

papers.title: Real-Time Recurrent Qubit-State Discrimination on a Heterogeneous AI-Engine-FPGA Accelerator
papers.abstract:
Qubit readout, or qubit state discrimination, remains one of the slowest and most error-prone operations in superconducting quantum processors, making fast, accurate, and hardware-efficient classification essential for scalable quantum computing. Conventional discriminators integrate the I/Q record into a single point, discarding evidence a relaxing qubit leaves behind; full-resolution feed-forward classifiers recover it but are too costly to deploy under this constraint. Recurrent classifiers retain full resolution far more cheaply, but their loop-carried hidden state cannot fit a single AI Engine (AIE) tile's register capacity and spills to data memory, adding latency that grows with sequence length.
  We present a hardware-aware LSTM accelerator for an AMD Versal device that resolves this by partitioning at the dependency boundary - independent input projections on the AIE array, the loop-carried update in programmable logic (PL) - keeping pace with a 64 ns input cadence under a 1,000 ns budget. On the qubit affected by mid-readout state transitions, our design matches a full-resolution feed-forward network's accuracy (96.59% vs. 96.37%) using 403x fewer parameters and roughly 103x fewer DSPs while cutting relative error by 68.2% over GMM, 43.6% over QubiCML, and 16.82% over MF-NN. Using 4 out of 400 AIE tiles and 17 DSP58, it needs 2.2-8.2x fewer DSP58 blocks than QubiCML and MF-NN, and the AIE-PL partition cuts exposed tail latency by 60.3% versus a pure-AIE mapping and DSP58 usage 31.1x versus an all-PL implementation. Across eight qubits, a compact variant reaches 96.78% mean accuracy, the strongest hardware-deployed operating point. Temporal resolution and recurrent-state placement must then be treated jointly when designing low-latency quantum readout accelerators.

papers.title: A thermodynamic correction layer for machine learning interatomic potentials
papers.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials enable atomistic simulations with near \textit{ab initio} accuracy over large length and time scales. Foundation models extend this capability across the periodic table but inherit the thermodynamic description of the electronic structure methods used to generate their training data. Small errors in relative phase stability can therefore produce large errors in transformation temperatures. We introduce an additive thermodynamic correction layer that shifts phase free energies towards an assessed reference without retraining or modifying the base potential. A first order thermodynamic construction converts the required phase free energy shifts directly into configuration energy targets, which are fitted using a linear atomic cluster expansion and refined iteratively from measured free energies. We apply the method to melting and solid to solid transformations across elements with different crystal structures using a foundation GRACE model. After the correction, all transformation temperatures lie within the prescribed tolerance of the assessed values, including Ca, Ti, and Zr, where a solid to solid transition and melting are corrected together. Static energy curves, bulk moduli, and liquid structure remain close to those of the base model. Vacancy formation energies, thermal expansion, and liquid density depend on the corrected phase balance and change where the correction is large. The method requires neither retraining, differentiable dynamics, nor access to the parameters of the base potential. It provides a modular route for combining transferable atomistic models with assessed phase thermodynamics.

papers.title: High-Q, high-power spin Hall nano-oscillators with thick NiFe layers enabled by SiC substrates
papers.abstract: Spin Hall nano-oscillators (SHNOs) are nanoscale microwave sources with potential applications in local spin excitation, neuromorphic computing, and oscillator-based Ising machines. Further improvements in output power and coherence are essential for these applications, and increasing the thickness of the ferromagnetic layer offers a promising route toward this goal. However, this comes at the cost of higher drive currents, which increase Joule heating and can degrade device performance. Here, we show that this bottleneck can be overcome by SiC substrates. By comparing otherwise identical W/NiFe nanoconstriction SHNOs on Al2O3, Si, and SiC, we find that the high thermal conductivity of SiC enables stable auto-oscillations in NiFe layers as thick as 10 nm, while the optimum performance occurs at 7 nm. The best SiC device reaches an average output power of 13.1 pW and a mean quality factor of Q = 23,000, representing the highest reported simultaneous output power and coherence for a single free-running SHNO. These results establish SiC and thermal substrate engineering as a route to thick-ferromagnet spintronic oscillators for coherent microwave generation in nanoscale devices.

papers.title: RepoTrace: Improving Requirement Tracing in Multi-Round Agent Interactions
papers.abstract:
Code agents have become increasingly capable of performing software engineering tasks through interaction with software environments. However, agents tend to degrade as the number of interaction rounds increases, making it difficult to maintain existing software during iterative modification. We analyze 2,656 agent trajectories in EvoCode-Bench and identify requirement focus misalignment as a recurring failure pattern, where agents struggle to distinguish the primary modification targets of a requirement from unrelated code.
  We propose Repotrace a requirement-driven repository understanding harness that combines repository structure with requirement semantics to construct a requirement-code correspondence and injects it into the agent context. This correspondence enables code agents to follow the repository architecture, trace requirements across multi-round interactions, and identify the core code elements corresponding to the current requirement. Experiments show that Repotrace improves the mean per-round reward (MPR) across different models (e.g., +19.99 on GLM-5.2) and agent harnesses (e.g., +10.22 on Claude Code). Across rounds, Repotrace increases the average per-round reward from 0.163 to 0.371 on Terminus-2 with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, while reducing average regression errors by 56.78%. We release the source code and agents' trajectories to support future research.

authors.institution: Shanxi University of Finance and Economics

papers.title: Do Round Numbers Hold Prices? Occupation Densities and Depth-Conditioned Hazards in the Limit Order Book
papers.abstract: Prices cluster at round numbers, a pattern often interpreted as evidence that these levels act as price barriers. This pattern also admits a mechanical explanation: more liquidity rests there, and prices take longer to leave deeper queues. Limit order book data allow us to distinguish these mechanisms through a tick-grid framework in which local time counts departures and level-wise volatility reflects the departure hazard. Using data for five Nasdaq stocks throughout 2025, we find that round levels attract more liquidity but do not exhibit longer depth-adjusted durations. Intel and SoFi show directional effects, with departures biased away from round levels.

papers.title: Analytical modeling of the gamma-ray morphology of TeV halos around moving pulsars
papers.abstract: We aim to derive an analytical prescription for the line-of-sight-integrated particle distribution around moving pulsars, suitable for constructing spatial templates of the associated TeV-halo gamma-ray emission without resorting to computationally expensive numerical integrations. We consider electrons and positrons continuously injected by a moving source, undergoing isotropic diffusion and radiative energy losses. Assuming spatially uniform target photon fields, as appropriate for the cosmic microwave background and approximately valid for the interstellar radiation fields, the projected particle distribution provides a useful proxy for the inverse-Compton gamma-ray morphology. We show that the line-of-sight integration of the particle distribution can be performed exactly, reducing the calculation to a single numerical integral over the injection history. Under the additional assumptions of constant injection luminosity and a simplified treatment of energy losses, we derive a fully analytical expression that factorizes into an energy-dependent spectral term and a dimensionless spatial term describing the energy-dependent morphology. Comparison with the exact calculation shows good agreement over a broad range of energies and spatial scales, with appreciable deviations primarily at particle energies approaching the cutoff of the injection spectrum and at large distances from the source, where the emission becomes fainter. Our results enable the construction of physically motivated, energy-dependent spatial templates for gamma-ray halos around moving pulsars, capturing the morphological asymmetries induced by proper motion without computationally expensive numerical integrations. This makes them particularly suitable for systematic morphological and spectral analyses of extended gamma-ray sources.

papers.title: PersonaScienceBench: Evaluating Scientific Agents with Diverse Simulated Researchers
papers.abstract: Scientific agents collaborate with researchers whose expertise and preferences differ, but benchmarks usually hold the collaborator fixed. We introduce PersonaScienceBench: 200 tasks from five benchmarks across four scientific domains. Simulated researchers provide context and feedback according to persona profiles, while task objectives and grading remain fixed. Agents encounter researcher preferences only through conversation. Across eighteen modelconfigurations, task performance, fact recovery, and self-repetition reveal different strengths. Detailed GPT 6 Astra analyses show distinct agent responses across researcher profiles; interaction traces illustrate targeted clar ification and workflow revision. These behaviors can differ even when final scores match. PersonaScienceBench therefore evaluates how agents collaborate with diverse researchers alongside whether they complete the task.

papers.title: Pinching Antenna and Relay Assisted Joint Indoor Outdoor NOMA Communications with SWIPT
papers.abstract: This paper investigates physical layer security in waveguide-based pinching antenna systems with a mobile eavesdropper. Assuming perfect knowledge of the legitimate user's location and only statistical information about the eavesdropper's position, the ergodic secrecy rate is analyzed under Gaussian and practical finite-alphabet signaling. Since the exact ergodic secrecy rate does not admit a tractable closed-form expression, a closed-form analytical upper bound is derived using Jensen's inequality. The resulting expression serves as an efficient objective for antenna position optimization without requiring exhaustive Monte Carlo simulations. Numerical results verify the tightness of the proposed upper bound and show that the optimized antenna position closely matches the optimum obtained from Monte Carlo optimization. Furthermore, practical finite-alphabet signaling is shown to exhibit secrecy-rate saturation at high SNR, identifying an effective operating SNR region. Although the antenna position is optimized using the Gaussian-based upper bound, it remains effective for practical signaling.

papers.title: Counterexamples to congruences in finite p-groups
papers.abstract: Let $K$ be a conjugacy class of a finite $p$-group $G$. H\'ethelyi, K\"ulshammer and the author asked whether the number of conjugacy classes contained in $KK^{-1}$ is always congruent to $1$ modulo $p-1$, and whether, dually, the number of irreducible constituents of $\chi\overline{\chi}$ is congruent to $1$ modulo $p-1$ for every $\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G)$. We construct a group of order $7^7$ for which both congruences fail.

papers.title: Temperature-dependent magnetic properties of the antiferromagnet Mn$_2$Au
papers.abstract: Mn$_2$Au is one of the most promising materials for antiferromagnetic spintronics due to its high N\'eel temperature, moderate anisotropy, layered spin structure allowing current induced spin-orbit-torques, and ultrafast spin dynamics. Further understanding and control of the magnetic order in Mn$_2$Au for ultrafast spintronics applications via ultrashort electric/optical means requires accurate understanding of how its magnetic properties depend on temperature. Here we present atomistic spin dynamics simulations of the temperature-dependent macroscopic magnetic properties of Mn$_2$Au single crystals. We introduce a spin Hamiltonian based on previous ab initio calculations which produces temperature-dependent scaling of the anisotropy constants with magnetisation consistent with Zener-Akulov-Callen-Callen power laws. The calculated temperature dependence of exchange stiffness follows a scaling law with magnetisation of $m^{1.83}_e$ , and predicts a temperature-dependent domain wall width that agrees very well with direct simulation. Our model provides an understanding of temperature-dependent magnetic properties of Mn$_2$Au that enables large-scale simulation of the working conditions of spintronic devices.

papers.title: Exponentially large mu-coefficients
papers.abstract: Using webs, we prove that Kazhdan-Lusztig mu-coefficients for symmetric groups grow at least exponentially with the rank, already for pairs labeled by a three-row rectangle.

papers.title: The modular characters of $\text{Sp}_{10}(2)$
papers.abstract: Using computational methods, we determine the irreducible $3$- and $5$-modular characters of the symplectic group $\text{Sp}_{10}(2)$ for blocks with non cyclic defect groups, with one ambiguity in the principal $3$-block.

papers.title: Data-Driven Stochastic Control of Delayed Air-Conditioning Systems
papers.abstract: We consider a stochastic optimal control problem arising in the operation of industrial air-conditioning systems with delayed activation effects. The delayed transition between inactive and operational regimes induces a non-Markovian structure in the controlled dynamics. We derive a regression-based discrete dynamic programming algorithm on nested state-control grids. We give a probabilistic proof of convergence of the idealized time-discrete dynamic programming problem to the continuous-time value function. Numerical experiments based on calibrated multidimensional forecast-tracking Ornstein--Uhlenbeck models illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology.

papers.title: AIPC: Evidence-Guided Agent Workflows for PyTorch Project Deployment
papers.abstract:
Deploying and optimizing a PyTorch inference project on a dedicated accelerator, especially an on-device NPU, requires more than using a framework device API as with CUDA. The project must be converted into hardware-runtime artifacts and adapted to the target toolchain and application interface. Differences in model formats, quantization flows, operator support, and toolchain interfaces create cross-layer problems spanning PyTorch/ONNX models, toolchains, runtimes, and device execution. LLM Agents can invoke tools to address such problems, but may drift because of insufficient domain knowledge, large configuration and repair spaces, or poor path selection.
  We propose AIPC (AI Porting & Conversion), an Agent method for deploying PyTorch inference projects. AIPC combines structured Skills with toolchain, runtime, and profiling evidence to drive cross-layer diagnosis and repair, organizing model adaptation, artifact building, on-target execution, accuracy repair, and performance optimization into one deployment flow. We evaluate AIPC on the on-device NPU path of Qualcomm QAIRT across vision, speech, LLM, and diffusion models. In two optimization cases, 6/7 Skill-arm Whisper-Small runs meet predefined accuracy and latency criteria versus 0/6 control runs, while YOLO-Worldv2 achieves a 2.791x end-to-end speedup versus 1.599x for the control. Under a pre-fixed deployment contract, Skill, tool permissions, and check conditions, some runs achieve zero in-run human intervention (0-HITL). We also examine Qwen3.8-27B as a locally deployable model for driving an Agent workflow.

papers.title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
papers.abstract: Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair, in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org.

papers.intro:
Many theoretical papers in statistics, machine learning, operations research and mathematics rest on long technical proofs with many tedious details. Even after several rounds of proofreading, an author can easily overlook a detail that seems unimportant, such as a boundary case, a missing regularity condition, or a step that needs an assumption the paper never states. Most of the time, such gaps have no effect on the main conclusions.

Many theoretical papers in statistics, machine learning, operations research and mathematics rest on long technical proofs with many tedious details. Even after several rounds of proofreading, an author can easily overlook a detail that seems unimportant, such as a boundary case, a missing regularity condition, or a step that needs an assumption the paper never states. Most of the time, such gaps have no effect on the main conclusions.

A proof assistant such as Lean [1], with its mathematical library Mathlib [2], accepts a proof only when every step follows from the definitions and earlier results, so no gap can pass unnoticed. Formalizing a paper in Lean is therefore a reliable way for authors to find and close the gaps in their own proofs, and the result is a paper whose mathematics is Lean-verified. Formalizing a research paper by hand, however, can take weeks of work from someone fluent in both the paper’s field and Lean. Recent agentic systems formalize informal mathematics automatically, but a research paper raises two problems that a machine cannot settle alone. First, natural language is ambiguous. A statement can admit several readings, and a formalization of the wrong one proves something the author never meant. Second, when a statement turns out to be false, there are usually many ways to fix it. The repair that changes the least in logic may still miss what the author intends, for example by giving up the part of the result the author cares about most. Both problems depend on the author’s intent, so the author has to take part in the process. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based pipeline that helps authors improve their own papers. PaperFormalizer points the author to each gap in the proofs, recommends how to close it, and produces a Lean-verified version of the paper, while the author keeps every decision about what the paper claims.

The pipeline has two stages, natural language review and autoformalization (Figure 1). In the first stage, one agent transcribes the TeX source into a dependency graph whose nodes are the statements of the paper. A second agent then checks each node closely for correctness and ambiguity and proposes repairs for the problems it finds. Whenever the agent is unsure what a statement is meant to say, it stops and asks the author, in natural language and TeX symbols, and the author decides on every repair that would weaken a main result. Once the paper passes this stage, the pipeline formalizes each statement in Lean automatically. The final output is a revised paper and a report of what was changed, together with the Lean code. We used PaperFormalizer on three of our own papers. Five of the seven results in one paper and 15 of the 29 results in another needed some revision, and for each of them the pipeline proposed a repair that largely preserve the statement of the main results in the paper. (Section 5 and Table ).

We designed PaperFormalizer for authors who want to strengthen their own papers, before submission or after publication. The pipeline makes its key decisions together with the author, because the right reading of a statement and the right repair of an error depend on what the author intends. A repair proposed without the author is only the pipeline’s best guess, and the author may have a different reading in mind or prefer a different fix. PaperFormalizer is therefore a tool for improving a paper together with its authors.

There is some recent work in this direction. OSVerify [3] and Rethlas-OSV review the mathematics of solutions and papers in natural language, passing only audited findings to human experts. PaperFormalizer sits between these two scenarios and puts the author in the loop, with the goal of producing a verified version of the author’s paper. papers.title: Optimal Non-Homogeneous Improvements of the Anisotropic Hardy Inequality
papers.abstract: We consider the Hardy inequality associated with a strongly convex Finsler norm $F$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and we study its optimal non-homogeneous improvements in the whole range $1<p<\infty$. We show that the anisotropic Hardy difference controls a weighted critical Sobolev norm when $1<p<n$, a weighted exponential integrability of Trudinger type when $p=n$, where the Hardy term is replaced by its Leray logarithmic correction, and a weighted H\"older seminorm when $p>n$, proving in each regime that the logarithmic weights appear with the optimal exponents. In the borderline case $p=n$ this extends to general functions the optimal exponent previously known only for anisotropically radial functions. The proofs rely on a common ground-state reduction, combined with a splitting into an $F_o$-radial and a mean-free part for $1<p\le n$, and with an anisotropic Morrey representation formula for $p>n$.

papers.title: Optimal ratcheting dividend policies with resets
papers.abstract: We study an optimal dividend policy problem under ratcheting and bankruptcy constraints. Firms face a tradeoff between the negative signal of a dividend reduction and a potential future bankruptcy. In contrast to previous works, the dividend rate is allowed to decrease after incurring a negative impact on equity valuation in accordance with a large empirical literature on the topic. We provide an explicit necessary and sufficient condition for the finiteness of the value function and prove the differentiability of the value function, and its characterization via viscosity solutions and the so-called supercontact property. The value function is given by the solution of a two-dimensional variational inequality combining optimal stopping, singular and impulse controls. We show that the problem is equivalent to a one-dimensional setup simplifying both mathematical and financial analysis. Finally, we provide a numerical study of the model and a sensitivity analysis with respect to the model parameters. We show the relevance of over-reaction to financial news on the manager's optimal policy.

papers.title: Smart charging without rebound peaks: Wholesale price feedback limits distribution grid peaks from price-responsive electric vehicles
papers.abstract: Studies on price-optimized EV charging consistently find that the common price signal synchronizes charging of the entire fleet of cars in the cheapest hours and creates new "rebound" load peaks in low-voltage grids. Almost all of these studies treat wholesale prices as exogenous, i.e., unaffected by the shifting EV load. This paper argues that this assumption overstates the problem: charging in low-price hours raises the wholesale price in those hours, which spreads charging across hours in equilibrium. I simulate price-optimized charging under real-time prices calibrated to German 2025 data. Even when adjusting for the increase in electricity demand, the coincident import peak of the local grid rises by 260%. After adding a model of equilibrium wholesale prices that takes the price-quantity feedback into account, the increase is reduced to a mere 5%. Allowing for vehicle-to-grid, the export peak rises by 115% and falls by 6%, respectively. The result holds across vehicle and charging parameters, charging constraints, renewable scenarios, network charges, price functions, peak measures, and simulation assumptions. Rebound peaks remain possible where vehicle adoption runs ahead of the national average or where charging power is high, but they are much smaller than the literature consensus suggests.

papers.title: Optimised growth of epitaxial D019 Mn3Ge(0001) thin films via single target sputtering
papers.abstract: Materials with chemical identity Mn3X, where X is Sn, Ga, or Ge, are Heusler alloys with intriguing properties that are fundamentally and technologically interesting. They have topological properties with a non-trivial band structure that identify them as Weyl semimetals in the bulk. Their magnetic properties, which give rise to the topological band structure through spin-orbit coupling, are determined by their Kagome lattice structure, making them chiral non-collinear antiferromagnets. Among these materials, Mn3Ge is particularly interesting because it has a larger Berry curvature, leading to a large anomalous Hall conductivity and motivating potential spintronic applications. The desirable properties are only obtained when Mn3Ge has the D019 crystal structure, so producing an easily reproducible growth recipe is the main objective of this paper. Here we show that ultra-high-quality thin films of Mn3Ge with D019 symmetry can be grown from a Mn5Ge target on an Al2O3(0001) substrate with a Ru(0001) seed layer. The expected non-collinear antiferromagnetic order was confirmed by the finding of weak zero-field magnetisation (0.0086 +/- 0.0002) mu_B/Mn that does not saturate at high magnetic fields and has a Neel temperature of (291 +/- 2) K.

papers.title: Optimizing Physical Neural Networks through Device Variable Selection
papers.abstract: Physical neural networks (PNNs) leverage device physics in electronics, optics, and related domains to enable energy-efficient neural networks. Broken-isomorphism PNNs replace linear operations with multivariate physical transformations, modifying how input signals are mapped to device variables. We exploit network architectures emerging from these mappings by treating the routing between signals and input variables of physical devices as trainable parameters. This approach expands device-level tunability of the physical transformations while, at the system level, demonstrating improved expressivity of PNNs with negligible additional inference overhead. This discrete routing is optimized by training a categorical distribution using Gumbel-Softmax reparametrization. We evaluate this approach using experimentally calibrated differentiable models of multivariate electronic RNPUs for MNIST and CIFAR-10 classification. Using variable selection, we improve the MNIST classification accuracy for a small CNN model from 94.5% to 96.9% and the accuracy of CIFAR-10 from 62.8% to 68.0%. Our method uniquely leverages the induced biases of broken-isomorphism PNN architectures, paving the way towards more efficient physics-based neural network inference.

papers.title: Engineering Lightweight Burrows-Wheeler Transform Construction on the GPU via Prefix-Free Parsing
papers.abstract: The Burrows-Wheeler transform (BWT) is the core of many compressed full-text indexes and most read aligners. The fastest BWT constructions on GPUs need about $20$ bytes of device memory per character, which severely limits the texts that can be processed there. For example, on our GPU with 24 GB device memory, this is only about 1200 MiB. Prefix-free parsing (PFP) can be used to reduce the memory requirements of BWT construction algorithms in main memory. But, it uses hash tables and inverted lists which are not suited for GPUs. We show that PFP-based BWT construction can work with only sorting, scanning, and simple data-parallel procedures. This results in our GPU construction gpupfpbwt that on an NVIDIA RTX 3090, reduces the peak memory on an English text 11.9 bytes per character. There, it can processes 2108 MiB input files, which is 1.8 times larger than what the current state of the art libcubwt can handle. It is faster than or on par with libcubwt on eight of nine repetitive texts but 2.0 to 3.2 times slower on five of six non-repetitive ones, i.e., it provides a trade-off between required device memory and throughput.

papers.title: How characterisations of traces and central elements fail: sharp violation constants via michelson contrast and noncentrality
papers.abstract: A positive functional is a trace if and only if it satisfies any one of many inequalities, the first being Gardner's $|\varphi(X)|\le\varphi(|X|)$; positive central elements are characterised similarly. We ask how strongly these characterisations fail. For $\varphi=\mathrm{Tr}(\rho\,\cdot)$ on a matrix algebra the natural scale is the Michelson contrast $\delta$ of the density. For Gardner's inequality the sharp constant depends on $\delta$ and on the contrast $\delta'$ of $|X|$ only through their product: it is $(1-\delta^2\delta'^2)^{-1/2}$, the secant of the angle whose sine is $\delta\delta'$. On a finite von Neumann algebra the contrast is the wrong parameter, since every central density gives a trace; the governing parameter is the noncentrality, defined through the central condition number $\kappa_Z(\rho)$ of the central envelopes of $\rho$ (the largest and smallest elements of Halpern's central spectrum). A transfer principle lifts sharp matrix constants to exact constants in terms of $\kappa_Z$ in every finite von Neumann algebra. For 38 trace characterisations the constant is exact in 23 cases, has proved bounds in 13 and is known only numerically in two; for instance it is $\cosh(\frac12\ln\kappa_Z)$ for Gardner's inequality and for the subadditivity of the modulus. On matrix algebras the finite exact violations vanish at the trace to the orders $\delta$, $\delta^2$ or $\delta^4$, and outside factors and abelian algebras no function of the contrast describes the constants. We also find the sharp constants of the Novikov-Tikhonov characterisations of central elements, sharp bounds for three unnormalised trace functionals, and sharp contrast thresholds below which subadditivity of the square root and the power-mean inequality cannot fail. A numerical search, certified as a lower bound for each supremum, supports conjectured values for the remaining inequalities.

papers.title: On tame amenable flows and generalized Newelski's conjecture
papers.abstract:
We are developing some topological dynamics below a given ambit. We define and study Bohr compactifications below ambits and other related objects. We describe a natural epimorphism from the Ellis group of an ambit to the Bohr compactification below its Ellis semigroup ambit. The first main result says that, assuming tameness and hereditary amenability, this natural map is an isomorphism of topological groups. This is an abstract dynamical generalization of Newelski's conjecture, or rather a theorem of Chernikov and Simon that a natural map from the Ellis group of the flow $(S_G(M),G)$ to the definable Bohr compactification of $G$ is an isomorphism when $G$ is a definably amenable group definable in a NIP structure $M$. We give two proofs of our main result: a shorter dynamical proof and an analytic proof. In the course of the dynamical proof, we prove some results on the universal compactification flow and on the generalized Bohr compactification below a given ambit which admits a left continuous semigroup operation extending the action of $G$. The considerations around the analytic proof yield a description of the measured structure of amenable tame minimal flows, which is the second main result of this paper.
  We also study specializations of the above abstract topological dynamics context to model theory contexts to recover some known and to obtain some new notions and results. The main new results in the model theory contexts are: (i) a description of the Bohr compactification of the group of automorphisms of a sufficiently saturated model $\mathfrak{C}$ of a first order theory $T$ below a certain fundamental ambit associated with $\mathfrak{C}$; (ii) transfer of amenability of a NIP theory $T$ to amenability of the Ellis semigroup ambit; (iii) a version of Newelski's conjecture for spaces of local types with a description of Bohr compactifications below such spaces.

papers.title: ALLMTS: Automated LLM-based Medical Triage System
papers.abstract: Telephone triage is a safety critical task: from a brief intake note, a nurse must decide whether a caller needs an ambulance, an emergency department, an appointment, or self care at home. Queried directly, large language models (LLMs) are unreliable: they over-escalate routine cases and cannot justify their recommendations against an auditable clinical standard. We present the Automated LLM-based Medical Triage System (ALLMTS), which grounds every disposition in the same commercially maintained telehealth guidelines nurses use. Rather than asking an LLM to triage, ALLMTS makes it execute the guideline: it selects the appropriate guideline and evaluates its triage assessment questions. The disposition follows deterministically from the first positive answer, using the same traversal rule a nurse follows. We evaluate ALLMTS on 566 synthetic, expert-validated scenarios spanning 14 dispositions and designed to test specific guideline questions. ALLMTS achieves 0.95 accuracy, compared with 0.47 for a raw-LLM baseline. On a curated 50-scenario subset released as an open benchmark, ALLMTS reaches 0.98 accuracy, on par with the 0.944 correct disposition rate that a five nurse expert panel recorded on those same scenarios. Critically, on that subset the baselines have over-triage rates of up to 0.50 (0.44 on the full dataset), whereas ALLMTS reduces the over-triage rate to at most 0.02 while maintaining low under-triage. These results support coupling LLM language understanding with executable clinical guidelines for triage from intake notes.

papers.title: Phonon-Dressed Quasiparticles in Epitaxial Scandium Nitride Resolved by Soft X-ray ARPES
papers.abstract: Electron-phonon interactions govern quasiparticle energies, lifetimes, and temperature-dependent band structures in semiconductors. However, direct momentum-resolved experimental evidence of their impact on quasiparticle electronic structure remains scarce, particularly in nitride semiconductors. Here, we present conclusive experimental evidence of electron-phonon interaction-induced quasiparticle renormalization and pronounced spectral broadening in p-type scandium nitride (ScN), using soft x-ray angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. First-principles spectral-function calculations due to electron-phonon coupling reproduce the measured spectra, capturing a pronounced quasiparticle kink ~2.3 eV below the valence-band maximum, phonon satellite features arising from long-range electron-phonon coupling, and a direct bandgap zero-point renormalization of -124.3 meV within the non-adiabatic Allen-Heine-Cardona approach. We further show that the anomalous temperature-induced increase in the direct bandgap in ScN originates from the combined effects of thermal expansion and electron-phonon coupling, contributing comparably near room temperature. Our results establish ScN as a model platform for visualizing electron-phonon coupling and provide a quantitative benchmark for predictive first-principles descriptions of quasiparticle renormalization in semiconductors.

papers.title: Nanoscale mapping of native defects in Td-MoTe2 and their impact on graphene-based van der Waals heterostructures
papers.abstract: We investigate native defects and their impact on the electronic structure of Td-MoTe2 and graphene/Td-MoTe2 van der Waals heterostructures using scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy. STM reveals a high density of circular, hollow surface defects that we attribute to Te vacancies. STS on pristine MoTe2 shows semimetallic, V-shaped dI/dV spectra with subtle low-energy states. The vacancies suppress the tunnelling conductance below the Fermi level without introducing new sharp defect-related resonances, consistent with a vacancy-induced redistribution of Mo-Te spectral weight rather than the appearance of new electronic states. In the heterostructure, graphene preserves these MoTe2 fingerprints with no noticeable graphene doping or charge transfer. Our results demonstrate that isolated native Te vacancies act as spectroscopically weak perturbations to the low-energy electronic structure of graphene. The graphene overlayer further screens their impact on the electronic structure, making graphene/Td-MoTe2 heterostructures intrinsically tolerant to such interface defects.

papers.title: Local Broadband Gigahertz Spectroscopy via SQUID-on-Tip DC Readout
papers.abstract: Superconducting microwave circuits are shaped by their local electromagnetic environment, yet standard microwave measurements do not resolve the local fields and device features that govern their behavior. Here, we combine microwave spectroscopy, nanoscale magnetic sensing, and topographic imaging in a single tapping-mode SQUID-on-tip microscope. The nonlinear Josephson response converts local GHz excitations into Shapiro steps, enabling quantitative measurements of microwave frequency signals and their excitation strength using only DC readout. Applied to a superconducting coplanar waveguide resonator, local spectroscopy reproduces the power-dependent resonance and nonlinear bifurcation observed in microwave transmission measurements. Spatially resolved measurements map the microwave response while simultaneously recording topography and static magnetic features, including vortices and Meissner screening currents. Electromagnetic simulations reveal how coupling through the superconducting probe leads limits spatial resolution and guides localized detector designs. Together, these capabilities establish a platform for correlating microwave circuit dynamics with the local structural and magnetic environment of superconducting devices.

papers.title: Projection-Based Federated Learning on Compact Submanifolds with Geometry-Independent Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: Federated learning trains a shared model across clients without exchanging their data, yet the updates they transmit still leak information about individual records. Enforcing differential privacy is harder still when the model parameters lie on a Riemannian manifold. Existing methods rebuild the noise added for privacy in the geometry of each new iterate, aggregate through intrinsic maps that often lack a closed form, and prove convergence only in restricted regimes. We introduce DP-RFedProj, a record-level differentially private federated learning method for compact submanifolds that aggregates through closed-form projections and privatises gradients in a fixed ambient geometry. Each client may run any stochastic first-order optimiser, take several local steps, and participate only intermittently. An explicit record-level $f$-DP guarantee holds for the entire training transcript, independently of the manifold, the aggregation scheme and the local optimiser. We establish convergence of DP-RFedProj when each client runs Riemannian SGD locally and the server aggregates by projected averaging, and show that privacy enters the rate through a term scaling with the manifold's intrinsic dimension rather than the ambient one. Synthetic experiments on federated PCA over the Grassmann manifold corroborate these findings. On EEG motor-imagery classification with SPDNet, whose weights lie on the Stiefel manifold, the method outperforms a Euclidean baseline at every privacy budget considered. In both experimental settings, our accounting requires five to six times less noise than that of the closest prior method for the same budget, which translates into higher utility.

papers.title: Intersection multiplicity of a sparse curve and a trinomial curve
papers.abstract: Let f $\in$ C[x, y] be a trinomial and let g $\in$ C[x, y] be a sparse polynomial with N monomials (N $\ge$ 1). We address the problem of bounding the local intersection multiplicity of the bivariate polynomial system f = g = 0 at an isolated root q $\in$ (C * )^ 2 only in terms of N . Our main result establishes that the local multiplicity of the system at any isolated solution q $\in$ (C * ) ^2 is at most (N -1)(N +2)/ 2 , independently of the degrees of f and g. Furthermore, we know that this bound is sharp for N = 3.

papers.title: Absolutely universal projective embeddings of long-root geometries of orthogonal type
papers.abstract: Let $G$ be a split Chevalley group of type $B_n$ ($n \geq 3$) or $D_n$ ($n \geq 4$), let $L$ be its Lie algebra and $\Gamma$ its long-root geometry, namely $\Gamma$ is the line-grassmannian of the polar space associated to $G$. It is well known that $L$ hosts a projective embedding of $\Gamma$, called the adjoint embedding, which realizes $\Gamma$ as a projective variety in the projective geometry of the underlying vector space of $L$. It is also known that $\Gamma$ admits the absolutely universal projective embedding, which is such that all projective embeddings of $\Gamma$ can be obtained from it as projections. When the field $F$ over which $G$ is defined is finite, the universal embedding of $\Gamma$ is just the same as the adjoint embedding. The same is not necessarily true when $F$ is infinite. Indeed, as we shall prove in this paper, the universal projective embedding of $\Gamma$ lives in a direct sum $K\oplus L$ for an $F$-vector space $K$, the dual of which is isomorphic to the derivation space $\mathrm{Der}(F)$ of $F$, which in general is non-trivial. Accordingly, the adjoint embedding of $\Gamma$ is universal if and only if $\mathrm{Der}(F)$ is trivial, namely $F$ is either perfect of positive characteristic or algebraic over its minimum subfield.

papers.title: AudioFM: Towards General Purpose Audio Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Learning audio representations that effectively bridge holistic global soundscapes with fine-grained acoustic moments is a long-standing goal in self-supervised learning. Recording-level contrastive objectives encourage agreement between pooled audio representations, but do not explicitly supervise local time-frequency representations. We introduce AudioFM, a self-supervised framework that combines recording-level contrast with patch-wise masked latent discrimination. Using visible acoustic context, a student predicts representations of masked patches and identifies their corresponding full-view teacher targets among candidates from other recordings. We further incorporate weaker supervision from eligible temporal neighbors to encourage local temporal consistency. Extensive evaluations show that AudioFM achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse audio domains in linear probing, fine-tuning, and zero-shot transfer, demonstrating superior event detection, robust scene-level understanding, and strong domain generalizability.

papers.title: Methyl radicals dynamics on (100)--(2x1):H diamond surfaces based on refined variational transition state calculations of gas-surface reaction rate coefficients
papers.abstract: Theoretical modelling of diamond growth should ideally provide estimates of the growth rate depending on experimental conditions. To that end, a description of all possible reactions related to the competing adsorption, desorption and migration mechanisms is required. Here, we provide precise calculations of the reaction rate coefficient of methyl-related reactions on hydrogen-terminated (100) diamond surface, as $\mathrm{CH_3}$ is known to be the main growth precursor in chemical vapor deposition (CVD) growth of diamond. To achieve this goal, we successfully combined Density Functional Theory (DFT) and variational transition state theory (VTST), allowing to extend our analysis to barrierless reaction. Our rigorous treatment of the quasi-free rotation of $\mathrm{CH_3}$ adsorbates on the surface allows us to overcome numerical errors for the finite difference calculations of the vibrational spectra for evaluating the partition functions of the system. Our results suggest that the mechanism that deplete the $\mathrm{CH_3}$ concentration the most is the absorption on a surface radical site. We also evidence the anisotropy of $\mathrm{CH_3}$ migration along the dimer of the (100)-(2x1):H surface. In a more general perspective, the calculated reaction rates coefficient for methyl reactions and migration presented in this work, together with the data for hydrogen reaction and other main gas surface reactions, bridge the gap between the atomic-scale description and the large-scale modelling of diamond growth.

papers.title: Modeling the CNOT gate in Germanium double quantum dots
papers.abstract: We model a controlled-NOT (CNOT) gate mediated by exchange interactions in a realistic Ge/GeSi hole spin-qubit device. We use for that purpose a computationally efficient framework based on a compact dressed basis of many-body singlet and triplet states, which enables fast time-dependent simulations that would be prohibitive within a conventional configuration-interaction approach. We discuss the dominant sources of infidelity in ideal (noise-free) devices. On the one hand, the nonadiabaticity of the tunnel barrier ramps, enhanced by the transverse component of the exchange interaction, imposes limits on the speed of the CNOT gate. On the other hand, the AC Stark shift of the conditional resonance and the off-resonant driving of the complementary transition can significantly degrade the gate fidelity and call for a careful optimization of the driving conditions. Finally, we investigate the impact of quasi-static charge noise on the fidelity of the CNOT gate. We find that the capture of charges near the qubits can strongly disrupt the conditional operation, while the nanometer-scale motion of charges results in a loss of fidelity that sensitively depends on the position and strength of the corresponding dipole. Our results quantify the requirements on barrier control, microwave driving, and charge-noise stability for high-fidelity two-qubit operations in Ge/GeSi hole-spin qubits.

papers.title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
papers.abstract:
A vulnerability costs more to fix the later it is discovered. As coding agents generate code faster than developers can review it, software needs a first line of defense screening each new function in real time. LLM agents have recently become capable of finding real-world vulnerabilities by working as a security expert would: they run analysis tools, explore the surrounding code, test hypotheses and weigh the evidence before forming their own judgement. This reasoning, however, spans many model calls, so that each verdict takes minutes of compute, far too long for real-time screening. Faster detectors, which fine-tune deep learning models or prompt an LLM for a direct verdict, are less accurate: they judge a function without the context an agent gathers, and an LLM's generated verdict is unreliable even when given some of it.
  We present REVA (REal-time Vulnerability Analysis), an AI vulnerability detector that brings the security context and code understanding components behind agentic detectors into a single forward pass of an LLM. For each new function, REVA gives the LLM a pre-computed threat model of its module, lightweight static analysis findings and call-graph information. REVA leverages a trained probe to read the LLM's internal representations of the new function in this context. On PrimeVul's held-out test set, REVA on GLM-5.3-Flash reaches 60.0% accuracy in about one second per function. This matches VulTriage (59.2%), the state-of-the-art agentic detector, run on the same LLM, while being over 250 times faster and less than a tenth as costly. On the same prompt, the probe is 14% to 17% more accurate than the LLM's own direct verdict. Across three open LLMs, REVA is at least as accurate as VulTriage, and about 10% more accurate on two of them. An LLM's internal representations thus encode much of what agentic detectors obtain through reasoning.

papers.title: Sustainability of TSFM Deployment and Pretraining: From Carbon Footprint Analysis to Mitigation via Pruning
papers.abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) offer strong zero-shot forecasting capabilities, but their high pretraining cost raises a practical sustainability question: does this upfront investment pay off over a full deployment lifecycle, compared to supervised standalone models that must be periodically retrained? We model the cumulative carbon cost of different approaches across a realistic industrial scenario: Chronos-2 amortizes its pretraining cost within months for large or frequently queried deployments, but a classical model remains cheaper indefinitely for small or rarely queried ones. For cases where reducing the TSFM's own cost matters, we show that removing a single encoder block (7.9% of parameters) via a gradient-free pruning criterion yields a consistent 6 to 9% reduction in FLOPs, CO2 emissions, and latency, at essentially no cost to zero-shot forecasting performance across a 25-task benchmark.

papers.title: Local obstructions and certified computations for perfect powers in power sums
papers.abstract: Let $S_k(x)=1^k+\cdots+x^k$. We study perfect-power values of $S_k(x)$ by combining local valuations with finite congruence certificates. For an irregular Bernoulli pair $(p,r)$ with $e=v_p(B_r)\ge1$, we prove a valuation formula uniform for $k\equiv r+1\pmod{p^e(p-1)}$, subject to an explicit condition on $v_p(x(x+1))$. This gives explicit families of nonexistence results in which both $x$ and $k$ are unbounded. We also determine all solutions of $S_k(x)=y^n$ for $3\le x\le10^6$ with $x\equiv0,3\pmod4$, leaving $k$ and $n\ge2$ unrestricted and including squares. This extends Hajdu's fixed-$x$ classification in the same residue classes. A uniform restriction on the normalized odd part of $S_k(x)$ and finite certificates exclude every $k\ge6$; the remaining exponents are checked by exact integer arithmetic. The certificates admit independent verification. We further prove a limitation of congruence tests of bounded prime-power depth and solve the equation for every $x\equiv28\pmod{5\,110\,664}$.

authors.institution: Budapest University of Technology and Economics

papers.title: Spatial variability of CH4-to-CO conversion pathways in irradiated gas giant atmospheres: implications for chemical relaxation and 1D quench schemes
papers.abstract: Close-in gas giant atmospheres are in chemical disequilibrium. Solving 3D kinetics to capture one source of this disequilibrium, transport-induced quenching, is computationally demanding, so simplifications are used. General circulation models (GCMs) relax abundances on the timescale of a single conversion pathway. 1D models place a quench level and hold abundances vertically uniform above it. We test both simplifications on CH4 against aerosol-free, solar-composition GCM simulations with thermochemical kinetics for HAT-P-11b, HD 189733b, HD 209458b and WASP-17b. We find ten CH4-to-CO conversion pathways, varying with depth, longitude and planet. A single pathway controls CH4 quenching on the three cooler planets; on WASP-17b two compete. The CH4 quench level is 3D: where the atmosphere is hotter, or a faster pathway takes over, the conversion timescale shortens, the quench level rises and the quench-level abundance falls. On WASP-17b the pathway switch lifts the quench level over the substellar tropics, deepening equatorial CH4 depletion. A 1D quench treatment with the Zahnle & Marley timescale typically locates the quench level within a factor of two in pressure for CH4 and about four for CO on every planet. It fails above the quench level, where every quench scheme holds abundances vertically uniform. The minor carbon carrier, CH4 or CO depending on the planet, is wrong by up to two orders of magnitude, on HD 189733b in opposite directions at different latitudes. Quenching sets an abundance at the quench level but does not fix it thereafter; even without photochemistry, transport and conversion keep that abundance spatially structured.

papers.title: On the isomorphism problem of Cayley digraphs
papers.abstract: A finite group $G$ is called a DCI-group provided any two Cayley digraphs $Cay(G,S)$ and $Cay(G,T)$ are isomorphic iff the two connection sets $S$ and $T$ are images of each other via automorphisms of the group $G$. Building on the vast literature on CI- and DCI-groups we present an updated list of possible DCI-groups. In addition, we give an alternative proof that does not rely on deep results from group theory. We also point out the three most important open problems related to the classification of DCI-groups.

papers.title: Observational evidence of the Gaia-Enceladus-Sausage merger's influence on the opposite side of the Galactic Center
papers.abstract: The Gaia-Enceladus-Sausage (GES) merger, which occurred approximately 8-11 Gyr ago, is a key event that shaped the Galactic inner halo. Its remnants have been studied extensively and are known to dominate the halo on the Near-side of the Galactic Center (GC), i.e. the side facing the Sun, but systematic evidence for whether the Far-side (the side beyond the GC as seen from the Sun) is similarly affected has been lacking. Using 14,056 red giant stars selected from SMSS DR4 and Gaia DR3 through stringent quality cuts, we compare the metallicity distributions, velocity-space distributions, velocity dispersions, anisotropy parameters, and action-space properties of the Near- and Far-sides. We find clear observational evidence for the influence of GES on the Far-side: it hosts the same metal-rich component peaked at [Fe/H] ~ -1.4, and its metal-rich population (-1.7 < [Fe/H] <= -1.3) shows GES-typical features consistent with the Near-side, namely a "sausage"-shaped velocity distribution and a velocity anisotropy as high as beta ~ 0.8-0.9. Action-space analysis shows that 10.86% +/- 0.23% of Far-side stars carry the GES dynamical imprint, consistent with 11.56% +/- 0.16% on the Near-side. The Far-side shows a residual prograde rotation that persists under increasingly aggressive disk-removal cuts, indicating a genuine kinematic signal rather than disk contamination, and a battery of robustness tests confirms that the symmetry is not an artifact of measurement uncertainties, residual disk contamination, or incomplete Sagittarius-stream removal. These results demonstrate that GES shaped the entire inner halo (r < 28 kpc) globally and symmetrically, with its imprint clearly present on the Far-side as well as the Near-side.

papers.title: Results for distinct covering systems with a prime minimum modulus $q \ge 11$
papers.abstract: We prove that if the smallest modulus of a covering system is a prime $q \ge 11$, then the sum of the reciprocals of the moduli is at least $1+10^{-28}$. This improves on a previous more general bound of the first two authors in this particular case. We also show that it is impossible to construct a covering system using distinct multiples of $q$ as moduli. Finally, we show as a corollary that it is impossible to construct $10$ distinct covering systems with the property that no modulus is used in more than one of the covering systems.

authors.name: Alexandros Kalogirou
authors.institution: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics

papers.title: Reading the Registers of Honorius III without Manual Line Transcription: Forced-Aligned HTR, End to End, Modular or Hybrid
papers.abstract: Unlocking medieval archives at scale is bottlenecked by the cost of line-level diplomatic transcriptions and manual abbreviation expansion. Focusing on the registers of Pope Honorius III (1216-1227) over 5,000 letters surviving in full only as manuscript images - we show that existing, line-break-free expert transcriptions (edition drafts) suffice to train end-to-end hand-written text recognition (HTR) that jointly transcribes and expands heavily abbreviated Latin. Using forced alignment on 860 unaligned edition entries across 394 pages of Reg. Vat. 9, we automatically bootstrap 13,122 training lines without manual alignment of segmented lines. While the generic CATMuS baseline struggles on this domain (18.9% CER) and a modular space-free HTR + word-segmentation pipeline (cf. Camps et al. 2021) plateaus at 15.6% WER, our from-scratch hybrid Conformer - combining CTC with bidirectional subword attention decoders, iterative self-realignment and n-best LM rescoring - achieves 4.7% CER and 8.7% WER (8.4% WER with ROVER system combination), nearly halving errors on clause-final words (22.7% to 12.2% WER). These figures are measured on the test lines that align with the transcription (86% of all test lines for the best hybrid). Furthermore, we address a tension between paleographic fidelity and editorial normalization: training on targets that preserve scribal name initials reduces the WER against the manuscript text on the 31 affected test lines from 13.3% to 9.2%, at a small cost against the expanded transcription (WER +0.3 points, CER +0.4). Finally, extensive ablations show that none of an auxiliary diplomatic CTC head, a copy mechanism, a permutation decoder or masked-image pretraining improves on direct end-to-end supervision, while strict padding-mask propagation and per-line beam termination make inference batch-invariant.

papers.title: The mathematical journey of spatial reciprocity
papers.abstract: Over the past three decades, evolutionary game theory in structured populations has witnessed explosive progress. Counterintuitive cooperative phenomena discovered in simulations have stimulated the development of rigorous mathematical theories to describe the underlying dynamics. In this paper, we review these theoretical advancements, including pair approximation and coalescent theory, which offer analytical solutions to evolutionary games on networks. We summarize the key results obtained by these theories, while also discussing their limitations, such as high computational complexity and constrained flexibility when applied to complex models. We therefore suggest that mathematical approaches provide a complementary tool for understanding cooperation in structured populations alongside simulations.
