authors.institution: Institute for Technical Physics and Materials Science

papers.title: P-stable degree sequence regions for bipartite and directed graphs
papers.abstract:
The switch Markov chain is a natural method for sampling graph realizations with a prescribed degree sequence, and $P$-stability is a general sufficient condition for its rapid mixing. Since $P$-stability is often difficult to verify directly, we develop an approach based on the simpler and more readily verifiable property of \emph{full graphicality}.
  We consider bidegree sequence regions obtained by fixing the two class sizes, the common degree sum, and lower and upper bounds for the degrees in each class. Such a region is fully graphic if every bidegree sequence satisfying these constraints has a bipartite realization. Our main result shows that every fully graphic region of this form is $P$-stable. More precisely, for class sizes $n$ and $m$, the perturbation ratio is at most $(nm)^5$. It follows from a known theory that the switch Markov chain is rapidly mixing on every such region. We also show that full graphicality can be tested on a canonical extremal bidegree sequence and use this characterization to derive several new explicit sufficient conditions.
  By encoding loopless directed graphs as bipartite graphs, we develop a parallel theory for directed degree sequences. This gives analogous extremal characterizations, sufficient conditions for full graphicality, and $P$-stability and rapid-mixing results for directed degree-sequence regions. The encoding process allows most corresponding statements for the two cases to be formulated and proved in one run.

papers.title: Spectroscopic Survey of Small Solar System Bodies with Ariel
papers.abstract: The small Solar System bodies (SSSBs) preserve records of the formation and evolution of the Solar System. In particular, the near-infrared wavelength region around 3 $\mu$m provides crucial insights into the origin and transport of hydrated materials and organics, although it is difficult to observe from the ground because of strong telluric absorption. We assess the observability of SSSBs as complementary science to the ESA Ariel space mission, operating in the visible to mid-infrared wavelength range (0.5--7.8 $\mu$m). Using the NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris system, we evaluate the visibility of known SSSBs from 2032 to 2035. Our analysis shows that Ariel can spectroscopically characterize up to 402 unique SSSBs under a conservative limiting visual magnitude of $V=13.6$. If observations can be extended to somewhat fainter targets ($V=16$), the number of observable SSSBs could increase to 2144. Assuming operational scenarios in which one SSSB is observed every 3, 7, or 30 days over a four-year mission, the total numbers of observable targets would be 357, 209, and 49, respectively. We further model the spectral energy distributions of candidate targets to evaluate their observational performance. We demonstrate that Ariel can resolve critical absorption features, such as those at 2.7 $\mu$m and 3.4 $\mu$m, with a higher spectral resolution than the previous infrared survey with AKARI. Observations of SSSBs with Ariel can provide insights into the distribution and evolution of life-forming materials in the Solar System and constitute a scientifically compelling component of Ariel's complementary science program.

papers.title: Phonon-assisted shift-current from first-principles: application to AlN monolayer
papers.abstract: In this work, we present a first-principles approach to investigate phonon-assisted shift current in extended systems. Our method combines the special displacement technique with real-time simulations based on the dynamical Berry phase. Merging these two frameworks enables direct access to non-linear optical responses at finite temperatures, while naturally incorporating phonon scattering and phonon-assisted electronic transitions into the time-dependent dynamics. This allows us to capture temperature-dependent features and lattice fluctuations that are essential for a realistic description of non-linear photocurrent generation. As a representative example, we apply our approach to the shift-current response of a monolayer of hexagonal AlN (h-AlN). This system provides an ideal testing ground because it features an indirect band gap and lacks inversion symmetry. Moreover, h-AlN layers of different thicknesses have been fabricated and characterized in a variety of experimental settings, opening the concrete possibility of testing our predictions. Our results demonstrate the relevance of phonon-mediated processes and the importance of temperature in determining the magnitude and spectral features of the shift current in layered materials.

papers.title: From Linear to Polylogarithmic: Dynamic Submodular Maximization over Matroids
papers.abstract: We study the problem of submodular maximization under a matroid constraint. In this problem, there is a monotone submodular function $f: 2^{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ and a matroid $M(N, I)$, accessible via value and independence oracles and the goal is to find the independent set $S \in I$ maximizing the objective function, i.e., $f(S) = \max_{I \in I} f(I)$. In the fully dynamic setting, the active ground set $N \subseteq N$ evolves through element insertions and deletions. The goal is to maintain a solution $S \subseteq N$ with $S \in I$ and $f(S) = \max_{I \subseteq N,, I \in I} f(I)$ after each update. Two approximation algorithms have been proposed to solve this problem: D\"utting et al. developed a $(4+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm with an expected amortized update time of $O\!\bigl(\frac{k^2}{\epsilon} \log k \log n \log^3 \frac{k}{\epsilon}\bigr)$, and Banihashem et al. achieved a similar approximation with a better update time $O\!\bigl(k \log k \log^3 \frac{k}{\epsilon}\bigr)$. However, these methods both become inefficient when the rank $k$ of the matroid is large (e.g., when $k = n^{o(1)}$). The central open question in this line of work is whether a fully dynamic algorithm with polylogarithmic update time exists. We resolve this question by presenting the first fully dynamic algorithm for submodular maximization over matroids with polylogarithmic update time. Our algorithm maintains a $(4+\epsilon)$-approximate solution with expected amortized update time $poly(\log n, \epsilon^{-1})$, where $n = |N|$. In particular, the update time is independent of the matroid rank $k$, thereby eliminating the dependence on $k$ and settling the open problem.

papers.title: Complex Domain Inverse Problem Formulation for 4D Flow MRI Super-Resolution
papers.abstract: Four-dimensional flow magnetic resonance imaging measures blood velocity fields in three dimensions throughout the cardiac cycle and is increasingly used to assess hemodynamics. However, these measurements are limited by low signal-to-noise ratios and limited spatial resolution, which can compromise their accuracy and reliability. To address these limitations, we investigate the feasibility of spatial resolution enhancement through a complex-domain inverse problem formulation inspired by MRI acquisition principles. Three inversion methods are evaluated: a closed-form approach (FSR), a Plug-and-Play alternating direction method of multipliers (PnP-ADMM), and a pretrained network that takes the forward operator as input (RAM). On simulated data, all three methods outperform 4DFlowNet at x2 and x4 super-resolution factors. On aortic phantom data at x2 super-resolution, PnP-ADMM and RAM achieve lower root-mean-square error than 4DFlowNet in almost all cases. These results highlight the potential of the proposed formulation and support further development and validation.

authors.name: Aur\'elien de Turenne
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Aging dynamics and generalized superposition principles in carbon black-carboxymethylcellulose hydrogels
papers.abstract: Aqueous dispersions of hydrophobic carbon black (CB) particles can be stabilized by carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), forming CB-CMC hydrogels whose microstructure is controlled by the relative CB-to-polymer content. At low CMC content, CB particles form a percolated, electrically conductive network, whereas at higher polymer content, CB particles act as isolated physical crosslinkers within an electrically insulating polymer matrix [see Legrand \textit{et al.}, Macromolecules 56, 2298-2308 (2023)]. Combining rheology and electrical impedance spectroscopy, we show that these two regimes exhibit markedly different aging dynamics. Conductive hydrogels exhibit logarithmic elastic recovery associated with a percolated CB network, whereas insulating hydrogels exhibit a combination of logarithmic and power-law stiffening, accompanied by dielectric polarization associated with confined ionic motion. The insulating hydrogels further exhibit a time-aging superposition principle, as their viscoelastic spectra measured in a time-resolved fashion can collapse onto a single master curve. Under steady shear, the viscoelastic response measured perpendicular to the flow also obeys a time--shear-rate superposition principle. Remarkably, the scaling between the shift factors under shear is reminiscent of critical-gel behavior, unlike that observed during aging at rest. Finally, time-resolved rheo-USAXS measurements performed during shear-rate cycles reveal structural rearrangements of CB particles and clusters that correlate with rheological hysteresis. These results provide a microstructural basis for understanding the nonlinear rheology of insulating CB-CMC hydrogels and establish generalized superposition principles as a unifying framework for their aging and flow behavior.

papers.title: Thermosolutal Marangoni instabilities in a weakly viscoelastic falling film with soluble surfactant
papers.abstract: We examine the linear stability and nonlinear evolution of a heated falling film containing a soluble surfactant and a weakly viscoelastic liquid. The stress response is described by the short-memory Walters model, while surface tension depends on temperature and surface concentration. An Orr--Sommerfeld analysis and its long-wave limit determine how elastic memory and the two Marangoni stresses enter the instability threshold. A five-field weighted-residual model is then derived to describe finite-amplitude disturbances. The bulk and surface transport equations are written with compatible fluxes, which conserve their combined projected surfactant inventory in a periodic domain. The numerical examples show that solutal Marangoni stress suppresses disturbance growth and reduces the amplitude of the nonlinear waves. Thermal Marangoni stress increases the maximum growth rate, although its effect on the width of the unstable wavenumber band is different. Elastic memory changes both the onset and the finite-wavelength response. The nonlinear profiles develop a main hump and capillary ripples, accompanied by variations in bulk concentration, surface concentration, and interfacial temperature. These results describe the competition between thermocapillary forcing, surfactant redistribution and elastic stress within the retained long-wave model. The larger elastic parameters are interpreted as formal predictions of the truncated constitutive equations, rather than as a controlled extension to strongly elastic flow.

papers.title: On the number of pioneers in high-dimensional critical percolation
papers.abstract: We prove that for critical percolation in high dimension the expected number of pioneers on any set containing the origin is of the same order as the probability that a simple random walk starting from the origin exits the set. Our proof works in all dimensions $d>6$, under the usual assumption that the two-point function is of the same order as the Green's function. As an application we obtain a sharp uniform quantitative bound on the probability that the cluster of the origin intersects any given ball.

papers.title: Sharp volume tests and entropy thresholds for quasilinear elliptic inequalities with gradient reactions
papers.abstract: We investigate positive weak solutions of $-\Delta_m u\ge u^p|\nabla u|^q$ on complete noncompact Riemannian manifolds without curvature, volume doubling, or Poincar\'e assumptions. For the superhomogeneous mixed reaction we derive a curvature-free integral volume test by combining two first-order estimates with a recurrence for the mass of a \emph{fixed} density. The same approach organizes the pure-gradient and capacity criteria and yields sharp finite hierarchies of iterated-logarithmic growth bounds, with counterexamples on smooth model manifolds. In the subhomogeneous region, vanishing lower growth of $\log V(R)/R^{m-q}$ forces the Liouville property. On the homogeneous line $p+q=m-1$, we obtain the optimal strict lower-volume-entropy threshold $(p+1)((m-1)/p)^{p/(p+1)}$ for $p>0$ (and $1$ for $p=0$), together with examples at equality. The existing six-region classification is not claimed as new; the advances concern refined volume hypotheses and their model sharpness. The tests remain valid for smooth weighted measures and for locally bounded positive Sobolev solutions. Sharpness is understood within the stated model families; no characterization from volume alone on an individual manifold is asserted.

papers.title: The measure equivalence classification of Baumslag-Solitar groups
papers.abstract:
In this article we show that all the nonamenable Baumslag-Solitar groups with nonunimodular Bass-Serre tree, i.e., $\mathrm{BS}(p,q)$ with $|p|,|q| 
eq 1$ and $|p|
eq |q|$, are measure equivalent to each other, thereby completing the measure equivalence classification of Baumslag-Solitar groups: each $\mathrm{BS}(p,q)$ belongs to one of three measure equivalence classes according to whether it is amenable ($|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$), virtually isomorphic to $\mathbf{F}_n 	imes \mathbf{Z}$ ($|p|=|q|
eq 1$), or is nonamenable with nonunimodular Bass-Serre tree ($|p|,|q| 
eq 1$ and $|p| 
eq |q|$). More generally, we obtain the similar classification of the generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups of rank $1$ (i.e., groups that act cocompactly on a tree with edge and vertex stabilizers infinite cyclic).
  Our proof also establishes a classification of all treeable lcsc groups into exactly six measure equivalence classes. Our new contribution which completes this taxonomy is: all nonunimodular nonamenable treeable lcsc groups are measure equivalent.
  Along the way we obtain several results about type $\mathrm{III}$ equivalence relations and graphings of independent interest. For example, we show that every ergodic type $\mathrm{III}_0$ graphing admits an ergodic hyperfinite subgraph for which the natural factor map of Krieger flows is an isomorphism.

papers.title: Speeding up Log-Sum-Exp: Kernel Fusion at the Memory Wall, Integer Arithmetic at the Compute Wall
papers.abstract: While the Log-Sum-Exp (LSE) function is a foundational numerical primitive for stable log-domain computation in modern machine learning, its fast and efficient computation on generic platforms (\ie, CPUs and GPUs) has been underexplored, potentially creating execution bottlenecks for large workloads. On GPU, the de facto implementation torch.logsumexp dispatches a chain of nine sub-kernels per call, incurring redundant High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) traffic and launch overhead. On CPU, exp and log operations are hardware-hungry, limiting the computing efficiency. To address these bottlenecks, we propose two drop-in kernels to significantly accelerate LSE computation on both GPUs and CPUs: FuseLSE, a single-pass fused kernel that evaluates LSE's exp and log functions on the GPU's Special Function Unit (SFU); and IntLSE, which further replaces the LSE computation with approximated integer arithmetic for CPU computation. Our experiments, validated by benchmarks across workload sizes and hardware platforms, show that both kernels are ${\sim}10-11\times$ faster than PyTorch at small workloads and ${\sim}6\times$ faster on larger ones on GPUs, where the speed-up is attributed to reduced launch overhead and HBM traffic. On CPU, where no SFU is available, LSE computation dominates the cost, allowing IntLSE to gain ${\sim}3-6\times$ execution speed over FuseLSE.

papers.title: Operator systems in \'etale groupoid C*-algebras
papers.abstract: We study operator systems arising from positivity domains of \'etale groupoids with compact unit space. Extending Kavruk's enough unitaries principle we show that such operator systems are hyperrigid in the C$^*$-algebra they generate. We focus on operator systems of positivity domains in UHF algebras and, by identifying them with Cantor graph operator systems, we show that they are hyperrigid. Furthermore, we show that in general, such a characterization is not possible when the \'etaleness condition of the underlying groupoid is removed, due to the failure of reduced spectral and compact operator synthesis.

papers.title: CropReward: A Human-Preference Benchmark and Reward Model for Aesthetic Image Cropping
papers.abstract: Aesthetic image cropping (AIC) aims to improve image composition and aesthetic quality by removing extraneous or distracting content. Over the past decade, AIC methods have evolved from specialized vision models to multimodal large language models(MLLMs). Reliable evaluation that reflects human preferences is essential for benchmarking AIC methods and guiding model optimization. However, the current AIC evaluation relies largely on geometry-based metrics such as intersection over union (IoU), as well as image aesthetic assessment(IAA) models. Although inconsistencies with human preferences have long been observed, the robustness and reliability of these evaluation criteria remain underexplored. To bridge this gap, we first construct CropBench, a large-scale benchmark comprising 106,995 human preference pairs for 1,019 images, with each candidate set containing the original image and candidate crops produced by 14 AIC methods. A systematic study on CropBench reveals that the existing criteria, ranging from IoU to off-the-shelf IAA assessment models, only exhibit limited alignment with human preferences. Building upon CropBench, we further propose CropReward, an MLLM-based reward model that evaluates a candidate crop by comparing with the original uncropped image and outputs a score indicating explicit aesthetic improvement or degradation relative to the original. In addition, we employ CropReward to construct CropReward-300k, the largest AIC dataset to date, and further develop CropAlign, a preference-aligned AIC model trained solely with CropReward supervision, without human-annotated crop boxes. Experimental results demonstrate that CropReward aligns with human preferences significantly better than existing criteria. CropAlign also surpasses the state-of-the-art AIC methods, demonstrating the advantage of CropReward in guiding AIC model optimization.

papers.title: Speculative Diffusion is a Tale of Two Tradeoffs
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is a technique that accelerates the inference speed of autoregressive large language models (LLMs) by sampling from a faster, lower quality draft model. Traditionally, a fundamental characteristic of speculative decoding is that it is lossless with respect to the verifier distribution, guaranteeing speed without sacrificing quality. This differs from recently developed diffusion LLMs (dLLMs), which are notably able to achieve substantial speedups by degrading the quality of their outputs with less diffusion effort. Because diffusion models are able to sample faster than autoregressive models by generating tokens in parallel, they are considered strong candidates for draft models in speculative diffusion. While it is widely understood that diffusion models can sacrifice quality for speed, speculative decoding itself can also be generalized to generate lossy samples faster using more lenient acceptance criteria with respect to the verifier distribution. Presented with the two parameters of diffusion effort and speculative decoding leniency, this paper explores the full achievable Pareto frontier via joint variations of these parameters. Our experiments show that jointly varying diffusion effort and acceptance leniency can extend the speed-quality Pareto frontier over single step diffusion drafting.

papers.title: When Agents Fail: Model or Harness--Who's to Blame?
papers.abstract: LLM agents combine models with execution harnesses, so agentic benchmark performance reflects their joint behavior. We argue that harnesses should therefore be evaluated through their interactions with underlying models. We develop a framework combining five complementary measures: (i) Valid Completion Rate (VCR), how reliably agents finish normally and deliver evaluable results, irrespective of task correctness; (ii) Model-Harness Fit, how well a harness supports task achievement through valid completion for a given model; (iii) Cross-Model Fit, a harness's overall suitability across evaluated models; (iv) Interaction Residuals, pairing-specific execution strengths and weaknesses hidden by component-level summaries; and (v) Token Load, the token demands of agent execution, including failed attempts. We evaluate four general-purpose harnesses (OpenCode, Codex CLI, Pi CLI, and DeepAgents) with four core models, plus two fixed native model-harness systems, on six benchmarks covering context management, tool use, long-context planning, multimodal interaction, and artifact handoff. Including native references and stress conditions, 111 evaluation settings yield 52,168 trajectories. Harness rankings vary across models and benchmarks; task performance and valid completion can favor different pairings, and similar task scores can accompany distinct execution profiles. OpenCode ranks first in cross-model performance, while DeepSeek V4 Flash Preview maintains consistently high Mean VCR across harnesses on the shared four-benchmark panel. These findings support evaluating model-harness interactions, training transferable harness-use capabilities in models, and harness designs adapted to the model and task.

papers.intro:
Classical views describe intelligent agents as goal-oriented systems that continuously perceive their environment, maintain internal state, select actions, and improve behavior through feedback (Wooldridge and Jennings, 1995; Wang et al., 2024). An LLM agent implements this paradigm by integrating a large language model (LLM) into an executable system for perception, reasoning, and action in external environments (Yao et al., 2023). At the system level, an LLM agent combines its model with an execution layer, the agent harness, that connects the model to the environment (Guo et al., 2026; Kwa et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2026). The harness provides mechanisms for observation processing, context management, tool and action interfaces, workflow control, state management, execution, evaluation, and error handling. By controlling how information is presented to the model and how its outputs are executed, the harness shapes agent behavior and task performance (Zhang et al., 2025b).

Classical views describe intelligent agents as goal-oriented systems that continuously perceive their environment, maintain internal state, select actions, and improve behavior through feedback (Wooldridge and Jennings, 1995; Wang et al., 2024). An LLM agent implements this paradigm by integrating a large language model (LLM) into an executable system for perception, reasoning, and action in external environments (Yao et al., 2023). The harness provides mechanisms for observation processing, context management, tool and action interfaces, workflow control, state management, execution, evaluation, and error handling. By controlling how information is presented to the model and how its outputs are executed, the harness shapes agent behavior and task performance (Zhang et al., 2025b).

Under this system view, end-to-end benchmark performance reflects the joint behavior of the model–harness system rather than model capability alone (Yang et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2026). Yet most benchmarks remain task-centric, evaluating fixed model–harness configurations by task success or aggregate reward while treating the harness as part of the setup. These evaluations summarize system-level success; execution diagnostics and crossed comparisons provide complementary views of performance sources. Failures may reflect insufficient model capability, ineffective harness use, or harness limitations in observation processing, action interfaces, state management, or recovery (Ma et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026). An empirical issue study reports failures occurring only when particular model behaviors interact with harness parsing, control flow, or context handling (Chen et al., 2026). Conversely, high performance may partly reflect the harness’s task-specific workflows or additional computation (Lou et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). Controlled studies show that changing harnesses can alter performance and rankings with models and tasks fixed (Zhu et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026). Understanding agent failure therefore requires examining the model, the harness, and their particular pairing through crossed comparisons and execution evidence. This assessment distinguishes failure to solve the task from abnormal termination or invalid evaluator handoff: a run may complete validly without solving the task, or earn task credit despite abnormal termination.

Understanding agent failure therefore requires examining the model, the harness, and their particular pairing through crossed comparisons and execution evidence. This assessment distinguishes failure to solve the task from abnormal termination or invalid evaluator handoff: a run may complete validly without solving the task, or earn task credit despite abnormal termination.

The missing object of evaluation lies at the model–harness boundary. A model’s harness-use capability depends on how effectively it can interact with a given harness: the same interface, action space, or feedback mechanism may be easy for one model to use but challenging for another, while the same model may behave differently under different harness designs (Yang et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2026). Accordingly, harness difficulty should be understood as a model-dependent interaction cost introduced by the harness’s observation format, action interface, state management, control flow, and recovery mechanisms. When this cost exceeds the model’s harness-use capability, the harness may prevent the model from realizing its underlying capabilities; when the harness provides extensive task-specific support, it may improve performance by contributing part of the task-solving process. Existing task-level evaluations conflate these effects into a single outcome, making it difficult to distinguish model capability from harness effects (Messick, 1995; Zhu et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026). Therefore, evaluating agents requires examining both task achievement and valid completion, together with how these outcomes vary across model–harness pairings.

We develop metrics to analyze model–harness interaction through task performance and operational validity. Valid Completion Rate (VCR) measures how often attempts terminate normally with valid evaluator handoff, regardless of task correctness. Model–harness Fit and Cross-Model Fit summarize task performance from valid completions for individual models and across models. We analyze their diagnostic value and robustness, failure patterns, and resource use. We implement a common agent adapter for this study, preserving native execution loops under matched tasks and controlled execution conditions. We cross four general-purpose harnesses—DeepAgents, OpenCode, Pi CLI, and Codex CLI—with multiple models on six benchmarks: SWE-bench-45 (Jimenez et al., 2024; Chowdhury et al., 2024), Terminal-Bench 2 (Merrill et al., 2026), VitaBench (He et al., 2026), LOCA-Bench (Zeng et al., 2026), ClawMark (Meng et al., 2026), and AgentSkillOS (Li et al., 2026). Fixed native systems add complete-system references. Figure 1 summarizes the evaluation framework.

We develop metrics to analyze model–harness interaction through task performance and operational validity. Valid Completion Rate (VCR) measures how often attempts terminate normally with valid evaluator handoff, regardless of task correctness. Model–harness Fit and Cross-Model Fit summarize task performance from valid completions for individual models and across models. We analyze their diagnostic value and robustness, failure patterns, and resource use. We implement a common agent adapter for this study, preserving native execution loops under matched tasks and controlled execution conditions. We cross four general-purpose harnesses—DeepAgents, OpenCode, Pi CLI, and Codex CLI—with multiple models on six benchmarks: SWE-bench-45 (Jimenez et al., 2024; Chowdhury et al., 2024), Terminal-Bench 2 (Merrill et al., 2026), VitaBench (He et al., 2026), LOCA-Bench (Zeng et al., 2026), ClawMark (Meng et al., 2026), and AgentSkillOS (Li et al., 2026). Fixed native systems add complete-system references. Figure 1 summarizes the evaluation framework.

Harness rankings vary across models and benchmarks in both task performance and operational validity, which can favor different harnesses for one model. Their joint distribution distinguishes execution profiles among configurations with similar success rates: clean runs may leave tasks unsolved, while non-clean runs may succeed or earn continuous-score credit. Pair-specific VCR deviations beyond model and harness averages also change sign across benchmarks. Resource use varies across models and tasks: the lightest harness changes across configurations, and lower token use can accompany lower outcomes. Low use can reflect premature termination; high use can include repeated failed actions. Cross-Model Fit identifies a stable aggregate leader on the evaluated panel, but model-specific preferences and intermediate ranks depend on its models and benchmarks.

papers.title: Beyond Visible Speakers: Context-Aware Active Speaker Detection with Speaker Registration
papers.abstract: Active speaker detection (ASD) relies on audiovisual correspondence between speech and visible faces, yet this correspondence becomes unreliable in crowded scenes, or when visual evidence is unavailable. We introduce ROAM-ASD-C and ROAM-ASD-CR to extend ROAM-ASD with contextual and identity-aware reasoning. ROAM-ASD-C jointly reasons across simultaneously visible candidates, allowing other faces to provide complementary evidence when the target observation is ambiguous or incomplete. ROAM-ASD-CR incorporates registered-speaker representations derived from enrollment speech, allowing detection of whether a speaker is active even when that speaker is not visually observed. ROAM-ASD-C achieves state-of-the-art performance across five ASD benchmarks: 96.8% mAP on AVA, 98.9% on WASD, 88.8% on UniTalk, 98.7% on Talkies, and 99.5% on ASW. It also improves ROAM-ASD by up to 13.3 mAP under 75% target-track visual removal.
papers.intro:
Active speaker detection (ASD) aims to determine whether a visible person is speaking in an audiovisual scene. It is an important component of applications such as speaker diarization and multimodal human-computer interaction. Recent ASD systems, such as ASC [1], MAAS [2], ASDNet [7], Light-ASD [8], LoCoNet [15], TalkNCE [5], TS-Talk [4], and MuSED [13], have achieved strong performance on conventional benchmarks, with performance on AVA [10] approaching saturation at over 95%95\% mean average precision (mAP). Nevertheless, ASD remains more challenging in unconstrained recordings, where multiple candidate speakers, interfering voices, and domain variation make the correspondence between acoustic speech and visible faces ambiguous. This gap is reflected in recent in-the-wild benchmarks such as WASD [11] and UniTalk [9], where the best reported baseline performance reaches only 93.7%93.7\% and 83.2%83.2\% mAP, respectively.

Nevertheless, ASD remains more challenging in unconstrained recordings, where multiple candidate speakers, interfering voices, and domain variation make the correspondence between acoustic speech and visible faces ambiguous. This gap is reflected in recent in-the-wild benchmarks such as WASD [11] and UniTalk [9], where the best reported baseline performance reaches only 93.7%93.7\% and 83.2%83.2\% mAP, respectively.

The core of an ASD system is audio-visual fusion. Most existing methods rely primarily on global full-face features as visual evidence, which can be distracted by non-speech facial activity under in-the-wild conditions [11]. Many systems adopt predefined pairwise fusion paths, such as cross-attention, which can be less robust when one modality becomes unreliable or incomplete, for example under face occlusion. In our previous work, ROAM-ASD [14], we addressed these two limitations for challenging in-the-wild conditions. ROAM-ASD augments global face representations with fine-grained localized visual cues, such as mouth information, and fuses audio, face, and mouth streams through flexible joint self-attention with modality-dropout training. This design improves cross-domain generalization and robustness to missing observations, raising the state of the art (SOTA) on WASD and UniTalk to 98.8%98.8\% and 87.9%87.9\% mAP, respectively.

This design improves cross-domain generalization and robustness to missing observations, raising the state of the art (SOTA) on WASD and UniTalk to 98.8%98.8\% and 87.9%87.9\% mAP, respectively.

However, ROAM-ASD still makes its decision independently for each visible face and therefore does not exploit relationships among simultaneously visible speaker candidates. Such context can be particularly useful in crowded or ambiguous scenes, where multiple faces may exhibit speech-like movements or acoustic interference from background noise and overlapping speech may be present. Prior works have demonstrated the benefit of this form of reasoning. ASC [1] models relations among multiple visible speakers and their temporal context. MAAS [2] formulates speaker assignment through multimodal graph reasoning. LoCoNet [15] further incorporates inter-speaker interactions together with long-term within-speaker context. Motivated by this, we extend ROAM-ASD with inter-face contextual reasoning among simultaneously visible candidates.

Despite these benefits, such contextual reasoning remains restricted to the visible candidate set. When visual observations are unavailable altogether, conventional face-level ASD loses the audio-visual correspondence required to assign speech to a particular person. Since the same scene-level audio is available to every candidate, speaker identity becomes ambiguous without an additional identity cue. A complementary direction is to incorporate speaker identity into audio-visual modeling, for example through target-speaker detection [4]. Such approaches show that prior speaker information can help disambiguate speech activity. Motivated by this, we introduce speaker registration, allowing enrolled speaker identities to be represented in addition to visible face candidates.

In this work, we extend ROAM-ASD in two complementary directions. First, we introduce ROAM-ASD-C, which augments the track-level ROAM-ASD representation with inter-face contextual reasoning across simultaneously visible candidates. Candidate representations are jointly processed before the final per-face activity predictions, allowing other visible candidates to provide complementary evidence when several candidates compete for the same acoustic evidence or when the target candidate’s own observations are ambiguous or incomplete. The final ASD decisions remain independent binary predictions, preserving the ability to represent silence and simultaneous speakers. Second, we introduce ROAM-ASD-CR, which further augments the candidate set with registered-speaker representations derived from enrollment speech. Registered speakers participate in the context block alongside visible face candidates and receive their own activity predictions. This extends ASD beyond the visible speakers by allowing the model to determine whether a registered speaker is speaking even when visual observations are entirely unavailable. When visual evidence is available, the registered identity can additionally be associated with the corresponding face. We conduct experiments across five ASD benchmarks to evaluate inter-face contextual reasoning, robustness to missing target-track observations, and speaker registration. ROAM-ASD-C consistently improves ROAM-ASD across all five benchmarks, with larger gains in crowded, difficult, and visually degraded conditions, and when the target candidate’s own observations are incomplete. ROAM-ASD-CR further preserves standard face-level ASD performance while enabling registered-speaker activity detection when visual observations are entirely unavailable. The main contributions are: • We introduce ROAM-ASD-C, which extends ROAM-ASD from independent face-track prediction to inter-face contextual reasoning among simultaneously visible candidates. • ROAM-ASD-C consistently improves ROAM-ASD across five ASD benchmarks, achieving new SOTA performance of 96.8%96.8\%, 98.9%98.9\%, 88.8%88.8\%, 98.7%98.7\%, and 99.5%99.5\% mAP on AVA, WASD, UniTalk, Talkies, and ASW, respectively. The gains become larger under more challenging and crowded conditions. Examples are available athttps://wangpuup.github.io/ROAM-ASD-C/crowds.html. • ROAM-ASD-C improves robustness to incomplete target-track observations. Under 75%75\% visual evidence removal, it improves over ROAM-ASD by 3.13.1, 8.88.8, 13.313.3, and 10.710.7 mAP on AVA, WASD, UniTalk, and ASW, respectively. Examples are available at https://wangpuup.github.io/ROAM-ASD-C/modality.html. • We introduce ROAM-ASD-CR, which extends ASD beyond the question “which visible person is speaking?” to “is this registered person speaking, and which visible face corresponds to that identity?” Speaker registration provides the identity cue that conventional face-level ASD lacks when visual correspondence is unavailable, enabling ASD beyond the currently visible scene.

papers.title: Analytical Modeling of Latency and Energy Trade-offs in FiRa-Like BLE-UWB Ranging and Localization Systems
papers.abstract: Accurate position and distance information provided by Ultra-Wideband (UWB) can enhance a wide range of applications. However, its receive-mode power consumption makes continuous channel monitoring impractical for energy-constrained devices. Consequently, UWB systems often rely on Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to discover peers and establish sessions before ranging begins. Although both technologies have been studied in isolation, an framework capturing the latency and energy consumption of the complete workflow is still lacking. To address this gap, we develop a unified analytical model for BLE-assisted UWB systems, from device-to-device ranging to infrastructure-based localization. The model includes closed-form expressions for discovery, parameter exchange, and ranging, and evaluates the resulting latency and energy consumption. Evaluation of three representative BLE configurations shows that the scanner consumes 28-57x more energy per discovery than the advertiser. In addition, the 99th-percentile discovery latency is 2-3.4x higher than the mean and reaches up to 110 s in the lowest-power configuration. The one-time BLE setup overhead is amortized after 24-562 ranging rounds, depending on the discovery configuration. Overall, the analysis demonstrates that the BLE discovery phase can dominate both the latency and the energy budget during short UWB interactions, making discovery configuration as important as the ranging scheme.

papers.title: DJustify: Reason-and-Verify DJ Planning for Pop Transitions and Story-Driven Sets
papers.abstract: Automatic DJ systems mostly target electronic dance music, whose regular structure makes rule-based mixing relatively easier. Vocal-rich popular music is harder: which track to play next, where to cue it, and which transition to use are tied together, so fixed rules handle them poorly. We present DJustify, a pop AI-DJ that puts an LLM in a reason--propose--verify--repair loop and lets it choose the next track, cue points, and mixing technique together. The LLM samples several transition plans; an external acoustic checker then scores the rendered audio and triggers repair when a check fails. Sampling keeps several candidate transitions per track pair instead of one fixed mix. In blind listening tests our transitions beat Mosaikbox, a reimplemented crossfade, and a cue baseline that reuses the crossfade's cues; that last comparison shows most of the margin comes from cue placement. The same planner also picks and orders a set along an emotion arc: this improves story coherence over a no-story ablation, and within a set story and transition ratings show no measurable gap from a human DJ. The checker mainly adds reliability, not higher average quality: it repairs rare but audible errors such as cut vocals, while the planner stays non-deterministic.

papers.title: Quantifying Meaning with SCAPE-T: Semantic Complexity from Encoder-Only Transformer Attention
papers.abstract: Automated semantic complexity estimation remains underexplored in NLP, despite important applications in linguistics and interpretability. This paper defines semantic complexity as the code length required to uniquely specify a text's semantic meaning, and operationalises it via SCAPE-T, an attention-derived metric based on encoder-only transformers. Existing measures either model reader effort (readability, lexical difficulty), which correlates with surface features (word length, syntax), or quantify surface features directly (type-token ratio, word frequency). SCAPE-T targets semantic integration directly by combining three submetrics: (i) inverse-weighted self-focus (token-to-self), (ii) CLS focus (token-to-CLS), and (iii) inter-head redundancy (cosine similarity across heads), using layer-weighted aggregation; data-driven learning is confined to hyperparameter tuning for calibration. Development uses philosophical prose vs. MCTest stories; evaluation is on children's stories vs. technical Wikipedia articles, with pairwise accuracy on contrasts as the primary criterion. Baselines include readability, syntactic/lexical, and LLM-derived measures. SCAPE-T substantially outperforms all tested baselines under word-length control, with a pairwise accuracy of 78.5% (95% bootstrap CI: 76.1-80.4, N=10k pairwise comparisons; +12.7 percentage points over the strongest baseline); without that control, readability heuristics overtake, consistent with their reliance on surface features. On a short-terms abstractness dataset, SCAPE-T also leads. Ablations show each submetric contributes materially. Overall, the results show SCAPE-T isolates conceptual structure from lexical/syntactic confounds better than existing methods, and generalises across two held-out domains.

papers.title: HA-DiPO: Diffusion Policy Optimization for Heterogeneous Cooperative Transport
papers.abstract: Cooperative transport with heterogeneous legged robots requires coordinating different motion capabilities while supporting an unfixed shared payload. We present HA-DiPO (Heterogeneous-Agent Diffusion Policy Optimization), a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE). The framework decouples team-level coordination from embodiment-specific motion control: at the high level, a centralized critic uses team-value estimates to jointly train independent coordination policies, aligning robot-specific action responses with a shared transport objective; at the low level, embodiment-specific robust motion policies track the coordination commands. The high-level diffusion policies offer more flexible action distributions than single-Gaussian parameterizations, allowing potentially multimodal coordination responses to be represented. The coordination policies learn from scratch through reward-driven simulator interaction without demonstrations. At execution, each robot generates coordination commands using only local robot and payload observations, without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages. Simulation comparisons show that HA-DiPO achieves higher final mean returns and velocity-tracking success rates, as well as lower velocity errors, than the evaluated baselines. Real-world experiments further demonstrate quadrupedal-wheeled-legged and human-robot cooperative transport.

papers.title: Wave-branch classification of ideal MHD discontinuities in Q-variables
papers.abstract: The $Q$-variable formalism combines velocity and magnetic field into branches aligned with a selected MHD wave. For homogeneous ideal MHD, appropriate choices of the branch parameter $\alpha$ correspond to the fast, Alfv\'en, and slow characteristic families, with the background variables $\boldsymbol{Q}_0^{\pm}$ representing the propagation direction and speed of the corresponding characteristics. In structured plasmas, $\alpha$ may instead be selected from the dispersion relation of a global mode such as a kink wave. Recent work reformulated the ideal-MHD Rankine-Hugoniot conditions in $Q$-variables and established their exact equivalence with the classical conservative jump conditions. Here, we apply this formulation to the standard ideal-MHD discontinuity catalogue. We determine how the two discontinuity-frame branches $\boldsymbol{Q}^{\prime+}$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}^{\prime-}$, their sums, and their $\alpha$-normalised differences are constrained across contact, tangential, and rotational discontinuities and across the principal shock families. Material interfaces are distinguished by their normal branch content, rotational discontinuities by an Alfv\'enic tangential relation, and fast, slow, and intermediate shocks by the magnitude or orientation of the $\alpha$-normalised tangential branch difference. Perpendicular, parallel, switch-on, and switch-off shocks appear as geometrical or limiting cases. The resulting classification expresses the classical discontinuity conditions in a wave-aligned form and, through the characteristic interpretation of $\boldsymbol{Q}_0^{\pm}$, shows how ideal-MHD discontinuities constrain changes in characteristic propagation direction and speed across the interface. It therefore establishes the background interface structure required for subsequent studies of reflection, transmission, coupling, and mode conversion.

papers.title: Population-average trajectories and slopes in smooth random changepoint mixed models
papers.abstract: Two-slope mixed-effects models with subject-specific changepoints are widely used to describe biphasic longitudinal trajectories. Treatment-arm summaries are often reported using a single "typical subject" curve obtained by plugging mean parameter values into the subject-specific model. This can be misleading when changepoint timing varies across individuals, because averaging subject-specific curves is not the same as evaluating one curve at average parameter values. A related issue is that individual trajectories may bend gradually rather than change slope through a literal kink, with transition sharpness varying between subjects. We propose population-average estimands for two-slope mixed models with random changepoints and smooth subject-level transitions. These estimands target the treatment-arm mean trajectory and instantaneous slope by averaging over fitted heterogeneity in changepoint timing and transition sharpness. We use a baseline-anchored normal-convolution soft hinge, which preserves the broken stick interpretation, includes the abrupt changepoint model as a limiting case, and allows analytic evaluation of the changepoint-marginalized kernels under a truncated normal changepoint distribution for fixed transition sharpness. Averaging over the fitted transition sharpness distribution is then performed by deterministic one-dimensional quadrature. In an application to HIV-1 RNA data from ACTG Protocol 315, with censoring and heavy-tailed residuals, the marginal summaries reveal a more gradual population-level transition than conventional plug-in summaries. The marginal slope remains more negative for longer, and the marginal mean continues to decline after the plug-in curve has begun to flatten. These results illustrate the main reporting implication: in random changepoint models, representative subject curves should not be treated as population-average trajectories or slopes.

papers.title: Robust Single-Parameter Point Cloud Registration using Truncated Lp Functions
papers.abstract: We propose a novel method for robust point cloud registration with only one tunable parameter. Our method, dubbed TLP, uses truncated $L_p$ functions with different values of $p$ to assign priority scores to correspondences, select the hypothesis, and refine the final model. By leveraging the robustness of truncated functions, TLP effectively handles the high outlier rates commonly encountered in real-world 3D feature matching. We also exploit GPU parallelization to evaluate hypotheses efficiently, enabling registration from thousands of correspondences in under a second on average. With only one tunable parameter, our method offers greater practicality than multi-parameter methods that require dataset-specific tuning of several parameters. Evaluations on public benchmark datasets demonstrate that TLP achieves higher accuracy than state-of-the-art single-parameter methods. Furthermore, it outperforms two widely used multi-parameter methods on three of the four evaluated datasets while maintaining competitive runtime.

papers.title: Mapping the Milky Way with SDSS-V: Galactic Genesis Selection Function and Mock Catalog
papers.abstract: Robust chemodynamic mapping of the Milky Way requires accounting for the selection function of the survey used, the probability that a given star is included in the final catalog as a function of its observable properties. We derive the empirical selection function of the SDSS-V Galactic Genesis survey, the largest Milky Way Mapper program targeting red giant stars for Galactic structure studies. Treating the Galactic Genesis sample as a subsample of its 2MASS parent catalog, we model the selection function as a function of sky position, apparent H magnitude, and G-H color using a Bayesian binomial estimator, computing both a mean and maximum a posteriori (MAP) version. The resulting selection function reflects the survey's targeting strategy and observing history, including the transition from the pencil-beam SDSS-IV footprint to the fuller sky coverage of SDSS-V and the prioritization of the Magellanic Clouds. Using this selection function with the FIRE-2 Milky Way-mass simulations, we construct mock Galactic Genesis catalogs built on existing mock Gaia DR3 catalogs, injecting realistic photometric noise and applying the selection function via a per-star Bernoulli accept-reject procedure. We demonstrate the mock catalogs' utility with an example application to azimuthal metallicity variations in the disk. Furthermore, we release a Python package allowing users to recompute the selection function for their own samples and science cases. The package, selection function and mock catalogs will be updated and made available as the survey continues, extending the tools needed to reach the full scientific potential of SDSS-V Galactic Genesis.

papers.title: Physical Layer Security in Chirp Permuted AFBM
papers.abstract: We propose a physical-layer security scheme for affine filter bank modulation (AFBM), a waveform proposed for sixth-generation (6G) integrated sensing and communications (ISAC). AFBM contains two discrete affine Fourier transforms, one for precoding and one for spreading, and the scheme permutes, with one secret key per transform, the chirp sequence that each transform places between two Fourier stages. A wrong key is then conjugated by a discrete Fourier transform into a dense matrix, the restoration of complex orthogonality fails, and the intrinsic filter-bank interference reaches the detector. Over a doubly-dispersive channel, an eavesdropper with perfect channel state information, co-located with the legitimate receiver and holding either key wrong, keeps a bit error rate near 0.5 and a rate below 0.09 bit/symbol, also under a blind carrier-phase attack. Compared with a single-permutation variant, the double scheme costs about 2 dB of peak-to-average power ratio and enlarges the search space from 10^61 to 10^93.

papers.title: Wireless Signal Point Processes with a Reflecting Wall
papers.abstract: A long reflecting wall gives every wireless transmitter a mirror image, pairing its direct and reflected paths. Motivated by intelligent surfaces, we study the resulting signal point processes under two treatments: keeping the powers apart and superposing their point processes, or adding the powers transmitter by transmitter to form a recombined process. A threshold on inverse received power selects a region of transmitter locations, so Campbell's theorem reduces the mean measures to area calculations without assuming Poisson transmitters. For power-law path loss and paired fading marks, we derive the ratio of the recombined and superposed mean measures at large thresholds. The limit is independent of transmitter density and wall distance, but generally depends on the joint fading distribution. Under common fading, that dependence disappears and the limit depends only on the reflection coefficient and path-loss exponent. For Poisson transmitters, we derive paired count fluctuations and convergence of the count ratio. We also calculate the probability that the strongest individual path is direct. When the wall passes through the receiver, this probability has a closed form and the strongest received power has an exact Fr\'echet distribution. These results provide a reference model for wireless networks with reflecting surfaces.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Parkinson's Disease Classification from Resting-State Functional Connectivity
papers.abstract: Altered resting-state functional connectivity (FC) is a candidate marker for the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD). Publicly available PD datasets, however, are small and fragmented across sites, scanners and clinical criteria. Transfer learning mitigates data scarcity by reusing a model trained on larger cohorts, but represents their knowledge primarily through a single set of weights shared by all individuals. Motivated by precision neuroimaging, we propose a retrieval-augmented classification (RAC) framework that additionally places each target individual in the context of similar individuals from external cohorts. A graph convolutional autoencoder (GAE), trained on external PD and control cohorts, encodes these cohorts into a neuro-knowledge base. Each target individual is encoded using the pretrained GAE, and its nearest neighbors are retrieved from the external knowledge base. Their embeddings are combined with the target embedding using mean aggregation or attention for classification. A systematic comparison on the TaoWu cohort separated the contributions of encoder pretraining, retrieval, attention and partial fine-tuning. Pretraining improved mean classification accuracy from 60.5% to 66.0%. However, retrieval and attention did not consistently improve performance over the pretrained-only variants. Several retrieval-based configurations nevertheless showed modestly higher ROC-AUC than the randomly initialized baseline. Varying the number of retrieved neighbors and partially fine-tuning the encoder provided no consistent additional gains. Retrieval-neighborhood analysis further showed diagnostically mixed neighborhoods. These findings provide initial evidence that population-learned representations can be complemented by individual-specific retrieval in neuroimaging, although larger datasets are needed to determine when such contextual information improves classification.

papers.title: A nonstandard selfinjective algebra of Euclidean type
papers.abstract: Let $\Bbbk$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic different from $2$. We realize the four-dimensional selfinjective algebra $\Omega(1)$ as an admissible infinite cyclic orbit algebra of the repetitive Kronecker category. Thus an algebra long stated to be nonstandard is of Euclidean type in the orbit-algebra sense. We also identify a gap in an earlier proof of its nonstandardness and give an independent proof by determining all connected Galois covering sources of $\Omega(1)$. Together, these results disprove the implication from Euclidean type to standardness in the equivalence explicitly stated by Bocian--Holm--Skowro\'nski (2004) and Bocian--Skowro\'nski (2005). They also contradict the standardness conclusion of the Proposition in \S2.1 of Skowro\'nski (1989); its main theorem in \S1.5 assumes standardness and is not contradicted by this example.

A selfinjective algebra is of Euclidean type if and only if it is standard and representation-infinite domestic.

We use standardness in the sense of [12, §1.2]: an algebra is standard if it admits a Galois covering by a simply connected locally bounded category. papers.title: Energy cascades in atmospheric moist convection
papers.abstract: We analyze scale-by-scale budgets of velocity and buoyancy second-order structure functions using Large Eddy Simulation of the BOMEX trade-wind cumulus layer. The simulation utilizes a $10\,\mathrm{m}$ grid resolution under the anelastic approximation, incorporating moist thermodynamics to capture phase changes. The analysis of derived turbulence kinetic energy (TKE) and turbulence potential energy (TPE) budgets reveals four regions of distinct turbulence dynamics. For three of these regions, approximate balances holding over wide range of length scales are identified, highlighting the importance of interspace and pressure transport. Above the lifting condensation level ($\approx 800\,\mathrm{m}$), phase changes introduce forcing across all resolved scales, leading to an inverse TPE cascade spanning all scales. The TKE, inter-scale transfer is inverse above the vertical velocity integral length scale but below the horizontal velocity scale. In the upper cloud layer ($>1400\,\mathrm{m}$), forward inter-scale transfers are recovered despite ongoing phase changes. A phenomenological interpretation of these features, referring to the different formation stages of convective updrafts, is also proposed. Finally, 1D horizontal subsamples from the simulation show good agreement with recent airborne measurements, validating the numerical framework and confirming the departure of moist convective turbulence from standard energy cascade models.

papers.title: Global invertibility of polynomial mappings and connectedness of preimages of large spheres
papers.abstract: We prove that a polynomial mapping $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ with nowhere zero Jacobian determinant is a global diffeomorphism provided the preimage of large circles are connected. In higher dimensions this result fails and we present families of counterexamples. Yet, in dimension $3$, we prove that if the preimages of large spheres are connected, then the Jelonek set of the mapping is not homeomorphic to a line and, provided that it has codimension at least $2$, cannot have a single end at infinity.

papers.title: Evaluating Spiking MoveNet Deployability for Near-Future Onboard Spiking Satellite Pose Estimation
papers.abstract: SNNs are attracting interest due to their potential for energy efficiency and event-driven processing. However, neuromorphic hardware is not yet mature enough to enable embedded deployment of complex spiking network architectures. In this work, we investigate a spiking version of the MoveNet architecture tailored for autonomous spacecraft operation, aiming to evaluate the deployability of this complex architecture compared to the non-spiking version for embedded, fully event-based solutions in space applications. Using the RAPTOR dataset, we compare the performance and operational cost of the proposed S-MoveNet-Lightning architecture with its standard version, MoveNet-Lightning. Our results show balanced advantages in computational resources and architectural settings for spiking U-Net-like architectures. An evaluation of the performance and hardware footprint of the proposed Spiking Neural Network (SNN) approach for pose estimation shows that, on average, 2.2 times fewer multiplication and accumulation operations are required compared to the non-spiking solution deployed on FPGA platforms with the AMD Deep Learning Processor Unit (DPU). These results provide valuable insights into the feasibility and potential of SNNs in complex aerospace applications and highlight their role in balancing efficiency and performance, paving the way for event-driven solutions in embedded space applications.

papers.intro:
Targeting efficient on-board event-based solutions assisted by neural networks requires three key components: event-based datasets, event-based neural architectures, and neuromorphic hardware. Although the space industry has shown increasing interest in event-based applications, such as Earth-based Space Situational Awareness (SSA) systems [25], Earth Observation (EO) with the first satellite on-board SNN [37], event-based sensing applications [45], and event-based pose estimation [24], there are still few spacecraft pose estimation datasets and solutions, and even fewer for event-based approaches.

Targeting efficient on-board event-based solutions assisted by neural networks requires three key components: event-based datasets, event-based neural architectures, and neuromorphic hardware. Although the space industry has shown increasing interest in event-based applications, such as Earth-based Space Situational Awareness (SSA) systems [25], Earth Observation (EO) with the first satellite on-board SNN [37], event-based sensing applications [45], and event-based pose estimation [24], there are still few spacecraft pose estimation datasets and solutions, and even fewer for event-based approaches.

SEENIC [26] is the first event-based dataset for spacecraft pose estimation, comprising both synthetic and real event data acquired on a robotic test bench. Although this dataset is suitable for simple deep learning direct approaches [24], it remains challenging to use for complex or indirect machine learning approaches. The dataset has a limited variety of scenarios and a significant domain gap between the synthetically generated and real event data. SPADES [15] is another promising event-based dataset with mixed synthetic and real event data acquired on a robotic test bench, but it is still not available. Standard image datasets (grayscale, RGB, multispectral) released for pose estimation in the space industry mainly focus on reducing the domain gap between synthetic and real data. Some use a combination of synthetic and real images acquired on test benches, such as SPEED+ [31], which contains 60,000 synthetic and 9,531 real images. Designed to train Formal Neural Networks (FNNs), most standard pose estimation datasets are composed of independent 2D images, unlike event-based data, which preserves temporal correlation. This loss of temporal information penalises their use for time-correlated event-based networks such as Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs). As our main concern is operational cost behaviour rather than domain gap evaluation, and as no satisfactory event-based dataset is available, we decided to use the realistic RAPTOR dataset [14]. With over 120,000 synthetic images, the RAPTOR dataset was built using a physics-based simulator aimed at achieving a high level of realism.

Recent advancements in neuromorphic hardware, such as SPLEAT [37], Pulsar [38], Akida [33], and SynSense Speck [36], have shown promise for implementing Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) in various applications, including space systems. However, these neuromorphic devices remain in the research phase and face significant challenges. Many existing neuromorphic platforms do not support a range of network architectures or have specific workflows that complicate deployment, due to hardware limitations in their design, processing capabilities, or availability. Additionally, some of these systems, such as SynSense Speck, operate asynchronously, which can complicate integration into real-time and critical applications such as satellite pose estimation.

papers.title: WorldFailBench: Do World Models Understand Policy Failures?
papers.abstract: Robot policy evaluation informs deployment decisions and policy improvement, but physical testing and simulator preparation require substantial effort. World models offer a complementary route through closed-loop interaction in generated environments. Recent benchmarks have demonstrated their potential as policy evaluators through outcome-based evaluation (i.e., assessing task success or failure). However, such evaluation does not establish whether world models faithfully simulate how policies fail. Misrepresenting failures can lead to incorrect diagnoses of policy weaknesses and make policies appear ready for deployment even when small scene changes cause them to fail. We therefore ask: do world models faithfully simulate how and at which stages policies fail, and under what conditions they transition from success to failure? To answer this question, we introduce WorldFailBench with three evaluation tasks. Failure reason tests whether models reproduce the observable errors policies make. Failure stage assesses whether failures concentrate at the same stages of full-task execution. Failure boundary examines whether models reproduce the conditions under which policies transition from success to failure under controlled scene changes in simulation. The benchmark covers manipulation tasks in the LIBERO and RoboTwin simulation environments and real-world manipulation tasks performed by the G1 humanoid robot. Experiments across seven world models reveal substantial gaps in their understanding of policy failures, providing guidance for developing more reliable world models for policy evaluation.

papers.title: TCSP3.0: Template-Based Crystal Structure Prediction with Coefficient-Preserving Element Substitution and Structural Diversity
papers.abstract: Template-based crystal structure prediction (CSP) transfers a known crystal structure to a new composition by element substitution, so its accuracy depends on retrieving suitable templates, mapping elements and ranking the resulting candidates correctly. Auditing the original TCSP2.0 implementation on the T180 benchmark, we found that 469 of its 2,347 selected structures (20%) have the wrong composition, caused by element mappings that ignore stoichiometric coefficients and by sequential text substitution that cascades or corrupts element symbols. We propose TCSP3.0, which enforces coefficient-preserving mappings, substitutes species simultaneously on parsed structures and validates every candidate's composition and cell. It further adds periodic-number retrieval, soft oxidation-state evidence, radius-compatibility scoring, structural deduplication, and ORB-v3 machine-learning-potential relaxation and energy ranking of its candidates, as used by deep generative CSP baselines. TCSP3.0 achieves Top-1 and Top-20 match rates of 72.2% and 90.6% on T180, compared with 28.3% and 45.6% for TCSP2.0, and a Top-20 match rate of 74.0% on a new 800-target benchmark (T800). On T180 it also outperforms PNcsp+ and deep generative models CrystalFlow and MaskGXT (Top-1 72.2% versus at most 63.9%). Even without relaxation, TCSP3.0 reaches 67.8% at Top-1 and 90.6% at Top-20 in a median of 28 s per target on two CPU cores, about ten times faster than CrystalFlow. Paired ten-arm ablations on T180 and T800 show that most of the improvement comes from the correctness fixes; structural deduplication significantly improves the Top-5 match rate, embedding-based retrieval is required for coverage, and the remaining scoring features have small or null effects.

papers.title: Uniform observability criteria for linear time-varying systems
papers.abstract: Verifying uniform observability of a linear time-varying system generally requires its state-transition matrix. This paper develops necessary and sufficient conditions that can be checked directly from the coefficient matrices for two classes of systems. For constant dynamics with real spectrum and a measurable, essentially bounded output matrix, uniform observability is equivalent to persistent excitation of the output matrix on each eigenspace. An equivalent condition requires persistent excitation of the Kalman observability stack. The second result concerns cascades with a constant observable measured subsystem coupled to a hidden state. Under uniform regularity assumptions, linear combinations of output derivatives eliminate the measured state and yield an equivalent observability test for the hidden dynamics. When those dynamics have real spectrum, the test reduces to excitation on each eigenspace intersected with the kernel of the direct measurements. An application to arbitrary-order integrator chains with measurements of ranges to fixed anchors gives an exact excitation condition for the associated lifted LTV system. A second application treats direct hidden measurements and compares the condition with existing sufficient tests.

papers.title: Perceived Acceptability of Sensory Augmentation
papers.abstract: Sensory augmentation (SA) can extend how people perceive and engage with public environments through the body, offering opportunities to support shared multimodal experiences between deaf and hearing visitors. Designing such systems requires understanding which combinations of tactile stimuli and body locations users perceive as acceptable. We examined the perceived acceptability of fictitious yet feasible SA configurations in a museum use-case. Using a modified technology acceptance model, we surveyed 307 deaf and hearing participants about tactile stimulus types and body locations. The results showed significant effects of stimulus type and body location on acceptance, but no interactions with hearing status. Participants generally preferred temperature-based stimuli, subtle movement, texture, and tickling over vibration, and distal over proximal body locations. These findings suggest that tactile SA design should be guided primarily by embodied and contextual factors rather than hearing status, informing future systems for shared multimodal experience in public cultural settings.

papers.title: A frequency-resolved measurement of the scattering law in FRB 20210415C
papers.abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) show diverse temporal morphologies, shaped both by their intrinsic emission and by propagation effects such as residual dispersion and multipath scattering. Because several of these effects can broaden a burst asymmetrically, an asymmetric profile does not by itself establish multipath scattering. We measure the frequency dependence of the temporal tail in FRB 20210415C, a bright burst from the repeating source FRB 20210219C. The burst is detected across approximately 400-800 MHz. Frequency-resolved fits yield an empirical exponential-tail timescale, $\tau_{\rm emp}$, that follows $\tau_{\rm emp}\propto\nu^{\alpha}$. Two complementary treatments of the underlying pulse width give $\alpha=-3.95\pm0.07$ and $-4.14\pm0.08$. Both results are consistent with the commonly adopted $\nu^{-4}$ scattering law. The inferred scattering time is approximately 8.0 ms at 583 MHz, exceeding Galactic foreground estimates by a factor of at least $4\times10^{2}$. This favours a dominant contribution beyond the Milky Way, although the data do not localise the scattering screen. FRB 20210415C therefore provides a direct measurement of a scattering law commonly imposed in catalogue analyses.

papers.title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
papers.abstract: Many decision-making tasks are inherently multi-objective. Interactive evolutionary multi-objective optimization algorithms (iEMOAs) are particularly well-suited to help the decision-maker find their most preferred solution. However, many of these algorithms employ black-box preference models. For high-stakes decision-making tasks, like healthcare and defense, a high level of transparency is needed, for instance to support accountability. We propose an interpretable iEMOA which uses active learning to efficiently learn a tree-based preference model directly from pairwise comparisons. The survival operator of NSGA-II and NSGA-III is extended with the learned preference model to guide the algorithm towards the region of interest. An extensive experimental study compares the proposed method to a state-of-the-art black-box model and a state-of-the-art interpretable model. Results indicate that our proposed model outperforms the alternatives in terms of finding the most preferred solution at the cost of a slightly worse average final population. Finally, a case study on a real-life engineering problem illustrates how inspecting the learned model reveals which objectives drive the decision-maker's preferences.

papers.title: The Conditional Value of Costly Information in Collective-Risk Dilemmas
papers.abstract: Many high-stakes collective problems, e.g., climate mitigation and pandemic response, share a structure in which risk materializes unless a group threshold is met. This threshold is often uncertain, but uncertainty can be reduced at a cost. We study this information cost tradeoff in an evolutionary game theoretic model of social learning in the collective-risk dilemma, where individuals must cooperate to reach a possibly uncertain threshold to prevent collective loss. Individuals may pay a fixed cost to observe the threshold's true value and condition their cooperation on it. Across four threshold priors, we characterize risk levels at which cooperative equilibria emerge and show that low cost information increases group success. However, this effect is reversed at higher costs. We define a private \emph{value of information} and show that information is worth buying only when it is considerably cheaper than contributing. When purchased information is shared with the group, the cooperative tipping point shifts to lower risk levels. Despite bearing a private cost, above this tipping point buyers earn more in expectation than information free-riders. We then study these dynamics when information diffuses through a network, allowing nodes to relay it. Although fewer individuals pay for information, relaying increases group success, and noisy relaying does not reduce it. By contrast, false information does, especially when it originates at the hubs of heterogeneous networks, and large attacks can bring collective action close to collapse. Buyers act as a firewall against disinformation, confining it to source neighbourhoods, and once disinformation sources are removed, the population recovers. The value of costly information thus depends on its price, the level of risk, and how it is shared, and, in our setting, the effort of acquiring it also protects the population against disinformation.

papers.title: Automorphisms of $\mathbb{P}^1$-bundles over rational surfaces in positive characteristic
papers.abstract: We study $\mathbb{P}^1$-bundles over smooth projective rational surfaces over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>0$, together with the actions of their neutral automorphism groups. After an equivariant square birational reduction to the projective plane or a Hirzebruch surface, we classify the possible induced actions on the base and identify the families relevant to relative maximality. For $p\geq 3$, we prove that every such $\mathbb{P}^1$-bundle is equivariantly square birational to one whose neutral automorphism group is relatively maximal, and we classify all bundles with this property. We also describe all equivariant square birational maps between these relatively maximal bundles and determine which are stiff or superstiff, the analogues of rigidity and superrigidity for $\mathbb{P}^1$-bundles.

papers.title: Accurate measurement of Lithium Tantalate birefringence in whispering gallery resonators
papers.abstract: Lithium Tantalate (LTA) is an important ferroelectric crystal widely used in piezoelectric, electro-optic, and nonlinear optical devices. Although this crystal is very common, there is an ongoing debate regarding its birefringence magnitude, and even its sign. While some sources claim it to be negative, others maintain that it is positive. The issue is further complicated by the sample-to-sample variation in the crystal composition, ranging from congruent to stoichiometric. Here we report the experimental exploration of this question based on high-resolution spectroscopy of optical whispering gallery resonators fabricated from this crystal. These sensitive measurements unambiguously indicate that in the near-infrared range at room temperature the stoichiometric LTA is negative, while the congruent LTA is positive.

papers.title: Rethinking Multi-View Fusion for Urban Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Urban region representation learning encodes heterogeneous urban signals, such as mobility flows, points of interest, and land-use patterns, into unified embeddings for downstream tasks, including check-in prediction, crime forecasting, and service demand estimation. Existing approaches rely on globally shared fusion and joint optimization, implicitly assuming uniform modality importance and naturally balanced multi-objective training. However, urban data is inherently heterogeneous. Our empirical analysis reveals two structural issues: (i) modality utility varies markedly across regions, causing static fusion to overemphasize signals from certain modalities; and (ii) heterogeneous objectives exhibit persistent gradient imbalance, causing representational bias and unstable training. We present PRISM, a self-adjusting framework for adaptive multi-view learning. PRISM adapts sparse MoE routing to learn region-specific view allocations, while a PID (Proportional Integral Derivative)-inspired regulation mechanism mitigates gradient conflicts during optimization. Experiments on three large-scale urban datasets show that PRISM achieves competitive performance compared with strong multi-view baselines, while providing more stable optimization behavior and more balanced region representations.
