Cities are increasingly instrumented with sensing and digital infrastructures that continuously generate heterogeneous data from mobility networks, land-use registries, transportation systems, and socio-economic activities (Xu et al., 2025a). This data provides unprecedented opportunities for understanding urban dynamics. Yet, heterogeneity in terms of structure, granularity, noise ratio, and spatial coverage poses fundamental data integration and computational modeling challenges.

Urban region representation learning has emerged as a principled abstraction for addressing these challenges (Duan et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2027). Transforming diverse urban signals into compact embeddings enables computational models that capture latent spatial functionality and inter-region relationships in a unified vector form. These embeddings serve as reusable, transferable representations that support a wide range of analytical tasks, including check-in prediction (Liang and Zhang, 2023; Gong et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2025), crime forecasting (Butt et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2023), traffic modeling (Zhang et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2021b; Yang et al., 2022a; Yang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2027; Yang et al., 2021a; Yang et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2022b; Wei et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025b; Yang and Yang, 2020), and service demand estimation (Sun et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025a).

Structured multi-view fusion. Existing approaches treat each urban modality—such as mobility flow graphs, POI distributions, or land-use maps—as an independent structured signal that is encoded using graph or attribute-based models. Representative methods (e.g., MGFN (Wu et al., 2022), HAFusion (Sun et al., 2024), CGAP (Xu and Zhou, 2024)) jointly learn representations from multiple modalities and fuse them by means of concatenation, attention, or weighted aggregation. More recent studies extend this paradigm to cross-modal settings by incorporating additional sources such as street-view images (e.g., FlexiReg (Sun et al., 2025a)). While being architecturally diverse, these methods adopt a shared abstraction: heterogeneous views are integrated via globally shared fusion mechanisms under deterministic parameterization.

Multi-view urban representation learning typically introduces modality-specific objectives that guide the shared embedding towards distinct structural or semantic properties. These objectives are then jointly optimized within a unified parameter space without explicit coordination. Although general multi-task strategies (e.g., gradient normalization or projection) have been explored in other domains, they assume task symmetry and do not account for the spatially heterogeneous and modality-dependent dynamics intrinsic to urban data.

Despite their methodological variations, existing approaches rely on two implicit assumptions: (i) modality importance is spatially consistent across regions, and (ii) joint optimization of heterogeneous objectives naturally produces coordinated and balanced representations.

Motivating example. To evaluate these assumptions, we analyze on three city-scale datasets (see Figure 1). Figure 1a highlights task-dependent differences in modality utility: mobility signals are most informative for crime prediction, whereas land-use and POI features are more useful for service call prediction, suggesting differing underlying spatial dynamics. Notably, as highlighted by the red dashed oval, POI and land-use features contribute negligibly to the SF Crime task. This pronounced heterogeneity challenges the assumption of globally uniform fusion across modalities. Figure 1b further reveals a systematic optimization imbalance under conventional joint training (e.g., the red dashed oval). Gradients associated with different modality-specific objectives exhibit persistent magnitude disparities, allowing dominant modalities to steer the shared embedding space while suppressing weaker yet informative signals. Such imbalance induces representational bias and ultimately degrades cross-region generalization.

Following this analysis, we identify two coupled research challenges that remain unresolved in urban region representation learning:

Challenge 1 (C1): Spatially adaptive view integration. The predictive utility of each modality is inherently region-dependent, and yet existing fusion mechanisms assign contributions through globally shared parameters. This mismatch between local data characteristics and global fusion strategies incurs representational bias—commercial regions may be well-served while residential regions may be systematically under-represented. The challenge is to enable region-aware, adaptive modality selection that aligns representation capacity with spatial heterogeneity, without requiring region-specific supervision.

The challenge is to enable region-aware, adaptive modality selection that aligns representation capacity with spatial heterogeneity, without requiring region-specific supervision.

Challenge 2 (C2): Coordinated optimization under heterogeneous objectives. When multiple modality-specific objectives with different gradient scales, noise levels, and convergence rates are jointly optimized in a shared embedding space, objectives associated with certain modalities may contribute disproportionately large or more stable gradients, causing them to dominate the optimization process and suppress weaker modality signals, which in turn leads to imbalanced representations and unstable training. The challenge is to explicitly regulate the interplay among competing objectives so that all informative modalities contribute proportionally to the final representation.

papers.title: Higher Reasoning Effort Improves Reference Verifiability and Changes Reasoning Summaries in GPT-5.5
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly being used in different stages of scientific knowledge production, including the suggestion of references. These models can operate at different levels of reasoning effort and provide summaries of their reasoning processes. This raises two questions: Does increasing reasoning effort improve the verifiability of generated references, and do the resulting reasoning summaries reveal how the model's behavior changes with greater effort? We examined summaries from GPT-5.5 as it generated scholarly references for 1,000 papers under paired low- and high-effort settings. Generated references were matched to external bibliographic records, and reasoning summaries were scored for four predefined features and explored for additional features discovered by GPT-5.5. High effort increased the mean paper-level resolver-verified reference rate from 78.3% to 84.8%, and produced longer reasoning summaries. All four predefined features received higher scores under high effort. The discovered features changed less uniformly: some appeared equally often in both conditions, whereas others were more common under high effort. Within each effort condition, neither feature set showed a consistent increase in verification rates with higher scores.

papers.title: Complexity-guided Regularization for Generalizable Human Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Recent studies on generalizable human Gaussian splatting have achieved the notable progress in synthesizing novel views of unseen human subjects from multi-view images. Despite this progress, existing methods still struggle to represent fine-grained details of human subjects, which inherently involve high geometric and textural complexity. This is because previous methods do not impose a constraint on how densely Gaussians are placed, which often leads to blurry rendering results in complex regions. To address this problem, we propose a complexity-guided regularization scheme. The key idea is to leverage a complexity prior computed via the local entropy in geometric and textural characteristics of a clothed human. This effectively prevents Gaussians from being coarsely placed in complex regions, which facilitates the faithful reconstruction of intricate structures. Furthermore, we sample local patches predominantly from complex regions according to this complexity prior, which allows the model to be sufficiently supervised by local details. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method delivers state-of-the-art performance while maintaining the real-time inference speed in generalizable human Gaussian splatting. The code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/DCVL-3D/CGR-GS_release.

papers.title: Dynamic heart rate variability for classification of arrhythmia burden
papers.abstract: Purpose: Heart rate variability (HRV) may provide information beyond heart rate (HR) for identifying arrhythmia burden, but the value of temporal HRV variation remains unclear. This study developed a dynamic HRV measure quantifying the interquartile range of window-level root mean square of successive RR-interval differences (IQRRMSSD) and evaluated its utility in classifying total abnormal-beat and premature ventricular contraction (PVC) burden compared with the conventional RR-based HRV measure, RMSSD. Methods: Manually annotated 30-minute ECG recordings from 43 individuals were analyzed using overlapping windows. A linear support vector classifier was used to classify individuals as having high or low arrhythmia burden, defined using 1% and 10% burden thresholds. Four feature sets were evaluated: HR alone, HR with RMSSD, HR with IQRRMSSD, and all three measures. Performance was assessed using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation. Results: HRV-containing feature sets generally outperformed HR alone, depending on outcome and threshold. At the 1% threshold, IQRRMSSD showed particularly high sensitivity for total abnormal-beat and PVC burden ($0.970 \pm 0.064$ and $0.882 \pm 0.193$, respectively). At the 10% threshold, conventional RMSSD showed the strongest overall discrimination, achieving a ROC-AUC of 0.947 for PVC burden. Combined features sometimes improved the sensitivity-specificity balance but not overall discrimination. Conclusion: These findings suggest that a conventional RR-based HRV measure is informative for elevated ectopic burden, while a dynamic HRV measure may provide complementary information for lower-burden abnormalities.

papers.title: A curated multi-endpoint drug-protein bioactivity dataset with construct-aware protein targets
papers.abstract: Public drug-protein bioactivity resources commonly identify targets by UniProt accession, although one accession may represent distinct experimental sequences. We present Curate-DTI, a construct-aware dataset derived from the 1 July 2026 BindingDB export, with IC50, Ki, Kd and EC50 processed independently. The release contains 2,919,717 measurements, 1,291,872 standardized ligands, 9,668 sequence-defined protein entities and 2,275,683 endpoint-specific interactions spanning 8,336 reviewed UniProt accessions. Protein entities combine the accession with the reported experimental sequence, preserving constructs that accession-only processing would merge. Across the four endpoints, 4,204 endpoint-specific ligand-accession groups showed different classification labels across sequence-defined protein entities. Exact and inequality-qualified observations provide relation-aware classification evidence, whereas regression targets use exact values only. Connected Parquet tables preserve individual measurements, standardized structures, protein sequences, aggregated interactions and available assay and source provenance. The resource supports endpoint-specific classification and regression while allowing users to select molecular representations, protein representations and evaluation splits. Preprocessing code, a column dictionary, exclusion reports and validation summaries accompany the release.

papers.title: On the isomorphism of the spaces $\mathcal{k}$ and $\mathcal{K}$
papers.abstract: Let $1 \leqslant p \leqslant q < \infty$, let $\mathsf{X}$ be a separable $\mathcal{L}_p$-space and let $\mathsf{Y}$ be a separable $\mathcal{L}_q$-space. We show that the space $\mathfrak{L}(\mathsf{X},\mathsf{Y})$ of bounded linear operators from $\mathsf{X}$ into $\mathsf{Y}$ is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{L}(\ell_p,\ell_q)$ if, and only if, $\mathsf{Y}$ is complemented in its bidual. We also show that $\mathfrak{L}(\mathsf{Z},\ell_{\infty})$ is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{L}(c_0,\ell_{\infty})$ for every separable $\mathcal{L}_{\infty}$-space $\mathsf{Z}$. This extends and complements the earlier result of Arias and Farmer [On the structure of tensor products of $\ell_p$-spaces, Pacific J. Math.]. Based on this general result, we give a completely different proof of the main result of Astashkin, Le\'snik and Maligranda [Isomorphic structure of Ces\`aro and Tandori spaces, Canad. J. Math.], which states that the space $\mathcal{K}$ and its sequence counterpart $\mathcal{k}$ are isomorphic. Furthermore, we complete the picture by showing that the spaces $\mathcal{k}$ and $\mathcal{K}$, although isomorphic, are not isometric. Along the way, we show that for every infinite compact metrizable space $K$ the $\ell_{\infty}$-sum of copies of the space $\mathscr{M}(K)$ of regular Borel measures on $K$ is isomorphic to $( \bigoplus_{n=1}^{\infty} L_1[0,1])_{\ell_{\infty}} \approx \mathfrak{L}(\ell_1,L_1[0,1])$. This provides an abstract blueprint for another result of Astashkin, Le\'snik and Maligranda, namely that $\mathcal{K}$ is isomorphic to $( \bigoplus_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathscr{M}[0,1])_{\ell_{\infty}}$. Finally, we show that there are models of set theory without the Axiom of Choice in which the spaces $\mathcal{k}$ and $\mathcal{K}$ are no longer isomorphic. This last part was inspired by V\"ath's paper [The dual space of $L_{\infty}$ is $L_1$, Indag. Math. (N.S.)].

papers.title: Revisiting Direct Control: A Field Evaluation of Sensor Fusion Efficacy in Teleoperating Full-Scale Autonomous Vehicles via Bird's Eye View
papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, robot teleoperation serves as a critical safety fallback mechanism, requiring operators to assume direct control in the event of system failure. While recent research has pivoted toward high-level supervisory control or simulation-based studies, these approaches often fail to capture the physical dynamics and sensory demands of driving a full-scale vehicle. To address this gap, we evaluated the impact of spatial data representation on operator performance using a real car-sized vehicle in a field experiment with $N = 18$ participants. We compared three visualization interfaces: (i) a standard camera feed baseline, with two bird's-eye views (BEV) from (ii) a raw LiDAR point cloud, and (iii) a sensor fusion of LiDAR and camera data streams. Contrary to prior passive observation studies suggesting that sensor-fusion BEV may hinder awareness, our active-control results demonstrate that such representation significantly outperforms the standard LiDAR BEV in perceived usability ($p \leq 0.0001$) and cognitive task load ($p = 0.01$, NASA-TLX score: 34.58/100) while also being significantly better than the Camera-only view ($p = 0.043$). The fused interface also led to statistically significant reductions in task completion time ($p = 0.0461$) and superior usability (SUS: 77.9/100) compared to those of the Camera-only and LiDAR-only views. By synthesizing objective performance data with comprehensive subjective assessments, we demonstrate that BEV fusion maximizes safety margins while minimizing the operator's mental demand. These findings challenge existing teleoperation conventions and provide an empirically validated approach for designing robust remote piloting systems.

papers.title: Reducing the Uncertainty in Determining the Origin of Natural Commodities via Earth Embeddings
papers.abstract:
Verifying where commodities like timber were harvested is a forensic task, needed to detect illegal trade due to illegal deforestation or trade sanctions. Existing Gaussian-process models of wood chemistry give a Bayesian posterior
  over candidate harvest locations, but their credible regions in general do not deliver
  the coverage they promise (0.82-0.91 at the nominal 95\%). In this work we bring in a
  second, independent source of evidence: a prior over harvest locations learned
  from satellite (AlphaEarth) embeddings. We fit one classifier per genus that predicts presence from an embedding vector, supervised by occurrence records, and normalize its scores into a prior over the candidate grid. For
  such a prior to act on the prediction sets rather than merely mask cells, we
  build a cross-conformal predictor on the \emph{posterior cell mass}, so the
  prior moves every p-value while the coverage guarantee survives any
  misspecification of it. On four European genera, the embedding prior shrinks
  regions by up to 42\% compared to a uniform prior at no cost in coverage, which holds at 0.953-0.968
  against a nominal 0.95.

papers.title: Harnessing Electrostructural Bistability to Control Defects in Polarizable Materials
papers.abstract: Structural defects are central to the functionalities of materials. However, conventional approaches to defect control are often slow and imprecise. This work identifies and characterizes a distinct physical phenomenon of electrostructural bistability that provides a rapid and precise pathway for engineering materials with defect-controlled physical properties. A generalized theory of conductivity bistability is developed and experimentally validated to unify two distinct regimes: previously reported electrothermal bistability in weakly polarizable insulators, such as silicon, and electrostructural bistability in strongly polarizable materials, such as TiO$_2$. In agreement with the theory, experiments on TiO$_2$ demonstrate that bulk-homogeneous defect concentrations in electrostructurally bistable materials can be tuned rapidly and deterministically by controlling applied electric current. Abruptly interrupting the current quenches the system into long-lived, room-temperature metastable states with distinct properties. This establishes a practical, rapid, and scalable pathway for defect engineering with direct relevance to nonvolatile memory devices.

papers.title: RobotAgentBench: Towards Open-world Robot Autonomy
papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) have significantly improved robotic manipulation, yet deploying robots in the open world demands a higher level of autonomy beyond executing predefined tasks. Robot agents offer a promising paradigm for this transition, integrating task discovery, contextual reasoning, physical execution, and adaptive recovery into a closed interaction loop. However, existing benchmarks largely evaluate isolated capabilities, failing to capture the complexity of open-world robot autonomy. We introduce RobotAgentBench (RAB), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating robot agents in realistic, open-world household environments. Through an agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline, RAB constructs 50 diverse household layouts with interactive objects and physically grounded tasks, encompassing 90 atomic tasks, 18 short-horizon tasks, 8 long-horizon tasks, and 4 open-ended scenarios. RAB provides a multi-level evaluation of robot agent capabilities: (1) task-level assessments systematically examine five complementary dimensions: task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and robustness; (2) scenario-level evaluation assesses how agents integrate these capabilities to autonomously fulfill high-level user needs. Furthermore, RAB enables systematic comparisons of standalone VLA/WAM models and diverse robot agent architectures under a unified planning-execution-verification framework. Extensive experiments reveal substantial gaps between manipulation and autonomy, demonstrate the advantages of agentic architectures and recursive self-improvement, and highlight the remaining challenges toward open-world robot autonomy.

papers.title: Theoretically Sound Item Similarity Measures for Recommender Systems
papers.abstract:
Quantifying the similarity between items is fundamental to neighborhood-based collaborative filtering, yet many commonly used similarity measures are heuristics that lack theoretical justification. The use of heuristics forces practitioners to rely on empirical trial-and-error, offering little insight into why certain measures outperform others or how they might be improved. In this paper, we present a principled approach for designing item similarity measures grounded in probabilistic modeling and parameter estimation.
  By adopting this formal perspective, we derive two previously overlooked similarity measures based on the Bernoulli and multinomial distributions. Through an extensive ablation study we highlight the critical role of bias, probabilistic smoothing, treating the unknowns correctly, and choosing appropriate probability distributions. Finally, we show that the commonly used cosine similarity can be interpreted as the solution to a specific optimization problem, thereby providing a novel perspective on this decades-old heuristic.

papers.title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Item-item similarity is one of the oldest and most foundational signals in recommender systems: two items are assumed to be similar when the same users consume them. Despite the sparsity and scale of interaction data, the implicit assumption across the field is that item co-occurrence reflects genuine shared preference, capturing what users like together. In this paper, we demonstrate that a substantial fraction of observed item-item similarity is an artifact of variance in user activity rather than shared taste. Even if every user consumed items completely independently, differing only in their total consumption volume, standard similarity measures still detect strong associations between items. We term this phenomenon phantom correlation: spurious item association that emerges strictly from heterogeneous user activity in the complete absence of preference structure. Starting from minimal formal assumptions, we show that independent consumption under varying activity is described by a Rasch model, and we derive how the resulting association depends on item popularity for each similarity measure. By comparing our theoretical baseline against real-world benchmark datasets, we reveal the extent to which popular similarity measures reflect phantom correlation, which bears on how item co-occurrence is interpreted and used in collaborative filtering.

papers.title: The mass discrepancy problem in massive stars: an inferential perspective
papers.abstract: Bayesian inference has become a standard tool for inferring stellar parameters from stellar evolution models. However, comparatively little attention has been paid to how alternative Bayesian likelihood formulations influence inferred stellar parameters, and the resulting evolutionary mass discrepancy for massive main sequence stars. Here, we investigate the effects of mixing and alternative Bayesian likelihood formulations on the inferred stellar parameters and the resulting evolutionary mass discrepancy. We analysed a sample of seven double-lined eclipsing B type binaries with $\beta$ Cep components using one pre-computed MESA grid of stellar evolution models and observables such as mass, effective temperature, surface gravity and luminosity. Stellar parameters were inferred within a Bayesian inference method employing nested sampling and piecewise cubic interpolation across the model grid. We compared several inference strategies, including single-star and coeval binary models, with and without dynamical masses included in the likelihood function. Bayesian evidence and Pareto-optimal model selection were used to evaluate the preferred solutions. Our work reinforces that core-boundary mixing is required for all stars. Further, the inferential analysis demonstrates that different likelihood formulations may lead to systematically different inferred mass discrepancies. For the adopted input physics and the small sample of stars, we find that about half of the apparent reduction in the inferred mass discrepancy may arise from the construction of the Bayesian likelihood, while enhanced near-core mixing accounts for the remaining improvement. The preferred coeval solutions further indicate that the systems span central hydrogen mass fraction of $0.632$ -- $0.205$, with ages of $4.25$ -- $12.27$ $\rm Myr$ determined with precisions of $2$ -- $13\%$ under the adopted model input physics.

papers.title: EL-DIP: A Deep Image Prior Framework for Accurate,Efficient, and Noise-Robust Elastography
papers.abstract: Elastography is a key technique for non-invasive imaging, yet it remains severely ill-posed and sensitive to measurement noise, causing blurring and artifacts. We propose EL-DIP, a training-data-free framework based on deep image prior (DIP) that reconstructs heterogeneous shear modulus distributions. Inverse distance weighting interpolation enables arbitrary-shaped domains, and adjoint sensitivity analysis provides efficient gradient computation. Numerical and experimental studies show that EL-DIP accurately recovers inclusion geometry and modulus across different noise levels. Under extreme noise, image fidelity improves by approximately 97.1% over conventional methods. We believe that this method has great potential as a robust tool for biomedical diagnosis,biomechanical characterization, and non-destructive evaluation.

papers.title: On the Error Analysis of Triangular Transport Maps for Conditional Generation via MMD-based Objectives
papers.abstract: Conditional generative models parameterized by triangular transport maps are widely used for conditional sampling, yet theoretical guarantees on the quality of the conditional measures they produce remain scarce. We address this question for minimum divergence estimators of triangular maps. We use MMD-based objectives as a tractable setting in which the gap between joint and conditional errors can be analyzed precisely, and we measure performance through the average conditional estimation error, defined as the squared maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between the estimated and the true conditionals, averaged over the conditioning variable. We first show that the common practice of minimizing a joint MMD may fail to recover the conditionals: writing the joint and the conditional criteria as quadratic energies of the same conditional mean embedding residual, we prove that, for parametric classes, joint minimizers are generically inconsistent in the misspecified setting. We then analyze an estimator that directly minimizes the conditional criterion through a surrogate loss computable from joint target samples and reference samples. We prove a non-asymptotic error bound that decomposes the average conditional estimation error into approximation, estimation, and reference sampling errors, with fast rates independent of the ambient dimension in the parametric setting. Finally, for joint MMDs built from concentrating Gaussian kernels on the conditioning variable, we show that the joint criterion approximates a density-reweighted version of the conditional one, and we derive an error bound for the joint minimizer whose rate suffers from a curse of dimensionality in the conditioning variable. Our results suggest that training criteria for conditional generative models should target the conditional rather than the joint error, a principle that extends to other divergences and to dynamic transport.

papers.title: Six-Degree-of-Freedom Rotor-Load Cross-Spectral Density from Rotor-Plane Turbulence Cross-Spectra
papers.abstract: A frequency-domain response analysis of a wind turbine rotor requires the complete hub-load spectrum, but the customary scalar thrust and torque spectra retain neither the four in-plane components nor the coupling between them. This paper derives the full six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) rotor-load cross-spectral-density (CSD) matrix from the IEC Kaimal turbulence model. By decoupling the spatial order of inflow coherence from the temporal Doppler shift, the formulation introduces a two-index rotational-sampling kernel. Rotor symmetry and azimuthal averaging constrain the observed Doppler carrier strictly to blade-passing harmonics $pBf_{\mathrm{rot}}$, while the azimuthal aerodynamic transfer shifts the spatial coherence order to $pB+s$. A convergence study of the retained azimuthal order $s$ shows that $\lvert s\rvert\le4$ suffices, the assembled CSD then deviating from the full-band result by less than $10^{-5}$ in relative norm. The formulation is compared with OpenFAST simulations of a rigid floating wind turbine over nine wind speeds: the six auto-spectral densities agree closely below 1~Hz, and the present theory over-predicts the spectra near the 6P and 9P rotational harmonics.

papers.title: Rigidity and deformations of Besse families of minimal hypersurfaces
papers.abstract: We generalize Zoll families of hypersurfaces to Besse families of hypersurfaces, which are defined differential-topologically and may contain non-embedded and exceptional hypersurfaces. A contact-geometric discussion presents them as double Legendrian fibrations and shows that regular hypersurfaces are either spheres or real projective spaces. In analogy with the Berger conjecture on simply connected manifolds all of whose geodesics are closed, we show that every hypersurface of a Besse family on a sphere other than the 4-sphere is regular. On even-dimensional spheres other than the 4-sphere we obtain a stronger conclusion, generalizing a theorem of Gromoll and Grove about 2-spheres all of whose geodesics are closed: every hypersurface of a Besse family is regular and embedded. Moreover, building on work by Ambrozio and Guajardo, we provide metrics of non-constant curvature carrying Besse families of non-embedded minimal hypersurfaces in every odd dimension at least three, and Besse families of minimal hypersurfaces with exceptional hypersurfaces on orbifolds in every dimension at least two. We also give a short proof that manifolds admitting Zoll families of embedded hypersurfaces are homeomorphic to spheres or real projective spaces, recovering a recent result of Martins up to homeomorphism.

papers.title: Estimating Stability of Individual-Specific Predictions from AI-based prediction models using Bootstrap and Cross-validation Resampling
papers.abstract: Clinical prediction models are typically developed in a single finite dataset, which is one of many possible datasets that could have been collected. Applying the same model development procedure in another sample will provide different predictions for an individual. The degree to which an individual's prediction varies across development sets is referred to as prediction instability and is not captured by average performance measures. Resampling of the training data offers a practical way to assess instability, but its ability to do so accurately and reliably for different model choices is unclear. In a simulation study, we considered non-parametric, parametric, and out-of-bag bootstrap methods and repeated 10-, 5-, and 2-fold cross-validation (CV) to estimate metrics of prediction instability for Elastic Net logistic regression and Random Forest. The same metrics estimated in independent development samples provided the reference. We assessed individual-level prediction variance, empirical 95% range width, and mean absolute differences from the original prediction and true outcome probability. Instability increased in smaller development samples, was greater for Random Forest, and varied across the probability range. Repeated 5- and 10-fold CV underestimated prediction instability across scenarios. Default non-parametric bootstrap more closely approximated independent sampling for Elastic Net but often overestimated instability for Random Forest, as did parametric bootstrap. Out-of-bag bootstrap and repeated 2-fold CV generally agreed most closely with independent sampling, although no procedure was uniformly best. Resampling procedures should not be used interchangeably, nor should less variable predictions be taken as evidence of greater stability. To estimate prediction instability, prefer procedures that predict on held-out data and limit overlap between training resamples.

papers.title: Kinetic Handover Modeling in Nonstationary Cellular Networks with Fluid Spatiotemporal Stochastic Geometry
papers.abstract: Inferring directional handover traffic from aggregate mobility observations remains challenging because population density evolution does not fully describe the movement of individual users across cell boundaries. This paper develops a kinetic framework for geometry-induced serving-region crossings in nonstationary cellular networks, connecting boundary-normal velocity statistics with fluid spatiotemporal stochastic geometry (F-STSG) for density-based transport reconstruction. The framework distinguishes signed net population transfer from gross bidirectional crossings and reveals two information limits: density evolution does not uniquely determine physical pairwise transport, while first-order transport alone cannot resolve counter-moving crossings. We establish exact recovery conditions for potential transport and develop coherent and Gaussian mobility closures for estimating directional crossing rates. Sharp moment-constrained bounds further characterize the remaining uncertainty under bounded normal velocities without assuming a specific velocity distribution. An error bound links directional estimation accuracy to transport reconstruction and unresolved mobility information. The formulation also recovers the classical stationary Poisson--Voronoi handover law. Numerical experiments examine the information limits, reconstruction sensitivity, and closure accuracy. On 47 held-out vehicular simulation windows, F-STSG achieves lower net-flow reconstruction errors than three baselines, while auxiliary velocity statistics improve directional estimates under matched Gaussian mobility.

papers.title: Geometry of holonomic modules over the first Weyl algebra
papers.abstract: We give a geometric description of the formal local data of holonomic modules over the first Weyl algebra, the algebra of differential operators in one variable. The exponential part of the associated formal meromorphic connection is encoded by a truncated jet of an affine plane curve at infinity, and the regular part by a regular formal meromorphic connection. We prove that these geometric data uniquely determine the `elementary' blocks in the formal decomposition of holonomic modules. The resulting correspondence is equivariant under automorphisms of the first Weyl algebra, including the Fourier transform.

papers.title: Large deviations for observables with logarithmic singularity and differentiability of the pressure function
papers.abstract: We show that logarithmic observables of form $\phi(x)=\log(|x-b|)$ on the doubling map $T$ have exponential large deviations with respect to the invariant measure if $b$ is preperiodic but not periodic with respect to $T$ giving a counterpart to the known result of strictly stretched exponential large deviations in the case that $b$ is periodic. These results are established by showing that the topological pressure function developed for unbounded observables is differentiable at $0$.

papers.title: Adequacy radii for stepped-wedge trials with time-varying effects
papers.abstract: Complete stepped-wedge designs guarantee eventual intervention delivery, but their final periods contain no concurrent controls. Under exposure-time heterogeneity this creates a design-analysis tension: a constant-effect analysis can be precise while targeting a design-dependent contrast, whereas an exposure-time indicator (ETI) analysis targets a prespecified time-averaged effect but may be much less precise. We develop an adequacy radius that quantifies the size of exposure-time heterogeneity compatible with a prespecified tolerance for estimand mismatch, and combine it with precision calculations to compare complete wedges with rollout-constrained hybrid designs that retain a wait-list arm. For a balanced wedge with a wait-list under the Hussey-Hughes model, the wait-list share and the correlation act on the constant-effect GLS estimand through a single scalar; we prove that the radius increases strictly with the wait-list share and decreases strictly with the within-cluster correlation, but remains bounded. Numerical optimisation and a model-based redesign of a weekend allied-health trial show that intermediate hybrids make estimand-aligned ETI analysis materially more affordable, giving a robustness-precision frontier rather than a binary choice between a complete wedge and a parallel trial. A second trial, of digital adherence support for tuberculosis treatment, has the same radius but no detectable heterogeneity; its test of a constant effect would detect heterogeneity large enough to halve the coverage of the nominal interval only 37% of the time. The contribution is a diagnostic and design principle: when exposure-time heterogeneity is plausible, retaining concurrent controls reduces the price of analysing the estimand one intends to report.

papers.title: The Digital-Energy Recomposition of the Kitchin Cycle: Exploratory Evidence from U.S. IT and Irish Data-Centre Series (1995-2025)
papers.abstract: Using quarterly FRED and CSO Ireland data over 1995Q1-2025Q4, we examine whether U.S.\ IT investment and Irish data-centre electricity are recomposing the Kitchin cycle around energy- and compute-backed assets. Three findings stand out. First, a Quandt-Andrews sup-Wald test locates a significant break in the U.S.\ IT-GDP correlation at 2014Q3 (sup-W $= 9.69$; $r$ falls from $+0.45$ to $-0.12$); the Fisher $r$-to-$z$ test survives Bonferroni adjustment ($z = +3.11$, $p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.006$), whereas the analogous test on the imposed Cloud-vs-AI boundary does not ($p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.164$), so ``Strategic Decoupling'' pre-dates the AI Era by approximately six years. Second, in Ireland the synchronous AI-Era correlation between metered data-centre electricity and Real GDP is large ($r = +0.41$, $N = 16$) but \emph{collapses to $r \approx 0$ when Real GDP is replaced by Real GNP}, suggesting the headline is largely an artefact of the shared multinational tax-structure footprint between hyperscaler operations and Irish gross output. Third, the Irish cross-correlation profile is asymmetric in the opposite direction to a leading-indicator reading: the largest positive coefficients cluster on the $k < 0$ side (GDP precedes data-centre load), so compute capacity is better read as coincident or moderately lagging. Given the small AI-Era samples and the absence of a quarterly multinational-adjusted aggregate such as GNI*, all coefficients are exploratory; subject to these caveats, the U.S.\ Kitchin cycle is best dated to 2014Q3, and the Irish Energy-Data Nexus is dominated by multinational firm activity.

papers.intro:
The study of economic periodicity has long been a cornerstone of macroeconomic forecasting and investment strategy. Among the established wave theories, the Kitchin cycle, first identified by Joseph Kitchin in 1923, remains one of the most influential frameworks for understanding short/medium-term economic fluctuations. In his seminal work, “Cycles and Trends in Economic Factors”, Kitchin observed a minor cycle of approximately 40 months (3-5 years), driven by fluctuations in commercial inventories and capital investment.

In his seminal work, “Cycles and Trends in Economic Factors”, Kitchin observed a minor cycle of approximately 40 months (3-5 years), driven by fluctuations in commercial inventories and capital investment.

For nearly a century, the Kitchin cycle served as a reference point for asset allocation and production planning. It operated on a simple feedback loop: a surge in demand led to an accumulation of physical inventory (e.g., steel, coal, finished goods), eventually resulting in market saturation, price corrections, and subsequent inventory liquidation. This “inventory lag” provided a predictable rhythm that investors used to time market entries and exits.

However, the structural realities of the 21st-century global economy differ from the industrial landscape of the 1920s. We argue that the traditional Kitchin cycle, while theoretically elegant, may be losing relevance in its original form. The transition from a manufacturing-based economy to a digital-first infrastructure plausibly shifts the relevant “inventory” from physical warehouses to digital ones, specifically to compute power, semiconductor stockpiles, and energy contracts.

This paper introduces a revised framework: the “New Energy and Data Cycle.” We document an empirical “Strategic Decoupling” of U.S. IT investment from GDP, and ask when, on the data, it begins. While our nominal AI Era window is 2021Q1-2025Q4, a Quandt-Andrews sup-Wald test on the U.S. IT-GDP correlation locates the structural break in 2014Q3, several years before the current wave of AI investment; the corresponding Fisher rr-to-zz test on the pre/post-2014Q3 sub-samples survives Bonferroni adjustment (z=+3.11z=+3.11, pBonf=0.006p_{\text{Bonf}}=0.006), in contrast to the analogous test on the imposed Cloud-vs-AI era boundary (pBonf=0.164p_{\text{Bonf}}=0.164). The pattern we report is therefore best read as exploratory evidence consistent with a longer-running decoupling of IT capital formation from GDP, of which the AI Era is the latest segment, rather than as a phenomenon uniquely attributable to AI. In parallel, we examine whether energy consumption in data centers and semiconductor manufacturing behaves as a coincident or leading correlate of growth in the AI Era window.

Using quarterly data from the Republic of Ireland, a country with a globally significant share of data-center capacity, we examine whether the modern Kitchin cycle is better explained by the availability and consumption of electricity than by physical goods. We acknowledge that Irish GDP statistics are heavily influenced by multinational firm activity (FitzGerald, 2018), a well-documented limitation revisited in Section 7; accordingly, the Irish evidence is presented as an illustrative, not a confirmatory, case study. Our results suggest that power purchase agreements (PPAs) and data center load deserve consideration alongside traditional stock-to-sales ratios as candidate barometers of economic health in data-intensive economies.

papers.title: A non-perturbative topological persistence theorem for normally hyperbolic invariant manifolds
papers.abstract: Floer proved that, under a sufficiently small $C^0$ perturbation, a normally hyperbolic invariant manifold gives rise to a nearby invariant set whose cohomology ring contains a subring isomorphic to that of the original manifold. Using topological conditions, expressed in terms of the so-called covering relations, we generalize this theorem to a non-perturbative context. Our result does not require the existence of an invariant manifold before perturbation, nor does it require the original map to be smooth or invertible. For the proof, we develop an additional structure on the Conley index for maps on vector bundles.

papers.title: A Twisted Affine Interpolation of the $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$-graded Integrable Super-Liouville and super-Sinh-Gordon Equations
papers.abstract: This paper is a third one in a series devoted to the construction of $2D$, $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$-graded, integrable Toda field theories. The first paper introduced parabosonic models obtained from Rittenberg-Wyler color Lie algebras; the second paper explained how to deal with parafermions (the $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$-graded super-Liouville theory) from finite Rittenberg-Wyler color Lie superalgebras. This new paper extends the construction to the infinite case of (twisted) affine color Lie superalgebras. A $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$-graded extension of ${\widehat{\mathfrak{osp}(2|2)^{(2)}}}$ allows to interpolate the super-Liouville and the super-Sinh-Gordon models, recovered as special limits. The $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$-graded extensions of three frameworks are here discussed: the Polyakov's soldering, the Leznov-Savel'ev Lax pair (zero-curvature) formulation and the B\"acklund transformations. As a byproduct of the construction, the Hamiltonian reduction from the $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$-graded ${\widehat{\mathfrak{osp(2|2)}^{(2)}}}$ WZNW models induces a $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$-graded color Lie superalgebra which admits three inequivalent superVirasoro subalgebras; they are the ${\cal N}=2$ superVirasoro, the $(1,\frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{2},2)$ $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$-graded superVirasoro and the $(\frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{2},2,2)$ $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$-graded superVirasoro.

papers.title: Knowing When to Escalate: Disagreement Patterns for Uncertainty-Aware Content Moderation
papers.abstract: Agentic content-moderation systems increasingly rely on collective judgments from LLM agents, while aggregation methods commonly treat inter-agent disagreement as a reliability problem to be removed through consensus or voting. This framing is inappropriate for value-laden tasks, where disagreement may reflect irreducible value pluralism - a distinction standard uncertainty decompositions cannot recover, since they operate on output distributions and discard the reasoning behind each judgment. We propose Reasoning Trace Divergence Analysis (RTDA), which embeds model-generated justifications from perspective-differentiated agents and classifies each case by justification similarity and conclusion agreement. The resulting four-state taxonomy isolates convergent disagreement, where agents reasoning similarly but concluding differently, as a candidate signature of value-laden conflict. On 1,000 items from the Measuring Hate Speech corpus, this structural signal predicts human annotator disagreement better than magnitude-only and output-only baselines. We contribute a design principle: condition human escalation on the structure of disagreement, not its magnitude alone, with RTDA serving as a post-processing layer for systems that already generate reasoning traces.

papers.title: CA-HNM: Constraint-Aware Hard Negative Mining for Dense Retrieval with Structured Domain Models
papers.abstract: Dense retrievers are commonly trained with hard negatives selected from lexical or dense retrieval results. Retrieval proximity, however, does not indicate whether a candidate conflicts with explicit domain structure. We introduce CA-HNM, a constraint-aware hard-negative mining framework that combines retrieval-based candidate generation with deterministic incompatibility rules derived from a structured domain model. The framework removes known positives, constructs a local typed context around the query target, records relational, scope, target, and level mismatches, and uses the resulting candidates to fine-tune a standard dual encoder. Structured information is required only during offline negative construction. We evaluate CA-HNM on MOOCCubeX and Course-Skill Atlas with two encoders, two training losses, and ten seeds. Relative to a retrieval-rank-matched control, CA-HNM-Pure has higher mean NDCG@10 in six of eight dataset--encoder--loss configurations. Four hierarchical 95% bootstrap intervals are entirely above zero, mostly under triplet loss. In a separate experiment, CA-HNM-Mixed shows slightly higher mean NDCG@10 than a matched-mixed control on both collections. Structural variants show that changes in available structure can also change candidate eligibility and negative-pool composition. The results indicate that the contribution of constraint-aware selection depends on the training objective and the composition of the negative pool.

authors.name: Bertrand Laforge
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: The Capability Transfer: Cohort Reversal, Codified Expertise, and the Adaptability Tax of AI Transformation
papers.abstract: Most analyses of AI and employment ask which jobs are exposed. This paper asks what happens to the pipeline that produces experts. It extends the model of Caosun and Aral (2026) from a single worker to a firm with two cohorts, juniors and seniors, and studies how expertise formation changes when codified work is automated. Because junior work is the most codified, demand for juniors falls first; the stock of seniors falls later but further, as the pipeline stops replacing the experts who retire. In the baseline calibration, junior demand bottoms out about a fifth below its 2022 level before recovering most of that ground, while the senior stock falls by a quarter and later halves. Because expertise forms through unassisted practice on work that AI cannot do, the time needed to develop an expert from within rises from about five years to nine. The costs fall on a different party from the one that decides on adoption: a manager with a three-year horizon sets AI use to maximise near-term output, cutting the wage bill by 21 percent while the capacity of the firm on work AI cannot do falls by two-fifths and its output on that work goes unserved once the pipeline runs thin. Two key parameters are not yet measured, so the results are scenarios rather than forecasts. The paper proposes three indicators organisations can track: the unaided practice juniors get on work AI cannot do, senior time spent on such work, and the years it takes to develop an expert.

papers.title: Sexual dimorphism and sex-specific features of pediatric hand bone shapes via statistical shape modeling
papers.abstract: Understanding the envelope of shape variation encompassing both sexual dimorphism and growth-related changes in living tissue is a non-trivial task. In this work, we use statistical shape models (SSMs) and analyze demographic-stratified shape parameters to quantify sexual dimorphism and sex-specific shape changes. To this end, we developed a two-stage detection-segmentation framework that accurately segmented $n = 27664$ unique bone masks from a radiographic dataset of $n = 1456$ subjects with diverse ages and sexes (HD95 = $1.512 \pm 0.005$, ASSD $0.449 \pm 001$, Dice = $0.987 \pm 0.00004$, IoU = $0.975 \pm 0.0001$). Following SSM fitting, our follow-up analyses of stratified shape parameters highlighted the morphology of sexual dimorphisms for each bone and demonstrated sex-specific differences in shape development. Our results were consistent with existing literature and provided an unambiguous, data-driven methodology for characterizing tissue shape and its population-scale variation. This approach provides a potential methodological foundation for developing population-based models of anatomical variation and could be extended to investigate tissue growth and shape changes over time. Future work should evaluate the applicability of this methodology on alternative anatomical structures and imaging modalities, with the goal of validating these growth trajectories on longitudinal data.

papers.title: Computational complexity of the $H$-coloring problem in cubic graphs
papers.abstract: If $G$ and $H$ are two cubic graphs, then an $H$-coloring of $G$ is a mapping $f: E(G)\rightarrow E(H)$, such that for every $v\in V(G)$ there is a vertex $x\in V(H)$, such that $f(\partial_G(v))=\partial_H(x)$. If $G$ admits an $H$-coloring then it is common to write $H\prec G$. In this paper, for a fixed connected cubic graph $H$, we consider a decision problem, which we call $H$-coloring. In this problem, on the input one is given a connected cubic graph $G$. The goal is to decide whether $H\prec G$. A conjecture by Hakobyan and the author states that $H$-coloring is polynomial time solvable, if $H$ does not admit a $P_{12}$-coloring. Here $P_{12}$ is the unique cubic graph obtained from the Petersen graph by expanding one of its vertices into a triangle. In this paper, we disprove this conjecture under $P\neq NP$, by showing that $S_6$-coloring is NP-complete. Here $S_6$ is the unique cubic graph on six vertices having exactly one bridge. Our second result is an algorithm that solves $H$-coloring problem in time $O^*(c^n)$, where $H$ is a simple connected cubic graph, $n$ is the number of vertices of the input cubic graph $G$ and $c=\sqrt{8}\approx 2.8284$.

papers.title: ThinkLocoManip: A Whole-Body Control Agentic Harness for Legged Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose ThinkLocoManip, an agentic harness for legged loco-manipulation designed to tackle complex, long-horizon tasks in large-scale environments. Existing approaches typically follow either direct action generation or a plan-then-act paradigm, both of which can struggle with the generalization and error-recovery capabilities required for extended task execution. In contrast, ThinkLocoManip adopts an interleaved reasoning-and-acting paradigm, allowing the agent to continuously reason about its current state, execute actions, observe their outcomes, and adapt its strategy accordingly. Building on this paradigm, our agentic harness orchestrates a suite of specialized tools for perception, navigation, manipulation, and locomotion, enabling flexible composition of heterogeneous capabilities. Unlike existing robotic agentic harnesses, ThinkLocoManip explicitly incorporates locomotion as a tool domain for agent reasoning and execution. We further design a set of skills that explicitly account for both tool usage within each functional domain and coordination across domains, supporting effective execution of complex behaviors over long horizons. To tackle task failure during long-horizon interactions, we develop keyframe thinking mechanism to preserve critical execution context and support efficient error recovery. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that ThinkLocoManip substantially outperforms representative methods based on both direct action generation and plan-then-act paradigms across challenging long-horizon legged loco-manipulation tasks. Notably, ThinkLocoManip achieves a success rate of 77%, more than twice that of the strongest plan-then-act baseline (37.1%). Our experiments further validate the effectiveness of interleaved reasoning and acting, tool orchestration, and coordinated skill execution.

papers.title: V-Representability Beyond Singular Times in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory: The Hubbard Dimer Case
papers.abstract: We study the global $V$-representability problem in time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) for the two-particle Hubbard dimer model in the spin-singlet sector. In particular, we investigate whether the time-dependent density of the interacting system obtained for a given one-body external potential $u$ (the tunable control variable) can be reproduced by a non-interacting Kohn--Sham system beyond the singular times at which the usual inversion formulas break down. We deal with both the conventional formulation of TDDFT based on some time-dependent variational principle and the recently introduced geometric formulation of TDDFT (Phys. Rev. Lett. 136 (2026) 256401, Phys. Rev. A 113 (2026) 062222). For both principles, we prove global-in-time $V$-representability, show that singular times induce non-uniqueness of the time-dependent effective potential, and classify the set of solutions.

authors.institution: École nationale des ponts et chaussées

papers.title: SGL: Towards a Bridging Model for Heterogeneous Hierarchical Platforms
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the Scatter-Gather parallel-programming and parallel-execution model in the form of a simple imperative Scatter-Gather Language (SGL). Its design is based on past experience with bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) programming and BSP language design. SGL's novel features are motivated by the last decade's move towards multi-level and heterogeneous parallel architectures involving multi-core processors, graphics accelerators and hierarchical routing networks in the largest multiprocessing systems. The design of SGL is coherent with L. Valiant's Multi-BSP while offering a programming interface that is even simpler than the primitives of Bulk-Synchronous Parallel ML (BSML). SGL appears to cover a large subset of all BSP algorithms while avoiding complex message-passing programming. Like all BSP-inspired systems, it supports predictable, portable and scalable performance. Moreover, SGL's explicit data distribution will allow automatic or programmable load-balancing.

papers.title: Testing independence in contamination models
papers.abstract: We consider a bivariate contamination model in which the distribution of a gold standard is known, while the mixing weight and the distribution of the contaminant component are unknown, and we test whether the two coordinates of the unknown component are independent. Classical independence tests are meaningless here, since a mixture of product distributions is not a product distribution. Following the Inversion-Best Matching principle, we invert the model for every candidate weight and compare the inverted distribution of the unknown component with the product of its marginals. The weight is estimated where they are closest in a Cramer-von Mises sense, and the scaled minimal distance is the test statistic. An exact quadratic structure makes the estimator computable without numerical optimisation and yields a transparent asymptotic theory under both hypotheses. The null distribution is calibrated by a multiplier bootstrap. Simulations and applications to gene expression data and spam filtering illustrate the method.
