papers.title: Internal Discrepancy for Contrastive Learning: Generalization Bounds and Downstream Behaviors
papers.abstract: Contrastive learning has emerged as a popular paradigm for training representation models. While prior studies pursue more practical and less restrictive assumptions to enhance theoretical understanding of contrastive learning, they essentially describe the interconnections among representations within the data or induced by the function class. To encapsulate these assumptions, we propose the measure of internal discrepancy that quantifies the difference between the mean representation of positive samples and latent cluster centers. We then prove an internal discrepancy-aware generalization bound for downstream supervised tasks following contrastive learning, without requiring additional assumptions. This generalization bound not only serves as a unifying framework connecting various assumptions but also motivates us to further reduce the internal discrepancy, thereby introducing the relaxed k-means loss as an approximation. Moreover, we investigate the downstream behaviors of contrastive learning from the perspective of contrastive learning-incurred supervised losses. In the presence of class imbalance, we shed light on why contrastive learning can facilitate imbalanced learning. Finally, we investigate the optimality of these incurred supervised losses, proving several intriguing properties.

authors.name: Gangfeng Hu
authors.institution: The First People's Hospital of Xiaoshan District, Hangzhou

papers.title: Loss Factor of Axisymmetric and Rectangular Tapered Collimators from Optical to Inductive Regimes
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate the loss factor of axisymmetric and rectangular tapered collimators over a broad range of bunch lengths and geometrical parameters using the electromagnetic simulation codes ECHO and GdfidL. The calculations are performed for Gaussian bunches of rms length $\sigma_s$, with the collimator geometry characterized by the minimum and maximum apertures $b$ and $d$, taper length $L$, and chamber width $W$ for rectangular structures. For short bunches and tapered collimators with $d-b>b$, we extend the phenomenological formula previously obtained for axisymmetric to rectangular tapered collimators, describing the dependence of the loss factor on bunch length and taper geometry through an arctangent function of the scaling parameter $\mu d^2/(\sigma_s L)$. We demonstrate that this parameter is related to a Fresnel number and, by combining diffraction theory with the electrodynamics of the beam-induced image charge, analytically explain the factor of two between the coefficients $\mu=0.2$ and $\mu=0.4$ for axisymmetric and rectangular collimators, respectively. The resulting expression is applicable to rectangular collimators with $W/(2d) \geq 1.8$, extending its validity beyond the idealized flat geometry. For longer bunches, we identify the transition from the optical to the inductive regime and derive an analytical expression for the loss factor based on the cutoff wavenumber of the lowest relevant electromagnetic mode.

papers.title: Babysitting AI Agents: A User-Centered Taxonomy and Study of Agentic Delegation Failures
papers.abstract: Users are increasingly delegating tasks to AI agents, allowing agents to perform long-running, multi-step workflows on their behalf. However, agents may perform these tasks in ways that depart from users' expectations for how they should be carried out, leading to what we call agentic delegation failures. We leverage a large corpus of 163,487 Reddit posts, describing AI agent use, to develop MANDATE: a taxonomy of 23 failure categories organized into seven groups. A follow-up study with 73 AI agent users examined the relationship between prevalence and perceptions of severity and noticeability, finding that failures rated as more severe are considered harder to notice, and that prior experience with a failure is associated with greater noticeability. Finally, we assess the maturity of research on each failure and identify commonly encountered failures that have received little attention (e.g., agents running without making progress). Our findings inform opportunities to make delegation easier for users to oversee and better studied by the research community.

papers.title: When and Why to Use TMA: A Workload-Grounded Characterization of Tensor Memory Acceleration on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs
papers.abstract: The Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), introduced on NVIDIA Hopper, is used pervasively in production GPU kernels yet its usage is conspicuously selective: expert kernel developers in CUTLASS, FlashAttention-3, and FlashInfer apply TMA to some tensor operands within a kernel but fall back to cp.async, direct global loads, or distributed shared memory (DSM) for others. Vendor documentation describes the API, and recent microbenchmarking work characterizes TMA throughput in isolation, but neither answers the question practitioners actually face: given a memory operand in a kernel, should it use TMA, and if so, with or without cluster multicast? We address this gap with a workload-grounded characterization study on H100. We catalog the TMA, multicast, DSM, and cp.async choices made inside FlashAttention-3 forward, isolate the discriminating features through targeted microbenchmarks (transfer-size crossover, multicast scaling), and produce rules of thumb for the load-mechanism choice on Hopper. We further compare TMA multicast against DSM as competing cluster-broadcast primitives, and isolate the FlashAttention-3 paged-key-value (KV) TMA-vs-cp.async dispatch on H100 across page size, datatype, model shape, and execution phase. Our results yield concrete, predictive guidance on when TMA pays off and when multicast helps or hurts on Hopper, and we extend the analysis to server Blackwell (SM100) via a CUTLASS GEMM study on B200 that shows the qualitative dispatch rules carry across generations while absolute crossovers shift with tensor-core and bandwidth scaling.

papers.title: A Mathematical Theory of the Jacobian Lens
papers.abstract: Recent work from Anthropic introduced a new interpretability tool, called the Jacobian lens (J-lens, Gurnee et al., 2026). This method identified linear directions in the hidden states of frontier language models that had properties reminiscent of working memory-like representations. However, it is unclear what mechanistic properties of such features make them detectable to the J-lens. To this end, we introduce a mathematical theory of the J-lens, and show that it preferentially identifies coherent features -- directions that act like leading, spatially coherent Lyapunov modes. Small perturbations along these directions amplify across layers, remain roughly constant across token positions, and are consistent across different contexts. While we are agnostic to whether these properties are necessarily associated with a ``Global Workspace'', the analytically derived preferences of the J-lens nevertheless explain prior empirical applied to both model classes. We validate our analysis on a Bayes filter and a toy transformer, each optimally predicting next tokens emitted from a Hidden Markov Model (HMM). We show how modulating task parameters that change the coherence of features in the Bayes filter correspondingly and predictively modulates the response of the J-lens . We also introduce of a family of J-lenses built to emphasize different temporal scales of information processing in LLMs, which we call $\omega$-J-lenses.

papers.title: PEAR: Adaptive Advantage Reshaping for Perception and Exploration in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Effective multimodal reasoning requires a model to reliably utilize visual information while sufficiently exploring diverse reasoning paths. To achieve this goal, prior work combines visual dependency and token entropy to reshape sequence-level advantages, but scaling the contribution of token entropy by visual dependency can leave high-entropy tokens with low visual dependency underweighted, despite their important role in reasoning exploration. To address this limitation, we propose PEAR, an adaptive advantage reshaping method for improving perception and exploration in multimodal reasoning. PEAR retains visual dependency as the base signal and adds an entropy-based exploration gain only at high-entropy positions, with lower visual dependency leading to a larger additional gain. The fused signal is then mapped to positive token-level weights that reshape the sequence-level advantage. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B show that PEAR achieves the highest average performance among evaluated baselines across multimodal reasoning benchmarks, alongside leading results on textual reasoning and general multimodal benchmarks.

papers.title: Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface
papers.abstract: Ecological monitoring, carbon accounting and biodiversity assessment increasingly rely on annual Earth embeddings--learned vectors that compress a year of satellite observation for every ten-meter pixel on Earth, consumed in place of the imagery itself. What these vectors mean has not been established. Here we decompose two widely used embedding products and show that they contain individual ecological features, including fire, forest clearing and crop type, validated against independent reference data on events across six continents. The recovered concepts date abrupt canopy loss to the first post-disturbance growing season and resolve severity well enough to separate prescribed fire from wildfire. Small fires that recover quickly are detectable in one product but not the other, which instead separates crops more strongly.

authors.name: Robin Young
authors.institution: Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

papers.title: SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements
papers.abstract: Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. $P \leftrightarrow Q$ holds trivially for any two statements $P$ and $Q$ that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through $P \leftrightarrow \mathrm{True} \leftrightarrow Q$. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval, a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq+, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq

papers.title: False Belief Dissemination, Persistence and Mitigation in Multi-Agent Social Networks Through the Lens of the Mandela Effect
papers.abstract: Multi-agent social networks are emerging as communities in which agents communicate, retain memories, and publish information that others can find as evidence. These interactions create opportunities for false claims to spread and remain influential beyond their original sources, analogous to the Mandela effect in human societies, in which many people recall the same false memory. In this paper, we systematically study false-belief dynamics through the lens of the Mandela effect, focusing on dissemination, persistence, and mitigation. Specifically, we build a controlled framework connecting agent communication, private memory, and a shared simulated web to mimic information dissemination in practical social networks, supported by 540 fabricated claims spanning 8 domains and 4 plausibility levels. For dissemination, we measure how widely and quickly claims gain acceptance across models and communication topologies. For persistence, we withdraw agents promoting fabricated claims while retaining existing articles and memories, and track subsequent acceptance. For mitigation, we compare preventive measures applied before implantation with corrective interventions introduced after claims have spread. Experimental results show that evaluated models readily accept and disseminate fabricated claims, with dissemination reach as high as 96.0%. Dissemination reach varies with claim plausibility, domain, and network size and composition, while communication topology shapes dissemination speed across model families. Acceptance barely declines after fabricators withdraw, and targeted corrective interventions outperform the preventive measures without eliminating false beliefs. These findings identify persistent false beliefs as a safety challenge for multi-agent social networks and highlight the need to address both their initial dissemination and the accumulated evidence that sustains them.

papers.title: Tiny Recursive Policy: Recursive Latent Refinement for Visuomotor Control
papers.abstract: Behaviour cloning has become a powerful approach for robotic manipulation, but many modern policies reconstruct their internal representation from a fixed observation window at each prediction and do not maintain persistent latent context throughout execution. We introduce Tiny Recursive Policy (TRP), a parameter-efficient behaviour-cloning policy that combines persistent temporal state with recursive latent refinement. At each control step, TRP repeatedly updates high- and low-level latent states using a shared computation module before decoding an action sequence, and propagates the resulting state to subsequent predictions. We evaluate TRP across LIBERO-100, MetaWorld ML45, and the LIBERO-Mem benchmarks. TRP performs competitively across multi-task and few-shot settings and shows substantial gains on long-horizon and context-dependent tasks, while using significantly fewer parameters than large generative baselines. Execution-time perturbations show that reliance on the persistent carry increases with temporal-context demand, while training with carry perturbations substantially improves robustness to both carry and visual corruptions. Ablations reveal a strong interaction between persistent state and recursive refinement: the benefit of carry depends strongly on the amount of within-step computation, and the resulting performance cannot be explained by parameter count alone.

papers.title: Well-posedness of the Burgers' equation on the half-line through the Cole-Hopf transformation
papers.abstract: We rigorously establish the well-posedness of the initial-boundary value problem (IBVP) for the Burgers' equation on the half-line for data in Sobolev-type spaces. The formal solution to this problem was previously derived via the Cole-Hopf transformation and the Fokas unified transform method under the assumption of smooth, Schwartz-class data. In this work, we prove the validity of this formal representation for initial data $u_0\in \tilde{H}^{s+1}_x (0,\infty)$ and boundary data $g_0 \in H_t^{{(2s+1)}/{4}}$ where $1/2<s<3/2$. Well-posedness is established under two complementary conditions: (1) sufficiently small initial and boundary data, and (2) non-positive boundary data of arbitrary size. The latter condition utilizes the strong minimum principle for the corresponding linear heat equation to ensure the global invertibility of the nonlinear Cole-Hopf map. The proofs combine linear estimates for the heat IBVP with nonlinear bounds obtained through Taylor series representations and the algebraic properties of Sobolev spaces.

papers.title: When Personas Become Harmful: Guiding LLMs with Global Citizenship Values Alignment
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly being used by users from diverse demographics with pluralistic values and distinct backgrounds. Maintaining safety while respecting value-laden personas is uniquely challenging because persona-conditioned requests are often not overtly malicious, unlike those in existing safety benchmarks. Alignment methods aimed at adversarial requests therefore may miss the harm that emerges from persona use, leaving models to either refuse legitimate value expression or blindly follow unsafe personas. We construct a dataset of 11k controversial topics paired with value-based personas mapping to value dimensions from the Schwartz Value Survey. Through an agentic pipeline that iteratively refines the topic and persona, we surface and collect harmful responses from well-aligned commercial LLMs with a more than 47% success rate. We use UNESCO's global citizenship principles as a minimal common ground for distinguishing valid value expressions from harmful behaviors, and introduce a controllable alignment model that lets users balance persona adherence and safety at inference time. The resulting model is safer and more persona-adherent than baselines on most samples.

papers.title: What Makes a Question Curious? Measuring Model Curiosity in Human-LLM Interactions
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly act as partners in everyday communication. In these interactions, useful assistance may require not only answering, but also asking the right questions that surface knowledge gaps, assumptions, and alternatives. In this study, we refer to such epistemic question-asking as model curiosity, and introduce a theory-grounded taxonomy that distinguishes curiosity-oriented questions from generic model questioning. Across four conversation datasets, we find that curiosity-oriented questions remain rare (17-28% of all questions), but are associated with more exploratory and epistemically rich subsequent user responses, with varying patterns across datasets. We further conduct a human study to evaluate the usefulness of model curiosity, finding that curiosity can encourage exploration, especially in advice, creative, and research contexts. These findings have implications for building LLMs that ask more selectively to support deeper exploration and human-AI collaboration.

papers.title: "High-Quality" Data for Early-Stage Instruction Tuning: An Empirical Study of Data Quality Metrics
papers.abstract: "Data quality" is widely invoked in instruction tuning, but the term is often underspecified. We study it as an operational property by asking which simple example-level metrics, drawn from prior work on data selection, text quality, and instruction tuning, best predict training utility under a fixed finetuning budget. For each metric, we sort instruction-response examples by score, partition them into low, middle, and high bins with roughly equal token mass, finetune separately on each bin, and compare validation perplexity and LLM-as-judge scores for the models' generated answers as a function of cumulative training tokens. Our results suggest that answer-dense supervision, as captured by response ratio, is a stronger and more portable predictor of instruction-tuning utility than commonly used alternative proxies.

papers.title: Matter that learns what matters
papers.abstract: Can a material learn what deserves its attention? We show that it can in a model optical network, in which action outcomes train a persistent record in each link. The record biases whether a source is consulted and sets how strongly it changes a stored answer, so useful sources gain attention and influence without being identified in advance. The network's experience thus shapes the information available for its future learning. Resonant readouts make this learning fragile: reinforcement can carry a record past resonance, where it persists but its influence weakens. We derive bounds within which relevant signals guide the answer, irrelevant signals are rejected and stored answers remain open to revision. These bounds guide a learning rule that limits reinforcement as records form; in simulations, it acquires useful records and keeps them functional. When relevance changes, an obsolete record can block its own replacement. A local state that strengthens negative writing after unsuccessful actions releases obsolete records and completes the learning sequence more often. How a memory is read should decide how it is written.

papers.title: Ask Before You Answer: A Question-Driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture (QERA) for In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly asked to reason over a user's own web traces: group chats, community threads, activity logs and revision histories. On CL-bench Life, a benchmark of such real-life context learning, frontier LLMs solve fewer than one task in five. We find that the request is not the specification: over 80% of the benchmark's rubrics share less than 60% of their content words with the final request, as for a rule set two turns earlier or every record that meets the user's criterion, and LLMs answering directly pass only 67% of these implicit rubrics against 81% of the others. We propose QERA, a Question-driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture that asks before it answers. QERA first turns the request into a requirement checklist and typed information needs, filtered by code for faithfulness to the user's words; it then answers from the whole conversation, asks the same questions again with quotes verified by code, and applies a guarded local repair. It needs no training or rubrics and makes about four LLM calls per task. On all 405 tasks with four frontier LLMs, QERA attains the highest solving rate on every LLM (21.0% on average, against 18.2% for the strongest of three inference-time baselines and 14.6% for direct answering) and leads every baseline significantly when pooled across LLMs, while using fewer tokens than PSCI and 4-5% of the tokens of Ctx2Skill. Ablations on GPT-6-Luna show that the gain is settled before the answer, by a fixed answer protocol (+3.8 rubric points) and the request-specific questions (+1.6), and that it is concentrated on implicit rubrics, with checking afterwards refining mainly numeric requirements.

authors.name: Wentao Zhang
authors.institution: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Cracking into RACS - I. Measuring the cosmic dipole in the RACS-low3 and RACS-mid1 radio surveys with simulation-based inference
papers.abstract: We measure the dipole in the count of radio galaxies over the sky as seen by the Australian SKA Pathfinder (ASKAP) in the Rapid ASKAP Continuum Survey (RACS). Our analysis focuses on the third observational epoch in the 'low' passband (943.5 MHz; RACS-low3) and the first epoch in the 'mid' passband (1367.5 MHz; RACS-mid1). We find strong evidence for a systematic relation between flux density and the temperature at the time of observation, whereby reported flux densities are suppressed to a greater degree when the ASKAP antennas are warmer. We include this temperature response in our forward model as part of our Simulation-based Inference (SBI) pipeline, generating data realisations that are then used by a neural network to learn the likelihood function. Despite this model, RACS-low3 and RACS-mid1 both exhibit a dipole inconsistent with the kinematic dipole of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), adding further evidence for the 'cosmic dipole tension'. For RACS-low3, the dipole agrees in direction but has an amplitude four times in excess, while the dipole for RACS-mid1 is offset from the CMB and has an amplitude roughly five times in excess. Our findings underscore the importance of interrogating the data for systematic effects and showcase the power of SBI in handling them.

papers.title: Flexural Altermagnetism
papers.abstract: We establish flexural deformation as a versatile route for engineering altermagnetism in two-dimensional collinear antiferromagnets. By tailoring the flexure, we selectively break different symmetries to realize altermagnetic states with distinct wave symmetries and reverse their spin splitting. A tight-binding model and first-principles calculations for monolayer MnPS3 demonstrate d- and i-wave states and a switchable transverse spin current in the d-wave state.

papers.title: Then there is prompt injection, a malicious email, ...: The Wild Wide West of OpenClaw Agentic System Security
papers.abstract: AI-powered personal assistant frameworks such as OpenClaw combine LLM reasoning, persistent memory, tool invocation, local execution, and web-based workflows. These capabilities enable useful automation, but they also create security risks when untrusted inputs, model reasoning, tools, memory, and deployment configuration interact without explicit trust boundaries. This paper presents an empirical study of reported security concerns in OpenClaw using two complementary data sources: Reddit discussions and security-tagged GitHub issues. We analyze more than 25K Reddit posts from 13 OpenClaw-related subreddits and identify 162 security-relevant posts with 1,787 associated comments. We further collect 358 security-tagged GitHub issues and retain 180 issues describing concrete security concerns. Using qualitative analysis and evidence-grounded CWE mapping, we identify 521 CWE instances across 59 distinct weakness types, concentrated in access-control failures, sensitive-data exposure, injection, and unsafe execution. We also extract 543 practitioner mitigation suggestions and consolidate them into seven recurring strategies. To complement the empirical analysis, we present an evidence-grounded illustrative reconstruction of a representative sensitive-data exposure pathway using dummy secret values. Our findings show that OpenClaw security issues are not isolated implementation bugs; they reflect recurring trust-boundary failures across the agent execution pipeline. We discuss how these weaknesses map to both traditional software-security categories and agent-specific failure mechanisms, and derive implications for safer agentic systems, including explicit trust boundaries, least-privilege tool access, execution containment, runtime oversight, and defense-in-depth deployment.

papers.title: Making Small Code LLMs More Efficient for Secure Code Review with Neuro-Symbolic Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: As AI coding assistants generate more code, the need to review it for security flaws grows. Existing approaches leave a gap: static analyzers identify program sites but offer little explanation, while language-model explanations can be difficult to verify. Small open-weight code models could make security review available without sending proprietary code to a hosted service. We study whether fine-tuning helps these models turn security evidence into explanations that developers and tools can check. We present secSemScan, which pairs a static analyzer with a locally deployable model that writes a schema-constrained security monologue naming program sites, assigning a CWE, and giving a machine-parseable verdict. We also introduce OGSM (Oracle-Grounded Security Monologue), a dataset of 1,993 C/C\texttt{++} functions covering 22 CWEs in the taint and lifetime families. Each record pairs a function with analyzer-derived or fix-diff-derived evidence and a monologue. We fine-tune three open-weight code models in two stages, first on the output format and then on the monologue content. Because evaluation prompts supply the verdict and evidence, our results measure how well models use that information, not whether they detect vulnerabilities independently. On 355 test records, fine-tuning raised Qwen2.5-Coder-7B's verdict accuracy from 4.8\% to 96.6\%; DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B reached 78.9\%, and StarCoder2-7B reached 43.7\%. Qwen2.5-Coder-7B cited 87.5\% of Tier~1 oracle sites, and every line it cited belonged to the oracle evidence. The results suggest that fine-tuning helps small models produce more structured, evidence-linked security reasoning.

papers.title: Characterising canonical lifts of ordinary Calabi-Yau varieties
papers.abstract: We study Brantner-Taelman's canonical lifts of ordinary Calabi-Yau varieties and characterise their (quasi)canonical lifts in terms of rational $p$-adic Hodge theoretic data. We also show that these canonical lifts need not be of CM type and that the associated local Galois representations need not split as sums of twists of unramified representations, in contrast to classical results for abelian varieties and K3 surfaces.

papers.title: From Quaternions to Pentarnions II: quadratic differential equations
papers.abstract:
We investigate differential equations defined through elements of a nonassociative five-dimensional real algebra $\mathcal A_\gamma$, and show that every system of quadratic differential equations $\dot p=F(p)$ on $\mathbb R^5$ can be written as a differential equation over such a non-flexible quadratic algebra. We then study quadratic differential equations and their solutions over the whole family $\{\mathcal A_\gamma\}_{0\leq\gamma\leq1}$ of algebras while varying $\gamma$ across the parameter interval $[0,1]$, exploiting the fact that by definition, $\mathcal A_0$ contains Hamilton's quaternion algebra and that $\mathcal A_1=\mathbb{P}$ is the real Pentarnion algebra.
  We construct explicit Jacobi elliptic solutions that deform a quaternion-valued solution at $\gamma=0$ into a Pentarnion-valued one at $\gamma=1$, and an algebra-valued Riccati equation whose equilibrium $p=0$ loses stability at a critical value of $\gamma$. Numerical experiments indicate period doubling, coexisting stable periodic orbits and irregular dynamics.

papers.title: A Five-Dimensional Nonassociative Algebra: elliptic integrability and bracketing-dependent dynamics
papers.abstract: We introduce a five-dimensional nonassociative real algebra $\mathbb{P}$ whose one-generated subalgebras are complex while its left, middle, and right nuclei are all $\mathbb{R}$. This contrast permits an unambiguous one-element functional calculus but makes polynomial ordinary differential equations sensitive to bracketing. We classify the homogeneous quadratic words containing one fixed coefficient $B$ and two copies of $p$ that preserve $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{1,B,p\}$. For a fixed-coefficient family of Pentarnion ODEs interpolating between $B(pp)$ and $(Bp)p$, changing only the bracketing preserves the linearisation but changes the observed global dynamics. Exact balance identities isolate the associator contribution, while numerical diagnostics support bounded chaos at one endpoint and an attracting periodic orbit at the other. The flexibility defect $p(Bp)-(pB)p=-[p,B,p]$ also produces a rank jump: after polarisation, one-generated subalgebras have dimension three on a nonempty Zariski-open set, rather than at most two. On a canonical invariant three-dimensional space the resulting flow has two first integrals and an explicit periodic orbit on an elliptic curve. We also construct a dense five-dimensional quadratic flow with a full-affine-span Jacobi-elliptic solution. Its projective closure is an elliptic normal sextic, and representation by two ordered products selects the modulus $m=1/2$.

papers.title: A Mathematical Murmuration
papers.abstract: We give a summary of a large group activity presented to primary school children as part of a STEAM (STEM plus The Arts) event. We describe the routine we demonstrated, this was based upon the tutting dance form, and the murmuration of starlings. Indeed, this demonstrates movement/dance as both a viable and engaging form of teaching mathematics.

papers.title: On Lehmer's Problem
papers.abstract:
Let $m\geq 2$ be an integer, and let $d\geq 2$ be an even integer. We study monic, reciprocal, non-cyclotomic polynomials $$ P(x)=x^d+a_{d-1}x^{d-1}+\cdots+a_1x+1\in\mathbb{Z}[x]. $$ For a fixed residue class $r\in\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$, we prove that there exists an effectively computable constant $c_{r,m}>1$ such that the Mahler measure $$ M(P)\geq c_{r,m} $$ for every irreducible polynomial $Q$ whose inner coefficients satisfy $$ a_j\equiv r\pmod m \qquad (1\leq j\leq d-1). $$ Moreover, we explicitly compute the constant $c_{r,m}$ in terms of $r$ and $m$. For the residue classes $r=2$, $r=3$, and $r=m-1$, we obtain improved lower bounds for suitable ranges of the modulus~$m$.
  We also consider monic, reciprocal, irreducible, non-cyclotomic polynomials whose inner coefficients belong to two distinct residue classes modulo $m$. More precisely, if the inner coefficients with odd indices are congruent to $a\pmod m$ and those with even indices are congruent to $b\pmod m$, where $a\not\equiv b\pmod m$, then we prove the existence of a constant $c_{m,a,b}>1$ such that the Mahler measure $$ M(P)\geq c_{m,a,b}. $$ These results solve Lehmer's problem for several families of polynomials. We also construct infinitely many examples in every even degree $d\geq 2$ of monic, reciprocal, irreducible, non-cyclotomic polynomials over $\mathbb{Q}$, together with explicit information about their Mahler measures.
  Our proofs rely on Y. Bilu's equidistribution theorem and its effective version proved by C. D'Andrea \emph{et al.}, as well as on a method developed by P. Borwein \emph{et al.} While it is natural to consider Bilu's equidistribution results in conjunction with the Borwein {\it et al}. method to Lehmer's problem, we are not aware of any previous work in the literature that employs this particular approach.

papers.title: What Sketches Tell Us about LVLMs: Conventions, Grounding, and Localisation
papers.abstract: LVLM benchmarks tell us whether a model answers correctly, but not which visual conventions it has retained, nor where those conventions live. Sketches expose this hidden structure. A sketch removes texture, lighting, and photographic context while preserving the strokes humans judged sufficient for recognition. If an LVLM can operate on that abstraction, the surviving signal is structural rather than merely photometric. We introduce a training-free sketch probe with three readouts: temporal part-construction order, spatial attention-based grounding, and the mechanistic layer/head locus of grounding. We evaluate nine LVLMs on part order and five on the attention readouts, over two part-annotated sketch datasets. Three findings emerge. First, LVLM part order tracks human convention: models reproduce canonical orderings where human drawings converge, and become correspondingly variable where human orderings vary. Controls that blank, withhold, and mismatch the sketch locate this convention in the language model. Second, part-level grounding survives the abstraction: attention heads selected from the frozen model with an existing recipe recover part and object regions on object and scene sketches, with no grounding supervision. Third, the grounding signal concentrates in a narrow mid-network band whose location follows the base language model rather than parameter count in the two families we compare, and remains stable across object and scene sketches. The result is a practical diagnostic for sketch-driven LVLMs: no fine-tuning, no auxiliary segmenter, and a layer band that doubles as a head-selection prior, matching or improving grounding mAcc@0.1 in every model and dataset we tested.

papers.title: AV-QTSS: Class-Query Target Sound Spatialization in Multi-Source 360$^\circ$ Videos
papers.abstract: Spatial audio is central to immersive 360$^\circ$ media, yet existing audio-visual spatialization renders the scene as a whole, leaving no control over an individual source. We introduce Audio-Visual Query-conditioned Target Sound Spatialization (AV-QTSS): given a monaural multi-source mixture, a 360$^\circ$ video and a class query from the 13-class DCASE sound-event ontology, it generates the first-order Ambisonics (FOA) signal of the queried source alone. The omnidirectional mixture contains no explicit spatial cues, so direction has to be inferred from the video, where several objects may sound at once. We propose a query-conditioned dense binding localizer that predicts a spherical probability map over the whole scene, coupled to the renderer so both are optimized jointly. Experiments with one to four concurrent sources show improved localization and spatial accuracy relative to established methods and ablated variants, and the localizer transfers to real 360$^\circ$ recordings after adaptation.

papers.title: A lifting defect for oriented $t_3$ and $\bar t_6$ moves
papers.abstract: We study oriented $t_3$- and $\bar t_6$-moves through the problem of lifting Fox $3$-colorings to colorings by a nine-element Alexander quandle. We define a nonnegative integer lifting defect $\delta$ for oriented links and prove that it is invariant under these moves. For knots, the defect equals the rank of an alternating bilinear form obtained from a Seifert matrix, so it is even. We also prove that it is additive under connected sum. Let $K_s$ be the connected sum of $s\geq 1$ copies of $9_{46}$. Then $\delta(K_s)=2s$, so these knots represent infinitely many distinct equivalence classes under the oriented moves, and none is equivalent to an unlink. After forgetting orientation, each $K_s$ can be transformed into an unlink with $2s+1$ components by $3s$ ordinary $3$-moves.

papers.title: Searching for binary orientable sequences
papers.abstract: An aperiodic binary orientable sequence is a finite sequence of zeros and ones for which, for some integer $n$, all the subsequences of $n$ consecutive symbols, read either forwards or backwards, are distinct. Analogously, a periodic binary orientable sequence is an infinite periodic sequence of zeros and ones for which, for some integer $n$, all the subsequences of $n$ consecutive symbols, read either forwards or backwards, are distinct within a single period of the sequence. Such sequences have potential application in position-location applications. For applications, the longer the sequence (or the greater the period in the periodic case) the greater its utility, but yet while constructions are known for such sequences, and upper bounds on their length (or period) exist, the precise maximum length (or period) was previously unknown for anything other than small values of $n$. In this note the results of LLM-conducted searches for the longest possible aperiodic and periodic binary orientable sequences for $n\leq16$ are reported. In each case an example of a sequence of the maximum discovered length is also provided, and the maximum possible length is now determined for every $n\leq16$ for both the periodic and aperiodic cases.

papers.title: The fate of $s_{\pm}$ superconductivity in the bilayer nickelate La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$
papers.abstract: Motivated by the recent measurement of high-temperature superconductivity in the bilayer nickelate system La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ in the bulk as well as thin film samples, we seek to understand the role of the interlayer coupling in this system in dictating the pairing symmetry. Many proposals posit the existence of an $s_\pm$ superconducting phase in close competition with the mroe conventional cuprate-like $d$-wave state in both weak- and strong-coupling theories. However, at least in the latter, the effects of Coulomb repulsion and the double occupancy constraint have been largely neglected. In this manuscript, we propose a mean-field fractionalization treatment that captures the full $SU(2)$ particle-hole symmetry of the t-J model at half-filling, and show how a systematic treatment of this new symmetry leads to an added Coulomb pseudopotential constraint - one that is absent in the usual $U(1)$ treatment. We then apply this new fractionalization scheme to a simplified bilayer t-J model of La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, showing how the Coulomb pseudopotential suppresses the existence of $s_\pm$ symmetry in favor of $d$-wave pairing.

papers.title: Multiplicative vs. Additive State Coupling in Learned Optimizer Schedules
papers.abstract: We learn schedules for a continuous penalty relaxation of MAX-CUT by backpropagating through an unrolled classical solver. A state-blind schedule generalizes to instances substantially larger than those used for training. A state-adaptive bilinear schedule also generalizes out of distribution, outperforming its untrained baseline across 15 seeds ($t=4.1$). By contrast, an additive ablation with identical inputs and output heads is statistically indistinguishable from the bilinear model in distribution but performs worse than its own baseline out of distribution ($t=-11.7$). This separation appears without regularization and persists across a $30$ round weight-decay sweep: the bilinear advantage remains significant at every tested value, whereas the additive model never recovers. The results in this setting isolate how solver state enters the schedule, rather than state adaptivity alone, as the architectural distinction associated with out-of-distribution transfer.

papers.title: Machine Learning Applications in the Solar Interior and Atmosphere
papers.abstract: The solar interior and atmosphere constitute a strongly coupled, multiscale dynamical system defined by continuous temporal evolution. Predicting the state of this system requires modeling physical interactions that span disparate spatial and temporal scales, constrained by heterogeneous and sparse data. This chapter formalizes the Sun within the mathematical framework of dynamical systems theory, defining a global state vector ($\vec{S}$) governed by thermodynamical, kinetic, and magnetic properties. Because solar observations represent projected, multi-modal, and partially observable measurements ($\vec{O}[\vec{S}]$) of this hidden state, pure physics-based deduction is fundamentally constrained. We present a unifying thesis: the primary role of machine learning in heliophysics is to act as a structured family of mathematical operators---specifically Inference ($\mathcal{I}$), Emulation ($\mathcal{E}$), Propagation ($\mathcal{P}$), and Control ($\mathcal{C}$)---that reconstruct, simulate, and couple this global state vector across disparate physical layers. By framing the vast, multi-disciplinary literature within this unified state-space taxonomy, we demonstrate how data-driven techniques bridge observational gaps to resolve hidden multiscale couplings and dramatically accelerate the simulation of non-linear processes, establishing a rigorous pathway to predict the global evolution of the Sun.

papers.title: Automated identification of ivory carvings using machine learning: A proof-of-concept approach to detecting the illegal wildlife trade
papers.abstract: Despite a ban on the international trading of recently poached ivory, elephants are still killed for their tusks. Ivory and its products are mainly sold in online marketplaces. However, due to the huge volume and variety of adverts and the similarity of ivory with other materials that can be legally sold, it is hard for enforcement officials to identify illicit trading and prosecute sellers. Existing techniques for identifying elephant ivory, such as Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy and microscopy, can reliably distinguish ivory from other materials, but require physical access to the item and cannot be applied to photographs alone. As a result, these methods are unsuitable for screening the large volume of images posted in online marketplaces, leaving a gap for automated, image-based identification tools. In this proof of concept work, we investigate the potential of machine learning techniques for image analysis to automatically distinguish ivory objects from bone. We employ a semantic segmentation framework using a U-Net architecture with a ResNet34 backbone, leveraging transfer learning on an augmented dataset of 541 original images. Using a dataset of images of ivory and items resembling carved ivory, several models were trialled. On a distinct test set, the classifier achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.81 and an overall classification accuracy of 81% on confident samples. The paper presents the best-performing model as a proof of concept for developing a system that can effectively identify ivory and its products when indicative features of elephant ivory are present in an image. This work provides initial steps towards a machine learning-based framework designed to advise law-enforcement in detecting illegal elephant ivory trade.

papers.title: A general algebraic characterization of extremal $\Delta$-trees and $k$-cyclic graphs for degree-homogeneous VDB indices
papers.abstract: We present a general algebraic method for maximizing a vertex-degree-based (VDB) topological index $TI(G) = \sum_{uv \in E(G)} f(d(u),d(v))$ over the class of $n$-vertex trees with a prescribed maximum degree $\Delta \ge 3$. By expressing the edge multiplicities of the basis $\mathcal{B} = \{(1,\Delta), (\Delta,\Delta)\}$ via degree-sum identities, we reduce the maximization of $TI(T)$ to the minimization of an explicit discrete penalty function $G(x,y)$ over the non-basic edges. We formulate five analytical conditions on the weight function $f(x,y)$ that dictate the optimal edge distributions, yielding a complete characterization of the extremal trees across all congruence classes of $n \pmod{\Delta - 1}$. Additionally, we provide their explicit construction by attaching leaves to a core of internal vertices. Applying this framework, we obtain the complete characterization of extremal $\Delta$-trees for the Degree-Ratio Sombor ($DRSO$), Symmetric Division Deg ($SDD$), and Hyperbolic Sombor ($HSO$) indices for all $\Delta \ge 3$. Furthermore, the analytical conditions identify the exact degree thresholds for the Arithmetic-Geometric ($AG$) and Diminished Sombor ($DSO$) indices, showing that the same extremal family maximizes $AG$ if and only if $3 \le \Delta \le 8$, and $DSO$ if and only if $3 \le \Delta \le 4$. Finally, since changing the edge count from $m = n - 1$ to $m = n - 1 + k$ affects only the constant term in the decomposition while leaving the penalty function $G(x,y)$ invariant, the method extends directly to connected $k$-cyclic graphs.

Determining the extremal trees that maximize a VDB index among all nn-vertex trees with a prescribed maximum degree Δ\Delta is a fundamental problem in extremal graph theory. While over unconstrained nn-vertex trees the maximum of such indices is typically attained by the star graph SnS_{n} (as shown for D​R​S​ODRSO in [4, 13] and for H​S​OHSO in [5]), imposing an upper bound Δ\Delta on the vertex degrees partitions the extremal problem into Δ−1\Delta-1 congruence classes of n(modΔ−1)n\pmod{\Delta-1}. Existing studies generally address this problem in one of two ways: 1. Upper bounds tight for a single congruence class: Several works derive general upper bounds in terms of nn, mm, and Δ\Delta (see, e.g., Proposition 2 in [4] for the D​R​S​ODRSO index, or [25] for the A​GAG index), or systematically identify optimal edge bases for various VDB indices via linear programming [6]. However, equality in such bounds holds if and only if the tree contains exclusively basic edges—such as (1,Δ)(1,\Delta)- and (Δ,Δ)(\Delta,\Delta)-type edges—which is realizable only in a single congruence class (e.g., n≡2(modΔ−1)n\equiv 2\pmod{\Delta-1}). The remaining Δ−2\Delta-2 congruence classes, where internal vertices of intermediate degrees must occur, remain unresolved. 2. Index-by-index characterizations: When complete characterizations across all congruence classes are pursued, they are invariably carried out for one index at a time, most often via combinatorial edge-switching arguments restricted to molecular trees (Δ≤4\Delta\leq 4). For instance, extremal chemical trees (Δ≤4\Delta\leq 4) have been characterized for the S​D​DSDD index [3], general chemical BID indices [2], and recently for the D​S​ODSO [23, 20] and H​S​OHSO [16] indices.
