papers.title: Energy stability of explicit--implicit--null time discretizations for nonlinear degenerate parabolic equations with state-dependent coefficients
papers.abstract: We study nonlinear degenerate parabolic equations with state-dependent coefficients admitting a scalar energy potential. The explicit--implicit--null (EIN) method avoids severe time step restrictions of explicit time stepping and costly Newton--Raphson iterations required by a fully implicit treatment of the nonlinearity. Using orthogonal projection of the Kirchhoff transform, we prove nonlinear energy stability for first- to third-order EIN time stepping coupled with a wide range of spatial discretizations that admit self-adjoint positive semidefinite discrete operators. Under an upper bound for the diffusion coefficient on relevant stage segments, two IMEX coefficient conditions yield sufficient stabilization bounds without any time step restriction. The estimates dissipate the original convex energy and allow degenerate diffusion. We also extend the analysis to diffusion systems with a scalar energy potential in a fixed positive definite metric, and to consistent positive-weight quadrature discretizations. Applications include porous-medium flow, nonlinear heat transfer in plasma, and multicomponent diffusion.

papers.title: Parabolic Rectifiable Reifenberg for Measures
papers.abstract: We announce a structure theory for measures on $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}$ equipped with the parabolic distance. Our results include a parabolic rectifiable Reifenberg theorem for arbitrary Radon measures, qualitative and quantitative characterizations of regular parabolic rectifiability by Jones square functions, and sharp results for $L^p$ beta numbers. The results hold in every parabolic dimension and extend the theories of Edelen--Naber--Valtorta, Azzam--Tolsa and David--Semmes to space-time. The stated theorems and corollaries, together with their proofs, are formalized in Lean~4 with Mathlib.

papers.title: How Robust Are CNNs and Vision Transformers for Alzheimer's MRI Classification Across Datasets?
papers.abstract: Accurate assessment of Alzheimer's disease stages from MRI is important for understanding disease progression and supporting the development of computer-aided analysis tools. Deep learning models have shown promising results for Alzheimer's disease classification from MRI. However, when evaluated on single datasets, it is difficult to determine whether the observed performance reflects consistent architectural behavior or dataset-specific effects. In this work, we present a multi-dataset benchmarking framework with standardized preprocessing and evaluation. We compare five architectures: ResNet-50, ReXNet-150, Swin Transformer, ViT-Base, and ViT-Large. The models are evaluated across three MRI datasets representing severe class imbalance, train-test distribution mismatch, and large-scale augmentation. The results show broadly consistent performance patterns across datasets, with ViT-Large achieving the best performance on all three datasets and reaching up to 99.84% accuracy and 99.86% macro F1. Performance differences between architectures are most pronounced under distribution mismatch and considerably smaller in the augmented-data setting. Across datasets, lower class-level performance is observed primarily among adjacent early-stage categories, particularly Very Mild and Mild impairment. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating deep learning architectures across multiple data conditions rather than relying on single-dataset performance.

papers.title: Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust--Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly participate in negotiations on behalf of individuals and organizations, yet they remain vulnerable to manipulation, particularly in repeated multi-party interactions. Classical multi-agent systems address this challenge through explicit trust and reputation models, whereas existing work on LLM negotiation largely treats trust as an emergent phenomenon. We investigate whether LLM agents can form useful trust estimates from prior interactions and leverage them to improve future negotiation outcomes. We introduce a repeated, multi-party, multi-issue negotiation framework in which recurring agents participate in a sequence of negotiation games while one participant covertly attempts to prevent agreement. After each game, agents assess their counterparts and maintain pairwise trust estimates that carry over to subsequent negotiations. We compare trust-aware and trust-agnostic agents and analyze how explicit trust influences negotiation outcomes. Our results reveal a \emph{trust--agreement gap}: trust-aware agents can identify the adversary within a few games, but accurate trust estimates do not consistently translate into better agreements. Trust increases agreement rates by up to 23 percentage points, but only when agents are explicitly guided to use it in their decisions. Explicit trust can therefore improve repeated LLM negotiations, but its value depends critically on how trust is assessed and incorporated into agents' reasoning.

authors.name: Moumita Choudhury
authors.institution: Jashore University of Science and Technology

papers.title: The Helpful Agent Problem: When Emergent Cooperation Among LLM Agents Bypasses Intended Workflows
papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in collaborative settings where they pursue separate tasks while sharing resources and operating under review or oversight processes. Such settings create safety risks not only when agents are malicious, but also when they are simply trying to help. Prior work has largely studied adversarial or explicitly collusive behavior; we show that benign agents pursuing separate objectives can spontaneously cooperate in ways that bypass intended workflows. We call this the \emph{helpful agent problem}. We study long-horizon shared-resource environments in which agents sometimes depend on resources owned by their peers and cross-owner changes are normally mediated by a reviewer. When review becomes unavailable, agents begin making changes on one another's behalf despite having no shared reward or explicit incentive to cooperate. Crucially, these actions remain within each agent's local permissions while circumventing the system's intended oversight structure. We introduce \textsc{FavorBench}, a controlled benchmark with measurable downstream side effects, and adapt \textsc{CooperBench} to test the phenomenon in realistic repositories. Across two benchmarks and four models, we find that out-of-workflow favors emerge frequently. Further, in \textsc{FavorBench}, favors from at least three models cause significant harm to parties outside the interaction. These results reveal a distinct multi-agent safety challenge: cooperation itself can create pathways around system-level safeguards.

authors.name: Moumita Choudhury
authors.institution: Jashore University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Sheaves on nodal singularities I
papers.abstract: We study two families of moduli spaces of sheaves attached to the node, namely the punctual Hilbert schemes of the non-reduced plane curve $x^uy^v=0$, and the punctual Quot schemes of the module $k[[x]]^u\oplus k[[y]]^v$ over the reduced node $xy=0$. We compute their motivic generating functions for all $u,v$ and over every field. Both are specializations of a single rational function whose numerator counts matrices by rank, and they are related by the substitution $\mathbb{L}\mapsto Q\mathbb{L}$. This proves the Hilb--Quot correspondence for the node with independent ranks on the two branches. The main geometric ingredient is an elementary modification of an ideal along a branch of the curve, whose fibres are affine spaces of dimension equal to a contact length. We also construct stratifications of the Hilbert schemes into products of affine spaces and tori, and we formulate a branchwise Hilb--Quot--HOMFLY conjecture, which we test on the colored Hopf link.

papers.title: Bounds on polynomial approximations of the discrete logarithm function
papers.abstract:
We revisit a classical result of Coppersmith and Shparlinski showing bounds on how well polynomials can approximate the discrete log function. They showed that for any univariate polynomial $f(X) \in \mathbb{F}_p[X]$ with $deg(f) \leq D$, we have: $$ |\{ x \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times \mid f(x) = dlog(x) \}| \leq \sqrt{2 D p}.$$ We show two improvements: (1) For all $D$, we improve the upper bound above to $(1+o(1)) \cdot \sqrt{Dp}$. In particular, we give nontrivial upper bounds on the approximation even for $D > p/2$. This new upper bound is the Johnson bound from the theory of list-decoding of error-correcting codes, and in fact our proof uses a connection to that problem, as well as other combinatorial ideas.
  (2) For $D = 1$, where both the above bounds are $O(\sqrt{p})$, we give an asymptotically improved upper bound of $O(p^{2/5})$. This is based on the sum-product phenomenon of additive combinatorics.
  We also improve the [CS00] bounds on the number of points of the form $(x, dlog(x)) \in \mathbb{F}_p^2$ that any bivariate polynomial $Q(X,Y) \in \mathbb{F}_p[X,Y]$ with $deg(Q) \leq D$ can vanish on, with our new bounds approaching the analogue of the Johnson bound for this problem.

authors.name: Swastik Kopparty
authors.institution: Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada

papers.title: Logit--Koopman coordinates for scale-resolved forecast-error growth in a three-level Lorenz-96 system
papers.abstract: Forecast-error growth in multiscale chaotic systems involves both advancement toward saturation and evolution of the error's scale distribution. We introduce Logit--Koopman coordinates to describe these processes together. For error energies normalized by fixed reference levels, logistic growth has exponential odds as exact Koopman eigenfunctions and affine logits as growth clocks, with an explicit inverse to error energy. Several band clocks define a longitudinal coordinate for shared advancement and transverse coordinates for departures from the reference band-growth relation. An exact transformed error-energy budget resolves production, conservative redistribution, interlevel exchange and dissipation into contributions to clock speed and transverse motion; an equivalent reference-law decomposition exposes the effect of ensemble heterogeneity. In uncoupled and coupled three-level Lorenz-96 regimes, 200 forecasts per regime exhibit nearly affine band-mean logits ($R^2=0.965$--$0.993$), alongside distinct timing, residual and launch-anomaly correlations. Recovered error fields reveal net slow-to-fast interlevel error-energy exchange in the coupled control, which removes slow-level error energy at a nearly steady relative rate near 1.2 per model time unit. Fast-only initial perturbations nevertheless seed slow-level errors immediately; after this transient, their mean approximately follows the control growth curve delayed by about 0.7 model time units. The slower middle-band clock reflects the full physical balance and an error deficit maintained at the dominant wavenumbers, rather than the strongest transformed interlevel sink. The contribution is a prescribed reference geometry in which growth timing, relative scale-evolution and signed physical exchange become separately measurable.

papers.title: Experimental Mathematics: Discovering The Half-Derivative from First Principles
papers.abstract:
This expository paper grew out of two lectures in Miller's Math 409: The little Questions (Williams College, Fall 2026). We explore fractional derivatives by asking what a ``half-derivative'' might mean if applying it twice is to recover an ordinary derivative. Linearity and a natural guess for the half-derivative of a power function lead to a functional equation related to the classical factorial recurrence. Choosing the familiar Gamma-function extension gives the classical formula \[
  \mathscr{D}^{1/2}(x^n)
  \ =\ \frac{\Gamma(n+1)}{\Gamma(n+\tfrac12)}x^{n-1/2}. \] We derive $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$, evaluate $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt{\pi}$ using the Gaussian integral, and verify the half-derivative formula with an elementary integral. Along the way, we explore how the Gamma function generalizes factorials and binomial coefficients beyond their classical domains, encounter the double factorial, see why the usual product rule fails, and examine the half-derivative of $e^x$. We also explain why the original requirements do not determine a unique operator. The treatment emphasizes motivation, the benefits of experimentation through accessible calculations in test cases, rather than the general theory of fractional calculus.

papers.title: A Cubic Underestimator for Deterministic Global Optimization
papers.abstract: We propose a new underestimator with pointwise and Hausdorff convergence of order three for deterministic global optimization of twice continuously differentiable functions with Lipschitz continuous Hessians. The proposed underestimator is obtained by augmenting the second-order Taylor expansion with a cubic remainder term of the objective function yielding a valid global underestimator that can be used to obtain lower bounds in a branch-and-bound method to solve nonconvex global optimization problems. The underestimator is nonconvex, and finding its global minimum could be computationally expensive. Accordingly, we derive a sufficient condition under which the proposed cubic underestimator is edge-concave, so that its minimum over a box can be found by vertex evaluation, while retaining third-order convergence. We show that the maximum separation distance between the objective function and the underestimator decreases cubically with the width of the box. This higher order convergence enables the lower bounds to converge more rapidly to the optimal value as the variable bounds are progressively tightened. The proposed underestimator is incorporated into a deterministic branch-and-bound algorithm and compared with the {\alpha}BB and second-order edge-concave underestimators on a collection of 130 benchmark problems. The numerical results show that the proposed underestimator outperforms the compared underestimators in terms of both the number of explored branch-and-bound nodes and total CPU time, while maintaining a competitive computational cost per node. These results demonstrate that the proposed cubic edge-concave underestimator can provide more effective lower bounds and better computational performance in deterministic global optimization.

papers.title: AskGLP1: A Knowledge Graph LLM Agent for Exploring GLP-1 Experience from Online Patient Narratives
papers.abstract: GLP-1 medications are increasingly used for weight management, and many people share their experiences online. These narratives show why people take the drugs and what they experience, but they remain unstructured and disconnected from formal pharmacovigilance. We therefore present AskGLP1, a system that transforms online patient narratives into a knowledge graph (KG) and answers questions about medication experiences. Through an LLM-assisted pipeline grounded in the MedDRA terminology, AskGLP1 screens nearly 8.5 million Reddit posts for medication experiences and distills 163,135 of them, with 2,506 WebMD reviews, into a KG of 385,790 drug-side-effect and drug-purpose relations. We find that GLP-1 experiences are source- and drug-specific. Online narratives share the most common gastrointestinal symptoms with FAERS, but they foreground everyday burdens such as fatigue and food aversion, whereas FAERS reports more often include injection-site reactions and selected serious diagnoses such as pancreatitis. We further find that posts report less nausea and vomiting for tirzepatide than for semaglutide, more fatigue for Wegovy than Ozempic and for Zepbound than Mounjaro. Evaluations show that the agent answers with verifiable evidence and declines requests for medical advice. Our findings reveal gaps between what FAERS captures and what people report online, and they call for patient-centered approaches to pharmacovigilance. Code, prompts, and evaluation questions are available at https://github.com/ZhaoqianXue/AskGLP1.

authors.institution: Chandra Shekhar Azad University of Agriculture and Technology

authors.name: Zhongyin Wang
authors.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Zhe He
authors.institution: Xi'an University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Reflective Computing
papers.abstract: Interactive technology is increasingly built for speed, and generative AI now answers before a question is fully formed. Yet the capacity to pause, interpret and decide for oneself is central to wellbeing, learning and meaningful use. HCI has named paradigms for sensing emotion, changing behavior, calming attention and tracking the self. However, none of them takes human reflection, and the slowing down it requires, as its organizing aim. This article defines that paradigm, reflective computing, and derives it from what thirty years of designs lack. We analyzed 134 interactive systems from 17 ACM venues (1996-2026) in two phases. First, an abductive gap analysis read every system against reflection theory, and seven recurring gaps defined seven dimensions, namely tempo agency, invitational form, interpretive openness, reflective depth, temporal span, protected idleness and ethical non-extraction. Second, two independent coders scored every system with a codebook (Krippendorff's alpha 0.67 to 0.84 for five dimensions; ICC 0.82 for the overall score). The system sets the pace in 51 designs, 74 support only momentary use, only 12 scaffold reflection beyond description, and 56 papers are silent on the inner states they collect. No system expresses all seven dimensions strongly, and only 20 meet the definition. Slow and experience centered design comes closest, whereas persuasive technology and human-AI interaction score lowest. Factor and latent class analyses reveal two cultures of reflection, one working through form and the other through scaffolded thought, which only one system combines. Systems that let people set the pace score markedly higher, even with paradigm and form controlled (odds ratio 13.5). Hence, reflective computing is proposed as a paradigm whose aim is a human capacity rather than a system function, and which treats slowness as valuable only when people choose it.

papers.title: Environment Edits as a Corrective Signal for Reward Learning
papers.abstract: Robot corrections allow people to adjust a robot's behavior, but a single correction changes many features. Also, preferences about object attributes and relationships between objects cannot be expressed by moving the robot. We propose environment edits as a complementary form of feedback. The robot's motion is held constant as the human edits the scene, so the only explanation for the edit is the moved object. We introduce Feature Learning from Environmental and Robot-Relational Edit Traces (FERRET), which learns preferences from both robot and environment corrections. We show that environment edits are able to disambiguate features and learn preferences that robot corrections alone cannot.

papers.title: ActionRAG: Evidence-Refining Graph Diffusion for Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents need long-term memory that can recover precise and mutually consistent evidence from growing interaction histories, particularly when answers depend on relations among facts rather than isolated semantic matches. Current memory pipelines remain vulnerable at two stages: indexing errors can fragment repeated entities or merge distinct ones, and online retrieval often treats initial similarity scores as final even when the surrounding graph provides evidence for revising them. We introduce ActionRAG, a graph memory architecture that couples cautious indexing with query-time graph retroevaluation. Its indexing pipeline reconciles type labels and applies tiered entity resolution. Given a query, dual-channel entity and triple retrieval forms an initial evidence set and induces a bounded local graph. Query-conditioned receiver-normalized diffusion refines triple scores using local path structure. Seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization preserve direct evidence while recovering missed connections. We evaluate ActionRAG on MemoryAgentBench (MAB), which tests accurate retrieval, conflict resolution, long-range understanding, and test-time learning. Across its eight deterministic-scoring columns, ActionRAG achieves 55.1 average accuracy, improving over the strongest retrieval-based memory baseline by 5.4 points. Under MAB's query-time cost accounting, mean synthesis cost stays below \$0.001 per query on the four reported cost columns, and the sum of separately measured retrieval-side p99 components is 440.7 ms on our consumer Apple Silicon setup.

papers.title: SWIFT-Cell: Segmentation Without Iterative Flow Tracking
papers.abstract: Generalist segmenters such as Cellpose-SAM (CPSAM) outline cells accurately across stains but slowly; watershed detectors such as QuPath's are fast but less accurate. In time-critical use, such as interactive retrieval of cells from a user-drawn region, CPSAM at the reference settings takes 58-303 s per measured 8192 x 8192 region on an RTX 4500 Ada GPU, beyond a seconds-scale interactive target. We distil CPSAM into SWIFT-Cell (SWIFT), a 0.63M-parameter U-Net trained only on CPSAM masks of 1,202 H&E and IHC tiles. On three 8192 x 8192 development regions SWIFT takes 2.0-5.2 s on 4 CPU cores in int8, 2.5-5.1x faster than QuPath's detector on the same cores, and 0.36-0.49 s on a GPU. Against human annotations on eight H&E, IHC and ISH sets it keeps 95% of CPSAM's panoptic quality (PQ) on PanNuke (0.593 vs. 0.627) and is level on NuCLS (0.546 vs. 0.540). On Ki-67 IHC masks scored to the outline centre it is 0.205 PQ above QuPath's better mode, 0.079 below CPSAM and 0.027 below InstanSeg (CI includes 0; at the outer edge 0.008 below CPSAM); on 212 pathologist-outlined nuclei in Ki-67 fields of 12 untouched patients its recall is 0.925 (CPSAM 0.920, InstanSeg 0.901; paired difference CIs include 0); one method-blinded pathologist accepted its outlines in 96% of 100 fields (60 from two development tissue patients, 40 hematology; CPSAM 83%, QuPath 53%; tissue 100% for SWIFT and CPSAM); on ER/PR points from 12 patients its detection F1 is 0.882 (CPSAM 0.896, InstanSeg 0.857), and on 4-reader PD-L1 points 0.83 (CPSAM 0.85, readers 0.87). SWIFT is close to CPSAM in accuracy and faster than watershed detection.

authors.name: Devansh Lalwani
authors.institution: King Edward Memorial Hospital and Seth G.S. Medical College

authors.name: Anand Reddy
authors.institution: Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center

papers.title: When Protection Hurts: A Cytokine Storm Theory of Supply Chain Overreaction
papers.abstract: Supply chain resilience research has traditionally viewed defensive actions such as safety stock, backup suppliers, expedited transportation, and emergency sourcing as beneficial. However, disruptions such as the COVID-19 pandemic, the 2021 semiconductor shortage, and the Suez Canal blockage highlight how synchronized hoarding, duplicate ordering, and capacity reservation can amplify congestion and operational costs, sometimes worsening the original disruption. Motivated by this observation, we develop a decision-theoretic framework in which Protective Response Intensity (PRI) is an endogenous decision variable. We introduce Response-Induced Loss (RIL) to capture costs generated by defensive actions and characterize a unique optimal response that balances disruption mitigation against self-induced losses. We derive a closed-form critical response threshold beyond which RIL exceeds the original disruption intensity, a phenomenon termed a *Supply Chain Cytokine Storm*. We further propose the Cytokine Storm Index (CSI), measuring response-induced loss relative to the original disruption, and discuss its potential calibration using operational data. Extending the framework to interconnected supply networks, we derive a spectral stability condition distinguishing bounded decentralized responses from network-wide propagation. Numerical experiments show that optimal responses remain below the storm threshold, whereas proportional response heuristics can exceed it. Network responses converge or diverge according to the derived stability condition. Overall, our findings highlight that supply chain resilience depends not only on mitigating disruptions but also on keeping defensive responses proportionate to the shocks they are intended to address.

papers.title: Optimal solution ranks in the Max-Cut semidefinite relaxation
papers.abstract: For every $n$ and $r$ with $1\le r$ and $\binom{r+1}{2}\le n$, we construct a connected unweighted graph on $n$ vertices whose Max-Cut semidefinite relaxation has a unique optimal solution of rank $r$. The main examples are the Kneser graphs $K(m,2)$, whose unique optima have rank $m-1$. A six-vertex wheel supplies rank three, and attaching pendant vertices preserves both rank and uniqueness. For dense random graphs, we also prove a polynomial lower bound on the optimal rank.

papers.title: Preparing State-Selected Molecular Beams with high Efficiency using Quantum Cascade Lasers
papers.abstract: We demonstrate the ro-vibrational state-selective preparation of CO molecules ($v$ = 0, J = 0 $\rightarrow$ $v$ = 1, J = 1) in an internally cold molecular beam using a continuous-wave, narrow-linewidth distributed feedback type quantum cascade laser, with an output wavelength of 4.65 $\mu$m. Using a modulation-free wavelength stabilization scheme, we show that population transfer to near saturation levels can be obtained with sufficient long term stability, as needed for state-resolved scattering experiments. We show preliminary results of CO molecules prepared in the $v$ = 1 state, scattering from a clean Cu(100) surface. This study showcases the promise of QCL based excitation for state-selected molecular beam based scattering experiments, especially involving transitions in the mid-infrared domain ($\lambda$ > 4.5 $\mu$m) which are otherwise difficult to access using conventional sources.

papers.title: Revisiting the Schwarz Lemma for the Pentablock: Counterexamples and Sharp Interpolation Criteria
papers.abstract: Alshehri and Lykova (\emph{J. Geom. Anal.} \textbf{33} (2023)) formulated a Schwarz lemma for the pentablock $P$, giving a criterion for the existence of an analytic map from the unit disc $\mathbb D$ into the closed pentablock $\overline P$ that sends the origin to the origin and a prescribed point $\lambda_0\in\mathbb D$ to a given point $x_0\in\overline P$. We show that the sufficiency direction of their criterion is false. We identify the underlying error as the extension to the open unit disc of a Fej\'er--Riesz identity that is valid only on the unit circle. We establish a corrected necessary and sufficient interpolation criterion when the last two components are prescribed by a fixed rational $\Gamma$-inner function and resolve the special case $s_0=0$. Using the Poisson integral representation of the associated outer spectral factor, we obtain a sharp comparison between the corrected bound and the bound proposed by Alshehri and Lykova, with a precise characterization of equality. We further express the logarithmic difference between these bounds as a nonnegative Green potential, thereby quantifying the discrepancy in terms of the derivative of the first coordinate of the prescribed $\Gamma$-inner function. Finally, we formulate a variational problem over rational $\Gamma$-inner interpolants satisfying the prescribed two-point conditions. We show that the supremum of the associated outer-factor quantities determines the maximal admissible modulus of the first coordinate among pentablock-valued interpolants whose last two components belong to this class. Equivalently, this extremal problem reduces to minimizing the corresponding Green potential. We conclude by discussing the remaining problem of characterizing unrestricted Schwarz interpolation for the pentablock and its connection with the Lempert function.

papers.title: Visible Reasoning: User-Facing Decision Transparency for Generative AI Systems
papers.abstract:
Across multiple waves of computing, public trust in new technology has followed the emergence of governance mechanisms that made dominant risks legible and manageable. Generative AI shifts this pattern: these systems synthesize across heterogeneous sources, and users increasingly experience them as reasoning systems. The central question changes from "did it perform correctly?" to "can we trust how it arrived at its conclusion?"
  This paper introduces Filtered Decision Logs (FDLs), a user-facing transparency mechanism that makes decision formation visible without exposing raw chain-of-thought. FDLs pair each response with (i) a concise decision rationale, (ii) influence-ordered supporting data points derived from tool outputs, and (iii) relevance indicators showing which sources most shaped the conclusion. To operationalize evidence selection, we propose a trace-based method that reconstructs observability telemetry into a provenance tree and ranks evidence using four deterministic semantic and structural signals - Final Answer Similarity, Average Relevancy, Persistence, and Structural Proximity - combined via adaptive weighted scoring. We demonstrate FDLs across three domains: career advising (5 tools), investment analysis (4 tools), and travel planning (4 tools). In a formative evaluation with 50 participants (25 students, 25 working professionals in AI development), 92% rated the influence-ranked evidence as helpful for understanding and trusting the system's recommendation. Counterfactual tool-removal experiments confirm that removing the top-ranked source changes the answer more than removing a low-ranked source, validating that the ranking tracks decision dependence. We conclude that evidence-ranked transparency helps users identify misleading signals and missing context, enabling more confident acceptance, correction, or re-run of system decisions.

authors.name: Xinrui Nie
authors.institution: Jiangsu Province Key Laboratory of Anesthesiology

papers.title: SUDO: From Scientific Publications to Global Scholarly Discourse
papers.abstract: Scholarly Knowledge Graphs (SKGs) support literature search, scientific discovery, and agent-assisted research. Yet, most approaches to SKG construction pre-specify the knowledge unit to be represented, typically named scholarly entities or contribution-level statements, and retain only the publication content expressible through that unit. This choice produces two dominant yet distinct paradigms: concept-centric SKGs that preserve entities and local relations, and statement-centric SKGs that capture high-level discourse in sentences. In both cases, the graph reflects a chosen extraction target rather than how a paper constructs and communicates knowledge. We introduce SUDO, the Scholarly Upper Discourse Ontology, which defines how knowledge elements are organized and related to form a paper's research narrative, namely its scholarly discourse. Using linguistic principles that generalize across fields and tasks, SUDO enables each publication's scholarly discourse to be constructed from the bottom up as a coherent, source-grounded representation. Applied consistently across papers, the same structure connects their research narratives into a global scholarly discourse without discarding local context or provenance. We demonstrate SUDO's capabilities across a comprehensive suite of scholarly knowledge-modeling use cases and performance improvements on a downstream Large Language Model (LLM)-based scientific QA task.

authors.name: Henrique Santos
authors.institution: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul

papers.title: From Autonomous Knowledge Generation to Generalizable Property Prediction: A Precision-First Pipeline for Electro-Optic Materials Discovery
papers.abstract: Electro-optic materials, whose refractive index changes linearly with an applied electric field (the Pockels effect), set the speed and energy of optical modulators and microwave-to-optical links for quantum computing. Designing better materials requires optimizing composition alongside temperature, strain, and bias field. However, general repositories lack electro-optic tensor data. We present a pipeline that builds such a database from literature following the rule: "no value is better than a wrong value." The pipeline has five stages: physics-aware acquisition, layout-aware extraction via LLM and deterministic table parsers, a three-tier verification gate, cross-paper consensus using median and median absolute deviation, and a noise-robust surrogate model audited by leave-one-material-out (LOMO) testing. Physics enters directly: notation is mapped, point-group symmetry-forbidden Pockels components are rejected, equivalent labels are merged, and values carry provenance tags. In a run over 49 publications, the gate processed 816 candidates into 414 accepted, 215 held for review, and 187 rejected. Against a hand-certified gold standard of 303 values from 16 papers, the run achieved a precision of 0.51 and recall of 0.48 for exact record matches. Across four database snapshots, held-out materials where the surrogate model beat a predict-the-mean baseline grew from 1 of 4 to 9 of 13 as the database expanded from 10 to 22 materials. While not a controlled comparison, this trend supports the premise that a precision-oriented, physics-checked database can power forward models beyond its training set and clarifies requirements for inverse material design.

papers.title: No Value Is Better Than a Wrong Value: Finding and Handling Erroneous Data in Literature-Mined Datasets for AI
papers.abstract: Machine learning across materials science, chemistry, energy, and medicine increasingly relies on literature-extracted datasets due to a lack of curated databases. However, automated extraction introduces errors: text recognition misreads digits, units and notations are confused, values are misattributed, and LLMs hallucinate numbers. Drawing on our work building an electro-optic property database, we present a taxonomy of errors organized by their origin and signatures, alongside a layered framework for error detection. The framework combines schema and provenance checks, physical admissibility (bounds, symmetry, and governing equations), cross-source statistical consensus, model auditing, and suspicion-ranked review. In a production run, our verification gate halted 402 of 816 candidate values with typed reasons. Yet, an audit against curated references showed that 30 of 112 accepted values were defective; standard symmetry rules alone caught 21 of these. On measured BaTiO3 and KNbO3 tensors, constitutive identities caught 8 of 10 single-value errors and isolated the corrupted entries. In a controlled benchmark, the combined framework caught 81% of errors at 85% precision, including errors in single-report materials, bringing model accuracy on held-out data to within 3% of a model trained on clean data. Uncleaned data severely impairs discovery: 89% of the twenty largest values were errors, causing AI searches to prioritize false positives. Once bad numbers are controlled, missing measurement conditions emerge as the main limit, as distinct records become indistinguishable without full context. We outline directions for the field, including shared physics rule libraries and self-reporting databases.

authors.name: Andrew Lee
authors.institution: University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics

papers.title: VisGeo-PipeTrack: A Visual Geometric Servo Control Framework with MPC-RCAPID Control for UAV-Based Dynamic Pipes Tracking
papers.abstract: While unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed for pipeline inspection, prevailing research predominantly assumes static pipes. In real-world industrial environments, pipes often exhibit dynamic movements, such as vibrations. This imposes more stringent requirements on UAVs' adaptive control and computational efficiency than in static scenarios. Therefore, this paper proposes a servo control framework named VisGeo-PipeTrack, which utilizes geometric constraints to enable UAV tracking of dynamic pipes. To achieve efficient UAV positioning, YOLOv5 is employed to detect labels on the pipe. The positions are derived from visual geometric constraints based on these detected labels to enable precise localization. To address tracking control challenges, a model predictive control based real-time corrected adaptive PID (MPC-RCAPID) controller is proposed. This controller employs the Recursive Least Squares method for real-time model estimation and integrates rolling horizon optimization to dynamically adjust PID parameters. Experiments conducted on both the AirSim simulator and the Tello UAV platform validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Simulation comparisons with standard PID, fractional-order PID, adaptive PID, and fuzzy PID demonstrate that MPC-RCAPID achieves the shortest settling time (3.26 s) and the lowest average tracking error (3.52%). In physical experiments on the Tello platform, compared with standard PID control, MPC-RCAPID reduces the average tracking error by 55.52%, 26.72%, and 26.52% across the three test dimensions. These results demonstrate that VisGeo-PipeTrack facilitates efficient autonomous tracking in dynamic pipe environments.

papers.title: A new arrangement inequality (revised and extended version)
papers.abstract: We study the cyclic inequality \[ \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\,\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^a x_{i+1}^b\;\le\;\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^{(1+a+b)/2}\Big)^2, \] where $x_1,\dots,x_n\ge 0$ and indices are taken modulo $n$. Let $N(a,b)$ be the largest $n$ for which the inequality holds for all nonnegative $x_i$. We show that $N(a,b)$ is bounded above by an explicit quantity $N^*(a,b)$ obtained from the second variation at the constant vector, and we conjecture that $N(a,b)=N^*(a,b)$. For $a=b=1$ we prove that the inequality holds if and only if $n\le 8$, which settles the case left open in the original version of this paper. For $n=4$ the inequality holds whenever $1,a,b$ are the sides of a triangle, with an explicit remainder term. We show that $N$ is monotone along rays emanating from the line $a+b=1$; this corrects and extends an earlier monotonicity statement. Finally, any $n$ nonnegative numbers can be arranged so that the inequality holds; for $n\neq 6$ this is achieved by one of $n-1$ prescribed arrangements, which yields a volume bound for every such $n$.

papers.title: Dirichlet problem on locally finite graphs (revised and extended version)
papers.abstract: We study existence and uniqueness of solutions to the vertex-weighted Dirichlet problem on locally finite graphs. Let $B$ be a subset of the vertices of a connected graph $G$. The Dirichlet problem asks for a function whose discrete Laplacian is prescribed on $V\setminus B$ and whose values are prescribed on $B$. Each infinite connected component of $G\setminus B$ is called an end of $G$ relative to $B$. On finite graphs we show that the solution is the limit of an averaging process, with an explicit geometric rate given by the spectrum of the random walk, and is also the limit of the heat flow and the minimizer of an energy functional. On infinite graphs we prove two existence theorems: one with no assumption on vertex degrees, under a finite-width condition and summable data, and one for bounded data on graphs of bounded degree, where the solution is also unique among bounded functions. If there are no ends, the Dirichlet problem has exactly one solution. If there are $l$ ends, the solution set, when nonempty, has dimension at least $l$; each end carries a positive harmonic function vanishing on $B$. Calling an end parabolic when the random walk started in it hits $B$ almost surely, we show that this function can be taken bounded exactly on non-parabolic ends and is necessarily unbounded on parabolic ones, a discrete analogue of a theorem of Li and Tam. Consequently, bounded solutions are unique if and only if every end is parabolic.

papers.title: Second largest eigenvalue thresholds for the vertex-connectivity of regular graphs
papers.abstract: Let $\lambda_2(G)$ and $\kappa(G)$ denote the second largest adjacency eigenvalue and the vertex-connectivity of a graph $G$. For a non-complete $r$-regular graph $G$, Fiedler's inequality $\lambda_2(G)\ge r-\kappa(G)$ shows that $\lambda_2(G)<r-t$ forces $\kappa(G)\ge t+1$. The best such bound is known for $t=1$, by Zhang and Wang, and for $t=2$ with $r\ge4$, by Zhang. In this paper, for every $r\ge3$ and every integer $t$ with $2\le t\le r-1$, we give an upper bound on $\lambda_2(G)$ that forces an $r$-regular graph $G$ to satisfy $\kappa(G)\ge t+1$, and we determine exactly when this bound is best possible. For $\frac{r+2}{2}\le t\le r-1$, Fiedler's bound $r-t$ is already best possible. For $2\le t<\frac{r+2}{2}$, it is replaced by one of two explicit algebraic numbers, and the sign of an explicit polynomial $W(r,t)$, which never vanishes, decides which one applies. Each of the two numbers is attained exactly when $(r,t)$ satisfies an explicit arithmetic condition, and every extremal graph then consists of two cliques and an independent cut of size $t$. In this range our bound also improves a bound of Zhang that holds for every such $t$.

papers.title: VibeGame: Prompt-to-Game Development with AI-Native Engine and Self-Evolving Adversarial Agent Team
papers.abstract: Large language model agents have enabled software development through natural-language interaction, but extending this paradigm to end-to-end game development remains challenging. Building a playable game requires coordinating code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, while allowing developers to validate their integrated behavior through interactive testing. We introduce VibeGame, a framework for creating complete 2D game projects from natural-language prompts and optional reference images. Its AI-native game engine represents project state as schema-validated structured text and provides frame-synchronous runtime control, enabling agents to inspect game states, execute actions, and verify behavior at their own pace. Built upon this interface, we design an Adversarial Agent Team of eight specialized agents to separate implementation from review, so that problems are found and fixed through multi-round loops. For each conducted and accepted project, we further introduce a training-free self-evolution mechanism to distill it into reusable skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts for future development. We evaluate prompt-assets-to-game (PA2G), where agents are given an asset library, and prompt-to-game (P2G), where agents generate their own art. On a GameCraft-Bench subset, VibeGame in P2G consistently outperforms a range of agent harnesses in either P2G or PA2G with the same underlying model, including GPT-6.1-Sol.

authors.name: Haofan Wang
authors.institution: Changchun University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Extended LASMP: Language Aided Subset Sampling Based Motion Planner for Drone Navigation
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a command-aligned sampling distribution that incorporates navigation commands directly into the exploration process to improve the efficiency of sampling-based motion planning for quadcopters in three-dimensional environments. Inspired by the Language-Aided Subset Sampling Motion Planner, this paper extends command-aware subset sampling to aerial systems. Subset sampling is generalized to command-aligned regions, enabling structured 3D exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness. Natural language instructions are grounded into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints using a prompt-based large language model for entity extraction and instruction validation. Extensive simulations in complex environments demonstrate that the proposed method generates collision-free, consistent trajectories while significantly reducing sampling effort compared to uniform RRT-based planners.

authors.name: Chinwe Ekenna
authors.institution: University at Albany, State University of New York

papers.title: Symmetry-driven in-situ physical adjoint computing beyond reciprocity
papers.abstract: Nonreciprocity enriches wave control and information processing through directional transport, yet challenges conventional in-situ physical adjoint optimization, which relies on reciprocity to acquire adjoint responses. Here we demonstrate symmetry-driven in-situ physical adjoint computing (Sym-iPAC) in nonreciprocal systems, which enables access to adjoint responses on the original hardware through three classes of transpose symmetry: local geometric permutations, complex gauge reweighting, and latent symmetry in effective port dynamics revealed by Schur reduction. Experiments with programmable nonreciprocal microwave networks validate these transpose relations and yield adjoint gradients, enabling closed-loop optimization. These results establish experimentally accessible transpose symmetry as a route to in-situ physical adjoint computing beyond reciprocity.

papers.title: Physical Adjoint Learning in Wave Systems with Asymmetric Couplings
papers.abstract: Developing self-optimizing physical systems that learn directly from their response to external stimuli offers a promising route toward adaptive and intelligent machines. A key ingredient is the ability to evaluate optimization gradients within the physical hardware, bypassing the need for accurate numerical models. In wave systems, \textit{in-situ} adjoint methods provide this capability by exploiting reciprocity to physically realize the adjoint dynamics. However, this approach generally breaks down in nonreciprocal systems, where the adjoint field cannot be directly accessed through the original device. Here, we develop an \textit{in-situ} adjoint optimization framework that extends physical gradient computation to wave systems with asymmetric couplings through computationally low-cost similarity transformations between the forward and transposed operators. We utilize available degrees of freedom like tailored injected excitations, targeted measurements, and tunable parameters, to enable adjoint field reconstruction through forward experiments on the same physical platform. We demonstrate the versatility of the protocol through broadband transmission and isolation, coherent perfect absorption, programmable wavefront shaping, and spatially selective sensing. Our results provide a route to self-optimization in complex nonreciprocal wave systems through efficient physical gradient-based learning. The number of experiments required by the protocol does not increase with the number of optimization parameters, and the method remains applicable even when parts of the system are completely inaccessible.

papers.title: Designing Customer Feedback for Subscription Boxes
papers.abstract: Problem definition: Subscription box services often ask customers for ratings before choosing what to send. Responses are scarce, and longer questionnaires and finer scales lower completion. We study which candidate items a questionnaire should ask about, and in what format, when the platform then selects a fixed number of them. A design is judged by the expected value lost by not selecting the truly best items. Methodology/results: We approximate each ordinal rating by a Gaussian signal carrying its information at the cutoff between selected and unselected items. As equal numbers of responses per item grow, the ratio of this proxy's loss to the exact loss tends to one. With 1 to 100 responses per item, the two are within about 7 percent. Averaging the information over the prior instead can misstate the loss by about half. For an item far from the cutoff, the value of responses grows slowly at first and then faster, so our envelope rule values responses in blocks. In simulations with a correct prior it lowers the loss by 15 to 81 percent relative to an even spread, and on MovieLens ratings by 6 to 25 percent. Under the proxy, with responses allocated optimally, formats are ranked exactly by one number, the expected information per customer asked. Choosing the format this way comes within about 2 percent of the best on average. Managerial implications: Feedback should go to items whose place in the selection is unclear. Planning helps most when the platform's prior beliefs are informative and right. A platform unsure of its prior should widen it and send the questionnaire in waves. Calibrated on MovieLens ratings, a five-point answer carries about 1.7 times the information of a like/dislike answer, so at equal length the finer scale is better when it cuts completion by less than about 40 percent.

papers.title: Learning to Be Monitored: Causal Bounds and Intervention-Aware Post-Training Recipes for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring aims to detect potentially harmful behaviors in large language models (LLMs) from their CoTs. Intervention-based evaluations measure this property by asking whether a monitor can detect the role of an intervention from the CoT when the targeted behavior occurs, typically using minimal-criterion sensitivity ($\mathsf{TPR_{mc}}$) proposed by~\citep{guan2025monitoring}. However, a target behavior observed under intervention is not necessarily caused by it, and we show that this metric can overestimate how often a monitor detects target behaviors actually caused by the intervention. Specifically, we establish $\mathsf{TPR_{mc}}$ as an upper bound on this causal detection rate and derive a complementary lower bound, which provides a tighter evaluation framework for CoT monitorability. With this framework, we study whether LLMs can be trained to make their CoTs easier to monitor. We first construct a training dataset of paired control--intervention tasks spanning multiple intervention types. Using the dataset, we design and apply three intervention-specific training methods based on off-policy self-distillation, reinforcement learning, and on-policy self-distillation to train separate variants of each base model. Across various model-monitor configurations, all three methods generally improve CoT monitorability over the corresponding base models under our extended evaluation framework. Our code is available at https://github.com/xinyue-lxy/learning-to-be-monitored.

authors.name: Xinyue Li
authors.institution: Xi'an University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Putting Transformer Theories to the Test
papers.abstract: Several formal theories have been developed to characterize the capabilities and limitations of the transformer architecture, each employing different abstractions that capture different features of the architecture. Due to the differences in their underlying assumptions and conceptual frameworks, these theories can disagree in their predictions about what tasks transformers find easy or hard. We map out seven theories of transformer capability (Star-free, $\mathsf{AC}^0$, $\mathsf{TC}^0$, C-RASP, MPC, BAPO, and Sensitivity) and translate their results into a common matrix of predictions across a suite of tasks covering different computational structures. We provide new theoretical results to complete this matrix. We then evaluate theoretical predictions through controlled experiments measuring in-distribution sample complexity, length generalization, and pretrained language model performance. We find that no single theory explains the observed pattern of successes and failures. When a theory does not capture the transformer behaviors relevant to a task, its predictions break down; for instance, we show that the $k$-hop induction task is predicted hard by C-RASP because it does not model content-dependent attention, but we train small transformers on this task that length-generalize. Similarly, theories assuming hard attention like $\mathsf{AC}^0$ and BAPO predict binary majority to be hard, for which we also find success in practice. Together, our results point to several specific features that a theory of transformers must capture: soft rather than hard attention, dynamic content-dependent retrieval, bounded computation at each position, an account of learnability and inductive biases, and a combination of upper and lower bounds.

papers.title: OpenESM: Energy-Steered Models Are Scalable Foundation Learners
papers.abstract:
Energy-based models have shown promising properties for domain-specific tasks but remain challenging in modeling general-purpose scenarios. To bridge this gap, we design energy-steered models (ESMs) for foundational language modeling. ESMs integrate energy steering and token generation within a single architecture to leverage the energy-guided search to refine token generation. Specifically, ESMs first optimize a latent state over the energy landscape, then leverages the refined latent state for token generation. By performing such energy-guided pre-training on large-scale corpora, ESMs learn generally effective energy landscape where favorable tokens correspond to lower energy values. To explore the scaling behavior of ESMs, we pre-train ESMs on three large-scale corpora, then evaluate across 26 downstream tasks spanning a broad range of domains. Our results demonstrate that ESMs have promising scaling behaviors with increasing model size and training data, and outperform GPTs on most downstream tasks. These findings highlight ESMs as a promising architecture for large-scale pre-training and general purpose problem solving. We fully release the model weights and training infrastructure to enable the community to completely reproduce and extend our results.
  GitHub: https://github.com/datamllab/openesm HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/collections/guan-wang/openesm

authors.name: Guanchu Wang
authors.institution: University of North Carolina at Charlotte

papers.title: A Multi-Asset Dataset and Tail-Risk Framework for DeFi Yield Trading Derivatives
papers.abstract: Yield trading has emerged as a pivotal innovation in Decentralized Finance (DeFi) by decoupling principal from yield streams to enhance capital efficiency. Despite its significance, the field lacks fine-grained datasets for systematic empirical analysis. We address this gap by constructing the first large-scale benchmark dataset for Pendle, the pioneering on-chain interest rate derivatives protocol, spanning 24 months across 340 active markets with complete lifecycle observations. Our analysis reveals a structural market transition toward stablecoin-dominated "flight-to-quality" dynamics. To tackle the heavy-tailed nature of yield data, we propose Tail-MSE, an asymmetric loss function that prioritizes tail risk awareness through dynamic penalty weighting. Experiments across six state-of-the-art time series models demonstrate consistent improvements in volatility forecasting robustness, enabling the Tail-MSE Sniper strategy to achieve superior risk-adjusted returns in over half of all markets.

authors.name: Huaiyu Jia
authors.institution: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

papers.title: Nonlocal Einstein Relation in Confined Phonon Hydrodynamics
papers.abstract: Einstein relations connect carrier mobility to macroscopic transport coefficients and constitute a fundamental link between microscopic dynamics and transport. In phonon hydrodynamics, this connection is conventionally local: the drift-induced thermal conductivity is proportional to the local drift mobility. Here we show that this relation becomes intrinsically nonlocal under spatial confinement. We derive a nonlocal Einstein relation, $\kappa_H(y) = \int P(y-y')\mu(y'),dy'$, in which hydrodynamic thermal conductivity $\kappa_H(y)$ at one position depends on collective drift mobility $\mu(y')$ across the entire cross-section of the channel. In the small-Knudsen-number limit, our nonlocal theory recovers the viscous heat equation and the local Einstein relation. At finite Knudsen number, nonlocality produces intrinsic boundary slip and distinct size-scaling behavior of the drift mobility $\mu$ and hydrodynamic thermal conductivity $\kappa_H(y)$. First-principles calculations for graphite show that nonlocality broadens the channel-size window over which thermal conductivity exhibits superlinear size dependence. Temperature-dependent simulations further show that the nonlocal theory captures the emergence of a hydrodynamic peak in thermal conductivity normalized by ballistic conductance, whereas the local theory fails to accurately predict its magnitude. Our results establish a microscopic connection between collective phonon mobility and heat conduction beyond local hydrodynamics.

papers.title: Software Engineering LLMs: Why We Need Them and How Software Engineering Helps Build Them
papers.abstract: Software engineering (SE) expertise can shape how coding large language models (LLMs) are trained and which engineering capabilities they acquire. We examine this role through an industrial case study of capability-focused training for a 92B-parameter coding LLM serving more than 100,000 developers. We demonstrate how established SE knowledge can guide the selection of engineering capabilities, the construction of verifiable training data, and the evaluation of model improvements. To target repository-level refactoring, we developed RefactorForge, a pipeline that combines refactoring knowledge, established SE tools, and verification techniques to construct training data. Across 306 Python repositories, RefactorForge generated 5,704 executable tasks and retained 4,572 verified teacher trajectories totaling 72.51 million tokens. Incremental supervised fine-tuning on these trajectories, accounting for 0.46% of the preceding coding mixture's tokens, improved RefactorBench performance by 18.00 percentage points and SWE-Bench ProMax performance by 7.06 points. Under OpenCode, these improvements extended to SWE issue resolution, with gains of 4.97 points on SWE-Bench Verified and 1.23 points on SWE-Bench Pro. Improvements also persisted across other coding-agent harnesses, while greenfield repository generation showed mixed results. We report lessons from constructing capability-focused training data and evaluating its effects across engineering workloads. Building on this industrial experience, we propose a research agenda for expanding SE's role in transforming coding LLMs into SE LLMs: incorporating SE knowledge into model training, applying engineering methods to model development and maintenance, and systematically defining the engineering capabilities these models should acquire.

papers.title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Liver Lesion Segmentation and Structured Radiology Reporting
papers.abstract: Despite advances in automated liver lesion segmentation, a gap remains between image-derived predictions and clinically interpretable radiology reports. Bridging this gap requires quantitative measurements that are both reproducible and traceable. We present an evidence-grounded agentic AI framework that connects liver and lesion segmentation with deterministic quantification and structured reporting. TotalSegmentator-based nnU-Net models delineate the liver, Couinaud segments, and lesions, while computational tools extract volumes, dimensions, counts, and anatomical locations. A large language model (LLM) organizes these measurements into a predefined reporting schema, with numerical consistency checks against source measurements. On 51 LiTS cases, the segmentation stage achieved a liver Dice score of 0.947, lesion sensitivity of 75.6%, and positive predictive value of 68.9%. Exploratory screening of 25,494 MERLIN reports identified 10,208 (40.0%) with liver-related abnormalities. By connecting quantitative imaging evidence with agentic report generation, this work takes a step toward human-centered medical AI that prioritizes traceability and clinical relevance.

papers.title: Competitive exploration in structured environments
papers.abstract: Organisms must constantly weigh exploiting the resources they know against exploring for better ones. When foragers compete, the best behavior for each forager also depends on what its competitors do. How does competition change the strategic balance between exploration and exploitation? Here we address this question in a minimal model: two $\epsilon$-greedy temporal-difference learners on a one-dimensional lattice, who start at a small reward at one end and are unaware of a larger reward at the other. For a lone forager, the optimal exploration rate increases monotonically with the value of the distant reward, and with its distance up to a critical distance. When two foragers share the lattice and split rewards, the choice of exploration rate becomes a game whose Nash equilibria have both foragers exploring, both staying, or one exploring while the other stays (anti-coordination). Under local best-response dynamics, pairs of foragers often converge on both exploring or both staying, even when anti-coordination would be socially optimal. This social dilemma arises for a wide range of parameters, and it persists even in a simplified model without explicit spatial structure. A minimal, naturalistic signal, in which one forager informs the other that it has found the distant reward, can remove many of the dilemmas in which both foragers explore, and can produce a Nash equilibrium whose collective payoff exceeds that of every outcome available without signaling.

papers.title: On Reed-Muller-Type Codes Associated to Proto-Exact Categories
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show how to associate a family of binary linear block codes to the class of admissibly cofinitary objects in any proto-exact category with rank function. This family naturally generalizes the well-studied family of binary Reed-Muller codes, and recovers this classical family for suitable choices of category. We also expand the list of known examples of proto-abelian categories to include incidence categories of posets. As an application of this result, we construct a binormal, combinatorial, proto-abelian category of Kashiwara crystals associated to any root system. In the case that the proto-exact category is a category of $\mathbb{F}_1$-representations of quivers, we show how to reconstruct our family via the language of algebraic geometry codes, in particular motivating an extension to arbitrary finite fields. We provide explicit computations of the dimension and minimum distance for select families of $\mathbb{F}_1$-representations of quivers.

papers.title: Fast Path, Exact Path: One Library of Hardwired Operators for Streaming and Exact Canny Edge Detection on a Low-Cost FPGA
papers.abstract: Hysteresis edge tracking, the final stage of Canny edge detection, follows edge chains of unbounded length and therefore resists single-pass streaming; FPGA designs either approximate it or dedicate separate labelling hardware to it. We show that a single library of hardwired 3x3 operators, each with an identical two-clock latency, delivers both a camera-rate approximation and exact hysteresis on a low-cost Artix-7 (XC7A35T). The fast path streams camera pixels through the operators and K local hysteresis stages and commits each edge decision 262.15-720.63 microseconds after the pixel arrives (K = 1-8; system simulation with a datasheet camera model), that is, 3 + K camera lines later and 46-127x sooner than a frame-based processor can even begin at 30 frames per second. It provably never reports an edge that exact hysteresis rejects, recovers 76.6-96.1% of exact edges at thresholds 20/40, and on the 200 BSDS500 test images retains at least 98.6% of the exact path's boundary F-measure (ODS 0.470-0.477 versus 0.476). The exact path holds 128x128 tiles in block RAM, is exact within each tile, and replaces two-buffer iteration with in-place forward and reverse sweeps built into the same operator. This reduces hysteresis from 38-82 passes to 3-7 on pattern and photo tiles, accelerating the hysteresis step 6.6-21.7x (40x on a worst-case tile) and a complete tile 4.5-9.9x, with identical output. Both paths are bit-exact with software golden models at every pipeline stage and close timing at 50 MHz in at most 1455 LUTs. An optimised multi-core CPU remains faster on stored images, but it cannot begin until the frame is complete.

papers.title: Resource competition and survival for random walkers on complex networks
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of $W$ random walkers on a complex network where each walker requires an amount $\theta$ of resource at each time to survive. Resource is stochastically produced at each vertex of the network with a specified distribution. The survival time of the system of walkers is defined as the time required for all $W$ walkers to die. Using numerical simulations, we show that Erd{\H o}s-R\'enyi networks a have higher mean survival time than Scale-free networks as expected, but also that uniform distribution production leads to higher mean survival time than exponential distribution with the same mean. We derive an exact expression for the survival-time distribution under the assumption of independent walker lifespans, and use it to show that scale-free network topology produces strong dependence in the lifespans but homogeneous topology does not. We moreover demonstrate how the survival time can be substantially increased without changing the resource production or network topology by appropriately biasing the movement of the walkers towards low degree vertices on Scale-free networks, but has no effect on Erd{\H o}s-R{\'e}nyi networks.

papers.title: Statistical inference for boundary constrained parameters
papers.abstract: Estimation and inference under boundary constraints arises in many areas of statistics, but the available asymptotic theory remains limited and fragmented relative to the classical case, where the parameter lies in the interior of the parameter space. In this paper we derive a boundary-constrained analogue of the standard asymptotic expansion for a minimiser of a loss function, in which the deviation of the estimator from the population parameter is decomposed over lower-dimensional subspaces determined by the directional derivatives at the minimiser. Using this decomposition we show that the limiting distribution of the estimator is a mixture of point masses and truncated skew-normal distributions, with mixture probabilities determined by the directional derivative conditions. A consequence of this result is that the constrained and unconstrained coordinates do not separate: the presence of parameters on or near the boundary affects the sampling distribution of the unconstrained parameter estimators. We apply the expansion to obtain the asymptotic distribution of the quasi log-likelihood ratio statistic under a range of null hypotheses, and since the resulting mixture is not pivotal in the quasi-likelihood setting, we propose a simulation-based procedure for approximating critical values. The framework unifies and simplifies several existing results. We illustrate the methodology by testing for interactions in exponential family graphical models, where the parameters are subject to compatibility constraints that ensure a joint distribution exists.

papers.title: ZipFusion: Fusing Lossless KV Decompression with Attention for Efficient LLM Decoding
papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache places growing demands on GPU memory capacity and bandwidth as large language models serve longer contexts and more concurrent requests. Its footprint limits concurrency, while repeated KV reads during attention can make decoding memory-bandwidth bound. Prior lossless KV cache compression methods reduce transfers between devices but restore the uncompressed KV cache in GPU memory before attention. They therefore leave these repeated KV reads unchanged and require additional work and memory for decompression. We present ZipFusion, which enables attention to consume the losslessly compressed KV cache directly. ZipFusion co-designs the compression format and attention kernel to reduce the bytes read from GPU memory during attention. The kernel reconstructs the original values directly in registers using simple bit operations, avoiding a separate decompression pass and easing the memory-bandwidth bound. ZipFusion also reassigns memory freed by compression across layers to store additional KV cache. Its memory manager reserves space for ongoing generation and makes the remaining capacity available to new requests. We implement ZipFusion on top of FlashInfer and integrate it with SGLang. On an NVIDIA H100, ZipFusion achieves about 1.25x speedup over FlashInfer in decode attention. With 8K context, it improves model decode throughput by up to 26.3% over uncompressed SGLang under the same GPU memory budget. At each method's largest supported batch, it also delivers up to 2.76x the throughput of the best-performing lossless KV cache compression baseline.

authors.name: Yuetao Chen
authors.institution: National Health Commission of the People's Republic of China

authors.name: Hong Xu
authors.institution: Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine

papers.title: StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue
papers.abstract: Users of conversational assistants rarely state all requirements up front: they add constraints, amend them, withdraw them, digress, and return. Instruction-tuned LLMs fail here in two ways: active constraints stop being honored as turns accumulate (persistence failure), and withdrawn constraints keep being enacted (relapse). The only existing repair we know of is an external ledger that re-injects a compiled specification every turn. We propose StateWise, a self-improving approach that teaches a single LLM to maintain its own revisable constraint state, a typed state with tombstones for revoked constraints, so persistence and relapse are measured by executable checkers and ground-truth states are compiled for free. StateWise fine-tunes the LLM on two complementary skills, summarizing a dialogue into its constraint state and responding conditioned on that state, then self-trains on its own trajectories, keeping only turns that pass an exact round-trip check against the compiled state. This teaches 7-8B models to track the state almost perfectly but, surprisingly, not to obey it: on Llama-3.1-8B every supervised variant roughly doubles relapse. We therefore add a preference stage on self-generated relapse contrasts, where the rejected response enacts a revoked rule and the chosen one passes the round-trip check. On two backbones with held-out constraint families and unseen phrasings, StateWise cuts relapse by 8-22 points relative to supervised self-training, lifts conversation success by 8-19 points over the backbone, and beats an oracle compiled-ledger baseline on relapse with no inference-time scaffolding. We also characterize the recipe's cost on general instruction-following benchmarks and study weight interpolation as a mitigation.

papers.title: TriageRAG: Failure-Aware Self-Training for Adapting Retrieval-Augmented Language Models to Specialized Domains
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets large language models (LLMs) answer knowledge-intensive questions from retrieved evidence, but adapting a general-purpose RAG system to a specialized domain such as medicine is difficult when only an unlabeled corpus is available. Self-training approaches such as SimRAG address this by letting the LLM write its own question-answer pairs from domain passages and fine-tuning on the pairs that survive a round-trip consistency filter. We observe that these approaches treat every retained example identically: they never ask whether the student already knows the answer, already extracts it correctly from the retrieved context, or fails - and if so, whether the failure lies with the reader or with the retriever. To tackle this, we propose TriageRAG, a failure-aware self-training approach that probes the student on each self-generated question with and without retrieved context, triages it into one of four categories (known, solved, context-failure, retrieval-failure), and routes each category to the training signal that addresses it, including a parametric route that teaches the reader to answer when retrieval misses. Probing is cheap and repeated every round, so the training mixture follows the student, and the triage histogram doubles as a label-free diagnostic of where the domain gap lies. Experiments on 11 datasets spanning three domains with a Qwen3-4B backbone, and on CS-Bench with Qwen3-8B, demonstrate that TriageRAG outperforms a budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2-6.4 points and is the only method that recovers the closed-book level in every case where retrieval hurts the base model. A single ablation identifies the mechanism: round-trip filtering removes every training context that lacks the evidence, and a reader that never sees such contexts learns to over-trust noisy retrieval.

papers.title: Not All Information Is Worth Asking For: Decision-Informed Information Seeking with LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support decisions under incomplete information, where deciding what to look up and when to stop matters as much as the final answer. However, LLMs fall into an information trap: They pay for checks, i.e., costly pieces of evidence, that cannot change their decision or are not worth their cost, and they keep asking when the evidence is already sufficient. To this end, we propose Decision-Informed Value-of-information Acquisition (DIVA), a simple yet effective procedure for LLM information seeking based on the decision value of evidence. DIVA 1) lets the LLM specify a small decision model, i.e., how likely a bad outcome is and how each check would shift this probability, through short numeric questions and 2) values each candidate check by how much its imagined outcomes improve the decision net of its cost, stopping when no check is worth its cost. Its variant, DIVA-U, further accounts for the LLM's uncertain estimates of how strongly each check shifts this probability. DIVA is training-free and applies to any LLM. Across four domains and 20 LLMs, DIVA-U has lower regret, i.e., value lost relative to the best possible decision, than every LLM baseline on real-world data, mainly by stopping once evidence suffices, and DIVA cuts the regret of the best LLM baseline by 75% in synthetic scenarios where every check's reliability is given. Code: github.com/seunghan96/diva.

authors.name: Jun Seo
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Arlington

papers.title: The Formal Critical Coupling of the Four-Dimensional Anderson Model
papers.abstract:
In this work we present a formal renormalization-group (RG) calculation for the weakly coupled four-dimensional elliptic Anderson model. Under a scale-independent bare-coupling convention, and with the normalization $\lambda_{\varepsilon}$, the bubble-chain resummation yields the geometric series $\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{formal}}(\lambda)$, with a formal pole at $\lambda_c$. We stress that this pole is a feature of the formal bare bubble series. The argument combines Bogoliubov-Parasiuk-Hepp-Zimmermann (BPHZ) renormalization, a Hepp-sector motivated restriction to the bubble-chain subclass for explicit resummation, and an explicit summation of the resulting geometric series.
  Numerically, we illustrate the analytic building blocks of the formal expansion: the massive Green function, the bubble integral, the geometric resummation, the extraction of the formal pole from synthetic noisy data, a kurtosis diagnostic, and a phase diagram of the formal variance. These computations visualize the deterministic kernels and the formal resummation used above. Using spectral methods and nonlinear least-squares fitting, we verify the short-distance asymptotic behaviour of the massive Green function for $G=(1-\Delta)^{-1}\delta_0$, reproduce the logarithmic divergence of the bubble integral in four dimensions, compute the formal effective variance $\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{formal}}(\lambda)$ arising from the bubble-chain resummation, locate the formal pole at $\lambda_c$, and draw a schematic phase diagram of the formal variance in the $(\lambda,\log\varepsilon)$ plane. The kurtosis diagnostic uses a synthetic proxy for the non-Gaussian regime; the sharp change is imposed by construction. Nonlinear fitting of synthetic data recovers the formal pole within the statistical uncertainty of the synthetic noise. Our results illustrate the analytic formulas and the fitting procedure.

papers.title: Cheap AI-Assisted Reverse Engineering and What It Will Do
papers.abstract: Generative AI is putting the law of reverse engineering (RE) under severe strain. Existing IP and technology laws assume that RE is expensive and time-consuming, and that it requires specialized expertise. They generally allow it, but they rely on its difficulty as a filter to separate (permissible) RE from (impermissible) copying and theft. Generative AI is changing this equation by making \RE much faster, cheaper, and easier. AI systems can identify hardware components, extract firmware, decompile object code, and clone entire apps. The resulting struggle between technology vendors and reverse engineers will challenge a wide range of laws, including trade secret, copyright, anti-circumvention, computer misuse, and contract. In this article, we describe the ways in which AI is changing \RE, map these new practices onto existing laws, and sketch ways that the legal system could respond and their associated trade-offs.

papers.title: Understanding Communication Failures in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems aim to improve reasoning through debate, evidence sharing, and mutual correction, but interaction can also introduce failures that final accuracy alone cannot explain. Agents may converge too early, ignore dissent, suppress correct minority answers, or preserve a wrong framing across rounds. We present a corpus-grounded taxonomy of communication failures, built from 3,211 failed multi-round trajectories across medical QA, coding, finance, multi-hop reasoning, ethics, and embodied text tasks. Using this taxonomy, we analyze failure distributions across datasets and system designs, round-level error dynamics, recovery hardness, majority transitions, minority-signal suppression, and self-reported confidence. We find that failures are dominated by recovery/correction and consensus/decision problems rather than isolated first-round mistakes, with many emerging after agents first observe peer responses. Based on these findings, we recommend stronger disagreement handling, evidence verification, minority-signal preservation, and recovery checks before finalization.

authors.name: Xuan Wang
authors.institution: Shandong University of Science and Technology

papers.title: An In-depth Study of Stochastic Stellarator Coil Optimization
