papers.title: Elementary transformations of toric vector bundles
papers.abstract: We describe negative and positive elementary transformations of toric vector bundles in terms of Klyachko filtrations. We first determine the filtrations of the restriction of a toric vector bundle to an invariant prime divisor and then derive explicit formulas for the transformed bundle: only the filtration at the distinguished ray changes. As applications, we interpret adding and removing invariant boundary components of logarithmic tangent bundles as elementary transformations and recover the residue sequence for logarithmic cotangent bundles.

papers.title: Water as a Battery: Using Hydropower Flexibility to Support the Grid
papers.abstract: This study presents a two-layer optimization framework to determine the optimal sizing of PV, wind, and battery storage co-located with existing hydroelectric plants to support rapidly increasing data center loads while minimizing cost, grid reliance, and transmission upgrades. The outer layer uses Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to select capacity combinations, while the inner layer performs rolling-horizon dispatch simulations to model hourly energy balance among PV, wind, hydro, and BESS, considering operational constraints. Two case studies were analyzed. At The Dalles Dam (Oregon), favorable wind resources and land availability enabled deployment of 111.2 MW PV and 117.9 MW wind, with no BESS required. Hydro flexibility allowed the system to meet the load with minimal grid support. In contrast, Conowingo Dam (Maryland) faced land constraints and limited renewables to 130 MW PV, leading to higher grid dependence. Co-locating hydro with renewables significantly enhances reliability and cost effectiveness by leveraging hydro's dispatchability to balance daily and seasonal variable generation from PV + Wind, reducing the need for storage or costly grid imports. This analysis provides a framework to meet the 99.9% availability targets of this new load type on the grid with sustainable energy resources.

papers.title: UltraFlash: Accelerating Megapixel Visual Synthesis
papers.abstract: Megapixel visual synthesis with latent diffusion models requires operating far beyond the resolutions at which these models are typically trained. Cascade refinement is a leading strategy for this setting: it starts from a base image at a native resolution and progressively upsamples it to the target resolution through multiple refinement stages. Each stage typically performs a pixel-space resolution transition followed by latent-space denoising. While prior acceleration efforts mainly focus on reducing denoising cost, we identify a complementary and underexplored bottleneck: the repeated movement of representations through the VAE. We call these operations pixel-space transitions. In cascade pipelines, intermediate latents are often decoded to RGB, resized, and re-encoded before refinement, while final latents are decoded patch by patch with dense overlap to suppress boundary artifacts. We propose UltraFlash, a transition-efficient approach that accelerates these VAE-heavy operations. UltraFlash has two components. Latent Hyperloop replaces intermediate RGB round trips with a learned latent-space shortcut that approximates the decode-resize-encode transformation without repeated VAE decoding and encoding. Sparse Patch-based Decoding accelerates final reconstruction by addressing patch seams caused by inconsistent GroupNorm statistics and reusing cached statistics across patches, enabling sparse VAE decoding with much smaller overlap. Integrated into a state-of-the-art cascade baseline, UltraFlash reduces 4K generation latency by approximately 2x while improving image quality. These results show that optimizing pixel-space transitions can improve both efficiency and fidelity, offering an effective route toward fast, high-quality megapixel visual synthesis.

authors.name: Anh Nguyen
authors.institution: Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology

papers.title: Not One Belief: Answer Payloads, Persistence, and Dissociated Confidence Signals in Conversational Question Answering
papers.abstract: Conversational QA systems should fix errors when users push back and signal which answers to trust. We split each follow-up into its speech act (re-ask, agree, or challenge) and its payload (an answer string, correct or not), and measure four confidence signals on the same transcripts: verbalized confidence, length-normalized likelihood, a frozen hidden-state probe, and P(True). Answers change when the user supplies an answer string and almost never under the speech act alone: in every retained full-size cell, the correct answer converts at least four times as many wrong answers as re-asking or agreement. The four signals disagree. On Qwen2.5-7B the frozen probe rises with answer persistence rather than truth; this holds on held-out questions, with Llama-3-8B (cleaned answers) as support, but not on four other models. Among 81 Qwen2.5-7B errors that survive one re-ask, re-asking, a fresh chat, or abstain repair almost none, while a gold answer repairs 75-95%. In two preregistered replications, every repair rate without an answer string stays below 0.15; a larger post-hoc rerun excludes 0.15 except for the empty elicit. With BM25 TriviaQA evidence, sentences that contain the answer repair 67-76% of persistent errors versus at most 12% when they do not. An end-to-end contain-gate cuts harm on TriviaQA, but a deployable gate that does not know the gold answer repairs few errors.

authors.name: Duc-Vinh Tran
authors.institution: Trường Đại học Khoa học và Công nghệ Hà Nội

papers.title: Three BMO-type Spaces Characterizing Chord--Arc Curves
papers.abstract: In this note, we introduce three BMO-type spaces on a locally rectifiable Jordan curve and prove that it is a chord-arc curve if and only if these spaces coincide with equivalent norms.

papers.title: The Hidden Costs of Gatekeeping in Open Science: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from arXiv's Endorsement Policy Tightening
papers.abstract: Preprint servers and open science platforms have become core infrastructure through which scientific knowledge circulates on the Web, greatly facilitating the dissemination and diffusion of online scientific information. Yet to safeguard content quality, many of these platforms rely on existing members to vouch for newcomers; how such network-mediated gatekeeping reshapes entry barriers across different scientific communities remains systematically underexplored. To address this, I examine the potential unequal impacts of this mechanism through arXiv's tightening of its endorsement policy in early 2026. Using the metadata of three million arXiv papers and the co-authorship networks of each research community, I compare the influx and dynamics of first-time submitters before and after the policy across eight disciplines. The findings show that the policy reduced the entry of new authors, and this reduction was concentrated in fields where co-authorship ties are sparse, while fields with dense collaboration networks were largely spared. A comparison with a parallel preprint server in biology suggests that this likely reflects a shift in where researchers choose to post rather than a decline in research activity. These findings demonstrate that the network structure of a scientific community shapes who can enter online scientific production, advancing our understanding of how the Web's open knowledge infrastructure shapes inequality in the diffusion of science.

papers.title: A solution to Haagerup's problem: Normality of weights is commutatively determined
papers.abstract: We prove that a weight on a C$^*$-algebra is lower semi-continuous if it is lower semi-continuous on commutative C$^*$-subalgebras. This can be used to prove a von Neumann algebraic counterpart that a weight on a von Neumann algebra is normal if it is normal on commutative von Neumann subalgebras. This provides an affirmative solution to Haagerup's second problem (Problem 1.11) on normal weights posed in 1975.

papers.title: Properties of Oxygen-rich Asymptotic Giant Branch stars in the LMC and the Milky Way
papers.abstract: We investigate the properties of oxygen-rich asymptotic giant branch (OAGB) stars in the LMC and the Milky Way using infrared (IR) color-magnitude diagrams, two-color diagrams, spectral energy distributions (SEDs), and variability data. The observed SEDs are analyzed with radiative transfer models to constrain the properties of the central stars and their circumstellar dust shells and to estimate distances. For OAGB stars in the LMC, whose distance is well established, a set of representative OAGB models is derived by fitting theoretical SEDs to the observations. These models are subsequently applied to Galactic OAGB stars, for which Gaia DR3 parallaxes are often uncertain, to estimate distances from SED fitting. For Galactic Mira variables, distances are also determined using a period-magnitude relation calibrated with Mira stars in the LMC. We find that OAGB stars in the two galaxies exhibit broadly similar IR properties, and that the theoretical models successfully reproduce the observed IR characteristics, despite the extreme rarity of heavily obscured objects with optically thick silicate dust envelopes in the LMC. We further examine Galactic OAGB stars associated with OH, H2O, and SiO masers, including the relationship between absolute OH maser fluxes and IR colors. In addition, we investigate the IR properties of Mira-type OAGB stars and characterize their long-term variability using archival observations together with 16 years of WISE photometric data. Finally, we present a new catalog of 70,877 Galactic OAGB stars, providing a more reliable and comprehensive dataset for future studies.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction with Stable Measurement Mechanisms
papers.abstract: In applications such as air-quality monitoring, inexpensive sensor readings can help predict pollutant concentrations measured by a separate reference instrument. We study how to adapt conformal prediction intervals to a new population when reference outcomes are available in the source data, but only sensor readings and context, such as weather conditions, are available in the target. We assume that the measurement distribution at a given outcome and context remains stable, while context frequencies and outcome distributions may change. This model is a particular form of causal mechanism shift. Its statistical restriction has been studied as sparse joint shift. Using established marginal matching, predictive adjustment, and weighted conformal calibration, we examine what this restriction contributes to coverage and interval length for continuous outcomes. Gaussian analyses show how measurement stability can identify outcome changes and how retaining context can shorten prediction intervals. For Gaussian models with known source mechanisms, we derive exact coverage formulas in the large-calibration limit while keeping the unlabeled target sample finite. These formulas explain when sharing a correction across contexts is preferable to fitting separate corrections, and why estimating outcome variability is particularly sensitive to weakly informative measurements. Experiments on synthetic Gaussian data show a coverage gain over covariate weighting at the same mean length and a length reduction of about $8\%$ relative to pooled label adjustment at comparable coverage. On the Air Quality dataset, controlled shifts yield coverage gains with longer intervals, while spring-to-autumn and year-over-year transfers show substantial undercoverage.

papers.title: Length bounds and rigidity for ancient curve shortening flow on warped product surfaces
papers.abstract: We study ancient solutions to curve shortening flow on a class of warped product surfaces. For closed embedded ancient solutions whose curves are not null-homotopic, we prove that graphicality at every time is equivalent to a uniform length bound as $t\to-\infty$, and that these properties hold whenever the length is $o(\sqrt{-t})$. Under an additional positivity condition on the linearized height equation, every such solution with bounded length is a family of slices. We derive backward convergence to a limiting circle from the length bound and prove slice rigidity by an $L^2$ estimate for the height perturbation.

authors.name: Taehun Lee
authors.institution: Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources

papers.title: Compressive microendoscopy in the presence of noise and misalignment: the translational correlation advantage of graded-index fibers
papers.abstract: Multimode fibers (MMFs) offer a minimally invasive platform for deep-tissue and multisite in vivo optical sensing. Computational microendoscopy methods extend them into the high-resolution imaging domain, but are quite sensitive to experimental errors. This study investigates the robustness of microendoscopy based on compressive sensing (CS) by comparing step-index (SI) MMFs with graded-index (GRIN) fibers. Mode-expansion-based simulations are used to assess the accuracy of image reconstruction in the presence of fundamental photon noise and lateral fiber shifts. We show that both fiber types exhibit comparable noise sensitivity, but GRIN fibers are significantly more robust to lateral misalignment errors. These results establish GRIN MMFs as an alignment-tolerant platform for robust computational microendoscopy.

papers.title: QuantileMix: A Python package for quantile g-computation
papers.abstract: Health researchers often study how a mixture of pollutants or nutrients relates to health. Quantile g-computation addresses this question by giving each exposure an ordered score and fitting a model for the outcome. For example, dividing an exposure into four quantile groups gives scores 0, 1, 2, and 3. The model can compare score 1 with score 2 for every exposure at once. These groups need not contain equal numbers of observations when measurements are tied. A one-score increase can represent different changes in the original units for different exposures. QuantileMix provides selected quantile g-computation methods in Python. It returns estimates, confidence intervals, predictions, and diagnostics for continuous, binary, count, and survival outcomes. Other models handle measurement limits, outcomes with several categories, and counts with many zeros. Fitting and prediction use NumPy and SciPy and do not require R. The package includes a reference manual, runnable examples, and numerical comparisons with R.

papers.title: Recovering the Topology of a Real Plane Algebraic Curve by Tropical Homotopy
papers.abstract: We present a tropical homotopy method for computing the numbers of ovals and unbounded components of a real plane algebraic curve, together with the pairing of its ends at infinity. Under explicit support and nondegeneracy assumptions, the homotopy starts from a tropical patchwork and encounters finitely many events. At Morse event points, the curve changes by local surgery. To determine the global attachments, we follow descending separatrices of a single gradient-like field to a fixed collection of base curves. The order of their landing points defines a finite combinatorial state, updated by local rules that also handle events at infinity and simultaneous event points. This recovers component data without tracing the intervening curves. For the dequantizing lifting, given by the negative logarithms of coefficient magnitudes, we prove an explicit event window when the lifting is generic. For fixed support and coefficient signs, with independent, identically distributed log-normal magnitudes, the expected number of events is bounded by a constant divided by the standard deviation of the logarithms. When all event points are Morse, correctness is conditional on complete, correctly classified event data, a sufficiently small starting parameter, and correctly labelled and ordered landing points. A numerical implementation illustrates its behaviour on sparse curves of high degree and on coefficients spanning many scales; these conditions are not certified.

papers.title: No Cones, No Duals: A Fast and Scalable Solver for NRSfM
papers.abstract: Non-rigid structure from motion (NRSfM) aims to recover camera motion and time-varying 3D shape from tracked 2D image measurements. Recent high-performing methods show that shape-space factorization remains highly effective for this task. These methods often use costly solvers for two key steps. First, a semidefinite programming (SDP) cone solver to perform Euclidean correction. Next, an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) solver to recover the low-rank shape. These steps often scale poorly to long sequences and dense point tracks. We propose a fast, scalable NRSfM solver that avoids these costly steps. For rotation estimation, we introduce a differentiable Euclidean correction that directly optimizes small factors for each sequence. A row-polar projection then maps each estimated camera block to the closest row-orthonormal matrix. For shape estimation, we introduce an unrolled spectral-proximal solver. It combines reprojection-gradient steps with weighted singular-value shrinkage in the reshuffled shape domain. This solver further uses FISTA-style restart and continuation. The spectral shrinkage operator itself is classical, but we embed it in a fixed differentiable solver, while preserving NRSfM's geometric constraints. The proposed approach is category-agnostic, requires no external training data, and maps naturally to modern accelerator-friendly linear algebra primitives. Across sparse, dense, noisy, missing-data, and long-sequence benchmarks, our solver achieves substantial speedups with competitive reconstruction accuracy, including 7x-1000x runtime improvements on dense sequences with 28,887 tracked points.

papers.title: From Self-Confidence to Statistical Accuracy: Scaling Human-in-the-Loop Evaluation with Direct and LLM-Assisted Auditing
papers.abstract:
For large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), model-reported self-confidence is often miscalibrated, yet it may still be useful for efficient evaluation. At the same time, LLM-as-a-judge offers a scalable alternative to direct human auditing, but its practical benefit depends on calibration quality and inference cost.
  This paper develops a unified statistical framework for both evaluation routes under alternative sampling strategies. For direct auditing, confidence-stratified sampling is used to recover population accuracy from partially verified outputs without requiring calibrated confidence. Finite-sample uncertainty is characterized, and the analysis shows how highly uneven confidence strata affect audit efficiency and label allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, the judge is modeled through sensitivity and false-positive rate, yielding an error-corrected estimator with calibration uncertainty. The two routes are then compared through human-label and total-cost efficiency boundaries.
  Experiments on MMLU-Pro and MMMU-Pro show that miscalibrated self-confidence can still support statistically valid stratified auditing. Under highly imbalanced confidence distributions, proportional allocation substantially reduces estimation error relative to equal-per-stratum allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, only a small subset of target--verifier pairs satisfies the idealized human-label efficiency condition, and automated inference costs can further limit potential savings. These findings clarify the statistical and economic conditions under which confidence-guided auditing and automated verification are useful.

authors.name: Chenchen Kuai (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering
Jiwan Jiang (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering
Yunlong Zhang (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering
Zhiwen Fan (Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
Zhengzhong Tu (Department of Computer Science and Engineering
Yang Zhou (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering

papers.title: Duration-Aware World Models for Sleep Staging with Dwell-Time Constraints
papers.abstract: Closed-loop neuromodulation requires sleep staging that respects stage-specific minimum dwells: stimulation policies switch by sleep stage, and a policy change is permitted only after the current stage has persisted for its minimum duration. Discriminative classifiers fragment stage trajectories---for example, a 30 s Wake segment inside a 10 min N2 run---and even hidden semi-Markov smoothing leaves 11.3% of segments below the minimum dwell threshold. This paper presents a world model in which a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) learns dwell structure endogenously from EEG, via duration-aware latent sampling, a survival-curve dwell prior, and transition-matrix calibration, and a trajectory-level hard-constraint layer guarantees the minimum dwell at decoding. On SHHS-1 (200 subjects, 160/20/20, three repeated splits), the model reaches a test accuracy of 0.690 +/- 0.053 (95% CI over 3 folds) versus 0.641 +/- 0.042 for an identically split discriminative baseline, with macro-F1 +17.5 pp and better accuracy on all three folds. On Sleep-EDF the constraint layer cuts below-threshold segments from 71.8% to 0.1% with no accuracy loss (0.734 to 0.737), and an online locked scheduler reduces RL policy switches by 87% per night while keeping every policy run at least 90 s. To the best of the author's knowledge, this is the first system to couple learned dwell statistics with a decoding-time hard guarantee. Code and pretrained weights will be released.

papers.title: FlockWorld: Toward Population-Scale Multi-Agent Video World Models through Artificial Life Simulation
papers.abstract: Most action-conditioned video world models remain limited to a single player, while existing multiplayer models support only small, fixed groups of agents. We introduce FlockWorld, an artificial-life environment built on Reynolds's Boids algorithm for studying population-scale multi-agent video world models. Specifically, FlockWorld renders synchronized egocentric crops, assigns distinct colors to preserve camera-agent identity across views, exposes rule-derived accelerations as actions, and lets the number of camera agents be configured independently of the size of the surrounding population. We further introduce FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching on FlockWorld data to jointly generate synchronized egocentric videos for multiple agents. Our results suggest that joint generation benefits agent detection at density-matched settings and that diffusion forcing improves rollout fidelity. Together, FlockWorld and FlockDiT provide a controlled testbed for multi-agent video generation.

authors.name: Yunzhe Wang
authors.institution: Suzhou University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Carleson duality and endpoint structure of Euclidean flag Triebel--Lizorkin spaces
papers.abstract: The main purpose of this paper is to develop the duality theory of the homogeneous Triebel--Lizorkin spaces associated with the Euclidean flag, using the discrete Littlewood--Paley--Stein analysis. After establishing bounded analysis and synthesis maps, we describe the continuous duals by Carleson conditions. In the Hardy spatial range, the representing distributions satisfy an open-set Carleson condition when the sequence exponent is greater than one and a coefficient supremum condition when the sequence exponent is at most one; in the Banach spatial range the dual is a conjugate-exponent or a supremum space. At the supremum sequence endpoint, the closure of the flag test functions is characterized by a pointwise scale tail measured in $L^p$, and a coefficient pairing decomposes every functional on the full space into a regular part and a part that annihilates the closure. By means of a fixed-envelope modulation construction we show that this closure is proper for every finite spatial exponent and that the annihilator is nonzero when the spatial exponent is at least one. The same analysis and synthesis framework also yields complex interpolation, real interpolation in the spatial exponent, the lifting property and the standard mixed-norm embeddings.

authors.name: Chang Li
authors.institution: Suzhou University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Convergence of Independence Metropolis-Hastings Algorithms in High Dimensions: Iteration Lengths, Cutoff Profiles, and Diagnostic Unreliability
papers.abstract: We characterize the high-dimensional convergence of the arithmetic mean from the independence Metropolis-Hastings algorithm initialized at its proposal. Convergence is measured in the worst-case expected absolute error over bounded functions. We prove necessary and sufficient conditions for the mean to converge in relation to the importance weight. We precisely describe the logarithmic cutoff profile of the sharp decay to convergence where the relative entropy between the target and proposal determines the required iteration length. These results make connections between the required iterations of independence Metropolis-Hastings and importance sampling. For concentrating Bayesian posteriors, we illustrate how the required iteration time can be estimated providing concrete guidance for simulations. We justify the logarithmic cutoff analysis by showing a standard cutoff phenomenon is absent and prove that popular convergence diagnostics based on simulation output can validate inaccurate simulations.

papers.title: Multilinear extrapolation on Banach function spaces
papers.abstract: We solve an open problem on the multilinear Rubio de Francia extrapolation on Banach function spaces. The first result states that, under the assumption of boundedness of the multisublinear Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator, the multivariable boundedness on Banach function spaces can be extrapolated from some weighted Lebesgue space, including the cases where some exponents may be infinite. Under the same assumption, the second result asserts that if a multilinear operator is bounded on some weighted Lebesgue space, then its compactness can be extrapolated from some unweighted Lebesgue space to Banach function spaces. Our results do not require any convexity or concavity conditions on Banach function spaces. The main ingredients in the proof are a multilinear version of the Rubio de Francia algorithm, a stopping-time argument, convex analysis, and a compactness criterion on Banach function spaces. As applications of extrapolation theorems, we obtain multilinear extrapolation for the boundedness and compactness of commutators on Banach function spaces. These results can be further applied to specific operators, which cover both the full range case including multilinear Calder\'{o}n-Zygmund operators, multilinear pseudo-differential operators, and bilinear paraproducts, and the limited range case including the bilinear Hilbert transform, multilinear rough singular integrals, and bilinear oscillatory Fourier multipliers.

papers.title: The sharp leading asymptotics of the self-energy of the spinless Pauli-Fierz model
papers.abstract: We consider the ground state energy E_0(alpha, Lambda) of a single spinless non-relativistic electron coupled to the quantized radiation field with a sharp ultraviolet cutoff Lambda (the Pauli-Fierz model), with fine structure constant alpha = e^2/(4 pi). Lieb and Loss proved that C_1 alpha^(1/2) Lambda^(3/2) <= E_0 <= C_2 alpha^(2/7) Lambda^(12/7) for large Lambda and suggested that the upper bound, which comes from product states, gives the correct order. We prove that, for every fixed alpha > 0, E_0(alpha, Lambda) = (1+o(1)) c_alpha alpha^(2/7) Lambda^(12/7) as Lambda -> infinity, with an explicit constant c_alpha = 0.99338...; more generally, this holds uniformly in the joint limit Lambda/alpha -> infinity, alpha^(5/2) Lambda -> infinity, provided log(2+alpha) = o((Lambda/alpha)^(1/21)). Since our upper bound holds already for the infimum over product states, it follows that the ratio of E_0 to this infimum tends to one: electron-field correlations do not contribute to the leading term. The condition alpha^(5/2) Lambda -> infinity cannot be dropped, since for alpha^(5/2) Lambda -> 0 the vacuum trial state gives a smaller energy. The upper bound follows from a coherent state bound for the field energy in a fixed electron density. The lower bound combines a periodization of the field, a Born-Oppenheimer bound in which phase multiplication and a Hardy inequality in field space are applied block by block, and a lower bound on the magnetic Neumann Laplacian on a cube for band-limited fields; the key point of the last is that a band-limited field obeying a weighted gradient condition cannot concentrate its vorticity.

papers.title: The effective mass of the Pauli-Fierz electron: a cutoff-independent lower bound and the breakdown of mass renormalization
papers.abstract: We consider the Pauli-Fierz model of one spinless non-relativistic electron coupled to the quantized transverse electromagnetic field, without external potential, with a sharp ultraviolet cutoff Lambda and bare mass m. Let h = m_eff/m be the ratio of the effective mass, defined by the curvature of the fiber ground state energy at total momentum zero, to the bare mass; by scaling, h depends only on the fine structure constant alpha = e^2/(4 pi) and on lambda = Lambda/m. We prove two lower bounds. First, h >= 1 + 0.3441 alpha/(1 + 0.2985 sqrt(alpha) + 0.1252 alpha) for all alpha > 0 and all lambda >= 1; the bound does not depend on the cutoff, and with the band extended to the cutoff its first order coefficient in alpha is the perturbative one of Hiroshima and Spohn. The proof uses a coherent translation of the field applied to the ground state as a trial state; the term linear in the translation vanishes by minimality of the ground state. Second, for every fixed alpha, h grows faster than linearly: for every epsilon > 0, h >= lambda^(8/7 - epsilon) for all large lambda (8/7 is the limit of the method). Consequently iota_PF(alpha) := inf_{lambda > 0} h/lambda > 0, and for a fixed physical mass m_phys a bare mass reproducing it exists only if Lambda <= m_phys/iota_PF(alpha). This was expected, but not proved, by Lieb and Loss (2002). The proof of the second bound starts from the sharp self-energy asymptotics of a companion paper and uses a trial state obtained from the ground state by a phase depending on the field configuration. The new ingredients are an estimator for the position of the electron given by the local centre of a shallow level set of the photon cloud, the decoupling of a localized part of the field from the electron through a divergence-free external subspace, and a proof that shallow depressions near the edge of the localization window are rare.

papers.title: Extremal Trudinger-Moser inequality associated with many point vortices with multi-intensities
papers.abstract: We study the boundedness of extremal 2D Trudinger-Moser inequality associated with many point vortices with multi-intensities. Sufficient conditions for continuously-distributed measures are given in one-sided and two-sided cases.

authors.name: Yohei Toyota
authors.institution: National Institute of Technology, Nara College

papers.title: Minimum Contagious Sets in Trees with Degree-Proportional Thresholds
papers.abstract:
We investigate how large the minimum size of a contagious set can be among trees of a fixed order.
  Given a graph $G$ and $\rho\in[0,1]$, an inactive vertex $u$ becomes active when at least $\lceil{\rho d_G(u)\rceil}$ of its neighbors are active. An initial set of active vertices is contagious if the process eventually activates every vertex. We obtain exact values for the minimum size of a contagious set in perfect $d$-ary trees. We then determine the exact maximum of this minimum size over all trees of order $n$. We establish this result by bounding the number of pairwise disjoint resistant sets, each of which must intersect every contagious set, and constructing trees that attain the resulting bounds. Finally, by bounding the change in the minimum size of a contagious set under a leaf exchange, we show that, for $0<\rho\leq1$ and $n\geq2$, every integer between $1$ and this maximum occurs as the minimum size of a contagious set in a tree of order $n$.

authors.name: Jeong-Ok Choi
authors.institution: Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Fixed pilot sequences can overstate the gains of learned MIMO-OFDM receivers under power amplifier distortion
papers.abstract: Neural-network receivers are proposed to undo the distortion of a power amplifier driven close to saturation, where it is most efficient. They estimate the channel from pilots, known symbols sent in every frame. The pilots pass through the same amplifier as the data, so the channel estimate carries a small error that depends on the pilot sequence. If one sequence is always sent, as by default in the Sionna simulator, the error never changes, and a network can learn it instead of undoing the amplifier. We tested this in simulated two- and four-antenna orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing links; results are for binary pilots at the highest signal-to-noise ratio tested. A network with separate weights for each subcarrier lowered the bit error rate by 14 to 22% with its training pilot but raised it by 2 to 18% with every other pilot tested, and longer training widened this gap. A convolutional neural receiver following an open-source tutorial gained 37 percentage points more on its training pilot than on unseen pilots after short training, and 9 points more after nine times longer training, much of which also appeared with a linear amplifier. The gap shrank with amplifier back-off but persisted where the in-band distortion meets the 5G limit. On a channel with short delay spread, smoothing the channel estimate across subcarriers without training lowered the error rate on all 107 pilot sequences tested, by 30% on average. Learned receivers should therefore be tested on unseen pilots and against such simple baselines.

papers.title: Extrapolating learned dynamics across bifurcations based on generalized synchronization
papers.abstract: Predicting dynamics across bifurcations by extrapolating trained models is crucial in diverse fields of physics. Generalized synchronization provides a framework for understanding dynamical reconstruction by neural networks, especially in the context of reservoir computing. Building on this framework, we derive a formula combining pretrained readouts to reconstruct unseen chaotic dynamics. Using classical Lagrange interpolation theory, we derive rigorous bounds on readout errors and conjugacy residuals. Numerical examples demonstrate accurate prediction of chaotic dynamics across bifurcations.

papers.title: The divergence of continuously differentiable vector fields
papers.abstract: For $m\geq 2$, we give a complete characterisation of the continuous functions on $\mathbb{R}^m$ that are divergences of continuously differentiable vector fields. The characterisation is formulated in terms of distributions and, equivalently, in terms of the continuous dual of a suitably topologised subspace of the Arens--Eells space. The two implications yield contrasting applications. First, there exists a compactly supported continuous function which is the divergence of a bounded Lipschitz vector field but not of any continuously differentiable vector field. Second, every continuous function whose distributional partial derivatives are locally $m$-integrable (the critical exponent for Sobolev embedding) is the divergence of a continuously differentiable vector field.

papers.title: Zassenhaus Filtration and Ihara Constants
papers.abstract:
Let $X$ be a curve over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Denote by $N(X)$ and $g(X)$ the number of $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational points and the genus of $X$ respectively. The Ihara constant \begin{equation*} A(q)=\limsup_{g(X)\to\infty}\frac{N(X)}{g(X)} \end{equation*} measures the asymptotic abundance of rational points on curves over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
  In this paper, we study the Zassenhaus filtration of pro-$p$ groups arising from class field towers. By combining Golod--Shafarevich theorem, embedding problems and central class field theory, we establish a new criterion for the infinitude of class field towers. As an application, we obtain an improvement on the best known lower bounds of Ihara constant $A(2)$ and $A(3)$ which are explicitly given by \[
  A(2)\geq 0.317779\cdots \text{ and }
  A(3)\geq 0.496074\cdots. \]

papers.title: Movable Curves and Ample Normal Bundles
papers.abstract: We prove that the movable cone of a smooth complex projective variety is the closed cone generated by possibly singular curves with ample coherent normal sheaves, answering a question of Boucksom--Demailly--P\u{a}un--Peternell. For smooth curves, we establish the analogous equality in several geometric settings and give explicit constructions on blowups.

authors.name: Jingcao Wu
authors.institution: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

papers.title: Quantitative hyperconvexity and the Bergman distance
papers.abstract: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{C}^n$ be a bounded hyperconvex domain admitting a negative plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $u$ such that $-u(z)\le C\exp[-\eta(\log(1/\delta_\Omega(z)))]$ near the boundary, where $\eta$ is nondecreasing with $\lim_{t\rightarrow+\infty}\eta(t)=+\infty$. We present a lower bound for the Bergman distance $d_{B,\Omega}(z_0,z)$ by counting the iterates of a function determined by the generalized inverse of $\eta$. The bound tends to infinity as $z\rightarrow\partial\Omega$ for every such $\eta$; moreover, it recovers several known estimates. The proof combines a one-sided localization of Green sublevel sets with boundary estimates for the Bergman kernel and a capacity--volume inequality. We also obtain an upper bound for the Bergman distance along the axis of a family of complete Hartogs domains whose fiber radii decay faster than every positive power of the boundary distance in the base disc.

papers.title: A High-Order Geometric-Compatible DGSEM with Subcell Limiting for the GPR System
papers.abstract: We construct an equation-of-state-independent geometric-compatible finite-volume (GC-FV) method and a high-order nodal discontinuous Galerkin spectral-element extension (GC-DG) for a reduced Godunov-Peshkov-Romenski system on fixed Eulerian meshes. Density is recovered from $\rho=\rho_0\det(\mathbf{A})$, so mass conservation is a hidden companion law of the distortion equation. Starting from a straight-path Dal Maso-LeFloch-Murat fluctuation pair, minimum-change cofactor projections produce a single-valued density flux and exact induced local Lax-Friedrichs dissipation without jump quotients. The summation-by-parts property lifts the geometric two-state identity to high order and yields an equivalent subcell representation of GC-DG. We then blend GC-DG with the compatible GC-FV operator on the same Legendre-Gauss-Lobatto subcells. Because both operators induce the same boundary density flux, the global subcell blend retains the exact semidiscrete mass balance while suppressing shock-generated oscillations. A complementary modal/face-jump indicator supplies the elementwise blending coefficient. Numerical experiments verify high-order convergence, the expected temporal scaling of the fully discrete mass drift, and robust shock capturing for fluid, nonlinear-elastic, thermal-wave, and elastoplastic problems, including genuinely multidimensional configurations.

papers.title: Aspherical Symplectic Manifolds with Positive First Chern Degree
papers.abstract: For every integer $n\ge5$, we construct a closed aspherical symplectic manifold of real dimension $2n$ with positive first Chern degree. Each example is a flat torus bundle over the same compact hyperbolic surface, with arithmetic monodromy arising from an explicit indefinite quaternion division algebra over $\mathbb{Q}$. We identify its symplectic first Chern class with the pullback of the canonical class of the base and compute its degree explicitly. Asphericity rules out nonconstant pseudoholomorphic spheres for every tame almost complex structure. Thus these examples give a negative answer to the symplectic uniruledness question of Boucksom--Demailly--P\u{a}un--Peternell in every even real dimension at least ten.

authors.name: Jingcao Wu
authors.institution: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

papers.title: Beyond Wasserstein Proximity: Finding Better Transfer Sources
papers.abstract: Source selection often favors similar data, yet marginal proximity need not identify the most useful pretraining source. We motivate a conditional alternative through domain-adaptation theory and a regression example in which broader source variation improves estimation despite increasing Wasserstein distance. We examine five-day cryptocurrency volatility using ten Binance spot assets, six forecaster families, three seeds, and shared temporal cutoffs. Selecting the three farthest rather than nearest Gaussian-Wasserstein sources improves mean persistence-relative skill by 12.52 percentage points for MLP and 20.90 for Transformer, with positive post-hoc paired date-block intervals. Forward pilot selection improves mean skill over random transfer in all six families. Compact recurrent models achieve the lowest absolute mean errors, separating selection utility from forecasting quality. Retrospective five-candidate screening shows additional gains from farthest-first geometry before pilot ranking for MLP and Transformer. We distinguish across-target associations from within-target decisions and evaluate target heterogeneity, training seeds, and temporal-block sensitivity. Findings are exploratory for a fixed historical panel; the screening analysis measures no runtime saving.

affiliations.raw: School of Mathematical Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China

papers.intro:
Newly listed cryptocurrency assets provide short and uneven histories for volatility forecasting. Pretraining on another asset can improve the initialization available to a target forecaster, but choosing a source is a consequential decision: transfer can also preserve irrelevant structure. The practical problem is to identify a useful source for a fixed target, learner, and adaptation budget. Windowed Gaussian-Wasserstein distance offers a tractable summary of differences between time-series distributions (Chen et al., 2025). It is natural to prefer the closest source. We ask when a more distant source can instead be useful.

We ask when a more distant source can instead be useful.

Similarity has a sound theoretical rationale. Domain-adaptation bounds relate target risk to source risk, distribution discrepancy, and the error of a hypothesis that must work on both domains (Ben-David et al., 2010; Redko et al., 2017). Reducing discrepancy tightens these bounds when other terms are controlled; distance alone does not order sources with different predictive relationships or estimation quality. Matching feature marginals can also leave conditional differences unresolved (Zhao et al., 2019). These results explain why similarity may be insufficient, but do not themselves predict a benefit from greater distance.

There is a constructive reason to investigate that benefit. A source with broader informative variation can estimate a shared response more accurately while being farther away in marginal geometry. Finite target adaptation can retain this estimation advantage. Section 3 demonstrates the tradeoff in a simple regression model. For neural forecasting, a source with different activity or volatility scale might similarly expose transferable temporal structure. This is a mechanism to investigate, not one established by the present experiment. Evidence that initialization-dependent benefits can survive fine-tuning (Yosinski et al., 2014), and that learned data selection can combine similarity with diversity (Ruder and Plank, 2017), makes the question credible without implying a universal preference for dissimilarity.

Forecasting across heterogeneous series provides further context. Global models need not require identical marginal distributions (Montero-Manso and Hyndman, 2021), and domain-adapted forecasting can share temporal components while retaining domain-specific ones (Jin et al., 2022). Their benefits depend on what is shared and on the learning procedure. We therefore investigate the conditional hypothesis that for a fixed target and finite adaptation budget, more distant Gaussian-Wasserstein sources can yield lower forecast error than nearer sources, with the effect depending on the learner. A direct comparison of source-selection rules tests this hypothesis more closely than an association across targets of unequal difficulty.

The contributions are: (i) relating a statistical mechanism to a learner-specific reversal of nearest-source selection; (ii) separating selection gains from absolute quality using target-only, self-continuation, random-transfer, and HAR-style controls; and (iii) testing geometric screening before predictive validation against a matched random-screening comparator. Screening is retrospective; findings have exploratory, fixed-panel scope.

papers.title: The Weyl Problem for Planar CBB$(-1)$ Surfaces in Hyperbolic $3$-Space
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the Weyl problem for noncompact convex surfaces in hyperbolic $3$-space $\mathbb{H}^3$. We prove that any planar CBB$(-1)$ surface with countably many ends can be isometrically embedded as the boundary of a closed convex subset $X\subset\mathbb{H}^3$ such that each connected component of the ideal boundary of $X$ is either a round disk or a single point. By known rigidity results, such an embedding is unique up to isometries of $\mathbb{H}^3$. Moreover, we show that the assumption of countably many ends can be dropped if Koebe's circle domain conjecture holds.

papers.title: Network of limit sets in dynamical systems
papers.abstract: Points within a topological dynamical systems can be separated into transient and recurrent points. Most of the asymptotic properties of the dynamics is borne by the closure of the collection of recurrent points. This article presents a representation scheme for dynamics using the connectivity information in terms of the recurrent set. This representation is functorial and represents certain compositional features of dynamical systems.

papers.title: Amplitude-Dependent Damping of Gravity--Capillary Waves in Power-Law Fluids: An Energy-Dissipation Framework
papers.abstract: Classical gravity--capillary theory locates the restoring-force crossover, but the wave amplitudes and depths for which energy losses remain measurable depend on the constitutive response and on where viscous dissipation occurs. We develop a weak-loss mechanical-energy model for small-steepness progressive surface waves in memoryless power--law liquids. The full invariant of the leading inviscid strain field yields the deep-water bulk law $\dd A/\dd t=-C_tA^n$, with $C_t=4Kk^2(2k\Omega)^{n-1}/[(n+1)\rho]$, and the corresponding spatial law $\dd A/\dd x=-(C_t/v_g)A^n$. For finite depth we calculate bulk dissipation using a phase- and depth-resolved quadrature $J_n(kh)$ and formulate a separate oscillatory power--law bottom layer. We solve the latter numerically in periodic state, obtaining dimensionless integrated wall losses $I_{0.6}\simeq0.5432$ and $I_{1.4}\simeq0.4708$ and recovering the exact Newtonian benchmark $I_1=1/2$. These values make it possible to evaluate conditional finite-depth bulk--wall dominance boundaries rather than only their amplitude exponents. The theory is organized into restoring-force, attenuation, local propagation-length, and dissipation-mechanism regime maps; at fixed wave steepness it additionally predicts a capillary-side maximum of normalized temporal damping for $0<n<2/3$. Grid, time-step, domain, and energy-work checks support the reduced wall calculation, while the coupled bulk--wall approximation still requires independent free-surface numerical or experimental validation. The results provide a reproducible single-fluid reference for subsequent two-liquid interfacial-wave modeling.

papers.title: Robust Network Enhancement: Formulations and Approximations
papers.abstract: We study robust network enhancement problems that improve network performance through component upgrades, where both network utilities and enhancement costs are uncertain. We consider two formulations: a lower-bound problem that improves the minimum utility across feasible network structures and an upper-bound problem that improves the maximum utility. For the lower-bound problem, we develop an exact cut-generation reformulation and identify the robust separation subproblem as a key computational bottleneck. We characterize conditions under which fractional extreme points arise in the linearized robust formulation and demonstrate that such points can be optimal. For the upper-bound problem, we derive two exact reformulations and compare the strength of their linear relaxations. To improve computational tractability, we introduce a box approximation of the utility uncertainty set that preserves solution robustness and provides explicit performance guarantees for both lower- and upper-bound problems. Computational experiments on spanning tree instances show that the proposed approximation improves computational efficiency for both problems while maintaining solution quality close to that of the exact formulations.

papers.title: Squarefree Values of Random Polynomials
papers.abstract: In this paper we consider the error term in the expected count of squarefree values of a polynomial when evaluated at integers \(n\le N\). We prove a power saving on average over polynomials of fixed degree and height at most \(H\). Our results improve previous estimates of Browning and Shparlinski in that the required range of \(H\) is independent of the degree, but depends on \(N\)

papers.title: How Do Small Coding Agents Use Code Graphs and Embeddings?
papers.abstract: Coding agents are given embedding search and code-graph tools on the premise that a repository's structure is something the model lacks and the tool supplies. We test that premise on SWE-bench Verified with small open-weight models, stratifying tasks by a deterministic hop depth (the shortest code-graph path from code the issue mentions to code the gold patch changes) that a companion paper defines and validates. First, we ablate a localization agent's tool set (grep only; +embedding search; +graph tools; all) on a depth-balanced 160-task split and on all 500 tasks for ten models (six Qwen3 sizes from 0.6B to 32B with five decodings each, an FP8 control, three Gemma 4 sizes; 79k episodes). Structured tools double grep-only accuracy for Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 E4B; their gain peaks at 17-21 points at 1.7-4B and falls to 4-5 points at 32B (odds ratio 0.77-0.82 per doubling of parameters). From 8B up, about half of that gain is the form of the submission rather than finding the target; the fall from 14B to 32B is a fall in tool uptake at equal grep-only accuracy; and the same 4B size gains or does not gain from a tool depending on the checkpoint. Each extra hop multiplies the odds of correct localization by 0.50-0.67 at every size, and no tool set flattens that gradient: traces show the graph tools' gain is name lookup at hop 0 and one expansion at hop 1, and agents chain expansions in only 12-14% of episodes. A fixed repair model resolves 6-13 of 160 tasks from these localizations (oracle 26). Second, linear probes find direct call edges decodable under a within-anchor, degree-stratified protocol (AUC 0.74; 0.61-0.66 inside agent conversations), but below a lexical baseline (0.99), with two-hop edges at 0.57. Small agents carry a one-hop, largely lexical picture of their repository, in weights and in use. We release the agent, probes, logs and traces.

papers.intro:
Resolving a GitHub issue in a large repository starts with finding the code that has to change. Agentic systems for this localization step increasingly ship with structured tools: dense retrievers over function bodies, and query interfaces over a static code graph whose nodes are files, classes and functions and whose edges record containment, imports, calls and inheritance (Chen et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). The working assumption behind these tools is simple. An issue names some code; the fix lives some distance away along the dependency structure; a plain text search cannot bridge that distance, so the agent needs either a semantic index (to jump directly to code that means the right thing) or a graph (to walk to it). LocAgent (Chen et al., 2025a) made the assumption measurable by scoring SWE-bench tasks by the hop distance between the functions an issue mentions and the functions the patch edits, and reported that graph-guided agents degrade least as that distance grows. CodeAnchor (Lin et al., 2026) observed that SWE-bench Lite and Verified contain mostly one- and two-hop faults, and argued that evaluating structure-aware agents properly “requires a benchmark that sorts tasks by structural depth”.

This paper takes that argument seriously and asks three questions that the existing literature leaves open, using small open-weight models where the behaviour is cheap to measure many times over and where tool support plausibly matters most.

We compute, for every SWE-bench Verified task, a deterministic hop depth on a LocAgent-style graph built at the task’s base commit (Section 3). Unlike LocAgent’s measurement, which extracted mentions with GPT-4o, ours uses only regular expressions and the Python ast module, so it can be re-run, audited and varied. We ask how the 500 tasks are distributed over depth, whether depth predicts whether an agent localizes the fix after controlling for repository, tool set, number of gold functions and patch size (DepthGEE), how sensitive the label is to the two measurement choices that matter—how calls are resolved and how mentions are extracted (LabelVar)—and we release the labelled split.

On a 160-task subset balanced over depth we run a localization-only agent whose arms differ only in their tool set: G (grep, read_file, list_dir), E (G + embedding search over function and class texts), T (G + a name lookup and a one- or two-hop neighbourhood query over the graph) and ET (all tools) (Section 4). We measure accuracy by depth, run-to-run variance under sampling, which tool first exposes the gold code and whether exposure converts into a correct submission, sensitivity to retrieval quality, the effect of forcing the structured tool to be used, the effect of a larger step and context budget, and—because localization is only useful if it leads to a fix—how many issues one fixed repair model resolves when given each arm’s localizations (Section 5). We then rerun the four arms on all 500 tasks across a model-size curve: six Qwen3 sizes from 0.6B to 32B with five decodings each, an FP8 precision control, and three Gemma 4 sizes (Section 5.4).

We then rerun the four arms on all 500 tasks across a model-size curve: six Qwen3 sizes from 0.6B to 32B with five decodings each, an FP8 precision control, and three Gemma 4 sizes (Section 5.4).

The “Thousand-Graph Hypothesis” (Ding, 2026) proposes that an entity-only index suffices because self-attention materialises whatever relation a task needs; a recent probe shows that the runtime tool-call dependency structure of an agent is linearly decodable from Qwen3-32B residual streams (Sun & Kazakov, 2026). Neither probes the repository’s own call and inheritance graph. We do, with linear probes on definition-level activations, first in static file contexts (GlobalProbe, AnchorProbe) and then inside real agent conversations (ConvProbe). The design is driven by a negative result we obtained early on: a global pair probe reaches AUC 0.75–0.80 for call edges, but so does a probe that sees only one of the two definitions, and so does the in-file in-degree of the callee. Linked and unlinked pairs differ in properties of a single node. We therefore introduce a within-anchor ranking protocol with an in-degree-binned stratification that a node-level shortcut cannot pass, with bootstrap intervals over anchors and a lexical name-match baseline (Section 6).

The answers are consistent across two model families and six sizes, and point in one direction. • Hop depth is a strong, controlled predictor of failure. Each extra hop multiplies the odds of correct function-level localization by 0.47 (Qwen3-4B, three runs), 0.47 (Qwen3-8B), 0.54 (Gemma 4 E4B, three runs) and 0.55 (Qwen3-32B, all 500 tasks), with all p≤10−3p\leq 10^{-3}; across the scale curve the per-hop odds ratio is 0.50–0.67 at every size and barely changes with size. The label barely moves under alternative call resolution (κ=0.96\kappa=0.96–0.980.98). It is, however, sensitive to mention extraction: a strict extractor that counts only back-ticked code and traceback frames leaves 311 of 500 tasks without a mention. • For Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 E4B, grep alone is a weak baseline (12.8% and 9.6% function Acc@10) that any structured tool roughly doubles. For Qwen3-4B the embedding tool adds nothing (−1.1-1.1 points) and the graph tools add +8.1+8.1 points ([3.0, 13.5][3.0,\,13.5]). In every model, the graph-tool advantage is largest at hop 0, where the issue names the target and find_entity resolves the name directly, and at hop 1, where one graph_neighbors expansion reaches it; at hop 2+ the gain shrinks or vanishes, and in a GEE interaction model the depth slope of T is never significantly flatter than that of G (it is steeper in the Qwen models) while E has the flattest slope. Small graph-tool agents do not walk the graph; they look names up and expand once. Over the scale curve, the structured tools’ gain over grep rises from 7–9 points at 0.6B to 17–21 at 1.7–4B and falls to 4–5 at 32B (odds ratio 0.77–0.82 per doubling of parameters); from 8B up about half of that gain is the form of the submission (exact ids) rather than discovery; the fall from 14B to 32B happens at equal grep-only accuracy and is a fall in tool uptake (find_entity called in 96% of episodes at 14B, 45% at 32B), not an FP8 artifact; and the same 4B size gains +17.6+17.6 points from embedding search under one checkpoint and nothing under another. • Grep-only Qwen3-8B collapses into search loops (10 grep calls per episode, 40% of episodes hit the step cap, 41% never submit); a 50-step, 40k-token budget does not rescue it. Graph tools also change the form of what the agent submits: 85% of its top-5 function strings are exact entity ids, against 47% with grep only, which matters downstream. • Downstream, the localizations of G/E/T/ET lead a fixed Qwen3-8B repair prompt to 6/13/12/13 resolved tasks of 160 (oracle locations: 26). Resolution is almost entirely conditional on correct localization (24–27% versus 1–2%). • Inside the model, direct call edges are linearly decodable within anchor and in-degree bin (AUC 0.74 and 0.68 on the two held-out folds for Qwen3-4B; 0.73 and 0.66 for Qwen3-8B) and remain so inside agent conversations (0.61–0.66) including for edges no tool printed (0.59–0.60); but a one-line lexical baseline reaches 0.99, two-hop edges with the lexical cue removed reach only 0.57, and inheritance is not decodable beyond one-sided information. What is in the weights is a shallow, mostly lexical picture of direct dependencies.

papers.title: Linear Hashing Is Poissonesque
papers.abstract:
The Poisson approximation theorem states that when $m$ balls are tossed uniformly and randomly into $n$ bins, the distribution of the bin loads can sometimes be approximated by $n$ independent Poisson random variables of mean $m/n$. We show that when the balls are tossed via a random $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear map, the load distribution is still governed by this Poisson distribution, albeit in a (necessarily) weaker manner. This allows us to show that a random linear map behaves like a fully random map in the following ways:
  1. $\textbf{Expected loads.}$ We show that the expected value of the $r$th largest bin is governed by the $r$th largest value among $n$ independent Poisson random variables of mean $m/n$. Specializing to the canonical setting of $m=n$ and $r=1$, our bounds show that the expected maximum load when $n$ balls are hashed into $n$ bins by a random $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear map is no more than the corresponding expectation for a fully random map $\textit{plus}$ $\frac{3}2 + o(1)$. Specializing to $m\gg n\log n$, we show that the expected max load is $(1+o(1))m/n$ in this regime.
  2. $\textbf{Concentration.}$ When $m\gg n\log (1/\rho)$ balls are tossed into $n$ bins randomly, we expect with $0.99$ probability that $\textit{every}$ density-$\rho$ subset of bins will contain a $(1\pm o(1) )\rho$-fraction of the balls. We show that this remains the case if the $m$ balls are tossed using a random linear map, and our bound matches the $o(1)$-factor produced by the fully random case. This gives a stronger version of the Leftover Hash Lemma for linear maps. An implication of this is that all bins have load $m/n \pm O(\sqrt{(m/n)\log n})$ with probability $0.99$.
  We obtain these results by showing that the average of a log-potential on the bin loads is upper bounded by the cumulant generating function of a Poisson random variable of mean $m/n$.

authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.title: Faster Polyhedral Intersections in 3D
papers.abstract: The operation of intersecting two polyhedra, which can be reduced to clipping one polyhedron with a series of planes formed from another polyhedron, is central to intersection based mesh interpolation and material interface reconstruction. R3D is a robust library for such operation which implements the algorithm of Sugihara. In this paper, we present J3D, a new implementation of the clipping algorithm of Sugihara that provides substantial performance improvements over R3D.

papers.title: Log-Concavity and Fundamental Gaps on Complex Projective Domains
papers.abstract: We prove quantitative log-concavity and fundamental-gap estimates for Dirichlet Schr\"odinger operators on complex projective domains. With holomorphic sectional curvature four, the boundary condition $\mathrm{II}\ge\sqrt{44/5}\,g$ suffices in every complex dimension under $\operatorname{Hess} V\ge2|\nabla V|g$ and $\operatorname{osc}V\le4n$. It yields $\operatorname{Hess}(-\log\phi_1)>g$ and $\lambda_2-\lambda_1>\max\{n+2+\sqrt{n^2+5n+11},\,2n+14/3\}$. The main difficulty is to control the distinguished Hopf direction together with a transverse Hessian block whose dimension grows with $n$. We extend modified-Hessian first-contact arguments by retaining the Hopf term and using longitudinal and transverse rotational tests. A trace minimization reduces all gradient orientations to three extreme directions. A dimension-scaled logarithmic barrier then compares their contact costs with a single limiting profile. A radial spectral estimate supplies the required quadratic-in-dimension spectral threshold from a dimension-independent boundary curvature bound. For $n\ge3$ these are, to our knowledge, the first log-concavity estimates for domains in $\mathbb{CP}^n$ without symmetry assumptions. We also prove a sharp diameter bound and Hessian levels linear in $n$ under larger dimension-free curvature bounds.

papers.title: Supervision Without Blocking: An Evidence-Driven Redesign of OTP-Style Fault Tolerance for Cooperative Runtimes
papers.abstract: Actor frameworks on mainstream runtimes advertise Erlang/OTP-style supervision, but OTP's consistency contracts assume a synchronous, single-threaded supervisor, and ports inherit that assumption's absence as unexamined risk. We evaluated every supervision guarantee against pinned OTP documentation and source read verbatim, against the source of three further Rust actor frameworks at fixed revisions, and against the actor-model literature, recording the evidence behind each design decision. Blind adversarial audits and the cross-framework study surfaced 24 defect classes, of which eight reduce to one root cause: reconstructing, by explicit mechanism, the atomicity a synchronous supervisor gets implicitly. We introduce a supervision runtime that closes all 24 cataloged classes through supervisor-owned completion values, per-incarnation identity, and a single lifecycle state machine, validated by 241 tests including reverted-fix reproductions. The result holds OTP's verbatim-verified contracts while adding two properties OTP does not offer: a supervisor that remains responsive throughout group restarts, and message handlers that are never cancelled mid-execution. We delimit the forcing guarantees no cooperative runtime can honor.

papers.title: Spectral Tur\'an problems for complete bipartite expansions in linear hypergraphs
papers.abstract: An $r$-uniform hypergraph is linear if any two edges share at most one vertex. For a family $\mathcal F$ of $r$-graphs, let $\text{ex}^{\text{lin}}_r(n,\mathcal F)$ and $\text{spex}^{\text{lin}}_r(n,\mathcal F)$ denote, respectively, the maximum number of edges and the maximum spectral radius of an $n$-vertex $\mathcal F$-free linear $r$-graph. In this paper, we show that for $t\ge s\ge3$, $\text{spex}^{\text{lin}}_r(n,K_{s,t}^{+})\le \frac{(t-s+1)^{1/s}}{r-1}n^{1-1/s}+o(n^{1-1/s})$, where $K_{s,t}^{+}$ is the $r$-graph obtained from the complete bipartite graph $K_{s,t}$ by enlarging each edge with $r-2$ new vertices. This answers a problem of She, Fan and Kang in a stronger form. Moreover, our result implies that $\text{ex}^\text{lin}_r(n,K_{s,t}^{+}) \le \frac{(t-s+1)^{1/s}}{r(r-1)}n^{2-1/s}+o(n^{2-1/s})$, which improves the leading coefficient in the corresponding bound of Gao and Chang. We also give a construction which implies that $\text{spex}^{\text{lin}}_r(n,K_{s,t}^{+})=\Theta(n^{1-1/s})$ and $\text{ex}^\text{lin}_r(n,K_{s,t}^{+})=\Theta(n^{2-1/s})$ for $s\ge 4r-6$ and $t>(s-1)!$.

papers.title: Nonreciprocal magneto-optic beam steering of thermal emission
papers.abstract: Conventional thermal emitters obey Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation, which ties absorptivity to emissivity and places a fundamental limit on a range of radiative energy technologies and sensing systems. This constraint can be overcome using magneto-optic materials, which exhibit nonreciprocal thermal emission under an applied magnetic field. While the spectral nonreciprocity of magneto-optic devices has been explored theoretically and experimentally, nonreciprocal control over the direction of thermal emission has received far less attention. Here, we propose and numerically demonstrate nonreciprocal beam steering of thermal emission, wherein an applied magnetic field lifts the degeneracy between guided modes at +/- kx, enabling asymmetric and tunable directional thermal emission. We highlight a III-V semiconductor photonic structure operating at 24.5 um, a wavelength with few laser sources. This structure exhibits a nonreciprocity greater than 0.5 between +/- 75 degrees at 50 mT, a peak emissivity asymmetry over 0.6 at 150 mT, and 22 degrees of beam steering between 0 and 1 T. Our approach provides a solid-state means of steering a thermal beam, offering a potential route to magnetically controlled beam scanning of incandescent sources.

papers.title: Semantic SCL Decoding for Polar Codes
papers.abstract: Semantic error control coding (SECC) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving communication reliability by exploiting the inherent structure and semantic dependencies of transmitted information. This paper proposes a semantic successive cancellation list (SCL) decoder for polar codes carrying natural-language text. A fine-tuned byte-level language model provides next-byte priors, which are converted into conditional bit costs and incorporated directly into the SCL path metric before each pruning step. This allows the decoder to jointly exploit channel reliability and source structure while retaining the conventional polar coding framework. The language model can also be invoked only for bytes whose channel decisions are unreliable, trading decoding performance for latency. Simulations for length-512 polar codes show substantial block error rate (BLER) improvements over conventional CRC-aided SCL (CA-SCL) decoding. At rate R=0.75 and list size L=16, the proposed decoder achieves more than 1 dB of gain in BLER compared to CA-SCL with the same L. Moreover, with L=8, it outperforms conventional CA-SCL with L=256 in terms of BLER, while requiring about one quarter of the decoding time of the latter in the evaluated software implementation.

papers.title: Weak mixing and non-recurrence along finitely generated multiplicative semigroups of $\mathbb N$
papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal P$ be a finite nonempty set of primes, and let $S_{\mathcal P}$ be the multiplicative semigroup that they generate. We prove that there are an invertible weakly mixing measure-preserving transformation $T$ and a set $A$ of positive measure such that $A\cap T^{-r}A=\varnothing$ for every $r\in S_{\mathcal P}$. This gives a negative answer to Bergelson's 1996 question concerning recurrence along $\{2^m3^n:m,n\geq1\}$, and applies to every finitely generated multiplicative semigroup of positive integers. More generally, we give a sufficient condition for weakly mixing non-recurrence based on divisibility properties and separation by finitely many rotations of the circle. This criterion also applies to an infinitely generated multiplicative semigroup not contained in any $S_{\mathcal P}$ with $\mathcal P$ finite.

papers.title: Dynamic helimagnetism via charged spin current
papers.abstract: We present a theoretical and numerical study of classical, localized spins coupled to conduction electrons that carry both charge and spin currents, deriving the effective equations of motion from the s-d exchange Hamiltonian. Applied to a periodically arranged one-dimensional spin chain, these equations yield two current-driven helical phases: a static helix stabilized by a pure spin current alone, and a coherently precessing helix that appears once a small charge-current component is added. For a given helical wavenumber, the precession angular frequency $\omega$ and the canting ratio $\Delta$ toward the hard axis follow analytically from the equations of motion, while the wavenumber $q_{\rm helix}$ of the precessing helix is selected by a heuristically constructed effective Lagrangian. Direct numerical integration of the same equations of motion reproduces all three observables wherever it yields a coherent helix. The helix chirality is set by a long-range, current-generated Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM)-type coupling rather than an intrinsic DM interaction, so materials without bulk or interfacial DM interactions could also host current-controlled helical order. Because the helical pitch, precession frequency, and canting ratio are all continuously tunable by the current amplitudes, these helices could serve as probes of spin currents.

papers.title: A marked scheme representation for Voronoi volumes in the Brownian map
papers.abstract: For any fixed number $k\ge3$ of independent volume-sampled sites in the unit-area Brownian map, we represent the negative-power transform of their ordinary Voronoi volumes as a finite sum of marked planar scheme integrals. These integrals arise from the critical asymptotics of generating functions for face-constrained labelled planar maps. To connect them to Voronoi volumes, we use Miermont's zero-delay correspondence to interpret the labelled maps as quadrangulations with distinguished sites and then pass to the Brownian map scaling limit.

papers.title: Unveil the Mask: Jointly-Optimized Diffusion Masked Pretraining for Appearance-Agnostic Operator Verification
papers.abstract: Photorealistic avatar videos decouple the appearance of a rendered face from the person who operates it, which makes conventional face recognition unsuitable for identifying the operator. Verifying the operator therefore requires representations of how a face moves that are insensitive to what the avatar looks like. We propose a verification framework built without any external pretrained model. It uses two complementary modalities provided for each sample: facial landmark sequences and video frames. From the landmark modality, it learns motion representations by diffusion masked pretraining over grouped landmarks, guided by lightweight auxiliary tasks that predict behavioral cues such as motion intensity and eye openness, and turns them into operator embeddings with a contrastive linear probe. To generalize to unseen avatar generators, the pretraining input is randomly transformed to simulate how a generator may alter the operator's motion. From the video modality, it captures fine facial motion through differences between consecutive frames. The embeddings of the two modalities are combined into one. Our approach reaches an overall AUC of 0.769 on the WBA2026 benchmark. Linear probing shows that the video embedding retains little information about the avatar's identity, whereas the landmark embedding retains some, and fusing the two modalities improves verification in particular across speaking and listening modes.

authors.name: Katsuya Ogata
authors.institution: Fukuoka International University of Health and Welfare

papers.title: UniQuery: Unifying Vision Models with a Joint Query Head for Cross-Domain Pedestrian Attribute Recognition
papers.abstract: Pedestrian Attribute Recognition (PAR) predicts semantic attributes of individuals, such as gender, age, clothing and accessories, and its descriptions support attribute-based person retrieval and person re-identification. However, accurately recognizing fine-grained attributes across domains remains challenging due to occlusion, appearance variations, and shifts in image distributions. Ensembles of independently trained foundation encoders combine their logits with fixed fusion weights, so every attribute uses the same mix and the encoders are never trained together. We propose UniQuery, which instead jointly fine-tunes DINOv3 and CLIP for attribute-specific fusion. It combines two query heads, one for each encoder, with a joint query head whose attribute queries attend to tokens from both encoders, and the prediction is the average of the logits of the three query heads. We evaluate UniQuery on the benchmark of the UPAR Challenge 2027 at the WACV 2027 Real-World Surveillance workshop, where models are trained on PA100k, PETA and Market-1501 with a shared set of attributes. In leave-one-dataset-out experiments, UniQuery outperforms the independent ensemble in Challenge_Avg on both held-out datasets. Ablations show that learning fusion over independently trained encoders does not improve upon logit averaging in the mean over the two held-out datasets, while freezing the encoders lowers the Challenge_Avg of UniQuery. On the hidden test set of the benchmark, UniQuery achieves a Challenge_Avg of 0.8001.

papers.title: LENS: Likelihood Evaluation and Neighbor Smoothing for Attribute-Based Person Retrieval on Unseen Cameras
papers.abstract: Attribute-based person retrieval ranks surveillance images from a binary query of semantic attributes, but mean Average Attribute Degree of Match (mADM) drops on unseen cameras as predicted probabilities shift. Common pipelines rank gallery images by their L1 distance to the query, which penalizes a confident single-attribute mismatch no more than small uncertainties across many attributes, while post-hoc recalibration fitted on source validation data fails to transfer because the per-attribute maps fitted on source data do not match those of new cameras. We propose LENS (Likelihood Evaluation and Neighbor Smoothing), combining fine-tuned DINOv3 and CLIP models with a distilled student. LENS regularizes mutually exclusive attribute groups with group cross-entropy in training, scores gallery images by the log-likelihood of the exact query, and smooths gallery logits over nearest neighbors using DINOv3 appearance features from the same forward pass. On held-out datasets, all three changes raise mADM: the likelihood score improves all six retrieval metrics for the main ensemble and mADM for all 48 development models, and training-free kNN smoothing improves all 46 tested development models. On the hidden test set of the UPAR 2027 benchmark, LENS reaches 68.17 mADM.
