papers.title: Optimal Rates in Local and Central Limit Theorems for the Elephant Random Walk
papers.abstract: We determine the optimal rates of convergence in the local and central limit theorems for the one-dimensional elephant random walk in the diffusive and critical regimes, $0\le p\le3/4$. For every fixed initial distribution, we treat both exact finite-time centering and standardization and the normalization $S_n/\sqrt n$ (or $S_n/\sqrt{n\log n}$ at criticality). We establish uniform Edgeworth expansions for local probabilities and distribution functions, and use these expansions to derive the optimal convergence rates, which exhibit several phase transitions depending on the symmetry of the initial distribution, the normalization, and the type of approximation. Our approach uses elephant polynomials for precise characteristic-function expansions and a random recursive tree representation for global Fourier bounds.

papers.title: Rank-1 Weight-Corrected Trainable Weight Averaging for Out-of-Distribution Detection
papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection identifies inputs outside the training distribution. Rank-based analyses such as RankFeat and RankWeight suggest that OOD overconfidence is closely related to dominant low-rank components in feature and weight spaces. Since weight averaging operates directly in parameter space and improves model generalization, we consider it for OOD detection from a dominant-component perspective. Trainable Weight Averaging (TWA) assigns a single coefficient to each checkpoint, limiting independent control of dominant weight components. We extend TWA with leading rank-one weight components extracted by Singular Value Decomposition as correction directions, whose contributions are learned through the in-distribution classification objective. On ResNet50, our method improves over fine-tuning and standard TWA across the evaluated datasets with MSP and RankWeight, both with and without Outlier Exposure. Mahalanobis-based evaluation yields mixed results, indicating that the benefit depends on the OOD scoring protocol. Target-layer analyses with MSP and Energy favor correction near the classifier.

papers.title: A Deterministic Game-Theoretic Approach to Convexity-Preserving Property and Finite-Time Extinction of Level Sets for Geometric Equations
papers.abstract: We consider the convexity-preserving property and finite-time extinction of level sets for quasilinear geometric equations using a game-theoretic approach introduced by Kohn and Serfaty. To construct the game whose value function approximates the viscosity solution, we use the approach introduced by Sato.

papers.title: Inverse origami inspired by insect morphogenesis: geometric design of wrinkle structures for curved surface formation
papers.abstract: Insect exoskeletons abruptly acquire complex three-dimensional forms during metamorphosis from larva to pupa. This transformation occurs through the unfolding of preformed wrinkle structures inside the larval body under internal pressure. Inspired by this process, we investigate an inverse-origami strategy for fabricating curved surfaces. Whereas conventional origami produces three-dimensional objects by folding a flat sheet, this strategy produces curved surfaces by unfolding preformed wrinkle structures. The central design problem is to derive a wrinkle structure from a prescribed target surface. Our key idea is to regard a wrinkle structure as a unidirectional stretching field, which specifies at each point the stretch produced when the structure unfolds. We first derive such a field from the target surface geometry and then translate it into spatially varying wrinkle directions and spacing, so that the wrinkle structure unfolds into the target. The resulting numerical designs approximate the intrinsic metric of the target surface. We demonstrate the method on multiple target surfaces through numerical construction, mechanical unfolding simulations, and 3D-printed prototypes. This work provides a biologically inspired geometric design principle for encoding prescribed surface shapes in wrinkle structures, as well as a framework for designing and fabricating deployable curved surfaces.

papers.title: Controlled Block Proximal Linearized Method for Nonconvex and Nonsmooth Optimization
papers.abstract: We consider multiblock nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization without assuming bounded iterates or coercivity of the original objective. We propose the Controlled Block Proximal Linearized (CBPL) method, which incorporates a control potential into block updates while retaining the original objective, variables, and constraints. Under explicit control design conditions and the KL property, the control yields boundedness, finite length, whole-sequence convergence of the original variables, and convergence of objective values. At the limit, one limiting subgradient of the original objective vanishes on all effective comparison directions. We apply CBPL to graph-regularized nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF), CP decomposition, and independent-core matrix tri-factorization (NMTF) with $\ell_0$ norm sparsity constraints. We characterize their reconstruction-preserving scale degeneracies, proving that scale criticality is equivalent to graph collapse and that full criticality forces such collapse. Explicit controls provide compact sublevel sets and a uniform positive lower bound on graph action, including with an independent Tucker core, while retaining genuine reconstruction-changing directions. Each block admits an explicit projection and a computable safe step parameter. For ordinary NMF and CP models, whole-sequence convergence to a full critical point follows. Experiments with direct safe updates demonstrate convergence, sustained graph action, and controlled factor and core scales.

papers.title: Learning Scene Coordinate Reconstruction from Unposed Images via Pose Graph Optimization
papers.abstract: Learning-based structure-from-motion methods such as ACE-Zero have demonstrated strong performance in estimating cameraposes and scene coordinates from unordered image collections without requiring ground truth supervision. However, the lack of global and multi-view consistency constraints in ACE-Zero can lead to pose drift and misalignment, particularly in complex or ambiguous scenes. In this work, we propose a hybrid framework that integrates pose graph optimization (PGO) into ACE-Zero to refine camera poses and suppress incorrect refinements. We construct pose graphs directly from ACE-Zero outputs by extracting relative pose constraints from predicted scene coordinates. Furthermore, we introduce an uncertainty-aware optimization strategy by estimating confidence scores using geometric priors, including epipolar and optical flow consistencies across views. Our approach improves the robustness and accuracy of pose estimation, demonstrating that global geometric reasoning can effectively complement learning-based inference in structure-from-motion.

papers.title: A superprocess model for eDNA transport in random river environment
papers.abstract: Environmental DNA (eDNA) is increasingly used to monitor aquatic organisms in rivers, yet predicting its concentration and assessing the reliability of such predictions remain challenging because river flow fluctuates with long memory and models of eDNA dynamics are inevitably misspecified. We propose a stochastic modeling framework for eDNA concentration in rivers that addresses both issues. The eDNA concentration is described by a stochastic partial differential equation with transport, decay, source, and square-root multiplicative noise, and the flow velocity is modeled by a superposition of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-type processes with long memory. We show that the long memory of the flow velocity induces superdiffusive transport of eDNA, with the variance of the transported distance growing superlinearly in the ensemble sense. The proposed model admits a closed-form Laplace functional, based on which we prove the existence and uniqueness in law of the solution on an unbounded domain. We further evaluate the effects of model uncertainty through a robust control formulation based on the relative entropy, in which the lower and upper bounds of the expected eDNA concentration, together with the worst-case distortions, are obtained in closed form. The framework is applied to eDNA and flow velocity data collected for the upstream migration of Plecoglossus altivelis altivelis in a river in Japan. The results demonstrate that the closed-form bounds provide a computationally inexpensive tool for quantifying the range of eDNA concentrations that can be expected under model uncertainty.

authors.name: Hidekazu Yoshioka

papers.title: How Tuning, Reference Preview, Actuator Modeling, and Fallback Policies Change Quadrotor Controller Comparisons: A Reproducible Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Quadrotor controller comparisons commonly report a single tracking error, although the resulting ranking also depends on tuning effort, reference information, actuator prediction, optimizer fallback, and command timing. We quantify these effects for cascade PID, hover LQR, boundary-layer sliding-mode control (BL-SMC), linear MPC with LQR fallback (LMPC-F), a preview-enabled LMPC-F, and a geometric $SO(3)$ controller on a common nonlinear plant with rotor gyroscopic coupling, motor lag, and saturation. A primary study (556 episodes at 50~Hz) combines matched twelve-candidate tuning, 400 paired evaluation episodes, and a 48-cell MPC factorial; a confirmation study (1462 episodes) repeats the evaluation on 50 fresh realizations with tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. A matched twelve-candidate tuning protocol changed the mean-RMSE ordering obtained with the fixed baseline settings, moving BL-SMC from last to first; the new ordering recurred on the fresh realizations, and a 48-candidate budget left it unchanged. Reference preview substantially reduced MPC tracking error and, on the figure-eight task, removed fallback activity. On an abrupt step, the outcome depended on the interplay between fallback policy, predictor, and actuator authority. Command timing also changed the outcome: replaying measured command-call delays terminated three of four nominal MPC configurations on a desktop computer and all four on a Raspberry Pi~5, whereas capping the solver at 100 iterations removed every deadline miss in the tested nominal timing profiles. Controller rankings therefore depend not only on tracking accuracy but also on the tuning protocol, reference information, fallback behavior, and implementation timing. We propose a reporting checklist covering tracking accuracy, tuning effort, completion and failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing.

papers.title: A Warped Dust Ring in the CQ Tau Disk
papers.abstract: The diversity of planetary orbital architectures calls for observational constraints on radial variations in disk-plane orientation, or warps, yet such variations in dust disks remain poorly characterized. CQ Tau is a promising target because its misaligned inner disk and candidate gas warp suggest a radially extended warp. We present the ALMA 1.3 mm dust continuum image reconstructed from the real part of the visibilities, extracting the centro-symmetric disk structure. At an effective spatial resolution of $0.052'' \times 0.042''$ ($7.8 \times 6.3$ au), the image reveals a bright main ring at radii of $\sim20$--$70$ au and an unresolved compact emission component tracing the inner disk around the central star. Ellipse fits centered on the stellar position to contours tracing the inner and outer edges of the ring reveal radial variations in position angles and inclinations. At the inner edge ($\sim21$--$26$ au), the position angle and inclination span $214^\circ$--$233^\circ$ and $23^\circ$--$39^\circ$, respectively, while they span $231^\circ$--$235^\circ$ and $33^\circ$--$36^\circ$ at the outer edge ($\sim58$--$67$ au). Whereas a coplanar ring toy model fails to reproduce such variations, a warped ring model with the local tilt decreasing from $\sim4^\circ$ at $r = 20$ au to $\sim1^\circ$ at 60 au reproduces them. The high-pass-filtered real-part image reveals a pair of opposed curved negative residuals. Similar features appear only in the warped ring model, further supporting the dust warp. These results establish CQ Tau as an example of a warped dust disk and an important laboratory for investigating the connection between three-dimensional disk geometry and planet formation.

papers.title: A simple construction of smooth counterexamples to the Loewner and Carath\'eodory conjectures
papers.abstract: Alp\"oge recently announced smooth counterexamples to the Loewner and Carath\'eodory conjectures. We present a simpler construction based on a trigonometric function as a seed. Using this, for every positive integer $k$, we construct a smooth real-valued function on the plane, flat at the origin, whose Hessian eigenline fields have an isolated singularity of index $1+k/2$. A support-function parametrization realizes this index as an umbilic index of a non-real analytic $C^\infty$-regular surface germ in Euclidean $3$-space. The same framework, applied to a rapidly decreasing function on the whole plane, gives a strictly convex closed smooth surface with exactly one umbilic, of index $2$. This paper is self-contained with regard to the existence of an umbilic of index $2$ and the construction of a counterexample to the Carath\'eodory conjecture.

papers.title: Head Dimension Matters in Language Models for Long-Context Retrieval
papers.abstract: Multi-head attention retrieves and combines context representations through query--key interactions and value aggregation, with head dimension constraining the per-head representation space. In long-context processing, it remains unclear whether allocating a fixed parameter budget to fewer, wider heads improves information retrieval. In this paper, we investigate how head dimension affects the performance of long-context retrieval tasks. Our empirical studies reveal that pretraining loss and short-context non-retrieval task performance are not affected much by head dimension, while long-context retrieval performance improves with wider heads at fixed model sizes. We find that models with wider heads have a higher proportion of retrieval heads, associating more parameters with retrieval. Our ablation studies also show that the retrieval performance improves with wider heads even when the projection weights in attention modules are frozen during long-context continual pretraining, suggesting that wider heads not only benefit updates in attention modules but lead to more effective adaptation of components such as embeddings and MLPs.

papers.title: Electronic Responses in Solid Oxygen with Coexisting Structural and Magnetic Orders
papers.abstract: Solid oxygen provides a unique platform for studying the interplay between structural and magnetic degrees of freedom, as each O$_2$ molecule possesses an $S=1$ spin and weak intermolecular van der Waals interactions allow substantial structural flexibility. In addition, because of its small intermolecular hopping integrals, this system is known to be a strongly correlated electron system with a multiorbital nature. In this study, we examine electronic states and magnetic and dielectric responses using a multiorbital Hubbard model with Peierls-type electron-lattice coupling. This model provides a minimal description of the interplay between structural and magnetic degrees of freedom in solid oxygen. We apply the Hartree-Fock approximation to obtain the ground-state phase diagram. Antiferromagnetic order appears when the onsite Coulomb interaction is strong, whereas three nonmagnetic bond-ordered states emerge when it is weak. At intermediate interaction strengths, antiferromagnetic order coexists with each of the three bond orders. These three coexistence phases all break time-reversal symmetry; one preserves spatial inversion symmetry, whereas the other two also break it. The two inversion-breaking phases exhibit linear magnetoelectric responses, whereas the inversion-symmetric phase exhibits altermagnetic spin splitting and a piezomagnetic response. These responses may provide experimental signatures of coexisting magnetic and structural orders in high-pressure solid oxygen suggested by recent experiments.

papers.title: A Lambda Calculus Based on Quantum Logic
papers.abstract: We propose a typed lambda calculus based on quantum logic. We first present a natural deduction system for quantum logic with the Sasaki hook as its implication operation and then formulate a typed lambda calculus connected to this system through the Curry-Howard correspondence. We prove soundness and completeness of the former with respect to orthomodular lattices and strong normalization of the latter. The resulting lambda calculus has the characteristic feature that only one assumption is available in the typing derivation that serves as the premise of $\lambda$-abstraction. Under this restriction, ordinary currying is not available in general, but it is still possible to perform $\lambda$-abstraction by combining multiple assumptions into a single argument of product type and to construct a term corresponding to a deduction using the Sasaki projection.

papers.title: Extremal and global-time statistics of sluggish random walks with stochastic resetting
papers.abstract: We study the extremal and global-time statistics of a one-dimensional sluggish random walk, whose diffusivity decays as a power law of the distance from the origin, under Poissonian resetting to the origin. A change of variable maps the process onto a signed Bessel process, so that renewal theory applies. We obtain the exact Laplace transform of the distribution of the maximum over a finite window. At long times the centered maximum of the transformed process follows the Gumbel law, and in physical space the typical maximum grows as a power of the logarithm of the window length. The far-tail rate function does not depend on $\alpha$ in the Bessel variable, so the second-order dynamical transition known for Brownian resetting, between maxima produced by a single anomalously long inter-reset interval and maxima produced by an interval occupying essentially the whole window, holds for every $\alpha$. The time of the maximum is uniformly distributed in the bulk of the window, with boundary layers that shift its mean above the midpoint logarithmically in the window length. The last-passage time through the origin has an exact density, and the time elapsed since it converges to a Gamma law. Reflection symmetry makes the occupation time of the positive half-line and the last-passage time uncorrelated. The results reduce to the Brownian case and agree with simulations.

papers.title: A spinal-inspired spiking neural network for continuous finger-joint kinematics estimation from high-density surface EMG
papers.abstract: Decoding simultaneous and proportional finger kinematics from high-density surface electromyography (HD sEMG) remains challenging. Although data-driven methods have shown promising performance for finger movement decoding, their limited physiological interpretability remains a relevant limitation. This study proposes and evaluates a spiking neural network (SNN) that incorporates spinal-inspired structures and mechanisms to predict multi-joint finger kinematics from HD sEMG signals. The spinal-inspired SNN includes a spike-encoding computational model with input-noise variability, a phenomenological representation of Henneman's size principle, and excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance. HD sEMG and kinematic data were collected from 23 healthy participants performing grasping tasks under different elbow and wrist postures. Performance was assessed using six prediction metrics and compared against six baseline machine learning and deep learning methods. The proposed method showed a large and significant ($p<0.05$, rank-biserial correlation $r_{rb}>0.7$) improvement over all baseline methods across all accuracy metrics. Performance improved significantly with increasing spike encoder firing rates up to approximately 128 Hz, and with more regular input spike trains compared with a Poisson-like encoder. In contrast, the E/I balance did not significantly affect the decoding performance of the algorithm. The firing rate and inter-spike interval statistics of the SNN differed significantly across motor tasks. These results demonstrate that incorporating neurophysiological principles into SNNs improves prediction performance while providing additional physiological interpretability for simultaneous and proportional finger-kinematics decoding. This approach represents a promising step toward physiology-informed neural networks, with potential applications in motor rehabilitation.

papers.title: Crystal-surface polarity enables nonreciprocal transport in a centrosymmetric kagome magnet
papers.abstract: Every crystal surface breaks inversion symmetry even when the bulk is centrosymmetric, creating an intrinsic boundary polarity ($\mathbf{\mathit{P}}$). Here we show that this polarity enables zero-field nonreciprocal transport in the centrosymmetric kagome magnets TbMn$_6$Sn$_{6-x}$In$_x$. In symmetric TbMn$_6$Sn$_{4.4}$In$_{1.6}$ microdevices, opposing side surfaces exhibit second-harmonic longitudinal resistances of comparable magnitude and opposite sign. Reversing the spontaneous magnetization ($\mathbf{\mathit{M}}$) reverses both signals, whereas rotating $\mathbf{\mathit{M}}$ so that the toroidal moment $\mathbf{\mathit{P}} \times \mathbf{\mathit{M}}$ has no component along the current suppresses the response. In pristine TbMn$_6$Sn$_6$, the signal switches off across the spin-reorientation transition, providing a chemically ordered control of the same symmetry relation. Spatial potential mapping indicates that the nonlinear boundary contribution is distinct from the bulk linear conduction. Spin-orbit-coupled surface states associated with topological bands may enhance the effect. Crystal-surface polarity therefore offers a broadly applicable route to zero-field rectification in centrosymmetric magnetic conductors around room temperature.

papers.title: Survey of small amplitude waves in solar prominences
papers.abstract: Presence of small amplitude oscillation or waves in solar prominences was investigated by using archived data from a full disk H-alpha imaging spectroscopic observation. A total of 178 prominences on the limb were studied and it was found that there are plenty of evidence of oscillations or waves with preferential periods in 3 - 5 min (4 min) and 10 - 20 min (15 min). We found very clear signature of persistently propagating 4 min wave in 21 prominences and at least a hint of 4 min oscillation in 90 prominences in their Doppler signal. The 4 min waves are often found in prominences with a large horizontal size, and they propagate in nearly horizontal direction with a phase speed of 140 - 400 km/s. On the other hand, very clear evidence of the 15 min wave was found in 14 prominences and at least a hint of oscillation in 62 prominences in the Doppler signal. The 15 min waves preferentially propagate in vertical direction with a phase speed of 20 - 50 km/s. There is a positive correlation between the presences of 4 min and 15 min waves. The 4 min waves are interpreted as Alfvenic wave propagating along the coronal magnetic field supporting the prominences. Two scenarios are discussed for the 15 min wave, i.e., Alfvenic wave propagating vertically in prominence bodies and apparent cross-field propagation in magnetic structures. Prominences that harbor the short period waves or oscillations distribute over the entire solar latitude, suggesting that these waves are excited by ubiquitous disturbance in solar atmosphere. While it is also true that a number of prominences do not show signatures of oscillations nor propagating waves, and the reason of this diversity remains open question. Our study suggests that observing the 4 min waves in prominences will serve as a useful tool for tracing the coronal Alfvenic waves and the magnetic field supporting the prominences.

papers.title: Symplectic singularity as hyperK\"ahler cone
papers.abstract: We prove that any symplectic singularity has a structure of hyperK\"ahler cone. In particular, it is equivalent to the vertex of a conical symplectic variety, and it is automatically K-polystable.

papers.title: Depth Improves Training-Time Scaling for Difficult Tasks in Deep Linear Networks
papers.abstract: Neural scaling laws describe the predictable power-law dependence of model performance on training time, dataset size, and model scale, with the exponents quantifying how performance changes with resources. Recent theory has shown how scaling exponents are shaped by the data distribution and the structure of the learning task, but whether network depth can improve training-time scaling has remained unsettled. Through a refined analysis of deep linear networks, we clarify that the task spectrum determines when increasing network depth improves training-time scaling. For spectrally difficult tasks, increasing depth improves the asymptotic training-time scaling exponent, whereas for easy tasks, the exponent remains independent of depth, with depth affecting only a logarithmic correction at the boundary between these regimes. Remarkably, we find that a reparameterization of time governed by the predictor norm provides a unified description of the dynamics across task difficulties. Under this reparameterization, the loss follows a common scaling law whose exponent is independent of depth. Numerical experiments on a task derived from benchmark image data and with nonlinear networks exhibit qualitatively consistent task-dependent effects of depth on training-time scaling. Our findings advance the theoretical understanding of how task structure shapes the effects of network architecture on learning and offer a basis for studying scaling behavior across broader classes of neural networks.

papers.title: Momentum-selective graphene spectroscopy of moir\'e excitons
papers.abstract: Far-field photoluminescence probes only the light-cone corner of an exciton's momentum content, whereas energy transfer to nearby graphene integrates in-plane momenta up to the inverse spacer thickness $1/z$. For a WSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ heterobilayer we build the transition polarization $\bm{P}_n(\qv)$ of each localized moir\'e exciton from the registry-dependent vector dipole texture and use each $\bm{P}_n$ for both baths. The two baths rank the states differently: the graphene-rate ratios differ from the optical ones, their ordering inverts with spacer thickness, and the distance exponents at $z=10$\,nm spread by more than two units. These ratios are independent of the transition-dipole prefactor. Within the $C_3$-symmetric leading-harmonic model the chiral $p_+$ and $d_-$ states are also dark at normal incidence yet transfer to graphene at rates comparable to the bright ground state. Their graphene rate depends on the sign of the texture phase, a quantity invisible in far-field emission, which we determine from first principles. In a device this prediction requires a splitting, larger than the symmetry-breaking mixing, that protects the chiral partners. Graphene proximity thus acts as a momentum-selective near-field probe of moir\'e excitons, and we propose its use as a practical spectroscopy.

papers.title: An isometric embedding of the space of non-increasing sequences with non-negative terms into the Gromov-Hausdorff space
papers.abstract: The Gromov-Hausdorff space is a certain metric space induced by the Gromov-Hausdorff convergence, and we study an isometric embedding into this space. While the subspace of non-negative real numbers in the Euclidean space admits an isometric embedding, we prove that the subspace of $\ell^\infty$ consisting of non-increasing sequences with non-negative terms can be isometrically embedded into the Gromov-Hausdorff space.

papers.title: Collisional Evolution around A-type Stars with Strong Silicate Features
papers.abstract: Around luminous A-type stars, retaining micrometer-sized dust grains is difficult owing to the high radiation pressure that repels particles with sizes below the blowout limit. Yet such particles have been evidenced in the terrestrial zone around those stars, via pronounced silicate spectral features. An in situ planetesimal belt that collisionally replenishes the dust is expected to deplete quickly, limiting the lifetime of observable features. However, modeling of such systems often relies on a power-law description of the grain size distribution that has a lower size limit owing to blowout. Using more complex, collisional simulations instead, we investigated the temporal evolution of hypothetical planetesimal belts in the terrestrial zone around five A-type stars showing strong spectral silicate features. A collisional cascade that is modified by radiation pressure results in dust distributions that replicate observed spectral features without requiring other physical processes. While features can be altered by particles below the blowout limit, their magnitude is dominated by the emission of larger grains. Using the systems' ages, we investigated the origin of the planetesimal belt. For the three younger systems of our sample, a planetesimal belt that emerged from the protoplanetary disk phase can explain the observations. This is even possible for two older systems if the planetesimals are located at slightly larger distances than the dust, e.g., if the dust drifted inward owing to the Poynting-Robertson drag. Alternatively, a recent production of the planetesimals, for instance, in a giant collision event, could have happened only several million years ago.

A subgroup of these disks shows spectral features in the mid-infrared that are associated with silicates [e.g., 19, 6, 64, and references in their Sect. 1], most prominently around wavelengths of λ∼10\lambda\sim$10$ and 18 µ​m18\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}. Such features are interpreted as the emission of dust grains of at most several micrometers in radius and at temperatures of several hundred kelvin, thus being located in the terrestrial zone around the host stars (≲10 au\lesssim$10\text{\,}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{u}$).

A possible origin for such warm dust distributions is a collisional cascade in an in situ planetesimal belt [39]. However, as the planetesimals are collisionally processed with time, the dust mass diminishes, an effect that is mostly unaffected by the initial belt mass, as initially more massive belts process faster [23, 92, 50]. Thus, an in situ collisional cascade generally cannot produce a given infrared excess at arbitrarily large times. The time when the ability ceases increases along with the size of the largest planetesimals in the belt, but there are physical limits to this, due to the planetesimal formation processes [42, 54]. For silicate spectral features in observations of A-type star systems, another challenge exists. The radiation pressure of these luminous host stars removes dust grains below the blowout size out of the system [13, 57]. This process can remove grains comparable in size to those that are needed to produce the silicate features. Frequently, spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of warm dust distributions are modeled using a power-law description of the grain size distribution that has a lower size limit [19, 6, 64, e.g.,]. However, this simplified treatment of the size distribution has limitations. Generally, the relative abundance of small grains modifies the size distribution for larger grains [14]. In addition, assuming a lower cutoff that is set by the blowout of small grains is only valid if the timescale on which the blowout occurs is much smaller than the collisional timescale on which the subblowout grains are replenished. In the limit of tenuous and optically thin debris disks, the blowout timescale is independent of the dust number density, while the collisional timescale decreases with increasing dust number density. Thus, assuming a lower cutoff is disfavored for systems with a sufficiently high dust number density where the impact of subblowout grains might no longer be safely neglected. Thébault & Kral [80] numerically showed the large impact of subblowout grains on the size distribution and the resulting SEDs for warm dust distributions around A-type stars. Observationally, Mittal et al. [64] found that, although the minimum grain size increases with the stellar luminosity, this increase occurs at a lower rate than expected from radiation pressure alone. Ballering et al. [6, hereafter BA14] analyzed SEDs of A-type systems that show spectral silicate features and found that the required minimum grain sizes are on the same order, but often smaller than the theoretically estimated blowout sizes.

A possible origin for such warm dust distributions is a collisional cascade in an in situ planetesimal belt [39]. However, as the planetesimals are collisionally processed with time, the dust mass diminishes, an effect that is mostly unaffected by the initial belt mass, as initially more massive belts process faster [23, 92, 50]. Thus, an in situ collisional cascade generally cannot produce a given infrared excess at arbitrarily large times. The time when the ability ceases increases along with the size of the largest planetesimals in the belt, but there are physical limits to this, due to the planetesimal formation processes [42, 54]. For silicate spectral features in observations of A-type star systems, another challenge exists. The radiation pressure of these luminous host stars removes dust grains below the blowout size out of the system [13, 57]. This process can remove grains comparable in size to those that are needed to produce the silicate features. In addition, assuming a lower cutoff that is set by the blowout of small grains is only valid if the timescale on which the blowout occurs is much smaller than the collisional timescale on which the subblowout grains are replenished. In the limit of tenuous and optically thin debris disks, the blowout timescale is independent of the dust number density, while the collisional timescale decreases with increasing dust number density. Thus, assuming a lower cutoff is disfavored for systems with a sufficiently high dust number density where the impact of subblowout grains might no longer be safely neglected. Thébault & Kral [80] numerically showed the large impact of subblowout grains on the size distribution and the resulting SEDs for warm dust distributions around A-type stars. Observationally, Mittal et al. [64] found that, although the minimum grain size increases with the stellar luminosity, this increase occurs at a lower rate than expected from radiation pressure alone. Ballering et al. [6, hereafter BA14] analyzed SEDs of A-type systems that show spectral silicate features and found that the required minimum grain sizes are on the same order, but often smaller than the theoretically estimated blowout sizes.

An alternative explanation for the origin of the small and warm dust grains are giant collisions of large objects, such as planetary embryos, that are associated with the late stages of terrestrial planet formation [43, 44, 36, 26, 91, e.g.,]. If an in situ planetesimal belt could be excluded as the origin of spectral silicate features, the giant impact scenario would be strengthened. Besides, the powerful space-based mid-infrared observational window to study debris disks has just recently been opened again by the Mid-Infrared Instrument [69, 88, MIRI;] with its Medium-Resolution Spectrometer [83, 1, MRS;] on board the James Webb Space Telescope [25, JWST;], allowing for new detailed studies of spectral silicate features [20, 16, 87, e.g.,].

In this study, we investigate the collisional evolution of warm debris disks in the terrestrial zone around A-type stars that show strong spectral silicate features. Using collisional simulations, we can avoid simplified power-law treatments of the grain size distribution and test the hypothesis that the collisional evolution of a planetesimal belt is able to explain the silicate features as seen in observations. Based on those results, we use an analytical description of quasi-steady-state collisional evolution to assess whether the observed infrared excesses can be produced by a primordial planetesimal belt, that is, a belt that has formed during the protoplanetary phase or shortly after, or the planetesimal belt has to be of recent origin, for instance, was produced in a recent major collision event.

Using collisional simulations, we can avoid simplified power-law treatments of the grain size distribution and test the hypothesis that the collisional evolution of a planetesimal belt is able to explain the silicate features as seen in observations. Our collisional model will be described in Sect. II, followed by a presentation of our particular choice of parameters and simulation results in Sect. III. The analysis of the planetesimal belt origin is outlined in Sect. IV. After discussing our assumptions in Sect. V, we will conclude with a summary in Sect. VI.

papers.title: Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks
papers.abstract: Jailbreak benchmarks test one checkpoint and treat which jailbreaks break it as a property of its pretraining data and safety training. We ask whether another pretraining run of the same data, given the same safety training, would break on the same jailbreaks. For each of 25 pretraining data recipes, we take 1B base models from 3 pretraining seeds and give each the same safety post-training with 2 post-training seeds, for 150 models in all. We then collect 20 responses from every model to a shared set of jailbreak prompts and correlate the per-prompt non-refusal rates between every pair of models. On average, two post-trained copies of the same pretraining run have per-prompt non-refusal rates that correlate at 0.984. A different pretraining seed lowers the correlation to 0.811, and a different data recipe lowers it only slightly further, to 0.779. These results indicate that which jailbreaks break a checkpoint depends much more on its pretraining run than on its data, a pattern that holds in all 25 data recipes and at 150M and 300M parameters. In practice, the best of 91 attack templates found on one checkpoint stays the best after a new pretraining seed in only 27% of model pairs, against 67% after a new post-training seed. Each pretraining run also leaves a fingerprint: across 3,211 prompts, a model's per-prompt non-refusal rates identify its pretraining run among all 75 runs every time, and a random subset of 50 prompts still does so 98% of the time.

papers.title: Early Selection of Polar Ensemble Decoding with Successive Cancellation Style Component Decoder
papers.abstract: Parallel ensembles of successive cancellation (SC)-style decoders improve error-rate performance by decoding multiple representations of the received vector. Conventional ensembles, however, keep every member active until completion. To reduce computational cost while retaining the diversity gain of ensemble decoding, we propose early ensemble selection (EES), which ranks members using intermediate decoding states and retains a prescribed numbers of members at each predefined selection stage. Within the EES framework, we propose two selection rules, namely path-metric-based selection (PM-EES) and neural-network-based selection (NN-EES). We analytically characterize the computational cost of EES through stage-dependent decoder log-likelihood ratio (LLR) update counts and provide an information-theoretically motivated criterion for choosing selection stages. Simulations on the \((128,64)\) extended BCH code and the \(\operatorname{RM}(4,8)\) code show that suitable selection schedules approach full-ensemble error-rate performance with fewer decoder LLR updates.

papers.title: EARS: Evidence-Aware Retrieval via Sound and Motion for Budgeted Video Reasoning
papers.abstract: Uniform frame sampling can miss brief evidence in sparse-event videos when the VLM sees only K frames. We propose EARS (Evidence-Aware Retrieval via Sound and motion), a training-free, query-free front-end that ranks frames using optical-flow motion and audio energy, then applies temporal non-maximum suppression for diversity. The evidence score alone has frame-level AP 0.39; used only to select frames for the VLM, EARS with temporal diversity reaches localization AP 0.94, compared with 0.88 under Uniform sampling. In the updated matched study, at K = 1 EARS reaches XD-subset F1 0.660 versus 0.614 for centered Uniform (the paired interval includes zero); earlier backbone studies use separate protocols. On mostly-silent UCF-Crime, however, EARS slightly trails Uniform. A single configuration is used across both benchmarks; the new controls do not repeat the original held-out search. EARS therefore targets low-budget videos whose salient evidence aligns with motion or audio; on dense narratives or stealthy events, uniform or semantic selection remains preferable, and cheap modality statistics cannot reliably route between them. Code: https://github.com/mikeslin-ir/EARS

authors.name: Shih-Yao Lin
authors.institution: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University

papers.title: Forecasting Associations, Not Interventions: A Preregistered Causal Audit of Covariate-Aware Time Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Covariate-aware time series foundation models (TSFMs) accept a future path for a control variable and return a forecast, inviting what-if queries. The query is interventional; the models are trained on observational data. We determine whether their answers are the conditional slope $\partial E[Y|X]$ or the interventional effect $\partial E[Y|do(X)]$, at three levels. Theory: a Bayes-optimal observational predictor answers interventional queries associationally unless the adjustment set is available and used; for in-context least squares we derive the resulting confounding gap -- a model's effect estimate under an observational minus under a randomized context -- in closed form, a parameter-free reference line. Behaviour: on a preregistered grid with exact counterfactual ground truth, Chronos-2, TiRex-2, TabPFN-TS and TimesFM-2.5 all track this line ($R^2$ 0.90-1.00) and respond more confounded than regression itself (slopes 1.3-1.8), on linear and nonlinear structural models. Pairs of models with identical observational laws prove this is not an identifiability limit: when the effect is identifiable, least squares recovers 100% of the true effect difference, Chronos-2 75%, TiRex-2 34%. Representation: linear probes decode the data-generating regime (94-96%) and the true effect ($R^2$ 0.7-0.9) from embeddings that the forecasts ignore. On two physical systems with randomized actuators, pretrained models under-respond by 2-5x and ignore in-window confounding. Minutes of interventional post-training on 3,000 synthetic series cut the gap by up to 83% and transfer outside the training prior. Its forecasting cost is a replay-distribution effect: replaying the model's own pretraining prior cuts it from +47% to +10% MASE, and with low-rank adaptation yields a recipe meeting the preregistered criterion over three seeds (52-61% gap reduction at +1-3% cost) while improving the DoTime benchmark.

papers.title: A Measure-Geometric Theory of Robustness in Machine Learning
papers.abstract: This paper develops a foundational measure-geometric theory of robustness in machine learning. Robustness is formulated as escape from a retained task state relative to a reference measure on a data-bearing manifold, a perturbation gauge, and an admissible realization mechanism. The theory distinguishes the structural possibility of escape on the reference manifold from its ambient realization under mechanism-dependent observable readouts, while placing both within a unified geometric account. It introduces a mesoscopic organization of escape geometry, through which vulnerable mass, finite-scale morphology, delivered progress, and branch coherence are characterized by explicit laws as linked but non-identical robustness phenomena. By recasting robustness as the geometric formation, organization, realization, and persistence of escape, the theory provides a structural basis for analysis beyond scalar criteria.

papers.title: Long-time action stability for perturbed KdV near finite-gap tori
papers.abstract: We prove action and spectral stability near finite-gap tori of the periodic Korteweg--de Vries equation under autonomous analytic Hamiltonian perturbations of size $\varepsilon$. The estimates are uniform over prescribed compact families, without small-amplitude or nonresonance assumptions, and allow nearby initial data with infinitely many open gaps. Assuming a strong solution and a uniform higher Sobolev bound on $[0,T_0/\varepsilon]$, we permit one-derivative loss in the perturbing Hamiltonian's normal gradient. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ and initial normal Birkhoff size $r_0$, the tangential action variations and weighted sum of normal actions are bounded by $C_\delta(r_0^2+\varepsilon^{2\delta})$, while the spectral-gap variation in $\ell^2$ is bounded by $C_\delta(r_0+\varepsilon^\delta)$, for every $0<\delta<1/4$. A key ingredient is coercivity of the negative Hessian of the nonlinear KdV Hamiltonian on the full $\ell^2$ action space at every finite-gap action. We combine this with resonance analysis and corrected action observables evaluated along the solution. The hypotheses are verified for several local and nonlocal Hamiltonian perturbations.

papers.title: State-specific perturbation theory for configuration interaction singles: Theoretical analysis, benchmarks, and improvement with size-intensive level shifts
papers.abstract: We recently proposed a state-specific second-order perturbation theory based on the configuration interaction singles (CIS) state, termed CIS(2). Here, we clarify its theoretical connections, assess the accuracy of its excitation energies in greater detail, and develop size-intensive level shifts to improve both accuracy and convergence of its amplitude equations. We first derive the MP2 structure of its working equations and show that our previously introduced Hybrid partition recovers CIS(D) when the ground-state Fock operator is used and the residual Fock action on the CIS reference is neglected. For this partition, an expanded benchmark shows that using the CIS-state Fock operator improves Rydberg and especially charge-transfer accuracy relative to CIS(D), while slightly worsening valence accuracy. We analyze how the hole and particle densities contribute to these changes in excitation energy, which differ among the classes. We then introduce size-intensive level shifts that preserve the ground-state correlation contribution of noninteracting fragments while leaving the ground-state MP2 energy unchanged. With appropriately calibrated parameters, these shifts improve overall accuracy and substantially accelerate convergence without increasing the formal scaling of the amplitude solve. Different optimal parameters for valence and Rydberg states reveal the limitations of a common parameter. The analysis further shows that shifting the contracted-triples block contributes markedly to the excitation-energy correction in addition to accelerating convergence.

papers.title: On the Upsilon invariant and the Baldwin-Vela-Vick b-invariant of fibered knots
papers.abstract: For a null-homologous fibered knot $K$ in a rational homology sphere, Baldwin and Vela-Vick define a refinement $b(K)$ of the Ozsv\'ath-Szab\'o contact invariant. We prove that if the Ozsv\'ath-Stipsicz-Szab\'o concordance invariant Upsilon has slope $\Upsilon'_K(t)=-g(K)$ for some $t\in[0,\frac{2}{n+1})$, where $g(K)$ is the genus of $K$, then $b(K)>n$. This extends a result of He, Hubbard, and the author on the Upsilon invariant and right-veering monodromies. We also prove that the knot Floer homology of a fibered knot in the $g(K)-b(K)$ Alexander grading is nonvanishing. As an application, we give many families of fibered cable knots whose $b(K)$ invariant grows arbitrarily large. Finally, we prove that if a monodromy of a fibered knot is neither right-veering nor left-veering, then the third-to-top term of knot Floer homology is nonvanishing.

papers.title: Accuracy and efficiency of compact foundation models for surface-water mapping during floods
papers.abstract: Pretrained Earth observation models may reduce the effort needed to map surface water, but their value depends on the alternative against which they are compared. We evaluated Prithvi-EO-2.0-Tiny using the 446 hand-labeled Sentinel-2 chips from 11 flood events in Sen1Floods11. A fine-tuned model, a frozen-encoder model, and an identical randomly initialized architecture were compared with a similarly sized U-Net, a larger Prithvi model, and spectral-index thresholds. Experiments varied the number of training chips, excluded events from model fitting, and measured computational cost and prediction reliability. With 252 training chips, U-Net achieved a water intersection-over-union (IoU) of 0.856 on the official test set, compared with 0.833 for fine-tuned Prithvi-Tiny. Pretraining improved the tiny transformer over random initialization by a reported 0.046 IoU with 25 training chips and 0.023 with 252 chips, but did not reverse the U-Net ranking. Across 11 event-exclusion evaluations, mean IoU was 0.768 for fine-tuned Prithvi-Tiny and 0.777 for U-Net; the paired interval included zero. Fine-tuned Prithvi-Tiny processed a 512x512-pixel chip in 16.1 ms on a GPU and 258 ms on a laptop CPU, compared with 30.6 and 665 ms for U-Net. Errors were concentrated near water boundaries, and high predictive entropy identified many, but not all, erroneous pixels. These results support a specific role for compact pretrained models: lower measured computational demand with competitive accuracy, rather than consistent superiority. Event-dependent performance, shared hyperparameter selection, and the distinction between observed water and newly inundated land delimit the conclusions.

papers.title: Asymptotic analysis of Dirichlet problems in supercritically perforated domains via quantification by torsional rigidity
papers.abstract: We study the Dirichlet problem $-\mathrm{div}(A^{\varepsilon}\nabla u^{\varepsilon}) = f$ on varying open sets $D^{\varepsilon}$, with uniformly elliptic coefficients $A^{\varepsilon}$, in the regime where the solutions vanish in the limit for every source. For periodically perforated domains, this is the supercritical regime. We show that the torsional rigidity $T(D^{\varepsilon})$ is the natural normalization: up to a subsequence, $u^{\varepsilon}/T(D^{\varepsilon})$ converges weakly as measures to $kf$ for every continuous source $f$, where $k$ is a nonzero finite measure independent of $f$, which we call the effective measure. The key ingredient is an estimate comparing $u^{\varepsilon}$ with the product of $f$ and the torsion function, whose rate depends on the domains only through $T(D^{\varepsilon})$. We also show that this rate is optimal. No structural assumption on the perforation is needed, and the results hold for relaxed Dirichlet problems. Every nonzero finite measure arises as an effective measure, so the continuity of the source cannot be dropped in general. For rougher sources, we characterize the convergence by a condition on the domains alone, expressed through their torsion functions or, equivalently, their Poincar\'{e} constants. We also prove that the effective measure is local, satisfies optimal two-sided bounds and is monotone with respect to the coefficients, and we study the role of the antisymmetric parts of the coefficients.

papers.title: Music of the Deep: An acoustic blueprint of sperm whale codas
papers.abstract: Sperm-whale codas are usually described by the number and timing of their clicks. Earlier acoustic studies showed that individual clicks and longer coda sequences contain additional organization. We ask how that organization compares with music, whose smaller sounds also form larger units and ordered sequences. We compare codas with performed violin music, drum grooves, and sung melodies. Their sequences resemble music in some measures of predictability, yet codas show a different relationship between the smaller sounds within a unit and the order of units across a sequence. This combination was not observed in the musical references tested. Coda timing also varies coherently and carries information about individual callers. The recordings show another striking property: broad, reproducible variation along acoustic dimensions associated with human ratings of emotion, with a range comparable to human audio in most eligible tests. These findings motivate an acoustic blueprint that describes natural codas beyond their click timing. Its importance is apparent in synthetic audio: WhAM produces recognizable coda-like recordings, yet the tested clips remain distinguishable from natural codas in five of six acoustic comparisons after strict matching. The blueprint provides a fuller way to study natural codas and to evaluate how faithfully synthetic recordings represent them.

papers.title: JIT-MPE: Just-in-Time Multi-Pitch Estimation under Output Deadlines
papers.abstract: Live pitch displays, score followers and accompaniment systems must know which pitches are sounding within tens of milliseconds, but instrument-agnostic multi-pitch estimation (MPE) has mainly been designed and evaluated offline. We present JIT-MPE, a causal MPE model of 86k parameters for mixed ensembles. It gives an immediate estimate of each 20 ms frame and re-estimates the same frame as 20, 40, 80 and 160 ms of further audio arrive, so that a live display can show pitches at once and then refine them. We score each output only at a deadline by which it can be computed from the audio that has arrived, on five development sets and four held-out sets evaluated only after all design choices were frozen. At a 50 ms deadline, which reads the update made with 40 ms of lookahead, JIT-MPE is significantly more accurate than five of six published offline MPE systems in 38 of 45 comparisons (15 of 20 on the held-out sets) and less accurate in only two, although these systems read the whole recording and all but one have 6 to 170 times as many parameters; the sixth, supervised on URMP, is higher on four of the nine sets. The deadline costs little: on the held-out sets, JIT-MPE at 50 ms is within $-1.27$ to $+0.60$ points of recording-level macro F1 of its own final output with 160 ms of lookahead and within $-2.08$ to $+0.79$ points of a bidirectional model of similar size. Waiting pays off where the immediate estimate is weakest: the update at 50 ms adds 1.7-3.6 points over it on the development data and three of the four held-out sets, and raises the recall of reference frames in the first 20 ms after a note onset from 9.8% to 38.4% on the held-out AAM set. The slowest measured frame takes at most 4.15 ms on one CPU thread. Code and trained weights are available at https://github.com/Frieve-A/jit-mpe.

authors.name: Yoshiyuki Kobayashi
authors.institution: National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology

papers.title: Fast Calibration of Generalized Posteriors via Dirichlet Reweighting
papers.abstract: While generalized Bayesian inference offers a principled approach to uncertainty quantification under general loss functions, its practical performance depends critically on the choice of the learning rate. Generalized posterior calibration, which selects the learning rate so that the resulting credible sets attain nominal frequentist coverage, is computationally intensive because it relies on repeated posterior sampling across bootstrap datasets and candidate learning rates. To overcome this practical difficulty, we propose a fast calibration method that combines Dirichlet-weighted bootstrap perturbations with importance sampling to estimate coverage while reducing the need for repeated posterior sampling. We further extend the framework to hierarchical models, where group-specific learning rates are calibrated and stabilized via shrinkage. Illustrative examples using quantile regression, support vector machines, and hierarchical Huber regression demonstrate that the proposed method substantially reduces computational cost while maintaining accurate calibration.

papers.title: On the transformation of unbounded convergent sequences by linear operators on Banach lattices
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a weak variant of the concept of unbounded Dunford-Pettis linear operators, which we call unbounded weak Dunford-Pettis operators. We investigate the properties of this new class, establish inclusion and coincidence results involving unbounded Dunford-Pettis operators, and examine its relationship with the class of unbounded absolutely weakly continuous operators.

papers.title: Asymptotic stability of transonic steady nozzle flows
papers.abstract: In the present article, we prove the nonlinear asymptotic stability of stationary solutions to the quasi-one-dimensional barotropic Euler equations in a finite-length nozzle with variable cross-sectional area $A(x)$. We consider all stationary flow configurations arising from subsonic inflow: flows that remain subsonic throughout the nozzle, flows that pass continuously through a sonic state and remain supersonic up to the exit, and flows that subsequently return to the subsonic regime through a stationary shock. We prove that all these stationary solutions are asymptotically stable with respect to sufficiently small perturbations. No smallness restrictions are imposed on the mass flux, the magnitude of $A_x$, or the prescribed exit pressure, provided that the corresponding stationary solution exists. The only geometrical assumptions are that $A_{xx}>0$ at a smooth subsonic--supersonic transition, and $A_x>0$ at a stationary supersonic--subsonic shock. To the best of our knowledge, this gives the first nonlinear asymptotic stability result for a stationary flow passing smoothly from the subsonic to the supersonic regime in a finite-length nozzle. The principal analytical difficulty is the degeneracy of the characteristic structure at the sonic point. We overcome this difficulty by coupling energy structures adapted respectively to the subsonic and supersonic regimes. This coupling provides the dissipation needed to control the smooth sonic transition, and when combined with the dynamics of the shock, yields a unified nonlinear stability framework for smooth and discontinuous transonic nozzle flows.

authors.name: Masashi Ohnawa
authors.institution: Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology

papers.title: Fair Division of Lotteries
papers.abstract: We study fair division of uncertain items, where the utility of each item is a random variable whose realization is observed only after the allocation is determined. This uncertainty creates a distinction between ex-ante fairness, evaluated before utilities are realized, and ex-post fairness, evaluated after realization. We examine to what extent these two notions are compatible. We first identify conditions under which ex-ante envy-free allocations maximize ex-post envy-freeness probability. These include two-agent instances where utilities toward the same item follow the same distribution from a convolution-power family. For an arbitrary number of agents, we establish analogous optimality results when the common generator is non-atomic or log-concave. Beyond convolution-power families, we derive approximation guarantees for ex-ante envy-free allocations relative to the optimal ex-post envy-freeness probability under log-concave or symmetric utilities. We also study the computational complexity of evaluating ex-post envy-freeness probabilities, establishing hardness results as well as pseudo-polynomial-time algorithms.

papers.title: The Undecidability of FO3 and the Calculus of Relations with Just One Binary Relation
papers.abstract: The validity problem for first-order logic is a well-known undecidable problem. The undecidability also holds even for $\mathsf{FO}3$ and (equational formulas of) the calculus of relations. In this paper we tighten these undecidability results to the following: (1) $\mathsf{FO}3$ with just one binary relation is undecidable even without equality; and (2) the calculus of relations with just one character and with only composition, union, and complement is undecidable. Additionally we prove that the finite validity problem is also undecidable for the above two classes.

papers.title: Seeing Through Distractions: Context-Stable Attribution via the Least Core
papers.abstract: Shapley-value-based explanations are widely used for feature attribution in machine learning. However, in computer vision, a feature may reduce the target-class score when added to the complete genuine image, even when the predicted label remains unchanged. We formalize such features as contextual distractors and investigate their attributions under semivalues and the least core. Under a weak average marginal monotonicity assumption, we derive quantitative semivalue--least-core gap bounds and sufficient conditions based on the probability of sampling smaller contexts. We further show that shifting semivalue weights toward larger contexts decreases the signed gap. Finally, controlled image-classification experiments and evaluations on Salient ImageNet provide strong empirical support for our theoretical findings.

papers.title: An $O(n^{0.1537})$-Coloring Algorithm for 3-Colorable Graphs
papers.abstract:
We present a polynomial-time randomized algorithm that colors every $n$-vertex $3$-colorable graph with $O(n^{0.1537})$ colors. This improves upon the previous bound of $O(n^{0.1954})$ colors by Bansal, Huang, and Lee (SODA '27).
  To achieve this result, we introduce a new algorithmic framework for finding a large independent set from a solution to the vector coloring SDP. Combined with the (combinatorial) dense-progress algorithm of Kawarabayashi, Thorup, and Yoneda (STOC '24), this framework yields an $n^{1/6 + o(1)}$-coloring algorithm. Furthermore, we strengthen the SDP-based algorithm specifically for 3-colorable graphs to achieve $O(n^{0.1537})$ colors.

papers.title: GKZ Systems and Gauss-Manin Connections of Families of Projective Hypersurfaces
papers.abstract: Periods of projective hypersurfaces satisfy GKZ hypergeometric systems, which may have solutions that do not arise as periods. For deformations of Fermat hypersurfaces, we describe the Gauss-Manin connection in terms of images of contiguity operators between GKZ systems. These images are also realized as Fourier transforms of minimal extensions of Kummer modules.

authors.name: Ryo Negishi
authors.institution: Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology

papers.title: Boundary-condition independence of infinite-chain ground states in the $S=1$ $J$-$D$ antiferromagnetic chain
papers.abstract:
Extending the analytic machinery and using the numerical inputs from OpenAI's proofs of the Haldane gap, we study infinite-chain ground states of the $S=1$ $J$-$D$ antiferromagnetic model $H=\sum_j\{\boldsymbol S_j\cdot\boldsymbol S_{j+1}+D(S_j^{\mathrm z})^2\}$ for sufficiently small $|D|$. We consider two finite-volume settings: periodic chains with an even number of sites, and open chains with an odd number of sites and the same positive magnetic field in the $\mathrm z$ direction at both endpoints. We prove that the ground states in each setting have an infinite-chain limit along the full sequence, without passing to a subsequence, and that the two limiting states coincide. Convergence is uniform in $D$ on a fixed neighborhood of zero. The common limit is a symmetric locally-unique gapped ground state, and its local expectation values depend continuously on $D$. These conclusions concern the two specified constructions, not uniqueness among all infinite-chain ground states. They provide the input for the study of a topological phase transition in a forthcoming revision of our companion paper.
  The author formulated the problem and proposed the basic strategy. ChatGPT Astra made substantial contributions to the inductive estimates and to completing the proof.

papers.title: Scott-type inequalities for trinomial $h^*$-polynomials
papers.abstract:
Motivated by Scott's inequality for lattice polygons, we study normalized volume bounds for lattice polytopes $\mathcal{P}$ with $h^*$-polynomials $1+at^k+bt^\ell$, where $a,b\ge1$ and $1\le k<\ell$. For $\ell>2k$, the coefficients satisfy $a+1\le b$, and consequently ${\rm vol}(\mathcal{P})\le2b$. In the complementary range $k<\ell\le2k$, we establish the dimension-independent bound \[
  {\rm vol}(\mathcal{P})\le(2b+1)(k+\ell). \] On the boundary $\ell=2k$ with $b\ge2$, the sharper Scott-type inequality ${\rm vol}(\mathcal{P})\le4k(b+1)$ holds, confirming a conjecture of Higashitani, Nill, and the author. Equality holds if and only if $k=1$ and $a=3b+3$. Moreover, when $\ell=2k$ and $k,b\ge2$, we obtain an upper bound depending only on $b$.

papers.title: Do AI-for-Science Agents Preserve Model Safety?
papers.abstract: AI-for-Science agents are increasingly being used for formulating scientific hypotheses, running autonomous experiments, and interpreting evidence. These agents are constructed by integrating a large language model (LLM) into a domain-specific agent harness, which in turn can improve the LLM's scientific capability and enable the model to orchestrate scientific tools. In this work, we ask whether model safety is preserved when an LLM is integrated in an AI-for-Science agent harness. We evaluate five agent harnesses on 50 harmful chemistry requests. Specifically, we study how the safety behavior changes under direct prompting, two simple adversarial prompting strategies, and an adaptive attack. Across four recent GPT variants, our results show that the agent harness can increase harmful compliance even under direct prompting. More critically, we find that adaptive attacks that are largely unsuccessful against the base LLM suddenly become highly successful after the agent harness is introduced. Our results show that the safety behavior of the base LLM is not durable once a harness is introduced. Thus, as AI-for-Science agents become more capable and autonomous, the community needs to evaluate and align the agent using domain-specific safety benchmarks.

papers.title: Initial Data Gluing for Asymptotically Hyperbolic Spacetimes
papers.abstract: We give a new proof of Corvino-Schoen-type gluing, also known as gluing up to linear obstructions, for asymptotically hyperbolic spacetimes satisfying appropriate smallness conditions in arbitrary dimension. The results retrieve and improve on previous known smallness requirements on initial data to conduct such gluing, including the work of Chrusci\'el and Delay. Our technique is highly versatile and well-suited for gluing results in highly anisotropic geometric settings.

papers.title: EVM-Anchored Provenance for AI-Assisted Code Evolution: A Smoke-Scale Deployment Report
papers.abstract: We report a smoke-scale deployment of an EVM-anchored provenance framework for the state stream produced by AI-assisted code generation. The system comprises codebase-state-manager, an open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) server (MIT, v0.2.1) that exposes codebase state, transition, and reward operations to any MCP-compatible assistant, and CodebaseStateRegistry, a Solidity contract deployed on Base Sepolia that emits per-state commitment events. Payloads are pinned to the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) and indexed through a rebuildable SQLite mirror that resynchronizes by replaying contract events. We delimit precisely what anchoring does and does not attest (existence, ordering, and non-equivocation by the committer key; never truthfulness or fabrication-prevention) and outline the orthogonal supply-chain controls required to close that gap. Under an author-produced synthetic workload on a local Anvil simulator, the median commit costs 103,282 gas, modeled at US$0.0018-0.0035 in rollup fees per commit (US$17.9-34.8 per 10,000 states), and simulator latency for the create operation is 539.8 ms (p50) and 725.0 ms (p95) under loopback storage and instant mining. The live deployment holds 14 StateCommitted events verifiable on-chain; the last consumed 98,977 gas at 1 gwei (about US$0.30). All empirical figures are descriptive quantiles from a single author run; no testnet latency is reported, and no claim of superiority is made against any baseline. A receipts-trie consumption mechanism, a BountyEscrow use case, and a FAIR-aligned dataset publication pattern are specified as outlook and are not implemented. A property-by-property comparison against OpenTimestamps, Sigstore Rekor, Centrifuge AnchorRegistry, in-toto/SLSA, Radicle, and Lalli et al. places this work relative to the surrounding provenance landscape.

papers.title: ElevateHead: Decide Once, Then Commit: When the Action Head Matters for Multimodal Imitation
papers.abstract: Robots that learn from people often see several valid ways to do the same task: pass an obstacle on the left or on the right, open the microwave or move the kettle first. A policy that re-decides at every step can waver between these ways mid-task. We ask when the action head (the part of a policy that turns the state into actions) matters, and how it should make this choice. On a controlled task, heads that sample one way succeed far more often than a head that averages the ways when the demonstrations contain several ways and the state gives no hint which to take (+0.72 success with two ways); this trend was not reproduced on the other tasks we ran. We then present ElevateHead, a head that decides once at a learned decision point, commits to that choice for the episode, and exposes the choice as an input a user can set. We designed it by diagnosis: each version was frozen and tested on tasks it had not seen, and the next version changed only what a measured failure pointed to; predictions were registered before each run. The first four versions each fell below BeT on at least one held-out task. The fifth completed all four subtasks of the held-out Franka Kitchen task in 45.2% of episodes against 29.3% for BeT, the strongest baseline across our tasks (+0.160, 95% CI [+0.129, +0.188]); when a mode was forced, the first completed subtask matched it in 95% of successful episodes. Diagnosis also located where commitment breaks: varied start positions (repaired on the controlled task: commitment 0.22 to 0.81, success 0.74 to 0.91) and varied object placement (partly repaired: in an exploratory variant, commitment 0.03 to 0.59 on aligning with no detectable change in success). On held-out block stacking, version 4 was comparable to BeT and did not exceed it. A real-robot test with predictions fixed in advance is planned for a follow-up version of this paper.

papers.title: Cut a Wall, See a Wall: Identity Substitution in Occluded Point-Cloud Perception for Construction Robots
papers.abstract: Construction robots must label building elements they can only partly see. We show that when occlusion at test time removes whole regions of a scene, rather than parts of an object as in training, point-cloud segmentation networks do not simply miss the hidden elements: they relabel them, and the errors collapse onto a single sink class. With fixed synthetic layouts the column absorbs up to 70% of all test points; with randomized layouts the sink moves to the stair, predicted at 4.5-5.4x its true share across three training seeds. Baseline mIoU falls to 0.15-0.27 (fixed) and 0.36-0.72 (randomized), and up to 269 whole objects vanish in a single test set. Appending 14 hand-computed geometric features per point (GPE) restores mIoU to 0.54-0.92 and removes 64-100% of whole-object losses in every run, for PointNet++ and a PTv3-style transformer in both layout regimes; on real S3DIS scans it removes every whole-wall loss (10 to 0). In an as-built column check computed from the predictions, GPE raises the share of correctly checked views from 17-58% to 71-92%. Feature permutation on fixed, randomized and real scenes explains the pattern: each class relies on whichever cue is stable in its training data, position for height-banded slabs and beams, intrinsic shape for walls and stairs once their position varies. Occlusion augmentation is a strong alternative on mIoU, but in every setting it loses more whole objects than GPE (e.g., 25-35 vs. 0).

papers.title: Symplectic capacities and Weyl laws from Abelian Higgs min max theory
papers.abstract:
For a Hermitian line bundle $E\to Y$ over a Riemannian manifold $(Y^n,g)$, the self-dual Abelian--Higgs energy is defined by $
  \En^Y_{\eps,g}(u,a)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_Y
  \left(|\nabla_a u|_g^2+\eps^2|F_a|_g^2+
  \frac{(1-|u|^2)^2}{4\eps^2}\right)dV_g, $
where $u$ is a smooth section of $E$, $a$ is a unitary connection, and $F_a$ is its curvature. Pigati and Stern studied the energy as a codimension-two analogue of the Allen--Cahn energy to study minimal submanifolds in a Riemannian manifold.
  In this paper, we use this functional to define a nondecreasing sequence of symplectic capacities $\{c_k^{\AH}\}_{k\ge1}$ in dimension four by a min--max construction. In particular, we prove that $c_1^{\AH}$ is normalized on the ball and the cylinder. For the upper bound on the cylinder, we combine Gromov's theory of families of $J$-holomorphic spheres with Taubes's planar vortex. For the lower bound on the ball, we use the properties of the Abelian--Higgs theory developed by Pigati--Stern, together with a geometric estimate on smooth approximations to the double of the ball and an equivariant deformation of low energy sublevels. These estimates give the normalization without Seiberg--Witten theory.
  We then use Seiberg--Witten moduli spaces on $\CP^2$ and $S^2\times S^2$ to prove an upper bound on the higher capacities of balls and the formula $c_k^{\AH}(Z^4(a),\omega_0)=ka$. We also prove Euclidean Weyl laws for the capacity sequence and for the min--max sequence with the standard Euclidean metric. For these results, we construct AH sweepouts from moduli spaces of the solutions to the perturbed Seiberg--Witten equations.

papers.title: Keep your eye on the tank: A fresh look at an accelerating frame demonstration
papers.abstract: A water tank sliding down a frictionless ramp is a classic example of an accelerated reference frame. Along with other accelerated frames, Bartlett analyzed frictionless sliding, and showed that the liquid's surface is parallel to the surface of the ramp, rather than the base. Duzen and coworkers used liquid in an accelerating tank to help students explore motion, noting that the ramp case and riding on a cart accelerated by a hanging mass are equivalent. Munera used the second as a lecture demonstration. In both Refs. 2 and 3, students viewed accelerating tanks from the lab frame, which may be hard to observe at a distance. As the goal of these demonstrations is to understand the effects of the acceleration in the tank frame, tank-frame observations would be beneficial. Following Krulj and Slisko, a camera was mounted to an accelerated object to make in-frame videos of liquid-based equivalence principle demonstrations. Previous work did not quantify the actual acceleration of the tank; use of a Smart Cart simplifies this measurement.

papers.title: Planetesimal Delivery to Giant Planet Circumplanetary Disks: Bulk Ice Enrichment and an Ice-rich Iapetus
papers.abstract: The regular satellites of Jupiter and Saturn are substantially enriched in ice relative to the rock-rich solids of the outer Solar System. In addition, the satellites interior to Titan and distant Iapetus are icier than Titan itself. Collisional processes and subsequent migration can readily alter compositions deep in the planetary potential well, but producing a distant, ice-rich satellite with Iapetus's radius of about 700 km is a challenge \citep{mosqueira2026a}. We show that differential ablation and capture of icy and rocky fragments from differentiated outer Solar System bodies can explain the bulk Jovian and Kronian satellite ice enrichment and supply the substantial ice-rich inventory needed for Iapetus. For 1\,m--1\,km fragments with the canonical size-distribution index \(p=3.5\) and a source containing 30\% ice by mass, the fixed radial distance Saturn calculation deposits material with ice fractions of 0.66 (delivery of vapor-only rock) or 0.50 (with retained rock melt) at 20 Saturn radii and nearly pure ice at 60 Saturn radii. Following three-dimensional trajectories over repeated passages through the pressure-supported gas gives ice fractions of about 0.4 near 20 Saturn radii and 0.9 near 60 Saturn radii. The matching Jupiter calculation yields a similar bulk ice enrichment, with a corresponding compositional gradient across the Galilean satellite region. These delivery profiles supply ice-enriched material for satellite formation. Yet satellitesimal inward migration subsequently modifies the material incorporated into satellites and thus alters their bulk compositions. We briefly discuss the implications for the PDS~70 planetary system.

papers.title: Combinatorial models for Quasicrystals and Schur-Weyl Duality
papers.abstract: Quasicrystals were defined by Cain and Malheiro and Maas-Gari\'epy to model the decomposition of Schur polynomials into fundamental quasisymmetric functions. We define a new combinatorial model for crystal graphs of type $A_{n-1}$, called parsed content words, for which the decomposition into quasicrystals is particularly evident. We use the model to describe a combinatorial interpretation of Schur-Weyl duality and recover the classical combinatorial proof of the well-known expansion of homogeneous symmetric functions into Schur functions within our framework.

papers.title: Interaction of Strong X-mode Waves with Magnetized Pair Plasmas
papers.abstract: The interaction of strong ($a_0>1$), superluminal X-mode electromagnetic waves with magnetized pair plasma falls into two regimes set by $\varepsilon_{\rm B}\equiv a_0\omega_{\rm B}/\omega_0$, the ratio of the wave strength parameter to its frequency, in units of cyclotron frequency. For $\varepsilon_{\rm B}<1$ the wave propagates until induced scattering disrupts it. Using analytical theory and kinetic simulations, we show that the background magnetic field introduces a restoring frequency $\Omega_{\rm B}$ to scattering; when $\Omega_{\rm B}$ exceeds the scattering rate, the unattenuated length grows from $\simeq\varepsilon_{\rm p}^{-2/3}$ to $\simeq\varepsilon_{\rm B}^{1/2}/\varepsilon_{\rm p}$ wavelengths ($\varepsilon_{\rm p}\equiv a_0\omega_{\rm p}/\omega_0$; $\omega_{\rm p}$ is the plasma frequency). When $a_0^2>\varepsilon_{\rm B}>1$, the plasma current is nonlinear, and the wave is damped while riding a motional electric field, so one half-cycle appears attenuated. This framework has implications for the duration of fast radio bursts and whether they can escape their surroundings.
