papers.title: Double KV Cache Optimization on Apple Silicon: Block-FP4, Radial Quantization, and Fused Metal Kernels
papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) cache capacity and memory traffic are primary bottlenecks in long-context autoregressive inference. We evaluate five cache paths on an Apple Silicon M5 Max using MLX: a native bf16 baseline, block-scaled E2M1 FP4, a Python reference implementing radial quantization with a QJL-style residual, sequential FP4-to-Polar composition, and a fused Metal Polar kernel. On Apple Silicon M5 Max, fused Metal PolarQuant achieves 46.8 tok/s at 3,456 B/token - 3.64x compression versus the bf16 baseline and 1.84x faster than the Python Polar reference (25.4 tok/s), while slightly outperforming block-FP4 (41.5 tok/s at 3.62x compression). Sequential composition of FP4 and Polar (Double Optimization) yields no additive benefit: 4,241 B/token at 15.1 tok/s, worse than FP4 alone on both axes. The fused path establishes that radial coding can be competitive when packing, rotation, and reconstruction are placed in one device kernel, but this result does not extend to longer contexts. At 32K and above, all compressed variants collapse to 1.5-14 tok/s because the current attention path repeatedly reconstructs the full cache, retaining cumulative O(N^2) decode work. At 64K, the Metal variant runs out of memory when a 33.5 GB allocation exceeds MLX's 22.6 GB Metal buffer limit. Fused scaled dot-product attention operating directly on compressed KV, together with chunked pre-allocation, is required for long-context viability. These results separate representation-level compression from kernel and allocator effects and identify the conditions under which low-bit KV caching helps on unified memory hardware.
papers.intro:
Autoregressive Transformer inference reuses the key and value tensors produced for earlier tokens. This KV cache avoids recomputing the entire prefix at every generation step, but its capacity grows linearly with sequence length and batch size. The cache is read repeatedly during decoding, so its footprint is also a bandwidth cost rather than merely a storage cost. Analytical and empirical studies of Transformer serving identify this state as a central constraint on long-context inference [14]. Multi-query attention reduces the number of key/value heads [15], and grouped-query attention interpolates between multi-head and multi-query designs [1], yet large contexts still leave substantial persistent state.

KV compression addresses the remaining state without changing model weights. The design space includes scalar and group-wise quantization, sparse outlier retention, token eviction, cross-layer sharing, geometric transforms, and compressed-domain attention. These approaches make different tradeoffs. A compact representation can save memory but lose throughput if every decode step reconstructs the entire cache. Conversely, a specialized kernel can make a less compact layout faster by avoiding framework dispatch, intermediate tensors, and repeated format conversion. The representation and the consuming attention kernel therefore have to be evaluated together.

papers.title: Radial reduction, spherical splitting and root counts for two-sided quaternionic polynomials
papers.abstract:
We study quaternionic polynomials whose coefficients may occur on both sides of the variable, using their degree in the four real coordinates. Such polynomials can have no roots, or many more isolated roots than their degree. A simple root has an invertible real derivative, and its sign is the sign of that derivative's determinant.
  For a radial family, the roots over a non-real target reduce to one real equation. We obtain a sharp root bound and follow a change in the signed root count as roots escape to infinity.
  The main results concern spherical root sets for which the polynomial derivative is invertible in the two normal directions. Under a small polynomial perturbation, a sphere splits into simple roots corresponding to the zeros of a tangent vector field, when the derivative of that field is invertible at every zero. We obtain a sharp bound in terms of the perturbation degree and a signed count of two or of minus two.
  For even degrees, the construction yields polynomials with a single leading power and lower-degree terms whose simple root counts, divided by the fourth power of the degree, tend to one as the degree grows. An explicit quartic has 132 simple roots, and this count persists under small coefficient perturbations. For gradient perturbations, the roots correspond to equilibrium directions of an energy on the sphere. This correspondence gives energy thresholds for root disappearance and bounds the critical directions of polynomial orientation profiles in diffusion magnetic resonance imaging.

papers.title: Wave propagation analysis for a second strain gradient rod theory
papers.abstract: In this work, an enriched model describing the longitudinal wave propagation is established based on Mindlin's Second Strain Gradient (SSG) theory, which can describe the heterogeneity caused by the micro-structure interactions in the frame of continuum mechanics. The governing equation and associated boundary conditions are derived based on Hamilton's principle, then the dispersion relation of non-classical longitudinal wave together with the extra-waves appearing exclusively in SSG theory model are investigated. The investigations are based on the modal density, energy flow, and forced response of the rod. Wave transmission and reflection through planar interfaces based on the proposed model have been calculated. Finally, the results of the enriched model are well interpreted by comparing with the classical theory results, and some useful conclusions are derived on the SSG theory based model in the wave propagation characterization.

papers.title: Non-Induced Representations in Characteristic Zero
papers.abstract: This paper explores the failure of induction from all proper subgroups to generate the full representation ring, measured by a quotient group $Q_k(G)$. We extend existing results for cyclic groups to all finite abelian groups and calculate this quotient for all finite groups over fields of characteristic 0 by reducing to the abelian case. We briefly discuss extensions to positive characteristics via modular representation theory. Finally, we detail our result for certain well-known families of groups.

papers.title: Chemistry-resolved disagreement between Materials Project-compatible PBE(+U) and r2SCAN stability verdicts in the GNoME materials database
papers.abstract:
GNoME's stability labels rest on a Materials Project-compatible GGA/GGA+U workflow. Its authors report that 84% of discovered binaries and ternaries retain a negative decomposition energy under r2SCAN and 86.8% of tested quaternaries remain stable on the r2SCAN hull. We resolve that aggregate by chemistry over the 139,541 GNoME materials released with r2SCAN recomputations, a subset the dataset authors selected rather than sampled, using cluster bootstrap intervals over 8,429 structural-prototype proxy clusters.
  The aggregate conceals a 26.7-point spread at fixed element count, from 4.0% [3.3, 4.7] for plain quaternary intermetallics (no lanthanide, no 3d metal) to 30.7% [27.7, 33.8] for lanthanide-free 3d-containing quaternary oxides, a pair identified post hoc against a prospectively fixed threshold. Under our reading of the release's "All" reference set the two cells sit at 14.5% and 37.4%, preserving a 22.9-point spread. Presence of a Materials Project Hubbard-U-list element is strongly associated with disagreement, conditional on the other covariates, in a model over all 139,541 materials (cluster-robust odds ratio 3.45 [3.13, 3.80]). Neither selective U application nor hull proximity explains the association away: disagreement stays elevated outside the U-treated regime, and a natural cubic spline in the continuous PBE decomposition energy moves the odds ratio in the 117,018-material model only from 3.53 to 3.43 [3.07, 3.83]. For allocating a verification budget, composition supplements hull proximity rather than replacing it: over held-out cluster splits at a 20% budget, the two together surface 45.8% of disagreements against 40.4% for hull distance alone. An exploratory comparison against previously catalogued materials changes direction between populations. We measure disagreement between two workflows, not accuracy.

papers.intro:
Computational materials discovery has shifted from enumerating candidates to generating them. GNoME (Graph Networks for Materials Exploration) reported 381,000 new entries on the convex hull, the surface of lowest formation energy below which a composition has no cheaper decomposition into competing phases, for a total of 421,000 stable crystals (Merchant et al., 2023); subsequent releases, which widened the release criterion from the documented on-hull tolerance of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} eV/atom to within 1 meV/atom of the hull (Google DeepMind, 2023), brought the public summary file to 554,054 entries (our row count). Generative models such as MatterGen (Zeni et al., 2025) and expanded databases such as Alexandria have followed, the latter’s PBEsol/SCAN subset (Schmidt et al., 2022) using PBEsol geometries with SCAN energies rather than PBE. GNoME’s own stability verdicts, which are what this paper analyses, rest on density functional theory (DFT) calculations at the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) level (Perdew et al., 1996), executed in VASP (Kresse and Furthmüller, 1996) with Materials Project (MP)-compatible settings (Jain et al., 2013), including a Hubbard UU for eight transition metals in oxides and fluorides and the Materials Project 2020 (MP2020) correction scheme’s empirical anion and GGA/GGA+UU mixing corrections (Wang et al., 2021). The functional and correction choices differ across MatterGen, Alexandria and GNoME, so the question we ask of GNoME does not transfer to the others unchanged.

GGA formation energies carry errors of order 0.1 eV/atom (Kirklin et al., 2015), but formation-energy errors do not directly determine stability-verdict disagreement, because a decomposition energy compares a material against composition-conserving combinations of competing phases rather than against an elemental reference. We therefore analyse the released decomposition-energy outcomes directly. The need for chemistry resolution is practical: a laboratory choosing which predicted compound to attempt cannot act on an aggregate error rate, a database maintainer deciding where to spend a finite recomputation budget faces the same problem at scale, and aggregate benchmark scores against PBE-derived labels (Riebesell et al., 2025) do not show how sensitivity to the workflow varies across chemistry.

GNoME’s authors anticipated the question. They recomputed a subset with the r2SCAN meta-GGA, the regularised-restored form of the SCAN functional (Furness et al., 2020), and reported that 84% of discovered binaries and ternaries retain negative phase-separation energies (their term for the decomposition energy), with 86.8% of tested quaternaries remaining stable on the r2SCAN hull (Merchant et al., 2023). Supplementary Note 2 of that paper observes that the discrepancy concentrates near the hull and that the same effect appears in the Materials Project and the Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD), but gives no breakdown by chemistry. The authors released the underlying r2SCAN data with the statement that it is provided “expectantly serving as a foundation for analysing discrepancies between functional choices.”

We measure disagreement between two computational methods: a material released as stable at the PBE level whose r2SCAN decomposition energy is positive (defined precisely in Section 3.4). We do not establish which functional is closer to the truth for any material, and we say nothing about whether these compounds are stable in reality. We therefore use the term flip throughout and avoid calling flipped labels “incorrect”. Where we discuss practical consequences the operative quantity is the share of labels a higher-fidelity recomputation would revise, which is a statement about what the expensive calculation would say, not about nature. This constrains every claim that follows, including the budget model of Section 4.12, whose payoff is measured in disagreements surfaced rather than errors corrected.

papers.title: Ampe-DB: A Dataset for Human Activity and Interaction Analysis Using the Ghanaian Game Ampe
papers.abstract:
Human activity recognition benchmarks underrepresent culturally situated forms of movement and interaction. We introduce Ampe-DB, a multimodal dataset based on Ampe, a traditional Ghanaian game involving coordinated jumping, leg movements, and two-person interaction. It contains 637 canonical clips from 15 participants, with RGB video, two-person pose representations, participant and pair metadata, four-class movement labels, and derived binary movement-relation labels.
  We evaluate four-class movement recognition and binary movement-relation classification using three protocols: a duplicate-safe fixed benchmark, four-fold pair-held-out evaluation, and participant-held-out diagnostics for participants with complete class coverage. Baselines comprise a frozen Kinetics-400-pretrained R(2+1)D-18 RGB encoder, a two-layer bidirectional GRU for pose sequences, and validation-selected RGB-pose late fusion.
  For four-class recognition, RGB macro-F1 falls from 0.955 on the fixed benchmark to 0.418 under pair-held-out evaluation and 0.384 under participant-held-out evaluation. Pose is more robust, achieving 0.957, 0.811, and 0.839 across the same protocols. Fusion reaches 0.976 on the fixed benchmark and 0.824 under pair-held-out evaluation, but does not consistently improve on pose under participant shift. Binary movement-relation recognition also becomes substantially harder under held-out evaluation, especially for different-leg configurations.
  These findings show that strong fixed-benchmark scores can mask failures to generalize across people and pairings. Ampe-DB supports research on fine-grained movement recognition, human-human interaction, multimodal learning, and identity-aware generalization.

papers.title: Deletion, Substitution, Repair and Transplant: Component Attribution in BARBICAN, a Layered Prompt-Injection Gateway for MCP
papers.abstract: A neural classifier can fail completely inside a layered defense without any end-to-end number moving. We demonstrate this on BARBICAN, a fail-closed gateway for language-model tool mediation whose arbitration stage spent an entire recorded evaluation receiving text mangled by a misconfigured tokenizer. Correcting the misconfiguration lifts that stage's corpus-wide area under the ROC curve (AUC) from 0.392 to 0.855 and pushes system recall down, from 80.67% to 80.34%; a stub that answers "malicious" scores 80.77%, higher than either. The reason emerges once the stage's input distribution is examined: upstream routing hands it a band that is 96.82% malicious, and the enforcement design lets an incriminating verdict block while an exculpating one releases an input only through one narrow branch. Yet deleting it costs 673 detections. Substituting its verdict with a constant instead moves between 12 and 140 of 25,000 decisions. Transplanted into the arbitration stage, an off-the-shelf classifier that separates the band's inputs at an AUC of 0.916 changes 16 of 25,000 decisions. Measured against such detectors with operating points chosen away from the test data, the gateway leads on its own benchmark distribution and falls behind once that distribution changes. In our earlier gateway, the review model's band is 92.94% malicious and a constant verdict is as accurate as the review model. We argue that an ablation figure for any routed stage is unreadable without the class balance of the band that stage receives, and that deletion experiments need substitution experiments beside them.

papers.intro:
Language models increasingly act rather than only answer, and interfaces such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) have made that routine. The exposure this creates is structural: whatever a tool returns enters the model’s context as text, and text in context is instruction-shaped. A retrieved document, a code comment or an error message can carry directives that the model has no reliable basis for distinguishing from its principal’s own. Defenses against this have converged on a recognizable shape—deterministic rules dispose of the obvious cases, a semantic layer catches paraphrase, an expensive neural or LLM arbitrator adjudicates what survives, and a fail-closed default blocks whatever remains unresolved.

Each of those stages costs latency, memory or an inference call, so a layered defense must eventually say which of them earns its place. The standard instrument is ablation by deletion: switch a layer off, re-run the benchmark, attribute the drop in detection to the layer removed—an experiment one recent gateway describes as a component ablation that “isolates each layer’s contribution” [17]. Isolation is the claim worth examining. In a cascade a stage is not an independent module but a position, defined by the routing rule that decides what reaches it and by the policy that disposes of what it leaves unresolved; switching the stage off removes all three at once, and the resulting drop is their joint contribution, reported as one component’s. Outside security the point is settled—zero-ablation can overstate a neural component’s importance several-fold, because it moves the network off the data manifold rather than removing a function [23], and statisticians made the corresponding argument about dropped covariates earlier [33, 34]—yet deletion remains the convention by which layered defenses report what their layers contribute.

BARBICAN is such a system—a fail-closed gateway mediating MCP tool calls, developed within our own research group and renamed here so that it and its artifacts can be cited under a single stable identifier. Its recorded evaluation, 88.26%88.26\% accuracy over a balanced benchmark of 25,000 prompts, is logged in the artifact manifest of the code revision we re-execute, and our control run reproduces its confusion matrix sample for sample [22]; every measurement below is a departure from it. We regard our authorship of the system as a condition of the study rather than as a caveat: the interventions that follow require the source, the configuration history and the audit trail, together with a willingness to publish what they turn up, and an outside evaluator would have had none of the first three and every incentive to avoid the fourth.

The 4.8-fold discrepancy is not a measurement artifact but a consequence of what each operation removes: deletion takes the band out of review, so that the fail-closed rule covering unresolved reviews no longer applies and a looser release rule for allowed inputs does, and the detections lost belong mostly to that change. Both operations lose their detections through releases with weak residual evidence, so the size of the discrepancy depends on how those releases are enforced (Section 5.4).

Cascades are built so that expensive stages see little traffic, and the traffic they do see is not a random sample: it is what the earlier layers could neither clear nor condemn. The enforcement path compounds this asymmetrically: a verdict of “malicious” ends in a block, by escalation or by the fail-closed rule, while a verdict of “benign” is checked against further conditions before it may release anything, and with the gateway’s own semantic scores those conditions almost never pass: never in the control, 12 times in 7,453 when every verdict is forced benign. With those scores the stage’s output is close to a one-way signal, able to add blocks and nearly unable to remove them. Under these two conditions an arbitrator can gain little over a constant, whatever its quality, and accuracy converts into lost coverage rather than into avoided false positives; the ceiling limits what it can gain, not what it can lose (Section 5.12).

papers.title: Holo-NN: Holographic Nearest Neighbor Search via Compressive Sensing
papers.abstract:
In the age of AI, privacy-preserving approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search over high-dimensional embeddings has emerged as a critical yet frustratingly challenging domain, dominated by tradeoffs between speed, privacy, and accuracy. Traditional tree and graph-based indexing structures (e.g., HNSW, ScaNN) rely fundamentally on non-linear operations that are computationally intractable under Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) or blind server-side constraints.
  In this paper, we introduce Holo-NN (Holographic Nearest Neighbor Search), an algebraic framework that replaces data-dependent branching with a single linear projection. Our key observation is that while distances across a database are dense, neighborhood membership is inherently sparse: only a handful of points ever lie close to a query. By pairing locality-preserving feature transforms with Compressive Sensing, Holo-NN folds the entire database offline into a compact holographic sensing matrix. At query time, encrypted search reduces to a single, non-interactive matrix-vector multiplication---requiring no FHE bootstrapping, no multi-round interaction, and no client-side index state. This turns private retrieval into an embarrassingly parallel, accuracy-tunable computation that runs out of the box on both CPUs and GPUs, scaling efficiently to production databases. We offer a comparison against other state-of-the-art Private ANN algorithms to help situate the method in the broader context of production-grade private retrieval.
papers.intro:
Published in 1750, Cramer’s rule [19] established an exceptionally inefficient and computationally intensive method for solving systems of linear equations based on an exhaustive calculation of determinants. And yet, despite its inefficiency, it introduced an embarrassingly parallel mathematical primitive that modern high-throughput computational hardware can execute with extreme efficiency.

And yet, despite its inefficiency, it introduced an embarrassingly parallel mathematical primitive that modern high-throughput computational hardware can execute with extreme efficiency.

A similar paradigm shift governs modern privacy-preserving computation. The constraints imposed by fully end-to-end secure computation—such as Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) and Private Information Retrieval (PIR)—fundamentally alter algorithmic tradeoffs, introducing choices that would be sub-optimal in most other settings. In unconstrained plaintext environments, Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search is dominated by hierarchical graphs (e.g., HNSW [35]) and quantized inverted files (e.g., ScaNN [28]), which exploit non-linear geometric branching to achieve sublinear query times (𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log N) for hierarchical graphs such as HNSW). In contrast, in private, blind-server settings, data-dependent branching leaks memory access patterns, rendering graph traversals either insecure, reliant on non-colluding multi-server assumptions (e.g., PRECO [40]), or subject to heavy multi-round cryptographic overheads across garbled circuits, oblivious RAM, or sublinear PIR (e.g., SANNS [14], Tiptoe [29], Pacmann [48], Panther [32], Compass [49]). Under strict single-server privacy constraints, non-interactive systems are forced into an 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) linear scan of the entire database. When server compute and memory capacity are abundant relative to communication bandwidth and cryptographic circuit depth, algorithm design shifts toward strictly linear, non-interactive mathematical formulations.

papers.title: Subgraph Isomorphism, Integer Linear Programming, and Lattices: A Linear Algebraic Framework
papers.abstract: The subgraph isomorphism problem (SGI) asks a deceptively simple question: is a graph B found inside a parent graph A? Famously NP-complete and the subject of volumes of study, attempts to practically solve subgraph problems typically require specialized software or the focused application of problem-specific theoretical knowledge. Here we present a straightforward linear framework that neatly joins SGI to lattice theory and constrained satisfiability and, importantly, yields an easily implemented algorithm that naturally leverages consumer-grade hardware and off-the-shelf libraries to compete with state-of-the-art specialized solvers. We additionally show practical realizations in approachable settings, along with some benchmarks that reduce 6+ hour computations to seconds. Aimed at readability, we develop a series of computable algebraic invariants and demonstrate their application to familiar problems such as the Knight's Tour, with a focus on providing an accessible entry point for researchers in graph theory, abstract algebra, and students in general.
papers.intro:
The subgraph isomorphism (SGI) problem asks an apparently simple question: when is one graph contained inside another? Framed another way, given a pattern graph GBG_{B} on MM vertices and a target graph GAG_{A} on N≥MN\geq M vertices, how hard is it to find a copy of GBG_{B} inside GAG_{A}—or prove that no such copy exists? Easy to state, subgraph isomorphism is famously NP-complete [1], generalizing both the graph isomorphism problem [2, 3, 4] and the Hamiltonian cycle problem, with direct relevance to chemical informatics, circuit layout, computer vision, and network analysis.

papers.title: Minimum orders of clique oddomorphism counterexamples
papers.abstract: An oddomorphism to $K_n$ is a proper colouring with $n$ colours in which every vertex is designated odd or even, every vertex has in each other colour class a number of neighbours of its own parity, and every colour class contains an odd number of odd vertices. We prove that an oddomorphism witness to $K_n$ on at most $n+6$ vertices contains a $K_n$ minor with every branch meeting the witness's specified odd set. The conclusion holds inside any graph containing the witness and therefore applies to weak oddomorphisms. The bound is sharp: for every $n\ge8$ the minimum order of a graph admitting a weak oddomorphism to $K_n$ but having no $K_n$ minor is exactly $n+7$. The extremal example is a fifteen-vertex graph with an oddomorphism to $K_8$, obtained from the doubled theta graph of Kriesell and Mohr by adding one vertex adjacent to the seven roots; we give a structural proof that it has no $K_8$ minor, including their counting argument for the rooted case. A separate technical companion records further results on related root-apex graphs, an attachment theorem and a bounded nine-colour statement, together with their computational provenance; none of it is used here. The results do not resolve the unrestricted clique-target problem.

papers.title: Classifying Brazilian Monetary Policy States with Interest Rate Gaps and Markov Models
papers.abstract: This paper develops a monthly framework for classifying Brazilian monetary policy that distinguishes the level of monetary restraint, changes in that stance, and statistical regimes associated with Selic adjustments. The framework combines a seven-state deterministic classifier, an empirical Markov chain, a Gaussian hidden Markov model, and Markov-switching regressions. Project outputs provide 145 classified observations from May 2014 to May 2026, with a partial final month. Under the implemented nominal neutral rate convention, restrictive states account for 88.3% of observations. A four-state HMM achieves a lower BIC, whereas the three-state model records a lower temporal validation loss. Switching regressions select three Selic adjustment regimes after solutions with degenerate variances are excluded. An additional sensitivity exercise reduces the restrictive share to 51.0% when the neutral benchmark is interpreted as real, demonstrating how strongly the results depend on benchmark measurement. The contribution is an auditable comparative application for monetary monitoring. The findings describe historical patterns conditional on the data and specifications; they do not establish predictive superiority or causal identification.

papers.title: A Deterministic Security Runtime for LLM Agents on MPI and Batch-Scheduled HPC Systems: Consensus-Governed, Hardware-Rooted Supervision of Every Rank
papers.abstract: Large language model agents launch simulations on high-performance computing (HPC) systems, where one sbatch or mpirun can commit thousands of node-hours and a forged result can cost lives. Of 23 surveyed systems, none supervises the running job, and none holds when the control host is compromised. We fix both. Enclawed, our deterministic security runtime for AI agents, has until now served a single user; this work makes it a distributed runtime for parallel HPC and agent swarms. The Enclaweder, our hardware root of trust, keeps a compromised host from becoming a catastrophe. A launch gate decides every launch by policy alone, refusing what it cannot parse. Once the job runs, a swarm chain grants short leases against signed heartbeats and evicts on evidence, and a supervisor around every rank pauses it when its lease lapses and kills it on tampering. Each node signs with its Enclaweder's key, so the host can forge none of it. Enclawed needs no administrator privileges and plugs into existing clusters unchanged, over Secure Shell alone. Supervision leaves the compute loop of a 16-rank LAMMPS job unchanged, on graphics processors too, and adds about 3 s of start-up. Twelve live attacks on Enclaweder-keyed ranks, colluding coordinators included, ended fail-closed. Sixteen agents on a real model attempted 24 launches that planted instructions ordered; the gate denied all 24 and allowed all 108 legitimate ones. Enclawed's core and the HPC Agent Security Benchmark are open source.
papers.intro:
Scientific high-performance computing (HPC) is where large language model (LLM) agents will first spend real money unattended, because an agent that runs a simulation acts through the scheduler rather than through an application programming interface (API): it writes an input deck, picks a rank count and a wall time, and types sbatch or mpirun. Each of those commands runs with the submitting user’s full credentials on every node it touches, so a wrong or hijacked decision is executed with the operator’s authority. Current HPC controls cannot tell the two apart, since they authenticate the submitter rather than the behavior; a recent position paper names this the “hijacked authorized agent” problem [26]. Without a control that can tell them apart, facilities fall back on prohibition: at least one university center now bans agents from submitting or operating jobs without explicit per-action human approval.

Without a control that can tell them apart, facilities fall back on prohibition: at least one university center now bans agents from submitting or operating jobs without explicit per-action human approval.

A hijacked decision can do worse than waste node-hours: it can forge a result, and a forged simulation result can cost lives. A hijacked agent can run another build of the code, change one parameter or one line of the input deck, rewrite a restart file or a material table that the running job reads, or report numbers the run never produced, and none of these changes the form of the output. A forgery written into a running simulation is the hardest to detect, because every later step is computed from the forged state. Rerunning the job does not expose it either. Atomic additions in force accumulation on graphics processing units and the reduction order of MPI collectives make floating-point sums depend on scheduling, so two honest runs of one input already differ in their last bits; where the dynamics amplify perturbations, as hydrodynamic instabilities do, those differences grow, and a rerun that disagrees with the forged run cannot tell the forgery from the nondeterminism. A systematic forgery, such as an altered equation-of-state table, shifts the answer itself and survives every rerun with the same inputs.

Wherever simulation is the evidence for a design, the forgery passes into the design. The clearest case is the stockpile stewardship of the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA): the United States has conducted no nuclear explosive test since 1992, so its laboratories use simulation to predict the performance, safety and reliability of nuclear weapons and to certify them in the absence of testing [28]. Government and industry design and certify on physics simulation in the same way: weapons, aircraft, spacecraft and launch vehicles, ships and submarines, cars, trains and other vehicles, nuclear reactors, medical devices, precision machinery, and the structures, materials and drugs behind them. In each of these, a design certified on a forged result can fail in service, and when it fails, people die. A hijacked agent with scheduler access at such a site therefore puts lives at risk, not only an allocation.

The systems that let agents use HPC today sit at two layers. Agent frameworks such as Academy [23], URSA (Universal Research and Scientific Agent) [18], LAMMPS-Agents [3] (agents for the Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator, LAMMPS) and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory’s (LLNL’s) descriptive execution work [47, 46] give the agent the operator’s scheduler access and concentrate on capability. A second group gates the launch: Diamond Agent checks partitions, wall time and credit before placement [50]; LARA-HPC, a validation-driven workflow framework on the Fugaku supercomputer, removes shell access and submits only fixed templates that pass a dry run [10]; a few Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers allow-list operations and cap resources per site [39]. These gates reduce the risk, and we compare against them in Section 4.1, but three limits keep them from removing it. First, they stop at submission, so nothing watches the job after the scheduler accepts it. Second, they trust the host that runs the gate, so a compromised gateway or credential store removes the gate with it. Third, they are not deterministic in the sense a security reviewer needs: several let the LLM itself choose resources inside loose bounds, and none refuses a command it cannot fully parse.

papers.title: MOTIO: Agentic Skill Engineering for Reality-Grounded Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract:
We present MOTIO, an agentic skill-engineering system that turns ordinary human-action videos, reality-grounded 3D assets, motion references, and reusable robot skills into executable humanoid loco-manipulation programs. Through in-context task and contact reasoning, an agent constructs staged robot-native interactions and improves them using physics execution, multi-frame feedback, and human validation---without task-specific teleoperation or robot demonstration collection. Agentic 3D supplies metric product and environment assets, while existing whole-body, inverse-kinematics, and dexterous-hand interfaces realize the programs. Across 33 timestamped first approvals, the median recorded agent-turn time is 97.0 minutes and request-to-approval duration is 2.80 hours. Simulation-side layout and object variation prepare a long-horizon bottle-disposal skill for a continuous 101.75-second physical G1 execution in a scanned office; physical refinement reduces screw-tightening thread residual by 76.0%. Agent-generated skills additionally supervise BC/DAgger distillation into one shared reference policy, completing 18 simulated tasks under the same checkpoint without inference-time expert intervention.
Project page: https://iiiiqiiii.github.io/motio/
papers.intro:
Humanoid foundation controllers increasingly provide reusable walking, balancing, and whole-body tracking. Developing a new contact-rich task in a real environment additionally requires metric object geometry, interaction stages, and execution under robot dynamics. Human demonstration videos reveal the sequence and intent of contact events—reaching, grasping, turning, regrasping, releasing, and checking the terminal state—which can be translated into robot-space programs.

Human review selects executable skill versions for reuse.

Simulated skill executions also serve as expert references for one shared BC/DAgger policy, without new task-specific reinforcement-learning rewards.

papers.title: Learning Dexterous Manipulation: Hands, Simulators, Training, and Evaluation
papers.abstract: A dexterous hand can change an object's pose without setting it down. This survey covers 113 learning-based methods that attempt it, the hands they run on, the simulators they train in, and how they report results. The field has largely converged on one recipe: reinforcement learning on privileged state in a GPU simulator, distilled into a vision-only student for transfer to hardware. Almost half the corpus trains that way, nearly all of it in one simulator, whose own successors are barely used. A second and faster-growing branch learns from teleoperated demonstration instead, through vision-language-action models, diffusion policies, and systems whose contribution is the collection rig itself. Published work has tripled since 2022. Grasping remains the largest task family and bimanual coordination the fastest-rising, and almost every experiment runs on one of four hands. What the survey adds comes from reading released code and vendor specifications beside the papers. Eight hands that can be bought or built from published designs appear in no method paper here. Where the depth a hand sinks into the object it holds is reported at all, it is not measured in the physics that produced the motion. Section VII proposes a protocol for the unreported quantities; the body gives the counts behind every claim above.
papers.intro:
A hand is dexterous when it can change an object’s pose without putting the object down. That property, and not the finger count, is what separates a hand from a gripper. Bicchi [1] draws the same line in Sec. 1.1 between restraining an object and manipulating it with the fingers: restraint is a static question about whether the contacts prevent motion, while in-hand manipulation is a dynamic one about whether contacts can be broken and remade while the object stays held. A parallel-jaw gripper can hold almost anything and reorient almost nothing.

The classical theory of grasping is about holding, and it is good at it. Given a set of contact points and an assumption about friction, it can decide whether an object is immobilized, and what force each finger has to apply to keep it that way. What it cannot do is say what the fingers should do next. Contact is what makes that hard: a finger is either touching or it is not, and it can push but not pull, so the equations of motion change form every time a contact is made or broken. The standard treatment says as much about its own results, that immobilizing an object “does not guarantee stability”, and that “the nonsmooth nature of grasp dynamics, because of the unilateral constraints on displacements and forces, has made a thorough analysis very difficult” ([1, Sec. 1.5 and 1.8]). The tradition produced tests. You can check a candidate grasp against them; you cannot run them on a robot.

Learning changed what a practitioner has to produce. The old deliverable was a proof that a configuration holds. The new one is a policy that scores well over many simulated attempts, which means the simulator now stands in for the analysis and the score stands in for the proof. That is why the field moved, and it is also why this survey is organized as it is. It shifts two burdens onto the author. The simulator has to be faithful where fidelity matters. One recipe now carries most of the field. Train a policy with reinforcement learning on privileged state, the object pose, velocities and physical parameters the robot cannot sense, in a GPU simulator running thousands of environments in parallel; distill that teacher into a student that sees only what a camera and joint encoders provide; transfer the student. Fifty-four of the 113 method papers here train this way, most of them in one simulator, and about half of those add the distillation stage. In-hand cube reorientation is the recipe’s benchmark, inherited from [2] and still the task a new method is expected to show.

Instead of a simulator and a reward it takes human demonstrations through a teleoperation rig and fits a policy directly, as a vision-language-action model, a diffusion policy, or a data-collection rig whose design is itself the contribution. Section V counts them, and Fig. 1 shows how fast they have arrived. It is the newer literature, most of it from the last two years, and it trades the reward-design problem for a data-collection problem. Which of the two branches ends up feeding the other is not settled here, but the growth is the clearest trend in the corpus.

Both branches run on remarkably little hardware. Four hands carry almost every experiment in this corpus, led by the Allegro at 35 of the 113 papers; Fig. 3 gives the rest of the distribution. Eight further hands can be bought today or built from published designs and appear in the experiments of none of them. The hardware exists and is purchasable, so this is not a manufacturing lag, and Section III takes it up: a field whose results rest on four platforms is more fragile than its publication volume suggests.

What this literature cannot currently do is compare its own results. Nearly every paper states a success criterion, but they are not the same criterion, and only 70 of the 113 say how many trials a reported rate rests on. The criteria run from never dropping the object to reaching a pose within a tolerance each paper picks for itself. Two success rates from two papers on nominally the same task are usually not measuring the same event, and none of the surveys preceding this one supplies a protocol that would make them comparable. Section VII derives one, with the trial counts a stated confidence interval actually requires.

papers.title: A Model-Theoretic Formalization of AlKhwaremis ilm alfaraid
papers.abstract: This paper presents a model theoretic and computational formalization of AlKhwarizmis treatment of inheritance within the framework of Computational Fiqh. We first show that every inheritance configuration in a specified class is representable as a finite system of rational linear equalities and inequalities, and that such systems are decided exactly by Fourier Motzkin elimination over Q. We then define the fixed dimensional inheritance structure Vd with distinguished claimant coordinates, and prove that every admissible rational linear coordinate realization is isomorphic to Vd, this establishes the algebraic representation as canonical within that class. The complete first order theory Td of Vd is shown to be complete by construction and is explicitly distinguished from the decidability of the inheritance relevant fragment. The methodological principle is then related to a broader formalization of closed Fiqh domains via exhaustive case generation, Horn clause axiomatization, and terminating deduction, yielding domain relative computational completeness.

papers.title: Noninteger completely monotonic degrees of Stirling remainders and their derivatives
papers.abstract: For Stirling expansions truncated after at least two Bernoulli terms, we disprove the three real-degree conjectures recorded by Mahmoud and Qi for the signed remainders of the logarithm of the gamma function and their derivatives. We give a unified proof of the corresponding integer-degree formula, recovering known cases and resolving Zhu's conjectures for higher derivatives in this range. Every real completely monotonic degree lies strictly between the predicted integer and the next integer. We obtain a universal fractional lower bound through an explicit inverse function and a simpler rational bound valid for every derivative order. A local estimate for the negative part of the Laplace kernel's derivative with respect to its logarithmic variable makes the lower improvement proportional to the reciprocal of the combined truncation and derivative order. Together with a uniform upper bound, this determines the exact order of decay of the fractional excess for each fixed derivative order and for its supremum over all derivative orders. Sharper kernel estimates give stronger bounds for the first two degrees. The proof combines fractional positivity criteria, the classical Laplace representation, a sign characterization of the associated densities, and a convexity obstruction at the upper integer endpoint. All estimates used in the proofs are analytic. The exact real degrees and the optimal asymptotic constants remain open.

papers.title: RoboJev: An Open Vision-Language Judge for Robot Success Detection
papers.abstract: Many robot manipulation videos do not indicate whether the task was successfully completed. RoboJev-27B is an open-weight vision-language model that takes a task instruction, 10 frames of a manipulation attempt, and (if available) final frames from auxiliary cameras and predicts whether the robot accomplished the task. RoboJev-27B is a variant of JEV-27B-VL, trained with a rank-32 LoRA adapter on the language model only (keeping the vision encoder frozen) using 52,598 episode records. It also uses a source-specific KL penalty that applies only to research data, anchoring predictions closer to the original model on those sources. It uses a calibrated two-token readout that outputs success/failure probabilities in a single forward pass. On 268 held-out episodes of the same robot model (SO-101), RoboJev-27B attains 95.2% balanced accuracy and 0.993 AUROC. It also generalises to episodes collected by unseen labs/robots (AUROC = 0.890 over 459 episodes) as well as to clearly labelled community-collected episodes (accuracy = 93.3% over 135 episodes), where the base model attains an AUROC = 0.900 on the unseen-lab/robot subset with the same inputs. It takes 0.26 seconds per episode (median, serial) to infer on a single H100, which is about \$0.19 per 1,000 success predictions at \$2.69 per GPU-hour (not including media processing and serving costs). RoboJev-27B is released together with its inference code, along with a transparent evaluation: 20,628 predictions organized into 29 model/protocol entries are made available to facilitate browsing and to enable reproducible benchmarking of success detection. We also compare against strong API-based frontier VLMs, which take in fewer input frames (4 images from the primary camera only); note that this comparison is not strictly like-for-like because RoboJev-27B is given more frames at inference.
papers.intro:
An important ingredient for review queues, learned terminal rewards, or aggregate evaluation is knowing which episodes succeeded. Such labels are often not machine readable and cannot be easily derived from low-level heuristics (e.g. trajectory length, data origin, or smoothness). We therefore fine-tune an episode judge from JEV-27B-VL [1, 2] into RoboJev, an open-weight success detector for robot manipulation videos. Given a task instruction, ten evenly spaced frames from the primary camera, and the final frame from any auxiliary cameras, RoboJev outputs a calibrated success probability. Rather than building a different classifier for every task and environment, RoboJev can be used in a plug-and-play fashion. Rather than generating an explanation, RoboJev scores true / false tokens at a designated position. RoboJev is reusable across tasks and environments thanks to its well-defined inputs, consistent prompting protocol, and verifiable error logs.

We test RoboJev on held-out SO-101 rollouts, on lab/robot domains not included in the robot-specific fine-tuning, and on community videos that have clear labels. Community videos with ambiguous labels can still be inspected, but are not used for binary metrics. While the SO-101 split contains rollouts from the same physical environment as some of the training data, we leave out two entire tasks, as well as individual recording sessions. On this split, RoboJev-27B achieves 95.2% balanced accuracy. On the unseen-domain data, it achieves 0.890 AUROC, just under the 0.900 AUROC of the unadapted JEV-27B-VL run with the same input protocol. Alongside our released predictions, protocols, and a pinned checkpoint, this indicates that RoboJev is a useful and inspectable tool for policy evaluation, rather than indicating that fine-tuning yields generalizable improvements.

papers.title: Optical imaging with only the evanescent fields and without diffraction
papers.abstract: We report on a conceptual framework for optical imaging utilizing exclusively evanescent fields, effectively eliminating or attenuating standard optical diffraction. We present the theoretical foundation of this concept based on the decomposition of dipole radiation into evanescent fields and homogeneous propagating waves, exploring the explicit conditions required to suppress the latter. By successfully decoupling and removing the homogeneous component, optical tasks, such as sub-diffraction imaging, can be executed solely via evanescent channels, bypassing traditional diffractive limits. We discuss the physical feasibility of this approach and provide concrete examples of how this conjecture can be realized using currently available laboratory and industrial techniques. The realization of this concept promises to redefine core paradigms in optics and fundamental physics. Because the minimum achievable feature size is no longer governed by the operating wavelength, this approach enables an unprecedented increase in spatial resolution, offering a direct pathway to advance state-of-the-art semiconductor lithography and chip manufacturing.

papers.title: On the stability of second-order methods for DDEs and PDDEs
papers.abstract:
In this paper, a one-parameter family of second-order implicit--explicit (IMEX) multistep methods is studied for delay differential equations (DDEs). The analysis is based on the matrix problem $y'(t)=A y(t) + B y(t-\tau(t))$, where $A$ is Hermitian negative definite but $B$ is any matrix. For constant, grid-aligned delays, a field-of-values argument yields unconditional stability whenever a suitable generalized field of values $F_p(A,B)$ is contained in the open unit disk. For a constant non-grid-aligned delay, we show that quadratic interpolation does not reduce the corresponding stability disk. For genuinely variable delays, the method is formulated as a nonautonomous augmented system, and product-level sufficient conditions are obtained from a common quadratic Lyapunov inequality and from a quantitative slow-variation hypothesis.
  The approach developed herein is illustrated through several examples in which the discussed theory is applied not only to DDEs, but also to semidiscrete parabolic problems given by partial delay differential equations with a diffusion term.

papers.intro:
Many dynamical processes do not react instantaneously to their present state. Transport, maturation, sensing, communication, and decision making introduce finite time lags, so that the rate of change at time tt depends on information generated at earlier times. Even a single delay may change the qualitative behaviour of a model by creating or suppressing oscillations, moving stability boundaries, or producing bifurcations that are absent from the corresponding ordinary differential equation. Delay differential equations (DDEs) therefore provide a natural framework for feedback systems with memory, with applications ranging from population dynamics and epidemiology to physiology, chemical kinetics, control, and networked engineering systems; see, for example, [1, 2]. State-dependent delays are especially relevant when the travel, processing, or maturation time is itself affected by the evolving state, and they lead to a substantially richer dynamical theory than constant-delay models.

A DDE initial-value problem is infinite-dimensional, since its solution is determined by an initial history function rather than by a single vector. This distinction has direct numerical consequences. A time-stepping method must repeatedly evaluate an already computed approximation at delayed arguments, track propagated discontinuities, and provide a continuous extension or interpolation whenever a delayed point does not coincide with the mesh. These issues are central to the convergence and implementation theory of DDE solvers [3]. They become more delicate for time- or state-dependent delays: the delayed point moves relative to the grid, may cross mesh intervals as the solution evolves, and can make an otherwise explicit formula effectively implicit. Practical solvers for such problems consequently rely on continuous Runge–Kutta extensions, event handling, and residual control [4].

For one-step schemes, a substantial theory is available. P-stability of natural Runge–Kutta processes on constrained meshes was investigated in [8]; necessary or sufficient step-size conditions for θ\theta-methods were obtained in [9]; and a general framework for step-by-step methods with complex coefficients was developed in [10]. Since the delayed value is normally off-grid, the choice of continuous extension is inseparable from the stability question, as illustrated by the interpolation procedure of [11]. System-level results under suitable matrix or operator assumptions were established for natural Runge–Kutta methods in [12]. Later studies refined the distinction between delay-independent and delay-dependent regions for Runge–Kutta methods [13] and identified important barriers to unconditional stability for broad classes of implicit schemes [14]. papers.title: On the Evolution of Circumstellar Disks Modified by the Presence of a Binary
papers.abstract: Stars form within circumstellar disks, and some binary stars develop circumbinary disks surrounding the pair. Observations suggest that disks that form around binary star systems are less common than those around single stars. One possible explanation is that binary stars may disrupt or shorten the lifespan of their surrounding disks relative to those around single stars. To investigate this, we used the DISCO hydrodynamics code to compute the lifetimes of circumstellar disks with and without a binary. Our results indicate that binary systems can reduce the lifetime of a circumbinary disk by a modest factor of two to three compared to disks around single stars. This effect is present when the binary separation is at least one-tenth of the disk radius. While our findings show that binaries can shorten circumbinary disk lifetimes, this alone might not be enough to fully account for the scarcity of these disks.

papers.intro:
After the collapse of molecular clouds, stars typically form within disks of gas and dust, with the majority of these stars possibly forming in binary systems ([11]; [12]; [14]). The demographics of binary systems are consistent with the idea that most binaries form out of the same molecular cloud (see also [24]). In such systems, the process of star formation is accompanied by the development of circumstellar disks. Each star in the binary system may be surrounded by its own individual disk: the more massive primary star can host a circumprimary disk, while the less massive secondary star can host a circumsecondary disk. In addition to these individual disks, binary systems can also host a circumbinary disk that orbits both stars and their disks, encompassing the entire system (See Figure 1). All three types of disks have been observed in binary T Tauri systems such as GG Tau ([15]), DQ Tau ([35]), UZ Tau E ([16]), HD 142527 ([13]), and HD 100453 [13]).

Observations of young stars have compared the prevalence of circumprimary, circumsecondary, and circumbinary disks to disks around single stars ([25]; [17]). Studies have found that circumprimary/circumsecondary disks around each component of wide separation binary systems are more common than circumbinary disks, which are typically found in systems with smaller separations, seen, for example, in Figure 66 of [17]. These observations suggest that circumbinary disks are rarer than circumprimary/circumsecondary disks, raising the question of whether the presence of a binary system inhibits disk formation or enhances disk dissipation.

This distinction is worth emphasizing, since approximately half of all solar-type stars are in binary or multiple-star systems ([33]; [20]). Observational evidence shows that close binary companions can reduce the lifetime of circumstellar disks compared to those around single stars ([5]). In close binary systems, gravitational interactions between the stars and the surrounding disk can truncate the disk’s outer edge and excite spiral density waves that redistribute angular momentum. These effects restrict the disk’s radial extent and increase the efficiency of angular momentum transport, both of which shorten the disk’s overall lifetime ([3]; [29]; [1]; [2]).

This raises a key question: are circumbinary disks intrinsically rare, or do they simply dissipate more quickly in the presence of a binary? In this work, we carry out a fundamental study of how binaries affect disk evolution at high viscosity values, using scaling arguments to extend our findings toward lower viscosities thought to be more realistic in disks (see, e.g., [17]). Essentially, we are treating these models as an idealized set up to identify the structural and accretion response to the binary. For simplicity, we adopt a spatially uniform kinematic viscosity ν\nu. This assumption is an idealization used to clarify the influence of the binary. Because the models are initialized with a finite mass reservoir, the surface density evolves with time and the accretion rate gradually declines once truncation occurs. Although these viscosity values are intentionally higher than those inferred from recent observations, they are adopted here as an idealized choice to highlight how circumbinary disk lifetimes scale with binary separation and viscous transport. For comparison, the DSHARP survey [10] finds effective α\alpha-values two orders of magnitude lower than the values used here, and 3D circumbinary simulations such as [32] similarly report reduced levels of turbulence generated by the binary. Our goal in this first study is therefore not to reproduce physical turbulence, but to use a controlled and computationally efficient parameter range to establish how lifetime trends depend on viscosity in an idealized framework.

The dynamics of circumbinary disks have been studied extensively ([29]; [26]; [28]; [27]; [8]; [18]; [34]; for review see [22]). Previous reviews, such as those by [23], have explored how the gravitational interactions between the stars and the disk influence the structure and evolution, including the formation of circumstellar and circumbinary disks and the effects of binary system dynamics on disk gaps and resonances. Disks may be truncated at a specific disk size due to the binary’s gravitational influence. Positive torques generated by these interactions can drive material away from the inner region of the disk ([23]), impacting both its accretion rates and the disk lifetime.

We investigate the possibility that circumbinary disks are less common because their lifetimes are shorter. To do this, we use the DISCO hydrodynamical code ([9]) to simulate the evolution of circumbinary disks with different disk sizes (Rd), binary separation (aa), and viscosities (ν\nu). These simulations are carried out in both one-dimensional (1D) and two-dimensional (2D) configurations to examine how the disk lifetime τ\tau changes under each setup. In the 1D model, the binary is replaced by a single star. In contrast, the 2D model includes the full binary system, allowing us to capture the complex interactions between the stars and the disk, including resonances, gaps, and changes to the disk’s structure. By comparing these two models, we aim to determine whether the binary stars shorten the lifetime of the circumbinary disk.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In II, we describe how DISCO is used to simulate the dynamics of circumbinary disks. Section III compares disk lifetimes at different viscosities in single-star and binary star systems obtaining a disk suppression factor. Section IV introduces an analytical expression that summarizes all the data we find empirically.

papers.title: ArchGuard-APR: Architecture-Constraint-Aware Multi-Agent Program Repair Using Repository Graphs and Execution Feedback
papers.abstract:
Repository-level automated program repair must reason about more than a localized failing statement. A candidate change can satisfy a narrow test while violating dependency boundaries, modifying an unsafe path, or relying on context that omits relevant repository structure. ArchGuard-APR is an architecture-aware repair prototype that integrates deterministic repository analysis, immutable repository graphs, explicit architecture profiles, graph-guided context retrieval, role-based repair orchestration, patch-policy enforcement, isolated execution feedback, provider cost controls, and canonical source-free evidence.
  We evaluate the implemented pipeline through an exploratory paired feasibility study, not a confirmatory effectiveness experiment. Six executions were planned; four completed, and two black-4 conditions ended in pre-provider infrastructure attrition. Across two valid paired tasks, baseline and ArchGuard conditions each produced 0/2 successful repairs, and all four completed outputs were classified as invalid patches.
  The completed executions consumed 35,431 input tokens and 2,737 output tokens, for a total of 38,168 tokens, at a total cost of USD 0.1296325. No effectiveness advantage was observed, and the sample provides no useful inferential basis. The study instead establishes the engineering feasibility of composing architecture constraints with a reproducible repair pipeline and identifies patch validity and infrastructure robustness as the principal targets for future work.

papers.title: The geometric combinatorics of $k$-shuffle polynomials
papers.abstract: This paper is the second in a series of two which aims at introducing a new family of groups called $k$-shuffle braid groups, denoted $\mathcal{B}_{n}(k)$. We focus here on the geometrical origins of these groups, as first observed by Calegari in arXiv:2105.11265. The spaces we are interested in are spaces of complex monic polynomials of degree $n$ whose critical values lie in $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{1, e^{\frac{2\pi i}{k}}, \dots, e^{\frac{2\pi i (k-1)}{k}}\}$. We show that the $k$-shuffle braid groups are the fundamental groups of those spaces, which correspond geometrically to complements of $k$ translates of the discriminant variety. Moreover, we show that the $k$-shuffle braid groups $\mathcal{B}_n(k)$ inject into the larger braid groups $\mathcal{B}_{nk}$.

papers.title: Global $c^{1,\alpha}$ regularity and fine behavior at critical points for quasilinear elliptic equations with Orlicz growth and unbounded drift
papers.abstract: We investigate the global regularity up to the boundary and the fine pointwise behavior along the critical set for bounded weak solutions to general quasilinear elliptic Dirichlet problems in Orlicz-Sobolev spaces. Our structural framework encompasses operators with non-standard Lieberman-type growth alongside lower-order terms featuring natural gradient growth, an unbounded source term in $L^q$, and an unbounded spatial drift weight in $L^s$. To overcome the analytical obstructions posed by the unbounded drift across the anisotropic growth gap, we first establish global H\"older continuity up to the boundary via Moser iteration. We then construct a novel smooth regularization scheme for general homogeneous constant-coefficient operators, merging the approximation frameworks of Lieberman and Cianchi-Maz'ya, to derive global $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity up to the boundary through a variational perturbation approach. Building upon this global theory, we employ a geometric compactness and blow-up argument to prove that at any interior or boundary critical point where the gradient vanishes, the solution achieves an improved pointwise $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity. Remarkably, at boundary critical points, this quantitative improvement decouples from the lower-order terms and completely bypasses both the boundary datum regularity and the domain smoothness. Finally, we discuss the sharpness of the integrability threshold required for the unbounded drift weight in the subcritical regime.

papers.title: Explicit weighing matrices $W(n,k)$ for all $n \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ with $4 \le n \le 108$, and all $1 \le k \le n$
papers.abstract: We present an explicit weighing matrix $W(n,k)$ for every order $n\equiv 0\pmod 4$ with $4\le n\le 108$ and every weight $1\le k\le n$: 1512 matrices in total, each checked in exact integer arithmetic. Of these, 961 come from classical constructions (identity, direct sums, Kronecker products, Paley matrices and skew-Hadamard doubling) and 551 are Goethals-Seidel matrices, found by exhaustive search (24 matrices, $n\le 24$) or by simulated annealing on the periodic autocorrelation cost (527 matrices, $n\ge 28$). The note is self-contained as far as the methods are concerned: it presents all the construction methods used and the algorithm that selects among them, explains the algorithm step by step, proves every identity on which the constructions rely, and illustrates each method with a matrix taken from the catalogue. It does not reproduce the 1512 matrices, which are available in the repository. It also gives a short parity obstruction to Goethals-Seidel matrices $W(4m,4m-1)$ with $m$ even, and lists the generating sequences of thirteen matrices whose parameters appear as unresolved in historical tables consulted by the author; their status in the current literature is still being checked, and no claim of priority is made.

papers.title: Stochastic quantization and Osterwalder-Schrader axioms for quantum field theory models
papers.abstract: This PhD thesis constructs the $P(\Phi)_2$ Euclidean quantum field theory on $\mathscr{S}'(\mathbb{R}^2)$. We first construct the finite-volume measure of the $P(\Phi)_2$ model on $\mathscr{D}'(\mathbb{S}_R)$, where $\mathbb{S}_R$ is a two-dimensional sphere of radius $R\in\mathbb{N}_+$. To this end, we rely on Nelson's hypercontractivity estimate. We then use parabolic stochastic quantization and the energy method to construct the infinite-volume measure on $\mathscr{S}'(\mathbb{R}^2)$. This requires establishing the global-in-time existence of solutions to the corresponding stochastic partial differential equations with fixed cutoffs. The remainder of the thesis is devoted to verifying the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms: regularity, reflection positivity, and invariance under translations, rotations, and reflections. This combination of axioms, which is crucial for obtaining a non-trivial local relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski spacetime, had not been established in earlier constructions based on stochastic quantization.

papers.title: Sealed bets on emerging research topics: a protocol for judging early detection, applied to a detector and to eight research funders
papers.abstract: Tools that claim to detect emerging research topics are rarely judged on their own lists. Our main contribution is a protocol that makes such judgement possible. A bet freezes four things before its verdict can be known: the date of the photograph, the population of candidates, the verdict rule, and the comparison with chance drawn among the same candidates. The list has a fixed length, is read on two axes (champions and failures) against a computed ceiling, and is sealed by cryptographic fingerprint; sealing proves that a list existed at a date, not that it is right. A topic is a champion if its yearly volume of records triples within three years and reaches 100, a failure if it falls by 30%. We apply the protocol to one detector on PubMed/MEDLINE, in three separate blocks. On a retrospective benchmark (2017-2022), chance among the candidates yields 26.7 champions and 15.1 failures out of 120 slots; the detector yields 85 and 3, and under nine pre-registered variants of the verdict rule its champions stay between 2.5 and 5.0 times chance, with no more failures. The detector was developed with these verdicts known, and its specification is not published. Prospective validation rests on six sealed bets, judged in early 2029 and early 2030; only bets 5 and 6 test exactly the instrument of the benchmark. A secondary, exploratory study applies the same judge to eight research funders: under exact name matching, which may disadvantage grant texts, the detector's lists are more concentrated in future champions than the twenty topics named in the most grants of each funder (70.8% against 20.8% to 35.8%, chance 22.3%). We document data defects, negative results and the limits of each comparison.

On 6 December 2013 the US Food and Drug Administration approved the drug.

Many organisations publish lists of emerging topics. Commercial analytics platforms, public foresight programmes and academic methods all produce them. In a survey of public sources made in September 2026 (§2), we found no commercial provider and no public programme that publishes a verdict on its own past lists. Academic work usually reports retrospective splits, where the method is tuned and tested on a known past. Only a few lines of work score their predictions against an explicit external reference, and we found only one that froze its criteria at a date and then judged them out of sample.

papers.title: Beyond Brown's radial tests: admissibility, parabolicity, and a doubling-Poincar\'e prior that neither test decides
papers.abstract: For the estimation of a normal mean in $\mathbb{R}^m$ under quadratic loss, Brown (1971) proved that a generalized Bayes estimator $\delta_F$ is admissible if and only if a diffusion attached to the marginal $f^*$ of the prior $F$ is recurrent, and gave two radial tests: a sphere-average test for recurrence and a ray test for transience. He observed that both tests can be silent. We read his theory as the potential theory of the weighted Euclidean space $(\mathbb{R}^m,f^*\,dx)$ and ask what the modern theory of recurrence on weighted manifolds adds inside the zone where neither test applies. Three results. (A) If $f^*\,dx$ is doubling and supports a scale-invariant Poincar\'e inequality, the sphere test is already complete: recurrence, Brown's sphere test and the ball-volume test are equivalent, so geometric criteria can add decidable cases only on the inadmissible side. (B) They do add one. An explicit prior on $\mathbb{R}^3$ whose marginal is small along a lattice of circles at dyadic scales with spacing equal to the square root of the scale, is doubling and Poincar\'e, silences both of Brown's tests, and is transient by the ball-volume test; its generalized Bayes estimator is inadmissible. (C) Outside the doubling-Poincar\'e class the zone is two-sided: the same circles placed on one surface per scale give an admissible estimator, decided by a flux bound along a non-spherical exhaustion, and a logarithmic product prior gives an inadmissible one, decided by product heat kernels. A comparison lemma shows that any positive weight with Lipschitz logarithm is, up to constants, the marginal of a prior, so that explicit weights may be used throughout.

papers.title: On derived equivalences of exact structures on the category of representations $k[x]/(x^n)$
papers.abstract: From the perspective of homological algebra, exact categories are interesting because they possess derived categories. Typically, an additive category admits many exact structures. If the original category is sufficiently nice (for example, quasi-abelian), a classification of exact structures can be given in terms of certain Serre subcategories in the category of contravariant functors. It turns out that the derived categories of different exact structures are functorially related. This work is concerned with sufficient conditions for the derived equivalence of different exact structures on certain categories.
papers.intro:
Exact categories were first introduced by Quillen in 1972 for the definition of higher K-theory. The formalism of exact categories allows extending the apparatus of homological algebra from abelian categories to a wider class of additive categories. The question of classifying exact structures has been widely discussed in the literature. In [Rump], it was proven that on any additive category there exists a maximal exact structure containing all smaller ones. Later, an explicit description of the maximal exact structure was obtained for quasi-abelian categories, as well as for categories with split idempotents (see [Crivei] for details).

The formalism of exact categories allows extending the apparatus of homological algebra from abelian categories to a wider class of additive categories. The question of classifying exact structures has been widely discussed in the literature. In [Rump], it was proven that on any additive category there exists a maximal exact structure containing all smaller ones. Later, an explicit description of the maximal exact structure was obtained for quasi-abelian categories, as well as for categories with split idempotents (see [Crivei] for details).

Intermediate exact structures, which are neither maximal nor minimal, are of interest. In [En], a complete classification of exact structures on a category with split idempotents was given in terms of Serre subcategories of the category of contravariant functors ℱ​u​n​c​(ℰo​p,𝒜​b)\mathcal{F}unc(\mathcal{E}^{op},\mathcal{A}b) (Theorem 4.1). However, from a practical point of view, this theorem turns out to be difficult to apply, since the problem of finding all Serre subcategories is extremely complex. Nevertheless, in some cases, for example, for Krull-Schmidt categories of finite type, it is possible to obtain an explicit description of all exact structures on the category in its internal terms, using Auslander theory and almost split sequences. Furthermore, the problem of classifying exact structures on a category is closely related to the study of properties of the right/left abelian envelopes of the category, introduced by A.I. Bondal and A. Bodzenta in [BB]. It turns out that if an exact structure ϵ\epsilon is contained in an exact structure ϵ′\epsilon^{\prime}, then the abelian envelope of the category with the exact structure ϵ′\epsilon^{\prime} is a quotient category of the abelian envelope of this category with the exact structure ϵ\epsilon.

The main goal of the present work is to study the question of when two exact structures on a given additive category are derived equivalent. This question has hardly been discussed in the literature so far. Unfortunately, a criterion for the derived equivalence of exact structures has not yet been obtained. Nevertheless, the case of the category of representations mod−k⁡[x]/(xn)\mathrm{mod-}k[x]/(x^{n}) was studied, and a necessary and sufficient condition for derived equivalence was formulated for it (Theorem 6.5). These questions turned out to be closely related to the existence of spherical objects in the abelian envelope of the category with the minimal exact structure.

These questions turned out to be closely related to the existence of spherical objects in the abelian envelope of the category with the minimal exact structure.

The study of abelian envelopes of exact categories is also interesting from the point of view that the abelian envelope of the maximal exact structure always has a global dimension not exceeding 2 (Theorem 6.2), i.e., it is smooth. This allows considering it as a noncommutative resolution of the original category, possibly non-smooth (i.e., of infinite global dimension). Sometimes a smooth resolution can be given by the abelian envelope of a smaller exact structure.

papers.title: Sharp diameter estimates via integral geometry
papers.abstract: We prove that the diameter of a closed embedded surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is always less than the integral of the magnitude of the mean curvature, divided by $\pi$. We also prove a sharp variant for surfaces with boundary, and apply it to address a conjecture of Miura.

papers.title: Officially corrected errors persist in AI training data: preregistered measurements on EU law, Internet standards and retracted science
papers.abstract: Official texts are corrected after publication: EU corrigenda, verified RFC errata, retractions. We measured whether these corrections are present in four public datasets used to train language models, and what models answer about the corrected passages. In EurlexResources, a legal training dataset, 1,989 of 2,082 testable single-language corrections to EU acts (95.5%, 94.6-96.3) remain in their erroneous form; in a random sample of 100, 46 change the meaning, a figure, a cross-reference, the competent authority or the scope (20 without scope). At least 124 corrected EU-law errors and at least 60 verified RFC errata (38 classified "Technical") are reproduced in their erroneous form in FineWeb-2 and in a sample of FineWeb. About 12,200 retracted papers (11,700-12,500) are present in the peS2o corpus, 79% with no mention of the retraction; separately, 53% of a random sample of retracted papers are still cited at least a year after retraction (OpenAlex). Asked 59 questions on serious corrected errors without documents, five models gave the erroneous version in 45% of the answers in which they committed to one version (31-60% allowing for clustering by question): 53% for scope corrections, 32% for the others. One answer in 295 said it did not know. Shown both versions side by side, the models chose the corrected one in 53% of cases (49-57), and naming the act made no difference; when each version carried its date and the corrigendum label, the four larger models chose it in 99-100% of cases. A comparison between a legal masked language model and its base model is null, against our bet: we do not show that model answers come from the datasets measured. All steps were preregistered and their fingerprints timestamped in the Bitcoin blockchain; six controls failed, several bets were lost, and every deviation is reported. Data and proofs: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23642239.

The European Union publishes corrigenda to its acts in the Official Journal; a corrigendum does not change the original publication but states what should be read instead, and the consolidated versions on EUR-Lex include it. The RFC Editor publishes errata to Internet standards and marks some as “Verified”. Scientific journals retract papers, and the Retraction Watch database, now distributed by Crossref, lists the retractions.
