papers.title: Propositional formula minimization is $\Sigma_2^p$-complete under many-one reductions
papers.abstract: The Minimum Equivalent Expression problem (MEE) asks, given a propositional formula $\phi$ and an integer $k$, whether $\phi$ is equivalent to a formula with at most $k$ occurrences of propositional variables. While the problem is clearly in $\Sigma_2^p$, its completeness under polynomial-time many-one reductions has remained open since at least 1979. Buchfuhrer and Umans showed in 2008 that it is $\Sigma_2^p$-complete under polynomial-time Turing reductions. In this note, we present a proof discovered by GPT-Sol-6.1 which establishes that MEE is $\Sigma_2^p$-complete also under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
papers.intro:
The Minimum Equivalent Expression (MEE) problem is a fundamental computational problem in logic. Given a propositional formula ϕ\phi and an integer kk, the problem asks whether there exists a formula equivalent to ϕ\phi containing at most kk occurrences of propositional variables. The problem belongs to Σ2p\Sigma_{2}^{p}, since one can existentially guess a formula of the prescribed size and then verify its equivalence to ϕ\phi using a coNP oracle.

Determining the exact complexity of MEE has a long history. The problem was already listed as open by Garey and Johnson in 1979 [3]. In 1997 Hemaspaandra and Wechsung established hardness under polynomial-time many-one reductions for the class of problems solvable using parallel access to an NP oracle [4]. Subsequently, Buchfuhrer and Umans proved in 2008 that MEE is Σ2p\Sigma_{2}^{p}-complete under polynomial-time Turing reductions [1, 2]. Their result also established the corresponding completeness for bounded-depth formulas of every fixed depth at least three. The case of depth two, which amounts to minimizing DNF formulas, was proved earlier to be Σ2p\Sigma_{2}^{p}-complete under many-one reductions in Umans [7].

In this note, we resolve this question by proving that MEE is also Σ2p\Sigma_{2}^{p}-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. At a high level, our strategy follows that of Buchfuhrer and Umans [2]. Like them, we reduce from Succinct Set Cover, a Σ2p\Sigma_{2}^{p}-complete problem introduced by Umans [6]. In their construction, the size threshold of the final MEE instance depends on the minimum size of an equivalent formula for an auxiliary function. They have no explicit expression for this quantity, so they determine it with oracle calls to MEE, and this is why their reduction is a Turing reduction. It turns out that by using technical tricks we can modify their reduction so that the threshold can be written down explicitly, removing the need for oracle calls.

Our motivation for studying MEE comes from explainable AI (XAI), and in particular from our earlier work on logic-based explanations [5]. There we distinguish between local explanations, which explain the behavior of a model on a single input, and global explanations, which explain its behavior on all inputs. If a classifier is represented by a propositional formula ϕ\phi and the explanation is required to be completely faithful, a global explanation of ϕ\phi is a formula ψ\psi of minimal size that is equivalent to ϕ\phi.11 1 At first sight, it may seem odd to define an optimal explanation of a propositional formula as merely a smallest equivalent formula: how can explaining be reduced to optimizing size? The requirement of faithfulness does the real work here. A faithful explanation must describe fully how the formula behaves on all inputs, and so it can itself be interpreted as a formula computing the same function. The only thing left to improve is how easy the explanation is to understand, and one natural way to measure this is its size. When the size of a formula is measured by the number of occurrences of propositional variables, the problem of finding an optimal global explanation is precisely MEE.

papers.title: Admissible sets of integers in imaginary quadratic fields of class number 1
papers.abstract:
Let $\mathcal O_K$ be the ring of integers of a number field $K$. A finite subset $\mathcal H=\{\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_k\}\subset\mathcal O_K$ is said to be \emph{admissible} if for every prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ in $\mathcal O_K$, the reductions of the $\eta_i$ modulo $\mathfrak p$ do not represent every residue class. The diameter of a finite subset $S$ of $\mathcal O_K$ is defined to be \[\mathrm{diam}(S):= \max_{\eta_i,\eta_j\in S:\eta_i\neq\eta_j}|\mathcal N(\eta_i-\eta_j)|\] where $\mathcal N$ denotes the norm down to the rational field. This paper computationally investigates admissible subsets of rings of integers in imaginary quadratic fields of class number 1 (such as the Gaussian integers or the Eisenstein integers) that are large relative to their diameter. The motivation is twofold. Firstly, there is the improvement of results analogous to the question of an upper bound for the least gap between large rational primes, which has been one of the great number theoretic successes of the twenty-first century. A second motivation is that there is the opportunity to disprove a variation of the second Hardy-Littlewood conjecture.
  The calculations in the paper provide new records on the smallest distance between primes in the fields in question, and explicit counter-examples to a generalisation of the second Hardy-Littlewood conjecture in all bar one of the fields.

papers.title: The German Tank Problem & Navigating by Scent
papers.abstract: A robot searching for the source of an odor must eventually answer a deceptively hard question: have I arrived? Near the source, concentration gradients flatten, turbulence makes the signal intermittent, and a small robot often lacks the positional accuracy to map the plume. Here, we describe a lightweight remedy inspired by a World War II statistics conundrum: the German tank problem. To approximate enemy armament production, Allied analysts developed an estimator based on serial numbers from captured tanks. Analogously, we use the same procedure over sampled chemical sensor readings from a robot to create estimates for the peak concentration of an odor plume, and therefore the odor's source. Treating each sensor reading as an observation, our unbiased estimator needs only a running maximum and a sample counter. An exact confidence bound turns both numbers into a principled rule that the robot or UAV can use to determine whether to keep searching for the plume source or land. We derive the estimator and its bound, demonstrate its sample efficiency, and examine its robustness even when its assumptions fail. Finally, we summarize the estimator's role as the termination criterion for olfactory navigation.
papers.intro:
In any navigation task, a robot must have termination criteria for knowing it has arrived at its destination. One of the most difficult problems for a robot navigating by scent is having it estimate when it is “done”. In other words, how does the robot know when it has reached the global source of the odor, and not just a local maximum concentration of the plume? In the most simplistic perspective, this is analogous to one trying to climb a mountain in the fog without the ability to ever see the top - how would one know if they have reached it? If a robot is indeed near the source but does not yet know, it may circle around trying to maximize the gradient, in turn distorting the plume and creating more turbulence in the process.

If a robot is indeed near the source but does not yet know, it may circle around trying to maximize the gradient, in turn distorting the plume and creating more turbulence in the process.

Declaring “done” is hard for compounding reasons. A typical undisturbed plume becomes simultaneously more concentrated and more homogeneous toward its source. Before we formalized the algorithm in this paper, our olfaction-only UAV would spend several seconds circling the source, chasing ever-smaller gradients [8]. Many times, this distorted the plume so much that it created currents that pulled the UAV away from the source it was already near, and drained more of the battery. Coupled with the known drift of chemical sensors [5], this mandates a sense of urgency for the robot to find the odor source as fast and with as little movement as possible.

Turbulent plumes arrive as whiffs separated by blanks [2, 4, 20], so no single reading can be decisive by itself. In addition, small platforms often cannot precisely indicate where a sample was taken: on our UAV, payload-induced bias in the inertial measurement unit made long-horizon position estimates unusable [8, 10], ruling out methods that fuse concentrations with sample locations. Concentration-based maps hold little utility in environments with wind or HVAC systems due to the constant change in chemistry, and a robot may also not know what concentration to expect at the source. Termination criteria are therefore warranted to help the robot know whether it has arrived at the plume source or should keep searching.

papers.title: Does the Outfit Change the Price? Context Halo in Vision-Language Model Valuation of an Identical Low-Cost Necklace
papers.abstract: A chunky gold-tone chain necklace bought online for 2.43 USD was photographed four ways: worn with formal attire against a wood-panelled wall, worn at a party, worn with casual clothing in a recycling yard, and laid flat with no person present. We asked six frontier language models to estimate its price in 1,164 independent and sequential API sessions (4,604 logged rows) and compared estimates across settings. Among the four models that answered image prompts, the same necklace was priced 1.9 to 3.3 times higher in the formal photograph than in the flat-lay (all p < 0.01). Against the yard photograph, the ratio ranged from 1.23 (Grok 4.5, not significant) to 3.57 (Kimi K3), with Claude Fable 5 at 3.32. A text-only version of the task, in which the setting is described in words, produced formal-to-yard ratios of 2.2 to 3.9 in all six models, so the effect does not require pixels. Flat-lay estimates themselves were 7.8 to 18.7 times the receipt price, so part of any headline "outfit multiplier" computed against the receipt is baseline overestimate, not a context effect. A single instruction to ignore clothing and setting significantly reduced the effect in one model (ratio of ratios 0.77, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.91) and not detectably in the others; telling the model the photo came from a company website or a personal account changed nothing significant. Asked afterward whether a different outfit would have changed their number, Claude Fable 5 said yes in 24 of 24 sessions, GPT-5.6 in 69%, and GPT-4o in 18%, while GPT-4o also refused 79% of image estimation prompts. The study isolates a mechanism with one object and one wearer at about 10 sessions per model and condition; we outline the replication needed next, with multiple objects and a human benchmark. Data, code, and raw outputs are released.
papers.intro:
A halo effect is the tendency for a global impression to leak into judgments of unrelated attributes. It was described in ratings of military officers (Thorndike, 1920), shown to operate without the rater’s awareness (Nisbett and Wilson, 1977), and documented for attractiveness and perceived character (Dion et al., 1972). Vision-language models (VLMs) are now used to appraise objects from photographs: listings, insurance claims, resale, customs, and e-commerce moderation. If a model prices an object partly by the person wearing it or the room it sits in, appraisals will track social cues that have nothing to do with the object.

This study asks a narrow question. Holding one low-cost necklace fixed, does the photographed context change the price a VLM estimates? The question has three parts: whether the shift exists, whether it needs the image or survives when the setting is only described in text, and whether simple interventions (an explicit debiasing instruction, a stated source of the photo) remove it. A fourth, descriptive part asks what the models say about their own reliance on context when asked afterward.

papers.title: Reproducibility, Methodological Robustness, and Synthetic-Domain Selection Properties of AFINO for TESS Stellar-Flare QPP Analysis
papers.abstract: Quasi-periodic pulsation (QPP) searches in stellar flares depend on methodological choices that can affect both classification and the interpretation of recovered periods. A defensible assessment therefore requires explicit separation of reproducibility, robustness, and known-truth performance. We characterize the reproducibility, methodological robustness, numerical behavior, and synthetic-ground-truth selection properties of a frozen public AFINO implementation in the TESS context while keeping observational reference evidence separate from known synthetic truth. The frozen baseline reproduced five published TESS detections in the initial reproduction cohort. A ten-event observational pilot and a catalogue-scale robustness experiment then tested prospectively specified temporal-window and processing perturbations. At catalogue scale, 51 of 61 published-QPP references did not reproduce their frozen reference state under the F3A baseline, so robustness claims were conditioned on baseline-concordant references rather than interpreted as accuracy. In a separately developed synthetic programme, the untouched AFINO 0.5 rule was evaluated once on an independent HELDOUT set: 152 of 1800 synthetic positives were selected and no false selections were observed among 1800 synthetic nulls, with finite Wilson uncertainty. The resulting 156-stratum selection surface and period-recovery summaries remain conditional on the frozen synthetic domain and, for period recovery, on selection; they therefore provide a bounded characterization of methodological robustness and synthetic-domain selection behavior without establishing observational validation or a population-level correction.
papers.intro:
QPPs are recurring intensity modulations reported in solar and stellar flares, but the inference problem is methodologically difficult because flare evolution, colored noise, finite observing windows, detrending, gaps, and model choice can all produce or suppress apparent periodic structure. The literature represented in the frozen Bibliographic Audit II (BAII) includes Fourier- and wavelet-based significance testing, automated model comparison, blind methodological benchmarks, and machine-learning classifiers. That diversity motivates treating a QPP catalogue entry not as a self-authenticating physical label but as an output of a specified analysis procedure whose reproducibility and robustness can be tested. Methodological diversity and significance-testing concerns are represented in the frozen corpus by Inglis et al. (2016), Pugh et al. (2017), and Broomhall et al. (2019).

AFINO is an automated model-comparison framework that evaluates competing power-spectral models and uses Bayesian information criterion differences to identify a localized excess consistent with a QPP component. Large-scale AFINO applications predate the present programme, and the frozen BAII corpus also contains catalogue-scale TESS QPP work and neural-network classification. Accordingly, the contribution evaluated here is not framed as a first-ever catalogue, catalogue-scale AFINO study, or injection-recovery experiment. Its focus is the combined prospective architecture linking public-code reproduction, observational robustness, numerical diagnostics, development-only rule assessment, and independent synthetic held-out characterization. Catalogue-scale and machine-learning precedents include Howard and MacGregor (2022), Belov et al. (2024), Joshi et al. (2025), and Wang et al. (2025).

The resulting evidence is deliberately layered. The study can describe whether published reference classifications reproduce, whether classifications change under prospectively specified perturbations, whether binary decisions are stable across external optimizer seeds, and how the frozen rule behaves under designed synthetic truth. It cannot, from these evidence classes alone, establish observational physical truth or a population correction.

A central practical difficulty is that apparently similar QPP detections can arise from pipelines with different temporal support, preprocessing, stochastic-background assumptions, and decision rules. A catalogue-level agreement or disagreement is therefore ambiguous unless the underlying implementation and input contract are specified. The frozen literature audit supports this methodological framing without implying that one existing technique is preferred. It also motivates the prospective strategy used here: define the analysis choices before examining the corresponding robustness or held-out outcome, then preserve failures and inadmissible inputs rather than editing the design around the observed result.

papers.title: Resource-Performance Trade-offs in Intra-Aisle Robotic Picking: A Discrete-Event Simulation Comparison of Shuttle Configurations With and Without an Onboard Tote Lift
papers.abstract: This study compares two implemented intra-aisle robotic-picking configurations through discrete-event simulation. Without an onboard tote lift, two level-captive shuttles serve the two tested levels; with the lift, one shuttle remains on its horizontal level and its onboard mechanism moves the order tote to allow picks from the adjacent upper level. Thirty configuration-task-size experiments (n = 1-15 locations; ten replications each) yield 300 replication-level cycle-time observations. Two-sided Welch tests are applied to the replication means, with Holm adjustment across the 15 comparisons. The onboard-tote-lift configuration has longer mean cycle time at all tested task sizes. At n = 15, the means are 299.477 and 333.231 s/cycle, respectively: a 33.753 s increase (11.27%). The corresponding cycle-time-derived item rates are 180.314 and 162.050 items/h (-10.13%). These rates are calculated as 3600n divided by the scenario-mean cycle time; they are not measurements of the combined concurrent capacity of two level-captive shuttles. Importantly, task locations are sampled from different eligible-level sets in the two configurations, so the result concerns the implemented configuration-and-task-generation packages, not the isolated effect of a five-second tote-lift operation under identical picked locations. The study quantifies a cycle-performance difference alongside a reduction from two dedicated shuttles to one within the tested two-level block; it does not quantify system-level maximum throughput, investment cost, or reliability.

papers.title: Gaussian $\beta$-Markov Path Spaces without a Spectral Gap and the Araki--Woods Representations
papers.abstract: Derezi\'nski and G\'erard constructed the Gaussian $\beta$-Markov path space of a free Bose field in a form equivalent to the Araki--Woods representation, which suits nonequilibrium statistical mechanics with a quantum-field environment, but only for one-particle Hamiltonians with a spectral gap. We extend this construction, together with the equivalence to the Araki--Woods representation, to one-particle Hamiltonians without a spectral gap. The extension is intended for constructive quantum field theory at positive temperature and equilibrium statistical mechanics, for instance in the problem of the absence of Bose--Einstein condensation of quasiparticles whose number is not conserved.
papers.intro:
Klein and Landau [7] established the correspondence between stochastically positive KMS systems and periodic stochastic processes [7, Theorem 6.1, p. 385], related the two-sided Markov property for semicircles to a cyclicity property of the KMS state [7, Theorems 11.2 and 11.4], and identified the modular conjugation with a reflection of the process [7, Section 12]. These results hold for general stochastically positive KMS systems, and their generality makes them important. Dereziński and Jakšić proved return to equilibrium for a large class of Pauli–Fierz systems at small coupling [4], a problem of nonequilibrium quantum statistical mechanics in which the environment of a small quantum system is a free Bose field and the interaction is a perturbation linear in the field [4, Section 3.1]. The textbook [5] of Dereziński and Gérard develops the framework of Klein–Landau for quantum fields at positive temperature in a form suited to such problems of nonequilibrium statistical mechanics whose environment is a quantum field. In particular, it constructs the Gaussian β\beta-Markov path space of a free Bose field in a form equivalent to the Araki–Woods representation, which is the representation on which these systems are analyzed: a unitary map from its physical Hilbert space onto the Araki–Woods Fock space intertwines the time-zero fields with the Araki–Woods Weyl operators [5, Theorem 21.58, p. 635]. This equivalence connects the stochastic process with the operator-algebraic description of the environment, and it is this construction that the present paper extends. The Araki–Woods representations are treated in [5, Section 17.1.5, pp. 437–440], and their use in [4] is recorded in [5, Section 17.4, p. 473]. In the formulation of [5, Section 21.4], for an inverse temperature β>0\beta>0, a β\beta-Markov path space is a probability space with a time-zero σ\sigma-algebra, a β\beta-periodic group of measure-preserving automorphisms, and a reflection, which satisfy the β\beta-reflection property and the Markov property for the two half circles; the reconstruction theorem [5, Theorems 21.43 and 21.47, pp. 625–626] gives a physical Hilbert space, a Liouvillean, a modular conjugation, and a β\beta-KMS state. For a one-particle Hamiltonian hh, the Gaussian example has the covariance operator (−∂t2+h2)−1\left(-\partial_{t}^{2}+h^{2}\right)^{-1} with β\beta-periodic boundary conditions in the imaginary time tt; we use the Segal normalization, in which the field has covariance 12⟨⋅,(−∂t2+h2)−1⋅⟩\frac{1}{2}\left\langle\cdot,\,\left(-\partial_{t}^{2}+h^{2}\right)^{-1}\cdot\right\rangle, and its physical Hilbert space carries the Araki–Woods representation [1] of the free Bose field at the Planck density [5, Sections 21.4.5 and 21.4.6, Theorem 21.58, pp. 633–636]. The treatment of positive-temperature path spaces there follows Klein–Landau and Gérard–Jäkel [5, Section 21.6, p. 640], [6]. Although its stated hypothesis admits them, the construction there does not cover singular one-particle Hamiltonians, that is, nonnegative injective ones with infspec⁡h=0\inf\operatorname{spec}h=0, as explained in the next paragraph. For several problems, including return to equilibrium, this restriction is harmless. In [4], the one-particle Hamiltonian of the reservoir, the multiplication by |k|\left|k\right| on L2​(ℝd)L^{2}\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right), has no spectral gap, but the analysis does not use a path space: it is carried out on the Araki–Woods representation of the reservoir and the Liouvillean of the coupled system, and the field enters only through a form factor that satisfies an infrared condition [4, opening paragraph of Section 3, Sections 3.2–3.5, Assumption 3.B, and Theorem 3.4]. The path-space formulation is also useful in constructive quantum field theory at positive temperature and in equilibrium statistical mechanics, for instance in discussing the problem, well known in theoretical physics, that quasiparticles whose number is not conserved do not undergo Bose–Einstein condensation in equilibrium [9, Section 4.2]. The quasiparticles there have the spectrum A​|k|nA\left|k\right|^{n}, A,n>0A,n>0, and their density is the Bose integral without a chemical potential [9, (21) and (32)], so their one-particle Hamiltonian has no spectral gap. In contexts where infrared singularities or the occurrence or absence of Bose–Einstein condensation are discussed, the restriction is unsatisfactory, since these are governed by the behavior of hh near zero, for instance through the zero Matsubara mode h−2h^{-2} of the covariance. The aim of this paper is to remove this restriction, and the extension is formulated for use in these discussions.

papers.title: An event is a set, not a number: building the algebra of events before the probability measure in a school progression
papers.abstract: Asked what an event is, pupils often answer with a fraction. This paper argues that school probability should separate two learnings and order them: the algebra of events (random experiment, outcomes, sample space, events as sets of outcomes, the operations not, or, and) and the probability measure, which attaches a number to each event. Before learning to compute the probability of an event, pupils should learn to build, identify and handle the event. The thesis rests on the structure of finite probability, in which the rules are facts about events carried over by an additive function, and on the history of the subject, in which errors such as d'Alembert's two tosses concerned the weighting of outcomes and were resolved by refining events into equally likely outcomes. Five design principles are stated: two objects with two names; the event before its probability; modal judgements (certain, possible, impossible) on sets before numbers; the algebra of events taught as such, with the rules derived from it; the sample space as a modelling choice, with frequencies last, as statistical estimates, and the separation repeated for conditional probability and random variables. They are confronted with the probability chapters, from age 9 to 18, of the French-curriculum courses published at https://commeunjeu.org, with research and other curricula. In primary school events precede probabilities without set notation, which comes at age 12; the lessons apply the principles and prove the rules from events in lower secondary school. But, in the version analysed, events account for 18 to 44 percent of the exercises, proofs are hidden in upper secondary school, and automatically corrected calculations record only the number. It proposes number-free tasks on events for ages 6 to 8 and changes to the International Baccalaureate curriculum. No empirical evaluation is reported; hypotheses are stated.
papers.intro:
In the author’s teaching experience, pupils of thirteen who have “done probability”, asked what an event is, often answer with a number: “an event is one half”, “the event is three out of six”. The chapters analysed below list the same confusion among “two classic mistakes”; how frequent it is remains an empirical question (Hypothesis 1). A plausible reading is that such a pupil has met the event only inside a question—“what is the probability of rolling an even number?”—whose expected answer is a fraction, and that the two objects fused in that sentence have never been separated. One of them is a set: rolling an even number is the set of outcomes {2,4,6}\{2,4,6\} of the experiment. The other is a number: the probability 12\frac{1}{2} that a model attaches to that set. The everyday way of speaking about chance tends to dissolve the object into its measure: “the probability of an even number” names the event only as the argument of a number. French didactic research met a similar difficulty with area, where a surface, its area as a magnitude and the number that measures it have to be told apart (Douady and Perrin-Glorian, 1989); the event and its probability are the analogue of the surface and its measure.

This paper argues that school probability should separate two learnings and order them. The first is the algebra of events: recognising a random experiment, listing its possible outcomes, forming the sample space, describing an event as a set of outcomes, and operating on events with the words not, or, and—the complement, the union, the intersection—together with the two extreme events, the impossible and the certain. The second is the probability measure: attaching to each event a number between 00 and 11 in a way that respects those operations. The thesis is that, before pupils learn to compute the probability of an event, they should learn to construct, identify and manipulate the event itself; and that this order is the condition of a genuine modelling approach to probability, rather than the learning of a ritual—“favourable over total”—that produces fractions about objects the pupil has never built.

The thesis is not new in mathematics: since Kolmogoroff (1933), events form an algebra of sets and probability is an additive function on it, and Kolmogorov illustrates the definition with two tosses of a coin, whose four outcomes H​HHH, H​THT, T​HTH, T​TTT make “every event […] a set of elementary events” (Kolmogorov, 1950, §2). It is not new in research either. The review of Bryant and Nunes (2012) calls working out the sample space “the first and essential step in solving any probability problem” and the lack of intervention studies on teaching it “the most glaring gap” in the field; an intervention study then showed that ten- and eleven-year-olds taught the sample space as an object of its own progressed more than comparison groups (Nunes et al., 2014); and the framework of Jones et al. (1997) treats the sample space and the probability of an event as distinct constructs. In France, the inter-IREM commission described an event as “a particular set of possible outcomes” (Henry, 2001c), and Girard noted that the programmes of the time had no sets at their disposal any more (Girard, 2001). What this paper adds is an analysis of what the thesis requires of a progression over the whole of schooling, and a confrontation of a progression that claims to apply it with the chapters that implement it. The progression is that of the French-curriculum courses of the CommeUnJeu platform, from the fourth year of primary school to the final year of secondary school; the paper also examines the early years, which the French programmes leave without probability, and the International Baccalaureate (IB) curriculum, in which the separation is less developed.

The progression rests on five principles, which the paper states, justifies and confronts with the chapters: (i) two objects: an event is a set of outcomes, a probability is a number attached to it, and the two are never conflated in words or in notation (Section 5); (ii) the event first: in every chapter, outcomes and events precede probabilities, and every calculation begins by constructing the event—in primary school without any set formalism, the event being named by a sentence and built by listing the outcomes that make it happen, and from cinquième in the language of sets (Section 6); (iii) the modal before the numerical: “impossible”, “certain” and “possible” are first judged as relations between an event and the set of possible outcomes—none, all, some—before any number is attached (Section 7); (iv) the algebra of events is taught as such, and the rules of probability are carried over from it: the complement rule from the partition into an event and its complement, the addition relation from the double counting of the intersection (Section 8); (v) the universe is a model: the choice of the outcomes and the hypothesis of equally likely outcomes are modelling decisions; the frequency of an event in a series of trials is a statistic, which estimates the probability or tests the model, and it comes at the end of the chapter, as a related notion that links probability to statistics; and the separation of the two objects is repeated at higher levels, where conditional probability changes the measure and not the events, and a random variable is a function before it has a law (Section 9).

papers.title: RubriX: A Fast, Fine-Tunable Non-Autoregressive Rubric Judge
papers.abstract: Rubric-based evaluation asks which level of a rubric a response meets. It is usually done by prompting a large language model (LLM) as a judge, which needs a generative call per judgment and reads every level description, so its cost grows with the rubric. We present RubriX, a rubric judge whose architecture is inspired by contrastive language models (CLM): a LoRA-adapted encoder embeds the input and each level description, and a softmax over scaled cosine similarities gives a probability for every level without text generation. Trained on public rubric data and proprietary synthetic data, RubriX reaches 75.4% exact accuracy on held-out rubrics, against 57.1% for TypeSafe's Jev and 49.8% for a Qwen3-8B judge. On eight human-labelled benchmark sets it is within 6 percentage points of Jev's accuracy on most of them, while Jev keeps a larger lead on two and ranks responses best on average; against the results reported in the G-Eval paper, RubriX outperforms G-Eval with GPT-3.5 on every SummEval dimension and both QAGS subsets. With level embeddings cached, RubriX's latency stays at about 28 ms per judgment as level descriptions grow from 10 to 3,000 tokens, while Jev's (approximate network time subtracted) rises from 44 ms to 211 ms and the Qwen3-8B judge's from 32 ms to 516 ms, making RubriX 7.7x faster than Jev and 18.8x faster than the Qwen3-8B judge at 3,000 tokens per level.
papers.intro:
Evaluating AI systems increasingly comes down to one repeated decision: given a response and a rubric, which level of the rubric does the response meet? This is usually done by prompting a large language model as a judge [29], as in the rubric-based metrics of Ragas [10, 23] and the G-Eval metric [18] implemented in DeepEval [5]. These approaches are flexible, since any criterion can be written as text, but every judgment needs a full generative LLM call over the whole rubric, which makes them slow and costly when applied to every response and to long rubrics. Their scores also depend on prompt wording, decoding settings and output parsing.

Evaluating AI systems increasingly comes down to one repeated decision: given a response and a rubric, which level of the rubric does the response meet? This is usually done by prompting a large language model as a judge [29], as in the rubric-based metrics of Ragas [10, 23] and the G-Eval metric [18] implemented in DeepEval [5]. These approaches are flexible, since any criterion can be written as text, but every judgment needs a full generative LLM call over the whole rubric, which makes them slow and costly when applied to every response and to long rubrics. Their scores also depend on prompt wording, decoding settings and output parsing.

RubriX takes a different approach, with an architecture inspired by contrastive language models (CLM) [2]. The response and each rubric level are embedded with a language-model encoder, and small trained heads score how well the response matches each level. A rubric is scored without text generation, returning a probability for every level, and the level embeddings can be computed once per rubric and reused for every response. Our contributions are: • A non-autoregressive rubric judge whose cost does not grow with the rubric. RubriX scores a response against a rubric’s own level descriptions with a bi-encoder: one LoRA-adapted encoder embeds the input and each level separately, so a rubric of any size is scored without generation, and its level embeddings are computed once and reused for every response it judges. • Ordinal training for a CLM-inspired architecture. The original CLM treats options as unordered. We train with cross-entropy over each rubric’s own levels plus a ranked probability score whose weight adapts to the running magnitudes of the two losses, so the ordinal term keeps about an equal share of the objective throughout training without a hand-tuned weight. Weighting losses adaptively from their running statistics is established in multi-task learning [4, 12]; we apply a simple form of it to the ordinal term. • Training data. RubriX is trained on a criterion-capped mix of public rubric datasets and a proprietary dataset. • Evaluation and latency. We compare RubriX with Jev [25], a Qwen3-8B judge [21] and the published G-Eval results [18] on held-out rubrics and eight human-labelled benchmark sets, by accuracy and by ranking correlation, and show that with cached level embeddings its latency stays flat as rubrics gain levels and longer level descriptions, while judges that read the levels slow down. The RubriX-8B model is open source and available on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/CobuildX-AI/RubriX-8B, together with code to load it and score rubrics.

papers.title: GOWC: an open tool for observing-conditions prediction and observation planning, tested against site monitors and an exposure-time calculator
papers.abstract: GOWC (Global Observing-conditions Weather Catalogue) is an open web application that takes the user from a target to an exposure plan across 2,642 catalogued observatory sites. It computes seeing, airmass, extinction, precipitable water vapour, sky brightness and signal-to-noise from live Open-Meteo meteorology, including pressure-level profiles, and tests most of these outputs against an independent reference. The photometric SNR calculator, run with GOWC's own catalogue entries, reproduces the ING SIGNAL exposure-time calculator to a median 1.9 per cent over a 16-point magnitude-airmass grid on two instruments. Precipitable water vapour tracks the Paranal LHATPRO radiometer closely ($\rho=+0.95$, 606 nights) with a +43 per cent wet bias. Seeing is computed from the Tatarski $C_n^2$ chain integrated over the pressure levels above the site and calibrated to the ESO MASS free-atmosphere median at Paranal; matching it requires an effective Tatarski coefficient of 5.7, nearly twice the upper end of the published range, which quantifies how much turbulence four coarse pressure levels fail to resolve. Against ~20 months of ESO DIMM data the seeing forecast has a weak but significant night-to-night ranking skill ($\rho=+0.24$, 575 nights, at Paranal; +0.16 at La Silla). Surface wind alone does as well or better (+0.27, +0.41) and persistence does better (+0.42, +0.47), but the free-atmosphere term tracks MASS ($\rho=+0.35$) and carries information that surface wind does not (partial $\rho=+0.28$, +0.40). At held-out sites the absolute seeing scale is no better than a constant. GOWC therefore treats forecast seeing as indicative, shows measured values wherever a public site monitor exists, and states which outputs are measured, calibrated or unvalidated.
papers.intro:
Planning a night at an optical telescope involves several steps. The observer first confirms that the target reaches a usable altitude during astronomical darkness, then estimates the conditions for that night (seeing, transparency and sky brightness with the Moon up), and finally sets an exposure time that reaches the target signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Each step depends on the one before it, but the tools that serve them are usually separate. Visibility comes from planetarium software, conditions from a weather page or forecast, and the SNR from an instrument-specific exposure-time calculator (ETC).

The observer first confirms that the target reaches a usable altitude during astronomical darkness, then estimates the conditions for that night (seeing, transparency and sky brightness with the Moon up), and finally sets an exposure time that reaches the target signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Each step depends on the one before it, but the tools that serve them are usually separate. Visibility comes from planetarium software, conditions from a weather page or forecast, and the SNR from an instrument-specific exposure-time calculator (ETC).

Dedicated tools already address parts of this chain. Astroplan computes target visibility (Morris et al., 2018), the ESO ETCs and skycalc (Noll et al., 2012) model sky brightness and exposure times, and mesoscale turbulence forecasts such as MOSE predict seeing at individual sites (Masciadri, Lascaux & Fini, 2013). Large facilities also run their own ETCs and site monitors. Most catalogued observatories, however, including many small professional, university and amateur stations, have neither. An observer at such a site, or one comparing several sites for a single target, has to combine general-purpose tools that were not designed to work together.

GOWC (Global Observing-conditions Weather Catalogue) brings this workflow into one open web application covering 2,6422{,}642 catalogued observatory sites. Its design priority is that every reported number can be traced to a published physical model or an explicit calibration, with its assumptions stated. This paper describes those models, tests them against site monitors and a professional ETC, and identifies where the method breaks down. The results support exposure-time planning, airmass and dark-time scheduling, and a water-vapour forecast with a known bias. Forecast seeing is indicative only.

This paper makes four contributions. First, it sets out a reproducible forward planning chain covering visibility, seeing, extinction, precipitable water vapour, sky brightness and photometric SNR, driven by one shared physics module across a catalogue of 2,6422{,}642 sites rather than a single facility. Second, it benchmarks the SNR calculation against a professional ETC across a grid in magnitude and airmass, using the instrument constants an observer actually gets. Third, it measures the night-to-night skill of the seeing forecast over a 20-month hindcast, in which the model is run on archived weather and compared with ESO Astronomical Site Monitor measurements. It compares that skill with two baselines an observer already has, persistence and surface wind, and reports what the calibration implies about the input data. Fourth, it states for each quantity whether the output is backed by measurement, calibrated, or passed through without validation.

papers.title: Supercritical Geometric Optics for multidimensional scalar conservation laws
papers.abstract: This article studies the propagation, near a smooth non-constant ground state, of monophase oscillatory wave trains with small amplitude and very high frequency for multidimensional nonlinear scalar conservation laws. These oscillations lie beyond the classical regime of uniformly bounded variation. Two scenarios may occur. Under suitable compatibility conditions, the oscillations propagate. Otherwise, they are damped through shock formation. In the baseline supercritical regime, we give an explicit criterion distinguishing these two behaviors and justify the corresponding asymptotic descriptions. At higher frequencies, the propagation mechanism becomes more restrictive and is governed by compatibility conditions involving a Lie algebra. Under a natural local constant-rank assumption, we obtain a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of complete WKB expansions. We also prove cancellation under first-order incompatibility. Perturbing a non-constant background state limits the propagation of small scales compared with the constant-background case. Our constructions contribute to the understanding of the fractional smoothing effect conjectured by Lions, Perthame and Tadmor.

papers.title: Macro Mondrian Conformal Risk Control
papers.abstract: Conformal Risk Control (CRC) extends conformal prediction beyond the coverage setting to the control of general monotone loss functions, in a distribution-free and modelagnostic fashion. This makes it well-suited to problems with high-dimensional targets, such as the semantic segmentation task addressed in this work. However, CRC guarantees only marginal control, meaning that the risk is controlled on average over the data distribution. Under imbalanced distributions, the risk on inputs that contain rare objects may therefore remain uncontrolled, even when the marginal guarantee holds. We propose a new method that controls the risk on average over user-defined groups of the domain, drawing on Mondrian conformal prediction and macro-coverage algorithms. The method relies on a taxonomy, that is, a function that assigns a group to each data point, and reweights each point's risk by a coefficient that depends on its group probability, so that rare points contribute more than common ones. We illustrate the approach on two semantic segmentation datasets.

papers.title: Blendshape Generation for Models with Disconnected Parts: Adding ARKit/MediaPipe Blendshapes to Anime-Style Character Models
papers.abstract: Blendshape generation for 3D models has been extensively researched, but very few works address generating blendshapes for models with multiple disconnected parts. We present a case study of generating fixed facial expression blendshapes for commercial anime-style 3D character models with up to 11 parts per face. To make sure that our system can handle models in a way that is agnostic to topology, we train neural networks to generate deformation fields around the input meshes. We employ at least one network to independently process each part, and the relative positions of their outputs are coordinated by having each network also process the geometry of an anchor part. We use two mechanisms to improve accuracy: having the networks predict whether the output displacement is zero or not, and classifying blendshapes into different size groups and dedicating a network to each group. We also introduce a method to improve blendshape quality by enhancing bilateral symmetry. Our method is simpler than recent neural-network-based works and solves a real problem of the user community of these models.
papers.intro:
3D character models used in games and simulations are typically triangular meshes. The most widespread method to animate their faces is shape interpolation. It involves preparing multiple meshes, called blendshapes [9], with the same topology11 1 The vertices and their connections are isomorphic in the graph-theoretic sense. but different vertex positions. An expressive face requires several tens of blendshapes: commercial libraries for facial expression tracking such as ARKit [5] and MediaPipe [18] require 52. Creating them manually is labor-intensive.

We propose a novel data-driven method for blendshape generation for real-world, commercial 3D character models. Our specific task is to generate ARKit blendshapes for humanoid character models from VRoid [35], a platform for anime-style 3D avatars with an international audience [32]. Such models are created with software called VRoid Studio [34], but it does not generate the ARKit blendshapes.

Our specific task is to generate ARKit blendshapes for humanoid character models from VRoid [35], a platform for anime-style 3D avatars with an international audience [32]. Such models are created with software called VRoid Studio [34], but it does not generate the ARKit blendshapes.

The VRoid user community has been trying to solve the problem since 2020, referring to the ability to control VRoid models with ARKit face tracking as “Perfect Sync” [28]. Third-party developers built it into their avatar software [26, 24, 16]. Others published tools to transfer blendshapes from one VRoid model to another [25, 38]. Nevertheless, these solutions simply copy blendshapes from a source model [19] to the target. They do not work when the target has a different number of vertices or when certain facial parts are bigger or smaller than those of the source. (See Figure 9 for an example of the latter problem.)

Meanwhile, the graphics community has been researching blendshape generation under the name of “deformation transfer” [39]. Recent techniques successfully address differences in topology and shape between the source and the target [2, 37, 45, 23]. However, we encountered problems when trying to apply them to VRoid models. Many works assume that the input mesh has only one connected part, but the face of a VRoid model has up to 11 disconnected parts (Figure 2). Furthermore, they are either too simple or too complex. Some assume that there is only one blendshape to transfer [2], but we have 52. Some assume that the input blendshape can be arbitrarily sampled from a distribution [37, 11], but our blendshapes are fixed yet numerous. One even requires a video generation model to help estimate the target movement [23].

Our proposed method builds on previous research, enabling it to handle a variety of topologies and shapes. To deform a single part, we employ what we call a neural deformation field (NDF) network. It has two types of subnetworks: a number of shape encoders and a displacement decoder. The shape encoders transform the input mesh into a number of shape codes, and the displacement decoder converts the codes to a displacement vector for every vertex. We design them to address challenges specific to our task: the presence of disconnected parts and a sizable number of fixed blendshapes. Namely, we employ a set of networks, with at least one NDF network to process each part independently, while using the largest part, the face skin, to help the networks position their outputs. We improve the performance by introducing a classification loss and by adding more networks to the set so that each network is responsible for fewer blendshapes.

papers.title: Non-local Interfacial Energies in Grain Boundaries via Dirichlet-to-Neumann Map and Energetic scaling
papers.abstract: This paper deals with the variational analysis of edge dislocations arising in small-angle grain boundaries (Read--Shockley) and semi-coherent interfaces (van der Merwe). Using the Nabarro--Peierls approach to model edge dislocations, we reduce the two-dimensional isotropic Navier--Lam\'e system governing the linearized elastic energy to a one-dimensional non-local energy on the slip interface through a Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. We prove that the resulting boundary energy coincides, up to a multiplicative constant, with the fractional \(H^{\frac12}\)-Gagliardo seminorm of the displacement jump along the interface. Within this framework, we establish the existence of a unique global minimizer by combining our dimensional-reduction result with the characterization of De Luca, Goldman, and Ponsiglione. Indeed, we show that the optimal defect configuration is uniquely attained, up to translations, by an equispaced periodic array. Finally, we provide a physical rescaling that recovers the classical logarithmic energy regimes of both the Read--Shockley and van der Merwe models.
papers.intro:
The study of crystal defects, and in particular dislocations, is a central theme in materials science and solid mechanics, as these line defects represent the primary carriers of plastic deformation in crystalline solids [16]. While classical continuum elasticity provides an accurate description of the stress and strain fields away from the defects, it is no longer valid close to the dislocation lines; indeed, it predicts diverging elastic energies at the so-called defect cores. To bridge the gap between the discrete atomistic structure of crystals and continuum elastic theories, the seminal models of Nabarro and Peierls [20, 21] introduced a multiscale description in which the crystal is treated as a linear elastic continuum away from a prescribed slip plane, while a non-linear potential accounts for the atomic mismatch across the interface. The study of crystal defects, and in particular dislocations, is a central theme in materials science and solid mechanics, as these line defects represent the primary carriers of plastic deformation in crystalline solids [16]. While classical continuum elasticity provides an accurate description of the stress and strain fields away from the defects, it is no longer valid close to the dislocation lines; indeed, it predicts diverging elastic energies at the so-called defect cores. To bridge the gap between the discrete atomistic structure of crystals and continuum elastic theories, the seminal models of Nabarro and Peierls [20, 21] introduced a multiscale description in which the crystal is treated as a linear elastic continuum away from a prescribed slip plane, while a non-linear potential accounts for the atomic mismatch across the interface. In this paper, we aim to describe the emergence and the energetic characterization of dislocations in two distinct physical configurations: grain boundaries and semi-coherent interfaces. Both frameworks can be viewed, in a simplified setting, as the matching of two square crystal lattices along a one-dimensional interface.

For small-angle grain boundaries, as described by the classical Read–Shockley theory [23], the two phases consist of identical lattices that are slightly rotated with respect to each other, for instance by angles θ\theta and −θ-\theta. In the case of semi-coherent interfaces, whose classical description dates back to van der Merwe [27], the lattices have the same orientation but different spacing, resulting in a mismatch. In both cases, the geometric incompatibility between the two bulk lattices prevents a coherent matching across the interface. The accumulation of macroscopic elastic strain is then relieved through the formation of arrays of dislocations localized close to the interface.

From a variational point of view, this mechanism can be described through the competition between bulk elastic energy and the energetic cost associated to the formation of defects. A first rigorous derivation of the Read–Shockley logarithmic scaling without any a priori prescription on the number, position, or nature of the defects was obtained in the seminal work of Lauteri and Luckhaus [17]. Their result is composed of a delicate lower bound estimate and an explicit upper bound of the scaling, which has also been obtained by Scardia and Tolotti [25] by means of a different construction. Building on their deep analysis, Fortuna, Garroni, and Spadaro [9] subsequently upgraded their work to a Γ\Gamma-convergence result for grain boundaries. This sharp interface approach has also inspired recent phase-field models designed to incorporate crystallographic symmetries [3]. In a parallel direction, the first author, together with E. Spadaro, is currently studying a Lauteri–Luckhaus-type model for semi-coherent interfaces, with the aim of deriving the corresponding van der Merwe scaling. The resulting picture is consistent with the analysis developed in the present paper and suggests closely related qualitative mechanisms for grain boundaries and semi-coherent interfaces. Recently, the Read–Shockley scaling was also recovered in [14] by minimizing the discrete elastic energy associated to the Volterra potential.

papers.title: A curated global dataset of open science initiatives and policies
papers.abstract: Inventories of open science initiatives differ in scope, geographic coverage and classification, making it difficult to compare infrastructures, services, networks and policies. We developed COSMI Hub within the OPENIT project to bring these sources together in a curated dataset. The release archived on 8 October 2026 contains 1,186 records and 71 variables covering initiative identity, source provenance, geography, record level, operational status, thematic activities, governance, funding and external identifiers. We identified candidates through structured directories, policy documents, official websites and suggestions from the open science community, then checked identities, reconciled duplicates and assessed supporting evidence. The dataset distinguishes standalone initiatives, services, deployments, umbrella organisations and policy instruments. Records can be assigned several thematic dimensions, with uncertainty retained where evidence is incomplete. We describe the collection and coding methods, the data structure and file-level checks, together with considerations for reuse. The Zenodo release is fixed, whereas the companion dashboard is updated separately. Because we assembled the collection purposively, it cannot be used to estimate the worldwide number of open science initiatives.

papers.title: Bounds on the number of squares in recurrence sequences: $y_{0}=b^{2}$ (II)
papers.abstract: For binary recurrence sequences, $\left( y_{k} \right)_{k \in \bbZ}$, arising from the solutions of generalised Pell equations, $X^{2}-dY^{2}=c$, where $y_{0}$ is any positive square and $c=-2^{\ell}p^{m}$ for an odd prime $p$ and non-negative integers $\ell$ and $m$, we show that there are at most $4$ distinct squares with $y_{k}$ sufficiently large. From this result, we also show that there are at most $7$ distinct squares when $y_{0}=1,2^{2},\ldots,7^{2}$, or once $d$ exceeds an explicit lower bound, without any conditions on the size of such squares.

papers.title: Sequential versus fully conditional specification for tree-based synthesis of health data
papers.abstract: Disseminating synthetic data in place of original ones is a promising way to enforce privacy while complying with open science principles, especially in the healthcare domain. To keep pace with the rate at which researchers collect such data, there is a need for fast and flexible synthesis procedures. A popular class of such procedures is based on models of conditional distributions induced by decision trees. Such models can be combined into a synthetic distribution following two main approaches: sequential specification and fully conditional specification. However, there is currently no recommendation on which specification to use to optimize the risk-utility tradeoffs. In this work, we use both specifications to synthesize medical datasets by combining tree-based models of conditional distributions. We compare the quality of the resulting synthetic data using several metrics of risk and utility. Our results indicate no general superiority of either specification over the other. Sequential synthesis seems sensitive to the ordering of the variables, while the fully conditional specification involves more hyperparameters and incurs higher computational costs, which may limit its suitability for off-the-shelf synthesis procedures.

papers.title: Shape-Preserving Treatment Effects for Functional Outcomes
papers.abstract: By recording health measurements daily rather than at a few clinical visits, connected devices pave the way for more precise real-world evidence that measures how the effect of an intervention unfolds over time: does the response rebound, peak late, or oscillate? Yet causal methods for such functional outcomes remain scarce, and those that exist target the Functional Average Treatment Effect (FATE). Its pointwise averaging flattens the features patients share whenever their curves are misaligned in time, as is common with biosignals, where patients respond with their own timing. We develop a causal inference framework that captures the shape of the effect of a binary intervention, based on the phase-centered elastic mean from elastic shape analysis. We lift this mean from a sample statistic to a functional of the data-generating law and prove that it is well defined under explicit geometric assumptions. Because it is not linear, it yields three causal estimands instead of one: populational, individual and local. We identify the populational estimand by inverse-probability weighting and the local estimand through the conditional outcome laws, estimate them by weighting and by matching, and show that the individual one is not identifiable. On simulations with timing variability or heterogeneous effect shapes, our estimators recover the shape that the FATE loses. On real weight trajectories following GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation, they reveal a rebound that the FATE averages away. This framework thus gives clinicians a treatment-effect curve whose shape and timing reflect genuine patient trajectories rather than a misalignment artifact.
papers.intro:
In medicine, the gold standard to prove a drug’s effect is the Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT): as treatment is given at random, the treated and control groups have the same characteristics, so that any difference in outcomes observed in the two groups can be attributed to the causal effect of the treatment. Causal inference provides the formal framework for the analysis of such trials, and also for the far more frequent situation in which randomisation is absent. When only observational data are available, the standard formulation is to emulate a target trial (Hernán and Robins, 2016): one states the trial that would have answered the question, then adjusts for confounding to recover the causal effect under explicit assumptions.

Causal inference provides the formal framework for the analysis of such trials, and also for the far more frequent situation in which randomisation is absent. When only observational data are available, the standard formulation is to emulate a target trial (Hernán and Robins, 2016): one states the trial that would have answered the question, then adjusts for confounding to recover the causal effect under explicit assumptions.

The classical setting, where one studies the impact of a scalar treatment on a scalar outcome, has been intensively studied in the literature (Hernán and Robins, 2020; Imbens and Rubin, 2015), starting from a settled choice of the quantity to be identified and estimated, called the causal estimand. In that setting, the most common way to measure an average effect on the difference scale is the Average Treatment Effect (ATE). Write Y(1)Y^{(1)} and Y(0)Y^{(0)} for the potential outcomes of a unit, that is the outcomes that it would have under treatment and no treatment, respectively. The ATE is then the difference between their expectations τATE=𝔼⁡[Y(1)]−𝔼⁡[Y(0)].\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}=\mathbb{E}[Y^{(1)}]-\mathbb{E}[Y^{(0)}]. Note that ratio scales, such as the risk ratio, define an average effect as well. We work throughout on the difference scale.

However, in many applications, the outcome of interest is not a scalar but a function, more specifically a curve indexed by time. Examples include body weight over the year, hormonal variations, physical-activity intensity across the day. Outcomes of this kind are becoming ordinary rather than exceptional: connected scales, wearable devices and health applications now record them day by day, for large populations and over long follow-up. In this paper, we restrict ourselves to the setting of a binary treatment acting on such functional outcomes. Note that only the outcome is time-dependent and that the treatment is assigned once at baseline, which places our problem outside the literature on time-varying treatments, dynamic regimes, and marginal structural models (Hernán and Robins, 2020), where time parametrises the interventions themselves. First, one can always reduce the functional outcome to a scalar, for instance by taking the average of the curve over time, or by taking its maximum value. This aggregation, however, discards clinical information carried by the individual trajectories, and the resulting quantity may not answer the scientific question at hand. A single number cannot describe all the ways a treatment shapes the short-term and the long-term evolution of a trajectory. Alternatively, the functional outcome can be reduced to the distributions of its values at each time point, as done in Chabassier et al. (2026), to leverage the growing literature on distributional causal inference (Lin et al., 2023; Katta et al., 2024). This literature treats distribution-valued outcomes via Wasserstein barycenters, with specific functional causal estimands designed for this setting. However, these approaches discard the temporal structure in the trajectories: an increasing curve and a decreasing one can have the same distribution of values, but usually yield very different clinical interpretations.

In order to fully capture all the clinical information contained in the functional outcomes, one needs to develop suitable functional causal inference methodologies, able to estimate the impact of a scalar treatment on entire trajectories. Despite the growing availability of functional data, this field has received relatively little attention, especially regarding the choice of tailored estimands. Designing suitable causal estimands is, however, not as straightforward as in the scalar case. Indeed, given the higher-dimensional nature of functional outcomes, several causal estimands can be defined, each targeting a different aspect of the treatment’s impact. Some may capture the typical values the functional outcomes take at each time point, others the typical shape of the response over time: does it rebound, peak late, or oscillate? We review below the few existing proposals and their limitations, before presenting ours.

These works, however, leave aside a property of pointwise averaging that is well established in Functional Data Analysis (FDA): averaging at fixed time points does not preserve shape. This phenomenon is called amplitude flattening (Marron et al., 2015; Srivastava and Klassen, 2016; Srivastava et al., 2011): when curves are misaligned in time, the pointwise mean fails to capture the shape of the individual curves, spreading for example sharp peaks into low, wide bumps that are shorter than any individual’s. This misalignment of individual curves, called phase variation, is very common in functional data, especially biosignals. Consider for instance growth curves in children: while all children go through the same growth peaks, they do so at different ages, and the pointwise mean of their growth curves will not capture the typical shape pattern of a child’s growth curve (Srivastava and Klassen, 2016).

papers.title: A cohomology operation encoding the octahedral axiom
papers.abstract: We introduce a new secondary cohomology operation, the naturality defect product, associated with a graded natural transformation between the cohomology functors of two differential graded functors, and study its main properties. We then prove that a pretriangulated category satisfies the octahedral axiom if and only if the naturality defect product associated with the natural isomorphism given by a theorem of Heller vanishes on the homotopy category of acyclic complexes over it. This characterization extends immediately to n-angulated categories. As an application, we exhibit non-vanishing instances for the recently found examples of pretriangulated categories which are not triangulated. Finally, we show that horizontal composition of these natural isomorphisms preserves n-angulated structures, and we use it to obtain, from each of these examples and for every r >= 1, a pre-3r-angulated category which is not 3r-angulated.

Triangulated categories were introduced in the early 1960s by D. Puppe [Pup62] in the context of algebraic topology and by J.-L. Verdier [Ver96] in algebraic geometry. Since then, they have become a fundamental tool not only in those fields, but also in other areas such as representation theory, and have been studied extensively in the literature. Verdier’s axiomatization, however, included an additional axiom absent from Puppe’s, the so-called octahedral axiom.

papers.title: Regular Graphs Without Isomorphic Bisections
papers.abstract: A graph is bisectable if its vertex set can be split into two sets inducing isomorphic subgraphs. Ando conjectured that every cubic graph is bisectable, and Das, Pokrovskiy, and Sudakov proved it for large enough connected cubic graphs. We give a constructive proof that, for every $d\geq5$, there exists a non-bisectable $d$-regular graph of even order.

papers.title: Identities, Not Pairs: Distribution-Free False-Accept Control for Embedding-Based Verification
papers.abstract: Embedding-based verification often calibrates a false-accept threshold from all impostor pairs among $m$ identities, although these pairs share identities. We characterize a worst-case limit: when hub identities score highly against a fraction $\rho$ of the population, a calibration-only threshold with marginal false-accept rate (FAR) at most $\alpha$ under every identity-exchangeable law reaches the hub score on hub-free calibration sets with probability at most $(m+2)\alpha/(2\rho)$. Uniformly accepting near that score at levels well below $\rho/m$ therefore requires trial information. We propose COVE, which ranks the trial pair among all $N=\binom{m+2}{2}$ pairs formed by augmenting the calibration units with the probe and reference. Under identity exchangeability, its marginal FAR is at most $\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor/N$, with first possible acceptance at $1/N=O(1/m^2)$. The rule also retains this guarantee with a fixed symmetric cohort-normalized score using an independent cohort. On 6 benchmarks and 8 frozen encoders, realised FAR was consistent with the exact bound. Where both valid calibration-only baselines accepted nothing, COVE retained a median $100\%$ of the sampled oracle's true-accept rate over reliable comparisons. In contrast, an empirical quantile over dependent pairs reached 2.87$\,\alpha$ FAR, and a binomial upper confidence bound over pairs missed its nominal 95\% conditional-FAR target in up to 55\% of calibration draws. Symmetric CSLS raised COVE's true-accept rate by up to 4.3-fold in the tested settings. The code is available in https://github.com/salimkhazem/Cove.git
papers.intro:
A large class of vision systems decides whether two images show the same identity by thresholding the similarity of frozen embeddings: product and landmark retrieval, animal re-identification, near-duplicate removal in dataset curation, and open-set matching with foundation encoders such as DINOv2 or CLIP, whether deployed directly or tailored via parameter-efficient adaptation, visual prompting, or distillation [Khazem, 2026a, Khazem, 2026c, Khazem, 2026b] face and person verification rest on the same decision, but we do not study them. The operator of such a system specifies a tolerated false-accept rate (FAR) the probability of declaring a match between two different identities and it is typically small, 10−410^{-4} to 10−610^{-6}. The threshold is set on a labelled calibration set, and the standard recipe takes a quantile of the similarity over all impostor pairs, the m⁡(m−1)/2m(m-1)/2 pairs of images from different calibration identities, often with a binomial confidence bound that treats the pairs as independent draws. Those pairs are not independent: every identity appears in m−1m-1 of them, and an identity that resembles many others, a “wolf” in the biometric zoo Doddington et al. [1998], a “hub” in high-dimensional retrieval Radovanović et al. [2010], inflates many pair scores at once. This paper asks what can be guaranteed, without distributional assumptions, from mm calibration identities, and answers with a separation.

papers.title: Quadratic Returns for a Moving Water Tank: An Explicit Right Inverse and a Sylvester Representation
papers.abstract: Coron's return method established local nonlinear controllability of a moving water tank in sufficiently large time. We study the quadratic response at uniform equilibrium, where the acceleration input in the linearized model cannot excite the Fourier modes of the fluid with even indices. At three one-way wave crossings (T=3), we construct a nonzero smooth acceleration, whose first two final-state coefficients vanish. A planar curve reduces this cancellation to a scalar identity. At this reference acceleration, two integrations give an explicit control correction that preserves the linear return and produces any given leading change in the quadratic final state. The correction maps periodic $H^r$ targets with zero mean to $H^r$ controls for every nonnegative integer $r$. A contraction argument also gives local exact solvability of the quadratic final-state equation. Finally, a time-dependent Sylvester equation provides an alternative representation of the coupling responsible for the second-order correction. The associated change of state coordinates involves one spatial derivative, while the control correction preserves regularity in appropriate Sobolev spaces. These results concern the first two variation equations and not yet the fully nonlinear model.
papers.intro:
A tank moved by a single horizontal actuator can develop various fluid oscillations. The problem is relevant to the transport of partially filled containers, where the motion of the container also excites the liquid. For the inviscid Saint-Venant model at a uniform equilibrium, considered here, the acceleration (control input) in the linearized model excites only the spatial Fourier modes with odd indices. The modes with even indices can, therefore, be controlled only through nonlinear interactions.

In [1, 2], explicit motion planning for the linearized tank was developed. In [3, Thm. 2], Coron established local controllability of the nonlinear shallow-water model (inviscid Saint-Venant equations) in sufficiently large time by the return method. An obstruction below two one-way wave crossings (T<2T<2) was later proved in [4], whose unfolding and quadratic analysis are used here. However, this lower bound does not imply controllability at every longer time. papers.title: Comparing and measuring intermediate tail dependence
papers.abstract: The tail dependence function $\Lambda$ of a bivariate copula, and the tail dependence order based on it, cannot distinguish between copulas whose tail dependence coefficient vanishes; for all of them $\Lambda\equiv 0$. Such copulas, among them the Gaussian copulas with correlation $\rho<1$ and the lower tails of all extreme-value copulas other than the comonotonicity copula, are nevertheless ordered by the much finer information contained in their tail expansion $C(u w)\sim u^{\kappa}\ell(u)\,b(w)$, where $\kappa$ is the tail order, $\ell$ is slowly varying and $b$ is the tail order function of Hua and Joe. We introduce an asymptotic tail order $\preceq$ that refines the tail dependence order and show that it is lexicographic in the three quantities $\kappa$, $\ell$ and $b$. As a consequence, every real-valued measure that is monotone with respect to $\preceq$ is constant on all but countably many tail-order classes; meaningful measures of intermediate tail dependence must therefore be defined level-wise, and we construct such measures. Finally we determine where the fine structure resides: if the joint tail is ray-regular on the exponential scale, then $b$ is determined by the tail order and the one-sided derivatives at $\omega=1/2$ of the angular dependence function of Wadsworth and Tawn; it is a (possibly broken) product of powers. If the joint tail is log-concave on the exponential scale, $b$ is squeezed between two such products.

papers.title: The monotone part of Chatterjee's rank correlation
papers.abstract: Chatterjee's rank correlation $\xi$ measures how strongly a random variable $Y$ depends functionally on a random variable $X$, but it does not distinguish increasing, decreasing and non-monotone relationships. We ask how much of the dependence measured by $\xi$ is explained by an increasing relationship. For continuous marginals, $\xi$ is, up to a factor, a squared distance from independence in a Hilbert space geometry derived from the Sobolev scalar product for copulas. We answer it by the metric projection onto the closed convex set of stochastically increasing copulas in this geometry. The projection is explicit: it replaces every vertical section by its least concave majorant, and it coincides with the smallest stochastically increasing copula dominating the given one. It splits $\xi$ orthogonally into a monotone part $\xi^{\uparrow}$ and the squared distance to the class of stochastically increasing copulas; dually, $\xi^{\uparrow}$ is, up to a factor, the squared distance to the polar cone, which corresponds to negative quadrant dependence. The monotone part vanishes exactly for negatively quadrant dependent copulas, equals $\xi$ exactly for stochastically increasing copulas, and equals one only for the comonotonicity copula. In contrast to $\xi$, it is increasing in the concordance order and continuous with respect to weak convergence. Symmetrisation decomposes the measure of mutual complete dependence in the same way. Finally, the construction extends to arbitrary distributions via isotonic regression of conditional distribution functions. In particular, the plug-in estimator based on the empirical distribution is strongly consistent for every copula, without smoothing or tuning parameters.
