papers.title: From one particle to N particles: uniform transport-information and log-Sobolev inequalities for Coulomb gases on the torus
papers.abstract: We study how a functional inequality satisfied by the one-particle conditional distributions of a Gibbs measure, with a constant independent of the positions of the other particles, can be propagated to the whole N -particle system, with a constant independent of N , when the interaction is singular. Our model is the Coulomb gas on the torus T 3 in the mean-field regime. We distinguish two mechanisms. The first one is a dependent tensorization, governed by Dobrushin-Wu interdependence coefficients. It yields uniform Poincar{\'e} and transport-information W 2 I inequalities with fully explicit constants. We explain why this mechanism does not extend to the log-Sobolev inequality: the Zegarlinski-type coefficients, which require pointwise bounds on the interaction, are infinite. The second mechanism is a tensorization with a defect. Using a uniform bound on the partition function due to Duerinckx and Jabin, it yields a uniform log-Sobolev inequality for the Coulomb gas on T 3 at small charge. We identify the assumptions on the interaction under which each mechanism applies. All the results are then extended to the two-dimensional Coulomb gas and to periodic Riesz gases 1/|x|^s , 0 < s $\le$ 1. The extension to d $\ge$ 4 is also discussed.

papers.title: Encoding Time Series Dynamics with Sliding-Window Signatures for Online Forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting often relies on both past target values and exogenous variables as inputs. In many applications, however, the time series of interest are non-stationary and the relationship between target and inputs evolves over time, requiring forecasters that adapt online. Moreover, inputs affect the target not only through their current values but also through their recent joint dynamics. We address these challenges in three steps. First, to encode the series dynamics, we rely on signatures of the input paths over sliding windows. Motivated by the universality of linear functionals of signatures, we fit a regularized linear regression on these features to capture nonlinear, path-dependent effects. Second, the simplicity of the linear model allows us to update it online as new data arrives, using a Kalman filter to track dynamic effects. Third, to capture dependencies at several time scales, we combine forecasters built on different window lengths through online aggregation. For French national electricity load forecasting, our method outperforms various state-of-the-art approaches. It also remains competitive across several benchmark datasets with exogenous variables.

papers.title: Determinants of Dirichlet and Neumann Laplacians on Constant Curvature Surfaces with Geodesic Polygonal Boundary
papers.abstract: We express the zeta regularized determinants of the Dirichlet and Neumann Laplacians on compact Riemann surfaces with constant curvature metrics and geodesic polygonal boundary in terms of the Laplacian determinant on their closed conical doubles. The formulae apply without restrictions on the genus or number of boundary components. They involve explicit corner angle factors and a quotient of the Reidemeister and $L^2$ norms on the determinant line of cohomology. The proof combines a relative BFK gluing formula with the comparison theorem for analytic and combinatorial torsion on manifolds with boundary, due to L\"uck and Vishik. As an application, we give a rigorous proof of the Aurell-Salomonson formula for Euclidean polygons. We also obtain explicit determinants for spherical and hyperbolic triangles and certain other geodesic polygons from known formulae for their doubles.

papers.title: Acceleration of the BSS Algorithm
papers.abstract: Bartel, Sch\"{a}fer and Ullrich investigated the BSS subsampling algorithm, which is based on the work by Batson, Spielman and Srivastava. While this algorithm works well, the bottleneck is its complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\sigma^2nm^3)$ for a frame of $n$ vectors of dimension $m$ and oversampling $\sigma^2$. We continue their work by showing that the algorithm can be implemented in $\mathcal{O}(\sigma^2nm^{2.5})$. Moreover, for some special cases, an even faster implementation is possible. In particular, BSS subsampling of Fourier-type frames on a full frequency cube can be implemented in essentially $\mathcal{O}(\sigma^2m^2(n+m^{1.5}))$.}

papers.title: Survey on Favard length and rectifiability
papers.abstract: We overview recent results quantifying the Besicovitch projection theorem, focusing on the theory of quantitative rectifiability and connection to Vitushkin's conjecture.
papers.intro:
The study of relation between rectifiability and projections is a classical line of research in geometric measure theory, dating back to Besicovitch’s landmark article from 1939 [Bes39]. In this article we overview the efforts to quantify Besicovitch’s result, which were motivated by the theory of quantitative rectifiability and Vitushkin’s conjecture.

Other recent surveys on problems involving Favard length are [Łab14, Tay24]. In [Łab14] Łaba discusses in depth the Favard length problem, which we only briefly describe in Subsection 2.5. In [Tay24] Taylor concentrates on the connections to fractal geometry and non-linear projection theorems. Here we will focus on the theory of quantitative rectifiability and applications to the study of analytic capacity.

papers.title: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization reveals HiPIMS deposition rates exceeding direct current sputtering
papers.abstract: Pulsed sputter processes are essential for a wide range of applications from hard coatings to microelectronics. High power impulse magnetron sputtering (HiPIMS) offers unique possibilities for process design due to its high ionized flux fraction. Because of the high peak-current densities involved, correspondingly high plasma densities generate many ions. This enables tuning of kinetic energies by applying accelerating bias potentials. However, some HiPIMS processes have low deposition rates due to the back-attraction these ions experience with the negatively charged sputter target. Recent work in HiPIMS has targeted this problem, exploring complex pulsing schemes such as bipolar, multi-pulse, or chopped HiPIMS. These pulsing schemes introduce another problem: process complexity. As such, the process space, even with coarse intervals quickly blows up to 1E5-1E20 possible process combinations. This calls for efficient and intelligent sampling, which can be enabled by machine-learning algorithms such as Bayesian optimization. In this work we use multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) to efficiently sample the process space of pulse-packets, targeting high ionization flux fractions and deposition rates. Over 2,000 distinct processes were sampled during this exploration. Surprisingly, we found that many HiPIMS processes, including single pulse, can achieve deposition rates higher than DC references. In fact, at a working pressure of 1.0 Pa and moderate ionization rates of 5-20% we found that ms-scale pulses were ideal. We hypothesize these processes maximize gas rarefaction, creating a low-collision channel between the target and the substrate. These results showcase previously unreported behavior of pulsed sputter processes and challenge a long-held trade-off between film quality and speed in thin-film manufacturing.

papers.title: Synthetic Deformable Tubular Benchmark: A mechanically annotated dataset for evaluating deformable 3D reconstruction
papers.abstract: Evaluating deformable 3D reconstruction requires ground truth linking camera motion, surface deformation, material correspondence and image appearance. We introduce the Synthetic Deformable Tubular Benchmark, generated with LumenMorph, an open-source toolkit for creating, annotating and evaluating tubular scenes. The release contains 5,580 RGB images. Its baseline crosses three surface-motion conditions with moving and stationary cameras in six scene families; matched appearance variants cover only moving-camera finite-element actions in four families. Documented public and evaluation interfaces expose camera poses, geometry, depth, deformation fields, persistent material correspondences and discrete finite-element records. Persistent triangle identities and material weights let users track the same surface location across frames and query its three-dimensional trajectory. Separately implemented geometric and mechanical checks assess annotation consistency with the generating models. Structure-from-motion, optical-flow and supplied-geometry displacement-interpolation studies demonstrate how the resource distinguishes registration coverage from geometric accuracy, exposes camera- and surface-motion effects, and tests the benefits and mismatch of mechanical priors. Public readers, evaluation contracts and the configurable generator support reuse and extension. Data integrity, fixed-environment repeatability and retained-prediction score replay have distinct verification scopes. The benchmark provides a controlled synthetic reference without claiming anatomical or clinical realism.
papers.intro:
Deformable reconstruction in colonoscopy must distinguish camera motion from surface motion under limited visibility. A rigid reconstruction accumulated over time can absorb deformation into biased camera poses or geometry. Surface similarity alone may also conceal correspondence errors: a nearby surface point need not be the same material point—a fixed location on the wall followed as it moves. Evaluation therefore requires linked observations, material identities, geometry and visibility, together with explicit assumptions about the motion-generating model. Known camera poses alone do not resolve the inverse deformation problem.

We present the Synthetic Deformable Tubular Benchmark, a controlled synthetic resource (Cirauqui-Viloria, 2026c). It was generated with LumenMorph, an openly available generator and evaluation toolkit (Cirauqui-Viloria, 2026a). Figure 1 introduces the six scene families: one straight and five bent tubes, each observed under paired motion and camera conditions. A matched appearance extension changes lighting, reflectance and exposure on four of these same families. The resource links material trajectories, discrete finite-element (FE) records, image annotations and estimated reconstructions. This connection allows a user to ask not only whether a surface looks correct, but whether the same material points move correctly and whether missing surface support explains an apparently low error. Data, code and reproduction resources are identified in Sections 7–8.

This connection allows a user to ask not only whether a surface looks correct, but whether the same material points move correctly and whether missing surface support explains an apparently low error. Data, code and reproduction resources are identified in Sections 7–8.

The methodological contribution is a benchmark with an explicit, accessible and checked connection between image observations, camera states, persistent material identities, deformed geometry and discrete mechanical records. This integration lets researchers evaluate reconstruction accuracy, material-motion consistency and surface support under paired acquisition conditions, without introducing a new reconstruction algorithm. The novelty is the queryable connection, rather than any one annotation or the use of simulation alone. The reusable contribution has two parts: the fixed, versioned benchmark, with linked annotations and separately implemented consistency checks; and LumenMorph, the open-source generator and reader/evaluation toolkit for creating and studying additional tubular configurations. Reconstruction, optical-flow and supplied-geometry mechanical studies illustrate uses of these resources. They distinguish camera accuracy, sparse geometry, surface support and registration coverage, while a static phantom control examines performance on physical imagery under its declared acquisition contract. The engineered scene families provide controlled reconstruction diagnosis, not a sampled clinical population.

Existing resources address complementary evaluation needs. SimCol3D provides a synthetic depth and pose benchmark with separate anatomies for training and evaluation (Rau et al., 2024), while RealSynCol expands CT-derived geometry and image realism (Lena et al., 2026). C3VD and C3VDv2 provide phantom images acquired with clinical colonoscopes and registered dense labels (Bobrow et al., 2023; Golhar et al., 2026). DynamicColon, the dataset introduced alongside the ColonSplat reconstruction method by Smolak-Dyżewska et al. (2026), provides per-time-step point clouds to evaluate whole-scene motion, beyond appearance along the observed camera path. C3VD-DEFCOL combines parameterized peristalsis and centerline motion with depth-conditioned image translation, reporting 110 videos from 11 colon geometries and dense dynamic annotations (Luk et al., 2026). VR-Caps and SimIntestine extend simulation to capsule endoscopy (Incetan et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2025), and SimuScope incorporates deformable tissues in surgical simulation (Martyniak et al., 2025). Dense dynamic annotations and mechanical simulation are therefore established capabilities. The present work focuses on their auditable connection to persistent material identity, controlled acquisitions and reconstruction-pipeline evaluation.

papers.title: Adversary Brains: Hypothesis-Based Logical Signatures for Threat Actor Detection with LLMs
papers.abstract:
An adversary brain is an LLM-based model of a threat actor's behavior, held as an evolving logical signature: a hypothesis with enough structure that data can test it continuously, without a person re-interpreting it each time. Rather than any single observation, such as an IoC (Indicator of Compromise), it is the arrangement that becomes a detection, or intelligence, mechanism. Where YARA matches a file and Sigma matches a log line, an adversary brain matches the activity pattern of a campaign or threat actor. This is based on an intelligence analysis technique called Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (ACH), which the design lifts from the limitation of a few hypotheses at a time, to thousands, and then also operationalizes it for continuous detection purposes. Language models make the concept, and scale, practical: they turn prose reports into brains, judge matches, and drive the loop that keeps brains current. A partial pattern in a brain can also match a new value, such as a fresh C2 (command and control) domain name, assisting with the discovery of new indicators, and turning unknown unknowns into known unknowns, and potentially into knowns.
  The author would like to thank Ryan Moon for the collaboration, and Sounil Yu, Chris Inglis, Thomas Roccia, Marius Benthin, Israel Grimberg, Michal Kamensky, Justin Borland, Brandon Levene, John Hultquist, and John Bambenek for their feedback and assistance.

This text proposes a more AI-native way to do threat intelligence: running its claims as live hypotheses, with language models to make that practical at scale. Analysts already turn some claims about how an actor operates into detection rules. The rule may cite the claim, and its fires do not flow back to revise it. Here the claim itself runs against the defender’s own telemetry as data arrives, and its confirmed and dismissed fires raise or lower its standing, and can retire it.

papers.title: Simplifying 2-Bundle Descriptions of Invariants and Local Dynamics
papers.abstract: A string couples to a two-form gauge potential whose local descriptions need not fit together as a single global form. Principal 2-bundles provide a geometric description of this gluing. However, we recover surface amplitudes and quantum partition functions, as well as local classical field dynamics, without the 2-bundle formalism. For global phases, topological and index invariants, and twisted-sheaf moduli, established equivalences give alternative descriptions through cocycles, bundles, operators, or modules, with the required global compatibility data. For three-dimensional finite gauge theories with cohomological actions, Fourier transformation expresses the partition function as a sum of partition functions of ordinary finite-group gauge theories. An invertible local substitution reduces invariant classical actions for a class of 2-bundle connections represented by finite-dimensional crossed modules to ordinary gauge and tensor dynamics. These finite and local reductions explicitly eliminate field variables. A four-dimensional quadratic example instead admits a direct cochain evaluation even when an ordinary gauge-theory reduction fails. These results therefore do not require the additional 2-bundle presentation.
papers.intro:
A string in a background two-form field acquires a phase that depends on its worldsheet. If the potential BB is globally defined and f:Σ→Xf:\Sigma\to X is the worldsheet map, the phase is exp⁡(2​π​i​∫Σf∗​B)\exp(2\pi i\int_{\Sigma}f^{*}B). On a topologically nontrivial background, local potentials must instead be joined by one-forms on double overlaps and functions on triple overlaps. An abelian gerbe with connection organizes precisely these data [42, 1]. It is a basic example of a principal 2-bundle, the broader geometric object studied here [53, 58]. The resulting phase can change a spectrum or cancel an anomaly, so the global data are physically consequential [56, 23]. The physical effect is real. The question is whether obtaining it requires the 2-bundle presentation. It also arises across more general physical and mathematical topics. In each setting, we ask whether the higher presentation supplies information or an operation absent from the original description, or whether the stated result follows directly from cocycles, ordinary bundles, operators, modules, or a change of fields. Across the applications studied here, these descriptions suffice. In several cases, their equivalence with the higher geometric description is itself a theorem [42, 57, 36]. An equivalent presentation preserves the required data and operations; whether it simplifies their use is a further question. We therefore identify what the alternative actually does, from evaluating a phase to eliminating a field. The existence of a higher geometric interpretation does not make that presentation necessary for obtaining the result.

papers.title: The Proof-Theoretic Foundations of the Principle of Reiteration in Natural Deduction
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the proof-theoretic foundations of the principle of reiteration (R) in natural deduction, arguing that its legitimacy originates in the structural preservation of formulae within sequent calculus rather than in an independent logical rule. By examining singlesuccedent and multisuccedent sequent calculus, we demonstrate how logical operations transform principal formulae while preserving unaffected antecedent and succedent contexts. We subsequently analyse the schematic formulation of reiteration and compare natural deduction derivations with corresponding sequent calculus derivations. This comparison identifies two fundamental functions of reiteration, namely the reuse of previously employed formulae and the restoration of previously derived conclusions. We conclude that reiteration introduces no independent inferential content but explicitly represents the structural continuity of inferential dependencies already included into sequent calculus.

papers.title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
papers.abstract: The gap between AI capability deployment and safety assurance is structural and cannot be closed through internal evaluations alone. Analyzing documented harms (2017-2026) across the human lifespan reveals that disparate incidents --- from voice assistants endangering children to AI companions implicated in adolescent suicide and automated care denials for the elderly --- reflect a single failure: evaluating systems against an implicit adult user model. We introduce five developmental moderators structured into a Lifespan Vulnerability Matrix across six life stages. The matrix reveals a nonmonotonic risk distribution: vulnerability peaks at both ends of the lifespan, governance coverage is asymmetrical, and authority to convert model errors into real-world impact is scrutinized least. We then propose a set of lifespan design principles generalizing existing child-protective instruments, and an institution-agnostic, three-tier external evaluation framework --- comprising automated simulation, expert red teaming, and post-deployment monitoring --- indexed directly to matrix risk cells.

In February 2024, a fourteen-year-old died by suicide after an AI companion cultivated dependency and ignored suicidal ideation [28]. In November 2023, an insurer was alleged to have used predictive algorithms to systematically deny post-acute care to elderly enrollees [23, 54]. In February 2024, a finance employee transferred $25 million following a deepfake video conference with synthetic colleagues [17].

papers.title: Fuji: The Shape, Composition, and Spread of Demand Bursts on Robinhood Chain
papers.abstract: Demand on blockchain-based marketplaces arrives in bursts and at a high rate. On these platforms the data are completely visible, which makes it feasible to compare the bursty demand against the usual load. The congestion manifests as an increased demand for gas, the primary resource a blockchain sells. Existing studies consider how to price the gas. The demand itself, and what it is made of during bursts, has not been measured. We measure it on Robinhood Chain, a layer-2 blockchain that quickly became a venue for trading tokenized equities and memecoins. We collected the data from every block of its first three active months and more than 50 million Uniswap swaps that occurred during bursty periods. We find that a burst trades about as many pools as a quiet period, mostly different ones, and trades them harder, on top of elevated demand that accumulated for hours. With the bursts aligned on their peaks, the median peak is 2.5 times the usual load. Both the rise and the fall of the demand are described by the sum of two exponential functions with different timescales, a slow one of hours and a fast one of minutes. Against a matched quiet period, a burst has 1.05 times the pools, 1.40 times the trades, and 1.21 times the senders. We use two models to explain the arrival of bursts: externally triggered cascades and self-excitation. The former fits the data relatively better. Inside a burst, the entry of each trader into a pool is followed for about 24 seconds by more entries than the existing traders predict. Whether this is because of imitation or because of a shared signal is left open.

Figure 2 shows the gas usage during 82 minutes of this burst activity. This period contained 138,609138,609 swaps on Uniswap, touching 14111411 different pools. The periods of elevated demand on Robinhood Chain can be described by a slow and gradual rise and fall around an intense peak.

The research question we study in this work is how the resource demand concentrates both in time and across assets in an online marketplace, Robinhood Chain. The resource we study here is the gas, the unit of blockchain computation. A public blockchain makes the link between congestion, participation, and trading value observable. The transactions happening on the blockchain are organized into blocks. The block records the load and the transaction records the trades inside it in an immutable public database. Records like these have been used to study user preferences in a range of fields. Wu and Huberman [29] record votes on news stories, and Salganik et al. [23] record song choices in an experimental market. Different from our case, these platforms record cases without the platform’s load. On the blockchain, the platform load can be connected to the count and value of trades. Moreover, the gas price adjusts according to the demand. Existing studies look at the fee mechanisms [22, 7, 21, 19] in great detail, but, critically, they do not model the demand and the activity during periods of elevated demand.

Moreover, a burst that is caused by many trading pools has different implications from a burst concentrated in a few. The spacing between the bursts determines what the current burst says about the next one. As demand bursts can overlap, a burst cannot be easily identified by comparing it to nearby (in time) demand.

papers.title: Operator limits of random matrices: Edge universality and sharp approximations
papers.abstract:
We establish operator universality at the spectral edge of general Wigner matrices by showing that their suitably rescaled Lanczos tridiagonalizations, constructed from deterministic initial vectors, converge to the stochastic Airy operator with Dirichlet boundary condition.
  The result requires control of the entire tridiagonal structure on the scale relevant to the limiting differential operator. The Lanczos coefficients for non-Gaussian Wigner matrices are strongly dependent. We analyze their fluctuations by combining multi-resolvent local laws with quantitative control of Krylov subspaces and a comparison of the resulting Jacobi coefficients with those of the Gaussian ensembles. This approach identifies the limiting Brownian potential directly from the original matrix entries, without invoking Dyson Brownian motion in the step of Green function comparison. The resolvent limit yields joint convergence of edge eigenvalues, embedded eigenfunctions, and spectral measures.
  For Gaussian, Laguerre and circular $\beta$-ensembles we construct sharp couplings to the stochastic Airy, Bessel and Sine operators, preserving the finite-matrix laws. For fixed $\beta > 0$, their squared Hilbert-Schmidt inverse errors have almost-sure orders $n^{-1/3}, n^{-1}$ and $n^{-1}$, respectively, with $a > 0$ in the hard-edge upper bound. We also identify the positive leading order coefficient for the circular ensemble, whose second derivative jumps at $\beta = 2$.

papers.title: Infranormal Kazhdan subgroups and instability in finite actions
papers.abstract: We prove that the group $G=\mathbb{Z}[1/2]^3\rtimes(\operatorname{SL}_3(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathbb{Z})$ is finitely presented and residually finite, but is not stable in finite actions, answering a question of Gohla and Thom. The proof uses the infranormal Kazhdan subgroup $H=\mathbb{Z}^3\rtimes\operatorname{SL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ and its normal closure $N$ in $G$. A Kazhdan projection estimate shows that, in any $G$-action weakly contained in finite actions, every $H$-invariant measurable subset is also $N$-invariant. We construct an explicit sofic approximation of $G$ whose limit action contains a measurable subset that is $H$-invariant but not $N$-invariant.
papers.intro:
A residually finite group admits sofic approximations coming from genuine finite actions. Gohla and Thom call a group stable in finite actions if every sofic limit action is weakly contained in finite actions; see [5, Definition 3.7]. Equivalently, the statistics of finite measurable partitions in every such limit action must be approximable by those of genuine finite actions, as in Kechris’s notion of weak containment [6, Section 10]. They asked whether there exists a residually finite group that is not stable in finite actions [5, Question 3.12]. We answer this question affirmatively with a finitely presented example.

papers.title: Bodyseismography (BSG): Theoretical Foundation and Numerical Modeling
papers.abstract: Bodyseismography (BSG) records cardiovascular vibrations transmitted through the body and a supporting bed, enabling contactless assessment of cardiac mechanics. Relating these vibrations to hemodynamic features requires separating cardiac excitation from the effects of body and bed transmission. We develop a source-transmission-measurement framework that couples myocardial contraction and vascular recoil to directional BSG observations. The theory connects stroke volume, cardiac output, and blood pressure to observation and target Jacobians, establishes a local first-order target-observability criterion, and characterizes how additional sensing axes reduce ambiguities under specified source and transmission uncertainties. Numerical modeling combines four-chamber cardiac mechanics, cardiac-to-body excitation, and calibrated body-bed operators. Across 27 participants, a multilayer finite-element model with calibrated frequency correction achieves median Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.865 for the vertical channel and 0.682 for the planar-sum channel in matched-window waveform reconstruction. Controlled stroke-volume perturbations show that transmission reshapes feature sensitivity, including a reversal of the vertical feature association in 8 of 27 participant-specific transfer models. These analytical and numerical studies explain how cardiovascular sources and mechanical propagation jointly shape triaxial BSG and provide a physical basis for relating directional vibration features to hemodynamic changes.
